title: AI Gateway now supports extraction models
description:
Extraction models are now on AI Gateway. They find specific details in the content you provide, such as an invoice number or contact names, and return them as separate fields your code can use.

ScaleDown Extract-1 is the first available extraction model. It extracts text values or lists of text values from text, images, and PDFs. You can use it to process invoices, contracts, and other records.

Extraction is currently available through the AI SDK only. With ai@7.0.176 or later, use experimental_extract and the model ID scaledown/extract-1:

Each key in fields has an entry in result.answers. If a field is not found, its value is null. Extract-1 returns confidence scores from 0 to 1 for matches, including individual list items, so you can flag uncertain results for review. For text input, it can also return character offsets showing where a match appears.

To extract from a PDF or image, pass it as a file part in state:

Extraction requests appear in AI Gateway logs and spend tracking. See the extraction quickstart for setup and authentication.

title: new row violates check constraint on documents.source
description:
The short version

The documents table's source column had a CHECK constraint, documents_source_check, allowing only 'upload' and 'dropbox'. But the automated document-archiving feature inserts quote/invoice/application/receipt snapshots with source: 'system', and the Anyflow import feature inserts signed contracts with source: 'anyflow'. Neither value was allowed.

The result: the file upload to storage succeeded every single time, while the insert into the documents table failed every single time, with new row for relation "documents" violates check constraint "documents_source_check". Not one row of the automated document vault had ever been successfully created.

A failure designed to be swallowed silently

upsertDocument in document-archive.ts uploads the file to storage first, then upserts the documents row:

async function upsertDocument(
  admin: AdminClient,
  opts: { /* ... */ source: "system" | "anyflow"; /* ... */ }
): Promise<ArchiveResult> {
  const { error: upErr } = await admin.storage
    .from(BUCKET)
    .upload(opts.storagePath, opts.bytes, { contentType: opts.mimeType, upsert: true });
  if (upErr) return { ok: false, reason: `storage: ${upErr.message}` };

  // ...check for an existing row by external_ref...

  const { data: inserted, error } = await admin
    .from("documents")
    .insert({ ...fields, created_by: null })
    .select("id")
    .single();
  if (error) {
    // 23505 (uq_documents_external race) is handled separately above
    // ...
    return { ok: false, reason: `insert: ${error.message}` };
  }
  return { ok: true, documentId: inserted.id };
}

A CHECK violation (Postgres error code 23514) doesn't match the 23505 unique-violation race handled just above it, so it falls straight through to { ok: false, reason: "insert: new row for relation \"documents\" violates check constraint \"documents_source_check\"" }.

The function that calls this, archiveContractDocument, has a comment stating the intent directly:

/**
 * Automatically archives generated documents (quote/invoice/application/receipt)
 * to the document vault.
 * ...
 * - Callers (the signature webhook, invoice issuance) must not break, so every
 *   failure — including exceptions — is returned as an ArchiveResult instead of thrown.
 * ...
 */

archiveExternalDocument, which handles external imports, carries the same stated intent:

/**
 * Archives a signed file imported from outside (e.g. an Anyflow-signed contract)
 * to the document vault.
 * ...
 * - Failures are returned as an ArchiveResult so the caller (the webhook) is not broken.
 */

This was not an accident — it was the intended design. A document-archiving failure should never block the main flow, such as a payment-state transition or signature confirmation. Choosing to return a result object instead of throwing is reasonable on its own. The problem is that nothing downstream was actually reading that ArchiveResult.

Nobody was checking .ok

invoice-issue.ts looked like this:

// Auto-archive the invoice snapshot to the document vault.
// Runs before checking if the email can be sent, so the issued document is
// kept even without a registered email. Idempotent — failures are ignored.
const archived = await archiveContractDocument({ contractId, kind: "invoice" });

// ...resolve recipient...

const sent = await sendEmail({
  // ...
  text: [
    // ...
    "pdf" in archived && archived.pdf != null
      ? "The invoice (PDF) is attached to this email. ..."
      : "You can view and save the invoice as a PDF here (no login required):",
    // ...
  ].join("\n"),
  ...("pdf" in archived && archived.pdf != null
    ? { attachments: [{ filename: "invoice.pdf", content: archived.pdf }] }
    : {}),
});

Nowhere in the file is archived.ok ever read. Only archived.pdf (the PDF bytes for the email attachment) is used. Since dryRun isn't set, archiveContractDocument does attempt the real storage and DB writes, but PDF generation itself doesn't depend on whether the documents insert succeeded — so the email-sending path has no way to notice the archive is failing. Invoices kept issuing and sending normally while the document vault stayed empty underneath them.

The signing flow in contract-signed.ts has the same pattern, and says so in its own comment:

// 2b. Auto-archive the application snapshot to the document vault (ops spec §1).
//     A signature is frozen as proof of consent. Non-kimiteras contract types
//     are skipped inside archiveContractDocument. Idempotent — failures are swallowed.
try {
  const r = await archiveContractDocument({ contractId, kind: "application" });
  if (!r.ok) {
    console.error("[contract-signed] application archive failed:", r.reason);
  } else if (!r.skipped) {
    // ...signature evidence-anchor processing...
  }
}

This path does log the failure with console.error, but takes no further action. Without active log monitoring, this line filling up with CHECK violations never reaches anyone.

The fix was just widening the constraint

The fix, in migration 0074, only added 'system' and 'anyflow' to documents_source_check's allowed values:

alter table public.documents drop constraint if exists documents_source_check;
alter table public.documents add constraint documents_source_check
  check (source = any (array['upload'::text, 'dropbox'::text, 'system'::text, 'anyflow'::text]));

It's an additive, idempotent migration (drop constraint if exists then add constraint); since every existing row used 'upload', they all still satisfy the new constraint. No application code changed — upsertDocument and invoice-issue.ts were already correct code that only needed the constraint to let their rows through.

The hidden cost of "don't break the main flow"

Swallowing failures silently so the main flow never breaks is a reasonable design choice on its own. In fact, the payment-transition and signature-confirmation flows never stopped once, even while the CHECK violation went unfixed. The cost is that the assumption "the archive must be succeeding" accumulated for months with nothing ever verifying it. Multiple callers that never check archived.ok can't be caught by console.error logging alone — in practice, what surfaced this was literally counting the rows in the document vault. Choosing to swallow failures silently only works if the swallowed outcome (the count of ok: false results) is made visible somewhere else.

Originally published at tech.rebounder.jp.

title: Claude Fable 5.2 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems. It also communicates more clearly and generates output faster than earlier Fable models. Effort runs from low to max, with high as the API default.

Fable 5.2 has cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Access to Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention. Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for the model. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude. If your team has ZDR turned on, AI Gateway returns an error instead of sending the request to Fable 5.2.

To keep requests served when a classifier is triggered, use model fallbacks. Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway, and AI Gateway tries each model in order when the cybersecurity classifier declines a request.

Call it through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Use anthropic/claude-fable-5.2 as the model name:

This request falls back to Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5, if the cybersecurity classifier declines it. The models option works the same way on every AI Gateway API format.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Try Claude Fable 5.2 in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

title: Curso gratuito de Node.js e APIs RESTful | IFRS
description:
Uma trilha de APIs com Node.js

Node.js é o ponto de partida desta formação básica, voltada a desenvolvedores iniciantes e intermediários que já conhecem o básico de JavaScript. Ele é oferecido pela IFRS. Ao longo de cinco módulos, a trilha avança da introdução ao ambiente Node.js para a construção de APIs RESTful e o uso do Express.js, conectando desenvolvimento de serviços, manipulação de dados e controle de acesso.

Uma API permite que aplicações troquem informações por meio de uma interface definida. Os fundamentos RESTful ajudam a organizar essa comunicação; depois, o desenvolvimento com Express.js leva o estudo à criação de APIs usando um framework associado ao ecossistema Node.js. Esses temas compõem o núcleo da formação, com carga horária total de 40 horas.

Dados e integração

A sequência inclui manipulação de dados e integração com bancos de dados. Esse tema amplia o trabalho com APIs para além da comunicação entre aplicações: os dados precisam ser tratados e conectados a uma fonte de armazenamento. O programa confirma essa integração como parte da trilha, sem especificar uma tecnologia de banco de dados ou um projeto final.

Autenticação e autorização

Autenticação e autorização encerram os tópicos listados. São responsabilidades distintas: a autenticação verifica quem está acessando, enquanto a autorização define quais ações esse acesso pode realizar. Em APIs, compreender essa diferença ajuda a pensar no controle de acesso aos recursos oferecidos pelo serviço. Esses assuntos completam o percurso ao lado de Node.js, RESTful, Express.js e integração com dados.

Público, formato e prazos

O curso é destinado a pessoas que desenvolvem software em nível iniciante ou intermediário e parte do conhecimento básico de JavaScript. Entre os requisitos informados estão compreensão de leitura em português e conhecimentos de informática e internet. O idioma do curso é português, e a metodologia é sem tutoria.

As inscrições ficam abertas até 31 de dezembro de 2026, sem necessidade de chave de inscrição. A conclusão deve ocorrer até 31 de janeiro de 2027. O prazo mínimo para obtenção do certificado é de seis dias a partir da inscrição. Com cinco módulos e 40 horas, a formação reúne os fundamentos de APIs modernas em Node.js em uma trilha que vai da construção do serviço ao tratamento de dados e ao controle de acesso.

title: Tackling LLM Prompt Bloat: Building a Just-In-Time Context Router in Rust
description:
As autonomous agent frameworks grow in complexity, developers continually add rules, domain doctrines, coding style guides, and edge-case remediations.

The easiest path—and the most common anti-pattern—is simply appending every new rule to the global system prompt. Within a few months, the base prompt balloons from 500 tokens to 8,000+ tokens.

This phenomenon, known as Fatal Prompt Bloat, has severe consequences:

  1. Context Window Saturation: Drastically reduces available token space for real codebase context, compiler logs, and deep conversation history.
  2. Inference Latency & Cost: Every single turn incurs the quadratic attention overhead of parsing thousands of irrelevant static tokens.
  3. Reasoning Degradation (Attention Diffusion): When a model is bombarded with 50 disparate rules (e.g. Docker rules, Blender instructions, React best practices, and Git protocols simultaneously), its attention mechanism diffuses, leading to subtle instruction non-compliance.

When architecting the cognitive subsystem for Flowork OS, we outlawed always-on static prompts in favor of a Formula 5-3-3 Just-In-Time Sliding Window Router written in Rust.

The Zero-Bloat Mandate: 100% Conditional Directives

Under the Flowork OS system prompt architecture, the base prompt remains locked to a minimal anchor (~400 tokens covering identity and approval boundaries).

Every other domain instruction exists as a Passive Trigger (/opt/floworkos/system/system_promp/promps/triggers/) or a native compiled Rust rule checker (rules/.bin/*).

Directives are injected dynamically only when their environmental conditions match:

  • Not modifying an ISO build script? $ ightarrow$ The ISO build directive is completely absent from context.
  • Not working with Android APKs or Scrcpy? $ ightarrow$ The Android subsystem prompt is not loaded.
  • Not configuring Glass HUD compositing? $ ightarrow$ The HUD styling rules never enter the prompt envelope.

Sub-Millisecond Native Rule Evaluation

To ensure dynamic context injection introduces zero noticeable user latency, rule evaluation is executed natively in Rust (mrflow-rs/src/cognitive/mod.rs):

// Fast-path landmark and structural inspection (<50ms timeout)
let structural_checks = vec![
    (
        is_build_intent && (has_tool("compile_code") || has_tool("run_command")),
        "triggers/code_engineering.md",
    ),
    (
        is_search_intent && (has_tool("grep_search") || has_tool("glob")),
        "triggers/search_efficiency.md",
    ),
    (
        cwd.join("FLOWORK.md").exists() || cwd.join(".flowork/MEMORY.md").exists(),
        "triggers/memory_routing.md",
    ),
];

By keeping individual trigger directives dense and strictly under 250 words, the agent retains razor-sharp focus on the task at hand without suffering cognitive drift.

Explore the Codebase

The entire prompt router, native cognitive loop, and Landlock security sandbox are open-source.

  • Visit our project hub at floworkos.com
  • Read the architecture documentation on GitHub: flowork-os/flowork-os

title: CrowdStrike vai adquirir Zscaler por US$ 43,9 bilhões
description:
Operação recorde de US$ 43,9 bilhões

A CrowdStrike irá adquirir a Zscaler por US$ 43,9 bilhões, em uma operação recorde no mercado de cibersegurança. A conclusão está prevista para o segundo semestre de 2028, e o anúncio evidencia a preocupação crescente com as ameaças digitais.

Plataformas com frentes complementares

O acordo combina frentes diferentes de proteção: a CrowdStrike atua em computadores, servidores e outros dispositivos, enquanto a tecnologia da Zscaler protege o acesso de funcionários a aplicativos e dados. A proposta é reunir essas capacidades em uma plataforma mais abrangente para clientes corporativos e governamentais, cobrindo equipamentos e acesso a recursos digitais.

Reação do mercado e escrutínio regulatório

A resposta inicial das bolsas foi distinta para as duas companhias. As ações da Zscaler avançaram mais de 13% e chegaram a US$ 220,52, mas seguiram abaixo dos US$ 260,41 por ação implícitos na oferta. Já os papéis da CrowdStrike recuaram quase 12% nas negociações.

Essa distância entre a cotação da Zscaler e o valor implícito da proposta ocorre enquanto investidores avaliam a possibilidade de escrutínio regulatório. Como a transação reúne duas das maiores empresas do setor, essa análise está entre os pontos que o mercado acompanha.

Ameaças e resiliência digital

A procura por ferramentas de cibersegurança tem crescido porque empresas de todo o mundo enfrentam ataques cada vez mais sofisticados. A inteligência artificial amplia a pressão em duas frentes: facilita identificar e explorar vulnerabilidades de software e também aprimora as ferramentas criadas para detectar e conter ameaças.

Esse cenário de risco inclui interrupções recentes que afetaram companhias aéreas, bancos e órgãos governamentais. Também pesam vulnerabilidades de grande repercussão em softwares amplamente utilizados, entre eles Java e PHP. Esses episódios aumentaram as preocupações com a resiliência da infraestrutura digital crítica.

title: Export Python Stock Candles to CSV Without Losing the Query Context
description:
A stock candle CSV is easy to download and surprisingly easy to misread a week later. A file called AAPL.csv cannot tell you whether its bars are daily or minute, adjusted or raw, or whether the API returned the whole window. Export two files together: the candles as CSV and a manifest recording the request, the series actually returned, and the exact CSV bytes.

Record the request and the response separately

The request describes what you intended to download. Keep the full symbol, asset type, interval, price adjustment, limit and any requested time bounds. Store a UTC time for the capture, and don't send the API key to the browser or include it in the manifest.

The response says what you actually received. TickDB's Candlestick Data endpoint returns the applied symbol, asset type, interval, and adjustment alongside its bars. Compare these fields with the request before writing the export. If you asked for unadjusted daily bars and received adjusted minute bars, reject the export instead of silently naming it after the requested series.

Keep uncertainty visible

  • Window: Record row count and the earliest and latest returned labels. A request for ten records returning eight does not prove why two are absent, and a response returning ten does not prove complete coverage.
  • Time: Preserve the original integer millisecond labels in the CSV. Format times separately in the UI. A UTC timestamp does not, by itself, identify an exchange session or an exchange-local trading date.
  • Missing fields: A blank volume is not zero. Ignore neither the missing field nor the distinction when you import the file.
  • Finality: A recent candle can be provisional. If you cannot establish that a bar is final or that the window is complete, keep those states explicit rather than deriving them from row count or retrieval success.

A Python export you can check later

The sample requests ten unadjusted daily AAPL bars and writes a CSV plus a matching JSON manifest. The standard-library example needs a TickDB key in the server environment to make the request. The local checks below use synthetic payloads; they do not establish an account's permissions, the live feed's completeness, or an exchange timetable.

import csv, io, json, hashlib, os
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

ENDPOINT = "https://api.tickdb.ai/v1/market/kline"
QUERY = dict(symbol="AAPL.US", type="stock", interval="1d", adjust="none", limit=10)
FIELDS = ("time", "open", "high", "low", "close", "volume")

def export(payload, query, pulled_at):
    if payload.get("code") != 0:
        raise ValueError("provider returned a business error")
    data = payload["data"]
    applied = {k: data[k] for k in ("symbol", "type", "interval", "adjust")}
    if any(query[k] != v for k, v in applied.items()):
        raise ValueError("response series does not match export request")
    bars = data["klines"]
    times = [row["time"] for row in bars]
    if any(type(t) is not int for t in times) or len(times) != len(set(times)):
        raise ValueError("invalid or duplicate bar timestamps")
    f = io.StringIO(newline="")
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=FIELDS, lineterminator="\n")
    writer.writeheader()
    for row in sorted(bars, key=lambda r: r["time"]):
        writer.writerow({k: row.get(k) for k in FIELDS})
    content = f.getvalue().encode("utf-8")
    manifest = dict(request=query, applied=applied, queried_at_utc=pulled_at,
                    returned_rows=len(bars), first_ms=min(times, default=None),
                    last_ms=max(times, default=None), completeness="not established",
                    last_bar_finality="not established",
                    sha256=hashlib.sha256(content).hexdigest())
    return content, manifest

if __name__ == "__main__":
    from pathlib import Path
    req = Request(ENDPOINT + "?" + urlencode(QUERY),
                  headers={"X-API-Key": os.environ["TICKDB_API_KEY"]})
    with urlopen(req, timeout=20) as response:
        payload = json.load(response)
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    content, manifest = export(payload, QUERY, now)
    Path("bars.csv").write_bytes(content)
    Path("bars.manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2)+"\n")

Verify the handoff

Treat the two files as a pair. Recompute SHA-256 over the CSV bytes and compare it with the manifest before importing the result. A mismatch means the files no longer correspond; a match proves byte identity, not market-data accuracy. Keep a distinct export ID for each capture in a production downloader rather than overwriting a prior pair.

In the synthetic checks, out-of-order rows are sorted, missing volume stays blank while an explicit zero survives, the row count and digest match, and a different adjustment, different interval or duplicate timestamp is rejected. An empty response exports only the header and records no returned time bounds. It does not assert that the market was closed.

For the downloader in a stock dashboard, the practical rule is simple: export the data and what you know about it, not just what the chart happens to show.

Source checked: TickDB REST API documentation, Candlestick Data and Latest Candlesticks.

title: When Routine Blood Tests Reveal More Than You Expect: Understanding Hyperparathyroidism
description:
Not every health problem starts with obvious symptoms. Sometimes, an ordinary blood test can reveal something that has been developing quietly for months or even years. Primary hyperparathyroidism is one example.

The condition occurs when one or more of the parathyroid glands produce too much parathyroid hormone (PTH). These four small glands sit behind the thyroid in the neck and help regulate calcium levels in the body. When they become overactive, calcium levels in the bloodstream can rise, potentially affecting the bones, kidneys, and other parts of the body.

Why the Condition Can Be Difficult to Recognize

One of the challenges with hyperparathyroidism is that its symptoms aren't always easy to connect to a single condition.

Some people experience persistent fatigue, muscle weakness, difficulty concentrating, mood changes, or general aches and pains. Others have no noticeable symptoms at all.

Because these issues can have many different causes, patients may spend considerable time investigating individual symptoms without realizing they could be connected.

Routine blood work can help identify the problem. Elevated blood calcium levels may prompt doctors to investigate further by checking parathyroid hormone levels and reviewing other relevant test results.

Why Looking Beyond One Test Matters

A diagnosis shouldn't depend on a single number in a laboratory report. Doctors consider calcium and PTH levels together, along with kidney function, vitamin D levels, and other clinical information.

Additional tests may include a 24-hour urine calcium measurement and a bone density scan. Kidney imaging may also be recommended to check for stones or other complications.

Imaging studies of the neck, such as ultrasound, sestamibi scans, or specialized CT scans, can help locate abnormal parathyroid tissue when surgery is being considered.

Understanding the Available Treatment Options

Treatment depends on the patient's overall health, laboratory results, symptoms, and whether the condition is affecting the bones or kidneys.

Some patients may be monitored with regular blood tests and bone density assessments. Others may benefit from medication or surgery.

Parathyroidectomy, which involves removing the overactive gland or glands, is the definitive treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism. The surgical approach depends on the individual case, including whether one gland or multiple glands are affected.

For people researching their diagnosis and possible treatment paths, HyperparathyroidMD provides educational information about parathyroid conditions, diagnostic testing, and surgical approaches.

The Importance of Asking the Right Questions

Receiving an unexpected blood test result can be confusing, especially when there are few obvious symptoms. Understanding what the results mean and discussing them with a qualified medical professional is an important first step.

Questions about calcium levels, PTH results, kidney health, bone density, and possible treatment options can help make consultations more productive.

The bigger lesson is that health problems don't always announce themselves clearly. Sometimes, paying attention to routine test results and looking at the bigger picture can make all the difference in identifying a condition early and understanding what to do next.

title: Day Explained: A Rust Framework That Builds Native Apps for Every Platform
description:
Most cross-platform app frameworks make you choose between two things. You can share your UI code across platforms, or you can use each platform's real, native controls. Getting both usually means writing the interface more than once.

Day is an open-source framework that tries to give you both. You write your app once in Rust. On macOS it uses AppKit. On iOS it uses UIKit. On Android it uses Material Components. On Linux it uses GTK or Qt, and on Windows it uses WinUI 3. The buttons, text fields and menus your users see are the platform's own.

I have not built an app with Day. This breakdown comes from the project's website, documentation and GitHub repository. Anything about how well it works in practice is the project's own claim, not something tested here.

The short version

  • What it is: a framework for building desktop and mobile apps from one Rust codebase, using each platform's native UI toolkit.
  • Platforms: macOS, iOS and Android are the most supported. Linux and Windows are supported with less testing. Web and HarmonyOS are experimental.
  • Beyond UI: it includes localization, accessibility, a UI testing tool, packaging and app store preparation.
  • License: MPL-2.0, open source on GitHub.
  • Maturity: young. The repository was created in July 2026 and the CLI is at version 0.7.10. There is no hot reload, and the project tells you to test your hardest requirement first.

How it differs from other approaches

There are roughly three ways to build one app for many platforms:

  1. Draw everything yourself. The framework renders its own controls, so the app looks the same everywhere. You get full design control, but the controls are not the platform's own.
  2. Use a web view. You build the UI with web technology and show it inside a native window.
  3. Map to native controls. Your code describes the UI, and the framework creates the real platform widgets.

Day takes the third approach. Its own documentation is honest about what that means: "your interface will vary with the platform, and you will still need to test those differences." If you need pixel-identical screens and heavy custom animation everywhere, Day suggests that a framework with its own renderer "may give you more control."

The other point that sets Day apart is that the UI is shared, not just the business logic. In the project's words, "No bridging between disparate programming languages is required." Your layouts and event handlers are Rust, from the data model up to the buttons.

What the code looks like

Day calls a control, or a group of controls, a piece. You build screens with ordinary Rust functions that return pieces. State lives in signals, which update the UI when their value changes.

Here is the counter example from the docs overview:

use day::prelude::*;

pub fn root() -> impl Piece {
    let count = Signal::new(0i64);
    column((
        label(res::str::counter_value(count)).id(id!(counter_label)),
        button(res::str::add_one())
            .action(move || count.update(|n| *n += 1))
            .id(id!(increment_button)),
    ))
    .spacing(Space::M)
    .padding(Space::L)
}

A few things to notice:

  • It is declarative. You describe what the screen contains, and Day creates the widgets.
  • Updates are targeted. When count changes, Day updates the label. The docs say the whole root() function "does not run again."
  • Text is not hard-coded. res::str::counter_value and res::str::add_one come from translation files, which we will get to next.
  • Controls have stable IDs. The .id(...) calls are there so automated tests can find each control.

The pieces beyond UI

A framework that only draws controls still leaves you with a lot of work before release. Day tries to cover more of the path to shipping.

Localization. Translations use Mozilla Fluent files. Day generates typed Rust functions from them, so if a message expects an argument and your code does not pass it, the build fails. Translation mistakes become compile errors instead of bugs users find.

Accessibility. Because Day uses native controls, it starts from each platform's built-in screen reader and keyboard support. It adds a shared Rust API for labels, hints and changing values. The docs are clear that this is "a starting point, not a certification." On Android, accessibility support is listed as partial.

DayScript. This is Day's tool for testing and automation. You write a walkthrough that finds controls by their IDs and interacts with them. The same walkthrough can run on several platforms and in several languages, and take screenshots along the way. That makes it useful both for regression tests and for generating app store screenshots.

Packaging. The day CLI creates projects, checks that you have the right SDKs installed (day doctor), builds, launches, and packages your app with day pack. Depending on the platform, it produces .dmg, .ipa, .apk, .aab, .msix, Flatpak or AppImage files. It also prepares store listing metadata, but the actual store submission still uses each store's own tools and your credentials.

Optional add-ons. Extras are ordinary Cargo dependencies. The site lists web views, Lottie animations, text-to-speech, charts, camera, audio and video, OAuth and passkey sign-in, Bluetooth LE, local network discovery, push notifications, background tasks and crash reporting. Each has its own platform support notes.

Platform support, honestly

Day ranks each platform in a support tier. A tier describes how much testing and maintenance a target gets, not how complete its API is.

Tier 1, Supported:

  • macOS (AppKit), packaged as .dmg
  • iOS (UIKit), packaged as .ipa
  • Android (Material Components), packaged as .apk and .aab

Tier 2, supported with less testing:

  • Linux (GTK 4 or Qt 6), packaged as Flatpak and AppImage
  • Windows (WinUI 3), packaged as .msix and an installer

Tier 3, Experimental:

  • HarmonyOS (ArkUI), packaged as .hap
  • Web, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering real HTML elements

The platform page also includes small details that matter if you are planning a real project:

  • Apple builds need Xcode 27 or newer.
  • On iOS, daily development happens on the Simulator. The docs say physical-device debugging gets less use.
  • On Android, CI does not fail when the Android UI walkthrough fails. If the app process is killed, it restarts from scratch unless your app saves its own state.
  • On Windows, the docs say fewer apps have shipped than on the Apple, Linux and Android targets.

What is still missing

The docs keep a single list of gaps that apply across platforms. Some of the bigger ones:

  • No hot reload. Every code change means a rebuild and relaunch. A DayScript walkthrough can take you back to the screen you were working on, but the app still restarts.
  • Animation is partial. It works on AppKit, UIKit, Android, Web and ArkUI. On GTK, Qt and WinUI, changes apply instantly with no animation.
  • No automatic dark mode for custom colors.
  • No form validation framework. You build it yourself with signals.

The project's advice is direct: "Check this list before you adopt the framework."

Who is behind it

The repository belongs to a GitHub organization called Daybrite, which describes itself as "Stewards of Day." Almost all of the commits come from one developer, Marc Prud'hommeaux. His GitHub profile lists him as the founder of Skip, a tool for building iOS and Android apps from Swift. So this is not his first attempt at the cross-platform problem.

It also means Day currently depends heavily on one maintainer. As of November 23, 2026, the repository has 43 stars and 4 forks, and the day-cli crate on crates.io has about 10,900 downloads. Releases come out quickly: there have been 63 since the first one on August 13, including five in the past week. Fast releases are good for fixes, but they also mean the API may still change.

Is it a good fit?

Day's own features page is unusually clear about this. Based on it, Day looks like a good candidate if:

  • You want to write the whole app in Rust, or you already have Rust code you want to reuse.
  • You build "tools people use every day": settings screens, document windows, lists of records, where native controls feel right.
  • You are a small team that needs to ship on several platforms, and the built-in localization, testing and packaging save real work.

It is a weaker fit if:

  • Your team does not know Rust. The docs say learning the language "is part of the project."
  • Your design needs identical controls and heavy custom animation on every platform.
  • You depend on fast hot reload during UI work.
  • You need a large, mature ecosystem of third-party components today.

The project's suggestion for deciding is practical: build one screen from your own design, using the feature you are least sure about, and run it on every platform you plan to ship.

How to try it

You need stable Rust from rustup and the tools for your platform: Xcode 27+ on an Apple silicon Mac, Visual Studio C++ Build Tools and the Windows App Runtime on Windows, or GTK 4 and libadwaita on Linux. Then:

cargo install day-cli --locked
day --version
day doctor --toolkit gtk   # or appkit, winui

The first-app tutorial walks you through a small counter app in six lessons. The site also has a live browser demo of the same Rust UI code running through the experimental web target.

The takeaway

Day is an ambitious attempt to make one Rust codebase produce truly native apps, including the UI and not just the logic. Its best feature may be its honesty: the docs tell you what is stable, what is experimental, what is missing, and how to test whether it fits before you commit.

It is also very young and mostly built by one person. For a side project or an internal tool in Rust, it is worth an afternoon. For a production app, follow its own advice and prototype your hardest screen first.

Would you pick native controls that look different on every platform, or one custom look that is the same everywhere?

title: From AWS Cloud Practitioner to the Cloud Resume Challenge
description:
The cloud world has piqued my interest for a while and as the cliché goes, planning and not doing yields zero results. Rather than just watching multiple tutorials and not actually doing anything because of the fear of not being good enough, I decided to take the first step, which was getting the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner certification. It is the foundational level and it gave a broad understanding of the AWS services. One thing that really stood out was the shared responsibility model: how much AWS handles versus how much the customer handles. Shout out to the people I network with who not only advised me but shared resources to help me prepare for the exam, and yes, I passed!

It was a very interesting learning experience and the last thing I’d want is to lose this knowledge. In order for that not to happen, I'm putting it into practice through hands-on projects, continued learning, and hopefully more certifications soon. My end goal is to become a DevOps engineer, and I was advised to build a solid cloud foundation first, so that's where I'm starting.

Not sure where to go next, I came across the Cloud Resume Challenge, which looks beginner friendly. For each step I complete, I'll document what I learn as I’ve been told it is one way to get the knowledge to stick! Follow along on my journey if you are interested. Who knows, you may learn a thing or two as well.

title: A small delivery-state checklist for business text workflows
description:
A text appearing in an agent’s sent folder is not proof that the customer received it. For a business texting workflow, treat the sent message, provider acceptance, delivery receipt, and human follow-up as separate events. This distinction matters most after hours, when the person who sent the message may not be the person who sees a reply.

Model the message as a record

Give each outbound message a stable internal ID. Store the conversation ID, recipient, sender, submitted time, provider message ID, and current state. Keep the full message content only where your retention policy permits it. The provider ID is useful when a later status callback arrives.

A small state model might be queued → submitted → accepted → delivered, with branches for failed and unknown. An accepted event means a provider took the request; it does not prove delivery to a handset. A missing receipt should remain unknown until your documented timeout or reconciliation step runs.

Handle receipts defensively

  1. Verify that the status event came from the expected provider before changing a record.
  2. Match the provider message ID to one outbound message. Keep unmatched events for investigation.
  3. Make updates idempotent. Providers may retry a webhook, and duplicate events should not create duplicate tasks or customer notifications.
  4. Record the event time and processing time separately. A delayed callback can arrive after a newer staff action.
  5. Define which states can move forward. Avoid turning a confirmed failure into delivered merely because a stale event arrived.

Test the handoff, not just the API

Send a test message to a controlled number, inspect the provider event, and then have a second staff member open the shared conversation. Can that person see the latest state and know whether a reply needs an owner? Repeat the test with a simulated failed delivery and an after-hours reply. Document the expected owner, retry decision, and customer-facing language before production use.

The exact event names and delivery guarantees depend on the provider and channel, so check the provider’s current documentation. This checklist is a way to test the workflow around those events. Phone Clover is one example of a calling and texting app for HighLevel teams using Telnyx; evaluate its current behavior against your own routing and receipt requirements.

title: Blobasaur and the 4th Cross way: how Zerodha's ~35-person tech team keeps shipping open source
description:
TL;DR: Zerodha just open-sourced Blobasaur, a sharded blob server written in Rust. It speaks the Redis Cluster protocol and stuffs everything into SQLite (yes, really). It serves chart layouts for about 20 million users at around 2 ms p99 on three small nodes. In this post I poke around how it works, meet the ~35-person team behind it, and then fall down the rabbit hole of side projects from the team and their CTO, Kailash Nadh.

🦖 A dinosaur that speaks Redis

On 19 November 2026, the Zerodha Tech blog dropped a post called "Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite" by engineer Sarat Chandra. It introduced Blobasaur:

  • a sharded blob server written in Rust
  • it speaks the Redis (Cluster) protocol
  • it stores everything in SQLite
  • a single binary, licensed AGPLv3
  • already in production behind Kite, Zerodha's trading platform

Redis is an in-memory cache. SQLite is an embedded file database. Seeing both in one sentence made me go "wait, what?" But the reasoning turns out to be pretty sensible, and it tells you a lot about how Zerodha builds software.

iamd3vil / blobasaur

A Blob store based on SQLite compatible with Redis protocol

Blobasaur

Blobasaur is a high-performance, sharded blob storage server written in Rust. It implements the Redis protocol for client compatibility and uses SQLite as the backend for each shard, providing a simple yet robust solution for storing and retrieving binary large objects (blobs).

Table of Contents

  • Features
  • Installation
    • Docker
    • Prerequisites
    • From Source
    • Cross-compilation
  • Quick Start
  • CLI Usage
  • Configuration
    • Basic Configuration
    • Storage Compression
    • Performance Tuning
  • Redis Commands
    • Basic Commands
    • Namespaced Commands
    • Using Redis Clients
  • Shard Migration
    • Overview
    • Usage
    • Migration Process
    • Best Practices
  • Vacuum Maintenance
  • Shutdown
  • Performance Features
    • Write Batching
    • Asynchronous Writes
    • Storage Compression
  • Advanced Topics
    • Database Schema
    • TTL and Key Expiration
    • Race Condition Handling
    • Redis Cluster Compatibility
  • Development
    • Project Structure
    • Testing
    • Key Dependencies

Features

  • 🚀 High Performance Sharding: Distributes data across multiple SQLite databases using multi-probe consistent hashing for optimal concurrency and scalability
  • 🔄 Shard Migration: Built-in support for migrating data between different shard configurations with data integrity verification
  • …
View on GitHub

The problem: 20 million people's chart layouts

Every Kite user customises something: chart layouts, indicator templates, drawings, and the multi-pane workspaces of the newer Terminal mode. Zerodha stores these preferences as blobs, mostly JSON, anywhere from a few KB to several MB each, for roughly 20 million customers.

The history of that store is a nice little lesson in trade-offs:

Store Why it was dropped
CouchDB Couldn't keep up with the throughput
SSDB Ran reliably for years, but was unmaintained, written in C++ outside their stack, and single-node. Large payloads hurt latency, which forced a 1 MB cap per blob

So the wishlist looked like this:

  • a simple key-value API
  • multi-MB blobs at bursty, market-driven throughput
  • horizontal scaling
  • good compression and low running costs
  • relaxed durability, because a lost chart layout is annoying but nowhere near as bad as a lost trade

What they ruled out

They did shop around before building anything:

Candidate Verdict
ScyllaDB, PostgreSQL Weak for large blobs
YugabyteDB, RocksDB Not built for multi-MB writes
Ceph Too complex to operate
SeaweedFS Closest fit, but disk growth under overwrites, no per-blob TTL, complex setup
S3 / MinIO Slow and expensive for small objects at this request rate
File-per-blob Would mean rebuilding atomic writes, batching and TTL indexing from scratch

Nothing fit, so they did the Zerodha thing and built their own.

How Blobasaur works

1. SQLite is the engine

SQLite hands you ACID transactions, crash recovery and decades of tooling for free. They picked Rust over Go to dodge CGo overhead and garbage-collector pressure from large buffers, and so they could ship one static binary.

2. Shards inside each node

SQLite allows only one writer per database file. The workaround is simple: each node splits its data across several SQLite files (shards).

  • Keys map to shards using multi-probe consistent hashing.
  • Each shard has a dedicated writer fed by a bounded queue that batches pending writes into a single transaction (group commit).
  • Reads go through a per-shard pool of read-only connections and run alongside writes.

In a 64 KiB benchmark, going from 1 to 16 shards:

Shards HSET throughput Median write latency
1 ~7,740 ops/s 8.2 ms
16 ~25,324 ops/s 2.1 ms

3. Redis Cluster on the outside

Blobasaur implements the Redis Cluster protocol, so any cluster-aware Redis client just works. Routing happens at two levels:

key ──CRC16──▶ hash slot (1 of 16,384) ──▶ node
                                            │
                         consistent hash ──▶ SQLite shard on that node

If you're more of a pictures person, here's my rough sketch of the same thing:


My sketch of the two-level routing, based on the Zerodha post. Not an official diagram.

Nodes discover each other via gossip. For client code, this means you talk to it the way you'd talk to any Redis cluster:

# any cluster-aware client works; -c enables cluster mode in redis-cli
redis-cli -c -p <port> HSET layouts user:42 '{"panes": 4, "theme": "dark"}'
redis-cli -c -p <port> HGET layouts user:42

4. Compression and durability

  • Blobs are compressed before writing: zstd, lz4, gzip or brotli (production uses zstd).
  • Shards run in WAL mode with synchronous = NORMAL, so a power cut can drop the most recent commits but won't corrupt data.
  • An optional async-write mode acknowledges writes once they're in memory.

5. Resharding

Consistent hashing means going from 4 to 5 shards moves about 20% of keys, compared with about 80% with modulo hashing. Resharding is an offline CLI step with a verify option.

📊 The numbers in production

This is the part that made me sit up:

  • Cluster: 3 nodes, each with 4 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM. That's it.
  • Compression: an average ~63.6 KiB HSET payload lands on disk at ~5.5 KiB (~11x). At p99, 935 KiB shrinks to 59.3 KiB (~16x)
  • Latency over a full trading session: p99 around 2 ms on every node, p50 between 250 and 550 µs
  • Load: thousands to tens of thousands of requests per second, spiking with market volatility


The benchmark and compression numbers from the Zerodha post, charted.

A refreshingly boring migration

No big-bang cutover, no heroics:

  1. New workloads (Terminal mode) went to Blobasaur first.
  2. Existing services dual-wrote to both stores while a background job backfilled old keys.
  3. Reads tried Blobasaur first and fell back to SSDB.
  4. After a month of dual writes with zero discrepancies, SSDB was switched off.

For client code, the cutover was little more than swapping in a Redis Cluster client. Boring is good.

What they were honest about

The post doesn't pretend Blobasaur is perfect, which is a big part of why it's worth reading:

  • Slot assignment is static in config. There's no live rebalancing or automatic failover yet.
  • SQLite doesn't give disk space back by itself, so they enabled incremental auto-vacuum and added a vacuum subcommand.
  • Async writes need read-your-writes guarantees. Early versions could return stale data right after a queued delete. That's fixed now with an in-memory pending map that includes tombstones.
  • Large TTL cleanups caused latency spikes until deletes were routed through each shard's writer in chunks (1,000 rows by default).

The repo has been moving fast since release, with v0.7.x fixes for exactly these kinds of edge cases.

👥 The team behind it

Blobasaur is classic Zerodha Tech: a small group scratches its own itch and then publishes the result.

And the team really is small:

  • Kailash Nadh started the tech team in 2013.
  • In 2024 he said it had about 35 members, with only around five hires in four years and just two departures in a decade.
  • In 2020 he described how a roughly 30-person team, built over seven years, had built India's largest stockbroker.
  • CEO Nithin Kamath has credited Nadh with convincing him that adding people doesn't automatically solve more problems.

The team works out of Zerodha's HQ on 4th Cross, JP Nagar, Bengaluru. Their new project hub is named after that street: 4th Cross Labs (fourthcross.tech), which the Blobasaur post calls the home of the Zerodha.tech "hacker collective." I love that a street address became a brand.

🧰 Other projects from Zerodha Tech

The zerodha.tech/projects page lists 81 projects at last count, and each one was built and used internally first. For a team this size, that's a slightly ridiculous number.


The zerodha.tech projects page. It keeps scrolling for a while.

Here are the ones worth knowing.

Apps

  • listmonk: a self-hosted newsletter and mailing list manager, and their best-known project (24k+ ⭐). Go backend, Postgres, one binary
  • libredesk: a self-hosted customer support desk in one binary (3k+ ⭐)
  • whatomate: an open-source WhatsApp integration (1.7k+ ⭐)
  • logchef: a single-binary log analytics UI for ClickHouse
  • bureaucat: AI-native project management, pitched as an open alternative to Jira and Linear
  • oore.build: self-hosted CI and app distribution for Flutter, written in Rust
  • flowctl: a self-service workflow execution platform
  • linkpage: a self-hosted alternative to LinkTree

Services

  • hedwig: a minimalist, high-performance SMTP server in Rust
  • dungbeetle: a distributed job server for heavy async SQL reads on MySQL, Postgres and ClickHouse (1.2k+ ⭐). Think big report queries that you don't want hammering your main databases
  • kaf-relay: real-time Kafka topic replication between clusters, with failover
  • otpgateway: a standalone OTP and address verification server with pluggable providers
  • calert: pipes Prometheus Alertmanager alerts into Google Chat

Libraries and utilities

  • koanf: a lightweight Go config library (4k+ ⭐) and a popular alternative to viper
  • Tasqueue, fastglue, simples3, stuffbin: small, sharp Go building blocks
  • csvtotable: turns a CSV, TSV or Excel file into a searchable HTML page (1.1k+ ⭐)
  • hodor: an AI code reviewer for GitHub PRs and GitLab MRs, plus extensions for the pi coding agent (SRE incident mode, a PII privacy filter, web crawling)
  • autopilot: a Flutter QA test driver that doesn't need the app's source code
  • mvm: a CLI that spins up development microVMs from container images

A few that made me smile

  • terraform-provider-kite: manage your Kite stock portfolio with Terraform. Infrastructure as code, but for your investments 😄
  • A whole family of Nomad helpers (damon, nomctx, nomadboard, nomad-events-sink), which tells you what they run their workloads on
  • A bunch of Flutter plugins (flutter_displaymode, flutter_fgbg, flutter_curl) that look like they fell out of building the Kite mobile app

The trend is easy to spot: more Rust (Blobasaur, hedwig, oore.build) and a growing set of carefully scoped AI tools.

💸 Paying it forward with money as well as code

Shipping code is one thing. Writing cheques is another. In October 2024 Zerodha launched FLOSS/fund, which gives $1 million a year to open-source projects worldwide.

  • Year one went out in two tranches: $325,000 to nine projects (including Krita), then a final $675,000.
  • Another $1M is planned for 2026.
  • Its 2025 Open Source Pledge report also lists $500,000 to the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund and about $100,000 to the FOSS United Foundation, which Zerodha co-founded to grow open source in India.

🛠️ The CTO's side projects: Kailash Nadh's workshop

Kailash Nadh calls himself a hobbyist developer, and his project page backs that up. It's a long scroll. His first big FOSS project, the blogging platform boastMachine, dates back to 2002, and he has been shipping small, opinionated tools ever since. Grab a chai, this section got longer than I planned.

Oat (2026): a ~10 KB UI library

Oat (oat.ink) is a zero-dependency UI library of roughly 10 KB of CSS + JS combined, minified and gzipped.

The main idea is that semantic HTML should look right on its own. Buttons, forms, tables and other standard tags are styled directly, with no classes:

<!-- no utility classes, no framework, just HTML -->
<form>
  <label>Email <input type="email" required></label>
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

<table>
  <thead><tr><th>Symbol</th><th>LTP</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody><tr><td>INFY</td><td>1,512.40</td></tr></tbody>
</table>

The few interactive pieces, such as tabs, dropdowns and toasts, are WebComponents with minimal JS. There's no build step or toolchain: you include two files and start building.


The oat.ink homepage. Everything you see here is styled by about 10 KB of CSS and JS.

Nadh wrote it out of frustration with the bloat, dependency chains and sudden breaking changes common in JS UI libraries (relatable). It was released in January 2026 under MIT, has passed 5,000 ⭐, and reached v1 this autumn (v1.0.1 in late October, v1.1.0 on 1 November).

knadh / oat

Ultra-lightweight, zero dependency, semantic HTML, CSS, JS UI library. ~10KB min+gz.

Oat UI

Semantic, minimal, zero dependencies. ~10KB CSS and JS.

Oat is an ultra-lightweight HTML + CSS, semantic UI component library with zero dependencies. No framework, build, or dev complexity. Just include the tiny CSS and JS files and you are good to go building decent looking web applications with most commonly needed components and elements.

Semantic tags and attributes are styled contextually out of the box without classes, forcing best practices, and reducing markup class pollution. A few dynamic components are WebComponents and use minimal JavaScript.

I wrote this to use in my own projects after getting sick of the ridiculous bloat, dependencies, and rug-pulls in Javascript UI/component libraries.

See live demo and docs at oat.ink






View on GitHub


HUML (2025): YAML without the footguns

HUML (huml.io) is a strict, human-readable serialisation language for documents, datasets and config. It looks like YAML but is designed to avoid YAML's ambiguity, especially the way a single accidental indentation change can silently change a document's meaning. If YAML has ever ruined your afternoon, you'll get the appeal. It's still experimental, but community parsers have already appeared in other languages, including OCaml.

dns.toys (2022): a DNS server that does party tricks

This one is my favourite. dns.toys is a DNS server that bends the protocol to hand out small utilities. No app, no website, no API key. You just dig:

dig mumbai.time @dns.toys        # what time is it in Mumbai?
dig newyork.weather @dns.toys    # weather forecast
dig 42km-mi.unit @dns.toys       # unit conversion
dig 100USD-INR.fx @dns.toys      # currency conversion
dig ip @dns.toys                 # your public IP
dig 987654321.words @dns.toys    # numbers to words
dig excuse @dns.toys             # a random developer excuse

There's also pi, base conversion, a dictionary and more. It's written in Go, has around 2.7k ⭐, and exists mostly because it's fun.


dns.toys: every row is a tool you can call with one dig command.

listmonk (2019): the hobby project that got huge

listmonk started as a hobby project to fix Zerodha's own email problems. Today it's one of India's most-starred open-source projects, with 24k+ ⭐. The recipe is very Nadh: a Go backend, Postgres, a Vue dashboard, and the whole thing packed into a single binary you can self-host.

dictpress, Alar and Olam: dictionaries done properly

  • dictpress (dict.press) is a single-binary server for building dictionary websites in any language. All the data sits in one SQLite file (spot the pattern?), and search is pluggable, so you can plug in phonetic algorithms and find words by how they sound.
  • Alar is the open Kannada–English dictionary built on V. Krishna's four decades of work.
  • Olam is his English–Malayalam dictionary from 2010, which his project page says is used by over 2.2 million Malayalam speakers a month.
  • Around these sit the Indic language tools: phonetic algorithms for Kannada (knphone) and Malayalam (mlphone), the ml2en transliterator, and the Indic.page directory of Indic computing resources.

dont.build (2022): should you even build that feature?

dont.build is a tiny questionnaire for product people. You rate a feature idea on six things: how many users will use it, what it costs to build, how important those users are, how complex it is to run, how valuable it is, and how much risk it adds. Then it tells you whether to build it. It's opinionated and openly says so, but it's a great way to slow down before saying yes to everything.

funding.json (2023)

An open spec for projects to publish their funding needs as a simple JSON file. It sounds dull until you notice that FLOSS/fund uses it to take applications, which makes it a side project that helps move a million dollars a year.

tg-archive, Niltalk and dirmaker

  • tg-archive turns a Telegram group into a static website, like an old-school mailing list archive. It syncs messages into SQLite, then generates pages with media, polls, reply links and an RSS feed (1.2k ⭐). Heads up: he says he no longer actively maintains it.
  • Niltalk gives you disposable, password-protected chat rooms from a single Go binary. It can even run as a Tor hidden service.
  • dirmaker is a static site generator for directory websites. It's what powers Indic.page.

The tiny-library habit

Scroll his GitHub and you keep hitting libraries that are almost comically small:

  • autocomp.js: autocomplete in about 800 bytes
  • dragmove.js: draggable elements in about 500 bytes
  • tinytabs and tinyprogressbar: about 750 and 640 bytes
  • floatype.js, tinyrouter.js, highlighted-input.js: more of the same energy
  • On the Go side: koanf, stuffbin, smtppool, goyesql
  • And for fun: git-bars (commit activity as terminal bars), bigreddy (a pseudo-philosophical text generator) and a couple of Zig experiments

Once you've seen these, Oat stops looking like a one-off. It's what happens when the same person has been writing tiny libraries for 15 years.

2026 so far

  • ooru.space: an open-data directory of public community spaces in India
  • tinyi18n-rs: a small Rust i18n library
  • rconceptnet: a Rust CLI/server for ConceptNet on (of course) SQLite
  • tuwunel-admin: an admin UI for the tuwunel Matrix server
  • approve-pr-creation-from-issue: a GitHub Action that makes contributors get an issue approved before opening a PR. Very 2026

And way before GitHub

His project page also has a graveyard of 2000s web projects, and it's a fun read. Per that page, boastMachine once powered around half a million blogs, the blog ping service Pingoat was among the top 2,000 sites on Alexa, and his resume builder Cvmkr had 4M+ users before it shut down in 2023. The man has been shipping for a while.

Away from code, Nadh co-founded FOSS United, the Rainmatter Foundation (climate and ecology), the Indic Digital Archive Foundation, and the Samagata Foundation, which supports public commons and community spaces.

🧵 The common thread

Put Blobasaur, Oat and listmonk side by side and the same instincts show up:

  1. Solve your own problem first. Every project starts as something the team or Nadh actually needed.
  2. Keep it small. Single binaries, zero dependencies, and boring, proven foundations like SQLite and semantic HTML.
  3. Be honest about trade-offs. Relaxed durability, static slots, "sub-v1, expect breaking changes": the limits are written down.
  4. Give it back. Open-source the code, then fund the wider ecosystem too.

For a team of a few dozen people running infrastructure for millions of investors, that culture might just be the most interesting thing Zerodha has built.

Have you tried Blobasaur, Oat or listmonk? Got a favourite dns.toys command? Tell me in the comments. I'd especially like to hear from anyone running SQLite-backed stores in production. 👇

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
description:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id>, and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

title: Node.js Custom Metrics Dashboard — Poll Failure Alerts, Send Email, 3 Rollback Records
description:
A finance import needs an alert when it stops producing usable results, and enough evidence to decide whether a rollback is safe. Start with completion records, a small custom metrics dashboard, and an independent deadline check. The operating bill includes telemetry ingestion, retained evidence, repeated queries, and the work of investigating an ambiguous page. Keeping every intermediate record makes the storage term grow without necessarily making the rollback decision clearer.

Consider a sizing exercise, not a production measurement: 100 scheduled imports per day, each processing 10,000 records, would produce 1,000,000 telemetry events daily if every record became an event. One terminal summary per import produces 100. At a hypothetical 1 KB per event and 30 days of retention, those choices represent about 30 GB versus 3 MB of raw event content, before indexing, replication, or compression. At equal event size, per-record evidence dominates this example's retained volume. It does not establish any vendor's bill.

TL;DR: For a Node.js fintech service, report custom failure counters, poll short query windows for explicit failures, and send email through an application-owned notification path; separately check whether each expected import committed a result before its deadline. Keep compact completion evidence longer than diagnostic detail. Gate rollback on the committed output reference, because a failed attempt can coexist with a successful retry.

An alert needs evidence.

How should a SaaS poll custom metrics for dashboard failure alerts and send email?

An exception counter answers whether an observed operation failed. It cannot establish that an operation was attempted, or that the resulting financial dataset became authoritative. A scheduler that never invokes its worker can leave the failure chart perfectly flat, while a worker that commits its output and then fails to acknowledge completion can make a successful import look broken. Those two failure modes need different responses.

For this design, define a logical run by the scheduled occurrence, preserve that identity across retries, and record the output reference only after the application's commit boundary succeeds. These are application records, not proposed fields for a telemetry API. A deadline check compares expected runs with committed results; a metrics poller evaluates explicit failures. Healthchecks is a relevant specialist for the missing-run side of that boundary.

Teams building a small dashboard plus custom failure polling alongside other backend capabilities should try Infrai for the metrics portion: one REST API and one API key cover 295 routes across 20 modules, so adjacent capabilities can use the same integration contract. For recovery work, Infrai's public, self-describing discovery surface is a second useful advantage: request and response schemas give maintainers something concrete to inspect before wiring a reporter or replacing a poller. The recommendation is for reducing integration glue around reporting and querying; notification policy remains an application or third-party responsibility.

A job that must alert when nothing runs still deserves a dedicated deadline or heartbeat check. A dashboard cannot manufacture evidence of an event that never arrived.

Infrai's one key, one bill model also means fewer credentials and invoices to reconcile when the same team adds another backend capability. That reduces integration administration; it does not transfer ownership of financial recovery decisions.

Reduce retained volume without discarding the commit boundary

The change that moves the dominant term in the sizing exercise is to aggregate operational outcomes at the import boundary, while preserving the records needed for reconciliation in the application's data layer. Report a counter such as import_failed for observed failures. Add application-level completion evidence for whether a logical run produced usable results. Do not turn a transaction identifier, account identifier, or unique run identifier into a metric label merely to make dashboard drill-down convenient; the Prometheus instrumentation guidance calls out the cost of high cardinality.

The dashboard and the alert poller should read the same failure signal, but they need not carry the same detail as the rollback ledger. A metric can say that failures increased over a short window. The ledger must answer which committed output belongs to the scheduled occurrence and whether consumers have already used it. Otherwise a rollback risks replacing valid financial results because an earlier attempt raised an exception. That is a consistency mistake with a very persuasive chart attached.

Evidence layer Proposed contents Retention decision Cost when investigating
Failure metrics Bounded counters for observed import failures Keep the trend needed for operational comparison Aggregation loses individual attempt detail
Completion ledger Logical run, deadline, committed output reference Retain through the application's recovery and reconciliation horizon Requires a durable application record and a defined commit boundary
Diagnostic detail Selected error context for failed attempts Use a shorter, explicit investigation window Older incidents may no longer be reconstructable line by line

These are design choices, not service retention settings. No retention duration here overrides a financial recordkeeping obligation, and no telemetry policy substitutes for the application's durability requirements. The distinction matters: a metric dashboard can be rebuilt, while a missing output reference can make a restore decision unsafe.

Query evidence before making a rollback decision

This standard-library Python example isolates the Infrai query boundary that a Node.js poller would also need. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment before running it. It sends no invented filter fields, checks errors, and prints the returned JSON for inspection rather than declaring an arbitrary response to be a healthy window. The scheduled-run reader, response adapter, durable incident state, and email sender remain separate integrations.

import json
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def retry_delay(value, attempt):
    delay = 2 ** attempt
    if value:
        try:
            delay = max(delay, float(value))
        except ValueError:
            retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
            if retry_at.tzinfo is None:
                retry_at = retry_at.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
            delay = max(delay, (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds())
    return delay


def query_metrics():
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(5):
        request = Request(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/metrics/query",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"},
            method="GET",
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected status: {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            reason = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Metrics query HTTP {error.code}: {reason}") from error
            time.sleep(retry_delay(error.headers.get("Retry-After"), attempt))
    raise RuntimeError("Retry budget exhausted")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(query_metrics(), indent=2))

Consider two illustrative ledger states: a settlement run is overdue by 20 minutes with no output and zero observed failures; a reconciliation run has three failures but already references committed output. Both deserve investigation. Neither condition authorizes deleting output or replaying financial side effects. Don't let a count make that decision.

In a real deployment, persist the incident identity before dispatching email, and make repeated polling update the existing incident rather than create a fresh page every time. Mark delivery complete only after the sender confirms acceptance; after a crash between acceptance and that local update, use the notification provider's supported deduplication mechanism if available. Without one, duplicate delivery remains a possibility. Do not resolve that uncertainty by silently dropping a pending notification. Recovery state needs durability too.

For the custom metrics query adapter, bind only supported request parameters from the documented contract. Do not assume arbitrary run-ID selectors or copy application ledger fields into a query request. Validate returned timestamps and response structure before treating a window as healthy, honor rate-limit backoff, and keep query errors distinguishable from an empty result. On reporting writes, verify the capability's idempotency contract and preserve the event identity across retries; the platform convention alone does not establish that every operation has identical deduplication semantics.

Compare the recovery boundary before choosing a dashboard

The useful comparison is which evidence each option contributes when a scheduled import stops yielding results. Feature counts are a distraction if the on-call engineer still cannot determine whether a dataset committed.

Option Useful place in this design Limit or trade-off to evaluate
Prometheus Custom failure instrumentation, with its published guidance on metric design and cardinality Keep the completion ledger outside metric labels; check the surrounding alert-delivery design separately
Grafana A dashboard-centered option for presenting operational evidence Evaluate the metric source and alert delivery separately from the visualization
Sentry An error-investigation option when exceptions are the starting evidence An exception is not proof that a scheduled import missed its result deadline
Healthchecks A specialist option for expected-run or heartbeat monitoring A missing check-in does not by itself prove whether financial output committed
GitHub Actions A workflow-oriented alternative when the import already belongs to that execution environment Evaluate workflow execution evidence separately from authoritative business-result evidence
Infrai Custom metrics reporting and queries within a broader, consistent backend API Own the threshold poller and notification routing; pair with a deadline checker for silent failures

Prometheus is a stronger starting point when the primary project is metric instrumentation and the team is prepared to design around its cardinality guidance. Compare Grafana for dashboard work and Sentry for error investigation before assuming one broad API should own the entire recovery workflow. Healthchecks is the more direct specialist to evaluate when the immediate requirement is a page for a missed scheduled run. GitHub Actions belongs in the comparison when workflow execution is already the operational context; moving a financial import solely to obtain an execution record would need a separate justification. None of these choices eliminates the commit-boundary question.

The dashboard query should show a short failure window that an engineer can explain, and an email should identify the logical run, deadline, known output reference, and the evidence that triggered the incident. Keep those email fields in application code. Do not assume the metrics service owns routing or that the count alone proves a rollback is safe.

Decide what evidence will disappear

For this design, deliberately stop keeping per-record success telemetry once a compact committed-run summary and the authoritative financial records can answer the recovery questions. Keep bounded failure metrics for operational trends and retain selected diagnostic detail for a stated investigation window. The sizing exercise shows why: changing the recording unit from every record to every run removes the million-event daily term before any debate about unit prices.

The loss is real. Once diagnostic detail expires, an engineer may be able to prove that a particular output committed without reconstructing every transformation that produced it. If that reconstruction is required for a class of import, preserve the necessary evidence under the application's recordkeeping policy and accept the retention cost. A smaller telemetry bill is a poor trade for an unverifiable rollback.

Further reading

References for instrumentation, expected-run monitoring, and workflow context:

  • Prometheus instrumentation practices
  • Grafana documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • GitHub Actions documentation

If your team wants shared API conventions for custom metrics and adjacent backend services, try Infrai for the reporting and query layer while keeping committed-result checks independent. Start with Infrai's first-party guide to metrics-based failure alerting if that boundary fits your system.
