title: My layout check kept returning an empty list. I was reading it as a verdict.
description:
My layout check kept returning an empty list. I was reading it as a verdict.

I generate carousel covers from HTML, render them in headless Chromium, and publish one four times a day. Before a cover ships, three checks run against the PNG: no two blocks overlap, nothing is cut at the edge, the logo keeps its margin. In October a cover passed all three and still read wrong. The title promised an answer, and the big number sat between the title and the sentence explaining what it referred to. Anyone swiping to the second slide met "193x" before knowing the subject.

So I added a fourth check for reading order. It measures ink per pixel, groups rows into blocks, labels each block as title, definition or number, and compares their vertical positions. The check is ordinary. What took four versions to get right is that a check can return green while measuring nothing at all.

Version one trusted the document

The first version knew the order from the HTML: title first, definition second, number third. It read the y coordinate of each block position and compared them.

That held until the title wrapped to two lines. The second line arrived as its own block, the check called it the definition, and the first line of the real definition became the number. The three positions were still in increasing order, so the check passed. It passed while labeling the wrong rows.

The fix was to stop using the document as data. A block is what it measures: a filled band of rows with a height and a width. Nothing in the check reads the HTML any more, only the PNG.

Height alone put the number in the title slot

Font size survives the render as band height, so the tallest band is a good first guess for the number. On a cover with a single digit, the number band measured 114px tall and 90px wide, while the two title lines measured 91px and 72px tall with widths of 686px and 507px. Height separates those three.

Then came a cover whose number was "85". Two digits at 150px measure 584px wide, wider than any single-digit number the check had seen. A cutoff on width at 0.35 of the 904px content column, 316px, was enough for one digit and wrong for two. The number got labeled as text, became the title because it was the tallest text block, and the check reported:

FALHA: 0 numero(s), 1 titulo(s)

That message is not a verdict about the cover. The check could not see a number, so it had nothing to compare. I had been treating both outcomes as failures of the same kind for weeks.

The current classifier uses both dimensions, plus a floor relative to the tallest band:

alturas = sorted(b["h"] for b in bs)
ref = alturas[int(len(alturas) * PERCENTIL_REF_ALTURA)]
estreitas = [b for b in bs if b["h"] > ref * 1.5]
h_max = max(b["h"] for b in bs)
estreitas = [b for b in estreitas if b["h"] >= NUMERO_MIN_REL * h_max]
for b in bs:
    b["classe"] = "NUMERO" if b in estreitas and \
        b["w"] < CONTEUDO * FATOR_LARGURA_NUMERO else "TEXTO"

The floor arrived on 21 November, from a cover where the number was "99%" at 429px wide and 145px tall. A filled badge above it was 431px wide and 46px tall. Width could not tell them apart, and the badge passed the 1.5x test because its 46px is more than 1.5 times a 20px text line. Height could: nothing below half the tallest band is a number.

The reference for "tall" moves with the art

The first version compared each band to the median height of all bands. On a seven-band cover the median was 29px, and the 114px number passed easily. On the small art used as a control, with three blocks (title 90, number 114, definition 33), the median was 90. The number needed more than 135 to qualify and had 114. It became text, the title became the tallest block, the function that reads the order found no number and returned an empty list.

The median was measuring the middle of the list, and the middle of the list changes when the list gets shorter. The first quartile held in both cases: 21px on the seven-band cover, 33px on the three-block art, with the number above 1.5x in both. The reference had to be the text line, not a statistic that floats.

A control has to reproduce the defect

A test that only passes is worth nothing. The cover that started this had the number between the title and the definition, so the control rebuilds exactly that: it crops the real blocks out of the real cover, paints over everything below the title, and pastes the number and the definition in the wrong order. The rule that reads the result is the same function as the main test.

y = onde_apaga + VAO_CONTROLE
for g in (numero[0], defi):      # the wrong order
    f = fatia(g)
    nova.paste(f, (MARGEM_X, y))
    y += f.height + VAO_CONTROLE

Two versions of this control failed before it worked. In the first, the gap between the pasted blocks was 24px and the grouping gap is 30px, so all rows merged into one block, the classifier labeled that block as a number, and the order came out empty. The control "rejected" the art because it could not measure it, which is the same bug it was supposed to catch.

In the second, measured on 17 October, the control art was reduced to three slices. With the top bands removed, the first quartile rose to 72px, the 105px number needed 108px, and the order came out empty again through a new path. The fix was to keep the top of the real cover and recompose only what sits below the title, so the reference stays where it was.

An empty list is now an explicit failure with its own message. It says the measurement did not happen, and it does not count as the defect being caught.

What it prints now

Here is the check on the cover from 22 November, a deep purple background that the per-piece wrapper declares as (88, 3, 124). The wrapper overrides the palette, the measurement window and the file name. It imports the shared module and never copies the rule, because two copies of a rule are two rules, and only one of them survives the next edit.

y 269.. 441  hmax= 54  wmax= 690  -> TITULO
y 473.. 581  hmax= 28  wmax= 881  -> DEFINICAO
y 624.. 947  hmax=168  wmax= 903  -> NUMERO

ordem lida: TITULO -> DEFINICAO -> NUMERO
ok: titulo, definicao, numero

== controle negativo: a ordem errada tem que reprovar
ordem da arte com defeito: TITULO -> NUMERO -> DEFINICAO
ok: reprovou

Seven blocks were measured on that cover. Four belong to frame elements (the top line, a rule, a badge, the source note), they land in the definition class, and they do not disturb the order because only the first block of each class is compared. The check exits non-zero when the order is wrong, when a block is missing, or when either the main art or the control art produces an empty list.

The lesson I keep relearning: a verifier is code, and code that cannot measure returns a value that looks like an answer. "No number found" and "the number is in the wrong place" are different facts, and only one of them is about the image. Building the control so that it produces the real defect, from real pixels and through the same function, is what separates the two.

Se esse tipo de teste já te deu um verde que não significava nada, conta nos comentários o que estava sendo medido de verdade. Cada verificação que passa por motivo errado é uma armadilha que eu prefiro aprender pelo relato de outra pessoa.

title: AWS Global Accelerator now preserves client IPs for NLBs with TLS listeners
description:
AWS Global Accelerator now preserves the client IP address for traffic sent to Network Load Balancer (NLB) endpoints with TLS listeners. You can terminate TLS at your NLB and still see the original client IP address in your application. This means you can apply security groups, geo-blocking, rate limiting, fraud detection, audit logging, allowlists, and compliance controls based on the real client IP.

Previously, you couldn't add an NLB with a TLS listener to an accelerator that had client IP address preservation enabled. You had to choose between terminating TLS at the NLB and seeing the real client IP address. With this launch, you get both. This helps with workloads that need TLS termination at Layer 4, such as non-HTTP TCP protocols, applications that require static or Elastic IP addresses, and high-throughput traffic where a Layer 7 load balancer isn't a fit.

To enable this feature, add an NLB with a TLS listener as an endpoint to an accelerator with client IP address preservation setting turned on, the same way you add any NLB. No additional configuration is required! Client IP address preservation for NLBs with TLS listeners is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions, excluding the AWS GovCloud (US) and China Regions. Standard Global Accelerator pricing applies.

To learn more, see Client IP address preservation in the AWS Global Accelerator Developer Guide and Create a listener for your Network Load Balancer in the User Guide for Network Load Balancers.

title: Object Storage Service for App Data Backup: Lifecycle-Cost Trade-offs
description:
For an app storing healthtech data, the best object storage service for data backup is the one that can move a 2 GB report, apply automated file lifecycle rules, and protect an authenticated customer from another tenant's object. I would choose a standards-compatible object store only after proving those three paths with production-shaped files. The service name is secondary.

The operational rule is straightforward: generate into a private object key, publish only after a complete write, issue a short-lived read capability, and make retention a policy that is tested like code. Keep the application out of the byte stream whenever the platform can transfer directly. That leaves the API responsible for authorization and metadata, while the storage path handles throughput and range reads.

How should an object storage service handle app data backup?

A report is not merely a blob. It has an owner, a generation, a retention class, and a recovery expectation. I use a key such as tenant/2026/10/report-<id>/generation-3/report.pdf, but that path does not authorize anyone. The database record remains the source of truth for tenant membership, report state, and revocation.

For a large file, the write protocol needs an explicit state transition:

  1. Create a pending report row with a unique report ID.
  2. Stream or upload parts to a private temporary key.
  3. Verify the final byte count and checksum that the storage API reports.
  4. Mark the generation ready in one database transaction.
  5. Return a download capability only after that commit.

This ordering handles the awkward middle states. A worker can die after the object is complete but before the row changes. A reconciler can find that object and either finish the transition or quarantine it. A row can also say ready while the object is absent, and a read-path check should turn that into a controlled failure with an alert rather than a blank response.

Why is direct streaming worth the boundary?

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat retries as normal traffic. Proxying every byte through the API makes retry behavior, connection limits, and memory pressure part of the application release. Direct transfer moves the heavy path to the storage boundary, but it does not remove application responsibility: the API must validate the tenant, report state, expiry, and requested disposition before it grants access.

In Go, the important code is the decision boundary, not a vendor SDK call. The storage interface can be backed by an S3-compatible service, a self-hosted implementation, or another provider without changing the authorization rule.

package reports

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrNotReady = errors.New("report is not ready")

// AuthorizeDownload keeps tenant ownership in the application database.
type Report struct {
    TenantID string
    ObjectKey string
    Ready bool
}

type Store interface {
    PresignGet(ctx context.Context, key string, expires time.Duration) (string, error)
}

func DownloadURL(ctx context.Context, store Store, report Report, tenantID string) (string, error) {
    if report.TenantID != tenantID || !report.Ready {
        return "", ErrNotReady
    }
    return store.PresignGet(ctx, report.ObjectKey, 10*time.Minute)
}

The ten-minute value is a policy choice, not a security slogan. A shorter capability reduces exposure but can frustrate a slow connection; a longer one reduces repeat authorization calls but extends the impact of a leaked URL. Measure completion time by file-size bucket before setting it. Also record who requested the capability without logging the capability itself.

Where do lifecycle rules fail in practice?

Lifecycle management is useful for old report generations, temporary uploads, and backup retention. It is also asynchronous policy machinery. An object can remain visible for a period after its expiration condition is met, so a compliance workflow must not treat a lifecycle rule as the only deletion proof. The application should expose retention state, and a periodic inventory should compare expected objects with observed objects.

Use separate prefixes or tags for temporary and durable data. A temporary multipart upload should have a bounded cleanup policy. A durable report should move through a small number of retention classes, each with a documented restore test. Avoid a rule that matches every object in a shared bucket: one broad filter can silently apply backup retention to exports or apply export deletion to evidence that must remain. AWS documents lifecycle filters and expiration behavior; the same design questions apply across object-storage implementations.

A useful test matrix includes a 10 MB report, a 2 GB report, an interrupted upload, a duplicate worker retry, an expired capability, and a report whose tenant record has been revoked. Run it in a non-production account, then repeat the recovery portion against a sampled production-shaped dataset. The number of test cases is small. Their failure modes are not.

How should teams compare services without chasing a leaderboard?

Start with interfaces and evidence. Check multipart upload behavior, resumability, range reads, checksum support, encryption controls, audit events, lifecycle filters, deletion semantics, and restore procedures. Then test the path that matters: an authenticated customer downloading a large generated report while another worker retries the same job.

Three common service families illustrate why a single ranking is misleading. Amazon S3 exposes lifecycle configuration and multipart upload primitives; Google Cloud Storage provides object lifecycle management and resumable uploads; Azure Blob Storage provides lifecycle management and block-blob upload patterns. Those are capabilities, not a recommendation. Their operational details, identity integration, event delivery, regional behavior, and observability still need to be checked against the team's controls and data residency requirements.

The comparison should fit on an engineering worksheet:

Question Evidence to collect Failure signal
Can a 2 GB report resume? Interrupted multipart or resumable upload test Restart begins at byte zero
Is tenant isolation enforceable? Cross-tenant authorization test Key naming is treated as access control
Does retention behave as designed? Expiry, inventory, and restore test Rule scope is wider than intended
Can responders explain a miss? Audit, metrics, and object-state records Only application logs exist

This method keeps price in its proper place. Storage, request, transfer, and retrieval charges can matter, but an apparently cheap tier is a poor fit if restoring a report is slow, opaque, or operationally risky. The trade-off is a real limitation: direct transfers improve large-file throughput, while a proxy gives the application tighter control over every byte and can be easier to audit for small files.

The incident lesson

The invariant is simple: never let a successful byte transfer stand in for a successful business transition. A complete object without a committed report state is orphaned data. A committed state without a verifiable object is a customer-visible failure. Idempotent job IDs, conditional state changes, private-by-default objects, and reconciliation close that gap.

This approach does not fit every workload. If reports are tiny, ephemeral, and never downloaded outside the API, direct delivery may add unnecessary moving parts. A proxy is the better choice for that small case. If records require legal hold, retention must be integrated with the applicable policy and review process rather than delegated to a generic expiration rule. A lifecycle-only design is unsuitable when deletion must be proven synchronously. For large authenticated healthtech reports, however, the decision is less about finding a winner and more about proving the transfer, authorization, and deletion boundaries under retry.

Small test. Big consequence.

Sources

  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • AWS, Object lifecycle management: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • RFC 3986, URI Generic Syntax: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986
  • Amazon S3, Multipart upload overview: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • Google Cloud Storage, Object Lifecycle Management: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle
  • Azure Blob Storage, Lifecycle management policy: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/lifecycle-management-overview

title: Engineering Out Duplicate Charges: Idempotency, State, and Reconciliation
description:
Most chargeback advice is aimed at operations teams: write clearer descriptors, answer the phone, refund quickly. One category is mostly an engineering problem, though: the duplicate charge.

A customer who is billed twice for one order has a legitimate complaint. Card networks treat it as a processing error. Visa, for example, has a dispute condition for duplicate processing. These disputes are usually not worth fighting because the customer is right. The only good strategy is to make sure the second charge never happens, and to catch it yourself before the cardholder does.

The broader operational checklist is covered in this guide to preventing Visa disputes, which recommends reviewing transaction logs so each sale is submitted only once. This article looks at how to enforce that rule in code.

Where duplicate charges actually come from

Duplicates rarely come from one obvious bug. They come from retries that are reasonable on their own but unsafe together.

Source What happens
Client double-submit The user clicks Pay twice, or the mobile app retries on a flaky network.
Client timeout + retry The browser gives up after 30s, but the server finished the charge. The user tries again.
Server-to-PSP timeout Your backend calls the payment provider, the socket times out, and you retry. The first request had already succeeded.
At-least-once queues A job worker crashes after charging but before acking. The message is redelivered.
Webhook redelivery A payment succeeded webhook arrives twice and each copy triggers a capture or fulfillment step.
Batch resubmission A POS or batch file is re-sent after a partial failure, and settled items go through again.

All of these share one root cause: a network failure leaves the caller unsure whether the operation happened. The fix is to make retries safe, not to stop retrying.

Layer 1: Derive the idempotency key from intent

Many payment provider APIs accept an idempotency key, often sent as an Idempotency-Key HTTP header. The IETF HTTPAPI working group has a draft standardizing this header. The provider stores the first response for that key and returns it on repeats instead of charging again.

The common mistake is generating the key per request:

# WRONG: every retry gets a fresh key, so every retry is a new charge
key = str(uuid.uuid4())
psp.charge(amount, card, idempotency_key=key)

The key must identify the business intent, not the HTTP attempt. Derive it from data that is stable across retries:

def charge_key(order_id: str, attempt_group: int) -> str:
    # attempt_group increments only when the user deliberately
    # retries with a new card or amount after a decline
    return f'order:{order_id}:charge:{attempt_group}'

If the user's card is declined and they enter a new card, that is a new intent, so increment attempt_group. If the network dropped, it is the same intent, so reuse the key.

Also check how long your provider keeps idempotency keys. Retention windows are finite. A retry that happens days later, for example from a stuck queue, may not be protected by the provider at all. That is why you need the next layer.

Layer 2: Own the state locally

Never rely only on the provider for deduplication. Keep a payment record with a database-enforced uniqueness constraint and an explicit state machine.

CREATE TABLE payment_attempts (
  id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id        TEXT NOT NULL,
  idempotency_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  amount_minor    BIGINT NOT NULL,
  currency        CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  state           TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (state IN
                   ('pending','authorized','captured','failed','unknown')),
  psp_reference   TEXT,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- At most one successful capture per order
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_capture_per_order
  ON payment_attempts (order_id) WHERE state = 'captured';

The partial unique index is the important part. Even if application logic fails, the database will reject a second captured row for the same order.

The charge flow then looks like this:

def charge_order(order, attempt_group):
    key = charge_key(order.id, attempt_group)

    row = db.insert_or_get(
        'payment_attempts',
        idempotency_key=key, order_id=order.id,
        amount_minor=order.total_minor, currency=order.currency,
        state='pending')

    if row.state in ('authorized', 'captured'):
        return row                      # already done, return the same result
    if row.state == 'unknown':
        return resolve_unknown(row)     # never fire blind

    try:
        resp = psp.authorize(order.total_minor, order.currency,
                             idempotency_key=key, timeout=20)
    except (Timeout, ConnectionError):
        db.update(row.id, state='unknown')
        return resolve_unknown(row)

    db.update(row.id, state='authorized' if resp.ok else 'failed',
              psp_reference=resp.reference)
    return db.get(row.id)

The unknown state is the whole point

When a call times out, you do not know whether the money moved. Treating that as failed and letting the user retry with a new key is exactly how duplicates happen.

resolve_unknown should either retry with the same key, which is safe while the provider still remembers it, or look up the transaction using your own reference, such as the order ID in metadata. Only mark the attempt failed once you have confirmed it.

Layer 3: Make webhook handlers idempotent

Webhooks are typically delivered at least once. Your handler must accept the same event twice without side effects.

def handle_event(event):
    with db.transaction():
        inserted = db.execute(
            'INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES (%s) '
            'ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING', [event.id]).rowcount
        if not inserted:
            return 200          # already handled
        apply_event(event)       # state transition, same transaction
    return 200

Recording the event ID and applying the state change in one transaction matters. If you mark the event processed and then crash before applying it, you lose the event. If you apply it and then crash before marking it, you apply it twice.

Also make apply_event a guarded state transition, for example UPDATE ... SET state='captured' WHERE id=%s AND state='authorized', so out-of-order events cannot move a payment backward.

Layer 4: Reconcile against settlement data

Prevention will not be perfect. A legacy integration, a manual terminal entry, or a resubmitted batch can still get through. Reconciliation is your detection layer, and it should run before the cardholder's statement arrives.

Pull the provider's settlement or transaction report daily and compare it to your ledger:

def find_suspected_duplicates(settled, window_hours=48):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for txn in settled:
        # card_fingerprint: a provider token for the card, never the PAN
        groups[(txn.card_fingerprint, txn.amount_minor, txn.currency)].append(txn)

    flagged = []
    for txns in groups.values():
        txns.sort(key=lambda t: t.settled_at)
        for a, b in zip(txns, txns[1:]):
            close = (b.settled_at - a.settled_at) <= timedelta(hours=window_hours)
            same_order = a.order_id and a.order_id == b.order_id
            if same_order or (close and not b.order_id):
                flagged.append((a, b))
    return flagged

Two checks are useful:

  1. Hard duplicates: two settled charges linked to the same order ID. This is almost always a bug, so auto-refund the second one and alert.
  2. Soft duplicates: same card, same amount, close together, with no distinct order behind the second charge. Send these to human review, since repeat purchases are legitimate.

Also check for orphans, meaning settled charges with no matching ledger row. Orphans often come from timeouts your system recorded as failures.

Decision table: what to do on each outcome

Outcome of charge call Local state Safe action
2xx, approved authorized Proceed to fulfillment
2xx, declined failed Allow retry with new attempt_group
4xx validation error failed Fix input; new intent if amount or card changes
409 / idempotency conflict unchanged Another request with this key is in flight or used different params; do not retry with a new key
Timeout / connection reset unknown Retry same key or look up by reference
5xx unknown Same as timeout; never treat as failure

Common mistakes and how to catch them

  • Random keys per attempt. Grep for UUID generation near charge calls. Keys should come from order data.
  • Treating timeouts as declines. Search your code for exception handlers around provider calls that set state to failed.
  • Disabling the Pay button as the only protection. That helps the UX, but a client-side guard is not a server-side guarantee.
  • Webhook handlers that fulfill without checking state. Send the same event twice in a test.
  • Capturing in two places. For example, both a webhook and a shipping job call capture. Pick one owner for the capture transition.

Tests worth writing 

def test_timeout_then_retry_charges_once(fake_psp):
    fake_psp.succeed_then_timeout()        # charge lands, response is lost
    with pytest.raises(PaymentPending):
        charge_order(order, attempt_group=1)
    charge_order(order, attempt_group=1)   # user retries
    assert fake_psp.successful_charges(order.id) == 1

def test_concurrent_submits_charge_once(fake_psp):
    run_in_parallel(lambda: charge_order(order, 1), n=10)
    assert fake_psp.successful_charges(order.id) == 1

The concurrency test often exposes read-then-insert races that a unique constraint would have prevented.

Summary

Duplicate charges come from ambiguity after failures, not from a single bug. Use four layers: intent-derived idempotency keys, a local state machine with database constraints, idempotent webhook handling, and daily reconciliation against settlement data. Together they turn "check your transaction logs" into a guarantee you can test.

title: App Backup Storage in 2026: Large-File Throughput, Lifecycle, and Trust Boundaries
description:
Use an object storage service with lifecycle policies for app backups, and keep the application out of the large-file data path. For a developer tool that accepts media uploads, the practical choice is usually AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or Backblaze B2, with a separate decision about which service may process metadata or orchestration.

Short answer: let the browser or upload worker send bytes directly to object storage, then apply retention rules there. Compare region availability, egress, storage tiers, deletion behavior, and recovery guarantees before comparing headline rates. I would use Infrai as a thin REST control plane for storage operations when a team values one HTTP surface and wants lifecycle configuration alongside other backend calls, but I would keep residency and immutability decisions with the storage specialist.

The experiment: move bytes without moving the trust boundary

The simple design is an app server that accepts a 4 GB recording, buffers or streams it, and then writes it to a bucket. It is easy to sketch and expensive to operate: the app becomes a throughput bottleneck, and every byte crosses a process that did not need to inspect the media.

The better experiment is narrower. The app authenticates the upload, creates a short-lived direct upload handoff, and records only the object key and policy metadata. The client sends the file to the storage service. A worker later verifies the upload, writes a backup manifest, and applies the lifecycle rule. The app owns authorization; the bucket owns bytes.

That boundary matters more than a small difference in storage-unit price. A useful test fixture is 10,000 media objects ranging from 50 MB to 4 GB, written in one region and read back for restore drills from the same region. Measure upload completion time, failed-part recovery, restore time, egress, and the age at which objects move to colder storage. Do not copy a provider choice from a benchmark that only uploads 10 MB files.

Bytes should take the shortest path.

Which object storage service should back up app data?

AWS S3 is the broad default when the system needs mature lifecycle management, regional choice, and a large ecosystem of SDKs and adjacent controls. Its object lifecycle documentation is explicit about transitions and expiration, which makes it a strong baseline for a backup policy that will grow beyond one rule.

Azure Blob Storage is the natural comparison for a product already organized around Azure regions, identities, and operational tooling. Its lifecycle management can be a good fit when the rest of the application already uses that provider's access model. Moving media between clouds later is possible, but it is a project with egress, verification, and metadata mapping to budget for.

Backblaze B2 is worth testing when a simpler object-storage surface and broad compatibility are more important than the larger cloud's surrounding services. It should still be evaluated against the actual restore path: storage tier behavior, regional availability, egress terms, and the operational tools used by the team matter more than a table of nominal rates.

One REST option occupies a different position in this comparison. It exposes backend capabilities through HTTP, so a TypeScript, Python, or other client does not need another storage SDK or client-library release cycle. Its public discovery surface documents request and response schemas with runnable examples. For Infrai, the relevant advantage is one REST API and one key: any runtime that can send HTTP can use the same control surface without installing a storage client library or managing a second credential for this backend workflow. A second, practical advantage is its public self-describing discovery surface, which lets a backup worker inspect the current lifecycle schema before deployment instead of relying on copied SDK types. That can remove integration friction for a solo team already coordinating several backend services.

Here is the boundary I would use:

Decision Better fit Why
Deep storage controls, regional options, and a large ecosystem AWS S3 Strong baseline for long-lived backup policy
Existing Azure identity and regional operations Azure Blob Storage Fits an Azure-centered application boundary
A focused object-storage specialist to test directly Backblaze B2 Keeps the comparison grounded in the restore path
One REST control surface across backend capabilities A REST storage gateway Reduces SDK and integration surface for the control plane

What should the lifecycle rule actually do?

Start with a restore promise, not a storage tier. For example, keep recent backups in the primary tier for the period needed for routine recovery, transition older backups only after restore tests pass, and expire data only when the retention policy permits deletion. Separate user-uploaded media from backup artifacts; they have different legal, product, and recovery lifetimes.

The rule also needs an owner and an audit trail. Store the policy version with the backup manifest. When retention changes, record the effective date rather than silently rewriting history. A lifecycle engine can delete an object correctly while the application still points at it, so cleanup should be paired with manifest reconciliation and a restore check.

For large uploads, incomplete multipart work deserves attention. The storage options differ in how they expose cleanup, and an abandoned upload can create operational noise even when no completed object exists. Test an interrupted upload, a retry, and a delete request. Those three cases reveal more about the real data path than a successful upload does.

The REST lifecycle capability is a reasonable fit for bucket policy configuration when a one-key workflow is the goal. Its minimum lifecycle interval is one day, and it does not provide an automatic rule for multipart fragments. That rules it out for hour-level expiry or a design that expects unfinished parts to disappear through lifecycle policy alone. The worker still needs explicit multipart cleanup and manifest reconciliation.

Here is the smallest useful control-plane check I would keep beside the worker. The request body is deliberately supplied by the current schema rather than guessed in an article; the route, authentication, retry behavior, and response handling are the parts worth standardizing in application code.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const bucket = process.env.BACKUP_BUCKET;
const lifecycleJson = process.env.LIFECYCLE_JSON;

if (!apiKey || !bucket || !lifecycleJson) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY, BACKUP_BUCKET, and LIFECYCLE_JSON are required");
}

async function setLifecycle(): Promise<unknown> {
  let delayMs = 500;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/bucket/set_lifecycle/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": `lifecycle-${bucket}`,
      },
      body: lifecycleJson,
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      throw new Error(`Lifecycle update failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : delayMs));
    delayMs *= 2;
  }

  throw new Error("Lifecycle update was rate limited after five attempts");
}

await setLifecycle();

That code does not make the gateway responsible for residency or immutability. It makes one narrow operation repeatable, observable, and safe to retry; the bucket policy still needs review by the person responsible for retention.

Review the policy before the first production write.

Where does data live, and who can delete it?

Region is not a label to add at the end of an architecture diagram. Select the write region, backup region, and restore region together. Confirm where the provider processes control-plane requests, where objects reside, and where logs or metadata are retained. The contract and the provider's current regional documentation settle those questions; an API abstraction cannot.

Deletion has a similar split. A normal object delete is useful for application cleanup, but it is not a substitute for object lock or an immutable backup vault. Infrai does not provide object versioning or WORM object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through those controls. A financial or compliance-grade immutability requirement belongs with a specialist storage configuration or an external immutable backup system.

There are other hard edges. The gateway does not offer cross-region automatic replication or a cross-cloud bulk migration tool. It also does not provide an independently configurable CORS route for browser-direct uploads. If your upload design requires self-service CORS rules, cross-region replication, or a contractual residency guarantee, choose the specialist provider that explicitly supplies that feature and verify the terms.

This is the processor boundary: use the control plane to coordinate a storage action, but do not assume it changes the storage provider's residency, retention, deletion, or processor commitments. The storage specialist remains the source of truth for those obligations.

My decision rule for a small team

I would shortlist the provider that passes four tests with the real media distribution:

  1. Direct uploads and multipart retries meet the large-file throughput target without proxying bytes through the app.
  2. Lifecycle transitions and expiration match the written retention schedule, including the minimum interval.
  3. Region, processor, deletion, and egress terms are acceptable to the people who own the data.
  4. A restore drill can rebuild the app's manifest and media set after an overwrite, partial upload, or accidental delete.

Try the REST gateway for the storage control plane if your main problem is integrating bucket operations into a broader backend and you can keep specialist storage responsible for residency, replication, CORS, and immutable retention. The advantage is concrete: one HTTP API and one key replace another client-library integration for this control path. Do not select it as the sole answer for WORM backups, cross-region replication, hour-level lifecycle expiry, or browser uploads that require self-managed CORS. Those are the limitation cases where S3, Azure Blob Storage, or another specialist provider is the better choice.

The cost model should stay visible, but it should not drive the whole decision. Count storage tiers, requests, egress, restore traffic, regional availability, and the engineering work needed to verify deletion. A service that looks inexpensive while every restore crosses a region is not inexpensive for a backup system.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai storage documentation and validate the lifecycle request against the current schema before wiring it into production.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • AWS S3 object lifecycle management
  • Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management
  • Backblaze B2 documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
  • RFC 3986: URI Generic Syntax

title: Go Secure SMS OTP Login Flow Recovery with Rate Limiting and Lockout
description:
A timed-out SMS request creates a recovery problem before it creates a retry problem: the backend cannot safely interpret silence as proof that nothing happened. TL;DR: put per-user, per-IP, and per-device rate limits before OTP delivery, preserve one logical send identity across supported delivery retries, and consume each successful login challenge atomically. Keep country policy, temporary lockouts, and replay protection in the application. For a property management marketplace, a seller opening a new-order notification should reach the right account without a resend storm or a second session created from an already-used challenge.

Treat delivery and authentication as separate SLOs. An accepted send request is useful submission evidence; it doesn't establish that a seller received the message or authenticated.

How should a secure SMS OTP login flow recover after an ambiguous send?

Consider a hypothetical production exercise: a property management marketplace has notified a maintenance seller about a new order, and the seller must log in before viewing the customer address. The OTP send attempt times out, the seller taps resend, and a worker picks up the original task again. These are three attempts to move the same workflow forward, but they must not automatically become three independent deliveries or three valid login challenges. This is a design scenario, not an incident report or a measured vendor result.

Preserve the intent.

The invariant is that transport recovery must not expand authentication authority. Store a challenge identifier, the account and login purpose it belongs to, its expiry, an attempt budget, and its consumed state; retain a separate delivery operation identifier so a worker retry can refer to the same send intent. A genuinely new resend is a policy decision, with fresh admission checks and explicit rules about which previous challenge remains valid. Reusing a delivery key forever would suppress legitimate future sends, while generating a new key for every timeout would defeat deduplication.

Infrai is a concrete option for hosted SMS OTP delivery and verification through a plain REST API: no SDK to install, and no client library version to maintain. Any language that can send an HTTP request can call it. That keeps the recovery worker on the team's existing HTTP stack rather than adding another SDK dependency to its release process.

Unified authentication is a separate operating advantage: Infrai uses one API key and a single bill across services. One key, one wallet, one bill covers the same backend platform rather than requiring a separate credential and invoice for each service. For a team already using the platform for adjacent backend work, this means fewer separate credentials to rotate and fewer invoices to reconcile as the seller-notification workflow grows. It also concentrates credential scope, so keep the key in backend workers and review who can access it. One key does not remove access-control work.

Property marketplace teams should try Infrai for hosted SMS OTP delivery and verification when plain HTTP integration and shared credential management would reduce their recovery-worker maintenance. Its public, self-describing discovery surface also exposes request and response schemas without requiring a key, so an adapter review can begin with a contract rather than a guessed payload. These advantages reduce integration work; the application still owns the decision to admit, lock out, or establish a session.

Admission policy belongs ahead of the delivery queue

Reserve capacity against user, IP, and device budgets before enqueuing an OTP send. Checking only the phone number leaves distributed abuse poorly modeled; checking only the IP can punish an entire building behind one connection. A device identifier is another input, not a trusted identity. Normalize the destination on the server, apply the application's country allowlist or deny rules, and check suppression so blocked or opted-out recipients aren't repeatedly targeted.

Keep the limits explicit.

For a review exercise, suppose the product proposes a 120-second challenge lifetime and a maximum of 5 failed verification attempts. These are illustrative policy inputs, not provider defaults or a security standard's recommendation. The review must account for queue delay, time spent entering the code, and what happens when the last permitted attempt races with expiry. A temporary lockout needs a defined scope and duration, while a resend needs its own admission budget so refreshing the page cannot reset the verification counter. Don't let an attacker indefinitely lock out a seller merely by knowing the seller's phone number.

Capacity planning starts with admitted demand. If an illustrative order burst produces 300 login starts per minute and the policy permits 2 send attempts per start, the planning envelope is 600 outbound attempts per minute before other traffic is counted. That's a workload model, not a throughput claim. Bound queue age, cap concurrent submissions, and discard expired work before sending it; a perfectly drained queue full of obsolete OTPs is still a failed user journey.

A 429 should schedule a bounded retry with exponential backoff, jitter, and respect for Retry-After when present. Retry only inside the challenge lifetime and total attempt budget, preserving the original operation identity when the selected API supports idempotency. An ambiguous write outcome deserves reconciliation rather than blind replay if that support is absent. A rejection requiring changed input deserves a surfaced error and a new decision.

Country admission rules and country-based spending circuit breakers belong in your backend policy. Don't infer either from the presence of a hosted OTP API. For a US/EU SaaS service, those controls also don't establish data residency or legal compliance; assess the relevant processing terms separately before approving deployment. The same distinction applies to automotive service updates: a notice about a job does not confer permission to authenticate as its recipient.

Buy versus build changes the recovery boundary

Compare how much verification state the platform team intends to own, and which evidence will let an on-call engineer distinguish a delayed submission from an exhausted challenge. There is no measured delivery ranking here. Run the same timeout, resend, and concurrent-verification cases against each candidate before committing to an adapter.

Option Buy versus build boundary Recovery trade-off and fit
Infrai Buy hosted SMS OTP delivery and verification through REST; build account admission and session policy. Fits teams avoiding another SDK and consolidating backend credentials. Review the capability contract and plan reconciliation around pull-based events.
Twilio Verify Evaluate a dedicated verification service rather than assembling verification from messaging alone. A specialist candidate when verification is the central buying decision; confirm retry, challenge, and abuse-control behavior against the intended deployment.
Vonage Verify Evaluate another dedicated verification product with its own workflow contract. Useful as an independent specialist comparison; test how its workflow maps to the application's resend and lockout rules before assuming portability.
Amazon SNS Evaluate SMS messaging as transport while retaining the OTP lifecycle in the application. Fits a deliberate build decision. The team owns challenge generation and checking, expiry, replay prevention, and operational recovery.

Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify deserve serious consideration when the buying requirement is a specialist verification workflow. Amazon SNS is the better architectural fit when the team deliberately wants messaging transport and accepts ownership of the authentication machinery. Neither approach removes the need to bind authentication to the correct seller account and purpose. A hosted service should earn its place by reducing the state machine the team operates, while the build option should earn its place through requirements that justify keeping that state machine.

Infrai's event model is pull-based, so an event-driven fallback design needs a reconciliation schedule and a freshness budget. An email OTP fallback requires application-owned verification logic. If voice, WhatsApp, or RCS is a purchasing requirement, compare specialists against that channel requirement before selecting the OTP transport. Those boundaries matter more to recovery design than a broad count of available APIs.

Inspect the retry contract before writing the adapter

The preventative code path starts with contract inspection. This complete Go program fetches the public OTP capability schema, checks the HTTP status, and prints the JSON document for review. Save it as main.go and run it with Go. The request is public and needs no key; the optional environment-supplied bearer header shows how an existing backend credential can be attached without embedding a secret in source.

The program retries only its read request. It doesn't send a message, validate a code, or implement the distributed challenge store. A send adapter must separately use the declared parameters, an environment-supplied bearer key, and a stable Idempotency-Key only where supported. This distinction keeps a runnable example honest without guessing a write payload.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) (time.Duration, error) {
    value = strings.TrimSpace(value)
    if value == "" {
        return fallback, nil
    }
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 64); err == nil {
        if seconds < 0 || seconds > 30 {
            return 0, fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds local wait budget")
        }
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second, nil
    }
    deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("invalid Retry-After: %w", err)
    }
    delay := time.Until(deadline)
    if delay < 0 {
        delay = 0
    }
    if delay > 30*time.Second {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds local wait budget")
    }
    return delay, nil
}

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, (2<<20)+1))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if len(body) > 2<<20 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery response exceeds local size limit")
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            base := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            delay, err := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), base)
            if err != nil {
                return err
            }
            time.Sleep(delay + time.Duration(rand.Intn(250))*time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if !json.Valid(body) {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery response is not valid JSON")
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The read client waits at most 30 seconds per Retry-After value and makes at most 3 attempts; a longer requested wait returns control to the caller instead of retrying early. Those are local example budgets. They are not OTP settings.

Before implementing the write path, inspect the selected capability's idempotency declaration. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention and a default 24-hour deduplication window, but a platform convention is not evidence that every operation supports it. More importantly, delivery deduplication and challenge consumption solve different problems: the first prevents repeated side effects for one send intent, while the second prevents a previously successful code from authorizing another login. Keep the latter in a shared transactional store rather than a worker's memory.

Recovery ends at a consumed challenge

A successful provider verification should trigger a transaction that checks the challenge's account, purpose, expiry, remaining attempt budget, and consumed state before establishing the authorized session outcome. Competing successes must converge on one consumption decision. Persist enough state to recover that decision if the client loses the response; replaying a successful code should not mint another independent session.

Expiry still wins.

For operations, record application-owned challenge and delivery-operation identifiers, queue age, retry count, verification failures, and lockout decisions without logging OTP values or bearer keys. Infrai's native response metadata specifies request_id, vendor, and latency_ms, which can help correlate a submission with the local recovery record; none of those fields proves handset delivery. Define separate objectives for admitted-request completion and successful authentication, and investigate the gap instead of reporting submission acceptance as delivery reliability.

This design does not settle whether SMS is an acceptable authenticator for a particular risk level. Use the NIST authenticator guidance as part of that decision, and choose another authentication method when the threat model requires it. Nor should a new-order notification automatically start a login challenge: send the business notice, then admit the seller's authentication request under its own policy.

Sources

References for the authenticator decision and the buy-versus-build comparison:

  • NIST Digital Identity Guidelines, authenticators
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify documentation
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation

If this recovery boundary fits your system, start with the first-party SMS OTP login design guide.

title: Amazon Aurora serverless for MySQL now supports up to 384 ACUs
description:
Amazon Aurora serverless now supports database capacity of up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition, a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU provides approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory with corresponding CPU and networking, so a single Aurora serverless database can now scale up to 768 GiB of memory. When the workload completes, Aurora serverless automatically scales down to zero. This makes Aurora serverless especially well-suited for agentic AI applications, which typically have bursts of activity, long idle windows, and unpredictable traffic patterns. Aurora serverless handles all of it automatically, scaling capacity with your agents, so you only pay for what you use. 
 
 With 384 ACU support, customers can now use Aurora serverless for even more demanding workloads while continuing to scale down to zero when not in use, paying only for the capacity consumed. For new clusters, select a supported Aurora MySQL engine version and set your maximum capacity up to 384 ACUs. For existing clusters on Platform Version 4, simply modify the cluster to update the maximum capacity setting (and the engine version if needed). There will be no downtime if your database is already on Platform Version 4. For existing clusters on older platform versions, upgrade to Platform Version 4 through a pending maintenance action. 384 ACU support is available for Aurora MySQL versions 3.14 and 8.4.10, running on Platform Version 4. 
 
To learn more, see Aurora serverless capacity in the Amazon Aurora User Guide. For pricing details and Region availability, visit Amazon Aurora Pricing.  To get started, create or modify an Aurora serverless database in the AWS Management Console.

title: SQL GROUP BY and HAVING: Find Your Top Customers and $3,000 Key Accounts in Eight Rows of Orders
description:
Before a quarterly review, someone usually gets asked two questions: who are our top three customers, and which accounts were worth $3,000 or more this quarter? The usual answer is a spreadsheet, a sort, and a lot of adding up by hand.

Both questions are four SQL keywords: GROUP BY, ORDER BY, LIMIT and HAVING. This walkthrough uses a made-up shop, Lakeside Office Supply, with eight orders. You can type all of it into DB Fiddle (free, no account needed, MySQL v9 selected).

Step 1: make the orders table

DB Fiddle has two boxes. The left one, Schema SQL, holds the table. Click inside it and type:

CREATE TABLE orders (
id INT, order_date DATE,
customer VARCHAR(40), amount INT);

Four columns: an id, the order date, the customer and the amount.

Leave a blank line and add the eight orders. Text goes in single quotes, numbers don't. Every row ends with a comma except the last one, which ends with a semicolon so the database knows the statement is finished:

INSERT INTO orders VALUES
(1, '2026-07-02', 'Maple Dental', 1250),
(2, '2026-07-15', 'Cobalt Legal', 860),
(3, '2026-07-28', 'Northside Realty', 2140),
(4, '2026-08-06', 'Cobalt Legal', 2310),
(5, '2026-08-19', 'Harbor Accounting', 640),
(6, '2026-08-27', 'Maple Dental', 980),
(7, '2026-09-09', 'Northside Realty', 1890),
(8, '2026-09-22', 'Cobalt Legal', 1270);

Four customers, eight orders, one quarter (July to September).

Step 2: total each customer with GROUP BY

In the right box, Query SQL, type:

SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer;

Click Run. GROUP BY customer collapses the eight rows into one row per customer, and SUM(amount) adds up that customer's orders. AS revenue names the new column.

You get four rows, but in no useful order.

Step 3: biggest first with ORDER BY

Delete the semicolon at the end of the last line, press Enter, and add:

ORDER BY revenue DESC;

DESC means descending, biggest first. Run it:

customer revenue
Cobalt Legal 4440
Northside Realty 4030
Maple Dental 2230
Harbor Accounting 640

Notice you can sort by revenue, the alias you just created. That works because ORDER BY runs after the totals are calculated.

Step 4: keep the top three with LIMIT

Remove the semicolon again and add one line:

LIMIT 3;

The full query now reads:

SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 3;

Run it: Cobalt Legal, Northside Realty, Maple Dental. That's question one answered.

One thing to watch: LIMIT without ORDER BY gives you three rows, but not necessarily the top three. Always sort first.

Step 5: key accounts with HAVING

Question two is different. It's not "the top N" but "everyone over a threshold". Replace the whole query (Ctrl+A, then type) with:

SELECT customer, COUNT(*) AS orders,
SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 3000
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

COUNT(*) adds the number of orders next to the revenue. Run it:

customer orders revenue
Cobalt Legal 3 4440
Northside Realty 2 4030

Those are the two accounts that get a thank-you call. Change 3000 to any other number and the list updates.

Why HAVING and not WHERE

This is the part that trips up most beginners. It's tempting to write:

-- This does NOT do what you want
SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE amount >= 3000
GROUP BY customer;

WHERE filters single rows before they are added up. No single order in this table is $3,000 or more (the biggest is 2,310), so this returns nothing, even though two customers are clearly over $3,000 in total.

HAVING filters the totals after GROUP BY. "Customers worth $3,000 or more" is a question about totals, so it needs HAVING.

You can use both in the same query. WHERE first narrows which orders count (say, one month), then HAVING filters the totals:

SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-08-01'
GROUP BY customer
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 2000;

The order of the clauses

SQL is strict about the order you write things in:

SELECT  ...
FROM    ...
WHERE   ...   -- filters rows
GROUP BY ...  -- makes one row per group
HAVING  ...   -- filters groups
ORDER BY ...  -- sorts the result
LIMIT   ...   -- keeps the first N

If you get a syntax error on a query that looks right, check this order first.

Same table, new question

The table didn't change between question one and question two. Only the query did. That's the real shift from spreadsheets: at work the orders table already exists, and every new question from your manager is just a new query. GROUP BY works on any column: customer, month, region or salesperson.

Checklist

  • [ ] Every row in INSERT ends with a comma, the last with a semicolon
  • [ ] GROUP BY names the column you want one row per
  • [ ] ORDER BY ... DESC before LIMIT, or the "top three" is random
  • [ ] Thresholds on totals go in HAVING, thresholds on single rows go in WHERE
  • [ ] Clause order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT
  • [ ] One total checked by hand (Cobalt Legal: 860 + 2310 + 1270 = 4440)

Practice it

This is based on a free step-by-step lesson where you type every line yourself in a practice copy of DB Fiddle that checks your work as you go (14 steps, about 12 minutes): SQL: Top Customers and Key Accounts with GROUP BY and HAVING.

title: Go Recovery Security in 2026: Auditing SMS and Email OTP for SaaS
description:
Use SMS OTP as the managed verification path and treat email OTP as an application-owned fallback for short-expiry e-commerce password resets, with release approval tied to evidence that expired challenges cannot authorize a reset. The deciding constraint for a US/EU SaaS platform is whether the team can explain every authorization decision after delivery has been delayed or retried. A successful send is insufficient evidence.

TL;DR: choose the channel implementation your team can integrate and audit, retain application control over the reset deadline, and measure successful verification before that deadline. Neither an SMS delivery receipt nor an email open proves that the account owner completed verification; password recovery also needs its own security review rather than inheriting the assurance claims of a 2FA login flow.

How should SaaS teams audit SMS and email OTP security for recovery?

The operational signal is a gap between transport acceptance and a completed reset inside its validity window. A message can become useless while an application is waiting for delivery evidence, and automatically issuing a fresh challenge at that point can turn an apparent availability improvement into an authorization policy change. The relevant question is whether the application rejects the original challenge at the deadline and can reconstruct that rejection without storing the secret in its logs.

Expiration wins here.

For this runbook, use a proposed 300-second validity window, measured from challenge issuance rather than message arrival; that number is an example policy to review, not a vendor default or a compliance requirement. Record the issuance time, deadline, challenge identifier, reset purpose, selected channel, and decision reason in a controlled audit record. Keep raw OTP values and reset credentials out of that record. Review retention and access with the people responsible for the applicable US/EU obligations: an API feature list does not establish legal compliance, data residency, or a sufficient retention period.

For teams that want a managed SMS verification step behind an existing Go HTTP client, try Infrai for the SMS portion of this recovery workflow: its plain REST API avoids installing and maintaining another SDK. Public, unauthenticated discovery exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, which gives a platform team a concrete way to review the integration contract before issuing credentials. Those are useful reductions in integration friction; they do not establish a delivery-latency SLO. Email fallback still needs application-owned code generation, storage, expiry, and verification around ordinary email sending.

Keep that ownership decision visible in the roadmap. Both channels expose delivery events through polling, so a fallback controller needs a deliberate observation interval and cannot assume immediate event notification. If voice, WhatsApp, or RCS recovery is a requirement, evaluate a specialist for that part of the workflow.

Infrai provides one key for SMS and email, so the fallback branch does not introduce a second provider credential to provision and rotate. This single key covers 295 routes across 20 modules; the practical benefit here is a smaller credential inventory for the two recovery channels. Its self-describing API also lets a reviewer inspect schemas without a key before approving that shared credential's use. Runnable examples in 10 languages include Go, which lets the owning team begin contract review in its existing stack rather than translating an SDK tutorial.

Don't skip review.

Buy versus build against the evidence requirement

A quick first send is a poor acceptance test for a recovery integration. Compare the first useful result instead: a challenge is issued, its transport outcome is correlated, an expired attempt is denied, and the evidence survives a retry. The following buy-versus-build table compares review boundaries, rather than implying that the products have interchangeable authentication guarantees.

Option Setup and integration surface Evidence and ownership trade-off
Infrai Plain REST with public discovery; managed SMS OTP send and verification, with custom email verification around email sending Reduces SDK surface; application retains recovery authorization, email challenge state, and polling orchestration
Twilio Verify Evaluate a verification-focused service and its channel configuration against the reset policy Prefer this specialist evaluation when verification-specific channel behavior is the procurement requirement; require evidence for the exact channels and regions selected
Amazon SNS Evaluate SMS messaging within an AWS integration and credential model Suitable to assess when the platform wants a messaging building block; explicitly assign ownership of the challenge lifecycle instead of treating publication as verification
Resend Evaluate a dedicated email API and sender setup for the email branch Suitable to assess when email delivery is the integration focus; require the application or a separate identity service to own the recovery decision
Amazon SES Evaluate an email-focused service within the AWS credential and sender-management model A reasonable email-branch candidate for an AWS platform; account recovery state and expiry still need an explicit application owner

Twilio Verify, Amazon SNS, and Resend are real alternatives at different layers. Their official documentation belongs in the review, but no latency ranking, regional compliance conclusion, or feature-equivalence claim follows from this comparison. If an existing identity platform already owns account recovery, extending its verified policy may create less on-call work than introducing a second challenge authority. That is the buy-versus-build question to resolve before writing an adapter.

Credential sprawl is also an operating constraint: count production secrets, rotation procedures, sender configurations, and incident owners for the actual combination you would deploy. A shared API credential can reduce integration inventory while increasing the importance of application-side access control. Do not equate fewer SDKs with fewer security responsibilities.

Implement the expiry boundary before connecting transport

Use five controls as the release boundary: an immutable issuance deadline, binding to the intended account and reset purpose, atomic single-use consumption, transport-independent audit evidence, and a fallback policy that preserves the original recovery deadline. These are application requirements. Do not infer their implementation from a provider accepting an SMS request.

Before wiring a send worker, inspect the API contract. This runnable Go program calls the read-only discovery surface, prints its JSON response, and needs only the standard library plus an INFRAI_API_KEY environment variable. Discovery itself is public; using the environment credential here demonstrates the HTTP authentication pattern without sending a reset or recipient data. Review the returned capability schemas before implementing SMS send or verify payloads.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY before running")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if !json.Valid(body) {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned invalid JSON")
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This request is read-only, so retrying it cannot issue duplicate challenges. Production write calls need their documented idempotency contract. Discovery success proves contract access, not delivery or verification success.

Keep authorization separate.

In production, reject the challenge at or after its deadline, check the intended account and purpose, validate the submitted secret through the appropriate verification path, then atomically consume the application challenge while rechecking expiry. A check followed by a separate update leaves room for two concurrent requests to pass. Enforce rate limits and define the behavior of concurrent challenges before exposing the reset flow to customers. A worker that resumes at second 305 of a 300-second window must discard that attempt, and a verifier receiving the correct code at second 300 must reject it; both decisions should have an audit reason that can be correlated to issuance without recording the code itself. These are policy examples to test, not reported production incidents.

The email branch deserves an explicit engineering estimate because the team owns its secret generation, protected storage, expiry, and verification. Sending an email is only one step. For SMS, keep the application's reset authorization separate from the managed OTP verification result so that the reset deadline remains enforceable even when the transport workflow completes later.

Verify the SLO with a capacity budget

Define a proposed journey SLO around eligible reset attempts that complete before their deadline, and report transport acceptance separately. Do not publish an achieved target until production evidence supports it. Segment the evidence by channel and the US/EU populations the service actually serves, while controlling access to recipient data; an aggregate success rate can conceal an unusable branch.

Polling consumes capacity.

For a planning example, 600 pending challenges checked every 10 seconds imply roughly 60 status checks per second if each challenge requires one check per interval, before resends, duplicate workers, or email fallback are counted. This is arithmetic for sizing a controller, not a measured throughput claim or a provider quota. If the queue wait plus observation delay consumes the remaining validity window, stop attempting the old challenge and return an explicit expired result. Never extend the deadline to make the delivery dashboard look healthier.

Verification should cover boundary times, duplicate submission, a worker resuming after expiry, a delayed delivery observation, and an email fallback attempted near the deadline. Require correlated records showing why each attempt was allowed or denied. For the email branch, review domain authentication against DMARC, and review the implications of Mail Privacy Protection before treating open telemetry as useful evidence. Neither source establishes that a particular reset reached its intended user.

Abuse controls belong in the same capacity review. Define business-layer geographic restrictions and country-level spending circuit breakers for SMS, plus per-account and per-origin request limits. Their thresholds should follow the application's threat model and traffic evidence. They are not substitutes for successful verification.

Roll back routing without reopening expired challenges

Release the channel decision behind an application-controlled routing setting, with one owner responsible for the challenge state and another explicitly assigned to transport operations if the responsibilities differ. Preserve request correlation and the original deadline across retries; for writes, use the documented idempotency mechanism and distinguish a transport retry from authorization to issue a new challenge.

If the rollout fails its journey SLO or cannot produce the required evidence, stop routing new attempts to that branch and return to the previously approved recovery path. Keep outstanding challenge state and audit records until the reviewed retention policy permits removal. Rolling back routing must not revive expired or consumed challenges, and stopping a worker must not be treated as recalling a message already in transit.

Approve the integration when the evidence chain is clear and the on-call ownership is affordable. Choose a specialist when its verification workflow or required channels remove more application responsibility than a common HTTP interface would.

References

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation
  • Resend introduction
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • DMARC specification
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection guide

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with the API contract and discovery guidance in the Infrai documentation index.
