title: Piramal Finance Scales Its Internal Agentic AI Assistant With MongoDB
description:
Piramal Finance Limited is a retail-led upper-layer NBFC with a pan-India presence. It offers a diverse portfolio of retail lending products spanning affordable housing loans, loan against property, microfinance, personal loans, insurance solutions, and more, as well as wholesale lending, which provides asset-backed, data-driven financing solutions across real estate and select non-real estate sectors.

As of June 30, 2026, the company has over ₹ 1,00,000 Cr of assets under management; it operates 780 branches and serves over 6 million customers across 26 states.

The company operates a distinctive phygital model combining high-touch engagement with high-tech capabilities, including machine learning models, agentic AI tools, and real-time dashboards. Underpinning this breadth of services is Piramal Finance’s "high-tech, high-touch" strategy. Unlike other financial institutions that rely on off-the-shelf software, Piramal Finance’s team built the company’s entire tech stack in-house.

MongoDB has been core to Piramal Finance’s tech stack since the company’s early days. Today, MongoDB Atlas’ flexible document model—combined with built-in capabilities like MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search—powers over 80% of Piramal Finance’s services, including its loan management system, which was migrated from PostgreSQL.

Building on this solid data foundation, Piramal Finance recently set out to solve its next big challenge: empowering its workforce with generative AI.

Building an internal agentic AI assistant for 18,000+ employees

In 2024, Piramal Finance decided to invest in agentic AI to help improve productivity and job satisfaction for its more than 18,000 employees. The company aimed to empower employees across the company—including those from engineering, operations, HR, and customer service—with AI tools.

Piramal Finance’s team wanted to build an intuitive, enterprise-wide agentic AI assistant that would serve as a one-stop shop for employees, from querying policies and tracking performance metrics to resolving customer issues and interacting with internal systems. The idea was to democratize access to AI and allow even non-technical staff to leverage state-of-the-art AI, without complex prompts or technical training.

Initially, Piramal Finance's team started building an architecture that stitched together several specialized third-party tools:

  • Neo4j, a graph database that stores data as nodes and the relationships between them, managed the dynamic permissions model. Because permissions depended on a user's position in the organizational hierarchy and their associations with other entities—and because those relationships changed in real time—access had to be evaluated at runtime rather than precomputed.

  • pgVector, an open-source extension that adds vector storage and similarity search to PostgreSQL, handled the vector workloads powering AI features.

  • PostgreSQL, an open-source relational database, handled operational data and analytical queries.

However, this setup introduced significant complexity and inefficiencies, and it didn't lend itself to running complex AI workloads at scale.

Piramal Finance’s team saw MongoDB Atlas as the best solution to move away from PostgreSQL’s credential management. Using MongoDB’s built-in authentication and authorization features, Piramal Finance was able to map MongoDB Atlas’s access control directly to its enterprise single sign-on and Active Directory, so employees could log in securely with their standard corporate credentials. Meanwhile,MongoDB Atlas’s built-in role-based access control (RBAC) capabilities automatically restricted sensitive data based on Piramal Finance employees’ job roles.

Piramal Finance soon realized that the power of the MongoDB Atlas platform could solve many of the other challenges that its fragmented database stack presented.

From a fragmented to a unified AI data layer: The power of MongoDB Atlas

As Piramal Finance’s internal agentic AI Assistant's enterprise knowledge base grew, the data architecture became increasingly complex. Although this separation allowed each database to specialize in its workload, it introduced significant operational overhead and complexity, as Piramal Finance explained in a recent conversation at MongoDB .local Mumbai.

Data had to be synchronized across multiple systems through ETL pipelines, resulting in update latencies of over 30 minutes before newly ingested content became searchable.

Figure 1. Piramal Finance’s data architecture before migrating to MongoDB Atlas.

As Piramal Finance explored options to unify its data foundation, it realized that MongoDB Atlas was both inherently built for AI workloads (thanks to its flexible document model), and that it had all the capabilities needed to scale an agentic AI solution on a single platform.

Kaushik Deb, Head of AI engineering, Piramal Finance, said: “An AI agent is only as good as the data behind it. MongoDB gives us one platform for all our data, which makes our AI simpler to build, easier to maintain, and more reliable in production.”

Figure 2. Piramal Finance’s data architecture after migrating to MongoDB Atlas.

During the architecture review, Piramal Finance’s team realized that most of the graph queries involved bounded traversals such as reconstructing document hierarchies, identifying parent-child relationships, and retrieving connected metadata—operations that did not require a dedicated graph database. The data model was redesigned to represent these relationships within MongoDB itself, using the flexibility of MongoDB Atlas’ document model and MongoDB’s aggregation framework capabilities.

The $graphLookup aggregation stage became central to the implementation, enabling recursive traversal of document relationships directly within MongoDB collections. Combined with operators such as $lookup, $facet, $unwind, and $project, Piramal Finance was able to replace Neo4j traversals with efficient aggregation pipelines, all while expressing complex relationship queries entirely within MongoDB.

MongoDB Atlas also allowed the team to consolidate structured metadata, document storage, relationship traversal, and search into a single platform. MongoDB Search handled keyword retrieval, while the aggregation framework combined metadata filtering, graph traversal, and ranking into unified retrieval pipelines, reducing application-side joins and simplifying backend services.

Today, there are 25+ MongoDB MCP servers live, powering Piramal Finance’s agentic AI assistant, which, combined with MongoDB Vector Search, allows for unstructured documents (e.g., 500-page policy PDFs) to be processed through Piramal Finance’s in-house pipeline (.score), chunked, embedded using in-house embedding models, and stored directly in MongoDB Atlas. MongoDB Vector Search delivers 3x faster retrieval performance compared to Piramal Finance’s former Postgres setup.

An incredibly efficient, smart agentic assistant

Since the launch of Piramal Finance’s internal agentic AI assistant, employee performance and productivity across all functions have improved, which has in turn improved customer experience and satisfaction.

Today, over 80% of Piramal Finance's 18,000 employees use the internal agentic AI assistant on a weekly basis, with an average of 15,000 daily queries handled by the platform.

Teams from all across the organization are benefiting from using the agentic AI assistant. HR teams experience a significant reduction in routine internal support tickets regarding benefits, travel policies, and payroll, as new hires and staff turn to the agentic solution for instant answers, supporting agents. Support agents who previously spent extensive time manually combing lengthy and complex policy manuals during live calls are now able to ingest real-time customer data and policy docs into the agentic assistant. This has drastically reduced handle times, improving first-contact resolution and customer satisfaction. Furthermore, sales representatives using the internal agentic AI assistant have seen a 2x improvement in performance compared to non-users during contest periods.

Piramal Finance’s tech team, including developers, are also greatly benefiting from using MongoDB Atlas. Knowledge graph and document updates that previously took up to 30 minutes in legacy setups now execute in just 15 seconds, eliminating operational downtime.  Working with MongoDB and being able to use MongoDB Atlas’ built-in capabilities such as MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search has also made developers’ jobs much easier.

With MongoDB, Piramal Finance has been able to turn what was initially a pretty simple AI assistant into a full agentic solution that orchestrates workflows across the entire organization. MongoDB Atlas has become the single source of truth for the internal agentic AI assistant, providing a simpler architecture and a scalable foundation for semantic retrieval, richer metadata, and future AI-powered knowledge discovery.

Looking to the future, Piramal Finance plans to use MongoDB’s capabilities to further expand its internal agentic AI assistant into a personalized, proactive coach for every employee in the company.

title: Shared-schema multi-tenancy in Spring Boot + Hibernate: the reference code we actually run
description:
Shared-schema multi-tenancy in Spring Boot + Hibernate: the reference code we actually run

Multi-tenancy is one of those architectural decisions that looks deceptively simple until you start implementing it.

You add a tenant_id column, make sure queries are scoped to the current tenant, and assume you're done.

But what happens when a request has no tenant context? What happens when Spring Security hasn't populated the authentication context yet? What about native queries, background jobs, or writes that attempt to associate an entity with another tenant?

We ran into these questions while building our SaaS application, PresenceWave.

Rather than publish another theoretical explanation of multi-tenancy, I wanted to document the implementation we actually use: shared-schema, discriminator-based multi-tenancy with Spring Boot and Hibernate 6.

We've also extracted the relevant implementation into an open-source repository. It contains the tenant resolution filter, Hibernate integration, write-time validation, database schema and integration tests.

This isn't a library you can add to your build.gradle. It's reference code extracted from our production application, intended to be read alongside this article.

We've deliberately kept some of the rough edges and limitations in the implementation. They're often the most useful part of an engineering discussion.

Three kinds of requests

Before getting into the architecture, it helps to understand the different kinds of requests a multi-tenant application needs to handle.

There are three distinct scenarios:

  1. No tenant yet. Login, magic-link validation, health checks and other requests that happen before authentication. There's no tenant to scope the request to.
  2. A tenant from an authenticated session. A logged-in user working within their own tenant. This is the primary use case covered by our reference implementation.
  3. A tenant resolved from the request, without authentication. For example, a visitor accessing a customer's public blog, links page or embedded widget through that customer's custom domain.

Our TenantResolutionFilter handles the first two scenarios.

The third is also part of our production application, and probably accounts for the largest volume of requests. However, that uses host-based tenant resolution, which is product-specific and outside the scope of this repository.

It's also a somewhat different problem. Public pages are supposed to expose certain information across an anonymous request. The interesting security question there is ensuring that anonymous writes, such as form submissions, are still associated with the correct tenant.

That's worth a separate discussion.

The isolation model, and why we picked it

There are three common ways to isolate tenants in a relational database.

Model Isolation Operational cost
Database per tenant Strongest A connection pool and migration run per tenant. Cost grows with tenant count.
Schema per tenant Strong Requires a custom MultiTenantConnectionProvider and migrations per schema.
Shared schema + discriminator column Enforced in the ORM One schema, one migration path. Cheap to add tenants, but isolation depends on queries going through Hibernate.

We use the third approach.

Hibernate 6 supports discriminator-based multi-tenancy natively. We configure:

  • hibernate.multiTenancy=DISCRIMINATOR
  • @TenantId on the discriminator column.
  • A CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver implementation.

Hibernate then automatically appends a tenant predicate to queries against tenant-scoped entities and populates the discriminator column on inserts.

We don't need to add WHERE tenant_id = ? to every repository method or pass tenant identifiers through every service call.

The ORM handles that for us.

The honest trade-off is that the isolation guarantee depends on every relevant code path going through Hibernate.

The implementation and test suite are designed to make that boundary explicit.

Architecture

The complete request lifecycle looks like this:

[INSERT ARCHITECTURE DIAGRAM FROM ORIGINAL ARTICLE HERE]

Four components do most of the work:

  • TenantResolutionFilter runs once per request, after Spring Security, and determines whether the request has a tenant.
  • TenantContextHolder stores that decision using a pair of ThreadLocal variables.
  • CurrentTenantIdentifierResolverImpl connects Hibernate to the tenant context.
  • TenantAwareAspect addresses a gap that Hibernate's read-side filtering doesn't cover: writes.

Let's look at each component.

Resolving the tenant: a filter that runs after security, on purpose

The tenant resolution filter needs to know who is making the request.

For authenticated requests, it reads the authentication information from Spring Security's SecurityContextHolder and looks up the user's tenant membership.

A simplified version of the implementation:

// web/TenantResolutionFilter.java (trimmed)

private void resolveTenant(String path) {
    if (!path.startsWith(TENANT_SCOPED_PATH_PREFIX)) {
        // Not a tenant-scoped endpoint: public request,
        // Hibernate runs in root mode.
        TenantContextHolder.setPublicRequest(true);
        return;
    }

    Authentication auth =
        SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();

    if (auth != null
            && auth.isAuthenticated()
            && auth.getPrincipal() instanceof UserDetails userDetails) {

        TenantUser membership = tenantUserRepository
            .findByUserEmail(userDetails.getUsername())
            .orElseThrow(() ->
                new IllegalStateException(
                    "Authenticated user has no tenant membership"
                )
            );

        TenantContextHolder.setTenant(membership.getTenant());

    } else {
        TenantContextHolder.setTenant(null);
        TenantContextHolder.setPublicRequest(true);
    }
}

Three outcomes come out of this method:

  • A non-tenant-scoped path.
  • An unauthenticated API request.
  • An authenticated API request.

Only the last one gets an actual tenant assigned.

There are two details here that are easy to get wrong.

1. Filter ordering is important.

Spring Boot registers its security filter chain at order -100.

We register our tenant resolution filter at order 1, after security, because it reads Authentication from SecurityContextHolder.

That authentication context doesn't exist until the security filter chain has run.

Interestingly, our production code used to have a comment saying the opposite: "keep before security".

It was wrong, and we corrected it while extracting the repository.

A stale comment pointing in the wrong direction on something this important is exactly the kind of thing worth checking in your own codebase.

2. The initial tenant lookup cannot itself be tenant-filtered.

When findByUserEmail runs, we don't know the tenant yet. That's precisely why we're running the query.

If it were a normal derived query against an entity annotated with @TenantId, Hibernate would append the tenant discriminator predicate using our fail-closed default tenant ID.

It would find nothing.

So we deliberately use a native query:

// tenant/TenantUserRepository.java (trimmed)

@Query(
    value = """
        SELECT tu.*
        FROM tenant_users tu
        JOIN users u ON tu.user_id = u.id
        WHERE u.email = :email
        """,
    nativeQuery = true
)
Optional<TenantUser> findByUserEmail(
    @Param("email") String email
);

Native queries bypass @TenantId entirely.

That's exactly what we need for this bootstrap lookup, but it's also why every other native query in a tenant-aware codebase needs to be reviewed carefully.

Hibernate's safety net only covers JPQL and derived queries.

Teaching Hibernate who's asking

The next component is CurrentTenantIdentifierResolverImpl.

Hibernate calls this resolver to determine the tenant identifier to use for the current operation.

Here's the relevant implementation:

// tenant/CurrentTenantIdentifierResolverImpl.java

public static final Long DEFAULT_TENANT_ID = -1L;
// Can never match a real row. Real IDs start at 1.

@Override
public String resolveCurrentTenantIdentifier() {
    try {
        if (TenantContextHolder.getCurrentTenantId() != null) {
            return TenantContextHolder.getCurrentTenantId();
        }
    } catch (Exception e) {
        return "" + DEFAULT_TENANT_ID;
    }

    return "" + DEFAULT_TENANT_ID;
}

@Override
public boolean isRoot(Object tenantId) {
    Boolean publicRequest =
        TenantContextHolder.getPublicRequest();

    return publicRequest != null && publicRequest;
}

Two decisions carry most of the design.

Fail closed, not fail open.

If a request forgets to set a tenant, it doesn't get access to all tenants' data.

It gets no data because -1 cannot match a real tenant ID.

The failure mode of a bug here is an empty result, not an accidental data leak.

isRoot() is the escape hatch.

When isRoot() returns true, Hibernate stops appending the tenant discriminator predicate.

We use this for public requests and background jobs that legitimately need to access data across tenants.

But we're not going to pretend this is a harmless switch.

It is the single riskiest part of this design because the ORM no longer provides automatic tenant isolation for those operations.

We register the resolver explicitly on the EntityManagerFactory, because we build it manually rather than relying entirely on Spring Boot autoconfiguration.

// config/PrimaryDataSourceConfig.java

return builder
    .dataSource(dataSource)
    .packages("com.example.multitenant")
    .persistenceUnit("primaryPU")
    .properties(Map.of(
        "hibernate.tenant_identifier_resolver",
        tenantIdentifierResolver
    ))
    .build();

Opting an entity in: one extends, two columns

We use a mapped superclass to make entities tenant-aware.

// tenant/TenantAwareEntity.java (trimmed)

@MappedSuperclass
public abstract class TenantAwareEntity {

    @Id
    @Tsid
    protected Long id;

    @ManyToOne
    @JoinColumn(name = "tenant_id")
    protected Tenant tenant;

    @TenantId
    protected String tenantIdFilter;

    @CreationTimestamp
    protected LocalDateTime createdAt;

    @UpdateTimestamp
    protected LocalDateTime updatedAt;
}

Notice that we have two tenant-related fields.

They serve different purposes.

  • tenant is a regular foreign-key relationship. It maintains relational integrity and can be used for joins.
  • tenantIdFilter is the discriminator column Hibernate uses for automatic tenant filtering.

The discriminator field is a String because that's what our resolver returns.

An entity opts into tenancy simply by extending this superclass.

For example:

// example/Project.java

@Entity
public class Project extends TenantAwareEntity {

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String name;
}

The repository doesn't need to know anything about tenants.

// example/ProjectRepository.java

public interface ProjectRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Project, Long> {

    List<Project> findByName(String name);
}

There is no tenant parameter in findByName.

Hibernate adds the discriminator predicate automatically.

That's the appeal of this approach: tenant isolation lives in one base class and one resolver, rather than being repeated across every repository method.

The gap Hibernate doesn't close: writes

@TenantId takes care of populating the discriminator column on inserts.

But it doesn't update or validate the tenant relationship.

Nothing inherently prevents application code from constructing an entity that points to another tenant, perhaps using an ID supplied by a client.

We address this with TenantAwareAspect.

The aspect intercepts save() and saveAll() calls across Spring Data repositories.

Here's the relevant code:

// tenant/TenantAwareAspect.java (trimmed)

@Before(
    "execution(* org.springframework.data.repository.CrudRepository+.save(..)) || "
    + "execution(* org.springframework.data.repository.CrudRepository+.saveAll(..))"
)
public void beforeSave(JoinPoint joinPoint) {

    if (!tenantAwareUtil.hasTenantContext()) {
        return;
    }

    Object entity = joinPoint.getArgs()[0];

    if (entity instanceof TenantAwareEntity tenantAwareEntity) {

        Tenant currentTenant =
            tenantAwareUtil.getCurrentTenant();

        if (tenantAwareEntity.getTenant() == null) {

            // New entity: stamp it from the current context.
            tenantAwareEntity.setTenant(currentTenant);

            tenantAwareEntity.setTenantIdFilter(
                "" + currentTenant.getId()
            );

        } else if (
            !tenantAwareEntity.belongsToTenant(currentTenant.getId())
        ) {

            // Entity points to a different tenant.
            throw new SecurityException(
                "Attempt to save entity with mismatched tenant"
            );
        }
    }
}

The intended behaviour is straightforward:

  • New entity without a tenant: assign the current tenant.
  • Existing entity belonging to another tenant: reject the operation.

We throw an exception rather than silently correcting the tenant relationship.

There is, however, a known limitation in this implementation.

The aspect only inspects joinPoint.getArgs()[0].

For save(entity), that argument is the entity itself.

For saveAll(collection), the first argument is a collection. The instanceof TenantAwareEntity check fails, and the call passes through without validation.

So saveAll() currently bypasses this aspect entirely.

We have deliberately left this limitation documented rather than quietly presenting the implementation as complete.

If your codebase relies on saveAll(), this needs to be fixed before adopting the pattern.

It's also a useful reminder that intercepting a repository method doesn't automatically mean you've handled every shape of its arguments.

Proving it, against a real database

Mocking the repository wouldn't prove much here.

The actual guarantee we're interested in is the SQL Hibernate generates and whether the database results respect tenant boundaries.

Our integration tests use Testcontainers to spin up a real PostgreSQL instance.

A simplified version of the tests:

// TenantIsolationIntegrationTest.java (trimmed)

@Test
void queries_AsAnotherTenant_DoNotSeeTheRows() {

    TenantContextHolder.setTenant(tenantA);

    Project alpha = projectRepository.save(
        Project.builder()
            .name("alpha")
            .build()
    );

    TenantContextHolder.setTenant(tenantB);

    assertThat(projectRepository.findAll()).isEmpty();

    assertThat(
        projectRepository.findById(alpha.getId())
    ).isEmpty();

    assertThat(
        projectRepository.findByName("alpha")
    ).isEmpty();
}

@Test
void queries_WithoutTenantContext_SeeNothing() {

    TenantContextHolder.setTenant(tenantA);

    projectRepository.save(
        Project.builder()
            .name("alpha")
            .build()
    );

    TenantContextHolder.clear();

    assertThat(projectRepository.findAll()).isEmpty();
}

@Test
void save_WithEntityOfAnotherTenant_IsRejected() {

    TenantContextHolder.setTenant(tenantA);

    Project foreign = Project.builder()
        .name("gamma")
        .tenant(tenantB)
        .build();

    assertThatThrownBy(
        () -> projectRepository.save(foreign)
    )
    .isInstanceOf(SecurityException.class)
    .hasMessageContaining("mismatched tenant");
}

These tests verify three different behaviours:

  1. Cross-tenant reads return no results, even when querying by an exact entity ID.
  2. A missing tenant context results in no data being returned.
  3. A write attempting to associate an entity with another tenant is rejected.

There's also a fourth test that deliberately sets publicRequest = true and verifies that it can see all tenants' rows.

That's an important test because root mode is a documented trade-off in this architecture.

A test suite that doesn't verify this behaviour would be hiding one of the most important parts of the design.

What we didn't smooth over

We left the limitations in the README rather than fixing everything before publishing.

These are useful considerations for anyone implementing this architecture.

1. Context doesn't automatically follow work onto other threads.

TenantContextHolder uses TransmittableThreadLocal.

However, that doesn't mean context propagation is automatically configured.

It requires TTL-aware executors or the TTL Java agent, neither of which is wired up in this reference repository.

A plain @Async method or @Scheduled job needs to set the tenant explicitly and clear it in a finally block.

Otherwise, it runs without a tenant context.

2. saveAll() bypasses the aspect.

As explained earlier, our aspect only inspects the first method argument as an entity.

A collection passed to saveAll() isn't inspected.

This needs to be addressed before relying on the aspect for collection writes.

3. Public requests are unfiltered.

When isRoot() returns true, Hibernate doesn't append the discriminator predicate.

There is no softer version of this behaviour.

Isolation for those requests depends on the application handler, not Hibernate.

4. Native queries are outside the safety net.

The initial tenant membership lookup deliberately uses a native query.

That's necessary because we don't know the tenant when performing the lookup.

But every other native query against tenant-scoped data needs to implement its own tenant restrictions.

5. The discriminator column needs an index.

The tenant discriminator should lead its own index.

Otherwise, tenant-scoped queries can end up scanning the table.

Our reference migration, V1__tenancy_core.sql, adds these indexes.

It's easy to overlook this when adding new tenant-aware tables later.

What's not here

This repository is intentionally scoped to the tenancy plumbing.

It doesn't include:

  • Resolving tenants from custom domains.
  • API-token authentication.
  • Tenant invitations and membership management.
  • Product-specific authorization rules.
  • Public visitor handling and anonymous form submissions.

Those are separate concerns from the narrower question of how Hibernate knows which tenant's rows it should return.

Try it, read it, take it apart

We've published the implementation as an open-source reference repository:

GitHub: https://github.com/JulioLabs/spring-boot-multitenant-starter

The README includes a suggested reading order:

  1. TenantContextHolder
  2. CurrentTenantIdentifierResolverImpl
  3. TenantAwareEntity
  4. Configuration
  5. TenantResolutionFilter
  6. TenantAwareAspect
  7. The isolation integration test

The docs/architecture.md file goes deeper into the request lifecycle and the implications of public-request handling.

We built this because we needed it for our own SaaS application, PresenceWave.

If you're evaluating shared-schema discriminator-based tenancy against schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant, hopefully seeing a real implementation — including its limitations — is more useful than another abstract description of the pattern.

I'd particularly welcome feedback from people who have implemented multi-tenancy with Hibernate:

  • Have you encountered other edge cases with @TenantId?
  • How do you handle tenant context propagation across asynchronous execution?
  • How do you enforce tenant consistency on bulk writes?
  • Have you found a better way to handle public or root-mode requests?

The intention here is to share something useful with the Java community and learn from people who have tackled the same problems.

title: I Wrote a Circuit Breaker and a Bitcask-Style WAL Engine for My Face Recognition API (With Real Code)
description:
A few weeks ago I shared what I learned building FaceMark, my facial-recognition attendance system (NestJS + Angular + a Python AI service). This post is the technical deep-dive I promised myself I'd write: the two components I built from scratch instead of pulling in a library, why I built them, and how they actually work.

Everything below is running code from the repo: ZiadtahaM/FaceMark.

Why build these myself?

Two reasons. First, both failure modes bit me in real testing: the AI service hanging froze my entire API, and restarting the Python service lost face embeddings stored as a pickle file that had corrupted once already. Second, I'm a junior developer, and I wanted to understand the patterns, not just import them. Both designs are straight out of Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann) - the circuit breaker from the reliability chapters and the storage engine from Chapter 3's Bitcask model.

Component 1: The circuit breaker (TypeScript, NestJS)

VisionService calls the FastAPI service over HTTP for every face registration and recognition. When FastAPI hangs (TensorFlow is loading, or it just died), each hanging request holds a thread. Enough of them and the whole API is unresponsive - a cascade failure caused by one dependency.

The breaker has three states:

export enum CircuitState {
  CLOSED = 'CLOSED',
  OPEN = 'OPEN',
  HALF_OPEN = 'HALF_OPEN',
}

The execute wrapper does four things: evaluates whether it's time to probe again, fast-fails while OPEN, caps every call with a timeout budget via Promise.race, and records the outcome:

public async execute<T>(action: () => Promise<T>, fallback?: () => Promise<T> | T): Promise<T> {
  this.evaluateState();

  if (this.state === CircuitState.OPEN) {
    this.logger.warn(`[${this.serviceName}] Fast-failing: Circuit is OPEN.`);
    if (fallback) {
      return fallback();
    }
    throw new ServiceUnavailableException(
      `[${this.serviceName}] Service is temporarily unavailable due to upstream instability. Circuit is OPEN.`
    );
  }

  try {
    // Enforce timeout budget capping
    const result = await Promise.race([
      action(),
      new Promise<never>((_, reject) =>
        setTimeout(
          () => reject(new Error(`[${this.serviceName}] Request timed out after ${this.timeoutMs}ms`)),
          this.timeoutMs
        )
      ),
    ]);

    this.onSuccess();
    return result;
  } catch (error) {
    this.onFailure(error);
    if (fallback) {
      return fallback();
    }
    throw error;
  }
}

State transitions are driven by counters, not timers:

private onFailure(error: any): void {
  this.failureCount++;

  if (this.state === CircuitState.HALF_OPEN || this.failureCount >= this.failureThreshold) {
    this.state = CircuitState.OPEN;
    this.lastStateChange = Date.now();
  }
}

Three consecutive failures trip CLOSED to OPEN. OPEN rejects immediately with a 503 for 15 seconds, then a single canary request probes the service in HALF_OPEN. If the canary succeeds, failureCount resets and the circuit closes; if it fails, it re-opens instantly (that's the HALF_OPEN || condition - one failed probe is enough to re-open).

For retries I use exponential backoff with full jitter (the AWS Architecture Blog variant):

/**
 * Exponential backoff with full jitter formula:
 * t = random(0, min(maxBackoffMs, baseMs * 2^attempt))
 */
public static calculateJitterBackoff(attempt: number, baseMs = 500, maxBackoffMs = 8000): number {
  const exponential = Math.min(maxBackoffMs, baseMs * Math.pow(2, attempt));
  return Math.floor(Math.random() * exponential);
}

Full jitter matters because without it, N clients retrying after a failure all wake up at the same computed times and hit the recovering service in synchronized waves. Randomizing across [0, exponential] spreads the load.

What it fixed: with the AI service killed, the API kept serving auth, courses, and attendance normally, and recognition endpoints returned instant 503s instead of hanging for 15+ seconds each. Before the breaker, killing FastAPI took the whole API down within about a minute of real traffic.

Component 2: A Bitcask-style WAL for face embeddings (Python)

Face embeddings (512-dim vectors from DeepFace/FaceNet512) live in the Python service. My first version pickled a dict to disk. It worked until the process died mid-write and I lost every enrolled face.

So I wrote BitcaskWalEngine, a log-structured append-only store. Every record on disk looks like this:

[CRC32: 4B][Timestamp: 8B][Tombstone: 1B][KeyLen: 2B][ValLen: 4B][Key][Value]

# 4 (CRC32) + 8 (Timestamp float) + 1 (Tombstone flag) + 2 (KeyLen) + 4 (ValLen) = 19 bytes
HEADER_FORMAT = "!IdBHI"
HEADER_SIZE = struct.calcsize(HEADER_FORMAT)

The design has four moving parts:

  1. Writes are appends only. A put serializes the embedding, computes a CRC32 over header + key + value, appends the record, fsyncs, then updates the in-memory index. No in-place updates, ever. The last record for a key wins.
  2. An in-memory Keydir maps each key to (offset, size, timestamp) in the log, so reads are one seek, not a scan. A second in-memory cache holds the vectors themselves for fast similarity search.
  3. Crash recovery is a sequential replay. On startup the engine scans the log front to back, verifying the CRC32 of every record. A record that fails its CRC (that's the torn write from a mid-write crash) is counted as corrupt and skipped - everything before it survives: 
def _recover(self):
    """Crash-recovery: Rebuilds Keydir and memory cache by scanning WAL sequentially."""
    self._file.seek(0)
    valid_records = 0
    corrupt_records = 0

    while True:
        offset = self._file.tell()
        header_bytes = self._file.read(self.HEADER_SIZE)
        if not header_bytes or len(header_bytes) < self.HEADER_SIZE:
            break

        crc, ts, tombstone, k_len, v_len = struct.unpack(self.HEADER_FORMAT, header_bytes)
        # ... verify CRC, rebuild keydir and cache
  1. Compaction and tombstones. Deletes write a record with the tombstone flag set rather than removing bytes. A garbage-collection pass eventually rewrites the log keeping only live records, which is how the file stays bounded despite being append-only.

There was also a pragmatic piece I enjoyed: the engine auto-migrates the old pickle file into WAL format on first run, so existing deployments upgraded without a manual step:

if not os.path.exists(self.wal_path) and self.legacy_pickle_path and os.path.exists(self.legacy_pickle_path):
    self._migrate_legacy_pickle()

What it fixed: I've since killed the AI service mid-write on purpose, repeatedly. Every time, recovery comes back with all valid records and a count of the corrupt tail it skipped. The pickle version failed this test the first time.

What I'd tell another junior dev

  • Write the pattern once by hand, then use the library. I now deeply understand what Resilience4j/Polly-style breakers and real LSM-tree storage engines do, because I felt the edge cases myself: the HALF_OPEN re-trip, the torn write, the replay ordering.
  • Design for the failure you already observed. I didn't add a circuit breaker because it sounded enterprise-grade. I added it because my API hung and I could reproduce it.
  • CRCs and fsync are the whole point. A WAL without integrity checks is just a file you append to and hope.

Honest caveat: neither component is production-grade. SQLite would replace my WAL with one dependency, and there are mature breaker libraries for NestJS. But as a learning exercise that also made the system genuinely more robust, I'd do it again.

I'm a junior full-stack developer (Angular, NestJS, TypeScript, Python) based in Alexandria, Egypt, currently open to junior roles and freelance work. If you're hiring, or you spotted something in my code you'd have done differently, I want to hear it:

  • Email: ziad.taha3456@gmail.com
  • GitHub: github.com/ZiadtahaM - full repo: FaceMark

title: AWS Doubled the Timeout for Lambda Event Functions. Are You Still Paying for Speed You No Longer Need?
description:
Introduction

On November 19, 2026, AWS doubled the maximum timeout for on-demand Lambda Event Functions (previously known simply as Lambda Functions) from 15 to 30 minutes (announcement). Anyone would read that and think: great, longer jobs can run on Lambda Functions now. That was my first thought too. Then a second question hit me: if we suddenly have twice the time, are we still paying for speed we no longer need?

Here's what I mean. With Lambda Functions, a function with more resources usually runs faster, but it also costs more. When a job crept toward the 15-minute limit, a common quick fix was to give the function more resources so it finished in time. Now that the limit is 30 minutes, could those functions run on fewer resources and cost less? And more broadly, with this much more room on the timeout, how should we think about sizing our functions from now on?

To find out, I dug into AWS's pricing, its own benchmarks, and recent independent measurements. The answer is more interesting than yes or no: the same change, running a Lambda Function on fewer resources, reduce costs, save nothing, or make it more expensive. It all depends on what your function spends its time doing.

In this post, I'll start by covering three basics of running Lambda Functions (resources, pricing, and the time limit). Then I'll share how I used to handle the old 15-minute limit. After that comes the heart of the matter: where fewer resources save money, where they don't, and where they cost you more. Finally, I'll share a simple test to help you decide whether fewer resources are worth it for your own functions.

The basics: resources, pricing, and the time limit

Let's start with three ideas that make the rest of this post easy to follow, even if you've never worked with Lambda Functions before.

How resources are configured: you set the memory, the CPU follows

Unlike a regular server, a Lambda Function has no CPU setting. Instead, CPU comes with memory: the more memory you give it, the more CPU it gets (memory docs).

Memory CPU you get What it means
Below 1,769 MB A fraction of one vCPU, in proportion to memory Double the memory, double the CPU: work runs about twice as fast
1,769 MB One full vCPU The most a single-threaded function can use
1,769 to 10,240 MB Extra cores, up to 6 vCPUs (AWS News Blog) Only multi-threaded code gets faster; single-threaded code just costs more

That's why giving a function more memory often makes it faster, even when it never uses the extra RAM.

How Lambda Event Functions are priced: you pay for memory × time

Lambda Event Functions are billed by the GB-second: one gigabyte of memory held for one second (pricing).

Think of it like renting a room, priced by size and by the hour. A bigger room costs more per hour, and keeping it longer costs more in total. And you pay for the room you reserved, even if you only use one corner of it.

What you pay for is the product of memory and duration, not either number alone:

Memory Duration GB-seconds (memory × duration) Cost per 1,000 runs (EU Ireland)
1 GB 10 s 10 $0.17
2 GB 5 s 10 $0.17
512 MB 20 s 10 $0.17
4 GB 10 s 40 $0.67

The first three rows mix memory and time differently, but they cost exactly the same. The last one costs four times as much.

How long a function can run: you set the timeout, up to a hard ceiling

Every function also has a timeout: if it's still running when the timeout hits, it gets stopped. Until November 19, 2026, the highest timeout you could set was 15 minutes, and that limit shaped how we all designed our functions.

How I used to beat the 15-minute limit, and what it really cost

Whenever I built a new Lambda Function, I sized it for the job: enough memory for the work, and a timeout with room to spare. But jobs can grow and loads can change: a function that finishes in 4 minutes in its first weeks can creep toward 15 as its workload grows. When one got close to the 15-minute limit, or went past it, I had three kinds of fixes to choose from.

The fixes I had: redesign, optimize, or add memory

  • Structural fixes: rethink whether one Lambda Function should handle the whole job, split the work across several functions orchestrated with a workflow service like AWS Step Functions, or move it to a container-based service with Amazon ECS.
  • Code fixes: make the function itself faster, for example by profiling it, using a more efficient algorithm, running independent calls in parallel, or batching requests.
  • Resource fixes, the quick one: give the function more memory, so it gets more CPU, runs faster, and finishes under the limit.

Structural and code fixes take time to design, build, and test, so the quick fix was often the pragmatic first step. It works in some cases, not in others. Which case you're in depends on what the function is actually doing while the clock runs.

Working vs waiting: when the quick fix pays off, and when it backfires

A function spends its time in one of two states:

  • Working (CPU-bound): the processor is busy, so a faster CPU finishes sooner.
  • Waiting (I/O-bound): it depends on something outside it, like an API call, a database query, or an S3 upload, so a faster CPU barely helps.

Picture a kitchen. A skilled chef chops a mountain of vegetables faster, but doesn't make the delivery truck arrive any sooner.

And here's the key point: Lambda Event Functions bill wall-clock time, not CPU time. In other words, a second spent waiting costs exactly as much as a second spent working.

You can see this clearly in real measurements:

In the top diagram, the function is working, so the extra memory bought time at no extra cost.

In the bottom diagram, it's waiting on a download, so the extra memory bought nothing and multiplied the bill: download speed stayed flat at about 620 Mbps.

So for a job that mostly waits, the quick fix can't help: you need a structural or code fix instead.

Mixed jobs: the quick fix works, but at a price

To make this concrete, let's follow one example through the rest of this post: a nightly report, the kind of job almost every team runs. Every night, a Lambda Function:

  1. Calls external APIs to fetch the day's data. These APIs are slow and rate-limited, so most of this step is waiting.
  2. Processes the data and builds the report. That's working.
  3. Uploads the report to S3. Waiting again.

A single Lambda Function is a common, sensible home for a job like this while it's small.

Now, if you give this function more memory, only the working part gets shorter. The waiting part stays exactly the same:

For jobs that mix working and waiting, extra memory often does the trick, but at a price: the higher rate also applies to every second of waiting. Looking back now, that's the part I keep thinking about. With twice the time available, can those jobs lower their memory and stop paying that price?

The new opportunity: stop paying for speed you no longer need

With 30 minutes available, a job no longer needs extra CPU just to finish in time. That means any memory that wasn't making the function proportionally faster can go. There are two places to look:

  • Time spent waiting, which more memory never speeds up
  • Work that can't make full use of extra cores

Waiting time: stop paying the high rate to wait

Let's start with the main one. For a mixed job, lowering memory lets the working part take longer, while the waiting part stays the same. So the saving comes almost entirely from the waiting part:

GB-s saved per run≈memory removed (GB)×waiting time (s)

Back to the nightly report. Say it has grown to spend 9 minutes waiting on external APIs and needs 9 minutes of processing on one full vCPU (1,769 MB of memory). To keep things simple, I'm assuming the code can spread its work across several cores, so the working time depends on memory. At 4 GB (about 2.3 vCPUs) the processing takes about 3.9 minutes, and at 1 GB (about 0.6 vCPU) it takes about 15.5 minutes. Here's what happens when memory drops from 4 GB to 1 GB:

In numbers, using x86 pricing in EU (Ireland):

Setting Memory Runtime GB-s per run Cost per 1,000 runs
Old: fits under 15 min with headroom 4,096 MB 12.9 min 3,093 $51.55
New: fits under 30 min with headroom 1,024 MB 24.5 min 1,473 $24.55

That's 52% less. The working part costs about 933 GB-s in both cases, so the entire saving comes from the waiting part: 3 GB removed × 540 s = 1,620 GB-s.

Imperfect multi-core scaling: less memory, about 24% cheaper

The second place to look has nothing to do with waiting. Above 1,769 MB, extra memory buys extra cores, and many workloads can't use them all efficiently.

AWS's own PyTorch inference benchmark found that 5 GB cost the same as 1 GB while running 5x faster. At 10 GB, the function ran 7.6x faster but cost more: about $80 versus $61 per million invocations (AWS News Blog).

Now imagine a batch job that needed 10 GB to finish in 13 minutes. With the same ratios, it would take about 20 minutes at 5 GB: only possible under the new limit, and about 24% cheaper. One honest caveat: AWS measured short runs back in 2020, so I'm assuming the same ratio holds for longer jobs.

Not every function qualifies: when there's nothing to save

Of course, lowering memory isn't a free win. If a function is all work and no waiting, there's nothing to save: as the top diagram in “Extra memory buys time for working, but not for waiting” showed, dropping from 1,024 MB to 128 MB just makes the job 8x slower for the same cost. The idea also doesn't apply in these cases:

  • The memory floor. If the job needs the RAM, you can't drop it. And memory needs can vary: a busy night with more data, or a larger input file, may need far more RAM than a typical run. Only lower memory if you're confident about the peak requirement, and check Max Memory Used across your largest runs, not just an average one. Running close to the limit invites garbage-collection slowdowns or out-of-memory errors.
  • The free tier. Inside 400,000 GB-s a month, the saving is exactly $0. One 30-minute run at 1 GB uses 1,800 GB-s, so only about 222 such runs fit. In the nightly report example, 100 runs a month are free either way.
  • Other compute types. Lambda Managed Instances don't bill per-request duration at all, and Web Functions are billed on active CPU time and stay capped at 15 minutes (pricing).
  • Some event sources. Amazon MQ, DocumentDB, and Kafka mappings created before November 19, 2026 (unless in provisioned mode) remain limited to 14 minutes (announcement).

Going lower can backfire: when less memory ends up costing more

This is the part that's easy to miss: lowering memory can make things more expensive, either per run or in ways that never show up as GB-seconds.

A trap behind smaller sizes: the cost curve isn't a straight line

AWS's prime-number benchmark (Operating Lambda, part 2), shown in the top diagram of “Extra memory buys time for working, but not for waiting”, also tested two sizes in between, and both cost more than either end:

Going from 1,024 MB down to 512 MB would have raised the bill by about 9%. Measure, don't assume.

Synchronous callers: your savings, their extra cost

If another Lambda Function calls this one and waits for the answer, the caller is billed too, for every second it waits. So if your function now runs twice as long, the caller's cost doubles as well.

Longer runs: what you pay for outside the bill

Lower memory means longer runs, and longer runs bring costs that never show up as GB-seconds:

  • More concurrent executions
  • Slower stream processing
  • Longer queue timeouts
  • More work lost when a job fails late

AWS covers these in the “Considerations and best practices” section of its 30-minute timeout announcement, which is worth reading before you change anything.

How to tell which kind of function you have

So how do you know which kind of function you have? There's a simple way to get a first idea: halve its memory, run it again, and watch how the runtime reacts:

One rerun only points you in the right direction, though. Before changing anything for real, compare a few memory sizes on realistic inputs, including your biggest ones, keep headroom on both time and memory, and weigh the hidden costs of longer runs covered in “Going lower can backfire.”

Conclusion

The 30-minute limit is more than extra runway. It's a good moment to revisit how we size our Lambda Functions:

  • Memory buys CPU, not shorter waits. Before adding memory, check where the time actually goes.
  • Speed is now a choice, not a constraint. If a function spends much of its time waiting, you can trade a longer run for a smaller bill. If it's all work, there's nothing to trade.
  • Measure before you change anything. The cost curve has bumps, and longer runs bring costs that never show up as GB-seconds.

There's a broader lesson here about provisioning: faster isn't automatically better.

  • If nobody reads the results of a nightly Lambda Function until morning, a function that takes 25 minutes and costs half as much is the better design, even though "slower" sounds wrong.
  • If someone needs the result right away, the faster, pricier setting may be worth every cent.

The rule to remember: you save roughly memory removed × waiting time. Run the quick test before changing anything.

In the end, that's what engineering comes down to. Not the fastest setting, not the cheapest one, but the one that fits your specific need. Understand what your workload actually does, choose for that, and revisit the choice when the rules change, as they just did.

Sources

A quick note on the numbers: the measurements come from AWS and Classmethod, while the nightly report example is a model I built on AWS's published prices.

  • Announcing 30-minute timeout for on-demand AWS Lambda Event Functions, AWS Compute Blog, Nov 19, 2026
  • Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, AWS News Blog (where existing Lambda functions were renamed Event Functions)
  • AWS Lambda pricing
  • Configure Lambda function memory, AWS docs
  • New for AWS Lambda: Functions with up to 10 GB of memory and 6 vCPUs, AWS News Blog, 2020
  • Operating Lambda: Performance optimization, part 2, AWS Compute Blog
  • AWS Lambda scalable network bandwidth, AWS What's New, Aug 2026
  • Raising Lambda's network bandwidth to 3,000 Mbps, measured, Classmethod DevelopersIO, Sep 2026
  • Elastic Cloud Forwarder troubleshooting, Elastic docs

title: Introducing Vercel X
description:
Today we’re launching Vercel X, a six-week accelerator for AI founders at the idea and pre-seed stages.

Join a cohort of 40 teams at our San Francisco HQ and build alongside Vercel’s product leaders, designers, and engineers.

The program takes no equity for participation and offers access to a program-wide pool of more than $9M in credits from Vercel, AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI, and other partners.

Applications are now open through November 29, 2026. The program runs from January 19 to March 2, 2027.

Vercel has worked with more than 100 early-stage teams from around the world across three accelerator cohorts. Alumni include Rex, Alloy Robotics, Interfaze, Cervo, and Hacktron. Interfaze and Rex are backed by Y Combinator, and Cervo was acquired by Altana Technologies.

Why Vercel X?

If you’re applying to Vercel X, you probably have an idea or project you haven’t been able to stop thinking about. The next stretch is figuring out exactly what you’re building and who it’s for.

We think you get through that stretch the Vercel way: by deeply understanding your customers, shipping quickly, and iterating to greatness.

The program includes:

  • Technical mentorship: Hands-on workshops and product feedback from Vercel’s design, product, and engineering teams.

  • Partner credits: Put credits toward hosting, compute, and model API usage as you build and test your product.

  • Founder community: A cohort of AI founders at the same stage, with weekly fireside chats featuring industry leaders.

  • Investor access: Mentorship from VC partners and the opportunity to present your company to investors, ecosystem partners, and the Vercel community at Demo Day.

Winning teams receive funding from Vercel Ventures and prizes from program partners.

Who should apply

We’re looking for technical builders with ambitious ideas and insatiable curiosity.

You don’t need a finished product or traction. Tell us what you want to build, who needs it, what AI makes possible, and why you’re the right person or team for the job.

Solo founders and teams of up to three can apply from around the world. You must be a Vercel customer and must not have participated in a traditional VC accelerator or raised an institutional seed round. See the additional eligibility requirements below.

All participants must spend the full six weeks in San Francisco and attend weekly events in person.

Apply to Vercel X

Applications close at 11:59 p.m. PT on Sunday, November 29, 2026. Decisions will be released in mid-December.

Apply to Vercel X →

Applicants must be Vercel customers at or above the age of majority in their jurisdiction, able to commit to the full six weeks in person, and not located in or otherwise subject to restrictions imposed by U.S. sanctions laws.

Vercel X program applications will be judged on the quality of the submission, the founder's background, and the overall potential for impact.

title: The Subset Font That Turned My Arabic Text Into Empty Boxes
description:
I was rendering product images for my shop: Arabic text, the brand name "STYLE POINT", and prices. Some words came out fine. Others came out as empty boxes. No error, no warning — just tofu where letters should be.

It took me a while to realize the bug wasn't in my code at all. It was in the font file.

The symptom: some words render, some don't

The broken words had something in common, but it wasn't obvious at first. "STYLE POINT" showed as boxes. Prices (digits) showed as boxes. The Arabic word "تشكيلة" showed as boxes — while other Arabic words rendered perfectly.

Three different kinds of text, all broken. That pattern was the clue: the problem wasn't the text, the layout, or the rendering library. It was the font itself.

The cause: a subset font

The font I was using, Cairo-Bold in .woff2 format, was a subset. A subset font is a font file with most glyphs stripped out to make it smaller — it only contains the characters the person who built it thought you'd need.

This one was missing:

  • Latin capital letters (so "STYLE POINT" became boxes)
  • Digits (so prices became boxes)
  • The Arabic letter ة in its final form (U+FE93) — so words like "تشكيلة" broke, even though other Arabic words were fine

That last one is the cruelest kind of font bug: it doesn't break all Arabic, just the words that happen to end in ة. Everything looks fine until exactly the wrong word shows up.

The fix: build one full font, and let the shaper do its job

I fixed it in two steps.

First, I built a complete font. Using fontTools, I merged the full Arabic and Latin versions of Cairo Bold (weight 700) into a single file, Cairo-Bold-full.ttf. One font file, every glyph I need, no more guessing which characters survived the subsetting.

Second, I stopped reshaping Arabic text by hand. I had been using a reshaping library to connect Arabic letters before drawing. I switched to letting Pillow do it natively, with proper shaping support (raqm/harfbuzz) and right-to-left direction:

from PIL import ImageFont, ImageDraw

font = ImageFont.truetype("Cairo-Bold-full.ttf", 84)
draw.text((x, y), "تشكيلة STYLE POINT 250",
          font=font, fill="white",
          direction="rtl", language="ar")

With the full font and native shaping, everything renders: Arabic, Latin capitals, digits, mixed text on the same line.

The lesson I now apply everywhere

Two rules I never break anymore:

  1. Never trust a font you didn't verify. A font file that works for your test words can still be missing the exact glyphs your real content needs. Check the full font, not the demo.
  2. Never rely on local() for Arabic fonts. In my YouTube pipeline I had the same class of bug: the system font wasn't guaranteed to exist. Now I always bundle a real Arabic .woff2 with @font-face (Cairo Bold for titles) — the font ships with the project, or it doesn't ship at all.

The bug looked like a rendering problem. It was a supply-chain problem: the asset I depended on was incomplete, and nothing told me so. The empty boxes were the only warning I got — and honestly, I was lucky to get even that.

I'm Wahib El Khadiri, a junior full-stack developer from Kénitra, Morocco. I build with React, Node.js and Laravel, contribute to open source, and teach React in Darija on YouTube. Portfolio: https://wahib-portfolio.netlify.app — GitHub: https://github.com/WAHIB-EL-KHADIRI

title: November 18, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Feature

Model routers can route to Google API endpoints on different hosts

A model router can now reference Google API backends on different hosts, for example the global aiplatform.googleapis.com endpoint and a regional endpoint such as us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com, and in different projects. Previously, every backend referenced by a router had to share one hostname.

Every backend referenced by a router must use https. Creating an API config with a router that uses http for any of its backends now fails; existing deployed gateways aren't affected.

For more information, see Configure model routing.

Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.53.01.03.

For the list of updated RPM packages and the patch update procedure, see 4.53.01.03 - Edge for Private Cloud release notes.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud, including security hardening across Edge runtime, management, New Edge UI, and Apigee mTLS components.

Changed the bcfks-cacerts file shipped with edge-gateway to an empty BCFKS store, and Apigee mTLS now rejects SHA-1-signed custom certificates. Before you update, move to your own BCFKS keystore and truststore at a different path on FIPS-enabled systems that use the default store, and re-sign custom mTLS certificates with SHA-256. See the update procedure.

Fixed

Resolved the following issues in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.53.01.03:

  • Fixed an issue where API proxy deployments that use the OASValidation policy failed with OpenAPI Specification path parameter validation errors after updating to 4.53.01.
  • Fixed an issue where running setup.sh -p uapim failed during edge-uapim-connector setup.
  • Added sanitization to certain error messages generated by Message Processors.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.4

On November 18, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.4.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.17.4.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

Support for Kubernetes pod topology spread constraints

In this release, you can configure Kubernetes pod topology spread constraints for Apigee hybrid runtime components (apigeeIngressGateway, connectAgent, ingressGateways, istiod, mart, mcpServer, redis, redis.envoy, runtime, synchronizer, and watcher) to distribute pods across availability zones and nodes (maxSkew: 1). You can enable and customize these constraints globally using the topologySpreadConstraints property or override them for individual runtime components using <component>.topologySpreadConstraints in your overrides.yaml file.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
586658318 Security fix for Apigee. Mitigates CVE-2026-114938 in the Apigee runtime, including customer-supplied Java code run by the JavaCallout policy. Customers don't need to change their callouts.
579213551 Fixed Message Processor memory leaks during proxy deployment, environment reload, and environment deletion: compiled OASValidation specifications are now shared by content hash, resources and debug session managers from superseded or failed environment loads are released, and HealthMonitorServiceImpl registrations are properly removed when unregistering health monitors.
576697209 Fixed an issue where the LLMTokenQuota policy counted tokens for responses served from the semantic cache by the SemanticCacheLookup policy; cached responses now count as zero tokens and do not record ai_llm_response_token_count in analytics.
572875915 Fixed an issue where the apigee-env Helm chart and Apigee operator ignored the synchronizer pollInterval configuration (synchronizer.pollInterval, envs[].pollInterval, and envs[].components.synchronizer.pollInterval); configured values now take effect, and values below 60 seconds are raised to 60.
567551009 Added support for mutual TLS (mTLS) per environment group between the Apigee hybrid MCP data plane and apigee-ingressgateway using the virtualhosts[].mcpMtls configuration in the apigee-virtualhost Helm chart.

  • Google Chat

Feature

Gemini 4 Neon (GA)

Gemini 4 Neon is a Google Frontier Model subject to Section 34 of the Service Specific Terms (for details, see Abuse monitoring) and delivers high-performance coding, multi-step reasoning, and multimodal understanding at low latency for agentic enterprise workflows:

  • Unified 1,048,576-token limit and long decodes: Supports a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit, where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response. Single foreground segments generate up to 65,536 output tokens for streaming and non-streaming requests. Long decodes (continuation_token) extend output up to 1,048,576 tokens (minus input tokens) on the Interactions API and GenerateContent (v1beta1). The Interactions API also supports asynchronous server-managed background execution (background=true).

  • Thinking levels (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and XHIGH): Supports four thinking levels, with HIGH as the default and XHIGH for deep reasoning workloads. Setting thinking_budget or thinking_level="MINIMAL" returns an HTTP 400 validation error.

  • Implicit context caching with durable caching: Supports automatic implicit context caching with durable caching enabled by default for shared prompt prefixes of 4,096 tokens or more (explicit context caching isn't supported).

  • Cache write control and pricing: Starting on January 12, 2027, Gemini 4 Hydrogen and later models support cache control features with TTL configuration. You choose what to cache and how long cached content stays valid through TTL configuration. Cache writes are billed at 1.25x the standard input token price by default, and longer retention costs more. For details, see Gemini 4 pricing.

  • Office and OpenDocument file inputs: Supports Microsoft Office (.docx, .dotx, .doc, .pptx, .ppt, .xlsx, .xls) and OpenDocument (.odt, .odp, .ods) files inline or from Cloud Storage (gs://), including inside multimodal FunctionResponse parts.

  • Capabilities, consumption options, and endpoints: Available on the global endpoint and in the us and eu multi-regions across GenerateContent, the Interactions API, and the OpenAI compatibility Chat Completions API. Supports function calling, code execution, computer use, URL context, and Agentic video understanding. Grounding options include Grounding with Google Search, Google Maps, Web Grounding for Enterprise, and Parallel and Exa Web Search. Consumption options include Standard PayGo with Usage Tiers, Priority PayGo, Off-peak PayGo, batch inference, and Provisioned Throughput.

For model specifications, code examples, and migration guidance from Gemini 3 models, see Gemini 4 Neon, the developer's guide to Gemini 4 Neon, and Get started with Gemini 4.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Issue

In GKE versions 1.35, 1.36, and 1.37, enabling application-layer secrets encryption on a new or existing cluster whose control plane stores cluster state in Spanner encrypts only Kubernetes Secrets (ENCRYPTED) instead of all Kubernetes API objects (ALL_OBJECTS_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED).

  • Clusters that already have encryption of all Kubernetes API objects enabled (ALL_OBJECTS_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED) continue to encrypt all objects.
  • Clusters where application-layer secrets encryption is in the ENCRYPTED state encrypt only Secrets and require manual Secret re-encryption after a Cloud KMS key rotation. To check which objects are encrypted in your cluster, see Verify that application-layer secrets encryption is enabled.

A fix to restore encryption of all Kubernetes API objects for newly configured clusters is in progress.

Feature

GKE Granular NAT is now available in Preview for Autopilot and Standard clusters running GKE version 1.37.1-gke.2611000 or later with GKE Dataplane V2 enabled.

You can use GKE Granular NAT to control outbound traffic and assign dedicated egress source IP addresses at the Kubernetes namespace level using the CloudNATGateway and TrafficSelector custom resources. Instead of applying a single NAT policy to an entire cluster, you can route egress traffic from specific namespaces through dedicated external IP addresses for Public NAT or dedicated subnet IP address ranges for Private NAT, without managing custom proxy instances.

For more information, see About GKE Granular NAT and Configure GKE Granular NAT.

Feature

QueryData generates Graph Query Language (GQL) queries from natural language questions about your Spanner Graph property graphs. Your AI agent and LLM applications can explore connected data without writing GQL. Specify graph_ids in your request to generate GQL, and use optional context sets to improve accuracy.

This feature is available in Preview. For more information, see QueryData overview.

title: How We Built Hover-to-Preview YouTube Cards in Vue & TypeScript
description:
Video results on Recipe Finder are cards with a thumbnail, a title and a view count. Hovering a card for a moment mounts a muted YouTube player under the thumbnail, so you can see the dish being prepared before you decide to open it. Moving the pointer away removes the preview.

Clicking the card opens the video on YouTube in a new tab.

Three requirements shaped the design. The preview must never start by accident. It must not load a third-party frame until someone actually wants it. And it must respect visitors who have asked for less motion. Each requirement maps to a part of the code below.

The pieces

The feature is split into small parts, each doing one job:

Piece Job
RecipeVideoCard.vue The card. Forwards pointer events, shows the loading bar and the play icon, and opens the video on click.
RecipeVideoPreview.vue The layer over the thumbnail: the cropped frame, the mute button and the progress bar.
useVideoPreview.ts The state machine: the dwell timer, the embed address, the messages from the player and the cleanup.
utils/videoPreview.ts Pure helpers: build the embed address, read a player message, compute the progress.
constants/videoPreview.ts Every delay, origin and player setting, in one file.
shared/AppCardLoadingBar.vue The thin bar along the top edge that shows a preview is on its way.

1. Start only when someone is resting on the card

A pointer that crosses a card on its way somewhere else should not start a video. The preview therefore waits 400 ms after the pointer enters (DWELL_DELAY_MS). If the pointer leaves during that wait, the timer is cleared and nothing loads.

Before the timer is even set, the code checks whether a preview is allowed at all. Only a device with a real pointer can rest on a card, so phones and tablets never get one. Visitors who prefer reduced motion never get one either.

function canPreview(): boolean {
  const videoId = getVideoId();

  return (
    isEnabled() &&
    !isNilOrEmpty(videoId) &&
    !unavailableVideoIds.has(videoId) &&
    window.matchMedia(VIDEO_PREVIEW.HOVER_MEDIA_QUERY).matches &&
    !hasReducedMotionPreference()
  );
}

function onPointerEnter() {
  const isPreviewStarted =
    dwellTimer !== undefined || !isNilOrEmpty(embedUrl.value);

  if (isPreviewStarted || !canPreview()) {
    return;
  }

  isPreviewLoading.value = true;
  dwellTimer = setTimeout(startPreview, VIDEO_PREVIEW.DWELL_DELAY_MS);
}

HOVER_MEDIA_QUERY is (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine). A video that could not play once, because its owner blocks embedding or because it has been removed, is remembered in a set for the rest of the visit. That card keeps its thumbnail and does not try again.

2. An embed built from one list of settings

The preview is a YouTube embed on youtube-nocookie.com, the privacy-enhanced domain. Its address comes from a single list of player settings: muted and autoplaying, with every control switched off, no keyboard shortcuts, no fullscreen, no annotations, and related videos limited to the same channel (rel=0). Two settings matter for the code that follows. enablejsapi=1 lets the page drive the player, and origin names the only page the player should answer to.

export function buildVideoPreviewUrl(
  videoId: string,
  pageOrigin: string
): string {
  const params = new URLSearchParams({
    ...VIDEO_PREVIEW_PLAYER_PARAMS,
    origin: pageOrigin,
  });

  return `${VIDEO_PREVIEW.ORIGIN}${VIDEO_PREVIEW.EMBED_PATH}${encodeURIComponent(videoId)}?${params.toString()}`;
}

The frame is created only when the dwell timer fires, so a card that is never rested on costs nothing. YouTube also refuses an embed that arrives without a referrer, which is why the frame sends strict-origin-when-cross-origin.

3. Talking to the player with postMessage

The player understands a message protocol. The page posts JSON strings to the frame, and the player posts JSON back. Three rules govern the conversation.

The handshake. The player answers only once it has started. So when the frame loads, the page sends a listening message every 250 ms until the player replies. Only then does it subscribe to state changes and errors.

function onFrameLoad(event: Event) {
  const frame = event.target;
  if (!(frame instanceof HTMLIFrameElement) || !frame.contentWindow) {
    return;
  }

  playerWindow = frame.contentWindow;
  stopHandshake();
  handshakeTimer = setInterval(
    () => sendToPlayer(VIDEO_PREVIEW_PLAYER_EVENTS.LISTENING),
    VIDEO_PREVIEW.HANDSHAKE_INTERVAL_MS
  );
}

Every incoming message is checked. The origin must be the youtube-nocookie domain, and the source must be the window of our own frame. Anything else on the page is ignored.

function handleMessage(event: MessageEvent) {
  if (
    event.origin !== VIDEO_PREVIEW.ORIGIN ||
    event.source !== playerWindow
  ) {
    return;
  }

  const message = parseVideoPreviewMessage(event.data);
  // ...
}

The player reports what changed. Each message carries only the fields that changed: currentTime, duration or playerState. Playing, paused and ended are handled as states, and an error marks the video as unavailable.

4. Hiding the player's own title and buttons

For the first three seconds of every video, the player shows its own title, its links and a pause button, and then fades them out. The API has no switch to turn that off, and we cannot change the player. So we crop it instead, and keep the card's overlay up for 3.4 seconds to cover the fade.

The frame is sized like object-fit: cover for 16:9 video, and it is 160 px taller than the video at the top and at the bottom. The player's title and links therefore fall outside the visible area. The sizing uses container query units, so it follows the card at every width.

<div class="absolute inset-0 overflow-hidden [container-type:size]">
  <iframe
    class="absolute top-1/2 left-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 -translate-y-1/2
           w-[max(100cqw,177.78cqh)]
           h-[calc(max(56.25cqw,100cqh)_+_320px)] max-w-none border-0"
  />
</div>

The pause button still sits under the card's play icon for those first seconds. While the preview plays, a black disc sits behind the icon, so it covers the player's pause button. When the overlay timer ends, the icon fades out.

isPlayerOverlayShown.value = true;
overlayTimer = setTimeout(() => {
  isPlayerOverlayShown.value = false;
}, VIDEO_PREVIEW.PLAYER_OVERLAY_MS);

5. Sound that behaves like YouTube

The mute choice is one module-level value shared by every card. Unmute one preview and the next one plays with sound too, for the rest of the visit, as on YouTube.

Browsers block sound until the visitor has interacted with the page. When the player reports that it paused while we had asked for sound, the preview switches to muted and plays again, so it never sits frozen.

if (state === VIDEO_PREVIEW_PLAYER_STATES.PAUSED && !isMuted.value) {
  // The browser refused to play with sound, so the preview carries on muted.
  isMuted.value = true;
  sendCommand(VIDEO_PREVIEW_PLAYER_COMMANDS.MUTE);
  sendCommand(VIDEO_PREVIEW_PLAYER_COMMANDS.PLAY);
  return;
}

A small mute button sits at the top right of the preview. Its click stops propagation, so it does not open the video behind it.

6. Progress, countdown and a loading signal

Three small signals show the visitor what is happening. As soon as the pointer enters, a primary-coloured indeterminate bar runs along the card's top edge. While the preview plays, the duration badge counts down the seconds that remain, and a 3 px bar along the bottom of the preview fills.

The progress calculation is a pure function. It clamps the result between 0 and 100, and it returns 0 while the length of the video is still unknown.

export function getVideoPreviewProgress(
  currentTime: number,
  duration: number
): number {
  if (duration <= 0) {
    return 0;
  }

  return Math.min(Math.max((currentTime / duration) * 100, 0), 100);
}

7. Cleanup, failures and the click

A preview must never outlive its reason to exist. One function, stopPreview, clears both timers and the handshake, removes the message listener and resets every piece of state. It runs in four places: when the pointer leaves, when the component unmounts, when the card now shows a different video, and when the visitor clicks the card, because the video then opens in its own tab.

// Lifecycle Hooks
onScopeDispose(stopPreview);

// Watchers
watch(getVideoId, stopPreview);

If the player reports an error, the video is added to the unavailable set, and that card keeps its thumbnail for the rest of the visit.

What we learned

  • Wait before you start. A 400 ms dwell separates a deliberate pause from a pointer passing over.
  • Check who is asking. The pointer type, reduced motion, the message origin and the message source each decide something.
  • Create the frame only when it is needed. Nothing loads until the dwell has passed.
  • Crop what you cannot configure. The player's title and pause button sit outside the visible area.
  • Remember failures for the visit. A video that cannot play keeps its thumbnail, and the page does not retry it.
  • Keep the numbers in one file. Every delay and setting lives in constants/videoPreview.ts, so tuning the feel means editing one place.

Try it

Open recipe-finder.org, search for a dish, switch to the cooking videos and rest your pointer on a card for a moment. On a phone there is no preview, so tap the card to open the video on YouTube.
