title: How to Estimate Kubernetes CPU and Memory Requirements with a Free Online Calculator
description:
One thing I've noticed when working with Kubernetes is that deploying an application is only part of the job.

You also need to think about resources.

How much CPU does your container need? How much memory should you allocate? What happens when you increase the number of replicas?

These questions matter whether you're running a small development cluster or managing workloads in a larger environment.

Getting resource requests and limits wrong can lead to scheduling difficulties, unnecessary resource allocation, or containers running out of memory.

Let's look at why Kubernetes resource calculations matter and how an online calculator can make the process easier.

Understanding Kubernetes CPU and Memory

Kubernetes allows you to define resource requests and limits for containers.

  • CPU requests help Kubernetes decide which node can accommodate a workload.
  • CPU limits restrict how much CPU a container can consume.
  • Memory requests help Kubernetes schedule workloads based on memory requirements.
  • Memory limits define the maximum memory a container can use.

CPU is commonly measured in millicores:

CPU value Equivalent
100m 0.1 CPU
250m 0.25 CPU
500m 0.5 CPU
1000m 1 CPU

Memory is commonly represented using Mi and Gi:

Memory value Equivalent
128Mi 128 mebibytes
256Mi 256 mebibytes
512Mi 512 mebibytes
1Gi 1024Mi

Understanding these values makes it easier to estimate the resources required by your applications.

Why Calculate Resources Before Deployment?

Imagine you're deploying an application with four replicas.

Each replica requests:

  • 250m CPU
  • 512Mi memory

Your total requested resources would be:

CPU: 250m × 4 = 1000m (1 CPU core)

Memory: 512Mi × 4 = 2048Mi (2Gi)

This is a straightforward calculation, but when applications have multiple containers, different workloads, and varying replica counts, resource planning becomes more involved.

That's why having a convenient calculator can save time.

Try the Free Online Kubernetes Resource Calculator

If you work with Kubernetes, you can use the Free Online Kubernetes Resource Calculator from DevUtilityKits to help with resource calculations.

It's a handy online utility to explore when estimating CPU and memory requirements for Kubernetes workloads.

Instead of doing every calculation manually, you can use a dedicated tool as part of your planning workflow.

Tool link: Kubernetes Resource Calculator – DevUtilityKits

Practical Situations Where It Helps

Here are a few examples where Kubernetes resource calculations are useful:

  1. New deployments: Estimate the CPU and memory needed before deploying an application.
  2. Scaling applications: Understand how increasing replicas affects total resource requirements.
  3. Cluster planning: Compare planned workload requests against available cluster capacity.
  4. Learning Kubernetes: Get more comfortable working with CPU and memory units.
  5. Resource reviews: Revisit allocation figures when application requirements change.

One important point: calculated totals are estimates, not a guarantee that a workload will fit on a particular node. Kubernetes scheduling also considers available capacity, existing workloads, system reservations, and other constraints.

For production environments, review actual application usage and monitor workloads before finalizing resource requests and limits.

Explore More Cloud and DevOps Utilities

Resource planning is just one part of a developer's daily workflow.

Docker, Git, Linux, networking, CI/CD, and infrastructure configuration all involve repetitive technical tasks.

DevUtilityKits provides a collection of free online developer utilities for these areas.

Take a look at the Cloud and DevOps Tools collection to discover more useful tools.

Final Thoughts

Kubernetes resource planning doesn't have to be complicated, but it shouldn't be overlooked.

Understanding CPU requests, memory requests, limits, and replica counts helps you make more informed deployment decisions.

If you're working with Kubernetes, give the Free Online Kubernetes Resource Calculator a try.

How do you usually estimate CPU and memory requirements for your Kubernetes workloads — manual calculations, monitoring data, or dedicated tools?

title: How to test email invitations end to end
description:
Every app with teams has someone inviting someone else. The invitation is the person's first contact with the product, and it goes through three places: the inviter's screen, an inbox and the invited person's browser. That's why it usually goes untested, and breaks without anyone noticing: the email doesn't go out, the link lands on the wrong page, or the person joins a team that isn't theirs.

With a real inbox your test can read, the whole flow becomes an ordinary test. This guide uses Playwright and the saci.cc npm package, but the ideas apply to any tool.

What's worth testing

Seeing the email arrive isn't enough. A good invitation test checks that:

  • The invite reaches the address that was typed, saying who invited them and to which team. Nobody clicks an email from a sender they don't know.
  • The link opens the accept page with the email already filled in, and the account created there joins the right team with the right role.
  • The link works only once.
  • Resending or canceling an invite turns off the old link.
  • An invite for one address can't be used by an account with another address. This is the one that becomes a security hole: a forwarded or leaked link must not let a stranger into the team.

Set up the key and the inboxes

Create a free key on your account page, put it in SACI_API_KEY and install the client:

npm install --save-dev saci.cc

Each invited person is a new inbox, made with createInbox(). That way each inbox gets a single invite, and tests running in parallel don't get in each other's way. Inboxes created with your key are private, which matters here: an invite link gives access to a team.

The inviter is already signed in. In Playwright, that's usually a storageState saved by a setup project, so the test's page is already the team owner's account.

The full test

First, a function that sends the invite through your app's screen and returns the email. It notes the time before clicking, to skip emails that were already in the inbox:

import { test, expect, type Page } from "@playwright/test";
import { createInbox, type Inbox } from "saci.cc";

async function invite(page: Page, inbox: Inbox) {
  const invitedAt = new Date();
  await page.goto("/settings/team");
  await page.getByLabel("Email").fill(inbox.address);
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Invite" }).click();
  return inbox.waitForEmail({ subject: "invited you", after: invitedAt });
}

The test invites a new address, checks the email, opens the link in a browser with no session and creates the account:

test("an invited person joins the team", async ({ page, browser }) => {
  test.setTimeout(90_000);
  const inbox = await createInbox();

  const email = await invite(page, inbox);
  expect(email.text).toContain("Ana Souza"); // who invited
  expect(email.text).toContain("Acme"); // the team
  const link = email.links.find((url) => url.includes("/invite/"));
  expect(link).toMatch(/^https:/);

  // Someone else, in another browser, signed out
  const guest = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();
  await guest.goto(link!);
  await expect(guest.getByLabel("Email")).toHaveValue(inbox.address);
  await guest.getByLabel("Password").fill("invited-password-123");
  await guest.getByRole("button", { name: "Join Acme" }).click();
  await expect(guest.getByRole("heading", { name: "Acme" })).toBeVisible();

  // The inviter sees them on the team
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByRole("row", { name: inbox.address })).toContainText("Member");
});

browser.newContext() is what makes the test count: without it, the link would open with the inviter's session, and the test would pass even with accepting broken.

Pick the link by its path

saci.cc finds the link to confirm an address, sign in or reset a password on its own, and returns it in the verificationLink field. A button like "Accept invitation" or "Join the team" is none of those, so don't count on that field for invites. Pick the link by its path, as in the test above, or with waitForLink inside invite():

const link = await inbox.waitForLink({ match: "/invite/", after: invitedAt });

Invitation emails usually have other links, like the logo, the privacy policy and "I don't know this person". Without match, waitForLink returns the verificationLink or, without one, the first link in the email, which is rarely the invite.

The link works only once

At the end of the previous test, open the same link in a new session. The app should refuse it:

const again = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();
await again.goto(link!);
await expect(again.getByText("This invite was already used")).toBeVisible();

Resending and canceling

When an invite is resent, the old link should stop working. Otherwise each resend leaves one more valid link out there:

const first = (await invite(page, inbox)).links.find((url) => url.includes("/invite/"))!;

const resentAt = new Date();
await page.getByRole("row", { name: inbox.address }).getByRole("button", { name: "Resend" }).click();
const second = await inbox.waitForLink({ match: "/invite/", after: resentAt });
expect(second).not.toBe(first);

const guest = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();
await guest.goto(first);
await expect(guest.getByText("This invite is no longer valid")).toBeVisible();

Canceling is the same test with the "Cancel" button and no second email.

Someone else's invite

Here the test needs two inboxes: the invited person's and someone who got hold of the link. The second person creates their own account and tries to use the invite:

test("an invite only works for the invited address", async ({ page, browser }) => {
  test.setTimeout(120_000);
  const [invited, other] = await Promise.all([createInbox(), createInbox()]);

  const link = (await invite(page, invited)).links.find((url) => url.includes("/invite/"))!;

  const intruder = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();
  await signUp(intruder, other.address, "another-password-456"); // your sign-up
  await intruder.goto(link);
  await expect(intruder.getByText("This invite is for another email")).toBeVisible();

  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByRole("row", { name: other.address })).toHaveCount(0);
});

If your sign-up sends a verification code, signUp calls other.waitForCode() along the way, as in the Playwright guide.

Some apps invite with an open link that anyone can use until the seats run out. The saci.cc Team plan invite works that way. Then the test is a different one: the link expires on time, stops working when the team is full and turns off when a new one is made.

In short

  • One inbox per invited person, made with createInbox() and your key.
  • Open the link in a browser.newContext(), so you don't accept with the inviter's session.
  • Pick the link by its path, with links.find or waitForLink({ match }): verificationLink doesn't cover invites.
  • Also test what must not happen: a reused link, an old link after a resend, an invite accepted by another address.

I build saci.cc, temporary email inboxes for end-to-end tests and AI agents. The npm package is saci.cc and the client is open source on GitHub.

title: As Apple works on AI agent features, banks are already blocking them
description:

We can already use third-party chatbots in this way, and we know Apple is working hard to turn Siri AI into an agent. However, before the company even gets the chance, banks are already blocking them, and this may be just the start …

Gemini Enterprise

Announcement

Gemini Enterprise: End of Gemini Code Assist entitlement for existing subscriptions

Bundled Gemini Code Assist entitlements for existing Gemini Enterprise Standard and Gemini Enterprise Plus subscriptions will end on March 31, 2027. After this date, the entitlement will be removed from existing subscriptions. Support for Gemini Code Assist until March 31, 2027 is limited to the Gemini 3.x model family only. Effective October 9, 2026, new Gemini Enterprise subscriptions no longer include an entitlement to Gemini Code Assist.

To transition your developer workflows, agentic coding assistance is available through Google Antigravity, which is included in Gemini Enterprise editions.

For more information, see the Gemini Code Assist sunset page.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Video generation upgrades to Omni 1.2 Flash

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is generally available (GA) and replaces Veo 3.1 for video generation in the global region. Omni 1.2 Flash improves clarity and instruction following.

To use video generation, an administrator must turn on the Enable video generation setting. For more information, see:

  • Generate a video
  • Manage web app features
  • Gemini Enterprise limitations

Breaking

Gemini Notebook Enterprise: Updated web addresses

The URL path for the Gemini Notebook Enterprise web app is changing in two ways. In both cases, existing links redirect automatically.

"go/" added: Starting immediately, go/ is being added to the URL path:

  • For Gemini Notebook Enterprise,
    notebooklm.cloud.google.com/us/
    changes to
    notebooklm.cloud.google.com/go/us/.

  • For Gemini Notebook within Gemini Enterprise,
    vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/notebooklm/global/
    changes to
    vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/notebooklm/go/global/.

The dates for this go/ path change are as follows:

Region Rollout date
global and us Live
eu Rolling out
All other locations Starting November 9, 2026

"lm" removed: Starting November 16, 2026, lm is being removed from the hostname:

  • For Gemini Notebook Enterprise authenticated with Google Identity,
    notebooklm.cloud.google.com
    changes to
    notebook.cloud.google.com.

  • For Gemini Notebook Enterprise authenticated with Workforce Identity Federation,
    notebooklm.cloud.google
    changes to
    notebook.cloud.google.

Action is required: if your organization uses a firewall, proxy, or secure web gateway that allows access to Gemini Notebook by a specific URL path. If this applies to you, Google recommends that you add the following URLs to your allowlist:

  1. Allowlist notebooklm.cloud.google.com/* and notebook.cloud.google.com/*

  2. If you use Workforce Identity Federation, allowlist notebooklm.cloud.google/* and notebook.cloud.google/*

  3. If you use Gemini Notebook within Gemini Enterprise, allowlist vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/notebooklm/*.

Google recommends allowing entire domains (/*) so that future path changes don't require additional updates.

If you don't allow /*, you must allow both /REGION and /go/REGION, where REGION is your location value: global, us, eu, asia-northeast1, au, ca, de, europe-west2, in, kr, or sg. For example, notebooklm.cloud.google.com/us/ and notebooklm.cloud.google.com/go/us/

Temporary workaround: If your firewall blocks users before you update your allowlist, users themselves can access the original URLs by removing /go from the URL and adding version=legacy. For example: notebooklm.cloud.google.com/eu/?project=1234567&version=legacy. This fix will fail when Google sunsets the legacy version.

You can use natural language to search, share, and manage your Adobe Creative Cloud assets, customize Adobe Express templates, apply Lightroom presets, and edit images.   • Memories inspection and filtering: On the Memories tab, switch between Unstructured and Structured views, filter memories by key:value scope pairs or scope chips, edit or delete unstructured memories, inspect structured memory profiles and underlying facts in the Memory details panel, and select View revisions to inspect revision history.
  • Instance and schema configuration: On the Configuration tab, view and edit Details, Generation (memory extraction toggle, perspective, and managed or custom topics), Retrieval (embedding model, configurable before you store the first memory), and Retention (expiration and revision history TTL), or click Schemas to add and edit profile schemas.
  • Agent integration snippets: Click Link to an agent to get installation commands and prefilled Python code (populated with your project, region, and memory bank ID) for connecting with Agent Development Kit (ADK) or retrieving memories.
  • Agent Runtime memory updates: On the Deployments page, deployed agents include key:value scope filtering and View revisions on the Memories tab, along with Generation, Retrieval, and Retention configuration controls under Service configuration in the Memory bank section.

For more information, see Set up Memory Bank, Fetch memories, Memory Profiles, and Memory revisions.

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.32

We've released version 6.32 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where abandoned queue records incorrectly calculated wait times from the call's initial queue entry rather than the time the caller entered the specific queue they abandoned from.

  • Fixed an issue where the call adapter header title on SmartActions and virtual task assistant screens was truncated with an ellipsis, preventing users from viewing the full text.

  • Fixed an issue where the agent adapter froze on Calling and didn't dial the customer during recovery calls following an unanswered in-app call.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls became unroutable and remained stuck in the queue until abandoned if an agent's browser delivered a delayed connection request after a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue in the CCaaS portal where active Spanish IVR queues were incorrectly displayed as Setup is required and grayed out when switching languages from English to Spanish.

  • Fixed an issue where transient network errors during platform validation incorrectly marked virtual agent credentials as invalid.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS and WhatsApp virtual agent chats became unresponsive and didn't escalate to a human agent when encountering a custom payload validation error.

  • Fixed an issue where campaigns didn't resume after being paused, resulting in repeated call session failures and missing participant information.

  • Fixed an issue where call-related actions such as disconnecting or updating status took up to 72 seconds to complete.

  • Fixed an issue where a Not Found banner incorrectly appeared in the call adapter when a phone number couldn't be matched in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where the In-email status bar in the agent desktop appeared white.

  • Fixed an issue where agents in the In-email status couldn't change their status directly from the status bar.

  • Fixed an issue where the first letter of uppercase acronym field names was incorrectly lowercased in virtual task assistant input placeholders.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly set to an Unresponsive status instead of receiving a missed call when a new deltacast offer arrived while the call adapter was already ringing.

  • Fixed an issue where agents became stuck in a projected state and stopped receiving calls after a caller abandoned the call at the moment of routing.

  • Fixed an issue where transient carrier timeouts during outbound callbacks were incorrectly classified as invalid numbers.

  • Fixed an issue where forced virtual agent callbacks booked through the Apps API were incorrectly routed to the original call's queue instead of the requested destination.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled callback capacity was under-calculated due to a mathematical rounding error.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls were prematurely disconnected if the initial connection request timed out and was retried.

  • Fixed an issue where valid Canadian phone numbers using newer area codes were rejected by the Callback call API.

  • Fixed an issue where certain agents were missing from the directory during outbound calls, preventing other agents from transferring calls or adding them to a call.

  • Fixed an issue where dynamic queues incorrectly offered a minimum of one slot even when WFM staffing was zero or resulted in less than one available slot.

  • Fixed an issue where Dynamic Agent Availability queues were saved without a required custom queue identifier, causing workforce management synchronization to fail silently.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce cases and contacts were incorrectly created for voice calls handled entirely by a virtual agent, even when the Create CRM records for calls attended by Virtual Agents setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where voice transfers addressed to a specific agent were never offered to the target and didn't expire, leaving callers on hold indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where NICE WFM session data exports didn't generate for instances with subdomains exceeding 20 characters.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual callbacks routed through external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) were missing captured virtual agent custom parameters, causing routing engines to lose the caller's intent.

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist transcriptions permanently stopped following transient network or quota errors.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound phone number restriction rules weren't applied to agents with the Allow unrestricted international calling setting enabled.

title: How UndoHaven encrypts snapshots so a host never sees file names
description:
I build UndoHaven; this post is about how it handles encryption.

UndoHaven is an unofficial third-party CLI for dsh, a local agent runtime. It takes an encrypted snapshot of a dsh home (plus AGENTS.md and skills/ under ~/.agents) and writes the files back after you quit dsh. Restore is a command, not a screen inside the app, so it does not run against a session that is still writing.

The default needs no account and no network. npx undohaven init (or undohaven snapshot later) writes ciphertext under $DSH_HOME/undohaven, or ~/.dsh/undohaven if DSH_HOME is unset. Storing the ciphertext next to the dsh home is intentional: the snapshot travels with that home. It is also the limit the homepage is explicit about. A full-permission agent can wipe a home directory, local backups included. The copy that survives that wipe is an export you take off the machine, a bucket you configure, or an upload after you log in.

The rest of this post is how those bytes are sealed, and what restore refuses to do.

A data key, wrapped twice

The client generates a 32-byte data key. It does not encrypt files with the passphrase itself. The passphrase is stretched with Argon2id (64 MiB of memory, 3 iterations, parallelism 1; the memorySize value is 65536 because hash-wasm counts kibibytes), and that wrapping key seals the data key with AES-256-GCM. A 24-word recovery code, in the BIP39 layout, is 32 bytes of entropy plus a checksum. It wraps the same data key a second time, but with HKDF-SHA256 over the entropy, not Argon2. The recovery code already has 256 bits of randomness. A human-chosen passphrase does not.

From the data key the client derives three more keys with HKDF-SHA256, each under a fixed info string: one to encrypt chunks, one to encrypt the manifest, and one to name chunks.

If you lose both the passphrase and the recovery code, there is no reset. init, a passphrase unlock, and a recovery-code passphrase change all write the unwrapped data key to local keys.json (file mode 0600, directory 0700) so later snapshots on this machine do not prompt every time. undohaven logout clears that field. chmod has no effect on Windows. keys.json sits in the same $DSH_HOME/undohaven directory as the ciphertext, so syncing or copying the whole home takes the key along. The encryption protects copies that leave this machine; it does not defend a machine that is already compromised. An export file and, if you log in, the server carry only the wrapped keys.

Content-defined chunks, keyed names, then padding

Each file is split with a normalized FastCDC cutter (Xia et al.). The gear table is a fixed SplitMix64 stream, so the same bytes cut at the same places on another machine. The defaults aim at a 1 MiB average chunk, with a 256 KiB floor and a 2 MiB cap, so a sealed chunk stays under a 4 MiB object limit.

A chunk id is not a plain hash of the plaintext. It is HMAC-SHA256 of the plaintext under the chunk-id key. Duplicate chunks still collapse for the same data key, which is what you want across one person's snapshots. A host that only sees the ids cannot confirm a guessed file the way it could with unkeyed SHA-256.

Each piece is optionally compressed with zstd if it is at least 32 bytes and the compressed form is actually smaller, then sealed: a version byte, a flag bit, a 12-byte nonce, AES-256-GCM ciphertext, and a 16-byte tag. On disk or in a bucket the sealed chunk is padded to a 64 KiB multiple (an UHVP header, the true length, then zeros). The stored chunk size is not the plaintext length, and it is not the exact ciphertext length either. Export files and the encrypted manifest are not padded that way.

Paths and per-file sizes live in the manifest, which is encrypted with the third derived key. The claim I will make about the hosted service is narrow: the server cannot see file contents or file names. That is spelled out on the encryption page.

What a snapshot refuses to pick up

The walker does not follow symbolic links or Windows junctions. It skips the undohaven data directory itself, node_modules, cache, common model-weight extensions, and any file larger than 64 MB. Credentials (.env, .credentials.yaml) stay out unless you pass --include-credentials. That flag is off by default. The free plan will still take a local snapshot that includes them if you opt in; it will not upload a snapshot that contains them.

Those cuts are practical. They also mean a snapshot is not a whole-disk image. Files that were never snapshotted cannot be invented later.

Restore runs after dsh has quit

undohaven restore --to SNAPSHOT_ID will not start if it thinks dsh is still up. UndoHaven itself listens on nothing; before restore it connects to 127.0.0.1 and ::1 on port 3999, plus UNDOHAVEN_DSH_PORT if set, to see whether the dsh desktop app is open. On Unix it checks session and desktop lock files through python3 flock or /proc/locks, and refuses the restore if neither method is available. On Windows it looks at tasklist for dsh.exe and at a named semaphore. The error is blunt: quit first, so a live writer cannot race the rollback. There is an escape hatch, UNDOHAVEN_ASSUME_DSH_STOPPED=1, which the code tells you not to set until dsh has actually exited.

If the home still has files, restore takes a safety snapshot first, tagged safety / before-restore, then writes the selected scope back. Files in that scope that are not in the snapshot are deleted; they are still in the safety snapshot. Scopes include all, sessions, storages, config, profile, scheduled tasks (--scope tasks), or a single session. For a full or config restore it also drops a removed tool-working-directory profile entry so a snapshot taken before dsh 0.2.2-rc.3 will still load on 0.2.2-rc.5. Session bytes, including workspace-root paths, are written as stored. dsh itself, not UndoHaven, moves the workspace root.

When dsh will not start at all, undohaven rescue --to SNAPSHOT_ID is narrower still. It does the same lock check and safety snapshot, then writes that profile's package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, and cordis.patch.yml back (--scope profile). It does not try to replay the whole home while you are still figuring out why the process will not boot.

The optional dsh-undohaven plugin can take snapshots on start, on a 6-hour timer by default, and when the plugin is disposed. The startup snapshot only runs when the local data key is already unlocked. If the installed dsh base package version has changed, startup pins the previous snapshot as pre-upgrade and also stores a storage-only snapshot. Restore still happens from the CLI after you quit, so it does not conflict with a session that is writing.

Try it

The CLI needs Node.js 24.9 or newer (undohaven-core itself accepts 22.19). As of 24 November 2026 (Asia/Shanghai), the published packages are undohaven 0.1.14, undohaven-core 0.1.15, and dsh-undohaven 0.1.12.

npx undohaven init
undohaven snapshot
undohaven list
# quit dsh first, including the tray icon
undohaven restore --to SNAPSHOT_ID --scope all

Write the 24-word recovery code down off the machine when init prints it. The crypto lives in the published undohaven-core package, in src/crypto.js, src/cdc.js, and src/byo.js.

Site: https://undohaven.com/

UndoHaven is an unofficial third-party tool compatible with dsh. It is not affiliated with DeepSeek.

title: I graded 14 Go and Rust MCP servers without running a single one
description:
MCP servers describe their tools to the model: a name, a description, an input schema and a few hints like readOnlyHint and destructiveHint. The directories that list MCP apps check those descriptions, and clients use the hints to decide what to run without asking.

Most ways to check them start the server and call tools/list. That means installing it, giving it credentials, and trusting it enough to run. For a quick look at someone else's server, or a CI check on a pull request, that's a lot.

mcp-check 1.3 reads the tool list from the source instead. For Go it understands mark3labs/mcp-go, the official go-sdk and mcp-golang. For Rust it understands rmcp, rust-mcp-sdk and pmcp. It reproduces the tools as the SDK would list them, schemas included, and then grades them. TypeScript and Python were already covered.

The run 

npx @isokron/mcp-check --repo github.com/grafana/mcp-grafana

I ran that against 14 well-known open-source Go and Rust servers on 23 November.

Server Tools Spec Claude directory ChatGPT directory Hidden text Quality
github/github-mcp-server (exact) 149 A B C A B
grafana/mcp-grafana 136 A F D A A
containers/kubernetes-mcp-server 87 C C D A B
hashicorp/terraform-mcp-server 68 A A B A B
zerodha/kite-mcp-server 22 A D A A A
tuananh/hyper-mcp 20 D F D A A
mark3labs/mcp-filesystem-server 14 A D A A A
strowk/mcp-k8s-go 9 A F D A A
isaacphi/mcp-language-server 6 A D A A A
Roblox/studio-rust-mcp-server 6 A F F A A
apollographql/apollo-mcp-server 5 A C A A A
elastic/mcp-server-elasticsearch 5 A A D A A

Two weren't graded. genai-toolbox builds its tools from configuration at run time, so there's nothing in the source to read. The checker says that, names the four registrations whose names it couldn't resolve, and tells you to grade the live list. I'd rather have that than a confident F.

What came up

  • Missing titles (8 of 12). The Claude directory asks every tool for a human-readable title. A name like search_within_files isn't one.
  • Hints left unset (8 of 12). The ChatGPT app directory wants readOnlyHint, destructiveHint and openWorldHint set explicitly on every tool. Left out, a client has to guess, and the safe guess is "ask the human every time".
  • No hidden instructions anywhere. Every server graded A on that section.

None of this is a security hole. It's the difference between being listed and being bounced, and between a client that knows a delete tool deletes and one that has to ask.

Caveats

Grades from source are approximate. The reader can miss a tool built at run time, and a schema it can't work out is marked unreadable rather than graded as empty. A live list is exact:

npx @isokron/mcp-check -- ./your-server --stdio

In CI 

- uses: isokron-ai/mcp-check@v1

With no inputs, it reads your source, runs nothing, and writes a job summary. Add min-grade: B to gate on it.

If you maintain one of these servers and a grade looks wrong, open an issue on github.com/isokron-ai/mcp-check with the tool name. That's how the Go and Rust readers got this far.

More: isokron.ai/mcp-check

title: Pretending to Delete
description:
Algorithms, a semester of SQL, and the slow realization that in real systems we mostly only pretend to delete.

A look back — long before any of the tools we argue about now.

This is the last of my memories of studying computer science — the database course, and the algorithms course that led up to it, closing out what I learned in school in the 1990s.

Algorithms

After data structures in my sophomore year, algorithms arrived as the course for learning to program "properly." The book was thick enough to be intimidating on its own. I worked hard at the front of it, held my breath through graphs, and somewhere around greedy methods and NP-hard and NP-complete I simply found it difficult. At first I took it for no more than a set of slightly cleverer ways to solve a given problem, but I kept turning back to it — in grad school, and later in working life — and for one reason or another it kept earning its keep. Ten years after graduating, when I set out to interview at Google, it was the book I gritted my teeth and opened again; what's left of it now is fragments.

INSERT / SELECT / DELETE

The database course came at the very end of my undergraduate years. There was a book, though it never quite felt like a textbook, and what I remember is SQL, all semester long. The sharpest thing that stayed with me — I can't reconstruct the exact tone — was a grad student who came in as our lab assistant and told us, "For the rest of your lives you'll need nothing else; just know SELECT." More than twenty-five years on, working with SQL that is still very much in use, I found myself thinking of him again.

There was the minor argument over whether SQL counts as a programming language, but it remains one of the most used, and by now whatever tool you pick probably supports it out of the box. Work on the backend and you'll get a fuller look; otherwise, the prophecy about SELECT has more or less come true. In the AI era, perhaps we'll be learning how to coax GPT into writing good SQL — a chain of person to GPT to SQL to database to machine that feels already half here.

is_deleted

In data structures and algorithms, the thing that took the most time was implementing delete — keeping the state from breaking, returning memory properly, holding everything together so that the far more frequent searches stayed fast. It was the part that gave me the worst headaches whenever I tried to build a system. In the database course, though, the most time went to a different question: how to make deletion recoverable. Real services carried the same worry — what happens when something deleted still needs to come back, and then what becomes of the backup — and the usual answer was to not actually delete anything, and only act as though you had.

It was a little deflating, honestly, how often adding an is_deleted field was all it took for a feature to work. Later I found the same idea already everywhere — page memory in the kernel, the way NAND flash behaves — less like rubbing something out with an eraser than throwing white paint over it. When a departed user signs up again, do you reuse what was there? And under certain laws, did you truly delete it? That one small question — "is it deleted?" — turns out to hold a great deal of room for misunderstanding.

P.S. On a single service it never shows, but once you meet scale, some things reveal enormous read performance the moment they're frozen read-only — and watching the same concerns come around again as domains and generations change, maybe there's something to the old line about none of it going to waste.

Adapted from my Korean essay on Brunch: brunch.co.kr/@chaesang/57

title: Travel Itinerary Planner Retrieval: Caching Fresh Media Reranking Signals
description:
Short answer: cache retrieval evidence, not the final itinerary. Keep a short-lived cache for query features and a versioned cache for media index results, then invalidate by content revision and destination policy. This costs more bookkeeping than a single response cache, but it prevents a changed opening hour or licensing rule from surviving inside a supposedly helpful trip plan.

The application here is a travel itinerary planner whose corpus contains media: destination guides, venue pages, transit clips, and editorial photos. The retrieval layer reranks those documents for each itinerary step. Its hard constraint is index cost at scale. Rebuilding every vector after every edit is wasteful; serving an old ranking without a freshness signal is worse, because users make real reservations from it.

The constraint: index work is the scarce resource

A planner request usually has three different clocks. The traveler’s wording changes per request, editorial content changes when a document is revised, and policy data changes on a schedule owned by another team. A cache design that gives all three one TTL cannot express those clocks.

I model a result as evidence with a provenance tuple: (document_id, revision, embedding_model, policy_version). The tuple is part of the cache key and part of the audit record. In payment systems I would never reconcile a ledger entry without its source version; search deserves the same exactly-once mindset when a ranking is copied into a user-visible plan.

The useful unit to cache is therefore a candidate set plus scores, not prose generated by the language model. Candidate sets are reusable across many itinerary prompts, while generated text embeds assumptions that are hard to invalidate. A 60-second query-feature cache can absorb repeated autocomplete traffic, and a revision-keyed candidate cache can live much longer without hiding edits.

How should a travel itinerary planner cache retrieval and reranking?

Use three boundaries, each with an explicit invalidation event:

Boundary Key material Invalidate when Main risk
Query features normalized query, locale, date window parser or policy version changes old interpretation
Candidate retrieval destination, filters, document revision, index generation document revision or index generation changes stale membership
Reranking evidence candidate IDs, feature vector, model version model, policy, or feature schema changes inconsistent ordering

The index generation is a monotonically increasing token published with each completed batch. Readers pin one generation for the whole request. That small rule avoids a mixed result in which the first page came from generation 41 and the second page came from generation 42. If a generation is unavailable, the reader can use the previous complete generation and mark the response as aged; it should not silently combine shards.

Pin the generation.

Here is the cache admission and freshness check in Go. The interface is deliberately generic so the same logic can sit over an in-process cache, a shared key-value store, or a disk-backed layer.

package retrieval

import "time"

type EvidenceKey struct {
    Destination string
    Revision    string
    IndexGen    uint64
    Model       string
    Policy      string
}

type Evidence struct {
    DocIDs    []string
    Scores    []float64
    ExpiresAt time.Time
}

func Fresh(e Evidence, now time.Time) bool {
    return now.Before(e.ExpiresAt) && len(e.DocIDs) == len(e.Scores)
}

func Admit(key EvidenceKey, e Evidence, now time.Time) bool {
    if key.Destination == "" || key.Revision == "" || key.IndexGen == 0 {
        return false
    }
    return Fresh(e, now)
}

The length check is not cosmetic. A partial write can leave IDs and scores out of alignment, which turns a cache hit into a relevance defect that is difficult to reproduce. Writes should be conditional on the generation token, and metrics should record hit, miss, stale, and rejected-admission counts separately. A single “cache hit rate” hides the failure mode that matters.

Invalidation is a data contract, not a timer

Every indexed document emits a revision event after its source transaction commits. The consumer records the event ID before applying it, so a retry cannot enqueue the same embedding job twice. The job itself is idempotent: (document_id, revision, embedding_model) identifies one intended write. If the event stream is delayed, the planner can still serve a prior complete generation, but the response carries the age and revision used for the audit trail.

A timer remains useful as a backstop. It catches missed events and bounds exposure, yet it must not be the primary correctness mechanism. For volatile facts such as opening hours, use a policy-specific freshness window; for stable editorial prose, revision keys can outlive that window. Your mileage may vary when upstream publishers cannot provide revisions; in that case, add a content hash and accept that freshness is probabilistic rather than pretending a TTL proves correctness.

The awkward case is a delete. Tombstones need to remain visible to the index builder until every serving generation that could contain the document has expired. Removing the cache key immediately only protects the next generation; it does nothing for readers pinned to the old one. Consider a venue page revised at 09:00 and removed at 09:03 while generation 41 is still serving a long-running itinerary request: the revision event must first make generation 42 exclude the document, the tombstone must remain consumable by any shard still building 42, and the serving layer must retain the provenance record long enough to explain why an earlier response contained the page. If the deletion is applied only to a key-value cache, an already materialized candidate list can continue to point at the venue; if it is applied only to the index, a stale reranking cache can reintroduce the old score. This is where teams often spend index budget twice: once rebuilding, then again repairing a result that still referenced a deleted venue.

Measuring cost without losing relevance

Track index CPU-seconds per published generation, embedding writes per revised document, cache bytes per destination, and the age distribution of served evidence. Pair those with retrieval recall on a fixed evaluation set and a freshness violation count. A cheaper index that raises violations is not a saving; it is deferred operational work.

Sample traces should carry the four provenance fields, the cache boundary that answered, and the invalidation event ID. Keep those fields for the retention period required by your compliance review. Do not log raw traveler queries when they can contain personal details; hash a normalized form and retain the salt outside analytics storage.

Rollout rules and the catch

Start in shadow mode: compute the versioned cache decision, but continue using the existing path, then compare rank changes and freshness ages. Promote one destination cohort at a time. Set an explicit rollback trigger, such as a rise in stale-result violations or a drop in judged recall, and roll back the cache policy rather than deleting generations that an in-flight request still needs.

The catch is that this architecture is not suitable when the product requires per-request, real-time inventory guarantees from an upstream system that has no revision or event feed. Keep a direct, uncached lookup for that slice, even if it raises latency. Conversely, a planner built only on slowly changing guides can use longer revision-keyed retention and a simpler invalidation worker. The decision follows data volatility and audit requirements, not a fashionable cache technology.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7234
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/

title: October 27, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI functions and improvements are available in Preview:

  • The ai.extract function lets you extract structured data from unstructured text directly within your database queries without needing external extraction pipelines. For more information, see Extract structured data.

  • The ai.classify function lets you categorize unstructured text into predefined labels directly within your database queries. For more information, see Classify text.

  • Parameter names and signatures for AI query engine functions (ai.analyze_sentiment, ai.summarize, and ai.agg_summarize) are updated. For more information, see Model endpoint reference.

    • The prompt and prompts parameters are renamed to input and inputs in scalar and batch functions respectively.

    • An optional additional_instructions parameter is added to ai.summarize and ai.agg_summarize to provide custom instructions to guide summary formatting, length, and tone.

    • In cursor-based versions of ai.analyze_sentiment and ai.summarize, the prompt parameter is removed.

    • ai.agg_summarize supports multiple positional signatures, including passing optional additional instructions and specifying model IDs.

Apigee X

Feature

The Apigee API Health & Availability dashboard is now generally available in Cloud Monitoring to help you monitor the health, performance, and availability of your Apigee API proxies in real time:

  • Golden signal scorecards: track aggregate Traffic (requests per second), Error Rate (5xx), and Latency (p95) scorecards.
  • Status code and error trends: visualize the Request Rate by Status Code chart over time and identify problematic APIs using the dedicated 5xx Error Rate by Proxy and 4xx Error Rate by Proxy charts.
  • Granular filtering: filter telemetry by project_id, location, and proxy_name to troubleshoot specific regions or proxies.

For more information, see API Monitoring.

Bigtable

Feature

You can use Apache Avro schema bundles to query individual fields within Avro records stored as serialized bytes in Bigtable. You can query your Avro data using GoogleSQL for Bigtable, continuous materialized views, and logical views. This feature is in Preview.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

Google Cloud VMware Engine

Feature

VMware solution on Google Cloud is generally available (GA). VMware solution lets you deploy, configure, and manage VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) on dedicated bare-metal Compute Engine instances within your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network under a Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model.

Key features include the following:

  • Provision dedicated bare-metal ESXi nodes (z3-highmem-192-highlssd-metal) directly in your project with deletion protection and Local SSD storage for vSAN.
  • Automate node preparation, Secret Manager credential storage, vSwitch and Dynamic NIC networking, Cloud DNS zone and record synchronization, vSAN storage initialization, and VCF installer appliance deployment by using Terraform and the VMware solution toolkit.
  • Distribute nodes across isolated availability domains by using spread placement policies to align with vSAN fault domains for high availability.
  • Connect ESXi nodes and VLAN-tagged Dynamic NICs directly to your VPC subnets without requiring private services access peering.

For more information, see VMware solution on Google Cloud overview and Compare VMware Engine models.

title: P2P Fraud Is a UX Problem: How One "Payment Confirmed" Button Empties Wallets
description:
A seller on a P2P marketplace recently lost his crypto to a classic case of P2P fraud — in a trade that looked completely normal.

The buyer tapped the button that marks a trade as paid. The interface updated. The trade screen showed the payment step as done. The seller, watching a countdown timer eat into his trade window, pressed "release."

His bank account was empty. It had always been empty. The "payment confirmed" state he trusted was never a confirmation of anything. It was the buyer's own claim, rendered by the interface with the same visual weight as a verified fact.

No hacking. No malware. Just one ambiguous button, one timer, and one moment of misplaced trust. This is how most P2P fraud actually works, and it is why I have come to see P2P fraud less as a security problem and more as a UX problem.

I work on community and growth at a mobile-first crypto project with a live P2P trading zone. I see these cases from the support side, and the pattern is almost always the same: the technology did not fail. The interface told a story that was not true, and the user believed the story.

The core bug: buyer-declared states wearing system-verified clothes

In most P2P trade flows, the payment step has two completely different events:

  1. The buyer declares "I have paid" (a self-reported claim)
  2. The seller verifies the money arrived in their own account (a checked fact)

Good interfaces keep these visually and structurally separate. Bad interfaces merge them into a single green checkmark.

When a buyer-declared claim is styled like a system verification — same color, same checkmark, same position in the progress bar — the UI is effectively lying. The seller reads "payment confirmed" and reasonably concludes the platform confirmed it. The platform confirmed nothing. It just recorded a tap.

This single design decision is behind a huge share of P2P fraud losses:

  • The "paid" button trick. The buyer marks the trade paid, sends a friendly message ("sent, please release"), and the seller releases against an empty account.
  • The fake screenshot. The buyer uploads an edited banking screenshot. Because the flow already trained the seller to accept in-app artifacts as proof, the image feels like one more confirmation.
  • Timer pressure. Trade windows count down. Verification takes a minute of opening a banking app. Releasing takes one tap. The interface rewards the fast, wrong action and punishes the slow, correct one.

None of these require the scammer to defeat any security system. They only require the scammer to understand the interface slightly better than the victim does.

What the fraud patterns teach us about design

Looking at real P2P fraud cases, the same design weaknesses keep appearing:

1. Proof is whatever the buyer uploads.
If your flow accepts a screenshot as evidence of payment, your flow accepts fiction as evidence of payment. The only trustworthy proof lives in the seller's own bank account, and the UI should say exactly that, at exactly the moment of release.

2. Reversible rails are treated like final ones.
Chargeback fraud works because a buyer can pay through a reversible method, receive the crypto, and then pull the payment back. Interfaces that display all payment methods as equally "safe" hide a real difference in risk. Method risk should be visible, not buried in a help page.

3. Leaving the platform feels like a shortcut, not an exit from protection.
Scammers constantly try to move the trade or the payment off-platform "to save fees." Users follow because nothing in the flow communicates that escrow and dispute protection end at the platform's border. The warning exists, but it appears once, early, in small text — not at the moment the user is about to step outside.

4. The dispute button is designed like an afterthought.
In too many trade flows, disputing is harder to find than releasing. Yet the dispute is the only action that freezes a bad trade while it can still be fixed. Once a trade completes, support teams, including ours, generally cannot reverse it. The safest button in the flow should not be the hardest one to reach.

Design fixes that actually reduce P2P fraud

If you are building or redesigning a P2P flow, these are the changes that matter most, in order:

Separate claim from verification in the state model.
Model the payment step as two states — buyer_claimed_paid and seller_verified_received — and render them differently. The claim can be neutral. Only verification gets the green checkmark. Never let a self-reported state borrow the visual language of a verified one.

Put the verification instruction on the release button itself.
At the moment of release, show: "Release only if the exact amount is visible in your own bank account. A screenshot or the buyer's message is not proof." This is not legal copy. It is the product working as intended.

Make dispute the path of least resistance.
When a trade is marked paid but the seller has not verified receipt, the dispute action should be at least as prominent as release. In our own P2P flow at UNC, the dispute option sits inside the trade itself, because a seller who cannot find it in ten seconds effectively does not have it.

Design timers that do not punish checking.
If your trade window expires while a seller is verifying a payment, your timer is a fraud feature. Pause the countdown when a payment claim is made, or extend it automatically while verification is pending.

Show counterparty risk where decisions happen.
Account age, completed trades, and verified-name matching between the platform profile and the payment sender should be visible inside the trade screen, not on a separate profile page the seller may never open.

Label payment methods by reversibility.
A small "reversible" tag on risky rails teaches users more than a blog post ever will.

The takeaway

P2P fraud is usually described as a user-education problem: "users should be more careful." But when the same mistake is made by thousands of different users, in the same place, in the same way, it is not a user problem anymore. It is a design signal.

The honest state model, the honest button label, the honest timer: these are small engineering choices, and they decide whether the next first-time seller keeps their money. Build the interface so that the truth is the easiest thing to believe.

Shahzad works on community and growth at UNC, a mobile-first crypto project built around verified human participation. Disclosure: the author is affiliated with UNC, whose P2P market is mentioned once above as an example of in-trade dispute placement.

title: Understanding public static void main(String[] args) in Java
description:
Introduction

In Java, public static void main(String[] args) is the traditional entry point of a Java application. When we execute a Java program, the Java launcher looks for a valid main method to start the application.

Let's understand each component.

1. Public

public is an access modifier. It allows the method to be accessed from outside its class. The Java launcher needs access to the main method to start the application.

2. Static

static is a keyword that makes a method belong to the class rather than an individual object.

The main method is static because the Java launcher needs to invoke it without creating an object of the class.

3. Void

void is a return type that indicates the method does not return any value.

For example:

void display() {
    System.out.println("Hello Java");
}

4. Main

main is the method name recognized by the traditional Java application launcher as the entry point of the program.

5. String[] args

String[] args is an array parameter used to receive command-line arguments. These arguments are passed when executing the program through the terminal.

Example:

class Student {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(args[0]);
    }
}

Execute:

java Student Abishek

Output:

Abishek

Here, args[0] accesses the first command-line argument.

How Does Java Execute the Main Method?

  1. We write Java source code.
  2. The javac compiler converts it into bytecode.
  3. The Java launcher starts the application.
  4. The JVM loads and initializes the required class.
  5. The launcher invokes the main method.
  6. The statements inside main are executed.

Conclusion

Understanding public static void main(String[] args) is essential for every Java programmer. It explains how a Java application starts, how the launcher invokes the main method, and how command-line arguments are passed to a program.

title: Amazon CloudFront is now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud
description:
Amazon CloudFront is now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. Organizations with strict EU sovereignty requirements can now deliver websites, applications, and APIs with the performance, security, and scale of CloudFront, all within the EU. Until now, customers had to build and run their own delivery and TLS termination infrastructure to keep traffic and data inside the EU.

With CloudFront in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, content delivery, TLS termination, logs, and customer configuration stay within the European Sovereign Cloud boundary. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions, and only EU-resident personnel operate it. This helps governments, healthcare, financial services and other regulated industries meet data residency and operational sovereignty requirements without trading away performance and scale. Customers use the same CloudFront APIs and console experience they already know making it easy to transfer over existing deployments and automations. If you plan to run media streaming or other high-volume workloads, contact your AWS account team and we can help you find the right solution, including options in AWS commercial Regions.

To get started, sign in to your AWS European Sovereign Cloud account and create a distribution in the CloudFront console. To learn more about available features and pricing, see the CloudFront Developer Guide and CloudFront pricing page in ESC.

title: Node.js Factors Influencing Lifecycle Policies for AI-Generated Property Image Storage
description:
Short answer: The factors that influence lifecycle policies are business state, private-link expiry, governance holds, regeneration or recovery value, and the throughput cost of moving large files. Use those signals together; file age alone is not a deletion policy.

A large AI-generated property image should live as long as its business purpose, access obligation, and recovery value justify. The least complex design is to give each object a retention state, keep the original immutable, create expiring download links on demand, and delete only after a recorded policy decision.

The useful signal is not "this object is old." It is "this object has no active lease, no legal or operational hold, and no recovery value left." That distinction keeps lifecycle automation from turning a quiet storage bucket into an incident.

The page is late.

No guessing.

Keep the deletion decision boring. The interesting part belongs in the evidence around it: which workflow owned the image, which lease was live, which hold was applied, and which policy revision made the transition eligible.

The page that arrives too late

The page fires when a resident cannot open a generated inspection image from a private portal. The on-call sees a 404 from the download service, a normal-looking object count, and a cleanup job that reported success overnight. Large files make this harder: a retry can consume worker bandwidth for minutes before anyone notices that the object was already deleted.

I start from the alert and work backwards. I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, and the useful lesson is consistent: the missing image is the final symptom. Earlier signals should have shown that an object moved from active to deletion_pending without a matching business event, or that a delete batch contained records whose download lease had not expired. A count of deleted objects is useful accounting; it is not proof that deletion was safe. Give the policy a revision such as 2026-01, record it with the decision, and keep the old rule available when an operator has to explain why a file was removed.

For a property-management workflow, the metadata record needs enough information to make the decision again: object identity, tenant or property scope, creation time, last authorized access, retention class, hold state, content digest, and the policy revision that made the object eligible. The image bytes and the decision record have different jobs. Keep them separate.

What factors influence lifecycle policies for AI-generated image storage?

The reader question sounds like a storage question, but the strongest inputs come from outside storage. AI-generated images may be intermediate renderings, published listing assets, resident-submitted documents, or evidence attached to a maintenance record. Those categories have different lifetimes even when their files are the same size and format.

A practical policy evaluates four gates:

  1. Business state: Is the image attached to an open work order, an active listing, or a closed record?
  2. Access state: Are there active sessions, download leases, or a pending export? An expiring link should be treated as a capability with a deadline, not as a permanent permission.
  3. Governance state: Is there a documented hold, privacy requirement, or retention class that prevents deletion? Security guidance for regulated data emphasizes defined safeguards and documented handling, so the policy should name its owner and evidence rather than hiding the choice in a cron expression.
  4. Recovery state: Can the image be regenerated deterministically, or would deletion remove the only useful artifact? A prompt, model configuration, source asset, and output digest are materially different from a recoverable copy of the rendered file.

The threshold is a policy decision, not a magic number. A short-lived preview can be deleted after its lease and workflow expire. A published image may need to remain while a listing is active. A record attached to a dispute may need a hold that outlives both.

There is a real trade-off here: keeping every original improves recovery, but increases the amount of private data that must be protected and the work a cleanup backlog can create. Deleting aggressively reduces that burden, but gives up forensic and regeneration options. The right boundary belongs to the record owner.

Why does large-file throughput change the design?

Large-file throughput changes what an operationally correct cleanup job looks like. Deleting metadata quickly while a transfer is still in flight creates a race. Rebuilding a full image to verify a digest consumes the same constrained path used by customer downloads. A queue that retries a timeout without an idempotency key can produce duplicate work, while a queue that retries a successful delete can produce a misleading error unless the delete operation is treated as convergent.

The worker should claim a small batch, re-read the decision fields, and make one idempotent transition. It should not stream the image merely to decide whether the object is eligible. This Go example shows the boundary; the storage adapter can use any object-store implementation that supports the required semantics.

type ImageRecord struct {
\tID             string
\tRetentionClass string
\tHold           bool
\tLeaseExpiresAt time.Time
\tDeleteAfter    time.Time
\tState          string
}

func EligibleForDelete(r ImageRecord, now time.Time) bool {
\tif r.Hold || r.State != "deletion_pending" {
\t\treturn false
\t}
\tif !now.After(r.LeaseExpiresAt) || !now.After(r.DeleteAfter) {
\t\treturn false
\t}
\treturn true
}

In production, the transition and the claim need a durable concurrency boundary. A worker that loses its lease should be safe to run again. The delete request should carry a stable operation identifier in logs, and the resulting state should distinguish deleted, already_absent, and blocked. Those outcomes support retries without pretending that every retry found a new failure.

Private delivery also needs a clean separation between authorization and transfer. The application checks the caller, records the intended object and expiry, then issues a link whose lifetime is bounded by the policy. The download path must not infer authorization from an object key that a caller can guess. A link that has expired should fail closed, while the record remains available for a controlled retry if the policy still permits it.

The instrumentation change that prevents the next page

I would instrument the policy evaluation before instrumenting the delete API. Emit a structured decision with the object class, policy revision, eligibility result, blocking reason, and age bucket. Do not log the private link or raw user data. Correlate the decision with the workflow event and the worker attempt.

The useful dashboard has three views: eligible objects waiting for work, blocked objects grouped by reason, and completed transitions grouped by outcome. Add transfer duration and bytes for downloads, but keep throughput separate from lifecycle correctness. A rising byte rate can be healthy; a rising mismatch between deletion_pending records and completed decisions is the earlier warning.

The alert should page on policy drift or an aging backlog, with a threshold based on the maximum tolerated delay for each retention class. A threshold set too low turns normal large-file retries into noise and teaches the on-call to ignore the page. A threshold set too high leaves a private delivery failure hidden. I would tune it against a replayable test set containing small previews, large originals, expired links, active holds, duplicate worker attempts, and objects that are already absent.

That test set matters because the dangerous bugs are temporal. Unit tests can prove the boolean rule; integration tests must prove that a lease expiring during a transfer, a policy revision, and a worker retry produce the intended final state. Run the same cases in a deployment check before changing the lifecycle worker.

A decision rule that survives change

Choose lifecycle behavior by evidence owned by the workflow, not by file age alone. Store the policy revision with the decision, make state transitions auditable, and require an explicit hold to override automatic cleanup. Keep original bytes immutable when their provenance matters, and use derived thumbnails or previews for high-volume access when the product permits it.

The design is portable because its contract is small: private object identity, bounded capability, durable metadata, idempotent transitions, and observable reasons. A storage backend can change without changing the policy question. The operational risk remains in the same place: deleting an object before the system has proved that nobody still needs it.

Further reading

  • NIST SP 800-66 Rev. 2, Implementing the HIPAA Security Rule: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/66/r2/final
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • W3C Trace Context: https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/

title: AWS WAF introduces simplified pricing
description:
AWS WAF now offers simplified pricing that follows what you protect instead of how you configure it. Previously, you paid separate charges for each web ACL, rule, rule group subscription, and capacity tier, making every security decision a billing calculation. Now, your bill follows three dimensions: the resources you protect, the traffic AWS WAF inspects, and the level of protection you apply. You pay a resource fee for each protected resource, a base request fee for every request AWS WAF inspects, and a premium request fee only for traffic evaluated by advanced protections like Bot Control targeted protections, Fraud Control, API Security, and AI Security.

AWS WAF's new pricing is available today in all AWS commercial Regions, including Cape Town, Hong Kong, Hyderabad, Jakarta, Malaysia, Melbourne, Mumbai, New Zealand, Osaka, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Taipei, Thailand, Tokyo, Calgary, Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain, Stockholm, Zurich, Tel Aviv, Sao Paulo, N. title: The morning our app launch broke Postgres
description:
🚨 The morning it broke

It was the first morning of our marketing sale. We had launched our mobile app shortly before, and it had been running fine. Then the orders started pouring in. A truckload of them.

The first sign was an SOS from a teammate: browsing was slow. I opened our observability dashboards and the alerts were already firing. Lots of red. Not the festive kind. Database connections were pinned at their limit and new requests were being turned away. The website, the admin panel and the app were all failing with the same error: Database connection failed.

I was the support engineer on duty, and I was on my own. My honest first thought was: oh my. 😳 Customers were complaining, on the busiest morning we'd had.

What helped most wasn't technical. The rest of the team stayed calm. They spoke to customers kindly while I worked, which let me focus on the database instead of the noise. Shout-out to them.

What the app changed

Our database had handled the website for a long time without trouble. On a normal day, each request borrowed a connection from the backend's pool, ran its queries and gave it back quickly. Sale-day traffic plus the new app broke that rhythm in two ways.

  • Connections were held longer. The app's background sync and polling kept a steady stream of requests coming, and some code paths didn't give their connection back as soon as they should have.
  • It sent queries in bursts. Each time someone opened the app, it fetched their profile, notifications and telemetry all at once. Multiply that by a sale's worth of shoppers.

Our database plan (1 GiB of RAM) allowed only 22 connections. On a normal day that was enough. On sale day, with the new app, it ran out.

Fixing it, and making it worse

I started with the obvious moves. I scaled the database cluster to clear out stale connections and put PgBouncer, a connection pooler, in front of it. Then I upgraded the database to a bigger plan with 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB of RAM. DigitalOcean sets the connection limit by memory, so it jumped from 22 to 97.

With all that new room, I raised the app's connection limit to 90. It felt like the right call. More room, more connections, more speed. Right?

It wasn't. Database CPU shot to nearly 100%. Pages that had been slow were now crawling. My fix had made things worse. 🫠

Here's why. Think of a traffic jam: letting more cars onto the road doesn't get anyone home faster. A database with 2 CPUs can only truly run 2 queries at the same moment. Every other active query waits its turn, and the more queries are fighting for those 2 cores, the more time goes on juggling them. Some of ours were also hitting unindexed columns, which means scanning whole tables. Ninety of those at once pinned the CPU.

That was the lesson of the morning: a connection limit is not a target. It tells you how many connections the database will accept, not how many it can serve well. The real limit is the CPU behind it.

The fix that held

So I went the other way. I cut the app's limit to 20 and made sure PgBouncer was running in transaction mode. Fifteen minutes later, everything was back to normal. 😮‍💨 From the first refused connection to full recovery took about 75 minutes.

Three changes did the work together:

  1. All traffic goes through PgBouncer. The backend no longer connects to the database directly. The pooler shares a small set of real connections among many clients. Think nightclub bouncer: only so many inside at once, and nobody hogs the dance floor.
  2. Transaction mode. A connection goes back to the pool the moment a transaction finishes, not when the client disconnects, so the app's long sessions stop holding connections hostage.
  3. A pool sized to the CPU. Twenty works on 2 CPUs because most connections are idle at any given moment, waiting on the network or the app. A common starting point for truly active queries is about two per CPU core. If the backend scales to two containers, each gets 10, so the total stays at 20.

One catch with transaction mode: anything tied to a database session doesn't carry over between transactions. That includes session-level SET commands, advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY and, on older PgBouncer versions, prepared statements. Check your ORM or driver is configured for transaction pooling before you switch.

Database CPU now stays under 45% at peak, and average API response time is under 150 ms.

How I knew it worked

I watched two numbers on DigitalOcean's database metrics dashboard. Connections told me what was failing. CPU told me whether a fix was working.

I didn't call it resolved straight away. I kept the database on the 2-CPU tier for 48 hours and watched both graphs through a full traffic cycle first.

What I'd do differently

Looking back, this was a launch problem as much as a database problem. We planned the app's features and its release, but not what its traffic would do to a database sized for the website.

  • Load-test a new client before launch. A mobile app talks to the backend differently from a website. Test the pattern, not just the endpoints.
  • Put a pooler in front of the database from day one. It costs little and removes a whole class of outage.
  • Size the pool to the CPU, not the connection limit. Start small, measure, then raise it.
  • Release connections in code, every time, even when a query fails.
  • Find the slow queries. Missing indexes make every query hold its connection longer.

A launch isn't finished when the app ships. It's finished when the system behind it survives its first busy morning.

For the engineers: what I check now

Alert on the early signal, not the failure: connections above 80% of the limit, and database CPU above 70% for five minutes. And when something feels off, this shows what connections are actually doing:

SELECT state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = current_database()
GROUP BY state;

The state to worry about is idle in transaction: a connection stuck inside an open transaction, holding a slot and often locks too. Behind PgBouncer, plain idle is normal; those are the pool's spare connections. In PgBouncer itself, SHOW POOLS; shows how many clients are waiting for a connection (cl_waiting).

The timeline

Minutes in What happened
0 Connections start climbing as sale traffic arrives.
75 Connections hit the limit of 22. The database starts refusing new ones.
90 Scaled the cluster to clear stale connections; started PgBouncer.
105 Upgraded to 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB of RAM; limit rises to 97.
120 Raised the app's limit to 90. CPU jumps to nearly 100%.
135 Cut the app's limit to 20; confirmed transaction mode.
150 Website, app and admin panel back to normal.
