title: Best colour contrast checkers for WCAG text pairs
description:
Best colour contrast checkers for WCAG text pairs

Checking two colours against WCAG 2 contrast is a defined calculation: relative luminance of the lighter and darker colours, then (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05). The tools that do that job are not interchangeable. Some only grade text. Some also cover the 3:1 bar for graphics and UI components in WCAG 2.1/2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.11. Some add colour-vision simulations. None of the options below is an APCA checker, and none replaces a full accessibility audit of real components, focus states, or text inside images.

This article was written with the assistance of AI.

This compares five tools whose official pages are built around the same task: enter a foreground and a background, get a contrast ratio, and see WCAG-style pass or fail grades. It is not a hands-on benchmark and not a single “overall best” ranking. Pick by workflow — a quick hex pair in the browser, sampling colours off a PDF or a native window, or explaining who a failing pair may affect.

The same checks apply to each tool: the contrast model and whether non-text 3:1 is shown as its own result; hex, RGB, HSL or HSV, alpha, and eyedropper support; preview, font samples, reverse, saved pairs, shareable URLs, or an API; colour-vision simulations and how the vendor describes them; browser versus an installed app, plus published price; and only the data-handling claims the vendor actually states. Missing claims are marked unknown. Ratios were not re-computed here.

WebAIM Contrast Checker

WebAIM’s Contrast Checker is a free page from WebAIM, a non-profit service center at Utah State University that has published accessibility resources since 1999. You enter foreground and background colours as RGB hex, or use a colour picker; an alpha value can be set on the foreground, and lightness sliders let you nudge a failing pair toward a target ratio.

It reports AA and AAA for normal and large text, plus a separate WCAG 2.1 AA result for graphical objects and user interface components (the 3:1 non-text bar). Large text is defined on the page as 14 point (typically 18.66 px) and bold or larger, or 18 point (typically 24 px) or larger. Permalinks use fcolor and bcolor query parameters. Appending &api returns JSON with the ratio and pass/fail states. WebAIM also offers a bookmarklet and a companion link contrast checker for links distinguished by colour alone.

WebAIM’s terms say the organization will not sell or otherwise give personal information submitted to it to external parties. Colour values appear in the page URL. WebAIM pages use Google Analytics; treat any broader telemetry claim as unknown beyond those terms.

Best fit: a widely cited, no-install checker, including the non-text 3:1 row, a documented definition of “large text,” and an API or bookmarklet. Trade-off: no colour-vision simulation on this page, and it is not a system-wide eyedropper for a PDF or a native app.

TPGi Colour Contrast Analyser

The Colour Contrast Analyser (CCA), currently listed as version 3.5.5, is a free desktop app from TPGi / Vispero. The open-source repository describes Windows and macOS builds (Electron; GPL-3.0). The product page says it can be used on websites, app UIs, social graphics, PowerPoint, PDFs, and InDesign — anywhere you can point an eyedropper.

Documented features include swapping foreground and background; WCAG 2.0, 2.1, and 2.2 results; HEX, RGB, HSV, and HSL entry; alpha on the foreground; sliders to adjust a failing pair; short or long copy-to-clipboard result formats; a preview for text and non-text contrast; a colour-blindness simulator with eight vision-deficiency settings; and language plus theme preferences. The GitHub README notes that the colour picker is for Windows and macOS only, which matches the supported builds.

CCA is free, with the usual GPL “no warranty” language. A dedicated, CCA-specific privacy policy describing local sampling versus any app telemetry was not found on the product page — unknown. There is no shareable URL workflow, because this is an installed app.

Best fit: testers who need to sample real pixels from a document, a design file, or a running interface, with non-text contrast and a built-in colour-blindness simulator. Trade-off: it requires an install, and it is the wrong shape for “paste this permalink into the ticket.”

WhoCanUse

WhoCanUse is a free browser tool (open source, GitHub: CoreyGinnivan/whocanuse) that starts from a contrast ratio and then shows how that pair may look under several visual conditions. The site describes regular trichromatic vision, several red/green/blue deficiencies, achromatopsia, plus simulations for cataracts, glaucoma, low vision, direct sunlight, and Night Shift. Population percentages are attributed to colour-blindness.com and Vision Australia; the site itself warns that those estimates do not add up to 100% and do not cover every impairment.

The project says contrast comes from chroma.js, grades also consider font size and weight, and colour-blind simulations use the color-blind library. Cataracts, glaucoma, low vision, and the situational modes are described as personally created simulations — useful as illustrations, not clinical measurements. A failing grade is explained as a combination that “offers some visual strain” and “should be avoided if possible,” which is broader language than a strict WCAG table.

No price or account is mentioned. The homepage describes client-side libraries for the math and simulations; whether the hosted site also runs analytics is not stated there — unknown.

Best fit: critiques where the question is not only “does this pair pass AA?” but “who might struggle with it, and under what conditions?” Trade-off: the simulations are approximations; it is less of a token-handoff or audit-export tool than WebAIM or CCA.

colourcontrast.cc

colourcontrast.cc is a free Colour Contrast Checker by Alex Clapperton. The live page (verified 22 November 2026) shows pass/fail for AA Large, AAA Large, AA Normal, and AAA Normal; background and foreground fields; RGB and HSL slider tabs; copy-to-clipboard; reverse colours; a “Save colours” control; a “Select Google font” control; and large and normal example copy. Query parameters work as a share mechanism: https://colourcontrast.cc/?background=ffffff&foreground=000000 reloads those values in the inputs.

A dedicated non-text / UI-component 3:1 row was not present in the page UI reviewed for this article. Alpha inputs and a system eyedropper were also not found there. How “Save colours” is stored, and for how many pairs, is not documented on the page — unknown. Choosing a Google font implies a request to Google Fonts for preview.

Best fit: a clean, shareable pair checker with HSL controls and a font preview, without installing software. Trade-off: no documented non-text contrast row, and no documented colour-vision simulator.

Colour Contrast Analyser

The colour contrast analyser on Uwarp is a free browser tool for foreground and background pairs. The product page says it computes WCAG 2.x relative luminance, (Llighter + 0.05) / (Ldarker + 0.05), and lists pass/fail rows it describes as “above 3:1” (AA Large), “above 4.5:1” (AA normal and AAA Large), and “above 7:1” (AAA normal). Those “above” phrases are the page’s wording, not the standard. WCAG 2 uses at least: a ratio of 3:1, 4.5:1, or 7:1 meets the relevant criterion. Equality counts as a pass. Inputs are six-digit hex fields plus RGB and HSL sliders. You can reverse a pair, save up to six recent combinations in localStorage on that device, preview large and normal copy, optionally choose from a Google Fonts list (described as the top 50 by popularity), and reload a pair from background and foreground query parameters.

The page is explicit about scope: WCAG 2.x relative luminance, “not APCA, not print ink or window tint simulation.” Ratio math is described as client-side, with colours “not uploaded for analysis.” Optional Google Fonts previews, if used, would still request those font files from Google.

What it does not document, compared with some tools above: a separate non-text / UI-component 3:1 result, foreground alpha, a screen eyedropper, or colour-vision simulations. The saved-pair limit is six, locally, on that browser.

Best fit: a quick, shareable hex-pair check in the same browser style as colourcontrast.cc, with a clearly stated WCAG 2.x formula and a small local swatch history. Trade-off: it is not a substitute for CCA when you need to sample pixels off a PDF or a native window, and it is not a substitute for WhoCanUse when you need deficiency simulations.

Choose by the job, not by a composite score

Use WebAIM when you want the most widely referenced browser checker, including the non-text 3:1 row and an official API. Use CCA when the colours live on screen in a file or app, not already as hex tokens. Use WhoCanUse when the review needs simulations and a reminder that a ratio is about people, not only a badge. Use colourcontrast.cc or Uwarp when the workflow is “paste two values, preview type, share or save the pair.” Between those last two, the documented differences are practical: Uwarp publishes a six-pair localStorage cap and an explicit “not APCA” scope note; colourcontrast.cc exposes a working ?background=&foreground= share URL and the same hex/RGB/HSL plus font-preview pattern, but does not document a non-text row or a save-limit.

If the work is a design system or a production UI, use more than one of these for different questions — token contrast, on-screen sampling, and simulation — and still inspect the real component states. A passing pair in a checker does not guarantee that placeholder text, disabled buttons, or icons meet the same bar.

title: You Can't Eyeball a Geometry Library
description:
I have a side project whose entire purpose is to make letters look like a teenager went at them with a spray can. You type a word, it fattens into one connected outline, then a stack of warps shoves it around until it reads as graffiti. It is a deeply unserious project. So naturally I spent a weekend building a forensic area-diff tool to referee it, because that is apparently who I am.

Here's how the unseriousness turned serious. One step in the pipeline is a polygon offset — grow a closed shape outward by N pixels to draw the outline. Textbook geometry, and JavaScript has at least three grown-up libraries that do it. The sensible move is to pick the one with the nicest README and never think about it again.

I thought about it. Turns out two of the three produce byte-for-byte identical geometry, the third quietly fibs, and you cannot see any of that with your eyes. Which is the whole point.

The project in question. Deeply unserious. Note the two boring faces on the bottom — a plain serif and a monospace — because they end up mattering far more than they look.

TL;DR: Three JavaScript polygon-offset libraries, tested with a symmetric-difference-area diff instead of eyeballing the shapes. Two turned out to be geometrically identical (0.000% apart) and just a speed pick between them. The third — the popular, ergonomic one — quietly drifted up to 10% on delicate serif shapes, while also being 10–30× slower. The numbers:

Engine vs. reference (XOR area) speed
JS port of the reference 0.000% 1× (reference)
WASM build of the same 0.000% 2–4× faster
The charming third one 0.4–2.8% (display) · up to 10% (serif) 10–30× slower

Why Can't You Just Eyeball Two Outlines?

Geometry is where visual inspection goes to embarrass itself. Two offset outlines of the same word can look pixel-identical in the browser and differ by thousands of points under the hood. Or look identical and be off by a third of a unit — nothing, a rounding shrug — that then compounds through a boolean union into a genuinely wrong shape. Show me two outlines side by side and I will confidently tell you they match. I will be wrong, and I will be sure.

A screenshot diff would have blessed all three libraries. A point count would have told me they were different without telling me whether the difference was a problem or a personality. Neither is the question I actually had.

For filled shapes the honest metric is area — specifically the symmetric difference. Lay outline A over outline B, keep the bits that belong to exactly one of them (an XOR), and measure that leftover area as a percentage of the reference. Two engines that truly agree score zero. One that drifts tells you how far, in a number that means something.

So instead of choosing a library, I built a tiny courtroom. Same word, same font, same offset distance, run through each engine, then diff against Clipper as the reference:

areaXOR(a, b) / areaFill(a) * 100   // 0% = geometrically identical

Which Libraries Turned Out to Be Identical?

First verdict, and it's the comforting one: two of the three "different" libraries scored 0.000% against each other. Every font. No daylight between them at all.

Which is not luck — it's a fact I could only know because I checked. One is a pure-JavaScript port of a famous C++ geometry library; the other is that same C++ hauled into WebAssembly. Same DNA, two upbringings. You'd hope the port is faithful, but "hope" is not a test, and reimplementations drift for a living — an off-by-one in a fill rule, a rounding mode nobody documented, an edge case the port author simply never hit. A flat 0.000% XOR area across a pile of wildly different letterforms is what "faithful" looks like when you make it say a number out loud.

And once you know they're twins, the choice stops being about right-and-wrong and becomes a drag race. The WASM build ran 2–4× faster for identical output. Done: fast twin in the hot path, readable JavaScript twin kept around as the reference and for headless scripts. Easy call — but only easy because the geometry question got answered first, instead of being assumed away.

Which Library Quietly Drifted?

The third library is the popular, ergonomic one. Gorgeous API, wonderful at boolean ops, firm handshake, remembers your name. Against the reference it scored 0.4% to 2.8% on the graffiti display fonts. Small enough to wave off — "close enough, ship it" — especially since, again, the shapes looked fine.

Then I added the narcs.

I dropped two boring reference faces into the test set — a plain serif and a monospace, the typographic equivalent of a hall monitor — right next to the loud graffiti fonts. The drift on those didn't stay small. It jumped to around 6% on the monospace and 10% on the serif.

That jump is the actual lesson wearing a disguise. The library drifted worst exactly where the geometry was most delicate — thin serifs, hairline stems, tight little counters — which is, of course, precisely the case you can least afford to get wrong. On a fat spray-paint letter a 10% error has nowhere to hide and nothing to ruin. On a hairline serif it has the run of the place. If I'd only tested the "real" inputs — the display fonts the project is actually about — the 10% case would never have shown up, and I'd have happily shipped a subtly broken outline on the exact shapes that expose it. The most boring font in the drawer was the most useful witness in the room.

Grey is the reference offset. Top: the WASM engine (green) traces it exactly — 0.000%. Bottom: paper.js (red) floats a hair outside the true edge, everywhere at once. That gap is the drift — and notice you only spot it because someone drew both lines on the same shape. Left to their own panels, all three outlines look completely fine.

It was also 10–30× slower than the WASM engine, so it managed to be both wrong and last. The slowness I'd have caught on my own eventually, the way you notice a room's gotten cold. The geometric drift I would not have — not without pointing a diff at the right quantity.

Why Was the Measurement Tool Itself the Bottleneck?

One more finding, filed under quietly-embarrassing. To score "quality" I'd written a metric that counts self-intersections in an outline — the classic smell of a warp gone feral. First implementation was the obvious one: every edge against every other edge, O(n²). Correct. Honest. Fine.

It was also, once the comparison grid grew to a hundred-plus renderings each carrying thousands of points, the single slowest thing in the whole project — slower than all the actual geometry it was hired to evaluate. I had built a courtroom and the bailiff weighed more than the defendant. The fix was to stop hand-rolling it and let the geometry library resolve self-intersections with a sweep-line (SimplifyPolygon, O(n log n)) and compare the result. Same signal, a whole complexity class lighter.

Say it plainly, because it's easy to forget: the tooling you build to measure a thing is also code, and it is fully capable of being the bottleneck. A benchmark harness slower than what it benchmarks. A linter slower than the compile. A quality metric slower than the render. All the same joke, and it's usually on you.

What's the Generalizable Lesson Here?

  • "Drop-in replacement" is a claim about the API, not the output. For anything numeric or geometric, prove it with a diff before you trust it. Two libraries agreeing on function signatures tells you nothing about whether they agree on answers.
  • Pick a diff that speaks the domain. For filled outlines that's symmetric-difference area — not a point count, and for the love of god not a screenshot. The right metric turns "looks the same" into "0.000%" or "10%, exactly where it hurts."
  • Test the inputs most likely to break, not the flattering ones. The dull serif I almost didn't bother adding is the one that ratted out the drift. Boring, delicate, and adversarial cases carry more information than the happy path — invite them.
  • Settle correctness as a number and the rest of the decision falls out. Two engines proven identical collapse to a pure speed pick; one that's slower and wrong disqualifies itself. A good measurement doesn't just inform the argument, it ends it.
  • Watch the harness, not just the subject. Your quality metric can be asymptotically worse than the thing it's judging. Weigh the bailiff.

The whole rig — diff harness, warp pipeline, and the graffiti it was all secretly in service of — is open source if you'd like to poke at it: github.com/jhalitschke/warp-lab.

title: Gradle Under the Hood: Hybrid JPMS Process Isolation & Dynamic Module Reflection
description:
Over the first four articles of our Gradle Under the Hood series, we explored source-driven incremental tracking, network-immune classloader harvesting, compile-only dependency isolation, and our federated plugin architecture.

Today, in Part 5, we tackle one of the biggest friction points in modern enterprise Java builds: How do you run build-time JPA tooling—like bytecode enhancement, schema validation, and query linting—against modular Java applications (module-info.java) without forcing developers to weaken their module encapsulation?

Let’s look at how we engineered JPersist v1.9.0 to support hybrid JPMS execution, dynamic ModuleDescriptor reflection opens, and vendor-specific provider settings out of the box.

The JPMS Build-Time Tooling Wall

The Java Platform Module System (JPMS) provides strong encapsulation and reliable configuration. However, build-time persistence tools—especially Hibernate—rely heavily on deep reflection (Field.setAccessible(true)) to inspect entity classes, generate metamodels, and validate schemas.

When a project introduces a module-info.java descriptor, standard Gradle workers running on a flat classpath hit a wall:

  1. Encapsulation Blockades: Unless the user explicitly adds opens com.example.domain to io.github.jpersist.tools.hibernate.orm; inside their production module-info.java, Hibernate throws an InaccessibleObjectException during schema validation or query linting. Forcing developers to pollute production module descriptors just to satisfy build-time linters is an anti-pattern.
  2. Process Fork Overhead: Running every project inside a forked JVM process (processIsolation) guarantees modular boundaries, but adds unnecessary startup latency for traditional, non-modular classpath projects.

The Solution: Hybrid Execution Isolation (JPMSWorkerSupport)

To get the best of both worlds, we designed JPMSWorkerSupport—a hybrid execution router that inspects the target source set's compiled output directory at task execution time:

static boolean isModularProject(File classesDir) {
    return classesDir != null && new File(classesDir, "module-info.class").exists()
}

Depending on whether module-info.class is present, JPersist dynamically chooses the optimal Gradle WorkerExecutor isolation strategy:

  • Non-Modular Projects (Classpath): Executes in-process using fast classLoaderIsolation, avoiding any JVM fork overhead.
  • Modular Projects (JPMS): Switches automatically to hermetic OS-level processIsolation, placing the user's classes and dependencies onto --module-path while keeping Gradle's worker action bridge files on the bootstrap classpath.

Dynamic ModuleDescriptor Inspection & --add-opens Injection

To prevent users from having to manually open their entity packages in module-info.java, JPMSWorkerSupport reads the compiled module-info.class binary directly using Java's standard java.lang.module.ModuleDescriptor API before spawning the worker JVM:

private static void appendDynamicUserModuleOpens(File moduleInfoFile, List<String> jvmArgs) {
    try {
        byte[] bytes = Files.readAllBytes(moduleInfoFile.toPath())
        ModuleDescriptor descriptor = ModuleDescriptor.read(ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes))
        String moduleName = descriptor.name()

        descriptor.packages().each { String pkg ->
            jvmArgs.add('--add-opens')
            jvmArgs.add("\${moduleName}/pkg={HIBERNATE_MODULES}".toString())
        }
    } catch (Exception ignored) {
        // Safe fallback if module-info.class cannot be parsed
    }
}

At runtime, JPersist automatically constructs the exact --add-opens <userModule>/<package>=io.github.jpersist.tools.hibernate.orm,io.github.jpersist.tools.hibernate flags for the forked worker JVM. Production encapsulation stays completely intact, while build-time tools get temporary, scoped reflective access.

Dual-Layer SPI Resolution (ModuleLayer vs. ClassLoader)

Because workers can now boot either on a JPMS --module-path or a traditional ClassLoader, our underlying SPI resolution layer (PersistenceServiceResolver) adapts dynamically inside the worker process:

  • When ModuleLayer.boot() contains our io.github.jpersist.tools.api module, factories (NamedObjectParserFactory, SchemaValidatorFactory, EnhancerProvider) are discovered via ServiceLoader.load(ModuleLayer.boot(), serviceType).
  • Otherwise, it falls back seamlessly to Thread.currentThread().contextClassLoader.

Fine-Tuning Provider Behavior with Custom settings

Real-world enterprise schemas often rely on custom SQL dialects, specific default schemas, or strict JPA compliance flags. In v1.9.0, we also exposed @Input @Optional MapProperty<String, Object> getSettings() across both LinterExtension and ValidationExtension:

persistence {
    main {
        validation {
            settings = [
                'hibernate.default_schema': 'APP_CORE',
                'hibernate.physical_naming_strategy': 'org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy'
            ]
        }
        linter {
            settings = [
                'hibernate.dialect': 'org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQLDialect',
                'hibernate.jpa.compliance.query': 'true'
            ]
        }
    }
}

These properties are serialized cleanly across the Gradle Configuration Cache boundary and passed directly into the isolated worker's SPI factory initialization.

The Engineering Win

By combining hybrid worker isolation with bytecode-level ModuleDescriptor inspection, JPersist v1.9.0 removes the friction of adopting JPMS in enterprise persistence projects:

  1. Clean Production Descriptors: Zero need to pollute module-info.java with build-tool-only opens directives.
  2. Zero Overhead for Legacy Modules: Non-modular subprojects inside the same multi-module build continue running in-process without spawning extra JVMs.
  3. Full Vendor Control: Custom dialects, naming strategies, and compliance settings propagate cleanly into isolated worker sandboxes.

Are you adopting JPMS (module-info.java) in your enterprise Java builds, and what build-tool hurdles have you run into? Let's discuss in the comments below!

🔗 Explore the complete JPersist architecture on GitHub: https://github.com/jpersist/persistence

title: [GUIA AWS CLOUD PRACTITIONER] #04 - ALCANCE GLOBAL
description:
A infraestrutura global da Amazon Web Services (AWS) permite que aplicações e serviços sejam implantados em diferentes partes do mundo, oferecendo recursos para melhorar a disponibilidade, reduzir a latência e atender a requisitos específicos de conformidade e custos.

Neste módulo, vamos explorar os principais componentes dessa infraestrutura, os critérios para escolher uma Região AWS e as ferramentas utilizadas para provisionar e gerenciar recursos.

1. Infraestrutura Global da AWS

A infraestrutura global da AWS é formada por diferentes componentes geográficos, cada um com uma função específica na entrega de serviços em nuvem.

Regiões AWS

As Regiões são áreas geográficas distribuídas pelo mundo que concentram a infraestrutura da AWS. Cada Região é composta por múltiplas Zonas de Disponibilidade.

A escolha da Região ou do conjunto de Regiões onde os recursos serão alocados depende de fatores como:

  • Demanda dos clientes.
  • Custos operacionais e de desenvolvimento.
  • Requisitos de conformidade.
  • Proximidade dos usuários finais.
  • Disponibilidade dos serviços necessários.

Zonas de Disponibilidade (Availability Zones — AZs)

As Zonas de Disponibilidade são locais isolados e independentes dentro de uma Região AWS.

Cada AZ possui infraestrutura própria de alimentação elétrica, rede e conectividade. Uma Zona de Disponibilidade pode ser composta por um ou mais data centers.

A separação entre as AZs permite distribuir recursos e reduzir o impacto de falhas localizadas em uma única zona.

Locais da Borda (Edge Locations)

Os Edge Locations são instalações menores, distribuídas estrategicamente pelo mundo, que armazenam conteúdo em cache próximo dos usuários finais.

Eles permitem entregar conteúdos, como imagens e vídeos, com menor latência, reduzindo a distância que os dados precisam percorrer.

Esses pontos de presença são utilizados pela rede de entrega de conteúdo (CDN) da AWS, principalmente por meio do Amazon CloudFront.

2. Principais Considerações ao Escolher uma Região AWS

A escolha de uma Região AWS deve considerar diferentes aspectos técnicos, legais e financeiros.

2.1. Conformidade

É necessário verificar as leis locais de proteção de dados e os requisitos regulatórios aplicáveis ao país ou à região onde os dados serão armazenados e processados.

Um exemplo é o RGPD (Regulamento Geral de Proteção de Dados), aplicado na União Europeia. Ele estabelece requisitos relacionados à coleta, ao acesso e à exclusão de dados pessoais, incluindo a necessidade de consentimento em determinadas situações.

2.2. Proximidade

A proximidade geográfica entre a Região escolhida e os usuários finais influencia diretamente a latência.

Selecionar uma Região próxima dos usuários reduz o tempo de percurso dos dados e pode melhorar o tempo de resposta das aplicações.

2.3. Disponibilidade de Recursos

Nem todos os serviços e recursos da AWS estão disponíveis em todas as Regiões.

Por isso, antes de escolher uma Região, é importante verificar se ela oferece os serviços necessários para a arquitetura planejada.

Um exemplo são as Regiões AWS GovCloud, que possuem controles específicos de segurança física, operacional e de pessoal para atender a determinados requisitos de agências governamentais dos Estados Unidos.

2.4. Preços

Os custos operacionais podem variar entre as Regiões AWS.

Entre os fatores que influenciam essas diferenças estão:

  • Alíquotas tributárias.
  • Incentivos fiscais locais.
  • Custos operacionais.
  • Leis de soberania de dados, que podem exigir que determinadas informações sejam armazenadas localmente.

Portanto, a Região mais próxima nem sempre será necessariamente a opção de menor custo.

3. Alta Disponibilidade, Agilidade e Elasticidade

Três conceitos importantes para compreender a infraestrutura global e a arquitetura em nuvem são alta disponibilidade, agilidade e elasticidade.

Alta Disponibilidade

É a capacidade de um sistema continuar operando sem interrupções significativas, mesmo diante da falha de componentes individuais.

Na AWS, uma das estratégias para alcançar alta disponibilidade é distribuir recursos entre múltiplas Zonas de Disponibilidade e, quando necessário, entre diferentes Regiões.

Essa distribuição reduz a dependência de uma única localização física.

Agilidade

É a capacidade de adaptar rapidamente a infraestrutura às mudanças nas necessidades do negócio ou do mercado.

A nuvem permite implantar, modificar e ajustar serviços de maneira mais rápida, sem depender exclusivamente da aquisição e instalação de equipamentos físicos.

Elasticidade

É a capacidade de aumentar ou diminuir automaticamente os recursos computacionais conforme a demanda.

Por exemplo, uma aplicação pode ampliar sua capacidade durante um período de grande acesso e reduzi-la quando a demanda diminuir.

4. Elementos-Chave da Infraestrutura Global da AWS

Os três principais elementos apresentados neste módulo são:

Elemento Características Finalidade
Regiões AWS Áreas geográficas compostas por múltiplas Zonas de Disponibilidade Distribuir recursos pelo mundo
Zonas de Disponibilidade (AZs) Locais isolados e independentes dentro de uma Região, compostos por um ou mais data centers Aumentar a disponibilidade e reduzir o impacto de falhas
Edge Locations Pontos de presença distribuídos geograficamente que armazenam conteúdo em cache Entregar conteúdo aos usuários com menor latência

Esses componentes trabalham em conjunto para permitir que aplicações sejam executadas em diferentes localidades e entreguem conteúdo de maneira eficiente aos usuários finais.

5. AWS CloudFormation e Infraestrutura como Código (IaC)

O AWS CloudFormation é um serviço que permite modelar e provisionar recursos da AWS por meio de arquivos de modelo, conhecidos como templates.

Essa abordagem é chamada de Infraestrutura como Código (Infrastructure as Code — IaC).

Em vez de criar e configurar cada recurso manualmente, é possível descrever a infraestrutura desejada em um arquivo e utilizar esse modelo para automatizar sua implantação.

Benefícios do CloudFormation

  • Automação: reduz a necessidade de configurações manuais.
  • Consistência: permite reproduzir configurações padronizadas.
  • Confiabilidade: reduz erros associados à implantação manual.
  • Escalabilidade: facilita a implantação de infraestruturas maiores.
  • Reprodutibilidade: permite utilizar o mesmo modelo em diferentes ambientes e Regiões.

Casos de Uso

O CloudFormation pode ser utilizado em diferentes cenários, como:

  • Automação de implantações em pipelines de CI/CD (DevOps).
  • Provisionamento padronizado de recursos.
  • Implantação de instâncias Amazon EC2.
  • Expansão de aplicações para múltiplas Regiões AWS.

A Infraestrutura como Código facilita o gerenciamento de ambientes complexos, permitindo que a infraestrutura seja versionada, reutilizada e implantada de maneira automatizada.

6. Formas de Interagir com as APIs da AWS

A AWS oferece diferentes maneiras de acessar e gerenciar seus serviços. As principais formas apresentadas são o acesso programático, o Console de Gerenciamento e as ferramentas de Infraestrutura como Código.

6.1. AWS CLI e SDKs — Acesso Programático

O acesso programático é indicado principalmente para desenvolvedores e profissionais técnicos familiarizados com programação e linhas de comando.

AWS CLI (Command Line Interface)

É uma interface de linha de comando que permite executar operações nos serviços AWS por meio de comandos e scripts.

Um exemplo de utilização é a automação de rotinas de backup de volumes Amazon EBS.

AWS SDKs (Software Development Kits)

São bibliotecas que permitem integrar as APIs da AWS diretamente ao código-fonte das aplicações.

Um exemplo é utilizar um SDK para implementar a gravação de arquivos no Amazon S3 a partir de uma aplicação.

6.2. Console de Gerenciamento da AWS

O Console de Gerenciamento da AWS é uma interface gráfica acessada pelo navegador.

É uma alternativa para iniciantes na computação em nuvem ou usuários que preferem gerenciar os serviços sem escrever comandos ou código.

Entre suas possibilidades de utilização estão:

  • Monitoramento visual dos recursos.
  • Consulta a painéis de faturamento e custos.
  • Gerenciamento de serviços por interfaces gráficas.
  • Acesso a serviços como Amazon QuickSight e Amazon Neptune.

6.3. Ferramentas de Infraestrutura como Código

Ferramentas como o AWS CloudFormation permitem descrever a infraestrutura de maneira declarativa e automatizar o provisionamento de ambientes completos.

Em vez de configurar cada recurso individualmente pelo Console, o usuário define o estado desejado em um template, que pode ser utilizado para implantar e reproduzir a infraestrutura.

7. Resumo do Módulo

Neste módulo, vimos como a infraestrutura global da AWS é organizada e quais fatores devem ser considerados ao escolher onde implantar recursos.

Os principais conceitos são:

  • Regiões AWS: áreas geográficas que concentram a infraestrutura da AWS.
  • Zonas de Disponibilidade: locais isolados dentro de uma Região, utilizados para aumentar a disponibilidade.
  • Edge Locations: pontos de presença que armazenam conteúdo em cache próximo dos usuários, reduzindo a latência.
  • Conformidade: atendimento às leis e aos requisitos regulatórios aplicáveis.
  • Proximidade: escolha de Regiões próximas dos usuários para melhorar o tempo de resposta.
  • Disponibilidade de recursos: verificação dos serviços oferecidos em cada Região.
  • Preços: consideração das diferenças de custos entre Regiões.
  • Alta disponibilidade: capacidade de continuar operando mesmo diante de falhas.
  • Agilidade: capacidade de adaptar rapidamente a infraestrutura.
  • Elasticidade: ajuste automático dos recursos conforme a demanda.
  • AWS CloudFormation: serviço de Infraestrutura como Código para automatizar o provisionamento.
  • AWS CLI e SDKs: ferramentas para acessar os serviços AWS programaticamente.
  • Console de Gerenciamento: interface gráfica para administrar e monitorar os recursos.

Conclusão

A infraestrutura global da AWS permite construir aplicações distribuídas, com maior disponibilidade e menor latência para usuários em diferentes partes do mundo.

Compreender a diferença entre Regiões, Zonas de Disponibilidade e Edge Locations é fundamental para planejar arquiteturas eficientes. Além disso, fatores como conformidade, proximidade, disponibilidade de serviços e custos devem orientar a escolha da Região.

Por fim, ferramentas como o AWS CloudFormation, a AWS CLI e os SDKs tornam o gerenciamento da infraestrutura mais automatizado, padronizado e reproduzível.

Esses conceitos formam a base para projetar e administrar soluções em nuvem que atendam às necessidades técnicas e operacionais de diferentes organizações.

title: Hermes Agent + local Gemma(llama)
description:
Switching Between a Home LLM and a Free Cloud Model — Safely

A practical setup with llama.cpp + Tailscale + OpenRouter + Hermes Agent
By Matis atelier

About the date of this information
Everything here reflects the state of the software as of August 2026, when I read the Hermes Agent source code directly because I could not find this behavior documented. Official documentation has probably improved since then. Check the current docs first; treat this article as the "why it behaves that way" companion, not as the final word. Config key names may have changed.
All IPs, keys, hostnames and paths below are placeholders.

1. The goal

I run an LLM at home (llama.cpp, Gemma 4 12B) and an agent (Hermes Agent) on a VPS. I wanted:

Situation Behavior
Home server is up Use the home LLM
Home server is down Use a free cloud model (OpenRouter)
The free model also fails Retry, and surface an error if it still fails

Why bother? The home box is not on 24/7 (power schedule), and free cloud models are rate-limited when you need them most. Combining both is cheap and resilient.

 Telegram / cron
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────┐   Tailscale (encrypted)   ┌────────────────────┐
│ Agent (VPS)  │ ────────────────────────► │ Home LLM server    │
│              │   Bearer token required   │ llama.cpp          │
└──────┬───────┘                           └────────────────────┘
       │ if unreachable / failing
       ▼
  OpenRouter  (openrouter/free)

2. Step 1 — Lock down the local server first

A local LLM endpoint is an unauthenticated compute resource unless you protect it.

a) Require an API key in llama.cpp

llama serve -m <model.gguf> --host <bind-address> --port 8080 \
  --api-key <long-random-token>

Generate the token with openssl rand -hex 32. In systemd, remember the trailing \ on every continued ExecStart= line, or the flag is silently dropped. Then daemon-reload and restart.

b) Reach it over a private network, not the open internet

Use Tailscale (or WireGuard). Important: both ends need the client installed. I assumed the VPS side already had it; it did not, so every connection timed out until I installed it. Verify with tailscale status on both machines.

c) Don't bind more widely than you need

--host 0.0.0.0 listens on every interface. The API key is a good last line of defense, but prefer binding to the Tailscale address (or firewalling port 8080 to the Tailscale interface) and restricting who can reach it with Tailscale ACLs.

d) Keep secrets out of chat logs, tickets and screenshots. If a token ever lands somewhere public, rotate it.

3. Step 2 — Register the server in the agent (the gotcha that cost me hours)

The obvious config:

model:
  provider: custom
  base_url: http://<tailscale-ip>:8080/v1

plus OPENAI_API_KEY in the environment. Result: 401 Invalid API Key — while curl with the same key from inside the same container returned 200.

Reading the credential resolver showed why. For a bare provider: custom with a base_url, the generic OPENAI_API_KEY fallback was only used when the host was openai.com / openai.azure.com. For any other host the key was silently dropped and replaced by a "no-key-required" placeholder. This looks like a deliberate guard against leaking a generic key to arbitrary endpoints — sensible, but silent.

Fix: register a named custom provider with an explicit key_env:

model:
  default: <model-name-or-path>
  provider: "custom:home-llm"
  api_mode: chat_completions

providers:
  "custom:home-llm":
    base_url: http://<tailscale-ip>:8080/v1
    key_env: OPENAI_API_KEY        # name of the env var that holds the token
    default_model: <model-name-or-path>
    request_timeout_seconds: 120   # see "Unresolved" below

fallback_model:
  provider: openrouter
  model: openrouter/free

Named providers resolve the key through the explicit key_env lookup and skip the hostname gate. I used OPENAI_API_KEY as the variable name; the code suggests any name works, but I did not test other names.

Note the model name: llama.cpp reports the model's file path as its ID in /v1/models, so that is what you put in default.

4. Step 3 — The fallback

fallback_model takes a single provider/model (a list is also accepted for a chain). When the primary exhausts its retries on a connection or rate-limit error, the agent switches over automatically. I observed it working:

Max retries (3) exhausted — trying fallback...
Primary model failed — switching to fallback ...

Choosing the fallback model mattered:

  1. A specific model that was retired (HTTP 404: No endpoints found) → total failure.
  2. A specific free model that was busy (HTTP 429) → total failure.
  3. openrouter/free — OpenRouter's router that picks from currently available free models and filters for features your request needs → far more resilient.

Caveat: free-tier rate limits are account-wide, so openrouter/free reduces, but does not eliminate, 429s. If the free fallback also fails, the request errors out after its retries (it does not wait forever); a scheduled job simply tries again on its next run.

5. Pitfall checklist

Symptom Cause Fix
Timeouts to the home server Tailscale missing on one end Install and join on both machines
401 with a correct key Hostname gate on generic env key Named provider + key_env
.env change ignored docker restart does not reload env; compose had no env_file Add env_file: .env, then docker compose up -d --force-recreate
Key looks like it ends in \r docker exec -it pseudo-TTY adds it to output Re-check without -t; the value was fine
systemd flag has no effect Missing trailing \ in ExecStart= Fix continuation lines
Every request times out with long prompts Draft-model / speculative decoding overhead and small context I removed the draft model and raised -c to 65536

6. Step 4 — Don't wait minutes when the server is powered off

When the home machine is powered off, nothing answers the TCP SYN, so there is no quick "connection refused". Each attempt waited roughly 30 seconds, and with retries plus an extra primary retry round, switching took about 3 minutes. Painful for every message sent while the box is off.

(request_timeout_seconds did not seem to change this. See "Unresolved".)

A fixed-time schedule is fragile: boot takes a while before the model is ready, and shutdown (mine is triggered by a power-consumption watchdog) is not at a precise time. So instead of trusting the clock, health-check the server and let reality drive the switch.

The agent CLI can change config at runtime — no container recreation:

hermes config set model.provider "custom:home-llm"
hermes config set model.default  "<model-name-or-path>"

Both keys must move together; changing only the provider leaves a local file path as the model name, which the cloud provider rejects.

Watchdog (run from cron every 3 minutes):

#!/bin/bash
# home-llm-watchdog.sh
set -u
source /etc/home-llm-watchdog.env   # chmod 600; defines HOME_LLM_URL, HOME_LLM_KEY, LOCAL_MODEL
STATE_FILE=/var/lib/home-llm-watchdog.state
LOG_FILE=/var/log/home-llm-watchdog.log

CURRENT=dead
code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 3 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${HOME_LLM_KEY}" "${HOME_LLM_URL}/models" 2>/dev/null)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && CURRENT=alive

PREVIOUS=$(cat "$STATE_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
if [ "$CURRENT" != "$PREVIOUS" ]; then
  if [ "$CURRENT" = alive ]; then
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.provider "custom:home-llm" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.default  "$LOCAL_MODEL"    >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
  else
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.provider "openrouter"      >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.default  "openrouter/free" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
  fi
  echo "[$(date '+%F %T')] $PREVIOUS -> $CURRENT" >>"$LOG_FILE"
  echo "$CURRENT" >"$STATE_FILE"
fi

*/3 * * * * /usr/local/bin/home-llm-watchdog.sh

Design notes:

  • State file → only acts when the state flips; no log noise or needless writes.
  • Keep the built-in fallback too. If the server is supposed to be up but crashed, the watchdog still detects it, and the retry-then-fallback path remains a safety net in between checks.
  • The secret lives in a 600 file instead of the script. (The first version I ran had it inline; don't copy that.)

Verified end-to-end: the machine powered on by its timer, and within 3 minutes the agent switched back to the local model by itself.

7. Security checklist

  • [ ] API key required on the local server
  • [ ] Private network (Tailscale/WireGuard), installed on both ends
  • [ ] Bind address / firewall narrower than 0.0.0.0 on the open internet
  • [ ] Tailscale ACL limits which nodes can reach the port
  • [ ] Secrets in 600 files, never in scripts, chat logs or screenshots
  • [ ] Rotate any token that was exposed
  • [ ] Prefer explicit key_env per provider over a generic key that could be sent to the wrong host

8. Unresolved

  • request_timeout_seconds appeared to have no effect on the effective wait; I did not find the cause. Renaming the providers key to match custom:<name> did not change it. Newer versions may differ.
  • A harmless warning about missing endpoint credentials appeared from an auxiliary (non-chat) task; it did not affect normal conversations.
  • Selecting which local model (e.g. Gemma vs. Qwen) is a separate layer from this up/down switch; I kept this to liveness only.

Summary

  1. Secure the local server (token + private network), on both ends.
  2. Register it as a named custom provider with key_env.
  3. Use openrouter/free as the fallback.
  4. If the box is power-scheduled, add a health-check watchdog that flips config with hermes config set.

Hermes Agent behavior described here was observed in August 2026. Check current official docs before relying on it.

自宅のローカルLLMと無料クラウドモデルを安全に切り替える

llama.cpp + Tailscale + OpenRouter + Hermes Agent で作る実践構成
Matis atelier

この情報の時点について
本記事の内容は 2026年8月時点 のものです。公式ドキュメントに該当の記述が見つからなかったため、Hermes Agent のソースコードを直接読んで挙動を確認しました。その後、公式情報は充実している可能性が高いです。まず最新の公式ドキュメントを確認してください。 本記事は「なぜそう動くのか」を補う読み物として使い、設定キー名などは変わっている可能性がある点にご注意ください。
文中のIP・キー・ホスト名・パスはすべてダミーです。

1. 目的

自宅でLLM（llama.cpp / Gemma 4 12B）を動かし、VPS上のエージェント（Hermes Agent）から使います。やりたいことは次の通りです。

状況 動作
自宅サーバーが起動している 自宅のLLMを使う
自宅サーバーが止まっている 無料のクラウドモデル（OpenRouter）を使う
無料モデルも失敗した リトライし、それでもダメならエラーを返す

自宅サーバーは電気代節約のため常時起動ではなく、無料クラウドモデルは混雑すると429で弾かれます。両方を組み合わせると、安く、かつ止まりにくくなります。

 Telegram / cron
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────┐   Tailscale（暗号化）   ┌────────────────────┐
│ エージェント │ ──────────────────────► │ 自宅LLMサーバー    │
│   (VPS)      │   Bearerトークン必須    │ llama.cpp          │
└──────┬───────┘                         └────────────────────┘
       │ 到達できない／失敗したとき
       ▼
  OpenRouter（openrouter/free）

2. 手順1：まずローカルサーバーを守る

ローカルLLMのエンドポイントは、保護しなければ「誰でも使える計算資源」になってしまいます。

a) llama.cpp にAPIキーを要求させる

llama serve -m <model.gguf> --host <待ち受けアドレス> --port 8080 \
  --api-key <長いランダムなトークン>

トークンは openssl rand -hex 32 で生成します。systemdで複数行の ExecStart= を書く場合は、継続行の行末に \ が必要です。抜けると、そのオプションが黙って無視されます。編集後は daemon-reload と再起動を行ってください。

b) 公開インターネットではなく、閉じたネットワークで繋ぐ

Tailscale（またはWireGuard）を使います。重要なのは 両端にクライアントが必要 という点です。私は「VPS側にもTailscaleが入っている」と思い込んでいて、実際は未インストールでした。そのせいで接続がずっとタイムアウトしていました。両方のマシンで tailscale status を確認しましょう。

c) 必要以上に広く待ち受けない

--host 0.0.0.0 は全インターフェースで待ち受けます。APIキーは最後の砦として有効ですが、できればTailscaleのアドレスに限定するか、ファイアウォールで8080番をTailscaleインターフェースだけに絞ってください。TailscaleのACLで、到達できるノードも制限できます。

d) 秘密情報をチャットログ・チケット・スクリーンショットに残さない。 もし公開の場に出てしまったら、トークンを再発行してください。

3. 手順2：エージェントにサーバーを登録する（数時間ハマったポイント）

最初に書いた、ありがちな設定はこうです。

model:
  provider: custom
  base_url: http://<tailscale-ip>:8080/v1

これに加えて環境変数 OPENAI_API_KEY を設定しました。結果は 401 Invalid API Key。ところが、同じコンテナの中から同じキーで curl すると 200 が返ります。

認証情報を解決するコードを読んで理由が分かりました。provider: custom と base_url だけを書いた場合、汎用の OPENAI_API_KEY は ホストが openai.com / openai.azure.com のときにしか使われません。それ以外のホストでは、キーが黙って捨てられ、"no-key-required" というプレースホルダーに置き換わります。これは「汎用キーが無関係な接続先に漏れないようにする」ための意図的なガードだと思われます。理屈は妥当ですが、何も警告が出ない点が厄介です。

対処：key_env を明示した「名前付き」カスタムプロバイダーとして登録します。

model:
  default: <モデル名またはパス>
  provider: "custom:home-llm"
  api_mode: chat_completions

providers:
  "custom:home-llm":
    base_url: http://<tailscale-ip>:8080/v1
    key_env: OPENAI_API_KEY        # トークンを入れた環境変数の「名前」
    default_model: <モデル名またはパス>
    request_timeout_seconds: 120   # 後述「未解決」を参照

fallback_model:
  provider: openrouter
  model: openrouter/free

名前付きプロバイダーは key_env の明示的な参照でキーを解決するため、ホスト名によるガードを通りません。環境変数名は OPENAI_API_KEY を使いましたが、コード上は任意の名前で動きそうです（他の名前は未検証です）。

モデル名にも注意してください。llama.cpp は /v1/models でモデルの ファイルパスをそのままIDとして返す ので、default にはそれを書きます。

4. 手順3：フォールバックの設定

fallback_model には1組のプロバイダー/モデルを書きます（リスト形式でチェーンにもできます）。メインがリトライを使い切って、接続エラーやレート制限になると、自動で切り替わります。実際にログで確認できました。

Max retries (3) exhausted — trying fallback...
Primary model failed — switching to fallback ...

フォールバック先の選び方で、結果が大きく変わりました。

  1. 提供終了したモデルを指定 → HTTP 404: No endpoints found で全滅
  2. 特定の無料モデルを指定 → 混雑して HTTP 429 で全滅
  3. openrouter/free を指定 → OpenRouterのルーターが、その時使える無料モデルから、リクエストに必要な機能（画像入力やツール呼び出しなど）を満たすものを選ぶ。圧倒的に安定

注意点として、無料枠のレート制限はアカウント単位なので、openrouter/free でも429が完全になくなるわけではありません。無料フォールバックも失敗した場合は、リトライ後にエラーになります（永遠に待つわけではありません）。定期ジョブなら、次回の実行で再挑戦されます。

5. ハマりどころ一覧

症状 原因 対処
自宅サーバーへの接続がタイムアウトする 片方にTailscaleが未インストール 両方に入れてネットワークに参加させる
キーが正しいのに 401 汎用環境変数キーのホスト名ガード 名前付きプロバイダー + key_env
.env の変更が反映されない docker restart は環境変数を再読込しない／composeに env_file が無い env_file: .env を追加し、docker compose up -d --force-recreate
キーの末尾に \r が付いて見える docker exec -it の疑似TTYが出力に付けていた -t を外して再確認。値自体は正常だった
systemdのオプションが効かない ExecStart= の継続行の \ 漏れ 継続行を直す
長いプロンプトで毎回タイムアウト ドラフトモデル（投機的デコード）の負荷、コンテキスト不足 ドラフトモデルを外し、-c を65536に増やした

6. 手順4：電源が切れている間、何分も待たされないようにする

自宅マシンの 電源が落ちている と、TCPのSYNに誰も応答しないため、「接続拒否」がすぐに返ってきません。1回の試行で約30秒待たされ、リトライや追加のリトライラウンドも重なって、切り替わるまで約3分 かかっていました。電源が落ちている間は、メッセージを送るたびにこれが発生します。

（request_timeout_seconds はこの待ち時間に効いていないようでした。「未解決」を参照。）

時刻で固定的に切り替える方式は脆いです。起動後、モデルが使えるようになるまで時間がかかりますし、シャットダウンも（私の環境では消費電力監視で）ぴったりの時刻に行われません。そこで、時計を信用せず、サーバーの生死を実際に確認して、その結果で切り替えます。

エージェントのCLIには、実行中に設定を書き換えるコマンドがあり、コンテナの再作成は不要でした。

hermes config set model.provider "custom:home-llm"
hermes config set model.default  "<モデル名またはパス>"

2つのキーは 必ずセットで 変えます。プロバイダーだけ変えると、ローカルのファイルパスがモデル名として残り、クラウド側に拒否されます。

ウォッチドッグ（cronで3分おきに実行）：

#!/bin/bash
# home-llm-watchdog.sh
set -u
source /etc/home-llm-watchdog.env   # chmod 600。HOME_LLM_URL, HOME_LLM_KEY, LOCAL_MODEL を定義
STATE_FILE=/var/lib/home-llm-watchdog.state
LOG_FILE=/var/log/home-llm-watchdog.log

CURRENT=dead
code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 3 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${HOME_LLM_KEY}" "${HOME_LLM_URL}/models" 2>/dev/null)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && CURRENT=alive

PREVIOUS=$(cat "$STATE_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
if [ "$CURRENT" != "$PREVIOUS" ]; then
  if [ "$CURRENT" = alive ]; then
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.provider "custom:home-llm" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.default  "$LOCAL_MODEL"    >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
  else
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.provider "openrouter"      >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
    docker exec hermes-agent hermes config set model.default  "openrouter/free" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1
  fi
  echo "[$(date '+%F %T')] $PREVIOUS -> $CURRENT" >>"$LOG_FILE"
  echo "$CURRENT" >"$STATE_FILE"
fi

*/3 * * * * /usr/local/bin/home-llm-watchdog.sh

設計のポイント：

  • 状態ファイルで、状態が変わったときだけ動作します。無駄な書き込みやログの増加を避けられます。
  • 標準のフォールバックも残す。 「起動しているはずの時間帯に落ちた」場合も、ウォッチドッグが検知しますし、検知までの間は従来のリトライ→フォールバックが安全網になります。
  • 秘密情報はスクリプトに直書きせず、600 のファイルに置きます。（私が最初に実行したスクリプトは直書きでした。真似しないでください。）

実機で確認できました。電源タイマーでマシンが起動し、3分以内にエージェントが自動でローカルモデルへ戻りました。

7. セキュリティチェックリスト

  • [ ] ローカルサーバーにAPIキーを要求させている
  • [ ] 閉じたネットワーク（Tailscale/WireGuard）を 両端 に入れている
  • [ ] 待ち受けを 0.0.0.0 のままにせず、バインドアドレスかファイアウォールで絞っている
  • [ ] TailscaleのACLで、到達できるノードを制限している
  • [ ] 秘密情報は 600 のファイルに置き、スクリプト・チャットログ・スクショに載せない
  • [ ] 露出してしまったトークンは再発行する
  • [ ] 誤った接続先に送られうる汎用キーより、プロバイダーごとの明示的な key_env を使う

8. 未解決の点

  • request_timeout_seconds が実際の待ち時間に効いていないように見えましたが、原因は特定できていません。providers のキー名を custom:<name> に合わせても変化はありませんでした。新しいバージョンでは挙動が違う可能性があります。
  • 補助タスク（チャット以外の処理）で「エンドポイントの認証情報が見つからない」という警告が出ましたが、通常の会話には影響しませんでした。
  • どのローカルモデル（GemmaかQwenか）を使うかは、今回の生死切り替えとは別のレイヤーです。今回は生死判定だけに絞りました。

まとめ

  1. ローカルサーバーを守る（トークン + 閉じたネットワーク）。しかも 両端 に。
  2. 名前付き カスタムプロバイダーとして key_env 付きで登録する。
  3. フォールバックには openrouter/free を使う。
  4. 電源スケジュールがあるなら、生死判定のウォッチドッグで hermes config set を使って切り替える。

本記事のHermes Agentの挙動は2026年8月時点で確認したものです。利用の際は最新の公式ドキュメントを確認してください。

title: AI SEO Agents: What They Can Publish Daily and Where Google Draws the Line
description:
Can an agent publish a blog post every day? Yes. Whether Google rewards it depends on one phrase in its spam policy.

I read the Google pages that decide this today. Here is what they say, and where I would draw my own line.

Free stuff: grab these first

  • The open source AI Employees (AI Employees). The page says "Open source, MIT licensed AI Employees. Free to hire." One of the eight is the SEO/AEO Employee: "Improves search content and answers your buyers' questions." The page lists 60 scheduled routines across the eight roles.
  • Google's spam policies (Spam Policies for Google Web Search). The section on scaled content abuse is the one that matters here.
  • Google's guidance on generative AI content (Using generative AI content). Short page. Read all of it.
  • Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content (Google Search Central). The standard your pages get measured against.
  • Google Search Console (search.google.com/search-console). Free. It shows whether your pages are getting impressions at all.
  • IndexNow (indexnow.org). A simple ping that tells participating search engines a URL was added, updated or deleted.

What Google actually says about AI content

Not "AI content is banned." It does not say that.

The generative AI page says generative AI "can be particularly useful when researching a topic, and to add structure to original content." Then the warning: using it to generate many pages without adding value for users may violate the policy on scaled content abuse.

The spam policy defines that term as many pages "generated for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users." It adds: "no matter how it's created."

The test is not who wrote the page. The test is whether the page helps the reader.

The same policy lists examples. A few that apply to agents:

  • Using generative AI tools to generate many pages without adding value for users.
  • Scraping feeds or search results to generate many pages.
  • Stitching content from different web pages together without adding value.
  • Creating multiple sites with the intent of hiding the scaled nature of the content.

If your agent does any of those on a schedule, it is not an SEO agent. It is a liability on a timer.

What an agent can safely do every day

Publishing daily is not the problem. What goes in each post is.

  • Research a keyword and read what already ranks. Reading is free and fast.
  • Draft a post with a point of view the other results do not have. One real number, one real example.
  • Pull sources and link to them. Authority links to real pages the reader can check.
  • Generate a hero image and the alt text. Google's page says to review metadata too, including title elements, meta descriptions, structured data and image alt text.
  • Add the URL to the sitemap and ping the engines. That is what Search Console and IndexNow are for.

What I would not hand to an agent

  • Fact-checking. Google's page is blunt: models "predict a likely sequence of words," outputs "may contain inaccuracies," and it is "critical to manually factcheck and review all AI-generated content" before publishing.
  • Claims about you or your clients. An agent will happily invent a case study. A human has to delete it.
  • The decision to publish ten near-identical pages. That is the scaled content example, word for word.

Tell readers how it was made

The generative AI page suggests giving readers context on how the content was created, "such as by providing more background information on how automation was used." I think that is good practice for trust, not only for Google. One line at the bottom of a post does it.

A realistic daily loop

  1. Pick one keyword from a list you wrote.
  2. Have the agent pull the top results and list what they all miss.
  3. Draft around the gap.
  4. You read it. You fix the facts. You cut anything you cannot stand behind.
  5. Publish, add to the sitemap, ping IndexNow.
  6. Check Search Console a week later. Keep what earns impressions, rewrite what does not.

Step 4 is the whole business. Skip it and you are on the wrong side of the policy page.

Where I would start

The SEO/AEO Employee in the open source library is built for the research and drafting half of that loop. It is free and MIT licensed. Install it, point it at one site, and read every draft before it goes live. If one post a day feels like too much to review, run one a week until it does not.

One small ask

If you run an agent that publishes for you, tell me in the comments what you check by hand before it goes out. I read all of them.

I run the Vibe Coding is Life community. Come say hi in the Facebook group or the free Skool community.

title: Clean Architecture for Backend Services: When to Use It and How
description:
Many engineering teams fall into one of two architectural traps: they prematurely over-engineer simple microservices with complex abstraction layers, or they neglect architecture entirely until their core backend becomes an untestable monolith where business rules are entangled with database queries.

When you mix your framework, database, and business logic into a single unlayered codebase, swapping infrastructure components becomes a nightmare. Testing unit logic requires spinning up real database instances, and simple feature additions start breaking unrelated parts of the system.

Here is how to evaluate whether your project actually needs Clean Architecture, and how to implement it cleanly without adding unnecessary friction.

The Checklist: Do You Need Clean Architecture?

Before introducing multiple layers of abstractions, evaluate your domain against three questions:

  1. Does your domain contain complex business rules that will frequently evolve?
  2. Will multiple teams touch and extend this service over several years?
  3. Is unit testability without external dependencies (like DBs or external APIs) non-negotiable?

If you answered yes to these questions, Clean Architecture earns its keep. Your core domain stays isolated at the center, completely untouched by database migrations, framework updates, or external vendor swaps.

However, if you are building a straightforward CRUD application, a temporary prototype, or a narrow-scoped microservice, skip the overhead. A clean, single-file or basic module layout will ship faster and remain easy to manage.

Step 1: Define Core Entities and Interfaces

The innermost layer consists of your domain entities and repository interfaces. This layer has zero dependencies on web frameworks, ORMs, or database drivers.

Here is an example in Python defining a domain entity and an abstract repository interface using Protocol:

# domain/entities.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol, Optional

@dataclass
class Order:
    id: str
    total_amount: float
    is_paid: bool = False

    def mark_as_paid(self) -> None:
        if self.total_amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Cannot process payment for non-positive amount")
        self.is_paid = True


# domain/interfaces.py
class OrderRepository(Protocol):
    def get_by_id(self, order_id: str) -> Optional[Order]:
        ...

    def save(self, order: Order) -> None:
        ...

Notice how the Order entity enforces business rules (such as validating payment amounts) independently of how or where the order is stored.

Step 2: Implement Pure Application Use Cases

The next layer contains your application use cases. Each use case orchestrates the domain entities and abstract interfaces to execute a specific business operation.

# use_cases/pay_order.py
from domain.entities import Order
from domain.interfaces import OrderRepository

class PayOrderUseCase:
    def __init__(self, repository: OrderRepository):
        self.repository = repository

    def execute(self, order_id: str) -> Order:
        order = self.repository.get_by_id(order_id)
        if not order:
            raise ValueError(f"Order {order_id} not found")

        order.mark_as_paid()
        self.repository.save(order)
        return order

Because PayOrderUseCase relies on the abstract OrderRepository contract, you can test this entire flow using an in-memory mock repository without touching a live database.

Step 3: Implement Infrastructure Adapters

The outermost layer implements the concrete infrastructure components, such as database repositories, external API clients, and HTTP controllers.

# infrastructure/postgres_repository.py
from domain.entities import Order

class PostgresOrderRepository:
    def __init__(self, db_session):
        self.session = db_session

    def get_by_id(self, order_id: str) -> Order | None:
        record = self.session.query(OrderORM).filter_by(id=order_id).first()
        if not record:
            return None
        return Order(id=record.id, total_amount=record.total_amount, is_paid=record.is_paid)

    def save(self, order: Order) -> None:
        record = self.session.query(OrderORM).filter_by(id=order.id).first()
        if record:
            record.is_paid = order.is_paid
        self.session.commit()

If you ever need to replace PostgreSQL with MongoDB, DynamoDB, or an external third-party API, you only write a new adapter. Your use cases and domain entities remain completely unchanged.

Balance Abstraction with Pragmatism

Clean Architecture is a tool to manage complexity, not a goal in itself. For large-scale systems or core business services, isolating your business logic ensures longevity and testability. For simpler, single-purpose utilities, favor flat structures to maintain development speed. The real engineering skill lies in recognizing which approach the current problem demands.

About me

Tanmay builds AI agents and automation for businesses and is open to freelance projects. Feel free to connect on LinkedIn.

title: Node.js PDF Template Observability: Trace Invoice HTML Changes Through Support
description:
Keep invoice HTML in the repository when engineers own the layout; choose a stored template when finance needs to edit it without a deploy. For customer support teams turning scanned invoices into searchable text, that ownership decision should also determine where a layout investigation starts.

Short answer: a PDF template management API versus HTML in a repo is a choice about who changes the file. Git gives layout changes the application's review and rollback process. Stored templates allow changes independently of application deployment. Give each layout one owner, then carry that ownership into the records used to investigate support tickets.

Search needs context. A support agent who finds an invoice should be able to distinguish its extracted text from the layout used to produce a replacement invoice. OCR reads a scanned document. Rendering creates a document. Neither operation establishes who approved its appearance.

How should support trace PDF template changes to invoice HTML?

Before: scanned invoice → extracted text → search result. A result may answer which invoice mentions a disputed charge, but the trace says little about where to correct the layout of a replacement document.

After: scanned invoice → extracted text → searchable support record → replacement request → one recorded layout owner. The original scan remains the evidence for the customer's uploaded document; the replacement has its own layout reference. This distinction matters when a support agent sees an old address on a scan and finance has already changed the address used for newly generated invoices. A fresh render should not silently become the explanation for what the original scan contained.

Record the boundary.

For repository HTML, attach the revision selected by the application to its replacement request. For a stored template, attach the reference your application actually selected and whatever revision evidence the chosen service supports. Don't assume a template name identifies immutable content. Establish that in your service evaluation before relying on it during an investigation.

This is an observability design recommendation, not a claim that every template API supplies a revision history. The useful question is concrete: can support identify both the document it searched and the layout used for its replacement? Consider a synthetic ticket with two attachments: an uploaded scan and a newly generated replacement. They may share an invoice identifier while containing different addresses. Joining every event on that identifier alone would hide which document supplied the searchable text. Give the scan its own identifier and preserve the replacement's selected layout reference, so an investigation can follow the actual document relationship rather than infer it from matching invoice numbers.

A small Node.js example makes ownership visible

The following TypeScript example uses synthetic support data. It models the handoff after OCR has supplied text and before a renderer creates a replacement PDF. The output is escaped invoice HTML and a structured event; an actual OCR service, search index, and PDF renderer remain separate integration choices.

Copy it into a TypeScript file and run it with a TypeScript-capable Node.js setup. The example keeps one rendering branch deliberately: the selected owner is engineering, so the HTML lives with the application. Its revision is an explicit example label, not a fabricated Git commit.

type SupportInvoice = {
  ticketId: string;
  invoiceId: string;
  scanId: string;
  extractedText: string;
  replacementReason: string;
};

type RepoLayout = {
  kind: "repo-html";
  owner: "engineering";
  revision: string;
};

const invoice: SupportInvoice = {
  ticketId: "SUP-1042",
  invoiceId: "INV-208",
  scanId: "scan-17",
  extractedText: "Invoice INV-208. Support renewal.",
  replacementReason: "Customer requested a readable copy",
};

const layout: RepoLayout = {
  kind: "repo-html",
  owner: "engineering",
  revision: "example-layout-3",
};

function escapeHtml(value: string): string {
  return value
    .replaceAll("&", "&")
    .replaceAll("<", "<")
    .replaceAll(">", ">")
    .replaceAll('"', """)
    .replaceAll("'", "'");
}

function renderReplacement(record: SupportInvoice): string {
  return `<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Replacement invoice</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Invoice ${escapeHtml(record.invoiceId)}</h1>
  <p>Replacement requested through customer support.</p>
  <p>${escapeHtml(record.replacementReason)}</p>
</body>
</html>`;
}

const html = renderReplacement(invoice);
const event = {
  event: "invoice.replacement.prepared",
  ticket_id: invoice.ticketId,
  invoice_id: invoice.invoiceId,
  source_scan_id: invoice.scanId,
  layout_kind: layout.kind,
  layout_owner: layout.owner,
  layout_revision: layout.revision,
};

if (!html.includes(escapeHtml(invoice.invoiceId))) {
  throw new Error("Replacement HTML is missing its invoice identifier");
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(event));
console.log(html);

Notice what the event records: the source scan and the selected layout. The extracted text stays out of the event. These are application-defined fields, not parameters for a vendor's logging API. Feed the text into your search workflow under its own access rules; use identifiers to connect an investigation across the handoff.

There's a useful trap here. Logging a revision label doesn't preserve a layout. The repository must retain the corresponding content, or the stored-template workflow must provide equivalent evidence. Otherwise the event gives support a precise-looking identifier that cannot answer the question.

The example also avoids treating OCR text as authoritative replacement invoice data. A scanned phrase is useful for retrieval, but this demonstration doesn't validate financial amounts, addresses, or line items. That validation belongs before a production rendering request.

Compare candidates through the change path

Evaluate Puppeteer, DocRaptor, and PDFMonkey against the same invoice and the same ownership question. Their documentation provides starting points for browser-driven PDF rendering, HTML-to-PDF conversion, and managed document templates respectively. Those are different places to put the rendering boundary. A product name alone doesn't decide who should approve a layout change.

Candidate Ownership question to test Trade-off to examine
Puppeteer Can engineering keep the HTML and rendering setup under the repository's review process? Repository control also leaves the rendering setup with the engineering team.
DocRaptor Can the application submit the exact reviewed HTML needed for this invoice? A conversion service doesn't by itself establish who approves changes to the submitted HTML.
PDFMonkey Does the managed-template workflow let the intended editor make and review a change? Independent edits require a deliberate record of which template content produced a document.

These are evaluation boundaries, not benchmark results. Test 3 synthetic inputs: a long customer address, a multi-page invoice, and an OCR result containing a literal less-than sign. The first two probe the layout; the third probes how your application handles extracted text. Don't interpret successful PDF creation as proof that the invoice is searchable or that its text extraction is correct.

Infrai offers a plain REST API with a single API key and unified billing. An HTTP-capable application can call it without installing a vendor SDK. The same key spans 295 routes across 20 modules, so a support workflow evaluating OCR and PDF generation can keep credential handling together. Its public discovery surface also supplies request and response schemas for checking the contract. Evaluate its stored-template and PDF-generation workflow with the same ownership test. The integration style is useful; it doesn't select the layout owner for you.

Check the contract first.

Here is a separate, read-only contract check for that candidate. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the service's documented HTTPS API base, including its version prefix, and INFRAI_API_KEY to your environment-managed key. Run this TypeScript in a Node.js setup with native fetch. Discovery is public and requires no key; the example uses the normal Bearer header to demonstrate the authenticated client's configuration without making a document write. It prints the discovery response for inspection before you implement template creation or rendering. No undocumented document fields are assumed.

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!baseUrl || !apiKey) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY");
}
if (new URL(baseUrl).protocol !== "https:") {
  throw new Error("The API base must use HTTPS");
}

async function inspectContract(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt++) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl!.replace(/\/$/, "")}/discovery`, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 2) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("Retry-After");
      const seconds = retryAfter === null ? NaN : Number(retryAfter);
      const date = retryAfter === null ? NaN : Date.parse(retryAfter);
      const delay = Number.isFinite(seconds)
        ? Math.max(0, seconds * 1000)
        : Number.isFinite(date)
          ? Math.max(0, date - Date.now())
          : 1000 * 2 ** attempt;
      await response.text();
      await new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  }
  throw new Error("Discovery retry limit reached");
}

inspectContract().then(
  (contract) => console.log(JSON.stringify(contract, null, 2)),
  (error: unknown) => {
    console.error(error);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  },
);

The deciding exercise is small. Ask engineering and finance to describe how a changed remittance address reaches the next replacement invoice. If both teams point to different editable copies of the same layout, resolve that ambiguity before selecting a renderer.

Does finance editing without a deploy weaken review?

It changes where review must happen. A stored template can be updated without an application deploy, which is useful when finance owns the content. That benefit needs an explicit approval process and enough retained evidence to explain a generated document. Check the candidate's actual editing and revision behavior rather than assuming it mirrors Git.

For engineer-owned layouts, Git review and rollback already travel with the code. That's a good reason to keep HTML in the repository. It's a poor fit if every routine finance edit then waits for an engineer to translate and deploy it. The right boundary follows the editor's job.

Pick one owner.

Can logs and alerts settle the choice?

They can expose an unclear boundary, but they can't appoint an owner. Start with structured records connecting the support ticket, source scan, replacement request, and selected layout. Then define an application check for missing ownership evidence before rendering; count failures and alert the team responsible for that handoff. Choose alert thresholds from the support workflow rather than inventing a universal number.

Keep separate signals for extraction and replacement generation. A generation success doesn't prove that OCR captured the original scan correctly, while a useful search result doesn't prove that finance approved the replacement layout. This separation gives an investigation a clear next step: inspect the scanned evidence, the extracted text, or the selected layout.

Choose repository HTML for engineering ownership and a stored template for finance ownership. Preserve the source scan relationship in either case. That makes the template decision useful to the support agent who must explain a document later.

  • PDF format standard, ISO 32000-2
  • Puppeteer documentation
  • DocRaptor documentation
  • PDFMonkey documentation
