title: Internxt Drive audit: reproducing 13 vulnerabilities without touching production
description:
13 findings, 13 test files, 13 test logs. That was the most consequential decision in the whole audit, and it had nothing to do with the vulnerabilities.

When I started reading internxt/drive-server-wip in October 2026, I made one rule before writing a single assertion: nothing in this project would touch a production system, a real account, or a network service I did not own. The repository is public. The backend is a NestJS application with Sequelize, PostgreSQL, Valkey, a Bridge service for storage credentials, SendGrid for mail, and a fairly large e2e test harness already in the tree. All of that can be pointed at loopback. So every finding would be reproduced against a local checkout of a pinned commit, with synthetic users and disposable services, or it would not be reproduced at all.

That constraint shaped everything else. A security report is only useful if a maintainer can run it. If reproducing a finding needs a real account, a production dataset, or access to infrastructure the maintainer does not have, the report becomes an anecdote. So each finding got its own self-contained proof of concept, its own log, source references pinned to the audited commit 7d7a8be2 from 28 October, and a hash of the archive. A maintainer could run C07 without reading C08.

The first thing to build was the runner:

set -euo pipefail
case_id=${2:-}
if [[ ! "$case_id" =~ ^C(0[1-9]|1[0-3])$ || ! -f "$source_file" ]]; then
if [[ ! -f package.json || ! -x ./node_modules/.bin/jest || ! -d test/helpers ]]; then
target="test/security-poc-${case_id,,}.e2e-spec.ts"
if [[ -e "$target" ]]; then
cp -- "$source_file" "$target"
trap 'rm -f -- "$target"' EXIT
export NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-vm-modules
export NODE_ENV=test
export RDS_HOSTNAME=127.0.0.1
export RDS_PORT=55432
export RDS_DBNAME=drive_audit
export RDS_USERNAME=audit
export RDS_PASSWORD=local_only_audit_password
export REDIS_CONNECTION_STRING=redis://127.0.0.1:56379
export REDIS_JOBS_CONNECTION_STRING=redis://127.0.0.1:56379
export PCREATED_USERS_PASSWORD=local_only_precreated_password
export NOTIFICATIONS_API_ENABLED=false
export SENDGRID_MODE_SANDBOX=true
./node_modules/.bin/jest --config ./test/jest-e2e.json --runInBand \
  --runTestsByPath "$target" --silent --forceExit

It takes a PoC source file and a case ID (C01 through C13). The first if rejects a bad ID or a missing file. The second refuses to run outside a checked-out repository with dependencies installed and a test/helpers directory. Then it refuses to overwrite an existing test file, copies the PoC to test/security-poc-<case>.e2e-spec.ts, and installs a trap that removes it again on EXIT. Every connection string is loopback: PostgreSQL on 55432 with TLS, Valkey on 56379. Every credential is synthetic and written into the report. NOTIFICATIONS_API_ENABLED=false and SENDGRID_MODE_SANDBOX=true exist so that no mail can leave the process even if a test path reaches the mailer by accident.

That trap line matters more than it looks. A PoC that leaves files behind changes the repository it claims to be testing. A PoC that overwrites an existing test can destroy evidence. A runner that happily executes against a non-loopback host turns a defensive test into something else entirely. These are small lines, and they are the difference between a reproducible report and a claim.

The installation step was equally deliberate, so that installing dependencies does not execute arbitrary package scripts or phone home, and 13 separate cases never share database state:

npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund
./node_modules/.bin/jest --config ./test/jest-e2e.json --runInBand \
  --runTestsByPath "$target" --silent --forceExit

--runInBand because a leaked handle should not hang a report; --silent --forceExit because the log should be readable in one sitting.

Why HTTP-level e2e tests rather than unit tests against the service classes? Because 2 of the 3 most interesting findings were invisible at the unit level. C07's broken behaviour was a side effect that happened before the method threw; a mocked repository would have shown the delete and the 403 as 2 independent, "correct" facts. C08 was a timing property: a token blacklisted for 120 milliseconds and re-accepted 350 milliseconds later can only be observed by sending real requests against a real cache, with a clock in the test. The repository already had an e2e harness, since createTestApp builds the actual Nest application with the actual modules and a mocked Bridge provider, so the honest reproduction used it:

export interface CreateTestAppOptions {
  enableAuthGuard?: boolean;
  enableValidationPipe?: boolean;
  enableTransformInterceptor?: boolean;
  enableExtendedQueryParser?: boolean;
}

export async function createTestApp(
  options: CreateTestAppOptions = {},
): Promise<NestExpressApplication> {
  const {
    enableAuthGuard = true,
    enableValidationPipe = true,
    enableTransformInterceptor = true,
    enableExtendedQueryParser = true,
  } = options;
  const moduleFixture: TestingModule = await Test.createTestingModule({
    imports: [AppModule],
  })

The application that comes up is not a stub. Real controllers, real guards, real Sequelize models against the disposable database, real Redis client against the disposable Valkey; only the Bridge, the external storage credential service, is mocked, because it would otherwise want to talk to infrastructure nobody should give a test. That decision matters for what a PoC can honestly claim. A mocked guard would have proven nothing about the guard. The point of running the whole stack locally was that every 403 and every 200 in the logs was produced by the same code that would produce it in production, with only the data and the network being synthetic.

Getting there was not free. The first PoC failed because a migration had not run against the disposable database; the second because the test configuration expected Valkey on a hostname that only exists inside the repository's docker-compose network, which is why the runner pins REDIS_CONNECTION_STRING to 127.0.0.1:56379 explicitly; the third because the mock Bridge provider was missing getLimit() and the application refused to finish booting. None of these failures said anything about the vulnerabilities. All of them had to be solved before a single finding could be demonstrated, and all of them produced changes that made the harness better rather than special-casing a single test. That is the actual work of building a reproduction, and it is invisible in the final one-pass log: the PoC that ships in the report is the fourth draft of a file whose first 3 drafts failed for reasons that had nothing to do with the bug.

1 thing was missing on the audited commit. The mock Bridge provider has no getLimit(), but the application calls it during setup. I added it with a patch and documented it separately from every finding:

diff --git a/test/helpers/test-app.helper.ts b/test/helpers/test-app.helper.ts
index c721448..a099f94 100644
@@ -23,6 +23,10 @@ class MockBridgeService {
+  async getLimit() {
+    return 1_000_000_000;
+  }
   async deleteFile() {

It changes test code only. It does not remediate a vulnerability. I wrote that sentence into all 13 reports on purpose, because a reviewer should never have to wonder whether the PoC quietly fixed the bug it claims to demonstrate. A test-only compatibility shim that is clearly labelled is boring. An unlabelled one is a reason to distrust the whole package.

Each PoC repeated the boundary check at the top of its beforeAll:

    if (process.env.RDS_HOSTNAME !== '127.0.0.1' || process.env.REDIS_CONNECTION_STRING?.includes('127.0.0.1') !== true) {
      throw new Error('PoC requires loopback PostgreSQL and Redis');
    app = await createTestApp();

  let sharings: typeof SharingModel;
  let invites: typeof SharingInviteModel;
  let roles: typeof RoleModel;
  let workspaces: typeof WorkspaceModel;
  let workspaceInvites: typeof WorkspaceInviteModel;
  let teams: typeof WorkspaceTeamModel;
  let members: typeof WorkspaceUserModel;
  let teamMembers: typeof WorkspaceTeamUserModel;
  let preCreatedUsers: typeof PreCreatedUserModel;
  let users: typeof UserModel;

  beforeAll(async () => {

If RDS_HOSTNAME is not 127.0.0.1, or the Redis connection string does not point at loopback, the test throws before a single fixture is created. That guard is part of the evidence. It turns "no production system was touched" from a promise into a checked condition that a maintainer can read and verify. Synthetic users come from createTestUser, folders are created directly through the model, keys are literal strings like local-key, and the database is called drive_audit with a user named audit. Anyone reading the log can see there is no real data in it.

The reason for 13 separate files rather than one suite was state. A shared suite accumulates it: one case leaves a user, a token, a sharing row, an invite, a workspace team behind, and the next case inherits that state. Then a passing test proves something about the previous test rather than about the vulnerability. Separate runs make each result attributable and each log short enough to read in a sitting. The cost is a lot of duplicated setup code: the same 20 imports, the same beforeAll, the same createTestUser calls appear in every file. That duplication is cheaper than ambiguity when the report is handed to someone who has never seen the codebase.

It also made the reports easier to write. Each one could say: here is the file, here is the commit, here is the command, here is the observed result, here is what was not tested. For the C07 case, the observed result was 3 assertions:

    expect(res.status).toBe(403);
    expect(await sharings.count({ where: { itemId: folder.uuid, type: 'private' } })).toBe(0);
    expect(await invites.count({ where: { itemId: folder.uuid } })).toBe(0);

For C08 it was 200, 401, 200 after a 350-millisecond wait. For C03 it was 200 and a missing row. Nothing in the reports claims an impact that the test did not measure.

The structure of each report followed from that: a summary stating the observed behaviour and the revision it was reproduced on; a details section with affected code, observed behaviour, suggested remediation, and an explicit scope paragraph; the PoC source and the test-only patch, clearly separated; the runner settings; the observed local result; and a limitations section. The same shape 13 times, so a maintainer reading the 8th report already knows where everything is. Repetition in the wrapper is not a flaw; it is what makes the package skimmable.

The hash of the archive was the last piece, and it exists for an unglamorous reason. A report of this size travels as a zip, and zips get re-downloaded, forwarded, and rebuilt. A SHA-256 on the cover email means the person who eventually reads it can confirm they are reading what I sent, not a version that lost a file or gained an edit somewhere in the chain. It costs 1 line and closes a whole class of "are we looking at the same thing" arguments before they start.

None of this was fast. Reading the sharing module, the auth module and the workspace module properly took the better part of 2 weekends; building and debugging the harness took another; writing 13 reports that each stand on their own took longer than finding the bugs. That ratio is normal and worth saying out loud, because the visible part of security research is the finding and the invisible part is everything that makes the finding believable. Anyone can claim a bug exists. The work is in making the claim cheap to verify.

The hardest part of the whole audit was not the code. It was writing down what a passing local test does not prove. A PoC establishes that a code path behaved as described on the checked commit. It says nothing about production reachability, deployment topology, log access, network position, certificate distribution, or whether the behaviour was ever exploited. Those answers belong to the maintainer, and no amount of local testing can produce them. Every report carried that boundary once, at the top, instead of a Severity section padded with speculation. That discipline is also why the reports went out privately: the tests were built to be reproducible, not to be published before a fix existed.

There is a tension in that discipline worth naming. A PoC that is too cautious proves nothing and wastes everyone's time; a PoC that reaches too far proves things that were never tested. The line I settled on: reproduce the code path exactly as a caller would reach it, claim exactly what the log shows, and stop there. No "an attacker could pivot to", no hypothetical chains, no severity theatre. The dryness is deliberate. A report that says "these 3 assertions failed in this order on this commit" is one a maintainer can act on in an afternoon, and one I can defend line by line a month later against every question of whether the finding was real.

On 28 October the archive went to hello@internxt.com and security@internxt.com: 13 findings, 13 PoCs, 13 test logs, source references, a hash. Getting a confidential channel to send it to had taken 8 days and an escalation to a national CERT. The technical work, by contrast, had gone almost exactly to plan. That asymmetry is the part of this story I still find strange. Building a harness that cannot hurt anyone took a weekend of careful, boring decisions. Getting an acknowledgement from the company took a month.

If you take 1 thing from this, take the trap line. A reproduction that cleans up after itself, refuses to run in the wrong environment, and states its own limits is worth more than a dramatic proof of concept. The rest of the audit (the disclosure timeline, the advisories that were published, the ones that were closed, the ones still in triage) is written up in the timeline post. This post is only about the part that worked.

title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
description: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Tested across five public security benchmarks, AAD successfully caught 87% of harmful instructions carried out by agents without adding runtime latency. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

title: Muse Ember now available on AI Gateway
description:
Muse Ember from Meta is now available on AI Gateway. It is a lightweight reasoning model for the high-volume parts of an agent run, such as coding sub-tasks, tool calls, and document analysis.

Muse Ember handles the bounded tasks agents repeat many times in a single run, like implementing a helper function, calling a tool, or summarizing a document.

The model accepts text, image, and video input with a 1M-token context window, so an agent can pass it code, screenshots, documents, and clips in the same run. Tool calling lets your application feed each result into the next step. Reasoning effort is adjustable from minimal to max.

Call it through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway.

Use meta/muse-ember as the model name:

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select meta/muse-ember in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Muse Ember in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

API Gateway

Feature

Call Google Cloud APIs from streaming gateways

Streaming gateways can now call Google Cloud APIs such as aiplatform.googleapis.com. A gateway with an effectiveStreamingMode of EFFECTIVE_STREAMING_MODE_ENABLED authenticates to backends whose host ends in .googleapis.com or .vertexai.goog with an access token for the gateway's service account. Other backends still receive an ID token. An existing streaming gateway switches when API Gateway next rolls out a gateway update, or immediately when you update it to a new API config.

For more information, see Securing backend services.

On November 3, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-8).

When unset, behavior is unchanged (installation default, typically 30 days).

Apigee hybrid v1.15.10 adds the ApigeeValkey custom resource definition (CRD), the apigee-valkey Helm chart, and the valkey configuration properties. ApigeeValkey is the replacement for the ApigeeRedis resource.

In version 1.15.10, the runtime continues to use ApigeeRedis. When you upgrade, install the new CRD with the other CRDs. Leave the new ao.args.valkeyBackend property set to its default value, false. You don't need to install the apigee-valkey chart or change your configuration.

For the supported upgrade sequence, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid. For more information about the resource, see Kubernetes resources.

  • roaringbitmap (pg_roaringbitmap) is upgraded from 0.5 to 1.2 for PostgreSQL 12 and later.

The new maintenance version is [PostgreSQL version].R20261013.02_04. If you use a maintenance window, then the updates to the minor and extension versions happen according to the timeframe that you set in the window. Otherwise, the updates occur within the next few weeks.

For more information about checking your maintenance version, see Perform self-service maintenance. To find your maintenance window or to manage maintenance updates, see Find and set maintenance windows. For more information about supported extensions, see Configure PostgreSQL extensions.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.108.0 is available. This release lets you pin node pools to reservation sub-blocks in the gke-node-pool module, adds Slurm support for Cloud TPU v5e, v5p, and v6e, and introduces the gcluster explain command to inspect blueprints and modules.

This release also exposes the wait_for_pods_ready configuration for Kueue in the kubectl-apply module and sets the recovery_timeout field to 0s by default for Pathways workloads.

Additionally, this release suppresses configuration drift for clusters and node pools in the ignore_changes argument of the lifecycle block for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), and upgrades the network modules for the Cloud Foundation Toolkit (CFT) to version 18.3 and later.

This update also checks credentials for Artifact Registry and Docker only when a job submission uses Crane to build container images.

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Salesforce federated data store

Connecting a Salesforce data source with Gemini Enterprise using data federation is generally available (GA). You can use the Gemini Enterprise app assistant to search across your Salesforce accounts, contacts, opportunities, cases, leads, and custom objects, get answers grounded in that content, and create, update, and delete records without needing to ingest the data.

For more information, see Set up a Salesforce data store.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

In GKE version 1.37.0-gke.3570000 and later, you can split each Local SSD on a node between ephemeral storage and raw block storage. When you create a cluster or node pool, use the capacity property of the --ephemeral-storage-local-ssd flag to set how much Local SSD capacity GKE formats for ephemeral storage. GKE leaves the rest of each Local SSD unformatted, so that workloads like databases and caches can use it as raw block storage. This feature is available in GKE Standard clusters. For more information, see Provision and use mixed Local SSDs for raw block and ephemeral storage.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Governance workflows in Knowledge Catalog support batch metadata change requests. You can group up to 250 create, update, and delete operations for entries and entry links into a single change request and curate batch proposals generated by the enrichment agent before approval. This feature is available in preview.

For more information, see About governance workflows.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud

Feature

Oracle Database@Google Cloud introduces Database Connections using which you can connect to your Oracle databases and execute SQL statements. For more information, see Create Database Connections and Execute SQL statements.

This feature is generally available (GA).

Sensitive Data Protection

Change

Sensitive Data Protection now records the last generated timestamp for data profiles with improved precision, close to the time when the resource data is read.

VPC Service Controls

Feature

General availability support for the following integration:

  • Service Management

Virtual Private Cloud

Feature

General Availability: VPC Flow Logs supports logging for IPv6 encapsulation flows. For more information, see IpConnection field format.

title: Build an Offline-First Zakat & Nisab Calculator in React Using a JSON API
description:
Zakat calculators are a nice small project: a bit of state, a bit of math, and some real-world concerns like offline use, number formatting and right-to-left text. In this tutorial we build one in React, using the Zakat API from QuraniAPI as the data source.

Important: this is a coding tutorial, not a religious ruling. Please confirm rulings and your personal calculation with a qualified scholar.

What the API gives us

The Zakat endpoint is documented on its API page and in the docs. The slug is zakat and the request looks like this:

GET https://quranicapi.online/api/serve.php?slug=zakat&lang=en

Use lang=all for all 9 languages, or a code such as en, ur, fr, de, ru, tr, ms, zh-CN or ja. The sample response I saw on the page contains:

  • zakat_rate: 2.5
  • nisab: an array with entries for gold (87.48 grams, 7.5 tola) and silver (612.36 grams, 52.5 tola), each with a translations object
  • items: guideline entries with a category (for example cash) and a translation string

It is listed as a premium API. Check the pricing page for plans (at the time of writing: $20/mo, $100/yr, or a $900 one-time full dataset). The docs say to request a key; check the docs page for the exact way to send it, since I won't guess at it here.

Step 1: a local sample (offline-first)

Because the live response may need a key, we ship a clearly labelled local sample that copies the shape above. If the network fails, the app still works.

// zakatSample.js  -- LOCAL SAMPLE copied from the public sample JSON.
// Check the docs page for the exact live response.
export const ZAKAT_SAMPLE = {
  zakat_rate: 2.5,
  nisab: [
    { type: "gold", unit: "grams", value: 87.48, tola: 7.5 },
    { type: "silver", unit: "grams", value: 612.36, tola: 52.5 },
  ],
};

Step 2: a fetch helper with a cache 

// zakatApi.js
import { ZAKAT_SAMPLE } from "./zakatSample";

const URL = "https://quranicapi.online/api/serve.php?slug=zakat&lang=en";
const KEY = "zakat-cache-v1";

export async function loadZakat() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(URL);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);
    const data = await res.json();
    localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(data));
    return { data, source: "live" };
  } catch (e) {
    const cached = localStorage.getItem(KEY);
    if (cached) return { data: JSON.parse(cached), source: "cache" };
    return { data: ZAKAT_SAMPLE, source: "sample" };
  }
}

Order of preference: live, then last cached response, then the bundled sample. Showing the source to the user keeps things honest.

Step 3: the React component

The calculator does one simple thing: it takes a total of zakatable wealth, compares it to a nisab amount the user supplies in their currency, and multiplies by the rate from the API. Converting grams of gold or silver into currency needs a price that this API does not provide, so the user enters the current nisab value themselves.

import { useEffect, useMemo, useState } from "react";
import { loadZakat } from "./zakatApi";

export default function ZakatCalculator({ locale = "en", currency = "USD" }) {
  const [info, setInfo] = useState(null);
  const [wealth, setWealth] = useState("");
  const [nisabValue, setNisabValue] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => { loadZakat().then(setInfo); }, []);

  const fmt = useMemo(
    () => new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency", currency }),
    [locale, currency]
  );

  if (!info) return <p>Loading...</p>;

  const rate = info.data.zakat_rate / 100;
  const gold = info.data.nisab.find((n) => n.type === "gold");
  const silver = info.data.nisab.find((n) => n.type === "silver");
  const w = parseFloat(wealth) || 0;
  const n = parseFloat(nisabValue) || 0;
  const reachesNisab = n > 0 && w >= n;
  const due = reachesNisab ? w * rate : 0;

  return (
    <section dir="auto">
      <p>Gold nisab: {gold.value} g. Silver nisab: {silver.value} g. (source: {info.source})</p>
      <label>Zakatable wealth
        <input type="number" min="0" value={wealth} onChange={(e) => setWealth(e.target.value)} />
      </label>
      <label>Nisab value in {currency}
        <input type="number" min="0" value={nisabValue} onChange={(e) => setNisabValue(e.target.value)} />
      </label>
      <p>{n === 0 ? "Enter a nisab value." : reachesNisab ? "Zakat due: " + fmt.format(due) : "Below the nisab you entered."}</p>
      <small>Confirm rulings with a scholar.</small>
    </section>
  );
}

Money math in floating point is fine for a display estimate, but for anything transactional use integer minor units.

Formatting and RTL tips

  • Intl.NumberFormat handles currency symbols and digits per locale. Try "ar-SA" or "ur-PK" with a matching currency such as SAR or PKR.
  • Set dir="auto" on text blocks so mixed Urdu/English content lays out correctly, or set dir="rtl" on the root when the whole UI is RTL.
  • Use CSS logical properties (margin-inline-start instead of margin-left) so one stylesheet works in both directions.
  • The API returns translations per language, so pass the lang parameter that matches your UI locale and read the matching key from the translations object.

Going further

Zakat is tied to a lunar year, so pairing the calculator with dates is natural. The Hijri Calendar API can help you build a reminder widget; check its page for the response shape. You can browse everything on the QuraniAPI home page, and the open repository is at sunnahsource-islamic-api on GitHub.

Wrap-up

We built a small component with a live, cached and bundled-sample data path, a simple 2.5% calculation using the API's rate, and locale-aware formatting. Next ideas: store the user's inputs locally, add a language switcher backed by the lang parameter, and show the guideline items text from the API under the result. Again, this is software only; please consult a scholar for your own zakat.

title: Spring AI's Model Layer: One API, Any Provider, Zero Rewrites
description:
Spring AI's Model Layer: One API, Any Provider, Zero Rewrites

If you have built an AI feature in Java, you have probably felt the same pain I did. You write the integration against one provider's SDK, the product works, and then a business decision, a price change, or a compliance requirement forces you to move to another model. Suddenly the code you thought was "done" is full of provider-specific request objects, response parsers, and retry rules.

Spring AI tackles this problem directly. Its model layer gives you a single, portable API for the kinds of models most applications use: chat, embeddings, images, audio, moderation, and decision models. Underneath, it connects to many providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google GenAI, Google Vertex AI, Amazon Bedrock, Mistral AI, Ollama, DeepSeek, and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

The practical promise is simple: you change configuration, not your application code. In this article I will explain how the model layer is organized, show how it fits with ChatClient, and walk through a small Spring Boot service that can switch providers without a single line of business logic changing.

The big picture

It helps to see Spring AI as a set of layers, each with a clear responsibility:

  • Models abstract the provider. You depend on a model interface such as ChatModel or EmbeddingModel, not on a vendor SDK.
  • ChatClient is the friendly, fluent entry point for talking to a chat model. It supports prompts, structured output, tool calling, and advisors that wrap each call.
  • Data and retrieval provide vector stores, document readers, and RAG building blocks, using one portable API across many vector databases.
  • Agents and protocols sit on top, for workflows that need planning, tools, and communication between agents.

This article focuses on the bottom layer, the model layer, because it is the foundation everything else depends on.

Six model APIs, one vocabulary

The model layer does not treat "AI" as a single thing. It defines one API per kind of model:

Model API What it does Typical use
Chat Text in, text out Assistants, summarization, extraction
Embedding Text in, numeric vector out Semantic search, RAG, clustering
Image Text in, image out Generating visuals, thumbnails
Audio Speech and audio processing Transcription, text to speech
Moderation Classify content for policy violations Filtering user input and output
Decision Choose among options with a model Routing and classification decisions

Each API has a consistent set of concepts: a model interface, options (such as the model name or temperature), and a response type. Once you learn one, the others feel familiar.

Why provider portability matters

Provider portability is more than a nice abstraction. It gives you concrete advantages:

  1. Cost control. You can route simple tasks to a cheaper model and reserve a premium model for hard ones.
  2. Resilience. If one provider has an outage or rate limits you, you can switch to another without a code release.
  3. Privacy and locality. You can run a local model with Ollama during development or for sensitive data, and use a hosted model in production.
  4. Evaluation. You can compare providers on the same prompts and pick the one that fits your quality bar.
  5. Negotiation and lock-in. Your architecture does not depend on one vendor's roadmap.

None of these advantages exists if your business code calls a vendor SDK directly. The abstraction is what makes them cheap to exercise.

Setting up the project

Start with a Spring Boot project and add the Spring AI starter for the provider you want to use first. Spring AI publishes a bill of materials (BOM), so you should manage the version through the BOM rather than hard-coding it on each dependency. The exact coordinates depend on the Spring AI version you target, so check the official reference documentation for the current setup.

With Maven, the shape looks like this:

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-ai-bom</artifactId>
            <version>${spring-ai.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-ai-openai-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Notice that the starter is provider-specific, but the code you write against it is not. That distinction is the heart of the design.

Configuration decides the provider

Provider settings live in application.yml. Credentials come from environment variables, never from source code:

spring:
  ai:
    openai:
      api-key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY}
      chat:
        options:
          model: gpt-4o-mini
          temperature: 0.2

Switching to Anthropic is a configuration change, not a code change:

spring:
  ai:
    anthropic:
      api-key: ${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}
      chat:
        options:
          model: claude-sonnet-4-5
          temperature: 0.2

Model names change over time, so treat the values above as examples and check the current model list in each provider's documentation before you deploy.

For local development, you can use Ollama and keep everything on your machine:

spring:
  ai:
    ollama:
      base-url: http://localhost:11434
      chat:
        options:
          model: llama3.1

Spring profiles make this even cleaner. Keep application-local.yml pointing at Ollama, application-prod.yml pointing at a hosted provider, and select the profile at startup with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE.

A provider-agnostic service

Now the important part: the service code. Spring Boot auto-configures a ChatClient.Builder when a chat model is on the classpath. Your service depends only on that builder:

import org.springframework.ai.chat.client.ChatClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class SupportAssistant {

    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    public SupportAssistant(ChatClient.Builder builder) {
        this.chatClient = builder.build();
    }

    public String answer(String customerQuestion) {
        return chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                        You are a concise support assistant for a digital bank.
                        Answer in the same language as the customer.
                        If you are not sure, say so and suggest contacting support.
                        """)
                .user(customerQuestion)
                .call()
                .content();
    }
}

This class does not mention OpenAI, Anthropic, or Ollama. Whichever provider is active at startup, the same code runs. That is the portability promise in practice.

Structured output: from text to Java objects

Free text is hard to use in a backend. Often you want a typed object. Spring AI can ask the model for JSON that maps to a Java record and convert the result for you:

import java.util.List;

public record TicketSummary(String category, String priority, List<String> keyPoints) {}

public TicketSummary summarize(String ticketText) {
    return chatClient.prompt()
            .system("Classify the support ticket and extract the key points.")
            .user(ticketText)
            .call()
            .entity(TicketSummary.class);
}

Structured output reduces brittle string parsing, which is one of the most common sources of production bugs in LLM integrations. It does not remove the need for validation. Treat the model's output as untrusted input: check ranges, enum values, and required fields before you act on it.

Embeddings: the other half of retrieval

Chat gets the attention, but embeddings are what make retrieval work. An EmbeddingModel turns text into a vector, and you store those vectors in a vector store. Here is a minimal example that embeds two texts and compares them with cosine similarity:

import org.springframework.ai.embedding.EmbeddingModel;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class SimilarityService {

    private final EmbeddingModel embeddingModel;

    public SimilarityService(EmbeddingModel embeddingModel) {
        this.embeddingModel = embeddingModel;
    }

    public double similarity(String first, String second) {
        float[] a = embeddingModel.embed(first);
        float[] b = embeddingModel.embed(second);
        return cosine(a, b);
    }

    private double cosine(float[] a, float[] b) {
        double dot = 0, normA = 0, normB = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            dot += a[i] * b[i];
            normA += a[i] * a[i];
            normB += b[i] * b[i];
        }
        return dot / (Math.sqrt(normA) * Math.sqrt(normB));
    }
}

In a real system you would not compare two texts on every request. You would embed your documents once, store them in a vector store such as PGVector, Redis, Elasticsearch, or Qdrant, and query by similarity. The point here is that the embedding code is the same regardless of which provider generates the vectors.

One caution: vectors from different embedding models are not compatible. If you switch the embedding provider, you must re-embed your corpus. Keep the embedding model choice as a deliberate decision, not a casual configuration tweak.

Testing without calling a real provider

Tests that call a live model are slow, expensive, and non-deterministic. Because your code depends on abstractions, you can test it with a fake. For example, a unit test can stub the model response and assert how your service builds the prompt and handles the answer. Keep a small number of integration tests that use a real or local model, and run them separately from your fast build.

This is also where the portability pays off in your test strategy: you can run the same integration suite against Ollama in CI and against a hosted provider in a nightly job.

Production concerns you should not skip

Switching providers is easy. Running them reliably is not. A few practices make a real difference:

  • Set timeouts and retries. Model calls can be slow. Define explicit timeouts and a bounded retry policy, and avoid retrying on errors that will not succeed on a second attempt.
  • Log carefully. Prompts and responses may contain personal data. Redact sensitive content and make logging levels configurable.
  • Track cost and latency per provider. Observability is part of the design. Spring AI exposes metrics and traces for the client, models, and vector stores, so connect them to your monitoring stack.
  • Control the prompt. Keep system prompts in version control and review them like code. A small wording change can alter behavior significantly.
  • Plan for model changes. Providers deprecate models. Pin the model name in configuration, and have a process for testing a replacement before you switch.
  • Guard the output. Use validation and, where needed, moderation models before you show or act on a response.

Common pitfalls

A few mistakes I see often:

  1. Leaking provider types into business code. If you import a vendor class into a service, you have lost portability. Keep provider-specific code in configuration.
  2. Assuming identical behavior. Providers differ in how they handle system prompts, token limits, and structured output. Test each provider you support.
  3. Mixing embedding models. Changing the embedding model silently breaks retrieval quality until you re-index.
  4. Hard-coding credentials. Use environment variables or a secrets manager.
  5. Skipping evaluation. Without a set of representative prompts and expected outcomes, you cannot tell whether a provider switch made things better or worse.

Where to go next

The model layer is the foundation, not the whole building. Once you are comfortable with it, the next steps are:

  • Add a vector store and build a small RAG pipeline with a document reader and a retrieval step.
  • Use advisors to add memory, logging, or safety checks around each call.
  • Introduce tool calling so the model can invoke your Java services.
  • Explore agent patterns such as chaining, routing, and orchestrator-workers when a single call is not enough.

Conclusion

Spring AI's model layer solves a problem that every Java team building AI features will eventually face: how to avoid being locked into one provider. By separating model APIs from provider implementations, and by letting configuration choose the provider, it gives you a clean path to switch models, control costs, run locally, and evaluate options without rewriting your business logic.

If you are starting an AI feature in a Spring Boot application, begin with the model abstraction, keep provider details in configuration, and invest early in tests and observability. Your future self, the one who needs to change providers on a Friday afternoon, will be grateful.

Have you already built an AI feature in Java? I would like to hear which provider you started with and what made you consider switching.

title: Cloud Hygiene Without Production Changes: A Safer First Assessment
description:
Teams often ask an assessor for administrator access just to find out what is already in the cloud account. That request creates risk of its own, and unvalidated findings can push people into rushed changes.

This piece is adapted from a MeritSOLV™ Research & Insights guide on running a first cloud hygiene assessment with read-only evidence. The example below is illustrative, not a client report.

Why inventories fall behind

Cloud estates get hard to govern when inventories and architecture records lag. Start by writing the account boundary in one sentence: which subscriptions, projects or accounts are in scope, and which are explicitly out. Then list the read-only exports the owners can provide, such as resource inventories, policy settings and cost reports. Treat everything found as an observation until an owner confirms it, and keep change requests in a separate list.

A scope statement can be short:

In scope: the two product-team subscriptions.
Out of scope: the inherited test account.
Evidence: policy exports, resource inventory, cost categories, approved screenshots.
Access: time-limited, read-only. No administrator role.

A read-only review: evidence first, changes later

A small product team operates two cloud subscriptions and one inherited test account. Rather than handing an external assessor administrator rights, it provides policy exports, a resource inventory, cost categories and approved screenshots in a time-limited read-only collection. The assessment finds publicly reachable storage configuration, inconsistent tags and missing cost allocation on a shared subscription. The report separates observed configuration from a confirmed exploitable condition.

Finding Evidence Risk owner decision
Unknown public exposure Resource policy and network path evidence Request validation before a severity claim
Missing owner tag Inventory export Assign an owner and a remediation window
Broad role assignment Role-binding snapshot Review least privilege with the platform team
No recovery drill Backup policy only Plan a restoration test

Avoid the false promise of a "no-impact scan." Even read-only collection can expose sensitive metadata and consume API capacity. Agree on account boundaries, sensitive-data redaction, access expiration and approved collection methods beforehand. Any production changes should go later through the normal change process.

Five steps that keep the first assessment safe

1. Agree which accounts, subscriptions and environments are in scope. Get written approval naming each tenant or account, environment, data category and excluded resource before requesting any export or permission.

2. Gather approved read-only exports and architecture diagrams. Prefer a limited evidence pack with configuration snapshots, logging coverage, role bindings and architecture boundaries over unrestricted cloud console access.

3. Inventory resources, owners, environments and labels. Normalize tags and ownership. Mark shared resources, test subscriptions and orphaned cloud identities so recommendations address the actual operating footprint.

4. Document cost and configuration observations as hypotheses that still need validation. Label each observation as verified, suspected or outside scope, and separate cost optimization from security exposure so risk rankings stay accurate.

5. Rank findings by exposure, business impact, effort and decision owner. Propose validated follow-up steps with an owner, estimated effort and the required change authorization. Do not present evidence collection as production remediation.

What done should look like

You want a reviewed inventory and a prioritized cloud observations worksheet, with provenance, version, owner and outstanding exceptions visible. The sponsor should be able to see what was decided, what was not, and which actions remain. State the population, sampling method and limits of any review. A scoped example is not a full assurance engagement.

When the worksheet is ready, hand it to someone outside the delivery team. Can they find the latest version, name the accountable owner, explain the top unresolved issue and say what the next authorized action is? If any of that lives only in someone's memory, the handoff isn't finished.

The mistake that shows up most often

Changing cloud settings while performing what was meant to be documentation-only discovery. The fix is not more paperwork for its own sake. Keep the smallest set of artifacts that shows scope, evidence, review and the next decision. Automate only after the responsibilities and exceptions are clear.

Working checklist

  • Agree which accounts, subscriptions and environments are in scope.
  • Gather approved read-only exports and architecture diagrams.
  • Inventory resources, owners, environments and labels.
  • Document cost and configuration observations as hypotheses requiring validation.
  • Rank findings by exposure, business impact, effort and decision owner.
  • Confirm who approves the final output and how corrections will be handled.
  • Archive the approved version and record the next review or follow-up date.

If you want a first step this week, pick one real account, write the boundary in one sentence, and collect only the read-only exports the owners will approve.

Questions that come up

Can cloud hygiene begin read-only?

Yes. A properly scoped review can document observations without modifying production resources.

Is a configuration observation a verified vulnerability?

Not necessarily. Findings should identify the evidence, the assumptions and the validation still needed.

For deeper reading, the guide points to NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 on configuration and access controls, and to NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0. This is general operational information, not legal, audit or certification advice. Review the cited standards and apply your organization's requirements.

The examples are illustrative, not reports of MeritSOLV™ client engagements.

Originally published at meritsolv.com.

title: A Risk Score Is Not a Decision: Building Smarter AML Workflows for Crypto Businesses
description:
AMLdark · Screen TRC20 USDT addresses for free

Live AML screening for Tron-based USDT addresses against OFAC designations, Tether's freeze list and darknet datasets. Free tier included.

amldark.com

What should your system do?

Reject the transaction? Freeze the account? Request additional information? Send it to a compliance analyst?

There is a problem with treating a risk score as a final answer: a number can describe a potential risk, but it cannot explain the entire situation.

This distinction becomes particularly important for businesses processing USDT, operating cryptocurrency exchanges, managing OTC transactions or building blockchain payment infrastructure.

As crypto adoption grows, companies need more than systems that simply identify suspicious addresses. They need systems that help them understand risk, prioritize investigations and make consistent decisions.

Let's explore how to build that kind of AML workflow.

  1. The Hidden Problem With Automated Risk Scores

Automated screening is useful because it can process information much faster than manual investigation.

However, automation introduces another challenge: false positives.

Consider three hypothetical situations.

Scenario A: Direct exposure

A wallet has a documented direct connection to an address associated with a sanctioned entity.

Scenario B: Indirect exposure

A wallet received funds from an address that interacted with a higher-risk service several transactions earlier.

Scenario C: Historical exposure

A wallet interacted with an address that was considered suspicious several years ago, but the available information does not establish a meaningful current connection.

All three situations might generate risk alerts.

But should they receive the same treatment?

Obviously not.

A responsible screening workflow needs to distinguish between direct and indirect exposure, consider transaction context and provide enough information for further investigation.

The objective should be better decisions, not simply more alerts.

  1. Why False Positives Are an Engineering Problem

False positives are often discussed as a compliance inconvenience.

In reality, they can become a serious operational problem.

Imagine a cryptocurrency exchange processing 10,000 deposits per day.

If its screening system generates hundreds of alerts that require manual investigation, the compliance team may struggle to keep up.

This creates several risks:

Legitimate customers experience unnecessary delays.

Analysts spend time investigating low-value alerts.

Important cases compete for attention with insignificant findings.

Operational costs increase.

Customer support receives more complaints.

Compliance teams may become less effective at identifying genuinely concerning activity.

This is why screening quality should not be measured exclusively by the number of detected addresses.

A useful system should help distinguish meaningful signals from background noise.

  1. Build a Risk Assessment Process Around Evidence

A better approach is to separate the detection stage from the decision stage.

Think about the process as four connected layers.

Layer 1: Detection

The screening system identifies relevant indicators, such as sanctions exposure, suspicious wallet connections or interactions with known high-risk services.

Layer 2: Context

The system provides additional information about the findings.

For example:

Is the exposure direct or indirect?

How many transaction hops separate the addresses?

Is the connection associated with USDT transfers?

When did the relevant interaction occur?

Is there more than one independent risk indicator?

Layer 3: Investigation

A compliance analyst evaluates the available evidence.

This stage may involve examining transaction history, customer information and additional external intelligence.

Layer 4: Decision

The business applies its documented risk policy.

Possible outcomes include standard processing, enhanced due diligence, additional information requests or escalation.

The important architectural principle is simple:

Detection should generate evidence. Decision-making should evaluate that evidence.

These responsibilities should not be confused.

  1. Transaction Graphs: Why One Wallet Is Never the Whole Story

Blockchain transactions create relationships between addresses.

These relationships can be represented as a graph.

Imagine a simple transaction chain:

Wallet A → Wallet B → Wallet C → Wallet D

If Wallet D receives USDT from Wallet C, looking exclusively at Wallet C may provide only a limited understanding of the available transaction history.

Additional analysis could reveal that Wallet C previously received funds from Wallet B, which had an earlier interaction with Wallet A.

This does not automatically make Wallet D suspicious.

It simply introduces additional information that may deserve attention.

When analyzing transaction graphs, several factors matter:

Hop distance

How many transfers separate the wallet being investigated from the identified risk source?

Transaction direction

Did the funds move from the risk-associated address toward the investigated wallet, or in the opposite direction?

Asset specificity

Was the relationship established through USDT transfers or through another asset?

Time relevance

How old is the connection?

Exposure concentration

Does the wallet have a single indirect connection or several independent relationships?

These distinctions are particularly important when investigating TRON-based USDT activity.

A transaction graph should help explain relationships, not create guilt by association.

  1. Why TRC20 USDT Screening Requires Its Own Perspective

USDT is available across multiple blockchain networks.

However, analyzing USDT on TRON is not necessarily identical to analyzing USDT on Ethereum or another blockchain.

The underlying infrastructure, transaction structure and operational characteristics differ.

For businesses working with TRC20 assets, a useful screening workflow should consider:

TRON address identification.

USDT token-transfer history.

Relevant sanctions information.

Tether freeze-list records.

Known fraud and darknet exposure indicators.

Connections between wallet addresses.

Risk information associated with transaction history.

Another important consideration is that native TRX activity and TRC20 USDT transfers are not interchangeable.

A system that only examines general blockchain activity may overlook information specific to the token being investigated.

This is why network-specific and token-specific analysis matters.

  1. Introducing Explainable AML: An Approach Worth Building Around

One of the most useful improvements a crypto business can make is moving from unexplained risk scores toward explainable risk assessments.

Consider the difference.

A basic screening interface displays:

Risk score: 78/100.

An explainable screening interface provides:

Overall risk assessment.

Relevant exposure categories.

Direct and indirect connections.

Supporting transaction information.

Relevant sanctions indicators.

Historical context.

Information requiring further investigation.

The second approach gives compliance professionals something they can actually work with.

It also makes it easier to document decisions and improve internal procedures.

For developers, this means thinking about AML data structures, reporting interfaces and investigation workflows from the beginning.

A good screening integration should not simply return a number and leave the rest of the work to the user.

  1. How AMLdark Fits Into This Workflow

This is an area where specialized cryptocurrency screening platforms become interesting.

AMLdark focuses on cryptocurrency AML analysis, particularly USDT TRC20 activity on the TRON network.

Its website describes several capabilities relevant to the workflow discussed above:

Wallet screening

Address analysis against sanctions-related information and other risk datasets.

Transaction graph analysis

Investigation of relationships between addresses through token-level transaction tracing.

Tether freeze-list checks

Screening against relevant Tether freeze-list information.

Risk categorization

Presentation of risk scores and individual exposure categories.

Additional network coverage

The platform also describes support for other blockchain networks, including TON and several additional ecosystems.

Developer-oriented functionality

API access, batch screening and webhook functionality are presented for businesses that want to incorporate AML checks into their operational workflows.

You can explore the platform and its available features here:

https://amldark.com

For development teams, the interesting question is not simply whether a screening service can return a risk score.

It is whether its underlying information provides enough context to support a meaningful investigation.

Before integrating any provider into production, evaluate its data sources, coverage, update frequency, API documentation, security controls and limitations.

  1. Designing an AML Workflow That Scales

A cryptocurrency business should not depend on individual analysts remembering how to handle every possible screening result.

The process should be documented and repeatable.

Here are five practical recommendations.

  1. Define risk categories clearly

Establish what low, medium and high risk mean within your organization's methodology.

Avoid treating a provider's numerical score as a universal legal standard.

  1. Document investigation decisions

Keep records of the evidence reviewed, the decision made and the person responsible.

  1. Establish escalation procedures

Define which findings require additional review and who is authorized to make the final decision.

  1. Review screening quality

Monitor false-positive rates, investigation time, unresolved cases and changes in data coverage.

  1. Reassess historical information

Risk intelligence changes. A result obtained months ago should not automatically be treated as a complete representation of current wallet risk.

These practices help transform AML from an isolated technical feature into a functioning operational process.

  1. The Future Is Not More Alerts. It Is Better Intelligence.

The cryptocurrency industry does not need systems that simply generate an endless stream of suspicious-wallet notifications.

It needs systems that help businesses understand why something was flagged, what evidence supports the finding and what should happen next.

This is especially important as stablecoins become increasingly integrated into payment infrastructure and international financial activity.

For developers, this creates an interesting engineering challenge.

The next generation of cryptocurrency applications will need to combine blockchain monitoring, risk intelligence, explainable analytics and human oversight.

The strongest solutions will not necessarily be the ones that produce the highest number of alerts.

They will be the ones that help organizations make better decisions with the information available.

title: Tool-Based Skill Integration: Giving Your Java Agent an activate_skill Tool
description:
Why this topic matters

Agent Skills are folders of instructions that an agent can load when a task needs specialized knowledge. A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md file: a short YAML header with a name and a description, followed by a markdown body with the instructions. The idea is simple, but the integration question is not. When your agent starts a session, how does the model learn that a skill exists, and how does the full instruction set reach its context only when it is needed?

The Agent Skills integration guide answers this with a core principle called progressive disclosure. Instead of loading every skill upfront, the agent works in three tiers. The first tier is a catalog of names and descriptions, which costs roughly 50 to 100 tokens per skill and is loaded at session start. The second tier is the full SKILL.md body, loaded only when a skill is activated and recommended to stay under about 5,000 tokens. The third tier is supporting resources such as scripts or reference files, loaded only when the instructions point to them.

This article focuses on one part of that lifecycle: activation. The guide describes two ways to deliver a skill's content to the model. One relies on the model reading the file directly with its file-read tool. The other is a tool-based approach, where the agent exposes a dedicated function, usually called activate_skill, that returns the skill content. The tool-based approach is the one you need when the model cannot read files, and it is useful even when it can. In this article I walk through why you would choose it, how the pieces fit together, and how to implement it in Java with Spring AI.

The two activation paths

The file-read path is the simplest. The catalog tells the model where each SKILL.md lives, and when a task matches a description, the model calls its normal file-read tool on that path. No special infrastructure is needed. The model receives the raw file, frontmatter included, as a tool result.

The file-read path has three limitations that matter in real systems:

  • It assumes the model has file access. A cloud-hosted agent, a sandboxed agent, or a chat product with no filesystem will not have it.
  • It gives you no control over what is returned. The whole file goes into context, including the frontmatter, and you cannot easily add metadata such as the list of bundled resources.
  • It leaves no place to enforce permissions, ask for consent, or record that a skill was used.

A dedicated activation tool solves all three. You register a function, the model calls it with a skill name, and your code decides what to return. The guide lists the advantages: control over the returned content, structured wrapping so the harness can identify skill content later, a listing of bundled resources without reading them, permission checks, and analytics.

The tool-based path is therefore not a different skill format. It is a different delivery mechanism for the same SKILL.md files. Skills authored for one client should work in another, and the activation tool is the adapter.

Step 1: Discover skills at session start

Before any activation can happen, the agent must find the skills. The guide recommends scanning at least two scopes. A project scope lives under the working directory, for skills that belong to a repository. A user scope lives under the home directory, for skills available across projects. Within each scope, the guide suggests scanning both a client-specific directory such as .claude/skills/ and the cross-client .agents/skills/ convention, so that skills installed by other compliant tools are visible.

Discovery looks for subdirectories that contain a file named exactly SKILL.md. It should skip folders such as .git and node_modules, and it should bound the search depth and the number of directories so that a large tree does not stall the session. When two skills share a name, the common rule is that project-level skills override user-level ones, and a warning should be logged so the user knows a skill was shadowed.

There is also a trust question. Project-level skills come from the repository being worked on, which may be untrusted, so the guide suggests loading them only after the user has marked the folder as trusted. This matters because a skill is, in effect, a set of instructions injected into the model's context.

Step 2: Parse the frontmatter leniently

Each discovered file is split into two parts: the YAML block between the opening and closing --- delimiters, and the body that follows. The guide recommends a lenient approach. A name that does not match its directory produces a warning but the skill still loads. A missing or empty description is the one case that causes the skill to be skipped, because the description is what makes disclosure possible. The guide also mentions a common compatibility problem: unquoted values containing colons, such as description: "Use this skill when: the user asks about PDFs, are invalid YAML that some parsers accept anyway. A good implementation retries with the value quoted."

For each skill you need three fields: the name, the description, and the absolute location of the file. The base directory, which is the parent of location, is derived when needed so that relative references such as scripts/evaluate.py can be resolved.

Step 3: Disclose the catalog to the model

The catalog is the first tier of progressive disclosure. It lists each skill's name and description, and optionally its location, inside whatever structured format fits your stack. The guide shows an XML example, but a bulleted list works too.

Where you place the catalog matters for the tool-based path. You can put it in the system prompt, or embed it in the description of the activation tool itself. The tool-embedding option keeps the system prompt clean and couples discovery with activation, which is why it pairs well with a dedicated tool.

The guide also provides a short behavioral instruction block. For the tool-based path, it tells the model that when a task matches a skill's description, it should call the activation tool with that skill's name before proceeding. The instruction is deliberately brief, because the skill content itself carries the detailed guidance once loaded.

Two rules keep the catalog honest. First, filtered skills must be hidden entirely, not listed and then blocked. A skill the user has disabled, or one that a permission policy denies, should never appear, because otherwise the model wastes turns trying to use it. Second, when no skills exist, the catalog and the tool should be omitted, not rendered as an empty block that confuses the model.

Step 4: Activate with a dedicated tool

Activation is the second tier. In the tool-based path, the model calls the tool, the harness looks up the skill, and the instructions come back as the tool result.

The guide offers a few design choices for that result. You can return the full file or only the body, with the frontmatter stripped. Most dedicated implementations strip it, because name and description were already captured during discovery. You can also wrap the content in identifying tags, which helps the model separate skill instructions from the rest of the conversation and lets the harness find the content again during context management. A typical wrapper includes the skill directory and a list of bundled files, without reading them.

The guide makes one point that is easy to miss. The tool should list supporting files but should not read them eagerly. The model loads a specific script or reference only when the instructions reference it, using its normal file-read capability. For large directories, the listing should be capped and marked as possibly incomplete.

There are two tips worth taking seriously. If you register a tool whose name parameter is an enum of valid skill names, the model cannot invent a skill that does not exist. And if no skills are available, do not register the tool at all. An activation tool with no valid options is noise.

Users should be able to activate skills directly as well, with a slash command or mention syntax such as /skill-name. In that case the harness intercepts the input, performs the lookup, and injects the content, so the model does not have to take an activation action.

A Java implementation with Spring AI

The following implementation follows the guide's structure. It scans two folders, builds a catalog, and exposes an activate_skill tool through Spring AI's @Tool annotation. The example assumes Spring Boot 3.4 or later with a chat model starter, such as spring-ai-starter-model-openai. The API shown here is Spring AI's annotation-based tool calling.

First, the skill record and the registry that discovers skills:

public record SkillDefinition(String name, String description, Path location) {

    public Path baseDirectory() {
        return location.getParent();
    }
}

@Component
public class SkillRegistry {

    private static final int MAX_DEPTH = 5;
    private static final int MAX_DIRECTORIES = 2000;

    private final Map<String, SkillDefinition> skills = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    public SkillRegistry(
            @Value("${skills.project-dir:.agents/skills}") Path projectDir,
            @Value("${skills.user-dir:${user.home}/.agents/skills}") Path userDir) throws IOException {
        // Scan user scope first, then project scope, so project skills override user skills.
        scan(userDir);
        scan(projectDir);
    }

    private void scan(Path root) throws IOException {
        if (!Files.isDirectory(root)) {
            return;
        }
        try (Stream<Path> paths = Files.walk(root, MAX_DEPTH)) {
            paths.filter(p -> p.getFileName().toString().equals("SKILL.md"))
                 .limit(MAX_DIRECTORIES)
                 .forEach(this::register);
        }
    }

    private void register(Path file) {
        try {
            SkillFrontmatter fm = SkillFrontmatter.parse(Files.readString(file));
            if (fm.description() == null || fm.description().isBlank()) {
                log.warn("Skipping skill without description: "{}\", file);"
                return;
            }
            if (skills.containsKey(fm.name())) {
                log.warn("Skill '{}' at {} shadows an earlier definition", fm.name(), file);
            }
            skills.put(fm.name(), new SkillDefinition(fm.name(), fm.description(), file));
        } catch (IOException | IllegalArgumentException ex) {
            log.warn("Skipping unreadable skill {}: {}", file, ex.getMessage());
        }
    }

    public Collection<SkillDefinition> all() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableCollection(skills.values());
    }

    public Optional<SkillDefinition> find(String name) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(skills.get(name));
    }
}

The frontmatter parser splits the file on the delimiters and reads the two fields the registry needs. A production parser would use SnakeYAML and apply the quoting fallback from the guide, but a small line-based parser shows the shape clearly:

public record SkillFrontmatter(String name, String description, String body) {

    public static SkillFrontmatter parse(String content) {
        if (!content.startsWith("---")) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing frontmatter");
        }
        int end = content.indexOf("\n---", 3);
        if (end < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unclosed frontmatter");
        }
        String header = content.substring(3, end);
        String body = content.substring(end + 4).strip();

        String name = null;
        String description = null;
        for (String line : header.split("\n")) {
            int colon = line.indexOf(':');
            if (colon < 0) continue;
            String key = line.substring(0, colon).strip();
            String value = stripQuotes(line.substring(colon + 1).strip());
            if (key.equals("name")) name = value;
            if (key.equals("description")) description = value;
        }
        if (name == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing name");
        }
        return new SkillFrontmatter(name, description, body);
    }

    private static String stripQuotes(String value) {
        if (value.length() >= 2 && (value.startsWith("\"") || value.startsWith("'"))) {
            return value.substring(1, value.length() - 1);
        }
        return value;
    }
}

Now the activation tool. It returns the body wrapped in the structured tags the guide recommends, and it lists bundled files without reading them:

@Component
public class SkillActivationTools {

    private final SkillRegistry registry;

    public SkillActivationTools(SkillRegistry registry) {
        this.registry = registry;
    }

    @Tool(description = "Load the full instructions of an agent skill. "
            + "Call this before performing a task that matches a skill's description.")
    public String activateSkill(
            @ToolParam(description = "The exact name of the skill to activate") String name) {

        SkillDefinition skill = registry.find(name)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown skill: " + name));

        try {
            String body = SkillFrontmatter.parse(Files.readString(skill.location())).body();
            return """
                    <skill_content name="%s">
                    %s

                    Skill directory: %s
                    Relative paths in this skill are relative to the skill directory.

                    <skill_resources>
                    %s
                    </skill_resources>
                    </skill_content>
                    """.formatted(
                        skill.name(),
                        body,
                        skill.baseDirectory(),
                        listResources(skill.baseDirectory()));
        } catch (IOException ex) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException(ex);
        }
    }

    private String listResources(Path base) throws IOException {
        // List, do not read: the model loads specific files on demand.
        try (Stream<Path> files = Files.walk(base, 3)) {
            return files.filter(Files::isRegularFile)
                        .filter(p -> !p.getFileName().toString().equals("SKILL.md"))
                        .limit(50)
                        .map(p -> "  <file>" + base.relativize(p) + "</file>")
                        .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));
        }
    }
}

Note that @ToolParam and the name argument are the only inputs the model controls. The tool resolves the name against the registry, which means the model cannot read an arbitrary file. The tool reads only files the registry discovered. That is a security property worth keeping: the activation tool is a lookup, not a file reader.

Finally, the catalog and the tool are wired into a ChatClient. The catalog goes into the system prompt, and the tool is registered as a default tool:

@Configuration
public class AgentConfig {

    @Bean
    ChatClient agentChatClient(ChatClient.Builder builder,
                               SkillRegistry registry,
                               SkillActivationTools activationTools) {

        String catalog = registry.all().stream()
                .map(s -> "- %s: %s".formatted(s.name(), s.description()))
                .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));

        String system = """
                You are a helpful engineering assistant.
                The following skills provide specialized instructions for specific tasks.
                When a task matches a skill's description, call activateSkill with the
                skill's name to load its full instructions before proceeding.

                Available skills:
                %s
                """.formatted(catalog);

        return builder
                .defaultSystem(system)
                .defaultTools(activationTools)
                .build();
    }
}

Two details in this wiring deserve attention. The catalog is built once at startup, which matches the guide's tier-1 behavior. And when the registry is empty, the wiring should skip both the catalog and the tool, as the guide advises. The version above omits that branch for brevity, but a production version should add it.

Context management

Once a skill is activated, its instructions sit in the conversation. Two problems follow. If the agent prunes or summarizes older messages to fit the context window, the skill can silently disappear, and the model keeps working without its instructions. The guide's answer is to protect skill content from pruning, either by flagging activation results or by recognizing the structured tags during compaction. The tags in the example above make that recognition straightforward.

The second problem is repetition. If the model activates the same skill twice, the instructions appear twice and waste tokens. A simple fix is to track activated skill names for the session and return a short acknowledgment instead of the full body on repeat calls.

The guide also mentions subagent delegation as an advanced option. Instead of injecting the skill into the main conversation, a separate session runs the skill and returns only a summary. This is useful for complex workflows that would otherwise flood the main context.

Security and trust

Three points deserve emphasis. The first is that a skill is untrusted instruction text. Project-level skills in a freshly cloned repository can steer the model, so loading them should depend on a trust decision by the user. The second is that the activation tool should resolve names against a known registry and never accept a path from the model. The example above does this by construction. The third is that bundled scripts are a separate permission question. If your agent can execute scripts from a skill directory, each execution needs the same scrutiny as any other tool call. The guide recommends allowlisting skill directories for reads so that the model does not trigger a permission prompt for every reference, but reads and executions are not the same risk.

When to choose each path

Use the file-read path when the model has a filesystem, the skills are local, and you have no need for permissions, analytics, or structured wrapping. It is the least code and the most portable across clients.

Use the tool-based path when the model cannot read files, when skills come from a remote registry or a database, when you need to enforce permissions or record activations, or when you want to shape the returned content. In a Spring application, it is the natural choice, because the registry, the permission checks, and the logging already live in your code.

Many agents support both. The guide notes that a dedicated tool is optional but useful even when the model can read files, which is a reasonable default if you are building a platform rather than a single script.

Key takeaways

  • Progressive disclosure keeps the base context small: names and descriptions at startup, full instructions on activation, and resources on demand.
  • The tool-based path is a delivery mechanism for the same SKILL.md files, useful when the model has no file access or when you need control over what is returned.
  • Discover skills in project and user scopes, let project skills override user skills, and gate project skills on trust.
  • Parse leniently, but skip any skill without a description, since the description drives disclosure.
  • Make the activation tool a registry lookup, not a file reader. The model should choose a skill name, not a path.
  • List bundled resources without reading them, and load them only when the instructions reference them.
  • Protect skill content from context pruning, and avoid re-injecting a skill that is already in context.

The guide is short, but it describes a complete lifecycle. If you are adding skills support to a Java agent, the tool-based path with Spring AI gives you that lifecycle in a few hundred lines, and the design decisions it forces, such as lookup over file access and tiered loading, are the ones that keep an agent predictable as the number of skills grows.

Sources

  • Agent Skills, "How to add skills support to your agent": https://agentskills.io/integrate-skills#integration-approaches
  • Agent Skills specification: https://agentskills.io/specification.md
