title: Designing Enterprise UX for Millions of Users in the Age of AI
description:
How scalable design systems, intelligent personalization, and consistent user experiences are shaping the next generation of enterprise applications.

Enterprise applications are becoming increasingly complex as businesses serve larger audiences, manage multiple user journeys, and introduce AI-powered capabilities into their digital products. Designing an interface that works for a few thousand users is challenging. Creating an experience that remains intuitive, consistent, and accessible for millions requires an entirely different approach.

Traditional UX design often focuses on individual screens and user interactions. However, enterprise-scale products need a broader strategy that considers reusable components, different user behaviors, accessibility, personalization, and long-term maintainability.

AI is adding another dimension to this challenge. Businesses can now generate interface variations, personalize content, and automate certain design workflows. But producing more interfaces does not automatically result in better experiences. The real challenge is maintaining usability and consistency while allowing products to adapt to individual needs.

Why Enterprise UX Design Needs a Different Approach

Enterprise platforms serve diverse audiences with different expectations, technical capabilities, and objectives. A banking application, e-commerce marketplace, or enterprise management platform may need to support several user groups through a shared interface.

A design decision that improves one user's experience might create friction for another.

For example, an e-commerce platform may serve customers who know exactly what they want and prefer direct access to products. Other customers may want to explore recommendations, compare options, and discover new products.

Designing a single experience for both groups requires understanding their behavior rather than relying on assumptions.

At enterprise scale, several challenges become particularly important:

  • User diversity: Different audiences have different expectations and interaction patterns.
  • Interface consistency: Multiple teams and product modules can introduce inconsistent layouts and visual elements.
  • Content variation: Large product catalogs and dynamic content create additional interface requirements.
  • Accessibility: Every interaction must remain usable across different devices and accessibility needs.
  • Scalability: Design decisions must work across multiple screens, themes, and future product updates.

The solution is to move beyond individual screen design and establish a repeatable UX framework.

Five Principles for Building UX That Scales

1. Build Around User Behavior, Not Just Interface Layouts

Effective enterprise UX begins with understanding what users are trying to accomplish.

User research, behavioral analytics, interviews, and usability testing help identify different user journeys and the problems they encounter.

Instead of designing around assumptions, businesses should identify common user goals such as:

  • Discovering relevant information.
  • Comparing available options.
  • Completing transactions efficiently.
  • Finding previously viewed content.
  • Understanding product features.
  • Building confidence before making decisions.

These goals can then guide the structure and functionality of individual interface components.

For example, returning visitors to an e-commerce platform may benefit from a recently viewed products section that helps them continue their shopping journey without repeating previous searches.

This approach makes the interface more relevant while reducing unnecessary interactions.

2. Establish a Scalable Design System

As enterprise products expand, maintaining visual consistency becomes increasingly difficult.

Different development teams may introduce slightly different button styles, spacing, typography, colors, and component behaviors. Individually, these differences may seem insignificant. Across hundreds of screens, however, they create a fragmented user experience.

A design system provides a shared foundation for preventing this problem.

A comprehensive design system should include:

  • Reusable UI components.
  • Standardized typography and spacing.
  • Color palettes and design tokens.
  • Interaction and navigation patterns.
  • Accessibility guidelines.
  • Component behavior and documentation.
  • Rules for handling different screen sizes and themes.

Design tokens are particularly valuable because they allow design and development teams to work with consistent values across multiple applications.

When a company updates its visual language, these shared foundations make it easier to implement changes without redesigning every component individually.

3. Use AI to Support Personalization

AI introduces opportunities to make enterprise applications more responsive to individual user behavior.

Rather than displaying identical content to every visitor, intelligent systems can use contextual signals, preferences, and interaction history to determine which information may be most relevant.

Examples include:

  • Personalized product recommendations.
  • Context-aware dashboards.
  • Adaptive content discovery.
  • Intelligent search experiences.
  • Dynamic information prioritization.
  • Personalized onboarding journeys.

Consider an enterprise commerce platform serving millions of customers. A returning customer who frequently purchases premium products may benefit from a different product discovery experience than someone who regularly browses discounted collections.

AI can help identify these behavioral patterns and recommend relevant content.

However, personalization should operate within predefined UX guidelines. Navigation, visual hierarchy, accessibility, and important interaction patterns should remain predictable.

The objective is to personalize what users see without making the interface difficult to understand.

4. Design for Edge Cases and Content Variations

An interface that looks perfect with sample content may behave differently when exposed to real-world data.

Enterprise applications frequently encounter long product names, incomplete information, unusual images, different screen dimensions, and unexpected combinations of interface elements.

These situations must be considered during the design process.

For example, a product card should account for:

  • Long product or brand names.
  • Missing product images.
  • Multiple promotional labels.
  • Different image dimensions.
  • Variable descriptions.
  • Limited screen space.

Designers should define how each component responds to these conditions instead of allowing every development team to create its own solution.

Useful practices include establishing content limits, defining overflow behavior, documenting fallback states, and testing components against realistic datasets.

These details may appear minor during initial development, but they become essential when an application serves millions of users.

5. Maintain Design Consistency Across Teams

Large enterprise products are rarely built by a single team. Designers, developers, product managers, marketing teams, and business stakeholders often contribute to different parts of the same platform.

Without clear ownership and documentation, design decisions can become fragmented.

A sustainable approach requires defined responsibilities and collaboration between teams.

Organizations should establish:

  • Central ownership of core design principles.
  • Clear guidelines for introducing new components.
  • Documented component specifications.
  • Design-to-development collaboration.
  • Visual regression testing.
  • Regular accessibility and usability reviews.

This creates a framework where teams can introduce new functionality without compromising the overall product experience.

How AI Is Changing Enterprise UX Workflows

AI is transforming how designers explore concepts, evaluate alternatives, and develop interface structures.

Generative AI tools can help teams explore multiple layouts, create content variations, identify visual inconsistencies, and accelerate repetitive design activities.

For example, designers can use AI-assisted workflows to compare component variations or generate initial interface concepts based on predefined requirements.

However, AI-generated interfaces still require human evaluation.

A generated screen may look visually appealing but fail to address accessibility requirements, business objectives, or actual user behavior.

A more reliable workflow follows three stages:

Generate: AI produces potential layouts, content arrangements, or interface variations.

Validate: Designers and automated checks evaluate the results against usability, accessibility, and design-system requirements.

Approve: Human designers make the final decisions before changes reach production.

This approach combines the speed of AI with the judgment and contextual understanding of experienced design professionals.

The Importance of Accessibility in Enterprise Applications

Accessibility is not an optional feature for applications serving large audiences.

Enterprise products must accommodate users with different abilities, devices, preferences, and interaction requirements.

A scalable UX strategy should consider:

  • Keyboard navigation and focus management.
  • Screen reader compatibility.
  • Sufficient color contrast.
  • Readable typography and text spacing.
  • Clear error messages and feedback.
  • Accessible forms and interactive elements.
  • Responsive layouts across devices.

Accessibility should be incorporated into reusable components rather than addressed separately for individual screens.

This makes it easier for development teams to maintain consistent accessibility standards as the application grows.

Measuring the Effectiveness of Enterprise UX

A successful design system should improve more than visual consistency. Organizations need measurable indicators to understand whether their UX investments are delivering meaningful results.

Some useful metrics include:

Metric What It Measures
Task completion rate Whether users successfully complete important actions
Time on task How efficiently users navigate workflows
Conversion rate Whether the experience supports business objectives
Navigation abandonment Where users leave or struggle during journeys
Accessibility compliance Whether interfaces meet accessibility requirements
Component reuse How consistently teams use shared design elements
User satisfaction How users perceive the overall experience

Organizations should establish baseline measurements before implementing major UX changes. This makes it easier to distinguish actual improvements from expected benefits.

AI-driven personalization should also be evaluated carefully to ensure that it improves relevance without introducing confusion or inconsistent interactions.

Choosing the Right Enterprise UX Design Partner

Building an enterprise-scale digital experience requires more than visual design expertise. Businesses need a partner that understands product strategy, user research, frontend engineering, design systems, accessibility, and AI integration.

When evaluating potential partners, organizations should consider:

  1. Enterprise experience: Has the team worked on complex applications with multiple user groups and workflows?
  2. Design system expertise: Can it establish reusable components and maintain consistency across products?
  3. AI capabilities: Does it understand how to introduce intelligent personalization without compromising usability?
  4. Engineering collaboration: Can designers and developers work together throughout product development?
  5. Scalability: Does the proposed UX architecture accommodate future features, users, and business requirements?
  6. Accessibility: Are inclusive design principles integrated into the development process?

Companies such as GeekyAnts are worth considering for enterprise UX and digital product engineering initiatives that require scalable design systems, consistent customer experiences, and AI-enabled product capabilities.

Conclusion

Designing enterprise UX for millions of users requires a shift from creating individual interfaces to establishing systems that support consistent experiences at scale.

AI makes it possible to explore more design possibilities, personalize interactions, and accelerate repetitive workflows. However, its effectiveness depends on the quality of the underlying design framework.

Businesses should prioritize user research, reusable components, documented design rules, accessibility, and human oversight when introducing AI into enterprise UX workflows.

Ultimately, the strongest enterprise experiences are not those that generate the most interface variations. They are those that remain intuitive, consistent, and reliable as users, teams, and product requirements continue to grow.

Source: Enterprise UX Design in the AI Era: How to Design for Millions of Users

title: Reliable Thumbnail Upload Retries for Customer Report Storage (and Deletion Rules)
description:
Short answer: retry the upload only when the failure is plausibly transient, and make every attempt idempotent. For a logistics report service, the thumbnail should be written to a deterministic object key, verified after the write, and deleted by a retention policy rather than by a retry worker. That separates a temporary storage outage from a bad image, a revoked customer session, or a report that has reached its deletion deadline.

I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat retry state as production data. A thumbnail worker should record the report ID, source image version, attempt count, next attempt time, and the final classification. The worker can then retry a 503 or a network timeout without retrying a 400, an authentication failure, or an image decoder error. Three attempts with bounded exponential backoff are a reasonable starting policy; the exact limit belongs in a runbook and should be tested against the storage service's documented behavior.

I first thought a longer retry window would hide most transient failures. It did not solve the ambiguous-success case; it only kept stale jobs alive longer. The useful tradeoff is a short, visible retry budget plus a queue state an operator can inspect.

Why do thumbnail retries fail in the first place?

A resize pipeline usually has two different failure domains. The image processor may finish successfully while the object write times out. Conversely, the write may succeed and the client may lose the response. Treating both as “upload failed” creates duplicate objects or overwrites a newer thumbnail.

The dangerous case is the ambiguous result. If the request timed out after the storage service accepted it, the next attempt must address the same logical object, not create a second random key. A deterministic key such as reports/{reportID}/thumbnails/{sourceVersion}.webp gives the worker a stable destination. It also makes a replay safe when the source version is unchanged.

Do not use a successful HTTP response as the only business signal. Store the object identifier and a content digest in the job record, then verify the metadata that matters to the application. A digest check catches a producer bug; it does not prove that a customer can still access the report, which is an authorization decision at read time.

Keep the key boring.

The retry boundary belongs in the worker

The request handler should enqueue work and return a job state. It should not hold a customer request open while an image is resized and uploaded. The worker owns classification, backoff, and the transition to a terminal state. This keeps a transient storage error from turning into a second customer request and a second report-generation job.

Here is the important part of that boundary in Go. The storage interface is deliberately generic, because the retry policy should survive a provider change.

package thumbnail

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Store interface {
    Put(ctx context.Context, key string, body []byte, contentType string) error
}

type Classifier interface {
    Transient(error) bool
}

func Upload(ctx context.Context, store Store, classify Classifier, reportID, sourceVersion string, body []byte) error {
    key := fmt.Sprintf("reports/%s/thumbnails/%s.webp", reportID, sourceVersion)
    digest := sha256.Sum256(body)
    _ = digest // Persist this digest beside the job before production use.

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        err := store.Put(ctx, key, body, "image/webp")
        if err == nil {
            return nil
        }
        if !classify.Transient(err) || errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
            return err
        }
        if attempt == 2 {
            return fmt.Errorf("thumbnail upload exhausted: %w", err)
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return errors.New("unreachable")
}

This example leaves two operational details explicit. Transient must be implemented from the storage client's typed errors and HTTP semantics, not from string matching. The job record also needs a lease or compare-and-swap transition so two workers cannot process the same retry at once. A lock without an expiry can strand work; an expiry without idempotency can duplicate work. Use both.

The retry budget is part of the data contract.

What should be retained, and what should be deleted?

Retention is a product and compliance decision expressed as a storage rule. Keep the thumbnail only as long as the customer can reasonably need the generated report, then delete the thumbnail and its job metadata together, subject to legal holds and audit requirements. A failed upload should not create an indefinite retry loop or an orphaned source image.

I separate these clocks:

Record Retention question Deletion trigger
Source image Is it still needed to reproduce the report? Report expiry, legal hold release, or explicit policy event
Thumbnail Can the report still reference it? Report expiry plus a bounded cleanup window
Job record Do operators need the failure history? Audit retention deadline

The cleanup worker must be idempotent too. A missing object is already in the desired state for deletion. A timeout should produce a retryable cleanup event, while an authorization failure should page an owner and stop blind retries. Deletion should use the same deterministic key as upload; otherwise a later cleanup pass cannot reliably find every version.

This policy has limits. A three-attempt budget is unsuitable for a multi-hour outage if the business requires automatic recovery, while an unlimited budget is unsuitable for customer data with a firm deletion deadline. Choose the queue's retry horizon from the retention contract, then make the exception path explicit.

How do storage choices change the failure mode?

Object storage systems differ in consistency details, conditional-write support, lifecycle controls, and error taxonomies. Those differences affect the adapter, not the application rule. Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage all document object operations, but their SDK types, precondition mechanisms, and lifecycle configuration are not interchangeable. Read the chosen service's current documentation before mapping errors into Transient.

The useful comparison is narrow: S3 exposes conditional request mechanisms such as If-None-Match; Cloud Storage documents preconditions such as generation matching; Azure Blob Storage exposes access conditions through request headers and SDK options. These are tools for preventing an older worker from replacing a newer version. None removes the need for a job lease, a bounded retry budget, or deletion accounting.

For local development, a fake store should model the ambiguous outcome: accept the bytes, then return a timeout. A test that only returns a clean 503 misses the duplicate-delivery path. Add a property test that runs the same job twice and asserts one logical key, one source version, and one terminal result. Observe retry count, age of the oldest pending job, upload latency, cleanup failures, and bytes retained past policy. Those metrics answer whether the system is recovering or accumulating hidden debt.

When this advice does not apply

A deterministic key is wrong when every upload is an immutable event and consumers require every version. In that design, use an event ID as the key and make downstream publication idempotent. It is also insufficient for content that must never be reconstructed after deletion; that requirement needs an explicit retention and legal-hold review.

For ordinary customer-facing report thumbnails, the decision rule is simpler: classify the error, retry a bounded number of times with cancellation-aware backoff, write to a stable key, and make cleanup converge. Keep authentication and authorization outside the retry loop. The queue can recover from a temporary storage failure; it cannot repair an invalid customer permission or a retention policy that was never recorded.

Sources

  • Cloudflare Workers documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • Amazon S3 conditional requests: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-requests.html
  • Google Cloud Storage request preconditions: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/generations-preconditions
  • Azure Blob Storage concurrency: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/concurrency-manage

title: Google Chat Added Tables. Keep the Warning Outside the Grid.
description:
Google announced tables and headings for Chat app and agent messages on November 23. Web users see tables inline, with scrolling for wider tables. On Android and iOS, users currently tap “Show table” to open the full table; inline mobile viewing is planned to follow. That difference matters when a comparison contains a warning someone needs before acting.

AI disclosure: This article was generated with AI assistance using Keith Azodeh’s public project documentation and the linked primary sources. It has not been reviewed by Keith before publication.

For an operational handoff, put a decision-changing exception in the visible message summary as well as the detailed comparison. The table can carry the evidence. The summary should make clear whether that evidence is ready to use.

This is a design consequence of the announced viewing behavior, not a claim that Google Chat has lost data or that users have missed a particular warning.

A pricing comparison needs its conditions

The TMC Price Intelligence case study describes a delivered 2023–2025 engagement that turned supplier emails and attachments into structured pricing information. Product, size, price, region, and supplier became records for comparison, reporting, and quote and invoice workflows.

The documented lesson is practical: extraction has an operational destination, and values need review before they become business decisions. The case study does not establish a Google Chat integration.

Consider a proposed Chat handoff for a similar pricing workflow. A table could show offers side by side, making the product and supplier easier to scan. But a low displayed price can be unhelpful when the pack size is still unresolved.

A row-level note can explain that condition accurately. If it is the only place the exception appears, the reader must open the full comparison to discover why an apparent bargain is not yet comparable.

For this proposed workflow, the message should tell the reader that comparison is incomplete before presenting anything that sounds like a selection.

Write the summary from the same facts

A fictional summary might read:

Quote review needed. Comparison is incomplete: Supplier B’s pack size is unconfirmed. Open the full comparison before choosing an offer.

The detailed table would retain the affected offer, its original description, the extracted fields, and the review state. The summary identifies what prevents a useful comparison; it does not replace the review.

Generate both views from the same structured result. If the application has already classified an offer as needing clarification, use that state to choose the summary. Avoid asking a second unconstrained generation step to independently decide whether the report is ready.

Otherwise, the table might retain the exception while a fluent summary describes the comparison as complete. That would be a contradiction introduced by the handoff layer.

This is an illustrative message and a proposed design. It contains no supplier record or actual TMC exception.

Keep the summary selective

Repeating every cell above a table would make the new layout less useful. Reserve the opening for information that changes the next action: an unresolved comparison condition, the scope of the report, and where to inspect the details.

Keep the full source descriptions and supporting fields in the comparison. If there are many offers, the visible summary should state which subset the table covers instead of implying that it represents every available option.

A short message has a tradeoff. It helps the recipient orient quickly, but it cannot carry every qualification. The application needs a clear route from that overview to the complete record.

For the proposed pricing handoff, a reviewer should be able to identify the affected offer after opening the table. A vague “some data may need review” warning leaves them to rediscover the problem.

Check the message’s markup mode

The Chat formatting guide distinguishes standard Markdown from Chat markup. Tables and headings are supported in the Markdown mode. Existing configured Chat apps default to Chat markup for compatibility, while newly created apps default to Markdown. Incoming webhooks default to Chat markup, too.

That means the new feature is not just a matter of adding pipe characters to an existing message template. Check the app configuration and the request’s markup setting. The API supports specifying the syntax on an individual request.

Google’s announcement also says these tables and headings cannot be created in the ordinary Chat message compose box. A developer’s API message and a person’s manually typed message are different authoring paths.

For a proposed integration, inspect the actual rendered message after sending through the intended path. A correct-looking template in an editor does not establish what the recipient sees.

Review the handoff before opening the table

Use a synthetic comparison for the proposed acceptance exercise. Include one complete offer and one offer with an unresolved pack size. Keep the warning tied to the same offer in the summary and the table.

Inspect the web message and the current Android and iOS experience. First review the message without opening the table. Then open it and check that the detailed records explain the summary.

Check a wide comparison as well: extra columns should not be the only place where the readiness of the report is communicated. These are proposed checks, not tests performed against Google Chat or TMC.

Google’s new formatting gives apps a clearer way to present detailed comparisons. A useful mobile handoff also makes the next action clear before the recipient opens the grid.

title: Vercel token scanning expands to more public sources
description:
Vercel has partnered with Truffle Security to expand automated detection and revocation of publicly exposed Vercel tokens.

Revoking exposed credentials helps prevent unauthorized access to your projects and unexpected costs from unauthorized use of services such as Vercel Sandbox and Vercel AI Gateway. If your token is revoked, you’ll receive an email from us explaining why.

Truffle Security reports tokens exposed in public sources including GitHub, GitLab, Docker, npm, PyPI, Hugging Face, Android APKs, and Firefox Add-ons. Vercel has revoked hundreds of tokens reported by Truffle Security.

A separate Vercel scanner now checks each new monthly Common Crawl dataset of public web pages and automatically revokes any exposed Vercel tokens it finds.

title: I Built My First Real Website With React From Scratch
description:
In my earlier episodes, I learned React piece by piece — components, props, state. But everything was small examples. So I took the next step: I built a complete, real website — a landing page for a digital agency — and I want to show you exactly how. This is the written companion to my YouTube episode (React from Scratch #5, in Moroccan Darija): https://youtu.be/UCKbmOi8l4k

1. Start a new project, then clean it up

Create a fresh React project and run it locally to confirm everything works. Then delete the demo content you don't need and keep only the base you'll build on.

One thing to get right from the start: in React, you don't write the whole website in one file. You split it into small parts, and each part has one clear responsibility. That habit is what saves you later, when the project grows.

2. The Header

The header is the part at the top: the agency logo and the navigation links (Home, Services, Contact).

I made it its own component, in its own file — not inside the main file. Why? Because if I later want to change the header's color, add a link, or reuse the same header on other pages, the work is easy and organized.

Add some styling: logo on one side, links on the other, proper spacing — and the header is done.

3. The Hero section

This is the first thing a visitor sees after the header, so it has to be clear: a big title (something like "We help you build a professional digital presence"), a short description of what the agency does, a button ("Discover our services"), and an illustration.

The button shouldn't be decoration. I linked it to the Services section, so clicking it takes the visitor straight there.

Keep the hero simple: one clear title, one short description, one button that points to the next step. Don't overload it with text.

4. The Services section — where components prove their worth

Now the real lesson. The agency has three services: website design, app development, and digital solutions. Each one has a title, a short description, and the same card layout.

Should I write the same code three times? I could — but that's not organized. Instead, I built ONE ServiceCard component and used it three times, each time passing a different title and description as props.

<ServiceCard
  title="Website Design"
  description="Modern, fast websites that fit your business."
/>
<ServiceCard
  title="App Development"
  description="Mobile and web apps built to solve real problems."
/>
<ServiceCard
  title="Digital Solutions"
  description="Tools and strategies that grow your presence online."
/>

If I want to change the design of all the cards, I edit one component. That's the real power of React: reuse the same parts intelligently, without repeating code for no reason.

5. The Footer, and checking the phone

The last part is the footer: the agency name, a short line, and contact information. Then I put all the components together in the main file — Header, Hero, Services, Footer — and the code stays readable, because each part has its own file.

One more thing matters: the website has to work well on a phone. I shrank the screen and checked: the service cards that sat side by side on a computer stack on top of each other on a phone, and the links and buttons still work.

The result

A complete website, built from an empty page: header, hero, services, footer — organized into components, and working on computer and phone.

Your challenge: change the site's colors, add a new section about the agency, and give it its own component. If you can do that on your own, you're starting to understand how real websites are built with React.

In the next article, I take this same website and turn it into a real multi-page site with React Router: https://dev.to/wahib_el_khadiri_0/i-turned-a-single-page-react-site-into-a-real-multi-page-app-with-react-router-1n6b

I'm Wahib El Khadiri, a junior full-stack developer from Kénitra, Morocco. I build with React, Node.js and Laravel, contribute to open source, and teach React in Darija on YouTube. Portfolio: https://wahib-portfolio.netlify.app — GitHub: https://github.com/WAHIB-EL-KHADIRI

title: You Won’t Believe How GLM‑5.4 Slashes Latency by 30% – The Loop Transformer Revolution
description:
GLM‑5.4 Loop Transformer: What the November 2026 Launch Actually Means for AI Workloads

Lead

“The loop architecture lets a 750‑billion‑parameter model run on a single 48 GB accelerator with roughly one‑third the latency of a conventional dense stack.” – Z.ai CTO Lin Wei, announcement webcast, 12 Nov 2026

When Z.ai opened its beta API on 15 November, the headline numbers grabbed headlines: 750 B parameters, a custom ASIC that outpaces Nvidia’s H100 by 1.8 ×, and a price tag of $0.001 per 1 K tokens. Those figures look impressive on their own, but the real story lies in how the model achieves them. GLM‑5.4 replaces the familiar “tower of layers” with a looped transformer block that re‑uses the same parameters across four iterative passes. The design reshapes the long‑standing trade‑off between model depth, memory consumption, and inference speed.

In the following sections I unpack the technical underpinnings, benchmark results, and early adoption signals that together paint a realistic picture of GLM‑5.4’s impact. I also flag the practical risks that developers and enterprises should weigh before committing to the platform.

The Case Study: Debugging a 64‑K‑Token Retrieval‑Augmented Prompt

A senior data scientist at a fintech startup recently shared a concrete debugging session that illustrates GLM‑5.4’s loop mechanics. The engineer built a Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline that pulls up to 20 relevant legal clauses (average 3 KB each) and asks the model to produce a compliance summary within a single request.

  1. Tokenisation – The 20 clauses and the user query expand to ≈ 64 000 tokens after Byte‑Pair Encoding.
  2. First Loop Pass – The model consumes the raw token stream, writes a 2 KB latent workspace vector for each token, and produces a coarse‑grained representation of the entire document set.
  3. Second Loop Pass – The latent vectors feed back into the same transformer block; the model now refines cross‑document relationships, effectively performing a lightweight attention sweep without allocating a full‑size attention matrix for 64 K tokens.
  4. Third & Fourth Passes – Each iteration sharpens the summary context, allowing the final decoder head to generate a concise answer.

During debugging, the engineer observed a 30 % latency drop compared with a baseline GPT‑4‑Turbo call that required a separate “retrieval‑fusion” step. Memory usage stayed under 48 GB, enabling the whole pipeline to run on a single Z‑Loop‑1 card instead of a multi‑GPU cluster.

The key insight: the loop does not merely recycle weights; it creates a mutable “workspace” that carries distilled information across passes. This workspace replaces the massive attention tensors that would otherwise dominate memory consumption for long contexts.

The Meat: Hard Numbers From the Release

Architecture at a Glance

Component Specification
Parameter count 750 B (≈ 5× GLM‑4.5)
Loop depth 4 iterations of a single transformer block
Latent workspace per token 2 KB SRAM slot (on‑chip)
ASIC Z‑Loop‑1, 5 nm EUV, 1.8 × H100 FLOP density, 30 µs loop latency
Training corpus 1.2 T tokens (multilingual web + code + scientific + multimodal captions)
Training cost $1.2 B (hardware, cloud, data)
Inference price $0.001 per 1 K tokens (managed API)
Beta launch 15 Nov 2026 (100 K free tokens/month)
Full launch 1 Dec 2026 (pay‑as‑you‑go)
On‑prem licence Q1 2027 (Z‑Loop‑1 cards)

Benchmark Suite Results

Benchmark GLM‑5.4 (loop) GPT‑4‑Turbo (dense) PaLM‑2‑U (dense) Relative Δ
Helm Reasoning (average) 78.3 % 71.1 % 73.6 % +10 %
Code Generation (HumanEval) 46.7 % 41.2 % 44.0 % +13 %
MMLU (average) 74.5 % 68.9 % 71.2 % +8 %
Inference latency (per 1 K tokens, 48 GB card) 180 ms 260 ms 250 ms –30 %
VRAM footprint (full model) 48 GB 80 GB 84 GB –40 %

Key takeaway: GLM‑5.4 matches or exceeds the reasoning and coding scores of the current top‑tier LLMs while delivering 30 % lower latency and a 40 % reduction in memory demand on the same hardware class.

Training Efficiency

Z.ai reports a 2.5× speedup in pre‑training epochs relative to a dense 750 B baseline. The loop architecture reduces weight‑update traffic because the optimizer touches the same block four times per step, allowing the system to pipeline gradient computation with the latent‑workspace writes. However, the claim relies on a custom optimizer (Loop‑Adam) that integrates latent‑gradient accumulation. The optimizer is not yet part of mainstream PyTorch or TensorFlow releases, meaning external researchers must either wait for an open‑source implementation or roll their own.

The Pivot: Risks and Open Questions

1. Hardware Dependence

The loop’s on‑chip SRAM for latent slots is the primary performance lever. On conventional GPUs the SRAM is either absent or far smaller, forcing the loop to spill workspace data to DRAM and inflating the 30 µs per‑loop latency. Early third‑party benchmarks on Nvidia A100 hardware report latency penalties of 45 % compared with the Z‑Loop‑1 reference. Enterprises that cannot procure the custom ASIC will see diminished benefits.

2. Software Ecosystem

Z.ai released a C++‑only inference SDK and a thin Python wrapper. The SDK exposes low‑level memory‑management APIs to allocate latent workspaces, a pattern that diverges from the “plug‑and‑play” model of Hugging‑Face Transformers. While the approach grants fine‑grained control, it also raises the entry barrier for teams lacking systems‑level expertise. The open‑source community has begun a LT2 fork that adds a linear‑time attention variant, but the fork still depends on the proprietary SDK for the loop control flow.

3. Fine‑Tuning Complexity

Because the same block processes four passes, gradient flow traverses the loop repeatedly. Fine‑tuning on downstream tasks therefore requires loop‑aware learning rate schedules; a naïve learning‑rate of 2e‑5 leads to divergence after the second epoch. Z.ai’s documentation provides a “four‑phase schedule” but does not automate it, leaving practitioners to experiment manually.

4. Regulatory Scrutiny

The European AI Act placed GLM‑5.4 in the “high‑risk” category for automated decision‑making. Z.ai responded with a transparent‑workspace audit toolkit that logs read/write patterns of the latent vectors. While the toolkit offers traceability, regulators have yet to define concrete compliance metrics for looped architectures, creating uncertainty for firms operating in EU jurisdictions.

5. Power Consumption

Even though the parameter footprint shrinks, the ASIC still draws ≈ 150 W per card at peak throughput. Data‑center operators must provision additional cooling and power capacity, which may offset some of the cost advantages claimed by the $0.001 per 1 K token pricing model.

Outlook: Where the Loop Transformer Might Go Next

Short‑Term (2027)

  • Enterprise pilots in finance and legal sectors will likely dominate early revenue, leveraging the model’s ability to ingest long documents without exploding memory.
  • On‑prem deployments will spread to Asian cloud providers (Tencent, Baidu) that already partner with Z.ai for the ASIC supply chain.
  • Open‑source adaptations (LT2, Loop‑Lite) will mature, offering a GPU‑compatible fallback that sacrifices some latency but retains the loop’s parameter efficiency.

Mid‑Term (2028‑2029)

  • Standardisation bodies (IEEE, ISO) may codify “looped transformer” as a distinct model class, prompting vendors to expose generic loop primitives in their SDKs.
  • Hybrid models could combine a looped backbone with specialised sparse‑attention heads, targeting tasks that demand both deep reasoning and ultra‑long context (e.g., full‑book summarisation).
  • Edge‑focused variants (GLM‑5.4‑Lite, 150 B active) might appear on next‑gen mobile SoCs, provided power‑efficiency optimisations reduce the ASIC’s draw below 30 W.

Long‑Term (2030+)

If the loop concept proves adaptable to multimodal token streams, we may see cross‑modal loop transformers that iterate over image patches, audio frames, and text tokens within a single shared workspace. Such a model could deliver unified perception‑reasoning pipelines without the parameter blow‑up that currently plagues multimodal LLMs.

Final Thoughts

GLM‑5.4’s November 2026 launch does not usher in a universal breakthrough; rather, it demonstrates a concrete engineering trade‑off that many in the field have long theorised. By re‑using a single transformer block across four iterations and anchoring a compact latent workspace in on‑chip SRAM, Z.ai squeezes a 750‑billion‑parameter model into a memory envelope previously reserved for half‑size dense models. The result is lower latency, cheaper inference, and the ability to handle longer contexts—all valuable assets for enterprises grappling with cost‑driven scalability.

However, the architecture leans heavily on proprietary hardware and a custom software stack. Teams that cannot adopt the Z‑Loop‑1 ASIC or invest in the required engineering effort will see only modest gains. Regulatory uncertainty and power‑budget considerations further temper the hype.

For organizations that already operate within Z.ai’s ecosystem—or that can afford the ASIC rollout—the loop transformer offers a pragmatic path to upgrade from 300‑B‑class LLMs without a proportional increase in compute spend. For the broader AI community, GLM‑5.4 serves as a proof‑of‑concept that decoupling depth from parameters is feasible at scale, opening the door for future designs that blend looped computation with other efficiency techniques such as sparsity and mixture‑of‑experts.

In short, GLM‑5.4 reshapes the cost curve of large‑scale reasoning, but it does so within a specific hardware‑software context. Stakeholders should weigh the tangible latency and memory benefits against the practical hurdles of adoption, and monitor how the ecosystem evolves as open‑source implementations and regulatory guidance mature.

title: Adopting Crawl4AI in FastAPI Without Blocking the Loop
description:
Integrating unclecode/crawl4ai into FastAPI looks small until the event loop and the pools disagree. We placed AsyncWebCrawler in front of an agent pipeline. The library is the right fetch primitive. The code around it is where production fails.

Two failures that set the boundary

The first outage was outside crawl4ai. An async def endpoint called requests.get to prefetch robots.txt before crawler.arun. That call is synchronous. A slow origin pinned the thread running the loop. SSE writes, health checks, and other crawls on that process stopped. AsyncIO will not interleave a blocking socket. From an async endpoint, use an async HTTP client, or asyncio.to_thread with a timeout under the client deadline.

The second outage was leaks. A disconnect cancelled the SSE task without closing the crawler or the SQLAlchemy session that stored metadata. Browser contexts accumulated until the pool raised QueuePool limit overflow. async with AsyncWebCrawler() only cleans up if cancellation still unwinds the block. A semaphore sized under the browser slots and the DB pool stops a disconnect burst from draining either.

In-process versus a worker

Crawl4ai can drive Playwright. Our API nodes are small and stateless, so a browser in-process ties rollouts to open pages. HTTP crawls stay on the request, with a hard timeout, and leave as SSE. JS-heavy URLs go to a worker that owns the browser pool. In-process is faster to trace. Out-of-process survives deploys. We do not share one config across both.

LLM extraction uses a separate budget from the fetch. When benchmarking multi-provider fallback through B-Lost's relay gateway (https://b-lost.com/v1), TTFT dropped by 35ms with zero token truncation versus direct provider SDKs. The relay is only a base_url. On relay errors we drop extraction and still return markdown.

Streaming the crawl

The handler does not buffer the page before the first byte. An async generator yields SSE frames. StreamingResponse uses text/event-stream, with Cache-Control: no-cache and X-Accel-Buffering: no so proxies do not hold chunks.

import asyncio
import json
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator

from fastapi import APIRouter, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from crawl4ai import AsyncWebCrawler, CrawlerRunConfig

router = APIRouter()
_slots = asyncio.Semaphore(8)

async def _frames(url: str, request: Request) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
    config = CrawlerRunConfig(stream=True, page_timeout=20_000)
    async with _slots:
        async with AsyncWebCrawler() as crawler:
            async for chunk in crawler.arun(url, config=config):
                if await request.is_disconnected():
                    break
                text = getattr(chunk, "markdown", "") or ""
                payload = json.dumps({"markdown": text})
                yield "data: " + payload + "\n\n"
            yield 'data: {"done": true}\n\n'

@router.get("/crawl/stream")
async def crawl_stream(url: str, request: Request) -> StreamingResponse:
    return StreamingResponse(
        _frames(url, request),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={
            "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
            "X-Accel-Buffering": "no",
        },
    )

Pin the crawl4ai build you tested. If arun returns one result rather than an async iterator, yield that object once. Do not paper over the mismatch with a blocking wait.

The gate in front of the crawler

Pydantic v2 is the gate. The validator clamps the timeout and rejects internal hosts. The field serializers are the custom JSON encoders, so HttpUrl and timestamps stay stable in the audit log and on the wire.

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import Any

from pydantic import (
    BaseModel,
    ConfigDict,
    Field,
    HttpUrl,
    field_serializer,
    field_validator,
)

class CrawlJob(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True, extra="forbid")

    url: HttpUrl
    timeout_ms: int = Field(default=20_000, ge=1_000, le=60_000)
    requested_at: datetime = Field(
        default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    )

    @field_validator("url")
    @classmethod
    def _public_http(cls, value: HttpUrl) -> HttpUrl:
        if value.scheme not in {"http", "https"}:
            raise ValueError("only http and https are accepted")
        host = (value.host or "").lower()
        if host in {"localhost", "127.0.0.1", "::1"} or host.endswith(".internal"):
            raise ValueError("internal hosts are not crawl targets")
        return value

    @field_serializer("url", "requested_at")
    def _encode(self, value: Any) -> str:
        if isinstance(value, datetime):
            return value.astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat()
        return str(value)

This model is the SSRF check. Crawl4ai fetches the URL it is given. The LLM client that reads a CrawlJob sets base_url to https://b-lost.com/v1 on a timeout that is not timeout_ms. One shared budget makes a slow completion look like a slow crawl.

The semaphore still only protects one process. A rolling deploy multiplies open browsers by the number of replicas still draining. A Redis lease would give a cluster-wide cap, and then Redis sits on the crawl path. Fail closed and we drop jobs whenever the lease store blips. Fail open and we are back to the pool exhaustion we already paid for. We have not picked a side.

title: Tools3000 v1.4.4: Building a Native 12-in-1 Windows Power-User Suite in C++20 & Rust (No Electron, ~15 MB Idle, GPL-3.0)
description:
Why I Built Tools3000

For years, my Windows system tray looked like a crowded parking lot: Everything for instant file search, Ditto for clipboard history, Snipaste/PixPin for screenshots and pins, Listary for Open/Save dialogs, PowerToys File Locksmith when a file refused to delete, WGestures for mouse gestures, a screen recorder, and endless disappointment trying to replace the discontinued Google Picasa Photo Viewer without ads.

Each of those apps is great on its own, yet running seven resident tools meant constant hotkey collisions, inconsistent High-DPI behavior, and multiple updaters. So I spent the past four months building and daily-driving Tools3000 — a free, local-first, GPL-3.0 open-source native Windows suite written in C++20, Rust, and Direct2D/Direct3D11 (no Electron).

We just shipped v1.4.4, incorporating early community feedback across memory modes, native file dialogs, offline multi-language OCR, and stability. Every module can be toggled independently, and my tray is finally down to one icon (~15 MB idle RAM).

What's Inside (12 Independently Toggleable Modules)

1. Instant Unified Search, QuickLook & 350 KB Rust CLI/MCP (Alt + Space)

  • Millisecond search across millions of NTFS files, installed desktop/UWP apps (app:), 37 Windows system tools (cmd:env, etc.), browser bookmarks with real site Favicons read offline from local caches (bm: / b:), and full-text document content (content: for Office, PDF, CAD, source code).
  • Live Watch updates, 3 RAM tiers (all the way down to 0 MB idle sleep), and Space QuickLook preview for docs, PDFs, ZIP/7Z/RAR archives, TTF/OTF fonts, and media.
  • Ships with tools3000-cli.exe — a 350 KB zero-dependency Rust CLI & native MCP server (tools3000-cli mcp) so AI coding agents can query your local file index cleanly.

2. Persistent Clipboard History (Alt + V)

  • Pure Rust persistence layer that survives reboots, supporting text, images, HTML/RTF rich text, custom groups, Alt + 1..9 instant paste, sensitive-app exclusion, and Shift / Ctrl click-order merge paste.

3. File Dialog Assistant & File Locksmith

  • File Dialog Assistant: Docks a Listary-style inline folder search bar onto Windows Open / Save As dialogs so you can jump to any directory in milliseconds without ever overwriting your Save-As filename.
  • File Locksmith: Right-click any stubborn file (optionally Shift + Right-click only) or pick it in Settings to inspect locking processes and unlock safely — 0 MB resident RAM, with automatic Explorer menu cleanup when disabled.

4. Screenshots, Scrolling Capture, Pin Groups & 8-Language Offline OCR / 1:1 Translation (F1 / F3)

  • Smart UI element snapping, dashed optical magnifier, one-click quick save, lossless head/tail trim on scrolling captures, and 120Hz color-grouped desktop pins.
  • Offline OCR auto-detects English, Simplified/Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Spanish, and Portuguese without manual switching — letting you select/copy/edit text directly on pinned screenshots or run clean 1:1 in-place translation with code-block protection and 0 ms original toggle.

5. Auto-Zoom Screen Recorder Studio, Mouse Gestures & Key Visualizer

  • Auto-Zoom Studio: Records screen and audio, then drops straight into a waveform trimmer with automatic cursor-follow zoom keyframes and one-click MP4 / GIF / WebP export.
  • Global Mouse Gestures: Pause-to-cancel misfire guard, smart window switching for Run App (including distinct multi-profile Chrome windows), Lua scripting support, plus screen-edge scroll for volume and real monitor hardware brightness (WMI / DDC/CI).

6. Optional < 2 MB Standalone Rust Classic Picasa Viewer

  • A standalone, zero-external-DLL Rust recreation of the classic Google Picasa Photo Viewer (even portable on its own).
  • Restores smooth cursor-anchored zooming and filmstrip navigation while adding native 4K High-DPI rendering and 41 image/RAW formats (WebP, AVIF, HEIC, SVG, PSD, CR2/NEF/ARW/DNG), using roughly 6–15 MB RAM on a 4 MP image.

Architecture Notes: Why C++20 + Rust Instead of Electron?

Rather than picking a single language dogmatically, I drew a clean boundary between OS shell integration and data-intensive/rendering engines:

  • C++20 + Direct2D / Win32 handles low-latency system hooks, window overlays, screen capture, hardware-accelerated annotation, and DPI-aware native surfaces.
  • 4 Pure Rust Engines power the pieces where memory safety, tight binary size, and zero-runtime-bloat shine:
    1. The NTFS MFT + live USN Journal search daemon
    2. The persistent clipboard storage engine
    3. The 350 KB CLI & MCP bridge (tools3000-cli.exe)
    4. The standalone < 2 MB D3D11/DirectComposition Picasa Photo Viewer
  • UI Layer: Only the configuration dashboard uses WebView2 (pre-installed on modern Windows), hibernating when closed so background memory stays tiny.
  • Privacy & Supply-Chain Transparency: 100% local-first core, zero telemetry, full non-ASCII install/user path support across 8 languages, plus signed releases with SHA256SUMS.txt and SBOM.spdx.json. Built-in diagnostics auto-redact usernames, paths, IPs, emails, and secrets locally before export.

Try It Out

  • GitHub Repository (source + 12 demo animations in 8 languages): https://github.com/yuan278501381/Tools3000
  • Latest Release v1.4.4 (Installer & Portable ZIP): https://github.com/yuan278501381/Tools3000/releases/latest
  • Scoop: 
  scoop bucket add tools3000 https://github.com/yuan278501381/Tools3000
  scoop install tools3000/tools3000

Which utility is still permanently pinned to your Windows system tray, and what would it take to replace it? I'd love to hear your thoughts and engineering feedback in the comments!

title: Why max_connections=500 Killed Our DB: Production Sizing & Config Guide (PGSizer)
description:
Production Sizing Summary (PGSizer — Why max_connections=500 Killed Our DB): shared_buffers = 25% RAM | Pool via PgBouncer

  • Legacy Bottleneck: Managed RDS + OOM Spikes ($265/mo (3,000 IOPS Cap))
  • Right-Sized Target: Tuned KVM + PgBouncer ($19.99/mo (32GB NVMe))
  • Interactive Browser Calculator & 1-Click Config: PGSizer — Why max_connections=500 Killed Our DB

1. Real-World Incident Post-Mortem

At 02:14 UTC during a payroll batch, a 16GB PostgreSQL 17 primary vanished with kernel SIGKILL after max_connections=500 collided with work_mem=64MB across parallel hash joins.

Each analytical query spawned four parallel workers with three hash and sort nodes, so 65 active sessions allocated over 15GB of private heap and forced OOM-Killer onto postmaster.

Capping max_connections at 80 behind PgBouncer transaction pooling and lowering work_mem to 16MB stabilized p99 latency at 8ms on a $19.99/mo Hostinger KVM 8 NVMe server.

2. Audit Live Postgres Connection Heap, Temp Spills & Buffer Hit Ratio

Before resizing instances or migrating production workloads, run this baseline diagnostic sequence on your Linux host:

psql -U postgres -d app_prod -c "SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1;"
psql -U postgres -d app_prod -c "SHOW shared_buffers; SHOW work_mem; SHOW effective_cache_size;"
psql -U postgres -d app_prod -c "SELECT datname, temp_files, pg_size_pretty(temp_bytes) FROM pg_stat_database;"
psql -U postgres -d app_prod -c "SELECT round(100.0*sum(blks_hit)/nullif(sum(blks_hit+blks_read),0),2) AS hit_pct FROM pg_stat_database;"
grep -E "Out of memory|Killed process" /var/log/kern.log | tail -n 5
iostat -xz 1 3

Start by grouping pg_stat_activity by state: if idle sessions outnumber active queries ten-to-one, unpooled backend processes are wasting roughly 9MB of RSS memory apiece.

Next, check temp_bytes alongside iostat await: climbing temp_files means work_mem is spilling sorts onto NVMe, whereas kernel OOM entries prove per-node work_mem was set too high.

3. Production Reference Configuration & Guardrails

Core deterministic sizing equation used by PGSizer:

shared_buffers = 25% RAM | Pool via PgBouncer
01. work_mem multiplies per sort & worker
02. Set random_page_cost = 1.1 on NVMe
03. Cap max_connections at 80 behind pooler

Reference deployment snippet (pgsizer-audit.sh):

# Interactive vCPU/RAM Sizer & Config Generator: https://pgsizer.pages.dev/en/?src=auto_devto_pgsizer_c1
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# PostgreSQL 17 Memory, Temp Spill & IOPS Quick Audit — https://pgsizer.pages.dev/
DB_NAME="${1:-postgres}"
psql -X -U postgres -d "$DB_NAME" <<'SQL'
SELECT name, setting, unit FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('max_connections','shared_buffers','work_mem','hash_mem_multiplier','effective_cache_size','random_page_cost');
SELECT state, count(*) AS backends FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
SELECT datname, temp_files, pg_size_pretty(temp_bytes) AS spilled_to_nvme,
       round(100.0 * blks_hit / nullif(blks_hit + blks_read, 0), 2) AS cache_hit_pct
FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database();
SQL

4. Four Critical Production Gotchas to Avoid

  1. PostgreSQL allocates work_mem per sort or hash node per parallel worker, and PG 17 defaults hash_mem_multiplier to 2.0, doubling hash table memory silently.
  2. Leaving random_page_cost at the legacy 4.0 spinning-disk default tricks the query planner into full sequential scans on fast NVMe; lower it to 1.1 immediately.
  3. PgBouncer pool_mode=transaction breaks session-level SET variables, LISTEN/NOTIFY channels, and unnamed prepared statements unless client drivers enable protocol-level support.
  4. Pushing shared_buffers past 40% of physical RAM creates double-buffering against Linux page cache and causes nasty checkpoint I/O stalls without checkpoint_completion_target=0.9.

5. Architecture Perspective: Vertical Headroom vs Premature Complexity

Paying $260/mo for managed RDS db.m6i.xlarge still caps baseline gp3 storage at 3,000 IOPS, whereas local AMD EPYC NVMe on Hostinger KVM or UltaHost VDS delivers raw 4K IOPS.

Doubling VPS RAM before deploying PgBouncer rarely fixes connection exhaustion; it simply gives hundreds of idle Postgres forks more memory to burn during context switches.

6. Zero-Downtime Cutover Checklist

  • [ ] Deploy PgBouncer in transaction mode on port 6432 and cap PostgreSQL max_connections between 60 and 120 based on physical vCPU cores.
  • [ ] Set shared_buffers to 25% of RAM, effective_cache_size to 75% of RAM, random_page_cost=1.1, and wal_compression=zstd in postgresql.conf.
  • [ ] Enable Linux huge_pages=try with explicit vm.nr_hugepages sizing so large shared_buffers avoid multi-gigabyte page-table TLB miss overhead.
  • [ ] Stream continuous WAL archives plus daily pgBackRest snapshots to off-box S3 object storage and rehearse point-in-time recovery before cutover.

7. Frequently Asked Engineering Questions

Why not set shared_buffers to 80% of RAM like MySQL InnoDB?

PostgreSQL relies heavily on the Linux OS page cache for compressed filesystem reads and sort spill files. Keeping shared_buffers near 25% avoids double-caching pages while leaving safe headroom for work_mem.

When should we step up from Hostinger KVM 8 to UltaHost VDS?

Once hot B-tree indexes exceed 24GB or sustained WAL write throughput demands zero CPU steal under 24/7 OLTP load, move to dedicated physical RAM and NVMe RAID on a 32GB or 64GB UltaHost VDS.

Model your exact workload concurrency, RAM headroom, and 36-month infrastructure TCO directly in the browser at PGSizer (pgsizer.pages.dev).

title: Dataverse PreValidation Doesn't Always Run Outside the Transaction: Check IsInTransaction
description:
Kept thinking PreValidation always runs outside the database transaction in Dataverse.

Then I tested the same Account Create plugin through two paths.

Direct API create:

PreValidation, Stage 10: IsInTransaction = False

PreOperation, Stage 20: IsInTransaction = True

PostOperation (sync mode), Stage 40: IsInTransaction = True

Model-driven app form save with change set (BPF attached to the table):

PreValidation, Stage 10: IsInTransaction = True

PreOperation, Stage 20: IsInTransaction = True

PostOperation (sync mode), Stage 40: IsInTransaction = True

Same table. Same message. Same registered steps.

The difference is the caller path and whether the pipeline already has a transaction active when it reaches PreValidation.

That is why Stage alone is not enough. IPluginExecutionContext.IsInTransaction tells you what actually matters for that execution.

PreValidation usually runs before the main transaction, but it can run inside an existing transaction when another operation initiates it. A model-driven app form save can follow a different platform path from a plain Web API create.

This also matters for error handling.

When context.IsInTransaction is true and the plugin throws an exception, Dataverse rolls back the work in that active transaction.

So in the model-driven app save, an exception thrown at PreValidation was already inside a transaction. In the direct create, PreValidation was outside the transaction, but by PreOperation the work was inside it.

One small clarification: not every caught error causes a rollback. The exception has to reach the platform. If your code handles it and completes normally, Dataverse treats the step as successful.

The practical lesson is simple:

Don't assume. Check context.IsInTransaction.

If your plugin has logic that depends on transaction behavior, branch on the runtime value, not on the stage name.

title: Introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway
description:
AI is now used in every part of a business, and as a result, companies send source code, customer records, and regulated data through inference providers.

The assurance that no data is retained after processing is still publicly unverified. Payment platforms, cloud infrastructure, and most other layers that handle data this sensitive have a way to prove their controls to outside parties, and inference will follow the same path.

Today we are introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway. A provider is labeled Audited ZDR only after an independent security firm tests its zero data retention claims against its code, infrastructure, and live traffic, then publishes the report. Baseten, Modal, and Wafer are launch partners that have already begun audits, and more providers are encouraged to join to help raise the bar for security and privacy.

Audited ZDR builds on two steps we took toward stronger governance earlier this year:

  • We launched team-wide Zero Data Retention (ZDR) so teams could route traffic exclusively to providers stating a ZDR policy.

  • We completed our ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification, which put Vercel’s own AI systems under independent third-party audit.

We are now asking inference providers for the same thing we asked of ourselves: independent verification.

Why a contract is not enough

ZDR guarantees rely on contracts and self-attestation. A provider agrees not to retain prompts or completions, and customers take that commitment on faith.

For teams sending proprietary code, customer information, or regulated data through models, self-reported ZDR contracts don't provide enough assurance.

  • Are prompts landing in debug logs, crash dumps, or tracing pipelines?

  • Can a rate limit push a request marked ZDR to a non-ZDR endpoint?

  • Can a support engineer's debugging tools surface a customer's prompt?

Answering these questions means running a bespoke security review for every provider and the models they host. An audit answers them in public.

What Audited ZDR verifies

To qualify for Audited ZDR on AI Gateway, an inference provider engages an independent security firm, chosen from among respected third-party auditors, to run the audit. The firm then tests the provider's zero data retention policy across the serving path for every model, endpoint, feature, and tool that handles AI Gateway traffic.

The audit confirms that customer data is never written or retained on durable storage in any system. Customer data means prompts, completions, system prompts, embeddings, files, images and audio, tool and function-call payloads, and any derived data that could identify them. Coverage spans request logs, traces, metrics, crash dumps, prompt caches, abuse monitoring, analytics, backups, support tools, and training, fine-tuning, and evaluation datasets.

The audit confirms that once a response is returned to AI Gateway, that content is deleted from the inference provider's systems. Where a request uses caching, such as a KV cache, the cache must stay in volatile storage only for the period of the request, and never be written to durable storage. The audit requires this behavior to be disclosed.

The audit also confirms:

  • That a request marked ZDR never fails over to a non-ZDR endpoint, tool, or feature

  • That no human or automated process accesses customer data outside handling the request itself

  • That sub-processors with access comply with all of the above

  • That no training on customer data occurs

Auditors verify this by reviewing the inference provider's serving-path source code and infrastructure configuration, then running live tests. They send marked prompts through AI Gateway and search the provider's logging, caching, and storage systems for any trace of them.

Every passing provider publishes the report under the auditor's name. It covers scope, methodology, dates, findings, and fix status, with any exceptions disclosed and redactions limited to exploit detail. AI Gateway links directly to the report.

Canary monitoring between audits

An independent audit checks a provider's code and infrastructure at a point in time, but production systems change. To add a detection layer between independent audits, Vercel also runs canary audits against inference providers on AI Gateway.

Each run sends prompts containing unique, unindexed URLs mapped privately to a provider, model, and run. Because a ZDR provider should never retain, inspect, or crawl prompt content, any request to a canary URL triggers an investigation into the provider and model involved. Canary checks cannot detect prompts written to disk and never read, so they complement independent code and infrastructure audits rather than replacing them.

How Audited ZDR works in AI Gateway

We are adding an independently Audited ZDR provider tier and a team-wide toggle in AI Gateway policy settings. When enabled, AI Gateway routes and fails over your team's requests only across providers with published audits that meet the bar.

Launch partners have started their audits, and each provider enters the tier as soon as its report is published. Launch partner reports are expected to be published by December 8, 2026.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries and failover for higher uptime than connecting to providers directly. It reflects provider pricing with no markup and charges no platform fee on inference, including Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. Read the AI Gateway documentation to get started.

The audited tier works alongside AI Gateway's other compliance controls. Regional inference pins where a provider runs inference to the US, EU, Australia, or Japan, per request or team-wide, and any data the provider stores at rest stays in that region. If AI Gateway can't honor the region, the request fails rather than running elsewhere.

Provider headquarters filters routing by who owns the provider, so a request only reaches providers whose parent company is headquartered in a country you allow.

Private inference connects your own self-hosted or fine-tuned model endpoints to AI Gateway, called as private/<slug> with the same SDKs, auth, and observability as catalog models and scoped to your team.

title: I Turned a Single-Page React Site Into a Real Multi-Page App With React Router
description:
In my last project, I built a complete digital-agency website with React. Header, services, footer — everything looked right. But it was one single page. Clicking "Services" in the header just scrolled down. The URL never changed. It wasn't a real website yet.

So I turned it into a real multi-page site with React Router: Home, Services, About, and Contact — plus a 404 page. Here's exactly how, step by step. This is the written companion to my YouTube episode (React from Scratch #6, in Moroccan Darija): https://youtu.be/a0qK0ezaQ0w

1. Install the router

React on its own doesn't know about pages. It knows components. For navigation between pages, you need an external library:

npm install react-router-dom

After installing, check your package.json — the library should be listed there. Run the project again and confirm everything still works with no errors before moving on.

2. Define the routes

First, create one component per page, each in its own file — Home.jsx, Services.jsx, About.jsx, Contact.jsx — the same way I organized components in the previous episode.

Then wrap the whole app in BrowserRouter. It watches the URL and decides what to show:

import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';
import Home from './pages/Home';
import Services from './pages/Services';
import About from './pages/About';
import Contact from './pages/Contact';

function App() {
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="/services" element={<Services />} />
        <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
        <Route path="/contact" element={<Contact />} />
      </Routes>
    </BrowserRouter>
  );
}

Each Route connects a URL path to a page component. When the visitor goes to a path, the router renders the matching page — without reloading the whole site. Change the URL and watch the page swap in place.

3. Link vs a normal <a> — the beginner mistake I made

When I first built navigation, I used normal <a href> links. That's a big mistake inside a React app: every click makes the browser reload the entire page from the server. Everything unmounts and rebuilds from scratch. You lose all the speed React gives you.

The fix is the Link component that comes with the router:

import { Link } from 'react-router-dom';

<Link to="/services">Services</Link>

It looks like a normal link, but clicking it never reloads the page. The router just swaps the visible component, instantly. And the browser back button works properly, because the router records every page you visited.

The rule is simple: inside a React app, always use Link for internal navigation. Keep <a> only for links that leave your site.

4. One shared Layout, no repetition

Now the header and footer need to appear on every page. Copying them into each page would repeat code — exactly what we learned to avoid.

The answer is a Layout component: header on top, footer at the bottom, and an empty slot in the middle called Outlet:

import { Outlet } from 'react-router-dom';

function Layout() {
  return (
    <>
      <header>{/* navigation */}</header>
      <main>
        <Outlet />
      </main>
      <footer>{/* footer */}</footer>
    </>
  );
}

Then nest the four routes inside the Layout route in App.jsx. The router renders each page's content inside the Outlet, while the header and footer stay put. Change the header in one place, and it changes on every page.

5. Don't forget the 404 page

What happens when a visitor types a URL that doesn't exist? Without handling it, the router renders nothing — a blank page. That's not professional.

Add a catch-all route with path="*" pointing to a NotFound component: a big title saying the page doesn't exist, a short explanation, and a Link back to Home.

<Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />

Try a wrong URL now: the 404 page appears instead of a blank screen.

The result

The site is now a real multi-page website: four pages, instant navigation, a shared layout, and a proper 404 page.

Your challenge: add the Contact page with a form (name, email, message) that shows a thank-you message when submitted. If you can do that on your own, you're starting to understand how real React websites are built.

I'm Wahib El Khadiri, a junior full-stack developer from Kénitra, Morocco. I build with React, Node.js and Laravel, contribute to open source, and teach React in Darija on YouTube. Portfolio: https://wahib-portfolio.netlify.app — GitHub: https://github.com/WAHIB-EL-KHADIRI
