title: Your USDT Wallet Risk Score Is Not a Verdict: Building Better AML Checks for Blockchain Applications
description:
AMLdark · Screen TRC20 USDT addresses for free

Live AML screening for Tron-based USDT addresses against OFAC designations, Tether's freeze list and darknet datasets. Free tier included.

amldark.com

A blockchain transaction can be perfectly valid from a technical perspective and still deserve a closer look from a compliance perspective.

This distinction is becoming increasingly important for developers building cryptocurrency exchanges, payment gateways, wallet applications, P2P platforms, and Web3 infrastructure.

Consider a simple scenario:

A user deposits 5,000 USDT into a cryptocurrency application.

The transaction is confirmed. The tokens arrive. The smart contract behaves as expected.

From the blockchain's perspective, everything worked.

But what does the application actually know about the incoming funds?

Does it know anything about the sending address's previous activity? Has the address interacted with entities associated with sanctions, fraud, or other high-risk activity? Are there indirect relationships that deserve investigation?

A transaction hash alone cannot answer all these questions.

This is where blockchain analytics and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) screening become important engineering considerations.

In this article, we'll explore how developers can think about wallet risk assessment, why simplistic risk scores can be misleading, and how to design more transparent screening workflows for USDT transactions.

  1. Blockchain Validity and Financial Risk Are Different Layers

One of the most important architectural decisions is separating blockchain transaction validation from compliance analysis.

These processes answer different questions.

Blockchain validation asks:

Was the transaction included in the blockchain?

Did the transaction execute successfully?

Which addresses participated?

Which tokens were transferred?

What was the transaction timestamp?

AML analysis asks:

Is an address associated with known risk indicators?

Does it have relevant sanctions exposure?

Are there documented connections to fraudulent activity?

What does its transaction history reveal?

Is further investigation justified?

A successful transaction does not automatically establish the legitimacy of the funds.

Likewise, an address appearing in a risk dataset does not automatically establish criminal activity.

Developers should avoid combining these two layers into a single yes-or-no result.

A better system preserves the original blockchain facts while attaching a separate, explainable risk assessment.

  1. Why USDT on TRON Creates an Interesting Engineering Challenge

USDT is used across multiple blockchain networks, including TRON and Ethereum.

However, developers should never treat every USDT transaction as technically identical.

USDT on TRON uses the TRC-20 token standard, while USDT on Ethereum follows the ERC-20 standard.

The transaction structures, contract addresses, network infrastructure, and available analytical data differ.

For applications supporting TRC-20 USDT, the screening process should consider:

The correct TRON network.

The relevant token contract.

The sending and receiving addresses.

Transaction identifiers.

Token transfer events.

Available historical transaction information.

This is particularly important when applications support deposits from multiple networks.

A token symbol is not a sufficient identifier.

A reliable implementation should use network identifiers and verified contract addresses to prevent accidental cross-network assumptions.

  1. Address Screening Is Not the Same as Transaction Screening

This is one of the most important distinctions in blockchain analytics.

An address represents a blockchain account.

A transaction represents a particular movement of assets.

An address may have thousands of historical transactions, but the risk context of each transaction can be different.

For example, imagine an address that previously received funds from a service identified in a blockchain intelligence dataset.

A basic address-level screening system might return a warning.

However, a more detailed investigation should consider:

When did the interaction occur?

How many transactions separate the addresses?

What was the transferred amount?

Was the exposure direct or indirect?

Is the underlying attribution reliable?

Has the relevant information been updated?

The distinction matters because risk should be evaluated in context.

A single historical interaction should not automatically determine the status of every future transaction involving that address.

  1. The Problem With Treating AML Scores as Absolute Truth

Many blockchain screening systems use numerical risk scores.

These scores can be useful because they make large amounts of information easier to interpret.

However, developers should be careful about how they expose them.

Imagine two addresses:

Address A receives a high-risk classification because of a direct connection to a documented malicious service.

Address B receives a similar score because of several indirect interactions with addresses that have previously been flagged.

The numerical results might look similar, but the underlying circumstances are not necessarily equivalent.

A good screening interface should explain why a score was generated.

Ideally, it should distinguish between:

Direct exposure.

Indirect exposure.

Sanctions-related indicators.

Fraud-related indicators.

Mixer-related indicators.

Historical versus recent activity.

Confirmed information versus uncertain attribution.

The goal is not simply to generate a number.

The goal is to provide enough context for a human reviewer to understand the result.

  1. Designing a Practical AML Screening Pipeline

For developers building cryptocurrency applications, it helps to think about AML screening as a separate processing pipeline.

Here is one possible architecture.

Stage 1: Transaction ingestion

The application receives a blockchain event.

For a TRC-20 USDT transfer, the system should identify:

Transaction hash.

Sender address.

Recipient address.

Token contract.

Transfer amount.

Block information.

Transaction timestamp.

The original blockchain data should be preserved for future reference.

Stage 2: Data normalization

Different data providers may use different formats.

Normalize addresses, timestamps, network identifiers, token amounts, and entity references before performing further analysis.

This reduces inconsistencies across different screening sources.

Stage 3: Risk intelligence lookup

The system checks relevant information from available intelligence datasets.

Depending on the provider, this may include sanctions information, known scam addresses, fraud-related entities, darknet exposure, and other blockchain risk indicators.

The system should also record the source and timestamp of the information.

Stage 4: Relationship analysis

Direct address matching is only one part of blockchain investigation.

Graph analysis can help identify relationships between addresses.

However, developers should avoid assuming that every graph connection represents the same level of risk.

The distance between addresses, transaction amounts, timing, and nature of the relationship all matter.

Stage 5: Risk interpretation

Instead of producing only a single number, the application should return structured findings.

For example, an internal result might contain:

Overall risk classification.

Relevant risk categories.

Direct exposure indicators.

Indirect exposure indicators.

Supporting transaction references.

Data freshness.

Recommended review status.

Stage 6: Human review and decision-making

A screening result should support a decision rather than automatically replace every compliance procedure.

Depending on the business, potential outcomes may include additional verification, enhanced due diligence, escalation to a compliance team, or further investigation.

The appropriate action depends on the applicable legal and operational requirements.

  1. False Positives: The Hidden Cost of Poor Screening

A screening system that identifies every unfamiliar wallet as suspicious is not a useful screening system.

False positives can create serious operational problems.

Imagine a cryptocurrency payment application processing thousands of transactions daily.

If the system generates excessive warnings without sufficient context, the compliance team may spend most of its time investigating low-quality alerts.

This can result in:

Delayed deposits.

Unnecessary customer support requests.

Increased operational costs.

Poor user experiences.

Reduced attention to genuinely significant cases.

This is why screening quality should not be measured only by how many suspicious addresses a system identifies.

Developers should also evaluate:

The quality of underlying attribution data.

The accuracy of entity matching.

The treatment of indirect exposure.

The freshness of intelligence datasets.

The consistency of risk classifications.

The explainability of individual alerts.

A useful system should help analysts prioritize investigations rather than overwhelm them.

  1. API Integration: Turning AML Screening Into Infrastructure

For cryptocurrency businesses, manual wallet checks may become inefficient as transaction volumes increase.

This creates a practical opportunity for API-based screening.

A typical integration could follow this workflow:

A user initiates a deposit.

The application identifies the relevant blockchain address.

A screening request is submitted.

The screening provider returns available risk information.

The application evaluates the response according to its internal policies.

A compliance workflow handles cases requiring additional review.

Developers should pay particular attention to several technical considerations.

Response consistency

API responses should have predictable structures so applications can process them reliably.

Timeout handling

A screening service should not cause the entire payment infrastructure to become unavailable.

Caching

Repeated requests for the same address may be handled more efficiently with an appropriate caching strategy, provided data freshness requirements are respected.

Auditability

The application should preserve enough information to reconstruct why a particular decision was made.

Data privacy

Wallet addresses and transaction information should be handled according to the organization's privacy and security requirements.

AML screening should become a well-integrated component of the architecture, not an isolated tool that developers remember to use occasionally.

  1. Five Questions Every Developer Should Ask Before Integrating an AML Provider

Before choosing a blockchain screening solution, technical teams should investigate more than its advertised risk score.

Here are five useful questions.

  1. Which blockchain networks are supported?

A provider supporting Ethereum may not necessarily provide equivalent analytical coverage for TRON.

  1. Which risk categories are available?

Understand whether the provider covers sanctions, fraud, scams, mixers, darknet exposure, and other relevant categories.

  1. Can indirect exposure be explained?

A useful system should provide enough information to understand relationships between addresses.

  1. How fresh is the underlying intelligence?

Risk datasets can change. Developers should understand update frequency and information timestamps.

  1. Is the API suitable for production workloads?

Investigate documentation, authentication, response structures, error handling, rate limits, and integration requirements.

The right provider is not necessarily the one advertising the highest number of supported features.

It is the one whose data, methodology, and infrastructure fit the application's actual requirements.

title: Readers Found Two Gaps in My AI Agent's Review Rules. Undoing an Approval Now Needs Its Own Flag.
description:
Originally published on hexisteme notes.

Two readers left comments on my earlier note about letting an AI agent withdraw evidence claims but not approve them. In my replies I admitted two gaps in my research tool. One was that the agent could still remove something I had approved, through the same path it used for withdrawals. The other was that a datum flagged as contradicted kept the flag but lost the value it was contradicted by. On November 18 I decided to fix both. This note covers what changed, how I checked it against the real store, and the gap the comments pointed at that I left open.

Where the earlier rule stopped

The earlier note set up a split for a batch of pending claims. The agent was delegated withdrawals. Passing a claim, which adopts it as evidence, stayed with me. Nothing in that rule said the delegation was limited to pending claims. That split covers two acts: approving and withdrawing.

One reader asked about reversibility and about who is on the hook for each decision. Answering that made me look at the transition table again, and it allowed passed → withdrawn. In my reply I wrote that an agent withdrawing a passed claim removes something I approved and stops it propagating, which is the expensive direction. The only code gate was the terminal check, and it treated every decision the same. A line in an agent-written review script that reversed one of my passes would be recorded with the same call and the same 8-character confirmation as a routine verdict on a pending claim.

So there was a third act the split had not named: undoing an approval. It needed its own door.

The first gap: undoing a pass

The transition table has exactly two transitions that leave passed: passed → failed and passed → withdrawn. Both count as undoing an approval, so both got the same treatment.

In the library, record_assessment_review now takes an explicit undo_approval argument. Recording failed or withdrawn on a passed claim without undo_approval=True returns TRANSITION_INVALID. With the flag, it is recorded. Passing the flag on a pending claim is refused too, because there is no approval to undo there. Transitions out of pending behave as before.

In the CLI, assess review on a passed claim without --undo-approval is refused before the confirmation prompt appears. With the flag, it first shows the approval being undone: who recorded it, when, and the reason. Then it accepts only the string undo- followed by the first 8 characters of the claim's id. Typing the 8 characters alone, which is what a normal review asks for, cancels. The flag on a pending claim is refused.

A script built to answer the routine prompt cannot reverse a pass by accident, because the routine answer cancels. Existing tests that reversed a pass were allowed one edit, adding undo_approval=True at the call site; their expected codes and states stayed the same.

The second gap: the counterpart was thrown away

The other reader described a listing where three pages on one vendor's domain said free, free, and freemium. In my reply I explained that my tool would count those as one source, and that for conflicting values it does less than you might expect. The pipeline already flagged some data as contradicted, and a review note surfaced that flag with fixed wording saying the contradiction in meaning was unconfirmed. It never picked a value.

Then I admitted the gap: the flag survived in the frozen input, and the value on the other side of the conflict did not. I could later show that a value was disputed, but not what it was disputed against.

The fix adds a conflicts field to the datum:

  • For a value conflict, it keeps the values that differ from the representative one, each with its source URL.
  • For a conflict between claims, it keeps the counterpart group's sentence with its source URL.
  • When the counterpart came through the path that withholds excerpts, its title is kept in place of the sentence.

When the frozen premise of a claim carries conflicts, the PREMISE_CONTRADICTED review note now names the counterpart and drops the wording that says the counterpart was not preserved. Claims frozen before this change have no conflicts, so their note keeps the old wording.

What the fix does not touch is the decision of what counts as contradicted. The detection conditions, distinct_values and cross_conflict, were explicitly off limits. The change records the counterpart and nothing else.

Why the empty case writes no key

The awkward detail was a hash. Each frozen claim premise refers to its datum by datum_ref, and datum_ref is a hash of the whole stored datum dict. If every datum got a conflicts key, even an empty one, every new report would produce different refs from the same data.

So the renderer writes conflicts only when it is non-empty. A datum that is not contradicted stores exactly the same dict as before, and its ref does not move. This follows a pattern already in the code: candidate fields such as basis and derivations are also left out when they hold default values, to keep existing ids stable. One of the new tests, test_no_conflicts_key_when_not_contradicted, pins this.

Checking it against the real store

Unit tests went from 1124 to 1135 passing. The new tests include test_undo_approval_cli_needs_distinct_confirmation for the cancel-on-routine-answer case and test_claim_conflicts_do_not_store_withheld_excerpt for the path that withholds excerpts.

Then I replayed the change over the existing data, read-only. The replay was not allowed to write to the stored data or record a real review. The log:

K 119 loaded, load errors 0
review history REVIEW_INVALID 0
PREMISE_CONTRADICTED 5 — same as the 11-08 list: True, old wording kept: True
stored reports 317, reports with a conflicts key 0
claim↔report binding: report found 66, not found 53, premise datum_ref mismatch 0
stored data fingerprint unchanged (read-only): True
1.0s

K is what my tool calls a claim. All 119 loaded without errors. The same 5 claims as in the November 8 replay got the contradiction note, with the old wording, which is what should happen when none of them carries conflicts yet. None of the 317 stored reports has the new key, because none was produced after the change.

The 53 "not found" needed a second look. For those claims the stored report's digest did not match, so the replay could not pair them with a report file. The datum_ref re-check inside load_inputs passed for all 119. I did not trace why those 53 digests differ; the replay only shows that it is not a datum_ref mismatch.

One more line went into the counsel module's docs. Counsel results are not frozen yet. Once they are, withdrawing a pending claim will break any counsel that cited it, and the delegation rule for withdrawals has to be decided again at that point.

What the comments did not fix

Two things stayed out of scope on purpose.

The first is retroactive enrichment. The 5 claims that already carry the contradiction note were frozen without their counterparts, and they still do not have them. Only reports produced after the change will name what a datum was contradicted by.

The second is the one I care more about. In my reply on revision binding, I wrote that claim files are immutable and the id is a hash of the content, so a review already attaches to one revision, and that the reviewer field is only the OS login name, so the "who" half is the weaker one. This change did not touch that. Undoing a pass now needs a flag and a distinct confirmation string, and the CLI shows whose approval is being undone. But the name it shows is whatever OS login ran the command. An agent running under my login would record reviews under my name, approvals and undo records alike. Reviewer authentication and signing were listed as anti-goals for this change, to keep it small.

So the separate flag guards against a mistake. A script that answers the routine prompt can no longer reverse a pass by answering it. It does not tell me who reversed a pass when the reversal was deliberate. Next I want to decide whether the reviewer field should carry anything an agent session cannot produce, or whether the terminal refusal from the earlier note is the only line I can actually defend.

Email list for these notes: hexisteme.beehiiv.com — no issue has gone out yet, so you would be on it before the first one. No welcome sequence, no course, no upsell.

More notes at hexisteme.github.io/notes.

title: AI Gateway now runs canary ZDR audits
description:
AI Gateway now runs canary audits against inference providers to detect when prompt content is read outside the inference path.

Contractual Zero Data Retention (ZDR) agreements and point-in-time security audits establish how a provider should handle your data, but production infrastructure changes continuously. Canary audits add a detection layer on top.

Each canary audit run:

  1. Mints unique URLs that exist nowhere else, each mapped privately to a specific provider, model, and audit run.

  2. Sends prompts containing those URLs through the normal inference path, with ZDR requested for covered providers and non-ZDR pairs included as positive controls.

  3. Watches for traffic. A ZDR provider should never retain, inspect, or crawl prompt content, so a canary URL should never receive a request.

  4. Records any request to a canary URL, identifying the provider, model, and run for investigation.

Canary audits complement contractual ZDR agreements and independent audits rather than replacing them.

Read more about AI Gateway security and compliance measures in the documentation.

title: API Testing with FastAPI and Pytest: A Practical Guide for Beginners
description:
API Testing with FastAPI and Pytest: A Practical Guide for Beginners


By Ezenwa Christian Chimeremeze

1. Introduction to API Testing

Let me tell you how I used to test my APIs.

I would start the server, open my browser, go to /docs, click "Try it out", type something, and see if it worked. If it returned 200, I would say "it works" and move on.

Then one day I changed one small thing in my code, and something else broke quietly. No error on my screen. No crash. Just wrong data coming back. My users noticed before I did.

That is when I learnt this: manual testing is not testing. It is checking.

API testing means you write code that calls your API for you, checks the response, and tells you immediately if something is wrong. You do not have to remember what to test. The test remembers for you.

In this tutorial, we will test a FastAPI app with Pytest. No big theory. Just practical tests you can run again and again.

If you followed my last article on Airbyte, PostgreSQL and FastAPI, this is the next step. Building the API is one job. Proving it works is another job.

2. What is FastAPI?

FastAPI is a Python framework for building APIs fast. And when I say fast, I mean two things: fast to write, and fast to run.

What I like about it:

  • You write normal Python functions, and FastAPI turns them into endpoints.

  • It validates your input automatically using Pydantic.

  • It gives you free interactive docs at /docs.

  • It is built on Starlette and Pydantic, so it is solid underneath.

Here is a small example we will test in this article. Create main.py:
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI(title="Beginner Testing API")

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float
    in_stock: bool = True

items_db = {}

@app.get("/health")
def health_check():
    return {"status": "healthy"}

@app.post("/items", status_code=201)
def create_item(item: Item):
    item_id = len(items_db) + 1
    items_db[item_id] = item
    return {"id": item_id, **item.model_dump()}

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
def get_item(item_id: int):
    if item_id not in items_db:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")
    return {"id": item_id, **items_db[item_id].model_dump()}

That is our whole API for this tutorial. Three endpoints: health check, create item, get item. Small enough to understand, big enough to test properly.

3. Understanding Pytest

Pytest is a testing framework for Python. People like it because it is simple.

You do not need to write classes. You do not need to remember plenty of setup. You write a function that starts with test_, you use plain assert, and Pytest does the rest.

Compare it to this thinking:

  • Without Pytest: You manually call the API, look at the screen, and decide if it looks correct.

  • With Pytest: You write assert response.status_code == 200 and Pytest decides for you.

Three words you need to know:

  • Test: A function that checks one behaviour.

  • Assertion: A line like assert response.status_code == 201 that must be true, otherwise the test fails.

  • Fixture: A reusable setup. For example, a fresh test client for every test, so one test does not pollute another.

We will use all three in this article.

4. Setting Up a FastAPI Testing Environment

Let us set up properly, so we do not have stress later.

Step 1: Create your environment
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Step 2: Install dependencies
pip install fastapi uvicorn pytest httpx
Why httpx? FastAPI's TestClient is built on top of it. Without it, your tests will not run.

Step 3: Project structure

Keep it simple:
my_api/
main.py
test_main.py
That is it. main.py is your app. test_main.py is your tests. Do not put tests inside main.py. Keep them separate.

Step 4: Create your TestClient

At the top of test_main.py, add:
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from main import app

client = TestClient(app)
TestClient lets you call your API without actually starting a server. It is fast, and it is perfect for beginners. You do not need to run uvicorn to test.

But there is one problem with this simple setup: our items_db dictionary will keep data between tests. If one test creates an item, the next test will see it. That can cause confusing failures.

We will fix that in Section 9 with fixtures. For now, just know it is coming.

5. Writing Your First API Test

Let us write the simplest test possible. The health check.

`In `test_main.py`:
def test_health_check():
    response = client.get("/health")

    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json() == {"status": "healthy"}
Run it:
pytest -v
You should see:
test_main.py::test_health_check PASSED`

That is your first automated test. One small thing, but it is powerful. From now on, every time you change your code, you can run pytest and know in seconds if your health endpoint still works.

Let me break down what happened:

  • client.get("/health") calls your API, like a browser would.

  • response.status_code is the HTTP code — 200 means OK.

  • response.json() is the body as a Python dictionary.

  • assert says "this must be true, or fail the test."

If you can understand this one test, you can understand all the others. They are the same pattern, just with different endpoints and data.

6. Testing Successful and Unsuccessful Responses

A good test does not only check the happy path. It also checks what happens when things go wrong.

Test a successful creation:

def test_create_item_success():
    response = client.post(
        "/items",
        json={"name": "Laptop", "price": 250000.0, "in_stock": True}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 201
    data = response.json()
    assert data["name"] == "Laptop"
    assert data["price"] == 250000.0
    assert "id" in data
*Test a successful fetch:*
def test_get_item_success():
    # First create an item
    create_response = client.post(
        "/items",
        json={"name": "Phone", "price": 150000.0}
    )
    item_id = create_response.json()["id"]

    # Then fetch it
    response = client.get(f"/items/{item_id}")

    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json()["name"] == "Phone"
*Test an unsuccessful fetch — item not found:*
def test_get_item_not_found():
    response = client.get("/items/9999")

    assert response.status_code == 404
    assert response.json()["detail"] == "Item not found"

This last one is important. Many beginners only test success. But users will request items that do not exist. Your API must return 404, not 500, not an empty 200. Your test proves it does.

7. Testing Request Validation

This is where FastAPI shines, and where many beginners get surprised.

FastAPI validates your input automatically because of Pydantic. If you send a wrong type, it will not crash. It will return 422 Unprocessable Entity.

Let us test that.

Test missing required field:

def test_create_item_missing_name():
    response = client.post(
        "/items",
        json={"price": 1000.0}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 422
We did not send `name`, which is required. FastAPI should reject it.

*Test wrong type:*
def test_create_item_wrong_price_type():
    response = client.post(
        "/items",
        json={"name": "Book", "price": "not-a-number"}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 422
Price should be a float. We sent a string that cannot be converted. FastAPI should reject it.

*Test extra check — default value:*
def test_create_item_default_in_stock():
    response = client.post(
        "/items",
        json={"name": "Pen", "price": 500.0}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 201
    assert response.json()["in_stock"] is True

We did not send in_stock, but our model says in_stock: bool = True. So FastAPI should fill it in. This test proves your defaults work.

Validation testing is not boring. It is how you prove your API will not accept rubbish data from the frontend or from a bad client.

8. Testing API Error Handling

Error handling is not just about status codes. It is about what your API tells the client when something goes wrong.

In our API, we have two main errors:

  • 404: Item not found
  • 422: Validation failed

We already tested both. Let us add one more layer: check the structure of the error.

def test_not_found_error_structure():
    response = client.get("/items/9999")
    data = response.json()

    assert response.status_code == 404
    assert "detail" in data
    assert isinstance(data["detail"], str)
Why check the structure? Because your frontend will depend on it. If your frontend expects `data["detail"]` and you change it to `data["message"]` one day, the frontend will break. Your test will catch that change early.

One more practical tip: never expose internal details in your error responses. A good error says "Item not found". A bad error says "KeyError: 9999 in items_db at line 24 in http://main.py". The first helps the user. The second helps an attacker.

In our test, we assert the detail is a clean string. That is a small way to enforce good error handling.

9. Organizing and Running Automated Tests

Now let us fix the problem I mentioned in Section 4 — tests polluting each other.

Our items_db is global. If test_create_item_success runs first and creates an item with id 1, then test_get_item_success will create an item with id 2, not id 1. That is confusing.

Solution: Use a fixture to reset the database before each test.

Update test_main.py to this clean version:

import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from main import app, items_db

client = TestClient(app)

@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def reset_db():
    # Runs before each test
    items_db.clear()
    yield
    # Runs after each test
    items_db.clear()
`@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)`

means "run this automatically before every test". Now every test starts with an empty database. No pollution. No guessing.

How to run your tests:
Run all tests
pytest

Run with details
pytest -v

Run only one file
pytest test_main.py -v

Run only tests with a keyword
pytest -k "not_found" -v

See coverage (optional but useful)
pip install pytest-cov
pytest --cov=main -v
How to organize when you grow:
my_api/
main.py
models.py
database.py
tests/
test_items.py
test_health.py
One file per feature. test_items.py for items, test_health.py for health. When you have 50 tests, you will thank yourself for organizing early.

10. Common Mistakes and Best Practices

These are mistakes I have made myself, and I see beginners make them often.
Mistake What To Do Instead
Only testing success cases Always test 404, 422, and invalid input
Hardcoding IDs that depend on test order Use fixtures to reset state, create fresh data in each test
Testing with a real database in unit tests Use TestClient and in-memory data for unit tests, use a separate test database for integration tests
Checking only status code Also check response body, fields, and error structure
Writing one giant test that checks everything One test = one behaviour. Small tests are easier to debug
Not running tests after every change Run pytest before you commit, every time
Exposing internal errors Return clean error messages, log the real error internally
Best practices I follow now:

  • One test, one behaviour. If a test fails, you should know immediately what broke.

  • Use descriptive names. test_get_item_not_found is better than test_2.

  • Test validation. If FastAPI gives you free validation, test that it works.

  • Keep tests fast. If tests are slow, you will stop running them. TestClient is fast. Use it.

  • Do not test FastAPI itself. You do not need to test that FastAPI can return JSON. Test your logic: your validation, your 404, your business rules.

11. Conclusion

API testing is not something you do after you finish building. It is part of building.

FastAPI gives you the API. Pytest gives you the proof that it works. Together, they give you confidence. You can change your code, run pytest, and know in seconds if you broke something.

In this tutorial, you learnt how to set up a testing environment, write your first test, test success and failure, test validation, test error handling, and organize your tests so they stay clean as you grow.

That is the foundation. The next step is to apply it to a real project — like the FastAPI + PostgreSQL API from my last article. Replace the in-memory items_db with a real database, use a test database, and write the same kinds of tests for your /records endpoints.

That is how I build now. One working endpoint, one passing test at a time.

Official Technical References

  • FastAPI Tutorial — https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/
  • FastAPI Testing — https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/testing/
  • Pytest Documentation — https://docs.pytest.org/
  • Pydantic Documentation — https://docs.pydantic.dev/
  • HTTPX Documentation — https://www.python-httpx.org/

I am Ezenwa Christian Chimeremeze, a Technical Writer and Python Engineer based in Imo State, Nigeria. I write about FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and AI systems — from what I have built, broken, fixed, and shipped myself, often from my phone using Termux.

title: Don't Use Rust Unless You Really, Really Need It
description:
This happened in 2023 and 2024. The Rust ecosystem has moved since then, and I'll note what's changed where it matters.

My plan was simple, and I was quite proud of it.

I'd noticed a pattern in engineering blogs. A company builds its backend in Python, Ruby or Java. It grows. Then it rewrites the hot parts in C++ or Rust and writes a celebratory post about it. So I thought: why not skip the middle step? If I'll end up in Rust anyway, I might as well start there and never worry about a rewrite.

I needed a backend for my own apps, and I'd spent most of my career as a front-end and mobile developer. I'd built a few backends, but not many. Rust looked like the perfect excuse to level up. Every video I watched said the same things: it's as fast as C, it's memory safe, you can use it for anything, and it's the future.

So I bought the books, worked through the tutorials, and learned the basics. I knew the learning curve was steep, and I accepted it. Pay the cost once, I told myself, and the skills will pay for themselves for years.

I want to be clear about my attitude, because it matters for everything that follows. I wasn't a skeptic looking for reasons to hate Rust. I wanted to love it. I was ready for mistakes, ready for the hard parts, and ready to keep learning for as long as it took.

Fighting the compiler

The first friction came from the language itself. Pass a value to a function, and it's moved, so you can't use it on the next line. Take a reference instead, and the borrow checker starts asking about lifetimes. Then come trait bounds you don't understand, and .clone() calls sprinkled around until the code compiles.

Some of that was simply me being new, and I own it. Ownership is a real concept, and it does get easier with practice.

But I judged it wrong. I told myself the friction was temporary, a small adjustment in how I think. In reality, friction you feel on small code doesn't go away on big code. It compounds. And for a backend whose job is to move data between HTTP and a database, I was paying that price for protection against memory bugs I'd never have had in a garbage-collected language.

Choosing a database library

The first real decision was how to talk to the database, and Rust had no default answer. Diesel, SQLx and SeaORM were all reasonable, each with its own philosophy. The community advice was basically "pick whichever you like". That's fine for an experienced developer. As a beginner, I had no basis for liking anything.

Whichever one I picked, a lot ended up written by hand. Diesel migrations are plain SQL files. SQLx is raw SQL by design, checked at compile time. I don't mind SQL. Every backend developer should know it, and it will outlive most of the tools built on top of it.

But a backend is mostly CRUD, and writing every query and migration by hand doesn't scale. Sooner or later you write helpers to stop repeating the same SQL everywhere. At that point you're building a small, worse ORM of your own, which is exactly what I'd hoped a library would save me from.

Looking for Rails

That's when I changed my mind about something. I'd started out happy to learn everything from the ground up. Now I just didn't want to reinvent the wheel. I wanted what Django, Rails, Laravel or NestJS give you: run one command, and get routing, an ORM, migrations, validation, auth and a test setup that already fit together.

The Rust ecosystem was huge. There were crates for almost anything. But a batteries-included web framework barely existed. Axum and Actix are excellent, but they give you routing and middleware and leave the rest to you.

Loco, a framework openly modeled on Rails, had only just been released and was very young. The most ambitious project I found was Pavex, by Luca Palmieri, the author of "Zero to Production in Rust". It was in closed beta. You signed up, waited for an invite, and needed an activation key from the project's Discord just to run its CLI. And as I understood it at the time, the plan was to charge for using it rather than release it as ordinary open source.

I still remember the conference talk. The pitch was that this framework would finally make Rust mainstream for backend development. Then came the news that it wouldn't be freely available. (Pavex has since been released under the Apache 2.0 license, but back then it was a dead end for me.)

In hindsight, this was the biggest warning sign of all. Even Node, an ecosystem I'm not a fan of, has NestJS. When a language with that much enthusiasm behind it has no widely adopted, batteries-included web framework, it tells you who the community is building for. Rust's strongest communities work on infrastructure, tooling and systems software. CRUD apps aren't their priority, and that's a perfectly reasonable choice. It just wasn't a good sign for me.

The runtime nobody mentions

With no framework, I assembled the backend myself, from bits of "Zero to Production in Rust" and a lot of blog posts. Routing, configuration, logging, the database layer: all wired up by hand.

Then I ran into a problem I didn't know could exist. Rust has async and await, but no built-in runtime to run them. In JavaScript, Dart or Python, the event loop is simply there. In Rust, an async function returns a future that does nothing until an executor polls it, and the language doesn't ship one. You pick a runtime yourself, usually Tokio, sometimes async-std or smol.

That choice is bigger than it looks. Many libraries are written for one specific runtime, so your choice decides which libraries you can use. Mixing them can crash at runtime with an error like "there is no reactor running". Changing your mind later means touching a lot of code. I went with Tokio, like most people.

I also kept running into the advice that you don't need async at all unless you know what you're doing. Maybe that's true for a systems programmer. But after six to eight years of Dart and JavaScript, I couldn't picture a server without async, and nobody explained what the alternative looked like. The official async book was unfinished for years, so beginners pieced it together from blog posts.

Here's an opinion many experienced engineers will disagree with. I understand how an event loop works. I just don't think an application developer should have to care. Good abstractions exist so we can spend our attention on the product. Needing to understand executors, pinning and Send bounds to write a CRUD endpoint isn't a badge of honor. It's a cost.

Back to the database

Picking Tokio sent me straight back to the database. Diesel was synchronous at the time. Calling it inside an async handler blocks one of Tokio's worker threads, so you either wrap every query in spawn_blocking or add a separate diesel-async crate. SQLx was async, but you had to enable the right runtime through a feature flag, and getting it wrong meant those runtime panics again.

This is when I noticed the pattern that would define the whole project. Every decision was tied to another one. Every time I moved forward on one thing, I had to go back and redo something I thought was finished. One step forward, two steps back.

Writing tests

Once I had a database library that played nicely with Tokio, I could finally write my CRUD endpoints. Then came testing.

cargo test works, but it's minimal. There's no watch mode. I added cargo-watch to rerun tests on save and tried cargo-nextest as a faster runner. With tests running in parallel against a shared database, the watch setup never worked reliably for me.

Everything around the tests had to be built by hand: a separate test database, migrations before each run, transactions that roll back or tables cleaned between tests, fixtures, helpers for logged-in users. Frameworks in other ecosystems hand you all of this on day one. I found myself rebuilding things I hadn't had to think about in years.

Mocking was the hardest part. Say a handler calls a Google API, and I want to check that my code called it correctly without touching the network. In most ecosystems you put the service behind an interface and let a dependency injection container swap in a fake. Rust has no mainstream DI container. The usual approach is a trait, passed in either as a generic parameter or as a boxed trait object. Generics spread type parameters through every struct they touch. Trait objects bring their own lifetime and async headaches. Crates like mockall help, but add even more ceremony.

If you're reading this and have no idea what the hell I'm talking about, believe me, I felt exactly the same. That's the Rust way of doing things. Nothing is easy.

The result was code I couldn't trust. The compiler guaranteed memory safety, but memory safety was never my problem. Only tests can tell you whether your business logic is right, and tests were the most painful part of the whole stack.

There's a popular idea in the Rust world that a strong enough type system makes unit tests almost unnecessary: get the types right, and the compiler proves your logic is right too. In theory, maybe. In practice, encoding business rules that way takes a level of Rust wizardry very few people have. And even if I had it, I'd still take the simplicity of a plain unit test and TDD over a clever type.

Deploying

After weeks spent on features that would have taken days elsewhere, I rented a server and tried to deploy.

Rust compiles to native machine code, so you build for a specific target: a CPU architecture plus an operating system. As someone who had only ever deployed JavaScript, I first had to find out which architecture my server even used. Then came cross-compiling from my laptop to Linux, which needs extra toolchains and linker setup. Then glibc: a binary built against a newer C standard library refuses to start on a server with an older one. Then OpenSSL, which kept failing to build or link.

After a lot of configuration, I finally had something that installed. I started it.

It died.

No error message. No panic. No logs. The process was simply gone. After a lot of digging through system logs, I found two words: segmentation fault.

I'd spent my career on front-end and mobile code. I'd never written C, never built a desktop app or a game. I had never seen a segfault in my life. It's what happens when a program tries to touch memory it isn't allowed to, and the operating system kills it on the spot. It's the classic crash of C programs, and exactly the kind of bug Rust promises to prevent. Yet I met my first one in the language whose main selling point is memory safety.

I spent three evenings on it. Rebuilding, tweaking, reinstalling, searching. I never found the cause. The problem lived at a level of the stack my career had never asked me to touch. I just wanted to ship a backend, and I ended up counting bytes in my operating system.

For the curious: in hindsight, I still don't know my exact cause, but I've since learned how this usually happens. Safe Rust can't produce a segfault on its own. When a Rust program segfaults, the crash almost always comes from C code underneath: a system library, or a mismatch between where the binary was built and where it runs. Rust's guarantees stop at that boundary. And when the operating system kills a process for a segfault, Rust never gets the chance to print a panic or flush its logs. That's why there was nothing to read.

Docker

So I turned to Docker, hoping it would make the segfault go away. Isn't that its whole promise? Describe the environment once, and it runs anywhere.

I'd avoided it at first because I thought containers would cost me performance, and if I was using Rust, I wanted every bit of speed. That was wrong. On Linux, containers share the host's kernel, and the overhead is close to zero. Looking back, it was a perfect example of the mindset Rust had pulled me into: optimizing for performance I didn't need.

Docker helped, but much less than I expected. The image still had to be built for the right processor, so my old problems came right back. And when something didn't quite match inside the container, the app simply refused to start, again with no clear reason why.

Honestly, that still surprises me. Every problem I had came from the gap between my machine and the server, and closing that gap is the whole reason Docker exists. With Python or Node, you take the official image and move on. With Rust, my problems didn't go away. They just moved into the Dockerfile.

Up and running

Eventually, the Docker version worked. My backend was live and answering real requests.

That should have been the moment of triumph. Instead, it was the moment I lost interest. Every step had felt like walking through a minefield, and I couldn't face writing more code knowing the next mine was waiting somewhere. And remember, this was me at my most motivated, determined to love the language.

I spent the next couple of months looking for a batteries-included framework in another ecosystem, found one, and I've been building with it happily for about two years.

When Rust is worth it

Remember my clever plan to skip the rewrite? It had a flaw I couldn't see back then. Rewrite stories are memorable because they're rare. A typical backend spends most of its time waiting on the database and the network, not running its own code. When one server isn't enough, you add another. The companies that do move to Rust usually rewrite one proven bottleneck, years in, not the whole product before they have a single user.

Earlier I mentioned the advice that confused me so much: you don't need async unless you know what you're doing. My conclusion, it turns out, has the same shape. Don't use Rust unless you're absolutely sure you need top performance, or you work with something low-level, like microcontrollers. Otherwise, it's going to be a pain in the ass.

If you love the language, you don't have to give it up. Use it where it pays off. I still write Rust for scripts that have to be fast and for custom lint rules that run on every file in a codebase. And if your app hits a real bottleneck, you don't need to rewrite everything. Keep your main language, write that one hot path in Rust, and call it through FFI. Most ecosystems make this easy, with tools like PyO3 for Python or napi-rs for Node.

title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August, September, and October.

November 2026 Summary

  • In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model.

  • About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one. OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December.

  • More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on.

Decision models account for 26% of all requests

Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive.

Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model.

They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model.

Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend.

Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models.

Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did.

This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively.

Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July

About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%.

New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%.

Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July.

A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps:

  • A voice model turns the user’s speech into text

  • A language model writes the reply

  • Another voice model reads the reply back to the user

Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled.

Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped.

For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both.

Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds

Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54.

Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five.

Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI.

But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

title: Risk-Tiered Checkout Friction: Routing Orders to AVS, 3DS, or Review
description:
Many card checkouts run every order through the same checks. One CVV rule, one AVS rule, one fraud score cutoff, and sometimes a 3-D Secure challenge on everything. That is simple to build. It also means your safest repeat customer gets the same friction as a first-time buyer shipping a gaming laptop to a freight forwarder.

The alternative is to match friction to risk. Low-risk orders pass with checks the buyer never sees. Medium-risk orders get a step-up challenge. Only the clearly suspicious ones get held or declined. The idea gets a brief mention in the broader discussion of eCommerce conversion optimization best practices. This article covers how to actually build it: the data flow, the decision logic, and the ways it tends to break.

The four outcomes

A risk-tiered checkout ends every order in one of four states:

Outcome Buyer experience Cost to you
Approve Nothing extra Fraud exposure if you're wrong
Step-up (3DS challenge) OTP, banking app prompt, or biometric Some buyers abandon
Review Order held, possibly delayed Analyst time, slower fulfillment
Decline Payment fails A lost sale if the buyer was legitimate (a false decline)

Every outcome has a cost. No single path is "safe." Your goal is to minimize total cost: fraud losses, chargeback fees, and the revenue lost to declines and abandonment.

Cheap signals vs. expensive signals

Sort your checks by who pays the friction cost.

Background signals. The buyer doesn't notice these.

  • AVS (Address Verification Service) result returned with the authorization
  • CVV/CVC match result
  • Device and browser fingerprint
  • Velocity, such as cards per device or orders per email in the last 24 hours
  • Account age and prior successful orders
  • Mismatch between IP geolocation, billing country, and shipping country
  • Order shape: basket value, resale-friendly SKUs, expedited shipping

Foreground signals. These add friction.

  • 3-D Secure challenge (EMV 3DS)
  • Manual review
  • Requests for extra documentation

The design principle: spend background signals freely, and spend foreground signals only where background signals leave real uncertainty.

Data flow: where each check actually happens

A common source of bugs is getting the order of operations wrong. AVS and CVV results come back with the authorization response. 3DS happens before authorization. So your decision logic has two phases.

Checkout submit
   │
   ▼
[Phase 1: pre-auth score]  ← device, velocity, account, order shape, geo
   │
   ├── score very high ──────────► Decline (no auth attempt)
   ├── score medium ─────────────► Request 3DS challenge
   └── score low ────────────────► Request 3DS frictionless or skip 3DS
   │
   ▼
Authorization (auth-only, no capture)
   │  returns: approval code, AVS result, CVV result
   ▼
[Phase 2: post-auth evaluation]  ← combine Phase 1 score + AVS/CVV
   │
   ├── clean ───────► Capture
   ├── ambiguous ───► Queue for review (keep auth open)
   └── bad ─────────► Void authorization

Two details matter here:

  1. Authorize first, capture later. If you capture immediately, a bad AVS/CVV result means issuing a refund instead of a void. Refunds cost more, and they can confuse the buyer's bank statement.
  2. The issuer has a say. With 3DS2, you send data to the issuer and it may decide to challenge or go frictionless regardless of your preference. Your code has to handle both responses on every path.

A decision table you can start from

AVS and CVV return codes vary by network and processor, so normalize them into a few categories first.

Pre-auth risk AVS CVV Action
Low Full / partial match Match Capture
Low Unavailable / not supported Match Capture
Low No match Match Review if high-value, else capture
Any Any No match Void (or step-up and retry)
Medium Any Match 3DS challenge before auth
Medium No match Match 3DS challenge + review
High Any Any Decline pre-auth or review

Note the second row. "AVS unavailable" is not a failure. AVS support is concentrated in a handful of countries. If you treat "unavailable" as "no match," you will decline a large share of your international customers.

Implementation sketch

Here is a minimal Python version of the two-phase router. Thresholds are placeholders. You tune them against your own data.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum

class Action(Enum):
    APPROVE = "approve"
    CHALLENGE = "challenge"
    REVIEW = "review"
    DECLINE = "decline"

class AvsResult(Enum):
    MATCH = "match"
    PARTIAL = "partial"
    NO_MATCH = "no_match"
    UNAVAILABLE = "unavailable"

@dataclass
class PreAuthContext:
    risk_score: float        # 0.0–1.0 from your model or rules
    order_value: float
    returning_customer: bool

LOW, HIGH = 0.3, 0.8
HIGH_VALUE = 500.0

def pre_auth_route(ctx: PreAuthContext) -> Action:
    if ctx.risk_score >= HIGH:
        return Action.DECLINE if not ctx.returning_customer else Action.REVIEW
    if ctx.risk_score >= LOW:
        return Action.CHALLENGE
    return Action.APPROVE  # still send 3DS data for frictionless if available

def post_auth_route(ctx: PreAuthContext, avs: AvsResult, cvv_match: bool,
                    authenticated_3ds: bool) -> Action:
    if not cvv_match:
        return Action.DECLINE  # void the auth
    if avs == AvsResult.NO_MATCH:
        if authenticated_3ds:
            return Action.APPROVE
        if ctx.order_value >= HIGH_VALUE or ctx.risk_score >= LOW:
            return Action.REVIEW
    return Action.APPROVE

In production, also persist the inputs and the decision for every order:

log_decision(order_id, phase="post_auth", inputs={
    "risk_score": ctx.risk_score, "avs": avs.value,
    "cvv": cvv_match, "3ds": authenticated_3ds,
}, action=action.value, rule_version="2024-06-01")

Without this log, you cannot tune thresholds later. You also cannot explain a decision when a customer or a dispute analyst asks.

Worked example: three orders, one router

Order A. Returning customer, $42, same device as the last five orders, AVS full match, CVV match. Pre-auth score 0.08 → no challenge requested. Post-auth: clean → capture. The buyer sees nothing extra.

Order B. New account, $310. The billing country differs from the IP country, and the shipping address is new. Pre-auth score 0.52 → request a 3DS challenge. The buyer approves in their banking app. Auth returns AVS no match, CVV match. Because 3DS authenticated, the router approves. This is the case a single strict AVS rule would have declined.

Order C. New account, $1,450, four different cards tried from the same device in ten minutes. Pre-auth score 0.91 → decline before authorization. You never send the auth, so the attempt doesn't show up against your authorization metrics.

That is three different levels of friction, each matched to the evidence.

Measuring whether it works

You need metrics per tier, not just overall totals:

  • Challenge rate and challenge abandonment rate. If abandonment is high, your medium band is too wide.
  • Review queue rate and review approval rate. If analysts approve nearly everything, those orders didn't need review.
  • Fraud/chargeback rate by tier. Chargebacks in the "approve" tier mean your low threshold is too loose.
  • Decline rate, plus an estimate of false declines. Track declined buyers who retry successfully with another card or contact support.

One trap is label delay. Chargebacks can arrive weeks or months after the order. If you tune thresholds on last week's data, the recent "approve" tier will look cleaner than it really is. Evaluate on cohorts old enough for disputes to have matured.

To estimate false declines directly, some teams use a small holdout: a tiny, capped slice of borderline orders that would have been declined goes to review instead. The approval outcomes show how many good buyers your decline rule was catching. Keep the slice small and the dollar cap strict.

Common mistakes and how to catch them

Treating AVS "unavailable" as a failure. Catch it by segmenting decline rate by billing country. A spike outside AVS-supporting regions is the tell.

Challenging everything with 3DS. This is safe but expensive in abandonment. Catch it by checking whether the challenge rate is close to 100% and whether conversion for challenged sessions trails unchallenged ones.

Capturing before evaluating AVS/CVV. You'll see refunds where voids should be. Audit for orders refunded within minutes of capture.

Ignoring issuer overrides. You asked for frictionless, but the issuer challenged anyway (or the reverse). Make sure both 3DS paths are covered by integration tests in your processor's sandbox.

Rules with no version. When fraud spikes, you need to know which rule set was live. Stamp every decision with rule_version.

Non-idempotent retries. A timeout on auth followed by a retry can create duplicate authorizations. Use your processor's idempotency key mechanism on every auth and capture call.

Optimizing one metric in isolation. Lowering the review threshold may cut chargebacks while quietly raising false declines. Always review fraud loss and declined revenue side by side.

Wrapping up

Risk-tiered friction isn't a single model or vendor feature. It's a routing problem with two decision points, pre-auth and post-auth, plus a feedback loop that matures slowly. Get the ordering right, normalize your AVS/CVV codes, log every decision with its inputs, and measure each tier on its own. Then the checkout gets easier for good buyers and harder for bad ones, which is the point.

title: Why Docker Silently Binds to 0.0.0.0 (And How to Trace Port Causality in Go)
description:
If you've spent any time working with Docker or Docker Compose, chances are high that you've written something like this:

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"

It looks completely harmless. You just wanted to connect your local GUI database client (DBeaver, TablePlus, pgAdmin) to PostgreSQL.

Except you just exposed your database to your entire local network and every public interface on your machine.

The Silent Wildcard Footgun

When you declare "5432:5432" without an explicit host IP prefix, Docker defaults to binding to 0.0.0.0 (the wildcard address in IPv4) and :: (in IPv6).

That means:

  • If your laptop is on a coffee shop or office Wi-Fi, anyone on that subnet can reach port 5432.
  • If this runs on a cloud VM without a restrictive security group, port 5432 is open to the entire public internet.
  • iptables rules are automatically modified by the Docker daemon to bypass standard host firewalls (like UFW) unless specially configured.

To bind exclusively to your local machine, you have to remember to explicitly write:

ports:
  - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"

Yet across millions of repositories and development stacks, developers constantly forget the 127.0.0.1: prefix.

The Causality Black Box: ss and lsof Don't Help

When you suspect an unexpected port is open and run standard Linux diagnostic commands:

$ sudo ss -tulpn | grep 5432
tcp   LISTEN 0 4096 0.0.0.0:5432 0.0.0.0:* users:(("docker-proxy",pid=14205,fd=4))

All you see is docker-proxy.

  • You don't know which container owns it.
  • You don't know which docker-compose.yml file declared it.
  • You don't know whether it was intended as public or an accidental wildcard binding.
  • If you have 30 containers running across 5 microservices, you are left manually running docker inspect across every container or grepping your codebase.

Building Lantern: Tracing Configuration Causality

To solve this visibility gap, we built Lantern, an open-source, local-first CLI written in Go.

Instead of merely listing sockets, Lantern traverses the full causality graph:

[ Listening Socket ]
        ↓
[ OS Process / docker-proxy ]
        ↓
[ Docker Container ]
        ↓
[ Docker Compose Service & Source YAML Line ]
        ↓
[ Reachability Verdict (PUBLIC / LOCALHOST / DOCKER) ]

1. Instant Reachability Audit (lantern scan)

Running lantern scan audits all listening TCP sockets and classifies their exposure:

$ lantern scan
PORT    PROTO   BIND ADDRESS    REACHABILITY   PROCESS         CONTAINER / SOURCE
5432    tcp     0.0.0.0         PUBLIC         docker-proxy    my-project-db-1 (docker-compose.yml:8)
8080    tcp     127.0.0.1       LOCALHOST      node            api-gateway

Any wildcard binding (0.0.0.0 or ::) is immediately flagged with a high-contrast PUBLIC warning.

2. Root Cause Explanation (lantern why <port>)

If you want to know why a port is open, Lantern produces the exact causal chain:

$ lantern why 5432
Port 5432 (tcp) is bound to 0.0.0.0 (PUBLIC)
├─ Process: docker-proxy (PID 14205)
├─ Container: my-project-db-1 (ID 8a1b2c3d4e5f)
├─ Compose Service: db
└─ Defined in: /home/dev/projects/api/docker-compose.yml:8
   Recommendation: Change '5432:5432' to '127.0.0.1:5432:5432' to restrict access to localhost.

3. Real-Time Terminal Watch Mode (lantern scan -w)

Developers frequently start and stop containers. With -w, --watch:

lantern scan -w --interval 2s

Lantern renders a live terminal dashboard that triggers an [ALERT] the moment a new wildcard exposure occurs.

Enforcing Guardrails in CI/CD

Catching exposure on developer laptops is great, but preventing it from merging into production repositories is critical.

We built two native CI mechanisms into Lantern:

1. Zero-Exit Flag 

lantern scan --fail-on-wildcard --ignore-ports 80,443

If any container or process binds to 0.0.0.0 on a port other than 80 or 443, the command exits with code 1 and emits native GitHub Actions error annotations (::error::).

2. Official GitHub Action

You can drop Lantern into any repository workflow with a few lines:

name: Security Audit
on: [pull_request, push]

jobs:
  port-audit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Spin up test environment
        run: docker compose up -d

      - name: Audit Port Exposures
        uses: DhyaanKanoja11/lantern-action@v1
        with:
          fail-on-wildcard: 'true'
          ignore-ports: '80,443'

It automatically formats a rich Markdown report on your GitHub Actions Step Summary page.

How to Try It

Lantern has zero runtime dependencies and is distributed across major package managers:

# macOS / Linux (Homebrew)
brew tap DhyaanKanoja11/tap
brew install lantern

# Windows (Scoop)
scoop bucket add dhyaan [https://github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/scoop-bucket](https://github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/scoop-bucket)
scoop install lantern

# Go toolchain
go install [github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/Lantern/cmd/lantern@latest](https://github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/Lantern/cmd/lantern@latest)

Open Source & Getting Involved

The entire project is MIT-licensed and built with standard library principles in Go:

  • GitHub Repository: github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/Lantern
  • GitHub Action: github.com/DhyaanKanoja11/lantern-action

If you've ever had a container expose an unexpected port, give lantern scan a run and let us know what you think!
