title: AWS Sign-In introduces configurable Sign-in duration of up to 90 days
description:
AWS Sign-In now enables developers and AI agents to stay authenticated for up to 90 days without frequent sign-ins or consent prompts. With this launch, administrators can configure Sign-in duration, which controls how long an OAuth Sign-in session remains active, for individual IAM users and roles.

This capability reduces authentication interruptions for long-running workflows and provides a more secure alternative to static access keys by using short-lived, renewable credentials. Existing session duration limits remain unchanged unless administrators explicitly configure longer durations.

Sign-In Duration supports AWS CLI (aws login), AWS MCP Server, and other OAuth-enabled applications. It does not affect AWS Management Console sessions. Customers can configure the setting using the IAM console, AWS CLI, or IAM API in all AWS commercial Regions.

To learn more, see the AWS Sign-In session management User Guide, Configure Sign-In duration on Role User Guide, Condition Key User Guide

title: A Crypto Swap Is More Than a Button: What Really Happens When You Exchange Tokens on TRON?
description:
TronSeven — Non-Custodial Token Swaps on TRON Network

Swap TRC-20 tokens on TRON with self-custody and open-source smart contracts. Low fees, verifiable on TRONSCAN.

tronseven.com

Most people think a cryptocurrency swap is a simple operation.

Choose a token. Select another token. Enter an amount. Press Swap.

A few moments later, the new tokens appear in the wallet.

But this simple interface hides an interesting technical process. Behind every successful decentralized exchange, multiple components must work together: token contracts, wallet signatures, liquidity mechanisms, transaction execution, and blockchain resource management.

For developers and Web3 enthusiasts, understanding this process is much more valuable than simply knowing where the Swap button is.

Let's look beneath the interface and explore what actually happens when exchanging tokens on the TRON network.

  1. The Swap Interface Is Only the Beginning

A decentralized exchange interface is essentially a communication layer between a user and blockchain infrastructure.

When someone initiates a swap, the interface must translate a simple user request into operations that a smart contract can execute.

Consider a practical example:

A user has 100 USDT (TRC-20) and wants to receive TRX.

From the user's perspective, this looks like a single exchange.

Technically, several things need to happen:

The application identifies the selected tokens and their contract addresses.

It retrieves pricing and available liquidity information.

It calculates an estimated output amount.

It determines the transaction parameters.

The wallet requests the necessary authorization.

The transaction is signed and broadcast.

The smart contract executes the exchange.

The blockchain records the resulting state changes.

The interface makes these steps look simple, but each one has its own requirements and potential failure points.

This is why a reliable swap experience should be evaluated beyond its visual design.

  1. Why Token Contracts Matter More Than Token Names

One of the easiest mistakes in cryptocurrency is assuming that a token's displayed name or symbol uniquely identifies it.

It doesn't.

A token called USDT, for example, should always be checked against its official contract address on the relevant blockchain.

On TRON, fungible tokens commonly use the TRC-20 standard.

TRC-20 defines how compatible smart contracts expose token functionality, including operations such as:

balanceOf

transfer

approve

transferFrom

allowance

These functions are fundamental to many decentralized applications.

For example, a decentralized exchange may need permission to use a particular amount of a user's tokens before executing a swap.

This is where token approvals become important.

An approval is not the same as completing an exchange. It grants a smart contract permission to spend tokens within the approved allowance.

Developers should make this distinction clear in their interfaces.

Users should also understand what they are approving, which contract receives permission, and whether the allowance is limited or unlimited.

A good interface should never make users guess.

  1. Liquidity: The Invisible Component Behind Every Swap

Here is a question worth asking:

If someone wants to exchange a large amount of one token for another, where do the destination tokens actually come from?

The answer depends on the exchange mechanism.

Many decentralized exchanges use automated market makers (AMMs) and liquidity pools.

A liquidity pool contains reserves of different tokens. Users trade against these reserves rather than matching directly with another person placing an order.

One widely known AMM model uses the constant-product formula:

[
x \times y = k
]

Where:

(x) represents the reserve of one token.

(y) represents the reserve of another token.

(k) represents the constant product, ignoring fees and other adjustments.

When a trade changes one reserve, the relationship between the reserves changes the implied exchange price.

This creates an important consequence:

The size of a swap matters.

A small exchange may have relatively little influence on the pool price. A large exchange compared with available liquidity can create substantial price impact.

This is why developers should pay attention to:

Available liquidity.

Estimated output.

Price impact.

Slippage tolerance.

Trading fees.

Minimum acceptable output.

A displayed exchange rate is an estimate, not necessarily a guarantee of the final execution price.

  1. Slippage: Why the Final Amount Can Be Different

Imagine that an application displays an estimated output of 500 TRX.

The user reviews the quote and submits the transaction.

However, before the transaction executes, the pool price changes because another transaction has affected its reserves.

The final output may now be lower than the original estimate.

This is slippage.

A decentralized exchange generally uses transaction parameters to limit how much the execution outcome can differ from the expected result.

For example, a minimum-output condition can prevent a trade from executing if the received amount falls below the user's specified threshold.

Developers should understand the relationship between:

Expected output: The amount calculated when the quote is generated.

Minimum output: The lowest amount acceptable under the transaction parameters.

Actual output: The amount received after successful execution.

These values are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A thoughtful exchange interface should communicate them clearly before the user signs anything.

  1. TRON Has a Different Resource Model: Energy and Bandwidth

This is one of the most interesting aspects of building applications on TRON.

Developers familiar with Ethereum often expect blockchain transaction costs to follow a single gas-based model.

TRON uses a different resource structure.

Two important resources are Bandwidth and Energy.

Bandwidth

Bandwidth generally measures the size of transactions stored on the blockchain.

Energy

Energy measures the computational resources required to execute smart contracts in the TRON Virtual Machine (TVM).

A token swap involves smart contract interactions, so Energy can become an important part of the transaction cost.

Users can obtain resources through staking or delegation. When available resources are insufficient, TRX can be burned to cover the required costs under the network's rules.

This creates an important design consideration for decentralized exchange developers.

The application should help users understand the potential resource requirements before they authorize a transaction.

It should also avoid making misleading claims that every swap is automatically free.

For developers building on TRON, understanding this resource model is essential when designing a smooth user experience.

  1. What Happens Between Signing and Confirmation?

A wallet signature is not the same as a completed blockchain transaction.

This distinction deserves more attention.

When a user approves a transaction in a compatible wallet, the wallet signs the transaction using the user's authorization.

The signed transaction can then be broadcast to the TRON network.

But the application still needs to determine whether execution was successful.

A responsible transaction lifecycle should distinguish between several states:

Prepared: Transaction parameters have been generated.

Awaiting signature: The wallet is requesting user authorization.

Broadcast: The signed transaction has been submitted to the network.

Confirmed: The network has processed the transaction.

Execution result: The application checks whether the smart contract operation succeeded.

A transaction ID alone should not be treated as proof that a swap completed successfully.

Developers should inspect the transaction receipt and relevant contract execution results.

TRONSCAN can also help users independently examine transaction activity.

This separation between submission and successful execution is important for both application developers and everyday cryptocurrency users.

  1. Security Should Be Part of the Interface, Not an Afterthought

A decentralized exchange can have an excellent design and still expose users to unnecessary risks if its security model is unclear.

There are several areas worth examining.

Smart contract permissions

Users should understand which contracts they interact with and what permissions they grant.

Contract verification

Where source code is available, developers and technically experienced users should examine whether verified contract information matches the deployed implementation.

Token identification

Applications should use reliable token contract addresses rather than trusting symbols or logos.

Transaction simulation

Where supported, developers can simulate state-changing operations before broadcasting them. This can help identify execution problems, although simulation cannot guarantee that the final transaction will succeed under later blockchain conditions.

Transaction transparency

Users should be able to inspect the transaction ID and verify what happened independently.

No interface can eliminate every smart contract or market risk. Good engineering makes important information visible rather than hiding complexity behind a convenient button.

  1. Evaluating the User Experience of a TRON Swap Platform

Technical architecture is only one part of a decentralized exchange.

The other part is how effectively the application communicates with its users.

A useful swap interface should answer five questions:

Which asset am I exchanging?

Which asset will I receive?

What exchange rate and price impact should I expect?

What permissions and network resources are required?

How can I verify the completed transaction?

These questions provide a practical framework for evaluating any TRON swap application.

They are also useful when comparing different wallet-connected exchange interfaces.

For example, TronSeven is a project worth exploring when looking at the TRON swap experience:

https://tronseven.com

Rather than judging an exchange solely by its appearance, examine its supported assets, wallet compatibility, transaction information, and available contract documentation.

The same evaluation criteria should apply to every platform in this space.

  1. A Developer's Checklist Before Building or Using a Swap Application

Here is a practical checklist worth keeping:

Area

What to examine

Token contracts

Correct TRC-20 addresses

Wallet integration

Clear authorization requests

Pricing

Accurate quote calculations

Liquidity

Sufficient available reserves

Slippage

Minimum-output protection

Network resources

Energy and Bandwidth estimates

Execution

Transaction receipt verification

Security

Contract permissions and verification

User experience

Clear status and error messages

A decentralized exchange is not just a smart contract with a graphical interface.

It is a complete interaction between wallets, blockchain infrastructure, token standards, liquidity mechanisms, and users.

Missing even one of these components can create a frustrating experience.

title: React in Action: State, Events, Inputs & Forms
description:

import { useState } from "react";

function Counter(){
    // let i=0;

    // let cout = 0

    function increment(){
        // count++
        // console.log(count)
        setCount(count + 1);
        //setCount(500);

    }

        if(count>0){

        setCount(count - 1)
    }
}

    function reset() {

        setCount(0);   
    }

    return(
        <div>
            <h1>Count : {count} </h1>

             <button onClick= {decrement}>-</button>
              <button onClick= {reset}>reset</button>

}

export default Counter;

To call your components inside App.jsx using tags like 

import Counter from './Counter';

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <Counter />
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

2. InputField

import { useState } from "react";

function InputField() {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Enter Your Name</h2>

      <input
        type="text" placeholder="Enter your name" value={name} onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)} />

        <h3>Hello, {name}</h3>

           {/* {name.trim() && <h3>Hello, {name}</h3>} */}

    </div>
  );
}

export default InputField;

*3.Show/ Hide Text *

import { useState } from "react";

function ShowHideText() {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false);

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Show / Hide Text</h2>

      <button onClick={() => setShow(!show)}>
        {show ? "Hide Text" : "Show Text"}
      </button>

      {show && (
        <p>
          Hello! Welcome to React.
          You are learning conditional rendering.
        </p>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

export default ShowHideText;

To call your components inside App.jsx using tags like 

import Showhide from './Showhide';

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <Showhide />
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

title: Best React Component Libraries in 2027 (Free and Paid)
description:
Picking from the best React component libraries is a decision you live with for years. Pick the wrong one and you spend months fighting its styles, its bundle or its license.

Most lists mix very different tools in one ranking. A headless primitive and a full design system don't solve the same problem.

This list groups 12 libraries by what they are for: headless primitives, full design systems and animated components. Each entry has the license and price as listed on the official site or npm in November 2026.

How do you choose a React component library?

Answer four questions before you look at screenshots:

  • Do you have a design already? If a designer hands you a custom look, use headless primitives and style them yourself. If not, a full design system gives you a finished look on day one.
  • How do you style? Tailwind projects fit shadcn/ui, HeroUI and the animated libraries. Mantine, MUI and Chakra UI ship their own styling systems.
  • Do you want the source in your repo? Copy-paste libraries (shadcn/ui and the libraries built on its CLI) put the code in your project. npm packages get updates for free but are harder to change deeply.
  • What does the paid tier cover? Several libraries are free at the core and charge for advanced components, blocks or templates. Check what you actually need before you budget.

Headless React component libraries

Headless libraries give you behavior, keyboard support and ARIA without styles. You bring the CSS.

1. Radix UI

Radix Primitives are unstyled, accessible components: dialog, popover, dropdown menu, tabs and more. They are MIT licensed and free. Many styled libraries build on Radix, including shadcn/ui. Best for teams who want proven primitives and full control of styling.

2. Base UI

Base UI is an unstyled React library from the team behind Radix, Floating UI and Material UI. It reached a stable 1.x release and is MIT licensed. shadcn/ui supports both Radix and Base UI. Best for new design systems that want an actively developed headless base.

3. React Aria

React Aria, from Adobe, offers over 50 components with behavior, adaptive interactions and internationalization built in, ready for your own styles. react-aria-components is Apache-2.0 and free. Best when accessibility and i18n are hard requirements, such as enterprise or government apps.

4. Ark UI

Ark UI is a headless library with 45+ accessible components powered by state machines (Zag.js). The same API works in React, Solid, Vue and Svelte. MIT licensed. Best for teams that ship to more than one framework.

Full design system libraries for React

These give you styled components, theming and a consistent look out of the box.

5. shadcn/ui

shadcn/ui is not a package. Its CLI copies accessible, Tailwind-styled components into your repo, so you own and edit the source. It is MIT licensed and free. The CLI also installs from third-party registries, which is how many of the libraries below are distributed. Best for Tailwind projects that want a solid default they can fully change.

6. MUI (Material UI)

Material UI implements Google's Material Design and is one of the oldest React libraries still in heavy use. The core is MIT and free. MUI X adds advanced components like the data grid, date pickers and charts, with paid Pro ($299 per year per developer) and Premium ($599 per year per developer) plans at the time of writing. Best for data-heavy admin apps that need a mature data grid.

7. Mantine

Mantine is a full-featured React library with more than 120 components and 70 hooks, plus forms, dates and notifications packages. MIT licensed and free. Best when you want one library to cover most of an app, without Tailwind.

8. Chakra UI

Chakra UI is an accessible component system with a style-props API and strong theming. Version 3 is built on Ark UI. The library is MIT and free; premium components are sold separately. Best for product teams that like styling through props and design tokens.

9. HeroUI

HeroUI (formerly NextUI) offers free, accessible components for React and React Native, styled with Tailwind. The open source package is Apache-2.0. HeroUI Pro adds paid templates and extra tooling. Best for Tailwind apps that want a polished default look across web and mobile.

Animated React component libraries

These sit on top of a base library. Use them for landing pages, marketing sites and the parts of an app that should feel alive.

10. Magic UI

Magic UI has 150+ free, open source animated components built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion. It is MIT licensed and installs through the shadcn CLI. Magic UI Pro sells templates and landing page sections. Best for landing page effects like marquees, number tickers and animated backgrounds.

11. Aceternity UI

Aceternity UI offers 100+ free components built with React, Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion, aimed at landing pages. A paid All-Access license adds premium blocks, templates and full pages, sold as a one-time payment. Best for bold hero sections and visual effects on marketing sites.

12. beUI

beUI is a free, MIT-licensed library of animated components for React and Next.js, built with Framer Motion and Tailwind CSS. Components install through the shadcn CLI as @beui, since beUI is in shadcn's official registry directory. They handle keyboard focus and reduced motion, and the component catalog covers inputs, overlays, charts, AI agent UI and blocks like a command palette.

beUI also has React Native components built with Reanimated and Gesture Handler, and beUI Pro, a paid library of animated blocks, pages and templates for web and React Native. Best for product UI that needs motion with accessibility handled, on web and mobile.

Best React component libraries compared

Library Style License / price Best for
Radix UI Headless MIT, free Proven primitives you style
Base UI Headless MIT, free New headless design systems
React Aria Headless Apache-2.0, free Strict accessibility and i18n
Ark UI Headless MIT, free Multi-framework teams
shadcn/ui Tailwind, copy-paste MIT, free Owning your component source
MUI Material Design MIT core, paid MUI X Pro and Premium Data-heavy admin apps
Mantine Own styling system MIT, free One library for a whole app
Chakra UI Style props MIT, paid premium components Token-driven product UI
HeroUI Tailwind Apache-2.0, paid Pro Polished web and mobile defaults
Magic UI Tailwind + Framer Motion MIT, paid Pro templates Landing page effects
Aceternity UI Tailwind + Framer Motion Free components, paid All-Access Bold marketing sections
beUI Tailwind + Framer Motion MIT, free, paid beUI Pro Accessible animated product UI

Can you combine React component libraries?

Yes, and most teams do. A common stack is a headless base or shadcn/ui for forms, dialogs and menus, plus an animated library for the parts users notice. Because shadcn/ui, Magic UI and beUI all install through the same CLI and share Tailwind tokens, mixing them in one project stays consistent.

If you are comparing the animated options, the beUI vs Magic UI page goes into the differences in more detail.

FAQ

What is the best free React component library?

It depends on the job. shadcn/ui is the most flexible free starting point for Tailwind projects, Mantine covers the most ground as one package, and Radix UI or Base UI are the safest headless bases.

Is shadcn/ui a component library?

Not in the npm package sense. It is a set of components and a CLI that copies their source into your project, so you own the code and update it yourself.

Which React component libraries have paid tiers?

MUI (MUI X Pro and Premium), Chakra UI (premium components), HeroUI (Pro), Magic UI (Pro templates), Aceternity UI (All-Access) and beUI (beUI Pro) all keep a free core and sell extra components, blocks or templates.

What is the best animated React component library?

Magic UI and Aceternity UI are strong for landing page effects. beUI focuses on animated product UI with keyboard support and reduced motion built in, and also ships React Native versions.

Takeaway

Pick by the job, not the ranking. Headless if you have a design, a full system if you need one, and an animated library on top for the moments that matter. Most of these are free at the core, so try two in a branch before you commit.

Browse the free animated components at beui.dev and install your first one:

npx shadcn@latest add @beui/command-palette

Originally published on beUI.

title: Vercel Sandbox snapshot creation is now up to 10x faster
description:
Vercel Sandbox now creates snapshots up to 10x faster. Median time to snapshot is under 0.4 seconds, down from 4.4 seconds. Snapshot restore speed has also improved by 50% from 500ms to 250ms at p50.

Snapshots are now able to write and restore by re-using frames within the Vercel Hive Snapshot (VHS) format. VHS now indexes data in a more efficient way which means that more read and write operations can be done in parallel. Snapshots can now restore more of your Sandbox base image in parallel with user data, leading to overall faster operations.

Persistent sandboxes, the default, snapshot automatically when a session stops and resume from the latest snapshot. This applies to all new snapshots, with nothing to configure. Existing snapshots keep the previous format.

Learn more in the snapshots documentation.

title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

Application Integration

Security

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability was discovered in the SubWorkflow task in Application Integration versions prior to September 11, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-074 security bulletin.

Feature

Application Integration agent skills

Application Integration agent skills are available in the public google/skills repository: application-integration-basics, application-integration-authoring, and application-integration-troubleshooting. AI coding agents that use these skills can help you set up Application Integration; build, publish, and run integrations through the REST API; and troubleshoot failed runs. For more information, see Application Integration agent skills and Build an integration with an AI agent.

Bigtable

Feature

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. This feature is generally available (GA) for instances in the Enterprise Plus edition. For more information, see Data type enforcement in Bigtable.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Google Cloud Migration Center
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/DiscoveryClient
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Group
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ImportJob
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/PreferenceSet
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ReportConfig
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Settings
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Source

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

Database Migration Service for homogeneous SQL Server migrations now supports Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations in general availability (GA).

With DAG migrations, you can use gcloud CLI and Database Migration Service API to migrate databases from self-managed SQL Server Enterprise Edition instances directly to Cloud SQL for SQL Server over a private network connection. DAG migrations don't require exporting backup or transaction log files to Cloud Storage, and support post-promotion reverse replication for zero-data-loss failback.

For more information, see About Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations and Migrate from self-managed SQL Server using Distributed Availability Groups.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Managed replica indexes for Cloud SQL for MySQL are generally available (GA). This feature lets you automatically retain and restore secondary indexes on read replica instances when Cloud SQL re-creates a replica.

Previously, re-creating a read replica deleted custom secondary indexes because primary backups don't have replica-only index definitions. With managed replica indexes, Cloud SQL tracks secondary index metadata on the primary instance, replicates this metadata to read replicas, and automatically rebuilds secondary indexes after replica re-creation.

Managed replica indexes are supported on instances that are running Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 or later, Cloud SQL Enterprise edition or Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, and maintenance version R20260726.00_05 or later.

For more information, see Read replica indexes overview and Create and manage read replica indexes.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (261001) is available. This image removes compromised CA certificates from the OS trust store. See the security bulletin for more details.

This image also adds support for running workload containers as a non-root user. Workload authors can require non-root execution with the tee.launch_policy.nonroot_container launch policy, and workload operators can enable it with the tee-nonroot-container metadata variable. For more information, see Non-root container execution.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Support for Brazil (br) region (GA with allowlist)

You can use the Gemini Enterprise app in the Brazil (br) in-country region with at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP) in region.

This location is available in GA with allowlist. To get access to this location for use with Gemini Enterprise, contact your Google account team.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Change

Use a single regional Agent Registry instance for Gemini Enterprise apps

For Gemini Enterprise apps, we recommend associating each Agent Gateway with a single regional Agent Registry instance in the same project and region as the gateway. Use the us-central1 registry for global and us apps, and the europe-west1 registry for eu apps.

This note updates the September 9, 2026 entry. For more information, see Register your agents and destination resources.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.17.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Support bundle diagnostics: Introduce cm support-bundle to collect environment metadata, configuration policies, health reports, and session logs into a compressed archive for streamlined troubleshooting.
  • Plain output mode: Add the persistent --plain flag (configurable via the CM_PLAIN environment variable or output.plain in config.yaml) to suppress decorative emojis, ANSI escape sequences, and Unicode borders for compatibility with screen readers and CI/CD log pipelines.
  • Dedicated exit codes for setup failures: Assign distinct exit codes (such as code 10 for credential issues) to configuration and authentication failures, preventing CI/CD pipelines from confusing environment setup issues with security findings.
  • Tailored CI/CD credential guidance: Provide environment-specific authentication guidance when running inside automated CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, and Jenkins instead of interactive login prompts.
  • Single-line JSONL statistics: Add the --jsonl flag to cm stats to output single-line JSON records with model and team attribution for seamless integration with Cloud Logging and log aggregation pipelines.
  • Granular sandbox and policy flags: Replace the overloaded --unrestricted flag with orthogonal flags (--sandbox=false) and configurable command policies to decouple container sandboxing from execution safety controls.
  • Sandbox configuration protections: Mount .git/hooks, .git/config, and .codemender read-only within writable execution sandboxes during cm fix and cm verify to prevent modifications to repository security policies.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a security warning when commands are executed with both sandbox isolation disabled and interactive approval skipped.
    • Enforced allowedRoots path boundaries across host discovery and remediation file operations to prevent traversal via dangling symlinks.
    • Supplied exact finding line ranges to remediation agents during cm fix to eliminate manual file scanning overhead.
    • Updated cm report import to properly treat findings without location data as file-level findings rather than defaulting to the first line.
    • Ensured cm session cancel routes requests to the session's original region regardless of local environment overrides.
    • Fixed finding status tracking in cm verify so unexploitable verdicts update the local state database rather than leaving findings open.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google SecOps

Fixed

Tools power-up: Environment filtering in Get Integration Instances

There was an issue where the Get Integration Instances action in the Tools power-up didn't correctly filter environments with names that contain an ampersand (&). This issue has been fixed in version 85.0 of the Tools power-up.

For more information, see Get Integration Instances.

Announcement

Following the March 26, 2025 deprecation announcement, Google SecOps is completing the final shutdown of legacy Google-managed BigQuery datasets and API keys associated with the chronicle-tla Google Cloud project:

  • Who is impacted: This shutdown applies only to non-Enterprise+ customers still provisioned on legacy chronicle-tla Google-managed BigQuery datasets (including tenants whose temporary transition exceptions expired in September 2025). Enterprise+ customers and customers using Bring Your Own BigQuery (BYOBQ) exports to customer-managed Google Cloud projects are not impacted.
  • When: Decommissioning begins on October 28, 2026.
  • Action required: To retain BigQuery access to Google SecOps data, configure export to a customer-managed BigQuery project (BYOBQ) or contact your account team to upgrade to Enterprise+.

title: CrowdStrike compra Zscaler em acordo de US$ 43,9 bilhões
description:
Acordo de US$ 43,9 bilhões

A CrowdStrike acertou a compra da Zscaler por US$ 43,9 bilhões, em uma operação totalmente em ações anunciada pelas empresas na segunda-feira, 23 de novembro de 2026. O valor fica próximo dos US$ 44 bilhões indicados no título do anúncio, e a transação ainda depende de aprovação regulatória.

As companhias esperam concluir o negócio por volta desta época no próximo ano, aproximadamente em novembro de 2027. Até lá, a aquisição permanece condicionada às autorizações necessárias; a conclusão é que permitirá a integração das plataformas descrita pelas empresas.

O foco de cada plataforma

Sediada em San Jose, na Califórnia, a Zscaler oferece produtos de cibersegurança em nuvem para cerca de 8 mil empresas. Entre eles está a tecnologia de confiança zero, que exige que funcionários se autentiquem a cada acesso a um sistema ou recurso interno da organização.

Essa exigência busca dificultar que invasores usem credenciais roubadas para conseguir acesso irrestrito à rede corporativa. A CrowdStrike, por sua vez, protege computadores, laptops, celulares e outros dispositivos conectados à rede de uma empresa por meio de software de proteção de endpoints.

Proteção combinada contra violações

Com a aquisição, a proteção de endpoints da CrowdStrike será reunida à plataforma de confiança zero da Zscaler. A combinação conecta a segurança dos dispositivos ligados à rede à verificação de quem acessa sistemas e recursos internos, duas frentes que as empresas pretendem integrar para defender clientes contra violações de dados.

As companhias afirmam que, juntas, as duas soluções poderão oferecer proteção superior aos clientes. Essa é a justificativa apresentada para unir os produtos: combinar capacidades que hoje estão em plataformas distintas e, segundo as empresas, reforçar a defesa contra o acesso indevido a dados corporativos.

Estratégia para a era da inteligência artificial

As empresas também associam a operação à adoção segura de inteligência artificial por seus clientes. Elas dizem que a integração das plataformas deve ajudar organizações a usar IA com segurança e que o acordo criará o “maior mercado endereçável individual” em cibersegurança, expressão usada para descrever a oportunidade comercial combinada.

A aquisição, portanto, tem duas justificativas declaradas: reunir tecnologias de segurança complementares e posicionar melhor as empresas para a era da IA. Essas metas dependem da conclusão do negócio e da integração das ofertas; por enquanto, o fechamento está previsto para cerca de um ano após o anúncio e sujeito à aprovação regulatória.

title: Show DEV: MovieVerse — A Movie Discovery App I Built With React 19 and the TMDB API
description:
Live demo: https://film2027.netlify.app
Source code: https://github.com/WAHIB-EL-KHADIRI/movieverse

MovieVerse is my flagship learning project — the app I built to go from knowing React to actually shipping something real with it. It is also the project I show recruiters when they ask what I can build.

What it does

  • Trending movies on the home page, loaded from the TMDB API
  • Search for any movie by title
  • Filters — release year and sorting (popularity, rating, date)
  • Detail pages for every movie, with full navigation via React Router
  • Favorites — save the movies you want to watch later
  • Dark mode and skeleton loaders while content is loading
  • Graceful error handling — when the TMDB API rate-limits, the app says so plainly instead of breaking

The stack

React 19, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, and the TMDB API. Deployed on Netlify.

What building it taught me

React Router in practice. Routing a real app with detail pages and filters is very different from reading about routes. (I wrote about the routing part in detail here: https://dev.to/wahib_el_khadiri_0/i-turned-a-single-page-react-site-into-a-real-multi-page-app-with-react-router-1n6b)

TypeScript catches the bugs you don't see. Typing the API responses forced me to understand the data shape instead of guessing — and the compiler caught mistakes before users did.

A real API means real failure modes. Loading states, empty results, rate limits, network errors — half the work of a "simple" movie app is handling everything that can go wrong between your UI and someone else's server. The skeleton loaders and the error messages are features, not polish.

Ship it, then show it. The demo is live, the code is public, and I'd rather get honest feedback on a real app than keep a perfect project on my laptop.

Try it, break it

Open the demo, search for a movie, save a favorite, switch to dark mode. If something breaks or feels wrong, tell me in the comments — that's exactly the feedback I'm here for. And if you're a junior dev building your own first real project: pick one API you like and build the whole thing around it. You learn more from one shipped app than from ten tutorials.

I'm Wahib El Khadiri, a junior full-stack developer from Kénitra, Morocco. I build with React, Node.js and Laravel, contribute to open source, and teach React in Darija on YouTube. Portfolio: https://wahib-portfolio.netlify.app — GitHub: https://github.com/WAHIB-EL-KHADIRI

title: npx -p playwright node script.mjs still threw ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. The fix was to stop trusting npx.
description:
I was taking screenshots of a website with a small Playwright script, written as an ES module, and ran it through npx. One of the commands I tried was this:

npx -p playwright node script.mjs

It ended in:

ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND

The reasoning looks airtight. -p playwright tells npx to make Playwright available, then run node script.mjs. The script imports Playwright. Playwright is available. Done.

It wasn't. After the second failure I stopped trying variations of the command and changed the approach entirely. This post is about why npx -p can't help an ES module find a package, what I did instead, why that kind of fix later broke on its own, and what I would do now.

The short version: npx puts things on your PATH. import never looks at your PATH. Those are two different lookup systems, and I was feeding the wrong one.

Failure, then failure again

I don't have a record of the exact first command I tried or its exact error, so I won't pretend I do. What I do have recorded is that npx -p playwright node script.mjs still ended in ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and that I changed approach after the second failure.

That second failure is where I stopped, and I want to explain why, because it's the part of this story I'd most like to keep.

When a command fails, the natural move is to try a slightly different command. Different flag, different order, quote something, clear a cache, try again. Each attempt is cheap, so it feels fine to keep going. But if the error is identical and the cause is identical, a third variation of the same shape is not a new experiment. It's the same experiment with a different spelling.

The rule I use now is simple: if the same operation fails twice for the same reason, don't run a third version of it. Find out why it fails, and switch to a different method. Retries for flaky things (timeouts, rate limits, a locked file) don't count. Two identical, deterministic failures do.

An honest note on sources: what I wrote down at the time was one line, "ESM can't resolve a package that npx provides," plus the workaround below. The fuller explanation in the next two sections comes from reading the npx and Node docs while writing this post.

What npx actually gives you

From the npm docs for npx, about --package:

"will be provided in the PATH of the executed command"

And about where it comes from, when the package isn't already in your project:

"installed to a folder in the npm cache"

[src:official:https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npx]

That's the whole contract. npx makes sure the package exists somewhere in the npm cache, and it puts that package's executables on PATH for the process it starts. That's what lets npx some-cli --flag work: your shell (or npx itself) looks up some-cli on PATH, finds the binary in the cache, and runs it.

Notice what's not in that contract: anything about where Node's module loader looks when your code says import 'playwright'. PATH is for finding executables. It's how a shell turns node into a file on disk. It has no role in resolving a bare specifier inside JavaScript.

So npx -p playwright node script.mjs did exactly what it promised. It put Playwright's CLI on PATH, then started node. My script never asked for the CLI. It asked the module loader for a package, and the module loader looked somewhere else.

Where import 'playwright' actually looks

Node's ESM documentation spells out the resolution algorithm. A bare specifier is a name like 'playwright' or 'some-package/sub', as opposed to a relative path or a URL. Bare specifiers go through a package lookup that, paraphrasing the spec's PACKAGE_RESOLVE step, does this:

  • Start at the folder of the module doing the import (the spec calls it parentURL).
  • Look for node_modules/playwright there.
  • If it's not there, move to the parent folder and look again.
  • Keep going until the filesystem root. If nothing is found, throw Module Not Found.

[src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html]

The anchor is the importing file's location. Not your current working directory, not PATH, not wherever npx happened to install something. If no folder above the script has node_modules/playwright, the walk reaches the root and fails. That's ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and it's the correct answer to the question an ES module asks when it imports a package by name.

"But NODE_PATH..."

If you've been writing Node for a while, you might remember NODE_PATH: an environment variable listing extra folders to search for modules. CommonJS still honors it. The modules docs say that if NODE_PATH is set, Node "will search those paths for modules if they are not found elsewhere" [src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/modules.html].

ES modules don't. The ESM docs have a short section titled "No NODE_PATH":

"NODE_PATH is not part of resolving import specifiers. Please use symlinks if this behavior is desired."

[src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html]

So even an approach that points NODE_PATH at the npx cache would not help an .mjs file. I didn't check whether npx sets NODE_PATH at all; for an ES module it wouldn't matter either way.

This is the gap in one sentence: npx extends the executable lookup, ESM uses the folder-walk lookup, and the only global escape hatch that used to bridge them (NODE_PATH) isn't part of ESM resolution.

What I did instead

Knowing what I know now, there are two directions: put Playwright somewhere on that walk, or stop using a bare specifier so there's no walk at all.

What I did at the time was the second one. ESM accepts absolute specifiers. The docs' example is 'file:///opt/nodejs/config.js', described as referring "directly and explicitly to a full path" [src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html]. An absolute specifier skips package resolution entirely. Node just loads that file.

Playwright was already on disk. npx had installed it into the npm cache at some point. I just needed to know where. I located the actual playwright package folder inside the npx part of the cache with find. I didn't save the exact invocation. The shape is a name search under the cache's _npx folder, something like this (illustrative, not the logged command):

find "<npm cache>/_npx" -type d -name playwright -path "*node_modules/playwright"

Then I imported Playwright by an absolute path into that folder, and it worked. No npx needed to make the package visible, which is what the title means: the fix was to stop relying on npx and point at the file directly.

I don't have that screenshot script's exact code in my notes. But the same day I wrote another small script, the one that renders cover images for these posts, and it uses the same pattern. This is its import line as it sits today, with my user folder and the cache folder's hash replaced:

import { chromium } from 'file:///C:/Users/<you>/AppData/Local/npm-cache/_npx/<hash>/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs'

A detail worth knowing if you're on Windows: I used the file:///C:/... URL form rather than a bare C:\... path. The Node docs recommend converting paths with url.pathToFileURL when you import a path, because URL and path rules differ in places like percent-encoding [src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html]. The line above is a hand-written URL. Building it with pathToFileURL is what the docs suggest; I haven't tried that version.

Then the fix broke on its own

Some weeks later I went to make a cover image and the Playwright copy in the npx cache was gone. The cover script's import pointed at a path that no longer existed. I didn't fix it. I rendered the same HTML with headless Chrome another way and moved on. That's how this post's cover was made, too.

In hindsight this was predictable, and I should have written it down at the time I made the switch:

  • The npm cache is a cache. The npx docs describe it as the install location and don't promise anything about how long things stay there. Anything that clears or prunes the cache can remove the folder my script depended on.
  • The folder name was not chosen by me. The <hash> segment is something npm picks. I didn't look into what it's derived from, so I can't tell you when it would change. I only know I was hardcoding a name I didn't control.
  • The dependency was invisible. The repository the script lives in has a package.json at its root, but Playwright isn't listed in it today. Nothing declares "this script needs Playwright." The only record is a long string inside an import statement.

So the fix was real, and it worked, but it swapped one problem (Node can't find the package) for a quieter one (Node can find exactly one copy of the package, in a place that can disappear without warning). I'd call it a good diagnostic step and a poor permanent solution.

There's a smaller safety point too. A hardcoded import into a cache folder runs whatever is in that folder. And per the same docs, a missing package gets "installed to a folder in the npm cache" when npx runs, so that folder is filled by npx, not by anything I reviewed or pinned. For a screenshot script on my own machine, that risk is small. For anything that runs with real credentials in its environment, I wouldn't want to load code from a folder nothing in the project pins.

What I would try now (all untested)

Everything in this section is what I'd reach for next time. I have not tried any of these for this script, so treat them as options to evaluate, not results.

1. Make it a tiny project with a real dependency (untested here).
Install Playwright as a dev dependency in the folder's package.json. Then node_modules/playwright sits directly on the folder walk that the ESM resolver performs, a bare import 'playwright' works, and the dependency is written down in a lockfile. This is the boring answer, and it fixes both problems: resolution and invisibility. The cost is one more dependency to install and keep updated. Given what happened, that cost looks small.

2. createRequire anchored somewhere else (untested).
module.createRequire(filename) builds a CommonJS-style require whose lookup starts from the path you give it. The docs say the argument "Must be a file URL object, file URL string, or absolute path string" [src:official:https://nodejs.org/api/module.html]. In principle you could anchor it at a folder that does have Playwright in its node_modules. But that's still a hardcoded location; if the location is the npx cache, I'd have the same disappearing-folder problem with extra steps. I'd only consider it if the anchor were a stable, deliberately installed location.

3. A symlink, as the Node docs suggest (untested).
The "No NODE_PATH" section says to use symlinks if you want that behavior. A node_modules/playwright link next to the script, pointing at a real install, would put the package on the walk without copying it. Pointing it at the npx cache would inherit the same fragility, so this is only as good as the target.

4. Use the resolver itself as a diagnostic (untested).
Before changing anything, I'd like to have asked Node directly where it thinks 'playwright' resolves from the script's location. I haven't looked up or tried the API for doing that, so I won't name one or describe its output. The point is to get the answer from the resolver instead of from my mental model of the resolver, which is the thing that was wrong.

5. NODE_PATH: no.
Per the ESM docs quoted above, it isn't part of import resolution, so it isn't an option for an .mjs file at all.

The part I actually took away

The technical lesson is narrow and worth having: PATH resolves executables, the ESM loader resolves packages by walking up from the importing file, and npx only touches the first. If you remember that, npx -p some-lib node script.mjs will look wrong to you before you run it.

The process lesson is the one I use more often.

Stop at the second identical failure. I didn't keep trying variations; I stopped at the second failure and switched approach. The one-line note I kept was right, but it was a conclusion, not an explanation. Writing down which lookup was failing would have made the later breakage easier to see coming.

When you switch approaches, write down what the new approach depends on. This is the half I skipped. "Imports Playwright from the npx cache at this exact path" is a dependency with an expiry date. One line next to the import would have explained the later breakage immediately.

A workaround that works is still a workaround. "It runs now" is a fine place to stop only if you also write down what would make it stop running.

Checklist for ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND with npx

  • Is your code importing the package, or running its CLI? npx helps with the CLI. It doesn't change where import looks.
  • Where is the importing file? ESM looks for node_modules/<name> starting from that file's folder and walking up. Your working directory and PATH don't matter.
  • Is the file ESM? .mjs, or "type": "module" in the nearest package.json, means NODE_PATH is ignored for import.
  • Did the same error come back twice? Stop varying the command. Read what each tool actually promises.
  • If you hardcode a path to make it work, write down why and what it depends on. Especially if that path is inside a cache.
  • Prefer a declared dependency over a discovered one. A package.json entry survives cache cleanups. A path you found with find might not.

I'm building an AI code reviewer (getdevreview.com) that tries to point out the issues that matter instead of everything it can find. There's a free tier if you want to try it on a pull request. If you've hit the npx-versus-import gap and solved it in a cleaner way, I'd like to hear how.

title: CMYK to Pantone without false precision: what ΔE can and cannot tell you
description:
Most CMYK to Pantone converters return one confident code. That confidence is usually misplaced. A CMYK value is a process build; a Pantone number is a spot ink. Converting between them is not a formula — it is a nearest-neighbour search through a reference table, and the answer depends on assumptions most tools never show you.

Here is what is actually happening, and how to read the result without over-trusting it.

1. CMYK is not a colour; it is a recipe for a press

The same C40 M20 Y10 K0 build can look different on coated stock, uncoated stock, newsprint, or a digital press, because ink, substrate and profile change what reaches your eye. Without an ICC profile and a rendering intent, a CMYK number has no single absolute colour meaning.

Tools that skip the profile have to assume something: a generic coated assumption, or a simple arithmetic conversion from CMYK percentages to RGB. Both are approximations. The honest output is not "the Pantone for your CMYK" but "the nearest reference under these assumptions".

2. Nearest-match search is a distance problem

Once both sides are expressed in a perceptual space such as CIELAB, you can measure distance. CIEDE2000 (ΔE00) is the current standard for how different two colours look to a typical observer, and a searchable converter should use it instead of raw Euclidean RGB distance.

A useful match reports:

  • the nearest coated reference and the nearest uncoated reference, searched separately
  • the ΔE00 distance for each
  • a couple of runner-up candidates, so you can see whether the nearest match is isolated or in a crowded neighbourhood

If a tool only gives one code with no distance, you cannot tell whether it is a near-exact match or the least-wrong option in a sparse region.

3. Coated and uncoated are different libraries

A Pantone C and U pair with the same number are not the same colour. Uncoated stock absorbs ink differently, so the printed result shifts. Searching a single combined library and labelling the result "Pantone" hides that difference. Search each library independently; the nearest C match may be several ΔE away from the nearest U match, and that gap is real information.

4. Community digital references are not spectral measurements

Unless you license Pantone's own data, any web tool is working from community-sourced digital approximations — values transcribed from guides or derived by measurement, with their own error. They are useful for shortlisting and for communication, not for colour-critical sign-off.

The practical workflow:

  1. Shortlist two or three candidates with a converter, using the coated and uncoated libraries separately.
  2. Look at the ΔE00 values. Under ~2 is close; above ~3–4 you are choosing a nearby colour, not matching one.
  3. Pull a physical guide and compare under your actual lighting.
  4. Confirm with your printer before committing a spot ink to a production run.

5. What to ask any converter

When you evaluate a CMYK-to-Pantone tool, check whether it:

  • states its CMYK assumption
  • searches coated and uncoated separately
  • shows the distance metric
  • warns that matches are approximations
  • gives you a shareable result so a colleague sees the same candidates

I build HueConvert, a free converter that tries to meet those criteria: it converts HEX, RGB, CMYK and HSL, searches coated and uncoated references separately with CIEDE2000, shows the nearest distance and two alternatives, and publishes a guide on why CMYK to Pantone results differ. No account is required.

If your job depends on the colour, the final check is still a physical guide and a conversation with your printer. A converter should help you narrow the field and show its uncertainty — not pretend the uncertainty is not there.

title: Kubernetes v1.38 Sneak Peek
description:
As we get closer to the release date for Kubernetes v1.38, the project develops and matures, features may be deprecated, removed, or replaced with better ones for the project's overall health. This blog post outlines some of the planned changes for the Kubernetes v1.38 release that the release team feels you should be aware of for the continued maintenance of your Kubernetes environment and keeping up to date with the latest changes. The information listed below is based on the current status of the v1.38 release and may change before the actual release date.

Deprecations and removals for Kubernetes v1.38

kubectl: WebSocket opt-out environment variables removed

kubectl has used WebSockets instead of SPDY by default for kubectl exec, attach and cp since v1.30, and for kubectl port-forward since v1.31. The KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS and KUBECTL_PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS environment variables let you turn that behavior off. These variables are going to be removed in v1.38. kubectl will then always try WebSockets first and fall back to SPDY when it needs to (the same as the current default behavior). If your scripts or CI environments set either of these environment variables, you can remove them since they will no longer have any effect.

To learn more, refer to KEP-4006: Transition from SPDY to WebSockets.

kubectl: name dropped from kuberc credential plugin allowlist entries

The kuberc file keeps kubectl user preferences separate from cluster credentials in the kubeconfig, including an allowlist of the credential plugins kubectl is allowed to run. In the beta kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 API, an allowlist entry can use name as an alias for command. The name field (not command) has been deprecated since v1.36.

With kuberc expected to graduate to stable in v1.38, the new kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1 API will not include name. If any of your allowlist entries use name, change them to command now.

To learn more, refer to KEP-3104: Separate kubectl user preferences from cluster configs.

Ongoing major changes

Future removal of cgroup v1 support

Support for cgroup v1 is being phased out. Since v1.35, the kubelet fails to start on nodes that use cgroup v1 unless you set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration. This option remains available in v1.38, but it should be treated as a short-term fix as support for cgroup v1 is planned to be removed in a future release. If you haven't already, please plan your migration to cgroup v2.

To learn more, refer to KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support.

Admission webhooks no longer receive authentication and authorization review requests

Since v1.37, the ExcludeAdmissionWebhookVirtualResources feature gate has been enabled by default. With it on, validating and mutating admission webhooks no longer receive requests for (virtual) writes to TokenReview, SelfSubjectReview, SubjectAccessReview, SelfSubjectAccessReview, LocalSubjectAccessReview or SelfSubjectRulesReview. Creating or updating a webhook configuration whose rules name one of these resources returns a deprecation warning, and the API server logs any existing configurations that are affected when it starts.

If you rely on a webhook to see these requests, you can turn the feature gate off for now, but note that the gate is planned to be locked on when the feature graduates to stable.

To learn more, refer to KEP-5793: Manifest Based Admission Control Config.

Breaking changes in Kubernetes v1.38

Container runtimes must report the cgroup driver

The kubelet in v1.37 and older supported releases provides a legacy mechanism to configure the cgroup driver. The modern way to do that is via the CRI RuntimeConfig RPC, which reports the cgroup driver that the container runtime recommends using. In v1.38, the kubelet defaults to not allowing the legacy configuration mechanism: it will be both deprecated and unavailable unless explicitly re-activated. As a result, v1.38 nodes will essentially require that your container runtime is running before the kubelet starts (to look up the expected cgroup driver); if the kubelet can't get the cgroup driver from the runtime even after retrying, it will exit with an error before even registering the node.

As part of this upcoming release, the cgroupDriver field in the kubelet configuration file will be deprecated. Not only is specifying that field going to be deprecated, the kubelet will actually reject it unless you reactivate the legacy mechanism by enabling the (temporary) LegacyCgroupDriverFallback feature gate. The kubeadm tool will also no longer set cgroupDriver to systemd by default, and its preflight checks will report an error if the runtime doesn't support the RPC. If any of your nodes run an older, incompatible container runtime, you should follow the instructions in the official v1.38 release notes about how to upgrade.

To learn more, refer to KEP-4033: Discover cgroup driver from CRI and kubernetes/kubernetes#136731.

Pod-level resources: swap behavior changes on LimitedSwap nodes

If you use pod-level resources on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2 and are configured with LimitedSwap, the kubelet in v1.38 will start applying swap limits based on the Pod's pod-level memory settings. This means that Pods whose pod-level memory request equals their memory limit will get no swap at all (both for the Pod and for every container in it), even if a container sets a memory request lower than its limit. Check any workloads that rely on swap before you upgrade, and be sure to read the official release notes for v1.38 for detailed advice.

To learn more, refer to KEP-2837: Pod Level Resource Specifications.

Featured enhancements of Kubernetes v1.38

The following list of enhancements is likely to be included in the upcoming v1.38 release. This is not a commitment and the release content is subject to change.

kubectl user preferences (kuberc) graduating to stable

kuberc, the separate kubectl configuration file for user preferences such as aliases, default options and a credential plugin policy, is expected to graduate to stable in v1.38.

To learn more, read Kubectl user preferences (kuberc) or refer to KEP-3104: Separate kubectl user preferences from cluster configs.

Pod-level resources graduating to stable

Pod-level resources, which let you set CPU, memory and hugepages requests and limits for a Pod as a whole, are expected to graduate to stable in v1.38. If you run Linux nodes with LimitedSwap, see the swap behavior change above before you upgrade.

To learn more, read Assign Pod-level CPU and memory resources or refer to KEP-2837: Pod Level Resource Specifications.

DRA support for partitionable devices graduating to stable

Partitionable devices let a Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver advertise a device such as a GPU both as a whole and as smaller partitions, and the scheduler allocates only combinations that fit within the physical device. The feature is expected to graduate to stable in v1.38, and the DRAPartitionableDevices feature gate will then be locked on.

To learn more, read Partitionable devices or refer to KEP-4815: DRA: Add support for partitionable devices.

EvictionRequest API (alpha)

Evicting a Pod isn’t always as simple as terminating it. Some applications may be in the middle of important work, such as data migration or cleanup, and terminating them without giving them time to prepare can cause disruptions.

The EvictionRequest API introduces a more coordinated way to evict Pods. It gives applications and controllers time to prepare before a Pod is evicted. For example, when a node needs to be drained or a Pod needs to be moved to another node, a controller can create an EvictionRequest to signal that this Pod needs to be evicted.

The eviction request controller coordinates with the responders configured for the Pod. These responders can perform application-specific tasks such as completing ongoing work, cleaning up resources, or migrating data before the Pod is terminated.

If no custom responder is available or responders don't complete the process, Kubernetes can fall back to the existing API-initiated eviction mechanism, which continues to respect PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs). The EvictionRequest API does not replace PDBs. It gives applications a chance to participate in the eviction process.

As this is an alpha feature, you will need to enable the EvictionRequestAPI feature gate and the relevant alpha API group. Check the v1.38 release notes and documentation, once they're available, to confirm exactly what's required.

To learn more, refer to KEP-4563: EvictionRequest API.

Want to know more?

New features and deprecations are also announced in the Kubernetes release notes. We will formally announce what's new in Kubernetes v1.38 as part of the CHANGELOG for that release.

The Kubernetes v1.38 release is planned for Wednesday, December 16th, 2026. Stay tuned for updates!

You can see the announcements of changes in the release notes for:

  • Kubernetes v1.36
  • Kubernetes v1.35

If you don't know where to start, join our monthly New Contributor Orientations where we teach the community how the project is structured, and we'll guide you on how to make your first contribution to the project.

title: AWS Partner Central expands analytics access with Partner Central Agents and Data Subscriptions
description:
AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers now have two new ways to access their analytics data in AWS Partner Central. Partner Central Agents answer questions in plain language, and Data Subscriptions deliver Partner Central data to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket every day.

Partner Central Agents answer questions about leads, marketing campaigns, opportunities and pipeline, and funding, without navigating dashboards or exporting to spreadsheets. AWS Marketplace sellers can also ask about usage, agreements and renewals, billing, collections, and disbursements. Partners can get the same answers in their own artificial intelligence (AI) assistants and agents through the Partner Central Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

Data Subscriptions deliver ready-to-use datasets to an S3 bucket daily, covering leads, marketing campaigns, partner account relationships, opportunities and pipeline, and AWS Marketplace usage, agreements, and renewals. Because the data lives in a partner's own S3 bucket, partners can connect it to the tools of their choice, such as a business intelligence (BI) tool, a customer relationship management (CRM) system like Salesforce or HubSpot, or a generative AI assistant, and build the reports they need.

Both features use existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and permissions, so partners see only the data they are already allowed to see, and exported data stays in their own AWS account.

These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Partner Central is available.

To get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central and ask an analytics question, such as "What are my top opportunities this quarter?" To set up Data Subscriptions, choose Settings, and then choose Data Subscriptions. To learn more, see Data Subscriptions in the Partner Central Guide.

title: I Built a Two-Language Christmas Game in Pure JavaScript — and Here's What It Taught Me
description:
Hi, I'm Marcos, an independent digital creator from Venezuela. I build interactive web experiences with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and I share my journey one project at a time. Today's project is a little Christmas game: you decorate a tree or assemble a nativity scene by dragging ornaments and characters onto a stage, and the app scores how correct your arrangement is.

You can play it right here: https://margus20.github.io/decoracion-navidad/

The idea behind the scoring

The trick of the whole game is that it does not check for a fixed picture. It checks for relationships. Each piece has a position stored as a percentage of the stage, and the rules are spatial: the star must be near the top, the nutcracker near the feet of the tree, the ornaments must not pile on top of each other, and the visual order from top to bottom has to be coherent. The same idea powers the nativity: baby Jesus in the crib, the crib inside the manger, the star above it, Mary and Joseph close to the scene, the animals on the ground and balanced on opposite sides.

// A rule is just a boolean over the pieces' positions
function ruleStarOnTop(figures) {
  const star = figures.find(f => f.dataset.personaje === 'estrella');
  if (!star) return false;
  return parseFloat(star.dataset.y) < 25; // top quarter of the stage
}

Each rule contributes points, and when the total reaches one hundred the game celebrates. I love this approach because it rewards understanding instead of memorizing coordinates, and it makes the same engine work for two different scenes with different rule sets.

The bilingual system, and the cache trap it exposed

The game switches between Spanish and English with a small dictionary I wrote myself, no i18n library. The interesting part is the color palette for the bow, the bulb, and the valance. At first the panel translated everything except the color names, and the title showed up as a raw key in capital letters. The culprit was not the code, it was the browser cache: one file had loaded fresh while another was still the old version in memory, so the two files were out of sync.

The fix that ended the whole fight was to stop depending on a second file for the palette. I gave the palette its own tiny dictionary inside the file that draws it, so the translation lives right next to the UI that needs it.

const PALETA_EN = {
  rojo: 'Red', amarillo: 'Yellow', anaranjado: 'Orange',
  azul: 'Blue', morado: 'Purple', plateado: 'Silver', original: 'Original'
};
function tColor(nombreOriginal) {
  const clave = nombreOriginal.toLowerCase().normalize('NFD').replace(/[\u0300-\u036f]/g, '');
  return PALETA_EN[clave] || nombreOriginal;
}

The lesson: when a feature looks broken in a way that contradicts your code, suspect the cache before you suspect the logic. Bumping a version query on the script tag, like ?v=23, is the cheapest way to force a fresh download.

Pinch to resize, without losing drag

Pieces are dragged with one finger or the mouse, but I wanted people to also grow and shrink a piece with a two-finger pinch, the way you would expect on a phone. The catch is that the same touch handler must decide in real time whether two fingers mean "pinch" or one finger means "drag". I track the distance between the two touch points and scale the zoom relative to the starting distance, clamped to the same limits the sliders use.

function distanciaDosDedos(e) {
  const t = e.touches;
  return Math.hypot(t[0].clientX - t[1].clientX, t[0].clientY - t[1].clientY);
}
// in the move handler, when two fingers are down:
let nuevoZoom = zoomPinchInicial * (distanciaDosDedos(e) / distPinchInicial);
nuevoZoom = Math.max(40, Math.min(300, nuevoZoom));
elemento.dataset.zoom = nuevoZoom;

The sliders update themselves to reflect the new size, so touch and the control panel never disagree.

Music that survives page changes

The game has three pages: a cover, the tree, and the nativity. The problem with music on a multi-page site is that every time you navigate, the browser tears down the old page and the audio stops. The solution is to remember the play state in localStorage. When a page loads, it reads that flag and resumes automatically if the user had left the music on.

// save the state whenever the user toggles it
localStorage.setItem('musicaActiva', activo ? 'true' : 'false');
// on page load, resume if it was on
const estado = localStorage.getItem('musicaActiva') === 'true';
if (estado) setTimeout(reproducir, 300);

One more detail I learned the hard way: the audio files I first used were really video files renamed to .mp3, and the browser refused them with a "no supported format" error. Renaming an extension does not change what is inside the file. Switching to real audio sources fixed it instantly.

Protecting the user from an accidental exit

Because a game has progress, I added a confirmation before leaving. The browser's own exit dialog is the one you see when closing a tab or reloading, and by design it cannot be styled or translated, so I built my own modal for the in-game "back" button instead, matching the game's gold-on-dark palette and the Bebas Neue font, and reading the current language.

const TXT = {
  es: { titulo: 'CONFIRMAR SALIDA', cancelar: 'CANCELAR', aceptar: 'SALIR' },
  en: { titulo: 'LEAVE GAME?', cancelar: 'CANCEL', aceptar: 'LEAVE' }
};

The honest takeaway: some dialogs belong to the browser and you cannot dress them up. The right move is to control the moments you can control, like the buttons inside your own page.

What I learned

This project taught me more than a tutorial ever did, because every bug was a real constraint. The cache desync taught me to isolate dependencies. The fake mp3 taught me that a file is its bytes, not its name. The pinch gesture taught me that a touch handler can be a state machine, not just a single action. And the exit dialog taught me to accept the limits of the platform and design around them.

If you want to play with it, the source is on my GitHub and the live demo is the link above. If you build your own scoring rules for a different scene, or you improve the flame or the drag, I would love to hear about it in the comments. Thanks for reading, and happy building from Venezuela.
