title: 116x Faster Is True. It Is Also the Wrong Number.
description:
The 116x number is not a lie. It is a measurement of the wrong thing. I ran the whole loop on my own fuzzy dedupe, a thousand names with typos, and the function really did get 110 times faster. The app got 48 times faster. Both numbers are from the same run, and the difference between them is the only thing worth writing about.

Fast-Anything does one thing: it profiles your app, finds the slowest function, has a coding agent rewrite just that function in Rust, proves the rewrite behaves the same on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. The headline number, 116x, comes from their fuzzy dedupe example: a Python dedupe of 700 names falling from 4.91 seconds to 42 milliseconds. I built my own version of the same job, 1,005 names with typos, 163 unique after dedupe, and ran the whole loop on it. My baseline was 2.61 seconds, then 2.57 on the repeat.

The scan took about seven seconds under the profiler and named the obvious suspect. dedupe was 99.9 percent of the run in a single call. Inside it, levenshtein ran 67,427 times and took 99.6 percent. The third function on the list was the typo generator, which the tool refused to port, correctly, because it calls random and no deterministic rewrite of a random function means anything. That refusal is the first thing the tool got right. A profiler that proposes porting your randomness is a profiler that has not understood your program.

The port step recorded one real call to dedupe and wrote a crate with a brief for the coding agent. I wrote the Rust myself, following that brief: the Levenshtein distance over characters, not bytes, because Python strings index by code point and a byte-based port would have failed on the first non-ASCII name. Then the tool replayed every recorded call plus the edge cases it derives, empty input, non-ASCII text, long inputs, against the Rust build. Thirty-five out of thirty-five came back identical. Per call, the function went from 2,536.8 milliseconds in Python to 23.1 in Rust. That is 110 times faster, measured, and close enough to the advertised 116 that the headline survives contact with my machine.

Then I ran the benchmark, which times the whole app, not the function. Five runs each, interleaved. Python: 2.60 seconds. Rust: 55 milliseconds. Forty-eight times faster end to end.

Forty-eight is the honest number and 110 is the true one, and they are different because the function is not the app. The app also generates a thousand names, prints a line, and starts a Python interpreter, and none of that got faster. The port moved the only part that was slow, and the slow part was 99.9 percent of the run, so the app still got dramatically faster. But the gap between 110 and 48 is the fixed cost of everything around the function, and no port touches that. A bigger app with more fixed cost would show a smaller end-to-end number from the same 110-times function. A smaller one would show a bigger number. The per-call figure belongs to the function. The end-to-end figure belongs to the app. Quoting the first as if it were the second is how a real speedup turns into a misleading one.

None of this makes the tool a gimmick. The loop worked exactly as described: scan found the hot function, the port was verified against real calls before anything was swapped in, and the swap is reversible. What it makes is a tool whose headline number needs a second number next to it, the one for the whole program. I would still port the hot function. I just would not tell anyone it made my app 116 times faster, because it made one function 110 times faster and my app 48 times faster, and the second number is the one a user feels.

What is the biggest gap you have seen between a function's speedup and the app's? I keep finding the fixed costs are larger than anyone admits before they measure them.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: November 09, 2026
description:
AI Hypercomputer

Feature

Generally available: Pathways on Cloud is now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Major features include the following:

  • Single-controller execution model: Coordinate multi-slice and multi-host Cloud TPU workloads from a single Python client process. Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and centralized scheduling to support both Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) and Multiple Program, Multiple Data (MPMD) workloads. For example, training and reinforcement learning (RL) loops.
  • Resilient and elastic training: Keep training jobs running across hardware interruptions with resilient training, including the following capabilities:
    • Elastic training: Dynamically scale down to healthy Cloud TPU slices during unplanned hardware failures and scale back up when replacement slices rejoin without restarting the entire job.
    • Suspend-resume: Automatically save and restore high-bandwidth memory (HBM) state to Cloud Storage during planned GKE preemption events.
    • Hot-swapping: Remap interrupted workloads onto standby or lower-priority Cloud TPU slices.
  • Colocated Python sidecar containers: Run custom Python code directly on Cloud TPU host VMs alongside Pathways workers. For example, multi-host data loading with Grain or RemoteIterator, and distributed asynchronous checkpointing with Orbax.
  • Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.
  • Cluster Director, Cluster Toolkit, and GKE integration: Launch JAX workloads on the Pathways runtime using Cluster Director or Cluster Toolkit (gcluster with --pathways and --pathways-headless), or by deploying Kubernetes JobSet manifests on GKE.
  • pathwaysutils utility package: Use the pathwaysutils Python package for advanced features such as the Shared Pathways Service, elasticity, and experimental.reshard for device-side data transfers across hosts over Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) or Data Center Network (DCN).
  • Standard libtpu.so layering and custom libtpu.so support: Pathways is layered over the standard libtpu.so shared library and provides a way to dynamically link in a user-provided libtpu.so at runtime using PathwaysJobSet.with_custom_libtpu in pathwaysutils.
  • Single-process profiling, observability, and compilation cache: Capture end-to-end JAX profiler traces across the client, proxy, resource manager, and Cloud TPU hosts from a single process. Reuse compiled XLA modules with a persistent compilation cache on Cloud Storage, and view Pathways control and data plane metrics in Cloud Monitoring.
  • Agentic workload debugging: Troubleshoot failed, crashing, or stalled Pathways workloads on GKE using the pathways-workload agent skill. With this skill, AI agents can inspect Cloud Logging container logs, node kernel logs, and GKE events to help identify root causes and fixes.
  • Supported Cloud TPU versions, JAX versions, and container images: Supports TPU7x (Ironwood), TPU v6e (Trillium), TPU v5p, and TPU v5e for JAX versions 0.12.0.1, 0.12.0, 0.11.2, 0.11.1, 0.11.0, 0.10.2, and 0.10.1, with container images published in Artifact Registry:
    • Image locations:
      • Pathways resource manager and worker: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/server:TAG
      • IFRT proxy server: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/proxy_server:TAG
      • Colocated Python sidecar: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/colocated_python_sidecar:TAG
    • Image tags: Replace TAG with one of the following tags, which are created automatically when a Pathways build passes qualification tests and is promoted to production:
      • YYYYMMDD-jax_JAX_VERSION: Pinned tag created by combining the UTC promotion date (YYYYMMDD) with -jax_ and the verified JAX version (JAX_VERSION) after per-version qualification tests pass. For example, 20261108-jax_0.12.0.1.
      • jax-JAX_VERSION: Rolling tag updated after per-version qualification tests pass to point to the most recent verified image for that JAX release. For example, jax-0.12.0.1 or jax-0.12.0.
      • latest: Rolling tag updated when a build passes qualification tests against the most recent supported JAX release.

For more information, see Introduction to Pathways on Cloud.

Smart batching automatically batches and offloads eligible AI operations for asynchronous evaluation. It improves query execution speed without requiring you to rewrite queries into complex array structures. In PostgreSQL 18 and later, this feature is enabled by default. title: Philippine Digital Banks Hold 22.4 Million Depositors and Less Than 1% of System Deposits
description:
The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas counted P138.5 billion in deposits across the country's digital banks at the end of 2025, spread over 22.4 million depositors (Source: Inquirer, 2026). The entire banking system held P22 trillion over the same period (Source: Inquirer, 2026). That is roughly one peso in every 160 of system deposits, for a sector that gets treated as if it already runs the country's money.

Growth Is Real; Balances Are Thin

Digital bank deposits rose 44% in 2025 while the depositor base jumped 81% (Source: Inquirer, 2026). Those rates look like a land grab until you divide them: P138.5 billion across 22.4 million depositors is about P6,200 per person. That is wallet money, not savings money. A deposit base that behaves like a wallet reprices overnight the moment a competitor runs a better promo.

The BSP Raised the Price of Looking Like a Digital Bank

Circular 1240, dated September 21, 2026, requires thrift, rural, and cooperative banks shifting to a digital business model to hold P1 billion in capital, the same floor as a digital bank license (Source: GMA News, 2026). Covered banks get six months to comply, and the requirement applies at the time of application. The BSP framed the rule as a level playing field, which is another way of saying it tired of small lenders marketing digital products while carrying small-lender risk. The licensing queue tells the same story: MariBank became the seventh licensed digital bank in July 2026, leaving three of the reopened slots unclaimed (Source: Inquirer, 2026).

One IPO Rewrote the Funding Math

Mynt, the parent of GCash, raised P60.9 billion in October 2026 in the largest IPO in Philippine history, listing with a market capitalization of P441.51 billion (Source: PSE, 2026). The detail worth studying is who bought: 140,725 GCash users invested about P1.1 billion through the app itself, many as first-time shareholders (Source: PSE, 2026). Distribution became capital formation. A fintech that already owns the daily transaction now also owns a channel into the same customer's investment account.

Payments Are Settled; Credit Is the Next Fight

Digital payments reached 64.7% of retail payments in 2025, up from 57.4% a year earlier, and QR Ph processed 2.47 billion transactions worth P1.16 trillion, passing cards for the first time (Source: GMA News, 2026). The payment layer is effectively won, which moves the fight to the balance sheet: credit, insurance, and wealth products. Underwriting there cannot lean on deposit collateral, because a P6,200 average balance secures almost nothing. Lenders will have to price risk from cash-flow data spread across wallets, payroll, and remittances instead.

Remittances Are the Quiet Rail Underneath

Cash remittances reached a record $35.63 billion in 2025 (Source: ABS-CBN News, 2026). September 2026 inflows rose 2.6% to $3.20 billion, the fastest growth in eight months (Source: GMA News, 2026). Full-year growth, though, may land as the slowest since 2020 (Source: BusinessWorld, 2026). For digital banks and wallets, that mix matters: remittance corridors remain the most reliable source of new money entering the formal system, and they are slowing.

What This Means for Builders

Compliance work is about to outrank feature work. When the capital floor rises and license slots run out, the differentiator stops being who ships a prettier app and becomes who can prove controls, reconcile ledgers, and document credit decisions. Yano.AI builds AI systems for document-heavy financial operations, and the questions lenders bring are consistent: how do you underwrite a borrower whose income evidence lives in three wallets, two payslips, and a remittance receipt? Teams that answer with auditable data will set the price of risk for everyone else.

FAQ

Q: How many digital banks are licensed in the Philippines?
A: Seven as of July 2026, with three license slots still unclaimed (Source: Inquirer, 2026).

Q: What capital does a digital bank need in the Philippines?
A: P1 billion. Circular 1240 now applies the same floor to thrift, rural, and cooperative banks that shift to a digital business model (Source: GMA News, 2026).

Q: Do digital banks hold a large share of Philippine deposits?
A: No. They held P138.5 billion against P22 trillion system-wide at the end of 2025, under 1% (Source: Inquirer, 2026).

Key Takeaway

The 2026 story is no longer about adoption. Payments crossed the halfway mark, digital bank deposits grew 44%, and the largest IPO in Philippine history belonged to a wallet company. What remains open is whether those 22.4 million wallet users become depositors who keep real balances, and whether a P1 billion capital floor makes that conversion easier or harder. If you run a wallet or lending product, what is your average balance per active user, and is it rising?

Sources

  • Philippine digital bank deposits reached nearly P139B in 2025
  • BSP sets P1-B capital requirement for banks shifting to digital models
  • Mynt, Inc. raises P60.9B in historic stock market debut
  • Digital payments accounted for 64.7% of total retail payments in 2025, says BSP
  • Philippines gets 7th digital bank as MariBank upgrades license
  • Cash remittances reach $35.63 billion in 2025
  • Cash remittances rose to $3.20B in Sept. 2026 - BSP
  • OFW remittances may grow at slowest pace since 2020

title: Your File Watcher Deleted the File You Just Saved
description:
The setup is about as simple as file-based automation gets: watch a folder, copy anything written there into a second folder, and — because a stale mirror is worse than no mirror — remove from the target whatever gets removed from the source. Four lines of chokidar and you're done.

Then someone hits Cmd-S in their editor, and the file vanishes from the target. Not corrupted, not half-copied. Gone. Sometimes it comes back a moment later; sometimes it doesn't. The source file is fine the whole time.

TL;DR: Most editors don't save into your file, they write a temp file and rename() it into place. A naive watcher sees unlink then add and, with delete-mirroring on, races itself into deleting the target. The fix is three ordered defenses: awaitWriteFinish so half-written files never get copied, a per-file debounce so a bundler's event storm becomes one copy, and a delay on every delete that gets cancelled the moment the path reappears. All three are in copy-watch, which is where the code below comes from.

Why Does Saving a File Look Like a Delete?

Because for a lot of software, it is one. An atomic save means the editor never leaves your file in a partially-written state: it writes the new content to a temporary file next to the original, fsyncs it, and then rename()s the temp over the target. rename() on the same filesystem is atomic, so a reader either sees the entire old file or the entire new one — never a truncated middle.

Excellent property. Terrible thing to watch naively. The kernel events you get are, in order:

unlink   notes.md
add      notes.md

Or, depending on the editor, a supporting cast of files you never asked about:

  • vim writes a probe file literally named 4913 into the directory to test whether it can create files there, then deletes it.
  • Some macOS editors stage the whole thing in a hidden .sb-a1b2c3d4 directory next to the file.
  • Copying onto exFAT or SMB volumes leaves AppleDouble siblings (._notes.md) carrying the resource fork.
  • iCloud Drive leaves notes.md.icloud placeholders for files that are visible in Finder but not actually on disk.

So a watcher that maps events one-to-one onto filesystem operations has already made two mistakes before any of your code runs: it will faithfully mirror junk, and it will faithfully mirror a delete that was never a delete.

Why Not Just Copy on Every Event?

Because add doesn't mean "this file is finished." It means "a directory entry appeared." A large asset written by a build step will fire add while it's still a few kilobytes of a few megabytes, and you'll copy the truncated version — with no error, because nothing failed. Truncated output that nobody reports is the expensive kind.

Chokidar's answer is awaitWriteFinish: don't emit until the file's size has stopped changing for a while.

const watcher = chokidar.watch(srcRoot, {
  ignoreInitial: !initial,
  usePolling: poll,
  interval,
  binaryInterval: interval,
  // Verhindert, dass halb geschriebene Dateien kopiert werden.
  awaitWriteFinish: {
    stabilityThreshold: stability,   // default 300ms
    pollInterval: Math.min(100, interval),
  },
  // ...
});

300ms is a compromise, not a law. It's the price of every copy — nothing is mirrored before it elapses — and it needs to be longer than the longest pause your writer takes mid-file. A bundler streaming output locally is comfortable at 300ms. A file arriving over a slow network mount is not; raise it there and accept the latency.

That handles one write. It does not handle the second problem: a bundler rewriting the same file four times in 200ms as it settles. Each of those is a legitimate, complete write, so awaitWriteFinish dutifully emits four events, and you do four copies where the first three are already garbage. Hence a second, separate timer — a per-file debounce, defaulting to 50ms:

const copyTimers = new Map();

const schedule = (map, key, delay, fn) => {
  clearTimeout(map.get(key));
  if (delay <= 0) {
    map.delete(key);
    fn();
    return;
  }
  map.set(key, setTimeout(() => { map.delete(key); fn(); }, delay));
};

Note the shape: keyed per path, and every new event for that path cancels the pending one. That's the primitive the delete fix needs too.

How Do You Make a Delete Safe?

You don't act on unlink when you receive it. You schedule the delete, and you let a subsequent add for the same path cancel it.

const deleteTimers = new Map();

const onWrite = (type) => (file) => {
  // Ein neu erscheinender Pfad annulliert eine noch offene Löschung.
  clearTimeout(deleteTimers.get(file));
  deleteTimers.delete(file);
  schedule(copyTimers, file, debounce, () =>
    run(type, file, (to) => copyFile(file, to, retries)),
  );
};

watcher
  .on('add', onWrite('copy'))
  .on('change', onWrite('update'))
  .on('unlink', (file) => {
    if (!deleteRemoved) return;
    clearTimeout(copyTimers.get(file));
    copyTimers.delete(file);
    schedule(deleteTimers, file, deleteDelay, () =>
      run('delete', file, (to) => rm(to, { force: true })),
    );
  });

Both directions cancel each other. An unlink drops any pending copy — no point copying a file that's gone. An add drops any pending delete — the atomic save's rename landed, so the "delete" was never real. The grace period (--delete-delay, default 400ms) is simply how long you're willing to wait to find out which of the two it was.

Pick it deliberately: too short and a slow rename slips through as a real delete, which is the original bug wearing a smaller hat; too long and genuinely deleted files linger in the mirror. 400ms covers a local rename() by three orders of magnitude and is imperceptible to a human deleting a file on purpose. Over SMB, raise it.

Worth being explicit about what this is not: it is not a correctness guarantee, it's a heuristic with a tunable window. There is no event that says "this was an atomic save." You are inferring intent from timing, and the honest thing to do is name the assumption in the flag's default rather than bury it.

What Should the Ignore List Actually Contain?

The tempting move, once you've seen 4913 and ._notes.md and .sb-a1b2c3d4 go past, is to ignore every dotfile and be done with it. Don't. That rule throws away .htaccess, .env, and the entire .well-known directory — for a folder being mirrored into a webroot, those are three of the files most likely to matter.

So the default list is deliberately narrow and enumerated:

export const DEFAULT_IGNORE = [
  /(^|[\\/])\.git([\\/]|$)/,
  /(^|[\\/])node_modules([\\/]|$)/,
  /(^|[\\/])\.DS_Store$/,          // macOS Finder-Metadaten
  /(^|[\\/])\.Spotlight-V100([\\/]|$)/,
  /(^|[\\/])\._[^\\/]+$/,          // AppleDouble Resource-Forks auf FAT/exFAT/SMB
  /\.icloud$/,                     // iCloud-Platzhalter
  /\.sb-[a-z0-9]+$/i,              // Atomic-Save-Verzeichnisse
  /~$/, /\.swp$/, /\.tmp$/, /\.crdownload$/, /\.part$/,
  /^4913$/,                        // vim-Testdatei beim Speichern
];

Every entry there is a name some piece of software chose for a file it intends to delete itself. That's the actual membership rule, and it's a much better filter than "starts with a dot."

Two more guards belong in the same category — cheap checks that turn a silent disaster into a startup error:

if (srcKey === destKey) {
  throw new Error('createCopyWatcher: "dest" darf nicht "src" sein');
}
if (destKey.startsWith(srcKey + path.sep)) {
  throw new Error(
    'createCopyWatcher: "dest" liegt innerhalb von "src" — das erzeugt eine Endlosschleife',
  );
}

A target nested inside the source is a feedback loop: every copy is a write inside the watched tree, which triggers another copy. It fills a disk in the time it takes to notice. And the comparison itself needs care on macOS, where the same path can arrive as NFD or NFC and comparisons are case-insensitive:

function normalizePath(p) {
  const normalized = path.resolve(p).normalize('NFC');
  return process.platform === 'darwin' || process.platform === 'win32'
    ? normalized.toLowerCase()
    : normalized;
}

Skip the normalize('NFC') and ~/Sites/Café compares unequal to itself depending on which program handed you the string.

What Doesn't This Replace?

rsync. If all you want is for B to look like A, this has been solved for decades and solved better:

rsync -a --delete ./dist/ ~/Sites/preview/

Pair it with fswatch and you have the same behaviour in two lines of shell, with none of the timing heuristics above — because rsync compares state instead of reacting to events, which sidesteps the entire atomic-save problem rather than defending against it.

A watcher earns its place only when something has to happen per file: purge a cache entry, trigger a reload, kick a deploy, transform the file on the way through. That's what the onEvent hook is for, and it's the only reason to accept the extra machinery.

It also doesn't preserve extended attributes, Finder tags, or resource forks — fs.cp copies content and mode, nothing more. Mirroring signed bundles or design files? Use ditto --rsrc --extattr. For build artifacts and source, it's irrelevant.

What's the Generalizable Lesson Here?

  • A filesystem event is a statement about a directory entry, not a statement about intent. unlink + add is one save operation about as often as it's two separate ones, and nothing in the event stream tells you which.
  • When you can't observe intent, encode the ambiguity as a tunable delay with a documented default — and say in the docs that it's a heuristic. A hidden 400ms assumption is a bug report waiting to happen; a documented one is a flag.
  • Use separate timers for separate concerns. Bundling repeat writes (debounce) and waiting out a possible rename (delete-delay) look similar and want different durations; merging them means one of the two is always wrong.
  • Make destructive operations cancellable and let the cheap signal cancel the expensive one. A pending delete that any new write annuls is strictly safer than a delete that has to be undone.
  • "Ignore all dotfiles" is the wrong abstraction for temp files. The real category is "files some program created and intends to remove itself" — enumerate those, and keep .env and .well-known working.

The other half of getting this tool to run at all — the sudo prompt, the macOS privacy dialog, and the EMFILE crash, none of which is actually about admin rights — is covered in the file watcher that looked like a permissions problem.

title: Workflow SDK now writes over WebSockets on Vercel
description:
The Workflow SDK now sends event writes and stream writes to Vercel Workflows over a WebSocket by default, replacing one HTTP request per write, or per write group for streams. No code change is needed beyond upgrading to workflow@5.2.0 or later.

Once you deploy the upgrade, new runs use it. In-flight runs finish on the deployment they started on.

Existing streaming code works as is. A step that writes a burst of chunks, like AI tokens, sends them over the WebSocket once it opens:

Streams keep pace with AI output

In a benchmark replaying an AI agent's token stream, v5.2.0, which writes streams over a WebSocket by default, delivered the full response 4.2× faster than v4.8.12, with no chunk delayed over a second.

Fewer HTTP requests for event writes

Every step start and completion is an event write, now sent over the WebSocket, so workflows with many steps make fewer HTTP requests. The added efficiency also improves performance and reduces costs. The queue handler opens the connection for every delivery.

Get started

Read the Vercel World documentation to get started. If you're on 4.x, start with the upgrade guide, since v5 is a major release.

title: What Backup and Disaster Recovery Tools Don't Recover (2026): Configuration, Identity, DNS, and Secrets Gaps
description:
Backup and disaster recovery tools recover data and servers, but a business also needs its cloud configuration, identity, DNS, certificates, secrets, pipelines, and people working again before customers can use the service. The best cloud operations setup for business continuity and disaster recovery combines a platform such as Control Plane that keeps the application running in more than one location, a data protection tool for backups, configuration kept as code, and a tested recovery order for everything else. This guide maps eleven recovery layers against what the vendors’ own documentation says their tools restore, and sets out the order in which services should come back.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Backup and DR products restore data and server images and leave most of the operating environment to you.

  • Most backup and DR products leave cloud IAM, DNS records, TLS certificates, encryption keys, and CI/CD pipelines to you.
  • A complete business continuity posture covers eleven layers, from volumes and VMs through people and communication.
  • Recovery order decides whether restored data is reachable. Identity and DNS come before compute.
  • Every recovery path must be timed and tested, including configuration, identity, and user access in the recovery environment.
  • Control Plane keeps the application tier running across multiple locations and clouds so that a location failure needs no recovery launch, and its declarative resources make configuration exportable and re-appliable.

What is the difference between business continuity and disaster recovery?

Business continuity, disaster recovery, and high availability solve related problems at different scopes, and confusing them leads to plans that protect servers but leave the business offline.

Term What it keeps running Typical scope Owner
High availability A single system or service, through redundant components and automatic failover One application, usually across zones in a region, sometimes across regions Engineering and platform teams
Disaster recovery Information systems after a major, usually physical disruption, by relocating to an alternate site The information systems at an affected site IT operations and infrastructure
Business continuity The organization’s business processes during and after a disruption, including people, communication, and third-party dependencies The entire organization Executive leadership, with IT, legal, and operations

NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 draws the continuity and recovery lines explicitly. A business continuity plan sustains business processes during and after a disruption, a disaster recovery plan covers major disruptions that require relocating information systems to an alternate site, and an information system contingency plan recovers a single system. The same publication defines a business impact analysis as the process that maps a system to the business processes it supports, including interdependencies, and characterizes the consequences of a disruption. Without that mapping, a team can restore every database and still miss the payment gateway dependency that keeps revenue at zero.

What do backup and disaster recovery tools actually recover?

Backup and DR products are engineered for data and compute, and the vendors’ own documentation shows where each layer is left to you.

Layer What usually recovers it What it leaves to you
Data and volumes AWS Backup, Azure Backup, Google Cloud Backup and DR, Veeam, Commvault, Druva Verifying data integrity and application-level consistency after restore
Servers and VMs AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (block-level replication), Azure Site Recovery, restore from backup products Post-failover steps such as public IP assignment, load balancer attachment, and connection-string updates
Cloud network configuration (VPCs, subnets, security groups, load balancers) AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery network replication (VPC-level configuration, in-AWS networks only, through a CloudFormation stack), Azure Site Recovery network mapping, Commvault Cloud Rewind, infrastructure as code Public IPs, network security groups, and load balancers, which Azure Site Recovery leaves to recovery-plan scripts or manual steps; keeping definitions as code and checking parity between regions
Cloud IAM roles and policies Infrastructure as code, if the roles were codified; IAM is not on AWS Backup’s supported list Keeping role and policy definitions as code and testing them in the recovery account
Workforce identity (Entra ID, Active Directory, IAM Identity Center) Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery, Commvault IDRecover (Active Directory, Entra ID, Okta), Veeam Data Cloud for Microsoft Entra ID Hard-deleted and on-premises Active Directory-sourced objects when relying on Entra Backup and Recovery alone, Active Directory forest recovery when relying on Microsoft’s own process, and IAM Identity Center’s fixed primary Region
DNS records and failover Exported zone files or infrastructure as code; Route 53 hosted zones are not on AWS Backup’s supported list Failover through data-plane health checks, short TTLs on failover records, and restoring DNS before applications
TLS certificates Re-issuance or certificates provisioned in advance in the recovery region Provisioning each recovery region ahead of time, since AWS Certificate Manager certificates cannot be copied between Regions
Secrets and encryption keys Multi-Region replication you set up per secret or key, or vault backups Creating multi-Region KMS keys yourself; Azure Key Vault restores only within the same subscription and geography
Application configuration and deploy pipelines Infrastructure as code repositories and CI/CD definitions in version control Predeploying pipelines in every region and replicating DR plans, credentials, certificates, and scripts
Third-party dependencies (payments, email, SaaS APIs) Nothing in the backup stack Documenting API keys, OAuth tokens, webhooks, service principals, and partner allowlists of your egress IPs, and testing integrations from the recovery environment
People and communication Nothing in the backup stack Out-of-band communication channels, phone bridges, runbook distribution, and role assignments

AWS states that in addition to data, you must redeploy the infrastructure, configuration, and application code in the recovery Region, and AWS Backup’s saved EC2 metadata, such as instance type, VPC, security group, and IAM role, is only used when restoring to the same Region. Generating infrastructure as code from existing resources after the fact is unreliable. Microsoft says exporting an ARM template from the portal is not a reliable way to turn pre-existing resources into templates usable in production, and exported templates can miss password parameters and stop at 200 resources per resource group. Terraform’s configuration generation for imports is labeled experimental and produces a best guess. Google’s Terraform export of existing resources is Pre-GA, and some resource types are not supported. The AWS CloudFormation IaC generator works only for resource types the Cloud Control API supports and models up to 500 resources per template. Configuration that is not in code before the disaster has to be rebuilt by hand under pressure. The tools that keep it in code are compared in CI/CD and IaC tools for disaster recovery and self-healing.

Why do identity, DNS, and secrets break recovery?

Identity, DNS, and secrets sit near the bottom of the dependency stack, so data, compute, and traffic all wait on them.

Workforce identity is the first bottleneck. Microsoft Entra ID soft-deletes only users, Microsoft 365 groups, cloud security groups, and applications, for 30 days, and hard-deletes all other object types immediately. Microsoft calls recoverability a shared responsibility and tells customers to keep tenant configuration in an external versioned repository exported with Microsoft Graph. Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery became generally available in June 2026; the Standard plan keeps daily backups for 7 days, a 30-day Premium plan is in preview, and it cannot recover hard-deleted objects or objects managed in on-premises Active Directory. Active Directory forest recovery has no end-to-end automation and is more a logistical and organizational challenge than a technical one, according to Microsoft, which recommends regular domain controller backups over snapshot restore. On AWS, the IAM control plane runs in us-east-1, so creating or changing roles during an event depends on that Region, and AWS advises against relying on global-service control planes in recovery paths. IAM Identity Center runs in one primary Region; multi-Region replication exists but not for account instances or Active Directory-sourced identities, and the primary Region cannot be changed.

DNS, certificates, secrets, and encryption keys form the second set of hidden dependencies. The Route 53 control plane is in us-east-1 while DNS answering is global, and AWS says to use data-plane functions such as health checks for DNS failover. AWS calls a TTL of 60 or 120 seconds a common choice for failover records because resolvers cache answers until the TTL expires. AWS Certificate Manager certificates are regional and cannot be copied between Regions, so each recovery region needs its own certificates in advance. AWS never automatically creates or replicates multi-Region KMS keys. Azure Key Vault backups can be restored only within the same subscription and Azure geography, and Microsoft-managed Key Vault failover is best-effort and leaves the vault read-only. Data encrypted with a key that does not exist in the recovery region stays unreadable after the restore.

What order should you restore services in?

Recovery is sequence-dependent, and the wrong order leaves restored services idle while teams rebuild the prerequisites beneath them.

Step What to restore Why it comes here
1 Out-of-band communication and the incident bridge Teams need a coordination channel that does not depend on the systems being recovered; CISA’s incident response playbook calls for out-of-band communications and phone bridges
2 Break-glass access to cloud accounts and recovery tools Break-glass accounts do not depend on the failed identity provider, so the team can sign in and rebuild everything else
3 Network, then workforce identity and internal DNS Self-hosted domain controllers and identity servers need VPCs, subnets, routes, and security groups first, and Microsoft says you often need to recover Active Directory and DNS before other application components; time sync comes up here because Kerberos and certificate validation depend on it
4 Secrets, keys, and certificates Encrypted data is unreadable and TLS endpoints fail without them
5 Data Databases and volumes restore once keys and network paths exist
6 Compute and application tier Application code needs identity, networking, secrets, and data in place, plus container images, service quotas, and monitoring already available in the recovery region
7 Traffic cutover with health checks and short TTLs Users should reach the recovery environment only after the application passes health checks, and TTLs must already be short before the event because resolvers keep cached answers
8 Verify access, payments, and integrations Users must sign in, payments must clear, and third-party APIs must respond
9 Plan failback The recovery environment’s state is recorded and the return to the primary site is scheduled

Steps without a dependency between them run in parallel, and large data restores usually start as soon as keys and network exist because they set the RTO floor. Azure Well-Architected guidance says to replicate DR plans, credentials, certificates, and scripts across regions, keep offline copies, and predeploy CI/CD pipelines in every region. AWS Resilience Hub notes that even with backups copied to a fallback Region, you are still expected to maintain a restore procedure and test and time it. Keeping these artifacts in one region or one cloud account creates a single point of failure that no backup tool fixes.

What are the best cloud operations solutions for addressing business continuity and disaster recovery?

No single product covers all eleven layers, so the strongest setup combines solutions that each handle a distinct part of the problem.

  1. Control Plane keeps the application tier running across multiple locations and clouds. A workload runs in every location of its Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s named set of locations, which can span AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) regions, plus Kubernetes clusters you run yourself or that Control Plane runs for you. Each workload gets Control Plane’s canonical endpoint, one HTTPS URL that uses DNS to route clients to the nearest healthy location, and replicas in other locations take over when a whole location fails. Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to a workload running at least two replicas across at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers. Configuration is kept as declarative resources that export and re-apply. Custom domains get TLS certificates automatically, and org secrets are stored on multiple cloud providers, so a workload references the same secret wherever its GVC runs. The business continuity solutions for high availability across on premises and cloud roundup covers this layer in depth.
  2. Hyperscaler-native DR and backup handles server replication and data protection into one provider’s cloud. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates server volumes at block level, and AWS Backup covers its supported resource types. Azure Site Recovery and Azure Backup provide VM replication and backup. Google Cloud Backup and DR covers workloads including Compute Engine, Persistent Disk, Filestore, Cloud SQL, and AlloyDB. The best cloud disaster recovery solutions for 2026 comparison scores them side by side.
  3. Data protection platforms provide backup, ransomware recovery, and identity backup. Veeam, Commvault, and Druva back up data across cloud and on-premises environments. Commvault IDRecover covers Active Directory, Entra ID, and Okta, and Veeam Data Cloud for Microsoft Entra ID backs up Entra ID. Commvault Cloud Rewind, now listed under Cloud Application Recovery, rebuilds cloud infrastructure and configuration along with data.
  4. Infrastructure as code and GitOps keep cloud configuration in version control so it can be reviewed and reapplied in a recovery account. Terraform, Pulumi, and CloudFormation define network, IAM, and security group state. The code has to exist and stay current before the disaster.
  5. A business continuity plan with a business impact analysis, out-of-band communication, and regular drills ties the technical layers to people and process. It covers third-party dependencies, communication channels, and decision authority.

Most companies need one solution from each of the first four types and a tested plan that ties them together. A backup product without codified configuration leaves identity and networking gaps, and a multi-location platform without data protection leaves backup and ransomware recovery gaps. The cloud vs on-premises disaster recovery guide covers where the recovery site itself should run.

How do you test that the whole business recovers?

AWS says the only error recovery that works is the path you test frequently, and a test that restores one database snapshot and declares success misses most of the recovery surface.

A complete drill rebuilds configuration and identity in the recovery account, applies the infrastructure as code, restores secrets and certificates, deploys the application, times the whole sequence against the RTO, and measures data loss against the RPO. Google’s DR guide says to test that permissions and user access work in the DR environment like they do in production. The drill should move traffic into the recovery DNS path with health checks and short TTLs, confirm that users can sign in, check that payment gateways and third-party APIs respond, and use the out-of-band communication channel. Every gap found becomes an action item with an owner and a deadline. Teams that skip the people and communication layer in drills find out during a real incident that the phone bridge was never set up. The steps for drilling without risking customers are in how to test failover without taking production down.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. When a location in a GVC fails, replicas in its other locations keep serving through the workload’s canonical endpoint. During the October 20, 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, 20 percent of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their GVCs. According to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry, their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime. Teams use the same model to survive a cloud provider outage without a DR runbook for the application tier.

Every Control Plane resource, including GVCs, workloads, identities, secrets, policies, domains, and volume sets, is a declarative item reached through one API shared by the console, CLI, Terraform, Pulumi, and AI agents. Control Plane’s CLI command cpln apply creates or updates resources from YAML or JSON files, is idempotent, and applies related resources in dependency order. Existing resources export as re-appliable YAML or as Terraform HCL. The Control Plane console’s Export GVC action saves a GVC with its workloads, identities, and volume set definitions as one file for backup and restore. Org-level secrets, cloud accounts, and agents are handled separately, and secrets are not included in the export.

Control Plane ships Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the docs include CI/CD examples for GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and CircleCI, so it complements the infrastructure as code you already run. Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s identity for workloads, creates an IAM role, GCP service account, or Azure managed identity in your own account, so no long-lived AWS, GCP, or Azure keys sit in your code. Org secrets are envelope-encrypted and stored on multiple cloud providers in cloud hardware security modules, and workloads reference them by name. Custom domains get TLS certificates automatically and are DNS geo-routed to the nearest healthy location. Volume sets support on-demand and scheduled snapshots with a retention period and restoring a volume to a snapshot. For cross-region data, Control Plane’s Template Catalog includes replicating databases, such as the Postgres Multi-Location template, which promotes a replica automatically with three or more locations, and pgEdge, which runs active-active multi-master Postgres. Volume-set data itself is not replicated between locations, and a volume can be copied on demand to another location.

Inside an org, nothing is permitted until a policy grants it, and a tamper-proof audit trail records who did what across the org. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

It works alongside the backup and data protection tools a company already runs. Those tools keep protecting data copies, and Control Plane keeps the application serving from healthy locations.

FAQ

Short answers on backup gaps, recovery order, identity, and testing.

What are the best cloud operations solutions for addressing business continuity and disaster recovery?

Control Plane runs the application tier active-active across locations and clouds, so a location failure needs no recovery launch. Hyperscaler-native DR tools such as AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, Azure Site Recovery, and Google Cloud Backup and DR handle server replication and backups. Data protection platforms such as Veeam, Commvault, and Druva cover backup and ransomware recovery, and Commvault and Veeam extend to identity backup. Infrastructure as code and GitOps keep cloud configuration repeatable. A business continuity plan with a business impact analysis, out-of-band communication, and drills ties these layers to people and process.

What is the difference between business continuity and disaster recovery?

Business continuity sustains the organization’s business processes during and after a disruption, covering people, communication, and third-party dependencies as well as technology. Disaster recovery is the part focused on relocating and restoring information systems after a major disruption. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 draws this distinction and uses a business impact analysis to map systems to the business processes they support.

Is DRaaS enough for business continuity?

DRaaS covers servers and data by replicating workloads to a recovery site and automating failover. It typically leaves most cloud configuration, workforce identity, DNS, TLS certificates, encryption keys, CI/CD pipelines, third-party integrations, and people and communication to you. Business continuity needs tools and plans for each of those layers alongside DRaaS.

What does a backup not recover?

A backup typically does not recover cloud IAM roles and policies, workforce identity, DNS records and failover configuration, TLS certificates, encryption keys and secrets, CI/CD pipelines, third-party integrations, or communication channels. AWS Backup keeps EC2 metadata such as instance type, VPC, security group, and IAM role, but uses it only when restoring to the same AWS Region. IAM, Route 53 hosted zones, Secrets Manager, and KMS are not on AWS Backup’s list of supported resources.

How do I back up cloud configuration like IAM, DNS, and security groups?

Define cloud configuration in infrastructure as code before a disaster and store the code in version control outside the primary cloud account. Terraform, Pulumi, and CloudFormation can define IAM roles, DNS zones, security groups, and networks. Generating code from existing resources afterward is unreliable. The AWS CloudFormation IaC generator supports only Cloud Control API resource types and caps at 500 resources per template, Terraform’s import configuration generation is experimental, and Azure ARM template export can miss password parameters and stops at 200 resources.

How do I recover Microsoft Entra ID or Active Directory after a disaster?

For Entra ID, use Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery, generally available since June 2026, which keeps daily backups for 7 days on the Standard plan, with a 30-day Premium plan in preview. It cannot recover hard-deleted objects or objects managed in on-premises Active Directory, and Microsoft recommends keeping tenant configuration in an external versioned repository exported with Microsoft Graph. Microsoft says its Active Directory forest recovery process has no end-to-end automation and describes it as more a logistical and organizational challenge than a technical one. Commvault IDRecover and Veeam Data Cloud for Microsoft Entra ID provide third-party backup, with Commvault covering Active Directory, Entra ID, and Okta and Veeam covering Entra ID.

In what order should systems be restored after a disaster?

Start with out-of-band communication and the incident bridge. Restore break-glass access next, then the network, workforce identity, and internal DNS, followed by secrets, keys, and certificates. Restore data once encryption keys and network paths exist. Deploy compute and applications, cut traffic over with health checks and short TTLs, verify access and integrations, and plan failback.

How often should business continuity and disaster recovery plans be tested?

Test at least quarterly, which AWS recommends for Elastic Disaster Recovery drills, and again after significant infrastructure or organizational changes, because AWS states that the only error recovery that works is the path you test frequently. Drills should rebuild configuration and identity in the recovery environment, time the full restore against the RTO, verify user access and third-party integrations, and use the out-of-band communication channel.

How does Control Plane support business continuity and disaster recovery?

Control Plane runs each workload in every location of its Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s named set of locations, across regions and clouds. Each workload gets a canonical endpoint that routes requests to the nearest healthy location, and replicas in other locations take over when a location fails. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to a workload running at least two replicas across at least two locations. Every resource is declarative, and existing resources export as re-appliable YAML or Terraform HCL. Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s identity for workloads, keeps long-lived cloud keys out of code, org secrets are envelope-encrypted and stored in cloud hardware security modules on multiple providers, custom domains get automatic TLS certificates with geo-routing, and volume sets support on-demand and scheduled snapshots. Control Plane works alongside existing backup and data protection tools.

title: How to Speed Up Python With Rust Without a Rewrite (One Function, 116x Faster)
description:
A Python fuzzy dedupe over 700 names takes 4.91s. Replace one function with Rust via PyO3 and the whole app runs in 42ms. That's 116x, and everything else is still the same Python you had yesterday.

That number comes from the README of fast-anything, an MIT-licensed CLI (2.6k stars as I write this) whose tagline is the whole argument: "Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow." It profiles your app (Python, Node, Ruby, Go, Java, PHP, C# and a few more), has a coding agent port the hot function to Rust, and refuses to switch the port on until it behaves the same as the original on real recorded calls. That last part is why I think it's worth a look, and the benchmark table also says something unflattering about a lot of full rewrites.

Most full Rust rewrites are about the résumé

My position: most "we rewrote it in Rust" projects are ego with a benchmark attached. A profiler would have told you where the time goes in an afternoon. The rewrite takes months, and the README is blunt about what comes with it: "months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/".

A commenter on the Hacker News thread (200 points, 163 comments) said it better than I can. caymanjim says people rewrite in Rust "so that they can make HN posts about rewriting a thing in Rust that didn't need rewriting."

There are honest reasons to rewrite. Memory safety is one, and several people in the thread argued it. But if the ticket says "it's slow", the rewrite is the most expensive way to fix it.

How fast-anything speeds up Python with Rust

Install it, have a Rust toolchain via rustup, and point it at a realistic workload:

npm i -g @el4cteo/fast-anything      # or: cargo install fast-anything
fast-anything go --agent claude -- python app.py

--agent takes claude, codex, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. If you'd rather drive each stage by hand, the subcommands are:

command what it does
scan -- <cmd> profiles the app, ranks functions by time × how portable they are
port [id] records up to 500 real calls, creates a one-function Rust crate + TASK.md
verify release-builds the port and replays every recorded call
enable / disable swaps the Rust in or out (one marked block, removed byte for byte)
bench times the whole app, original vs Rust, interleaved runs
report markdown + SVG card for your PR
doctor checks Rust, your runtimes and your agents

Python bindings use PyO3 and need Python 3.10+. Every port is its own small crate, and all of them share one .fast/target cache that you can delete whenever you like. If something looks off in production, FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 runs the original code.

scan wants "a representative workload, not the test suite." Take that seriously. Profile your unit tests and you'll end up optimizing your fixtures.

Why porting the outer loop beat porting levenshtein

This is the part I'd want every "just add a Rust extension" blog post to cover.

Fuzzy dedupe is the textbook case. You compare every name with every other name, and levenshtein is where the time goes. The obvious move is to port levenshtein. The README reports that porting only the inner levenshtein gave 35× and 1.9×. It doesn't say which benchmarks those two figures came from, but compare 35× with the 116× headline. The tool deliberately "ports the outermost loop it can, not the tiny function called inside it."

The reason is the boundary. Port the inner function and Python crosses into Rust once per pair of names, which for a quadratic loop can mean millions of crossings. Each crossing converts arguments and return values. Port the loop instead and you cross once, and Rust does all the comparisons on its own side.

Not everyone in the thread was convinced. efficax argued the FFI boundary "often means you lose any gains from rust to packaging up the data." ben-schaaf disagreed: "Not really true in Python. Data is already in the form of C structs". The outer-loop approach mostly settles the argument by paying the conversion once.

The tool also enforces this. A port that is correct but slower per call "isn't enabled either," because the call overhead can cost more than the work it saves. Since 0.6.2, go --agent sends a slow-but-correct port back to the agent for another try and keeps the best correct attempt. You can override it with enable --force, and then the slowdown is on you.

Verification is the actual product

The obvious objection to the tool is that "have Claude rewrite my hot path in Rust" is something you can type into any agent today. raincole said so on HN: "You can literally just type 'profile this app and find out the performance bottleneck' then 'rewrite it in rust' in your agent TUI".

Sure. Then the agent gives you a function that compiles and looks right, and it's wrong for any name with an accent in it.

That's the README's own demo. A port "compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it." Catching that is the job of verify, and it's the part of fast-anything that earns its keep:

  • It replays up to 500 real calls recorded from your actual workload.
  • It adds edge cases, with the original code supplying the expected answers: "NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs". The 0.5.0 changelog spells out non-ASCII as accents, CJK, emoji and combining marks.
  • Floats must match within 1e-9. The port must raise where the original raises, and in Python that means the same exception type. A Rust panic doesn't count.
  • It tells ints from floats and tuples from lists.
  • If the Rust changed after verify, build refuses to put it live.

Five hundred recorded calls is not a proof, and the README's "Proof, not vibes" slogan oversells it a bit. If none of your recorded inputs reach a branch, nothing checks that branch. Still, it beats the alternative most people actually use, which is "the agent said the tests pass."

Where this approach breaks

The README's benchmarks (an i5-10500 on Windows 11; C and C++ on a 4-core GitHub Actions Linux runner) show the limits plainly. These are whole-app times, not microbenchmarks:

app before after
Python fuzzy dedupe (700 names) 4.91s 42ms, 116×
PHP fuzzy dedupe (600 names) 2.94s 53ms, 55×
Go fuzzy dedupe (3,000 names) 3.02s 144ms, 21×
TypeScript fuzzy dedupe (2,000 names) 3.11s 155ms, 20×
Ruby fuzzy dedupe (400 names) 3.13s 228ms, 14×
C# fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) 4.03s 312ms, 13×
C mandelbrot (8 zoom levels) 431ms 127ms, 3.4×
Java fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) 3.50s 1.18s, 3× (11× on the function)
C++ fuzzy dedupe (6,000 names) 3.02s 1.09s, 2.7×

The slower the host language, the bigger the win, which is what you'd expect. For Java, the README says the rest of the time is JVM startup. Bolwin on HN said the results section "feels a bit like a joke," since C and C++ got rewritten in Rust for performance, and dellamonica pointed out the C# version is single threaded while the Rust one isn't. I read the compiled-language rows as mostly parallelism, with a little extra on top.

Other limits:

  • It only ports top-level, deterministic functions that take plain data. I/O, randomness, globals and functions that mutate their arguments in place are out. In Python that means module-level functions and @staticmethods, plus dataclasses, NamedTuples and numeric NumPy arrays.
  • Amdahl's law still applies. ThouYS made the strongest counterpoint in the thread: sometimes "the true performance hog is like sand, spread across the system." If scan shows a flat profile, no port will save you.
  • There may already be a library for it. dejaydev asked whether the result beats RapidFuzz, the maintained fuzzy-matching library. That's a fair question, and the README doesn't answer it.
  • Someone has to own the Rust. Almondsetat's worry, the trickiest code ending up "in a language you don't even know", is real. I'm fine with a 200-line single-function crate that sits behind a kill switch. A whole codebase in that state is a different matter.

What to do today

  1. Profile a real workload before you open a rewrite RFC.
  2. If one CPU-bound, pure function dominates, check for an existing C-backed library (numpy, RapidFuzz) first.
  3. If there isn't one, port the outermost loop, not the inner helper.
  4. Don't ship any AI-written port until it has been replayed against real recorded inputs and the nasty floats and Unicode.
  5. Benchmark end to end, and keep the off switch.

fast-anything automates steps 3 to 5. You can do them by hand too, but most people who say they will end up skipping step 4.

So: have you done a full Rust rewrite? Was it worth it, or would porting the slow 5% have gotten you the same result? I'd especially like to hear from anyone whose profile turned out to be all sand and no hotspot.

Sources

  • fast-anything repo, README and CHANGELOG: https://github.com/EL4CTEO/fast-anything
  • Hacker News discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50596155

title: We killed the PostgreSQL primary. Patroni brought writes back in 24.8 seconds
description:
How long does a PostgreSQL cluster stay without a primary when the primary dies without warning? Not a clean shutdown, not a switchover: the whole node gone at once while an application keeps writing.

We measured it on a real Patroni cluster with the default settings. The application went 24.8 seconds without being able to write, and then writes came back on their own on another node, with no manual action.

▶️ Video (1:40):

The setup

  • 3 PostgreSQL 16 nodes (pg1, pg2, pg3), managed by Patroni 4.1 with etcd as the consensus store (one etcd member per node).
  • Asynchronous streaming replication, one primary and two replicas.
  • Patroni defaults: ttl: 30, loop_wait: 10, retry_timeout: 10.
  • Cluster deployed and monitored with the HighAvailabilityData console (free).
  • Lab, not production: the three nodes ran on a single server, as separate processes with their own data directories, ports and etcd members. There was no load balancer in this test.

The application connects with a libpq multi-host connection string, so it always looks for whichever node accepts writes:

host=pg1,pg2,pg3 port=5441,5442,5443 target_session_attrs=read-write connect_timeout=1

It inserts about ten rows per second and, on any error, closes the connection and retries every 200 ms:

import psycopg, time

conn = None
while True:
    try:
        if conn is None:
            conn = psycopg.connect(DSN, autocommit=True)
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO orders DEFAULT VALUES")
        log_ok(conn.info.port)          # which node took the write
    except Exception:
        if conn: conn.close()
        conn = None
        log_error()
        time.sleep(0.2)
        continue
    time.sleep(0.1)

The number we report is the gap between the last write confirmed on the old primary and the first write confirmed on the new one. That is what your application actually feels.

The "power cut"

To simulate a node that disappears, we killed every process of pg1 at once with kill -9: Patroni, PostgreSQL and its etcd member. Nothing gets a chance to say goodbye: Patroni does not release the leader key and nobody is told that the primary is gone.

What happened, second by second

Time Event
0.0 s pg1 killed. The next INSERT fails.
0 – 24.8 s Every attempt fails: pg2 and pg3 are still read-only replicas, so target_session_attrs=read-write finds no node to write to.
~24.7 s The leader key in etcd expires. The replicas notice on their next loop, pg3 wins the race for the key and promotes itself.
24.8 s The application's next retry lands on pg3. Writes are back.

Later, when pg1 came back, we started it from the console and it rejoined as a replica of pg3 (Patroni uses pg_rewind if needed). The cluster was healthy again without rebuilding anything by hand.

Why ~25 seconds and not 2

Because Patroni is doing exactly what it should. The primary holds a leader key in etcd with a TTL of 30 seconds and renews it every loop_wait (10 s). When the primary dies, nobody can take over until that key expires. Depending on when the last renewal happened, that is somewhere between ttl - loop_wait and ttl seconds after the crash (20 to 30 s with the defaults), plus a moment for the replicas to notice and race for the key.

That wait is not wasted time. It is what guarantees that there are never two primaries at the same time (split brain). A replica cannot promote itself just because it lost contact with the primary: it has to win the key in etcd, and etcd only grants it once the old leader's lease is gone. If the old primary were still alive but cut off from the rest of the cluster, it would fail to renew its key and demote itself.

Can you make it faster?

Yes, by lowering ttl and loop_wait in the Patroni configuration. Patroni requires loop_wait + 2 × retry_timeout ≤ ttl, so you cannot shrink one without the others. Shorter values mean faster failover but also more chances of a false failover when the network or etcd has a hiccup of a few seconds. For most teams the defaults, about half a minute of write unavailability for an unplanned crash, are a reasonable trade-off. A planned switchover, by contrast, takes only a few seconds because the old primary hands over the leader key cleanly.

What this test does not show

  • A real network. All nodes were on one server, so there was no network latency or partition. On separate machines the numbers depend on your network and etcd.
  • A load balancer. With HAProxy in front, the application only sees the virtual IP, and you add HAProxy's health-check interval to the gap. That is where the 26–49 s range with default settings comes from.
  • Synchronous replication. We used asynchronous replication, so writes confirmed on pg1 in its last moment could be missing on pg3. If you cannot lose any committed transaction, use synchronous replication.
  • The console's own safety net. The HighAvailabilityData console can promote a replica itself if Patroni does not elect one in time. For this test we set it to wait longer than the TTL, so that the number above is Patroni's own election.

Reproduce it

  1. Build a 3-node Patroni + etcd cluster with the default ttl / loop_wait (we used the free HighAvailabilityData console, but any Patroni setup works).
  2. Run a write loop like the one above with a multi-host read-write connection string and log the node of every successful write.
  3. kill -9 Patroni, PostgreSQL and the etcd member of the primary at the same moment.
  4. Measure the gap between the last and the first successful write.

If you get a very different number, we would like to hear about it.

Disclosure: I work on HighAvailabilityData, a free on-premise console from NUTRADELIS S.L. for Patroni clusters.

More on how Patroni and repmgr decide failover: Patroni vs repmgr. Methodology of our HAProxy-based tests: failover tests.

title: Local AI Code Review and Security Scanning in VS Code with Ollama and Hushavyr
description:
I built Hushavyr because I wanted to review code and check for security issues inside VS Code while keeping my source code on my machine. It’s a free, open-source extension that combines static analysis with local AI code review through Ollama.

Hushavyr supports Java, Kotlin, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C#, PHP, and Ruby. I’m using Java in this demo because the JDBC example makes it easy to see what the scanner found and what the proposed fix changed.

From a security finding to a diff in VS Code

In the demo, a Java method looks up a customer by order ID. The method concatenates orderId into the SQL string, which creates a SQL injection risk. Hushavyr flags the line and proposes a PreparedStatement. I can inspect the diff in VS Code before applying the change.

Here’s the JDBC pattern behind the fix:

String sql = "SELECT customer FROM orders WHERE id = ?";

try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    statement.setString(1, orderId);

    try (ResultSet results = statement.executeQuery()) {
        return results.next() ? results.getString("customer") : null;
    }
}

The ? is a placeholder. setString binds the order ID separately as a value, so it can’t change the structure of this query.

I’d still check the full diff before applying it. Does the method return the same result when the order doesn’t exist? Does it close the statement and result set correctly? Those are the same questions I’d ask in a pull request review.

What runs locally

The built-in scanner can flag security issues and look for hardcoded secrets without loading an AI model. Optional analyzers such as Trivy and OSV-Scanner can check dependencies for known vulnerabilities.

Ollama runs the AI review on my machine. I can ask it to explain a finding in the context of the file or propose a code change. The security checks available for a file vary by language and installed analyzer.

Try it on your own code

  1. Install Hushavyr from the VS Code Marketplace.
  2. Open the Command Palette and run Hushavyr: Setup to choose a local model and any optional analyzers.
  3. Open a source file and run Hushavyr: Review Current File.
  4. If you request a fix, inspect the diff before applying it.

If you try it, tell me which language and local model you used. I’d especially like to hear about a finding you expected it to catch or a warning you’d dismiss. Those are concrete cases I can investigate.

Source code and issues on GitHub
