title: Node.js DNS Provisioning — Upsert, Conflict Detection, and Support Hostname Rollback
description:
Default to upsert for provisioning a customer support hostname, and treat rollback as a separate, authorized change with its own saved target. The deciding constraint is propagation delay: accepting a DNS write and moving every caller to the new destination are different milestones, so a faster write path cannot, by itself, justify retiring the previous support service.

TL;DR: Upsert makes a retried provisioning run a no-op instead of a duplicate-record error. Use create when an existing record must stop the operation as a conflict; use update when existence is a precondition. Keep the previous complete record intent available until the cutover has met your acceptance criteria.

Consider a support portal moving from one service to another while the Node.js provisioning worker may replay its work. The useful question is what a replay is allowed to mean. Reasserting an approved destination is reasonable. Silently taking over a hostname that belongs to another configuration is not an acceptable ownership decision.

The distinction matters more than the spelling of the SDK method. A storage architect would ask the same questions about a repeated object write: which identity is being reconciled, who owns that identity, and what protects a later version from an earlier writer? Those are design questions, not durability guarantees supplied by a DNS endpoint.

What must remain true while the hostname moves?

Record three invariants in the architecture decision. First, the provisioning job has authority over the intended hostname before it reconciles anything. Second, every change carries the complete record intent. Third, the saved rollback target survives the forward change. For these DNS operations, zone_id, record type, name, and content are all required; there is no partial write that infers the missing values. An update isn't a convenient way to send only the changed destination.

Keep both destinations available.

That is an operating requirement for this proposed cutover, with an explicit cost: the old support service remains part of the transition until the team can retire it. The alternative is a shorter overlap that accepts more exposure to clients still using the previous destination. No universal waiting interval follows from the write semantics here. Choose the interval from your DNS configuration and the observations your support service needs, rather than inventing a propagation promise.

There are three separate failure boundaries. A duplicate provisioning attempt should preserve approved intent. A stale forward attempt arriving after rollback must be rejected by your orchestration policy. A caller reaching the old destination after a successful write must still receive an acceptable service. Upsert addresses the first boundary; it doesn't establish an ordering protocol for the second or a readiness signal for the third.

For teams maintaining a Node.js provisioning worker, try Infrai for the DNS reconciliation step when keeping application code unchanged as the vendor behind a capability changes is the integration goal. Infrai provides one key, one bill, and one REST API with no SDK to install; the worker keeps the same API when switching providers instead of maintaining a separate SDK surface for each service. Infrai also provides public discovery with no key required, including request and response schemas, so an engineer can inspect the integration contract before arranging credentials. Neither advantage determines when the old support service can safely be removed.

Decision record: reconcile approved intent, preserve conflict detection

The decision is to make upsert the default only after authority and desired content have been established. Create remains an intentional conflict detector. Update belongs to a workflow whose record-existence precondition has already been satisfied.

The table compares integration choices for this decision, including where to start evaluating them. It makes no latency ranking: time to a first accepted write depends on the account, credentials, and zone you already control, while time to a useful cutover also includes application checks.

Option Setup and credential decision SDK and contract trade-off Appropriate boundary
Infrai Inspect public schemas before configuring the API key; its backend surface uses one key. A common REST contract reduces the application surface that changes with a vendor substitution. Try it for shared provisioning orchestration; retain separate cutover acceptance checks.
Cloudflare DNS If the support zone is already managed here, evaluate reusing that account's access arrangement. Compare a direct integration with the common-contract approach; keep the provider dependency explicit. Prefer a direct integration when Cloudflare-specific DNS behavior is a requirement.
Amazon Route 53 If the support zone is already managed here, evaluate the AWS credential and permission setup first. Decide whether a direct provider dependency fits the worker's existing AWS integration. Prefer direct integration when the design needs Route 53-specific controls.
Google Cloud DNS If the support zone is already managed here, evaluate the Google Cloud credential and permission setup first. Check whether another abstraction reduces work for an already Google Cloud-oriented worker. Prefer direct integration when Google Cloud DNS-specific controls drive the design.

These are alternatives, not interchangeable promises. Before selecting a direct provider, check its record identity and mutation semantics in its own documentation; an operation with a familiar name is insufficient evidence that replaying it has the same effect. The comparison leaves provider-specific conflict behavior unranked because this decision doesn't establish equivalence between those APIs.

Credential count is a poor standalone metric.

A common key reduces credential sprawl across integrations, but its permissions still need deliberate handling. Conversely, an existing direct-provider integration may have less setup work than introducing a new service. The relevant measure is how many contracts and access arrangements this particular worker must own, especially if a rollback needs to be executed by someone who didn't build the original integration.

Inspect the contract before putting a write on the critical path

The smallest safe integration example queries discovery and identifies the upsert capability by its published path. It uses Python's standard library, explicitly sets the method, checks HTTP failures, and retries rate limits. The discovery surface is public and requires no credential; this read-only example therefore needs no environment setup or API key. It prints the matching capability entry, rather than inventing an unverified write payload.

import json
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def retry_delay(value, attempt):
    if value is None:
        return 2 ** attempt
    try:
        return max(0.0, float(value))
    except ValueError:
        retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
        return max(
            0.0, (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds()
        )


def discover():
    request = Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
        headers={"Accept": "application/json"},
        method="GET",
    )
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected HTTP {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
            delay = retry_delay(error.headers.get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            time.sleep(max(2 ** attempt, delay))
    raise RuntimeError("Discovery retry budget exhausted")


manifest = discover()
matches = [
    capability for capability in manifest["capabilities"]
    if capability["path"] == "/v1/dns/record/upsert"
]
if len(matches) != 1:
    raise RuntimeError("Expected one upsert capability")
print(json.dumps(matches[0], indent=2))

This is contract inspection, not a cutover. The 30-second timeout and four-attempt retry budget are example client choices, not service limits or latency claims. The mutation adapter should take its path from discovery and its request fields from the capability schema. For authenticated writes, read the key from the environment and send Bearer authorization; keep error handling at least as explicit as in this read-only probe.

Before dispatching a mutation, persist the previous approved configuration and the proposed complete record intent. For an illustrative support hostname, that means retaining the old CNAME destination alongside the proposed new destination, together with the zone and name; those values must come from the actual configuration, rather than from a sample hostname copied into a worker. Printing a request or receiving a success response is not persistence of the rollback target.

Retries become subtle here. An identical upsert can be harmless while a delayed upsert containing an obsolete destination is harmful. Give the orchestration layer a way to reject stale intent before dispatch, and coordinate active workers when approving rollback. A generation check alone is insufficient if an already-dispatched forward write can still arrive afterward. Treat cancellation, in-flight work, and subsequent reconciliation as part of the rollback design.

Save intent first.

Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window; request deduplication and desired-state reconciliation solve different problems. Reuse a request identity for retries of one approved mutation, and distinguish a new rollback mutation from that forward action. Don't turn the window into a claim that obsolete work remains safe forever. A fresh transport request can still contain stale application intent.

Rejected default: create on every provisioning attempt

Create is rejected as the default because a replay should not become a duplicate-record error merely because the first attempt already established the desired record. Update is also a poor onboarding default: it requires the record to exist. Neither choice supplies the ordinary reconciliation behavior that provisioning needs.

Create still has a valid and valuable use case. If an existing customer support hostname means another team configured it and automation must stop, treating presence as a conflict is exactly the desired behavior. Don't follow that conflict with an automatic switch to upsert; doing so would erase the ownership boundary that justified create in the first place. Resolve authority first.

The resulting decision rule is narrow: choose upsert for approved repeatable provisioning, create for mandatory conflict detection, and update for an established record whose existence is required. Choose a specialist or direct provider when its particular DNS controls are part of the requirement. Keep rollback intent and cutover acceptance in your own orchestration, because successful reconciliation alone cannot certify that every customer has reached the new support service.

References

  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • Google Cloud DNS documentation

If the common-contract boundary fits your provisioning worker, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: How a desktop-only app's website can handle phone visitors, with no backend
description:
Originally published on claudictive.com.

A phone visitor on a desktop-only app's website is not a lost download if you give them a way to bring the link to their PC. On claudictive.com, a phone sees up to four buttons instead of the Windows download: email it to yourself, share it, a calendar reminder, and copy link. None needs a backend or collects anything new.

I build Claudictive, an in-game overlay for Claude Code, with Claude Code itself. It runs in games like World of Warcraft, League of Legends or Valorant, and it installs only on a Windows PC, through Overwolf. This is the short story of what we show people who find it on their phone, and why we skipped the obvious email form.

What happens when someone opens a Windows app's website on their phone?

They hit a dead end. The big button says download for Windows, a phone can't do anything useful with a Windows installer, and nothing on the page works on a phone.

I noticed it while looking at the site's own analytics and conversion. The write-ups I found solve the reverse problem: a desktop visitor and a mobile app. Branch recommends a "text me the app" page, and Mozilla's Send to Device widget is a form that emails a download link from a desktop browser to a phone. Both send the message from the site's side, through a server.

For our direction, phone visitor and desktop app, very little is written. The nearest thing is old redirect advice: in 2014 mobiForge quoted Google as saying "if there is no corresponding mobile page for a desktop page, then there should be no redirection at all". So the phone visitor stays on the real page, and the page has to offer them something.

Should you collect their email and send the link yourself?

That was option 2 in our decision record (ADR-031): collect an email address and mail the download link from our side. It looks like one form. Built safely, it is a lot more:

  • a transactional email provider and a verified sending domain;
  • abuse controls on a form that sends mail to any address someone types in, which means rate limits and a bot check;
  • a new section in the privacy page, because we would now hold email addresses;
  • a retention rule for how long we keep them.

Option 1 was to let the visitor send the link to themselves with the phone's own tools. I picked option 1. I wanted the method that would "reduce the privacy risks as far as possible", and I wanted something quick, relatively. An email form adds a new kind of data and a new thing to defend. The phone already has a mail app, a share sheet, a calendar and a clipboard.

How do you send a download link to your PC with no backend?

On a touch phone, each download button on the homepage, the use-case pages and the blog posts is replaced by a small panel. It reads: "On your phone? Claudictive installs on a Windows PC. Send yourself the link and grab it when you're back at your desk." The homepage hero swaps its download button for one that jumps to the panel in the download section.

The live download section at phone size (Chrome's phone emulation).

The panel picks phones with a media query, so a desktop with a mouse never sees it:

window.matchMedia('(hover: none) and (pointer: coarse)').matches

The buttons:

  • email_me_the_link: a mailto: link with no recipient. The visitor's own mail app opens with the subject and the link filled in, they type their own address and send it themselves. The address never touches our site.
  • share_to_another_app: the phone's share sheet (navigator.share), for sending the link to a notes app, a chat with yourself, or anything else.
  • remind_me_at_8pm: downloads a one-event calendar file (.ics) with the link in it and an alarm at the start time.
  • copy_link: copies the link to the clipboard.

Only the email button always shows. Share, the calendar reminder and copy appear only where the browser supports them. That matters, because a mailto: link needs a mail app set up on the phone, and on a phone without one, whichever of the other three the browser supports are still there.

The core of the email and the reminder is a few lines of plain JavaScript:

// mailto with no recipient: the visitor picks their own address.
'mailto:?subject=' + encodeURIComponent(TITLE) + '&body=' + encodeURIComponent(body)

// 20:00 local today, or tomorrow when it is already 19:00 or later.
var day = now.getHours() >= 19 ? now.getDate() + 1 : now.getDate();
return new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), day, 20, 0, 0);

The reminder uses floating local time, so it goes off at 8pm wherever the visitor is. I picked 8pm by thinking about my own routine and when I'm usually in front of the computer. From 7pm on, it is set for the next evening instead.

If the script fails for any reason, the page keeps its normal download button. Claude Code built the panel and the unit tests, which run it in a fake DOM and check the mailto and calendar-file builders. The parts only a real phone can prove, the mail app taking the mailto: and the calendar opening the reminder, I checked by hand on my own phone on the live site.

What do you count, and what stays on the phone?

We count the tap, and we don't count it as a download. The buttons send us nothing else. The privacy page says it this way: "On a phone this also covers the send-it-to-yourself buttons (email, share, calendar reminder, copy link): we only count the click. Your email address, your contacts and what you share stay in your own apps and never reach us."

That sentence was added to the privacy page in the same change as the panel. No new kind of data, no new storage, no new section.

When would we build the email form after all?

It is still an option. If the panel shows that people really want the link mailed to them, option 2 is written down with everything it needs. Until then, the phone's own tools do the job, and there is nothing new to protect.

title: How to continue a Claude Code task in Codex without re-explaining it
description:
If you use more than one AI coding agent, you have probably hit this. Claude Code stops at a usage limit halfway through a task. You open Codex to keep going, and it knows nothing: not the task, not what is done, not what you decided, not what is blocking. So you explain everything again from scratch.

I ran into this often, so I built pas-agent, a small open-source CLI that carries a task from one agent to the next. This post shows how to use it to move a task from Claude Code to Codex.

Why the next agent starts blank

Every AI coding agent keeps its own private session. When you switch agents, that session does not come with you.

But most agents read an instruction file when they start. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md. Codex, Cursor and OpenCode read AGENTS.md. Gemini CLI reads GEMINI.md.

pas-agent uses that. It keeps a small, local record of the task, the progress and the decisions in .pas-agent/session.json. When you switch, it writes that record into the file the next agent already reads at startup.

Install

pas-agent needs git on your PATH.

You can download a prebuilt binary for Linux, macOS or Windows from the latest release, or install it with Cargo (Rust 1.85+):

cargo install --git https://github.com/gfirik/pas-agent pas-agent-cli

Either way you get a single binary called pas-agent.

Step 1: start a session

In your project (any subdirectory works, the session lives at the git root):

pas-agent init --task "Add JWT auth"

Step 2: record progress as you go 

pas-agent update --completed "Login endpoint" \
                 --remaining "Token refresh" --remaining "Tests" \
                 --decision "Use jose, not jsonwebtoken, for edge runtime support" \
                 --next "Implement refreshToken()"

Flags can be repeated. You can also add blockers with --blocker.

Step 3: checkpoint 

pas-agent checkpoint "Login flow done"

A checkpoint snapshots the task, the git state and the changed files. pas-agent status shows the session with numbered lists, and pas-agent update --done 1 marks remaining item #1 as finished.

Step 4: hand off to Codex 

pas-agent export --to codex
codex

The export writes the session into AGENTS.md, and Codex reads it at startup. It now knows the task, what is done, what was decided and what comes next.

One thing to know: agents read their instruction file only when a session starts. So export before you launch the next agent. If it is already running, restart it or ask it to read AGENTS.md.

Let the agent keep it updated

You do not have to run these commands yourself. pas-agent is an ordinary command, so your agent can run it. Add something like this to your own part of CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md:

## Session handoff (PAS-Agent)
When you finish a piece of work, record it with
`pas-agent update --completed "..." --next "..."` (plus `--decision` / `--blocker` as needed).
At a milestone or before the session ends, run `pas-agent checkpoint "<summary>"`.

Your own files stay safe

export never overwrites a hand-written CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. It writes only inside a marked block (<!-- pas-agent:start --> to <!-- pas-agent:end -->) and leaves the rest of the file alone. Later exports replace only that block.

Which agents it supports

Right now export --to works for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Kiro CLI, Antigravity and Gemini CLI. Use --output <path> to write the context anywhere else.

Where the data lives

Everything is in .pas-agent/session.json at the project root. Commit it to carry the session across machines, or add it to .gitignore to keep it local. The CLI makes no network requests.

Since the session ends up in a file your agent treats as instructions, review changes to .pas-agent/ the same way you review changes to CLAUDE.md.

Status

pas-agent is in alpha. It works end to end, but the session format and commands may still change before 1.0. Next on the roadmap: shell hooks that update and export automatically when you switch agents.

It is MIT licensed. The code is on GitHub, and the docs are at gfirik.github.io/pas-agent. If you work with more than one AI coding agent, I would like to hear how it fits your workflow.

title: When Does a Rust Rewrite Actually Pay Off?
description:
Every few weeks there's a new "I rewrote my CLI tool in Rust and it's 47x faster" post that hits the front page. The benchmarks are real. The vibes are great. What's usually missing is the part where someone tells you when you should actually do this to your own codebase versus when you're just chasing a shiny number.

This post is a framework, not a hype piece. I've done rewrites that paid off in a week and rewrites that turned into six-month slogs for a 15% latency win nobody asked for. Here's how to tell which one you're about to sign up for.

🔥 The Pattern Behind the Posts

Most "rewrote it in Rust" success stories share three traits that don't get called out explicitly:

  1. The original tool was a CLI or daemon, not a web service behind a load balancer.
  2. The bottleneck was interpreter/VM overhead (startup time, GC pauses, GIL contention) — not application logic.
  3. The rewrite happened once, by someone who already knew Rust, not as a learning project billed to the business.

If your situation matches those three, a rewrite is probably going to feel as good as the blog posts claim. If it doesn't, you need to actually run the numbers before committing your team to months of borrow-checker therapy.

🧮 The Four Criteria That Actually Matter

1. Startup Latency

If your tool is invoked thousands of times per CI run, per request, or per shell command, interpreter startup cost compounds fast. This is the single strongest argument for Rust (or Go, or Zig) over Python or Ruby.

bash

Python: ~30-60ms just to boot the interpreter + imports

$ time python3 -c "pass"
real 0m0.032s

Rust: near-zero, dominated by exec() overhead

$ time ./target/release/noop
real 0m0.001s

Multiply that 30ms by 10,000 invocations in a CI matrix and you've found a real, measurable, dollars-and-minutes justification. If your tool runs once a minute as a long-lived daemon, this criterion is basically irrelevant — optimize elsewhere.

2. Binary Size & Distribution

If you're shipping to environments where you can't guarantee a runtime (containers you want under 10MB, embedded targets, CLI tools distributed via curl | sh), a statically linked Rust binary removes an entire category of "works on my machine" bugs.

dockerfile

Before: Python image

FROM python:3.12-slim

~150MB base, plus your deps

After: Rust static binary

FROM scratch
COPY target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/mytool /mytool
ENTRYPOINT ["/mytool"]

~5-15MB total

This matters enormously for serverless cold starts and edge deployments. It matters not at all if you're deploying to a fleet of VMs that already have a fat base image cached.

3. FFI and Integration Pain

This is the criterion people underweight the most. If your "slow" Python code is slow because it's calling out to a C library through ctypes or cffi, you might not need a rewrite — you need a cleaner binding layer, and PyO3 can get you 90% of the benefit without throwing away your application logic.

rust
// A PyO3 extension: speed up the hot loop, keep the rest in Python
use pyo3::prelude::*;

[pyfunction]

fn fast_checksum(data: &[u8]) -> u64 {
data.iter().fold(0u64, |acc, &b| acc.wrapping_mul(31).wrapping_add(b as u64))
}

[pymodule]

fn mymodule(_py: Python, m: &PyModule) -> PyResult<()> {
m.add_function(wrap_pyfunction!(fast_checksum, m)?)?;
Ok(())
}

python

Your application code barely changes

import mymodule
result = mymodule.fast_checksum(payload)

This is the move when 95% of your code is fine and 5% is a hot loop. A full rewrite here is wasted effort — you're paying full migration cost for a partial-codebase problem.

Conversely, if FFI is itself the pain — you're fighting segfaults from a C library binding, juggling GIL releases, or debugging memory corruption across a boundary you don't fully control — that's a real signal. Rust's FFI story (particularly bindgen and explicit unsafe blocks) tends to surface those bugs at compile time instead of in production.

4. Maintenance Cost, Honestly Accounted

This is the one nobody puts a number on, so let's try:

Rewrite cost estimate ≈
(LOC in original) × (hours per LOC to port + test)
+ (team ramp-up time on ownership)
+ (lost velocity on features during rewrite)
- (ongoing maintenance savings per year)
- (bug class elimination: null derefs, data races, etc.)

The last two terms are real and often underestimated — a memory-safe rewrite does eliminate entire categories of production incidents. But they accrue over years, while the first three terms hit immediately. If your team has one Rust-comfortable engineer and four people who've never touched the borrow checker, your "maintenance savings" line item needs an asterisk: savings assume the team can actually maintain it without that one person.

📊 A Quick Scoring Rubric

Before you start, score your situation 0-2 on each axis:

Criterion 0 (skip rewrite) 1 (maybe) 2 (strong signal)
Startup latency Long-running process Occasional CLI use Invoked thousands of times/day
Binary size No distribution constraints Some container bloat concerns Edge/serverless/embedded target
FFI pain None, pure interpreted code Minor bindings, mostly stable Frequent segfaults/GIL fights
Team Rust fluency Zero experience One experienced dev Multiple comfortable contributors

Score of 6+: rewrite is likely to pay off within a quarter. 3-5: consider a partial rewrite (hot path only, via FFI). 0-2: you're probably solving a boredom problem, not a performance problem — profile the existing code instead.

🤔 Before You Reach for cargo new

A lot of "it got 40x faster" numbers are really "we replaced an O(n²) algorithm" numbers wearing a Rust costume. Profile first. py-spy on Python, pprof on Go — find the actual bottleneck before assuming the language is it.

bash

Five minutes that might save you a rewrite

py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python myslowscript.py

If the flame graph shows your own algorithm dominating, fix the algorithm. If it shows interpreter overhead, GIL contention, or GC pauses as the dominant cost, now you have actual evidence for the Rust conversation instead of a vibe.

💬 Your Turn

Have you shipped a Rust rewrite that paid off exactly as promised — or one that quietly became a six-month tax on the team? What criterion from this list would have changed your decision going in?

Rewrites are seductive because they're fun. The discipline is making sure the fun project and the necessary project are the same project.

title: Idempotency Ledger for Agent Tool Calls That Retry Blindly
description:
An agent retry is not a request repeat. It is a new request that looks identical. When a model re issues a tool call after a timeout, the downstream system sees two valid writes, two charged payments, or two created tickets. The failure is structural: the caller carries state in its prompt, the callee carries state in its database, and no key ties the two together.

Why prompt level retry logic breaks at scale

Most agent frameworks implement retry as a loop around the tool function. The loop lives in memory. A process restart, a context compaction, or a supervisor failover erases the attempt counter while the side effect survives. The result is at least once execution with no deduplication, which the operations team discovers through a duplicate invoice rather than a stack trace.

Measurement matters here. A 2026 study titled "Do LLM Agents Act Exactly Once?" measures idempotency violations under retries, which indicates that test suites never forcing a retry cannot surface this class of failure (doi 10.5281/zenodo.24166026).

The write ahead ledger contract

Before the tool executes, the agent writes a row keyed on a deterministic intent hash. The hash covers tool name, normalized arguments, tenant, and a caller supplied window id. The row stores three fields that matter: key, state, and result reference. State moves through reserved, executed, and settled. A retry with the same key reads the existing row instead of calling the tool again.

Stage aware retry plus idempotency plus exactly once semantics is not a novel pattern, it is a well documented pipeline property (doi 10.52783/jisem.v11i2s.14608). Agents fail it because the retry decision is made by a language model rather than by the pipeline.

Three states that prevent duplicate side effects

Reserved means the intent is claimed but the tool has not returned. Executed means the tool returned a reference and the row is no longer eligible for a fresh call. Settled means the downstream effect is confirmed by reconciliation. A retry that lands on reserved must wait, not re issue. A retry that lands on executed must return the stored reference. A retry that lands on settled is a pure replay.

Dead letter handling belongs in the same table. When a reserved row exceeds its lease without reaching executed, the row is released and the intent is parked for human review rather than retried forever, a strategy already standard in payment pipelines that combine idempotency with dead letter queues (doi 10.32628/ijsrst52310495).

What breaks when the key is derived by the model

Keys must be computed by code, never generated by the model. A model that writes its own key will produce a new key on retry because the prompt changed by one token, which defeats the entire mechanism. The safest design derives the key in the tool wrapper from the normalized payload, and treats any model supplied identifier as metadata only.

Research on counterfactual repair of LLM agent failures (doi 10.48550/arxiv.2605.25338) addresses attributing failures to specific actions, which presupposes that a failing action keeps a stable identity across attempts.

Verification checklist before production

Force a timeout after the tool returns but before the agent records success. Confirm the second attempt reads executed and returns the original reference. Kill the process mid flight and confirm the lease expiry releases the row without duplicating the downstream object. Count rows in the ledger against objects in the downstream system and require an exact match. Any mismatch is a duplicate, not a rounding error.

Canonical: https://rausalbahtiar.dev/blog/agent-tool-call-idempotency-write-ahead-ledger

title: Test GLM-5.4 on a 32px checkout overflow, with and without a screenshot
description:
A 352px Pay button stuck out of a 320px checkout panel. GLM-5.4 identified the right edge and returned box-sizing: border-box both times: once from the code alone and once with a screenshot attached. Applying each declaration to a separate copy in Chrome produced identical 320px buttons. Only the reply with the screenshot could read the order reference printed above the button. That reference wasn't in the prompt text.

At 10:07 UTC on November 23, 2026, both calls to POST /v1/chat/completions returned HTTP 200. The requested model was coding-glm-5.4; both responses reported glm-5.4.

Input Edge identified Order reference Input tokens Output tokens
Code only Right null 573 28
Code + screenshot Right TXA-B4M 743 66

The screenshot added 170 input tokens for this PNG with the same prompt text. The output counts are separate; neither call reported a cache hit.

Keep one file for the prompt and one for Chrome

The test page contains no customer data. The HTML and prompt in this example are shorter than the ones used for the recorded run: they reproduce the overflow, not the exact token counts. Save the HTML as checkout.html and leave the placeholder in the file you'll send to the model.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>Checkout</title>
<style>
  .panel { width: 320px; margin: 32px auto; outline: 2px solid #687f7a; }
  .pay {
    display: block; width: 100%; height: 48px;
    padding: 0 16px; border: 0; box-sizing: content-box;
  }
</style>
<main class="panel">
  <p>Order ref: {{ORDER_REF}}</p>
  <button class="pay">Pay $12.00</button>
</main>
</html>

Save the following as prepare.py. Run python3 prepare.py before each pair to put a fresh reference in the browser copy only. Open rendered.html in Chrome with a 390px-wide viewport at 100% zoom. Take a screenshot that includes the reference and the whole button, and save it as before.png next to checkout.html.

from pathlib import Path
from secrets import token_hex

template = Path("checkout.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
reference = token_hex(4).upper()
Path("rendered.html").write_text(
    template.replace("{{ORDER_REF}}", reference), encoding="utf-8"
)

Give both requests the same CSS

Use Python with the openai package (python3 -m pip install openai). Set AIHUBMIX_API_KEY to a key for a funded test account; the AIHubMix quick start covers client setup. Save this as compare.py and run python3 compare.py in the same directory.

import base64
import os
from pathlib import Path
from openai import APIStatusError, OpenAI

template = Path("checkout.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
if template.count("{{ORDER_REF}}") != 1:
    raise ValueError("Use the unfilled checkout.html template")
question = (
    "390px viewport. Which edge of .panel does .pay cross? Give one CSS "
    "declaration that keeps the button full width and both 16px paddings. "
    "Read the order reference only if visible in a screenshot, else use null. "
    "Return JSON with keys edge, property, value, order_ref.\n\n"
)
text = {"type": "text", "text": question + template}
png = base64.b64encode(Path("before.png").read_bytes()).decode("ascii")
image = {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/png;base64," + png}}
client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://aihubmix.com/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["AIHUBMIX_API_KEY"],
    max_retries=0,
)
for name, parts in (("text", [text]), ("image", [text, image])):
    try:
        reply = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="coding-glm-5.4",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": parts}],
            max_tokens=1800,
        )
        print(name, reply.choices[0].message.content)
    except APIStatusError as error:
        print(f"{name}: HTTP {error.status_code}")

Both calls start a fresh conversation, use a 1,800-token output cap and leave temperature unset. Only the second gets before.png as an image_url part. The Coding Plan announcement describes vision on that plan. The AIHubMix channel guide lists image input without a verified vision flag. The exact transcription in this run is evidence for this particular PNG on this route.

Apply each proposed declaration to a clean copy

First check order_ref against your local browser copy. The text-only answer should contain JSON null. The image answer should match the fresh reference exactly. In the recorded run the text-only reply was plain JSON, but the screenshot reply wrapped its JSON in a Markdown code fence. Remove that fence before passing the reply to a JSON parser.

For the CSS check, start each candidate on its own copy of the broken rendered.html at 390px. Apply just the declaration from that reply. In the DevTools console, measure both edges with getBoundingClientRect():

const panel = document.querySelector(".panel").getBoundingClientRect();
const pay = document.querySelector(".pay");
const box = pay.getBoundingClientRect();
const style = getComputedStyle(pay);
console.log({
  edgesFit: Math.abs(box.left - panel.left) <= 1 && Math.abs(box.right - panel.right) <= 1,
  paddingIntact: style.paddingLeft === "16px" && style.paddingRight === "16px",
  labelIntact: pay.textContent.trim() === "Pay $12.00",
});

The repair passes if both edges line up within 1 CSS pixel, both paddings remain 16px, and the label is intact. Removing the padding would make the button fit but would fail this check.

On the recorded page, width: 100% with content-box gave all 320px to the button's content. Padding accounted for the extra 32px. Both replies put the padding inside the declared width with border-box. Chrome measured a 0px difference at each edge for each patch, with the original paddings and label intact. The model returned CSS; Chrome rendered the corrected page. The model didn't edit the PNG.

Keep that corrected screenshot out of your inputs. On this pair the code alone was enough to fix the layout, while only the screenshot supplied the reference. One page can't establish how often screenshots improve a repair.

Sources

  1. Original checkout and Chrome render after applying the model's CSS: same viewport and order reference.
  2. AIHubMix channel guide: request route and image-input status.
  3. Zixuan Li's Coding Plan announcement.
  4. MDN: box-sizing.
  5. MDN: getBoundingClientRect().

Keep reading

GLM-5.4: Debug a CSS overflow with a 320px test case

title: Object Storage for Browser Direct Uploads: Presigned URLs and Tenant Isolation
description:
Short answer: use private object storage with short-lived presigned URLs, keep tenant metadata in your database, and make multipart uploads the default for large media. For an edtech SaaS serving US and EU users, the least complicated choice is the provider whose region, CORS policy, and isolation model you can verify before launch. A single HTTP surface can reduce integration glue, but it cannot remove those checks.

The boundary that keeps your app out of the data path

The browser should upload bytes directly to storage. Your Node.js API authenticates the user, checks the tenant and object key, asks storage for a presigned upload URL, and returns that short-lived URL. The browser then sends the file to storage. Your app receives a completion event or records the object after a successful upload; it never becomes a media proxy.

That boundary matters for classroom video and large lesson recordings. A proxy ties bandwidth, timeout behavior, and failure recovery to your application fleet. Direct upload makes the storage service own those bytes while your database owns the facts about them: tenant ID, object key, course, uploader, size, and state.

This is where Infrai can fit early: its storage handoff uses one REST contract, so a Node.js service can call it with plain HTTP while the rest of a backend stays behind the same key.

The practical win is boring and useful: one REST API, one key, and no SDK install for this handoff. Any runtime that can send HTTPS can use the same contract, which keeps a small upload service from accumulating a second client library every time the product adds a backend capability. Infrai covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. The API is genuinely self-describing, with a public discovery surface and runnable examples, so the contract is inspectable before a key is issued.

Keep buckets private. Public-read URLs are unavailable in the storage capability described here, so this is not a fit for a permanent public file host, static website hosting, or an image CDN. Serve a fresh presigned download URL when an authorized viewer needs a file.

How should a SaaS app use presigned URLs for browser uploads?

Start with a tenant-scoped key such as tenant_42/course_8/lesson_3/video.mp4. The object key is not an authorization system by itself. Your API must derive or validate it from the authenticated tenant, and the database row should be the source of truth for ownership. Server-side metadata queries are limited: object listing supports prefix filtering, not arbitrary metadata search.

The API surface can stay small. The following TypeScript example shows the handoff shape with an explicit method and bearer token. In production, send the exact request fields documented by the discovery schema for your chosen expiry and content type; do not let a browser choose a bucket or tenant prefix. Before shipping, I would trace one complete upload on paper: the API authenticates a teacher, maps the request to tenant_42, writes an upload-intent row, issues a URL, and then waits for the browser's transfer result. If the browser retries, the object key remains stable and the database state machine decides whether the retry is allowed. If a student from another tenant guesses that key, the API refuses to mint a URL. That sequence is longer than a demo, but it exposes the exact place where isolation lives and prevents storage policy from being mistaken for application authorization.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function presignUpload(bucket: string, key: string) {
  const response = await fetch(
    `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/${bucket}/${key}`,
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({}),
    },
  );

  if (response.status === 429) {
    const waitMs = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "2") * 1000;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
    return presignUpload(bucket, key);
  }
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Presign failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  return response.json();
}

The retry is deliberately slow and bounded by your normal request deadline. For a create or publish operation, add an idempotency key; presigning itself should not be treated as proof that an upload completed. I started out assuming a storage listing could replace a media table. It cannot. Record the upload intent before issuing the URL, then mark it complete only after you have verified the object.

For a 2 GB lecture recording, use multipart upload. Create an upload, presign each part, upload parts from the browser, and complete the upload. A dropped connection then costs one part, not the whole file. Keep a cleanup job for abandoned multipart uploads because there is no automatic rule for deleting unfinished fragments.

Small files are different.

Which option fits isolation, regions, and setup?

There is no universal “best” bucket. The right answer depends on who controls tenant policy, where bytes must live, and how much provider-specific code you will carry.

Option Where it tends to fit Tenant-isolation trade-off
AWS S3 Teams that need the broadest mature storage controls and a large regional catalog Maximum policy surface also means more configuration and IAM to review
Cloudflare R2 Teams already operating at the Cloudflare edge and wanting an S3-compatible workflow Check regional and compliance requirements against your US/EU contract
Firebase Cloud Storage Mobile/web teams already using Firebase auth and rules Rules are convenient inside Firebase; a separate Node.js control plane adds another boundary
Infrai storage A SaaS that wants storage plus other backend modules behind one HTTP contract Validate CORS, region placement, and retention requirements before committing

Infrai's concrete advantage here is breadth behind a simple surface: one REST API and one key can cover storage alongside other backend capabilities, so adding a module does not require another SDK and credential flow. Its public discovery endpoint exposes request and response schemas with runnable examples, which is useful when I'm trying to get from zero to a first call without a configuration maze. Start by checking the storage discovery entry.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the storage handoff when your team values one HTTP contract and can keep tenant records and policy decisions in its own API and database. That is a developer-experience choice, not a claim that it wins every region or compliance review.

Where the simpler surface is the wrong tool

The catch is browser CORS control. There is no independent self-serve CORS route for this capability, so a flow that requires custom bucket CORS rules must validate compatibility first. A specialist with mature, user-managed CORS and policy tooling is safer when that control is non-negotiable.

Choose direct AWS S3 when you need object versioning, Object Lock (WORM), strict If-Match concurrency, cross-region replication, or bulk migration tooling. Those are explicit capability boundaries here, not small switches to flip. Firebase remains a sensible pick when Firebase Auth and Security Rules are already the center of your app. Your mileage may vary for US/EU residency: confirm the actual storage region and contract terms rather than inferring them from an API hostname.

Lifecycle policies have a one-day minimum, and there is no hourly expiry. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes. Plan a real billing path before production media lands in a bucket.

A decision rule you can test in one afternoon

Create two test tenants in the target US and EU deployment plan. Verify that tenant A cannot obtain a URL for tenant B's key, that an expired URL is rejected, and that a resumed multipart upload does not restart completed parts. Exercise a browser from the real origins you will ship; CORS behavior is part of the product, not a post-launch detail.

Then measure time-to-first-call, the number of credentials in CI, and the amount of provider-specific code in your upload service. I care about those numbers because they predict maintenance more reliably than a feature checklist. If the isolation tests pass and the single-contract benefit removes meaningful glue, Infrai is a reasonable fit. If a missing control blocks a requirement, pick the specialist and keep the boundary the same: your app authorizes, the browser transfers, and private storage holds the bytes.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://firebase.google.com/docs/storage
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS

Further reading

  • https://docs.infrai.cc

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.

  • Filtros inteligentes: segmentação cruzada por ano de referência, categoria comercial e região geográfica.
  • Camada de dados e exportação: ingestão de dados tabulares estruturados, validação tipada e exportação limpa dos recortes filtrados em CSV.

Por que usar e publicar Skills na Agensi

Transformar código validado, regras de negócio e contratos de dados em uma skill muda a forma como soluções técnicas são distribuídas e executadas:

  • Para quem utiliza: agentes como Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, DeepSeek, Grok e Gemini CLI conectam-se via MCP e carregam uma arquitetura pré-configurada em vez de improvisar o scaffolding a cada prompt.
  • Para quem cria: padrões de engenharia e automações testadas deixam de ficar restritos a repositórios locais e ganham distribuição direta e monetização na loja de criador.
  • Governança e previsibilidade: instruções explícitas e verificação de segurança reduzem ambiguidades e elevam a confiabilidade das entregas técnicas.

title: Is It Safe to Delete ~/Library/Caches on a Mac? How to Clear Cache Safely
description:
Yes—most subfolders inside ~/Library/Caches are safe to delete on a Mac, as long as you quit running apps first, remove only the contents inside (never the Caches folder itself), and skip Apple system caches and sensitive tool data. Apps automatically recreate their cache files the next time you open them, so the only normal side effect is a slightly slower first launch or re-downloading cached assets.

What you should not touch are macOS's system-wide /Library/Caches and /System/Library/Caches folders—macOS manages those itself. Also keep expectations realistic: clearing cache reclaims disk space, not RAM or CPU performance; in fact, rebuilding caches can briefly use a little extra disk and network activity right after cleanup.

On one developer Mac we measured using CleanBit's scan engine, general App Caches inside ~/Library/Caches held 5.42 GB across 65 items, Chrome Disk Cache (~/Library/Caches/Google/Chrome) held 4.37 GB, and dedicated developer caches living under ~/Library/Caches added over 1.2 GB more (including 575 MB for Swift Package Manager, 379.7 MB of Homebrew downloads, 261.7 MB of pip cache, and 24.1 MB of pnpm metadata). Even so, ~/Library/Caches was only a slice of the 124.29 GB scanned on that machine—far smaller than iOS DeviceSupport (24.1 GB du), CoreSimulator/Devices (43.0 GB du), Xcode DerivedData (15.3 GB du), and old node_modules folders (66.3 GB du). Always measure first so you know whether caches are actually where your storage went.

1. Check how much space ~/Library/Caches uses (read-only)

Before deleting anything, check the total size of your user cache folder and see which individual apps are taking the most space:

# Total size of your user cache folder (read-only)
du -sh ~/Library/Caches

# Top 20 largest folders inside ~/Library/Caches
du -sh ~/Library/Caches/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -20

If you also use web browsers with profile-level caches or developer tools that store caches outside ~/Library/Caches, you can inspect them read-only too:

du -sh \
  ~/Library/Caches/Google/Chrome \
  ~/Library/Caches/Firefox \
  ~/Library/Caches/Homebrew/downloads \
  ~/Library/Caches/pip \
  ~/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm \
  ~/Library/Caches/Yarn 2>/dev/null

Note: du reports total disk usage for a directory, not how much is safe to remove blindly. Some tools place virtual environments, downloaded browser binaries, or Apple system databases inside ~/Library/Caches, so always inspect folder names before deleting.

2. ~/Library/Caches vs. /Library/Caches: what is safe and what to leave alone

Location What lives inside Safe to clear? What happens after removal
~/Library/Caches/<third-party app> App thumbnails, HTTP/image caches, updater downloads Usually yes (quit the app first) App rebuilds the cache on next launch; first launch may feel slightly slower
Browser caches (~/Library/Caches/Google/Chrome, Firefox, com.apple.Safari, plus profile Cache/Code Cache) Cached web pages, scripts, images, and shader caches Yes (quit the browser first) Websites re-download assets on next visit; cookies, history, bookmarks, and passwords stay intact
Developer caches in ~/Library/Caches (Homebrew/downloads, pip, Yarn, org.swift.swiftpm, CocoaPods, go-build) Downloaded package archives and build intermediates Yes (when no build or install is running) Package managers re-download archives next time you install or rebuild
Risky subfolders inside ~/Library/Caches (com.apple.FontRegistry*, com.apple.spotlight*, CloudKit*, com.apple.finder, pypoetry/virtualenvs*, ms-playwright*, pnpm/dlx*, JetBrains*) macOS system indexes/databases, Python virtualenvs, Playwright browser runtimes, IDE indexes No—skip these Deleting them can break font rendering, Finder/CloudKit sync, local Python virtualenvs, or test runners until rebuilt/reinstalled
~/Library/Containers/<bundle-id>/Data/Library/Caches Caches of sandboxed Mac App Store apps Usually yes (quit the app first) Sandboxed app regenerates its cache on next launch
/Library/Caches (root Library) System-wide caches shared across all user accounts and daemons Leave alone Requires admin privileges and can cause glitches in shared services; macOS prunes these itself
/System/Library/Caches Core macOS operating system caches (SIP-protected) Never touch Protected by System Integrity Protection; attempting to modify it risks system instability

3. How to clear cache on a Mac manually (Finder & Terminal)

You do not need any third-party app to clear ~/Library/Caches safely. Follow this conservative sequence instead of wiping the whole folder at once.

Step 1: Quit all running apps first

Deleting cache files while an app holds open file handles or writes to a SQLite cache database can cause the app to crash, lose transient state, or keep disk space occupied until the process exits. Quit your browsers, editors, chat apps, and Xcode (Command + Q) before cleaning.

Step 2: Inspect and clear specific folders in Finder

  1. Open Finder and press Shift + Command + G (Go to Folder).
  2. Type ~/Library/Caches and press Return.
  3. Switch to List view (Command + 2) and sort by Size (enable Calculate all sizes via Command + J if sizes are blank).
  4. Select specific large third-party app cache folders whose apps are not running—skipping com.apple.* folders, password managers, cloud sync apps, IDEs, and anything you do not recognize.
  5. Press Command + Delete to move those folders to the Trash (never delete the parent ~/Library/Caches folder itself).
  6. Relaunch your apps to verify everything opens normally, then empty the Trash to reclaim the disk space.

Step 3: Clear browser caches safely (without losing logins)

  • Safari: Open Safari → Settings → Advanced, check Show features for web developers, then press Option + Command + E (or click Develop → Empty Caches). This clears web cache without removing cookies, history, or passwords.
  • Chrome / Brave / Edge / Arc: Open Delete Browsing Data, check only Cached images and files (leave Cookies and Passwords unchecked), and confirm.
  • Firefox: Go to Settings → Privacy & Security → Cookies and Site Data → Clear Data, and check only Temporary cached files and pages.

Step 4: Clean developer caches with their official commands

When large folders inside ~/Library/Caches belong to developer tools, their built-in cleanup commands are safer than rm -rf:

# Clean old Homebrew download caches
brew cleanup --prune=all

# Purge pip's HTTP and wheel cache
pip cache purge

# Remove unused pnpm store packages (do not delete ~/Library/pnpm/store manually)
pnpm store prune

Warning: Avoid running rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/* blindly. Wildcard deletion hits caches of currently running apps and background services, wipes Apple subsystem caches like com.apple.FontRegistry, CloudKit, and com.apple.finder, and can accidentally destroy Poetry virtual environments (pypoetry/virtualenvs), Playwright browsers (ms-playwright), or JetBrains caches stored inside ~/Library/Caches. Always target specific verified folders—or move them to the Trash first.

What if ~/Library/Caches is only a few gigabytes?

On many Macs—especially developer or AI-coding machines—~/Library/Caches is not the main reason storage is full. If your disk is still tight after checking caches, check our dedicated guides on whether Xcode DerivedData is safe to delete, cleaning iOS DeviceSupport and Xcode Simulators, finding and deleting old node_modules folders, removing leftover Claude Code git worktrees, and tracking down Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex disk space.

4. How CleanBit handles ~/Library/Caches (and its sandbox boundaries)

I'm the developer of CleanBit, a sandboxed Mac App Store disk space cleaner for macOS 15+ (v1.0.1 now supports 9 languages and per-group Smart Scan cleaning). Because blind wildcard cleaning inside ~/Library/Caches causes unnecessary breakage, CleanBit applies multiple guardrails before anything can be removed:

  • Running-app blocking (checked twice): CleanBit checks currently running apps during scanning and locks their caches so they cannot be selected—then re-checks running apps again immediately before deleting each individual item, along with verifying the file path, symlink target, and file identity.
  • Protected Apple & third-party bundle lists: CleanBit refuses to delete the ~/Library/Caches folder itself, automatically skips com.apple.* and macOS subsystem prefixes (FontRegistry, Spotlight, CloudKit, Finder, Keychain, and more), excludes sensitive tool paths (pypoetry/virtualenvs, ms-playwright, pnpm/dlx, JetBrains), and skips over 300 protected third-party app bundle patterns during broad cache sweeps.
  • Dedicated rules with no double-counting: Browser caches (Safari, Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Vivaldi, Firefox—without touching cookies, history, or passwords) and developer caches (Xcode, Homebrew, pip, Yarn, SwiftPM, CocoaPods, Go) are handled by their own specific rules so nothing is counted twice.
  • Sandboxed App Caches (~/Library/Containers): If you optionally grant Full Disk Access, CleanBit can also inspect Data/Library/Caches and Data/tmp inside sandboxed app containers after verifying each container's containermanagerd metadata matches its bundle ID.
  • Clear deletion control & honest sandbox limits: Recommended caches are deleted permanently by default so disk space returns right away (or you can switch Recommended items to move to Trash in Settings), while Review items always move to the Trash. Because CleanBit runs inside Apple's App Sandbox with no root privileges and no background helper daemon, it never touches /Library/Caches, /System/Library/Caches, /private/tmp, APFS local snapshots, or iCloud Drive synced files.

Scanning and your first 2 cleans are free on the Mac App Store (with monthly, yearly, or one-time lifetime options).

Originally published at getcleanbit.app/guides/is-it-safe-to-delete-library-caches-mac/. Written by the CleanBit developer with AI assistance; all measurements were taken on a real developer Mac.

LIV Golf's Funding Drought: What's Next for the Controversial Golf League?

The Saudi Funding Cliff: A Threat to LIV Golf's Survival?

LIV Golf, the controversial golf league founded by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), is facing a significant challenge. According to reports, PIF is set to stop funding the league after the 2026 season, leaving LIV Golf's future uncertain. In a recent statement, LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil acknowledged the funding cliff, but emphasized the league's commitment to delivering high-quality golf to its fans.

The PIF Funding Dilemma

PIF's decision to stop funding LIV Golf is not surprising, given the controversy surrounding the league's origins and the human rights concerns associated with Saudi Arabia's involvement. The league's launch in 2022 was met with widespread criticism, with many questioning the morality of accepting funding from a country with a questionable human rights record.

The PIF funding dilemma is a significant concern for LIV Golf, as it threatens the league's very existence. Without a stable source of funding, LIV Golf may struggle to maintain its current level of operations, let alone expand its reach and popularity. The league's reliance on PIF funding has been a major point of contention, with many critics arguing that LIV Golf's success is built on the back of Saudi Arabia's wealth.

The Impact on LIV Golf's Operations

The PIF funding cliff has significant implications for LIV Golf's operations. The league's ability to stage events, attract top talent, and maintain its current level of production quality is at risk. The uncertainty surrounding the league's future has already led to concerns about the stability of its staff, with some employees reportedly facing uncertainty about their job security.

The PIF funding cliff also raises questions about the league's long-term viability. Without a stable source of funding, LIV Golf may struggle to attract and retain top talent, ultimately impacting the quality of its events and the overall fan experience.

The Future of LIV Golf: What's Next?

So, what's next for LIV Golf? The league's CEO, Scott O'Neil, has emphasized the need for LIV Golf to adapt to the changing landscape, but the path forward is far from clear. The league may need to explore alternative funding sources, potentially through partnerships with other investors or sponsors.

However, finding a new source of funding will be a significant challenge, given the controversy surrounding LIV Golf's origins and the league's reliance on PIF funding. The league may also need to re-evaluate its business model, potentially shifting its focus from high-stakes, high-reward events to more sustainable, grassroots initiatives.

Key Takeaways

  • PIF is set to stop funding LIV Golf after the 2026 season, leaving the league's future uncertain.
  • The PIF funding cliff threatens LIV Golf's very existence, with significant implications for its operations and long-term viability.
  • LIV Golf may need to explore alternative funding sources, potentially through partnerships with other investors or sponsors.
  • The league may need to re-evaluate its business model, shifting its focus from high-stakes, high-reward events to more sustainable, grassroots initiatives.

Conclusion

LIV Golf's funding drought is a significant challenge, one that threatens the league's very existence. While the league's CEO has emphasized its commitment to delivering high-quality golf to its fans, the path forward is far from clear. The PIF funding cliff has significant implications for LIV Golf's operations, and the league will need to adapt quickly to survive. As the controversy surrounding LIV Golf's origins continues to unfold, one thing is clear: the future of LIV Golf is uncertain, and its very survival is at stake.

title: Why Rare-Answer Trivia Needs More Than Right or Wrong
description:
Open-ended trivia looks simple: a prompt, a text box, a clock. In practice it is nothing like a multiple-choice quiz. A prompt such as “name a sovereign country” has nearly two hundred valid answers. If every accepted answer is worth the same, the rational move is the first word that comes to mind. The game then rewards speed and popularity, not recall.

Krillion Unlimited is a free, no-login browser game built around that problem. You type answers to open-ended prompts. Valid answers are not equal. Common ones barely move you; rarer ones score more. This article is about that scoring ladder — why a rare-answer game needs more than right or wrong, and what a six-tier model changes for the player.

It is an independent game and is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by krillion.io.

A round, in brief

A standard expedition is seven prompts, with 25 seconds on each one. There are no multiple-choice buttons. You type an answer that fits the category. If the game does not accept it, the round does not end: the input is rejected and you can keep guessing until the timer runs out, or until a valid answer locks in. Minor spelling slips and some singular/plural variations on longer words are forgiven.

That loop is easy to learn and hard to play well. The tension is not “do I know anything in this set?” It is “can I find a valid member of the set that is not the one everyone else will type in the first two seconds?”

Six tiers, not one tick

On the official site, every accepted answer lands in one of six rarity tiers:

Tier Points Depth gained What it represents
Plankton 10 +100m The ultra-obvious first instinct
Too Clever 15 +150m A famous “smart” pick that thousands still guess
Schooler 30 +300m Solid mid-pack knowledge
Rare 60 +600m Sharper lateral recall
Deep Cut 85 +850m An abyssal pull almost nobody reaches under 25 seconds
One in a Krillion 100 +1000m Obscure, valid, and maximum depth

Each point is ten metres of depth, so a 100-point answer sinks you 1,000 metres, and a clean seven-prompt run can reach 7,000 metres.

The important design choice is not the metaphor. It is the spacing. A binary quiz only has to decide whether an answer belongs in the set. A rare-answer game also has to separate “everyone typed this,” “a lot of people thought they were being original,” and “almost nobody finds this in 25 seconds.” Without those bands, a player cannot tell a safe common answer from a genuine deep cut, and the prompt stops being a search problem.

The “Too Clever” trap

The 15-point band is easy to underestimate. When a prompt asks for an obscure country or a chemical element, a huge number of players reach for the same well-known “smart” example. It feels rare. It is not. The official site’s point is that those famous lateral picks belong in Too Clever, not in the 100-point trench.

That is useful as a scoring rule and as feedback. It tells the player: originality is not the same thing as the trivia-night favourite. The rarest valid answers are often quieter mid-sized members of the set, not the extreme everyone has already heard is “the obscure one.”

What this does to the 25-second clock

Because a wrong or misspelled guess does not end the round, the clock becomes a budget. You can spend seconds hunting for a deep cut. You can also spend them and leave with nothing. An expired clock scores no depth; even a 10-point Plankton answer still banks +100m.

The official guidance follows from that tradeoff:

  1. Skip the first one or two instincts. If an answer arrived in half a second, it is probably where the crowd is.
  2. Do not assume a famous “clever” pick is a 100-point answer.
  3. If an obscure spelling is rejected twice, lock in a guaranteed valid answer before the timer hits zero.

The game is not asking you to be obscure at any cost. It is asking you to be valid first, and then as rare as the remaining seconds allow.

An optional endurance mode, same ladder

The seven-prompt expedition is the standard shape. The official site also offers 3-Tank Endless Survival: you can descend past 7,000 metres for as long as three oxygen reserves hold. A tank is lost only when a 25-second round expires, or you skip, without a valid answer. A tank is refilled (+1, up to 3) only when you land a 100-point One in a Krillion answer.

That is a different pressure curve from the seven-prompt run, but it uses the same rarity ladder. The 100-point band is not just a high score; in survival it is also how you recover. I am describing the published rules here, not the implementation.

There is also a Pokémon-themed mode at https://krillionunlimited.co/pokemon, and you can play unlimited seven-prompt solo dives with no daily lockout and no account.

A note on independence — and on this article

Krillion Unlimited is independent. It is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by krillion.io.

This article was drafted with AI assistance and checked against the official site’s published rules before being prepared for publication. It does not describe the game’s internal implementation.

If you want to try the scoring ladder rather than read about it, the official game is here: https://krillionunlimited.co/.

title: Why "the agent said so" isn't verification: signed receipts for agent calculations
description:
AI agents state numbers with total confidence: a sum, a percentage, a unit conversion, a date pulled from a document. When something goes wrong, the question is never "was the model smart?" but "can anyone show this was checked?" Today the answer is usually a log line nobody can replay.

Deterministic checks vs a second model

An LLM judging an LLM is fine for tone or summaries, but for arithmetic and quotations it adds a second thing that can be confidently wrong. For claims that have one right answer, recompute them with plain code. For "the contract says 30 days", check that the quoted text, number or date really occurs in the text you supplied.

What a receipt should contain

The claim, the inputs, the rule version, the result, a timestamp, and a signature. With an Ed25519 signature, a third party needs only the public key to confirm that this exact check was run and the result was not edited afterwards. The receipt is evidence of a check, not a guarantee that the underlying data is true.

What I built

AgentVerify is a small open-source (MIT) service and MCP server that does exactly this: https://github.com/Bencoombes23/agentverify-checks. There is a free demo (see DEMO.md in the repo for the shared key; it runs on a free host that sleeps, so allow a minute for the first call).

Honest limits

It's early. No SLA, no payments taken (an optional x402 paywall exists but is testnet-only and off by default), the replay store is in-process, and it only checks text you give it, never fetching URLs. It is run with an AI assistant and I say so up front.

Question for you

If you ship agents that produce numbers, has anyone ever asked you to prove a check happened? What would you need a receipt to prove? Tell me it's useless if it is.
