title: Rust port: 177/177 match, 0.62x slower, 1 crash
description:
Rust port: 177/177 match, 0.62x slower, 1 crash

The leaf port matches 177 out of 177 recorded cases, runs slower than the Python it replaces, and enabling it as shipped crashes the app on launch. The tool knows about two of those three problems and says so in its own output. The third one it does not.

Yesterday I ran fast-anything on a fuzzy dedupe script: 10.06 seconds became 129 milliseconds, 78x faster, 34 out of 34 recorded calls matching. The same author shipped the bigger tool a week earlier — rust-anything, created 2026-11-16, 8,502 stars — and its pitch is the whole app, not the 5%: record what the app does, port it one piece at a time, prove each piece against the recording, and end with a pure Rust binary. I ran it on the exact same code to see what changes when the goal is the whole app instead of one hot function.

The setup

Same app as yesterday: 700 names, near-duplicates with typos, collapse within Levenshtein distance 2. Pure standard library, deliberately naive quadratic loop. Yesterday's clean baseline was 10.06s for dedupe(), with levenshtein called 151,315 times.

rust-anything 3.3.0, installed from npm. Its loop is: analyze -> bridge -> record -> port src/port.rs -> build -> diff -> gate, plus an app track (record / front-door / wire / lift) for moving the whole CLI.

go refuses the entry point

My first try was the one-command path, rust-anything go -- python3 dedupe.py. It ran the workload and then failed: no CPU profile was written: is the workload a node process? The profile step wants the repository root passed explicitly. With go . --lang python -- python3 dedupe.py it profiled fine — dedupe at 99% of the run, levenshtein at 98%, 151,315 calls, same shape as yesterday — and then refused:

error: every export of `dedupe.py` must stay in Python: levenshtein (not hot
in the profiled run; `go` ports one function), typo (not hot in the profiled
run; `go` ports one function), make_names (not hot in the profiled run;
`go` ports one function), dedupe (a command-line entry point: it stays in
Python, and `app front-door` takes the command line over when the whole app
moves)

This is the first real difference from fast-anything. The 5% tool ports whatever is hot, entry point or not. The whole-app tool will not port the function that owns __main__ — that belongs to the app track. So I ran the app track instead.

The front door: a Rust binary that runs Python

app record ran the CLI twice and stored 1 case (no-args), noting the timing line differs between runs and wildcarding it. app front-door scaffolded rust/app, a Rust binary with a clap parser that owns the entry point, and every command still runs the original Python underneath. Build and replay: 1/1 cases passed, fallback rate 100%.

That is the honest starting state of a whole-app migration: a Rust binary that is, for now, a launcher for the Python it will replace. The rest of the flow is supposed to drive the fallback rate to zero, one wired unit at a time.

analyze tripped over the tool's own install directory

One detour worth recording: analyze first reported the repo as TypeScript/JavaScript with 0 units. The cause was my own npm install rust-anything — the package.json and node_modules in the same directory made the language detector pick JS. Moving those out of the repo fixed it: the unit is dedupe.py, 69 lines, readiness 89, PyO3 bridge. The risk list it printed was accurate: string offsets and slicing, dynamic typing (3 places), clock and random numbers (make_names uses random.Random).

bridge ports the leaves, not the loop

bridge created rust/dedupe-rs for levenshtein and typo. dedupe and make_names stay in Python — again, entry points. So the unit to port is the two leaf functions, and the 151,315-call loop stays in Python, crossing into Rust once per call. The bridge has a --batch option for exactly this shape ("runs function over many param values kept in Rust"), which the profile output had hinted at, but the default bridge run does not apply it.

record: 177 cases, 143 of them throws 

Recorded 177 cases (143 threw) in rust/dedupe-rs/cases.jsonl
  levenshtein: 88
  typo: 89

The recorder feeds generated JSON values as arguments. For levenshtein that produces a genuinely interesting set: 34 cases return a value, 54 throw. The values include things like levenshtein(["a", 1], {}) == 2, levenshtein(null, null) == 0, levenshtein("x", []) == 1 — Python's duck typing doing its thing on lists and dicts. The throws are TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len(), KeyError: 0 (dict indexed by int), and friends.

For typo, all 89 cases threw. Every single one. The reason is structural: typo takes a random.Random object, and the recorder can only pass JSON values. All 89 errors are AttributeError: '<type>' object has no attribute 'choice' — dict, list, str, int, NoneType, bool. Not one recorded case exercises what typo actually does, because the input it needs cannot be expressed in the recording format. The tool's own docs suggest --pin-clock for random-dependent functions, but pinning the clock does not conjure a Random object into a JSON case either.

The port: Python-faithful, error for error

I wrote the port by hand (no agent is configured on this box, so go stops at TASK.md — same as yesterday). levenshtein reproduces CPython's semantics over JSON values: True == 1, len() TypeErrors with the exact message, dict KeyError: 0, "not subscriptable" for numbers and None, strings indexed by code point. typo reproduces the only behavior the recording covers: the AttributeError, with the type name filled in from the argument. That is a faithful port of the recording, and it is worth saying plainly what it is not: a port of typo.

$ rust-anything build rust/dedupe-rs
Built .../rust/dedupe-rs/python/dedupe_rs
$ rust-anything diff rust/dedupe-rs
177/177 cases match

fuzz — fresh inputs from a new seed, the check that is supposed to catch what the recording missed — was thin: 1/1 fresh cases match (1 round), and again 1/1 over two rounds with --cases 200 --time 60. One fresh case per round is not much of a net.

bench: the Rust is slower, and the tool says so 

function                  cases orig ns/call Rust ns/call   speedup
levenshtein                  88         1936         3446     0.56x
typo                         89         2349         3408     0.69x

Timed as callers call it, crossing included. Overall 0.62x (geometric mean);
0 of 2 functions at least 1.1x faster.
Do not ship this unit for speed: calling across costs more than the work
these functions do. Port a bigger unit (these functions together with their
callers), so one call does more work.

That is the tool being honest, and it is right — about the recorded cases. On those tiny inputs, mostly garbage, the PyO3 crossing costs more than the work. But the recorded cases are not the real workload. The real workload calls levenshtein 151,315 times on ~15-character names, where Python runs a 225-iteration bytecode loop per call and Rust runs a native one. So I measured the end-to-end run instead, 5 times interleaved, after fixing the crash below:

original (median of 5):        10.21s
Rust levenshtein (median of 5): 2.13s   -> 4.8x faster end to end

Same output both ways — 700 names -> 478 unique, same sample. So the bench (0.56x) and the workload (4.8x) disagree, and both are correct: they measure different inputs. The bench measures the recorded distribution; the workload measures the real one. The lesson is not that the bench lies — it is that a port proved on generated garbage tells you nothing about the calls the app actually makes, in either direction. And 4.8x is a long way from yesterday's 78x, for the reason the tool itself gave: the loop still runs in Python, crossing into Rust 151,315 times. Porting the leaf is worth 4.8x; porting the loop was worth 78x.

enable as shipped crashes the app 

$ python3 dedupe.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "dedupe.py", line 53, in make_names
    name = typo(name, rng)
TypeError: unsupported argument type Random

enable rebinds both levenshtein and typo to the Rust module in dedupe.py. The first thing the app does is make_names(), which calls typo(name, rng) with a real random.Random — and a real Random cannot cross the serde_json::Value bridge. The app dies before it reaches dedupe at all. The 177/177 diff never saw this coming, because the recording could not express the call the app actually makes. The kill switch works — RUST_ANYTHING_UNIT_DEDUPE=original runs the original — but a green diff that ships a crash on the first real run is exactly the failure mode the recording is supposed to prevent.

I narrowed the rebind by hand to levenshtein only. With that, the app runs and produces the same output: 700 names -> 478 unique, same sample — and the 4.8x number above.

gate fails, wire refuses, lift never happens 

FAIL  fmt        run `cargo fmt`      (cargo-fmt is not installed for this toolchain)
FAIL  clippy     (cargo-clippy is not installed for this toolchain)
pass  cargo test / unsafe / lockfile / ported / size / error cases / panics
pass  build / api / behavior  (177/177 recorded cases match)
Gate failed.

Two of the failures are environmental: this box's Rust toolchain has neither rustfmt nor clippy installed, and gate will not pass without them. The third failure mode I met along the way was recording — after I hand-edited dedupe.py to narrow the rebind, the gate noticed the source had changed since it was recorded and demanded a re-record. That check works as designed, and the re-record produced the identical 177 cases.

But wire requires a green gate, so the unit cannot be wired into the front-door binary, the fallback rate stays at 100%, and lift — the pure-Rust binary the whole pitch is about — is unreachable from here. On this box, the whole-app path ends at a Rust launcher that runs Python, with a leaf port that is slower per call and crashes the app if you enable all of it.

The take

fast-anything and rust-anything are the same idea at two scopes, and the same code exposes the difference. Porting the hot function as one unit, with the loop inside it, gave me 78x yesterday. Porting the leaves, with the loop left in Python crossing the boundary 151,315 times, gives me a bench that says 0.62x and a tool that tells me not to ship it for speed. The recording is the load-bearing part of the promise, and on this app it is thinnest exactly where the app is most real: the one function that takes an object the recorder cannot construct, and the one call path the app actually runs first.

That is not a verdict on the tool — the Prettier and json-server ports in its README are real, measured, and much bigger than my 69-line script. It is a verdict on what its proof covers at small scale: 177/177 is a statement about the recording, and the recording is a statement about JSON-shaped inputs. The app's first real call is not JSON-shaped, and that is where it fell over.

Sources

  • rust-anything, https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything — created 2026-11-16, 8,502 stars, v3.3.0, MIT. README results table (Prettier 19x, json-server) quoted from the repo.
  • fast-anything, https://github.com/EL4CTEO/fast-anything — same author, created 2026-11-21. Yesterday's numbers from my own runs: baseline 10.06s, 129ms median end to end, 78x, 34/34 verification calls matched.
  • All rust-anything numbers are my own runs on 2026-11-23: AMD EPYC VM, Python 3.12.3, rustc 1.100.0, rust-anything 3.3.0 via npm. Profile, record, diff, bench, gate, fuzz and enable outputs quoted verbatim from the tool.

title: How a Sales Career at MongoDB Will Set You Apart
description:
A sales career at MongoDB means owning the entire sales cycle, from pipeline generation to close, in a team-based culture where peers share what works, and career advancement follows results. MongoDB sellers say being stretched by challenging projects and coached by leaders who roll up their sleeves and work deals alongside them is exactly what accelerates their growth.

Our sellers often describe MongoDB as “the MIT of sales” and a place where you’ll earn your “PhD in sales.” “MongoDB gives you a very unique opportunity to cover accounts that stretch you, continue to push you, and make you grow in ways that you never thought possible,” says Brett Baker, Strategic Account Director. The people who have built careers in MongoDB sales agree. The work is demanding, and the product is complex, but our sellers say that challenge is also the draw.

At MongoDB, you own the sales cycle, win alongside colleagues who share what they learn, and get promoted when you deliver—all while enabling global enterprises to build and succeed in the AI era. Here’s what sales leaders and account executives around the world say makes selling at MongoDB different.

A culture built on more than hitting your quota

As a workplace, MongoDB is known for high performance and rigorous standards. But the people who work here tend to lead with something else when they talk about what makes the company unique.

"I describe MongoDB sales culture in three words: excellence, teamwork, and recognition," said Charlotte Crété, a sales development manager in Barcelona. "Excellence, because you'll be surrounded by brilliant colleagues and leaders who will push you to become great at what you do. Teamwork, because at MongoDB, I've never seen anyone close a deal ontheir own. And recognition, because we make sure to celebrate each other's wins and contributions."

The importance of teamwork to MongoDB’s sales culture can’t be overstated. The sales motion at MongoDB is a team sport in the truest sense, with everyone from account development representatives, solutions architects, customer success, professional services, legal, and senior leadership all moving together on a deal.

What's equally striking is how openly team members talk about harder moments. Lukas Kowalski, a commercial growth account executive for the DACH region, put it plainly: "Sales is a roller coaster. No, you can't succeed all the time. You will lose some deals. You will have some difficult customer conversations." What matters, he said, is what happens next. "At MongoDB, you have people left and right who went through similar journeys, who have similar challenges, and everybody's here to help you succeed."

Owning the full sales cycle

Selling at MongoDB is not a handoff culture. Account executives own their deals from the first conversation to close, and that full-cycle ownership is something our team views as a genuine differentiator for professional development.

"At MongoDB, you truly own the entire sales cycle, from pipeline generation all the way to closing," said Woojoon Chu, an enterprise account executive in South Korea. "By focusing on working directly with developers and selling real technical value, you build the complete skillset needed for salespeople in the AI era."

Ella To, a senior enterprise account executive in Hong Kong who joined MongoDB after working at Microsoft and Google Cloud, explained the shift: "When I came to MongoDB, I realized that I needed to develop my own ability to incite interest for customers, tell the MongoDB story, and connect our value to the customer's priorities." The result, she said, has been a meaningful transformation. "MongoDB helped me grow from someone who was mainly experienced in cloud selling into a complete enterprise seller."

Peer learning as a daily practice

Formal training is a priority at MongoDB, from structured enablement programs, methodology frameworks, onboarding academies, and dedicated sales leadership development tracks. But the learning culture that our people describe most vividly is the informal kind: the peer-to-peer exchange that happens every day across teams and geographies.

"Whenever someone finds a new solution to a problem or a new way of including AI into our operating rhythm, it will be shared immediately," explained Kowalski. "We are creating our own development sessions within our teams, but also within the broader sales organization."

Navdeep Arora, a regional director for Asia-Pacific, described a culture she called the "teach-back" approach: "You take a concept or something you've learned and teach it back to your peers. It sounds simple, but it's incredibly powerful because when you teach something, you develop a much deeper understanding of it yourself. Experiences like this happen frequently at MongoDB and have helped me evolve beyond being a sales manager into a more strategic and impactful leader.”

Career progression that's real

MongoDB's BDR to CRO program gives our career progression philosophy a name, but what makes it feel real to the people inside it is how concretely it shows up in day-to-day conversations with leadership.

"The BDR to CRO program at MongoDB is a true testament to development. It is a structured framework that is transparent and performance-based, which supports the career aspirations of salespeople moving into multiple levels of leadership," said Arora. "The program also helps people upskill and gear up for opportunities to move between regions or even cross-functional teams, creating endless opportunities for their next career move."

Brett Baker, a strategic account director in the U.S., described how that looks from a rep's seat. "MongoDB is an extremely fast-growing company, which naturally creates a lot of growth opportunities for its employees," he said. "My manager and my VP spent a lot of time with me speaking about the future and identifying areas of opportunity to accomplish my goals and achieve the promotions I was after.”

The moment is now

The market context adds its own layer of motivation. MongoDB sits at the intersection of data modernization and AI adoption—two of the most significant technology shifts of the decade—and the people selling it know it.

"I am 100% sure that MongoDB will be a major winner in both the AI and agentic era," said Kowalski. "We’re not talking about AI alone anymore. We're talking about agents, independent systems that use AI and use your data to really do the work for you."

At MongoDB, our reps aren’t just selling a data platform. They’re sitting with engineering leaders and IT decision-makers at the exact moment that they're deciding on how they build for the next decade. Baker added a seller's perspective on why MongoDB's position in that moment is so strong: "The market opportunity at MongoDB is unmatched. As a seller, there's really no better place to be than at MongoDB in technology."

Sales at MongoDB can be demanding. The standards are high, the product is complex, and the expectations around performance are real. But what comes through most clearly from the people who have built careers here is that the challenge is the draw, not the deterrent. They stay because they’re surrounded by people who take their growth seriously, because they’re given real ownership from early on, and because the market they're operating in keeps getting more interesting.

In the AI era, sellers who understand the data layer will be the ones who shape what comes next for some of the world’s largest enterprises and most cutting-edge startups. For anyone looking for a sales career that builds something lasting, that combination is hard to find anywhere else.

title: Build a Muslim Baby Names CLI and JSON Microservice in Go (stdlib only, cached, 9 languages)
description:
Name pickers are a common feature in Muslim parenting, family-tree and greeting-card apps. In this tutorial we build one in Go, using only the standard library:

  • a CLI that lists Muslim names filtered by gender and by a search term,
  • a disk cache so the data is downloaded at most once a day,
  • a small JSON microservice (GET /names?gender=female&lang=ur) that returns each name's meaning in the requested language, falling back to English,
  • unit tests with httptest, so the tests never touch the network.

The data comes from the public sample JSON of the SunnahSource Islamic Names API.

1. Look at the data 

curl -s https://sunnahsource.org/data/json/islamic-names.json

The response is a small document with an items array. Each item has an Arabic name, an English name, a gender and meanings in 9 languages (en, ur, fr, de, tr, ms, ru, zh-CN, ja):

{
  "title": "Islamic Names",
  "description": "Beautiful Muslim names for boys and girls with meanings",
  "is_free": false,
  "items": [
    {
      "name_ar": "عَلِي",
      "name_en": "Ali",
      "gender": "male",
      "translations": {
        "en": "High, elevated, noble",
        "ur": "بلند، عالی، شریف",
        "de": "Hoch, edel"
      }
    }
  ]
}

(Translations trimmed for space.) The public file is a sample with a handful of names. The full dataset is part of the paid API, see the pricing page. The code below works the same way with both, because the shape is identical.

2. Project setup 

mkdir names && cd names
go mod init names

Everything goes in one main.go. No third-party modules are needed.

3. Types that mirror the JSON 

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const sourceURL = "https://sunnahsource.org/data/json/islamic-names.json"

// Name mirrors one entry in the "items" array.
type Name struct {
    NameAr       string            `json:"name_ar"`
    NameEn       string            `json:"name_en"`
    Gender       string            `json:"gender"`
    Translations map[string]string `json:"translations"`
}

// Dataset mirrors the top-level JSON document.
type Dataset struct {
    Title       string `json:"title"`
    Description string `json:"description"`
    IsFree      bool   `json:"is_free"`
    Items       []Name `json:"items"`
}

translations is a flat map[string]string, so adding a new language on the server needs no code change.

4. Meaning with an English fallback, and filtering 

// Meaning returns the meaning in lang, falling back to English.
func (n Name) Meaning(lang string) string {
    if m, ok := n.Translations[lang]; ok && m != "" {
        return m
    }
    return n.Translations["en"]
}

// Filter returns names matching gender ("" = any) and a case-insensitive
// query against the English name or the meaning in lang.
func Filter(items []Name, gender, query, lang string) []Name {
    q := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(query))
    var out []Name
    for _, n := range items {
        if gender != "" && !strings.EqualFold(n.Gender, gender) {
            continue
        }
        if q != "" &&
            !strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(n.NameEn), q) &&
            !strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(n.Meaning(lang)), q) {
            continue
        }
        out = append(out, n)
    }
    sort.Slice(out, func(i, j int) bool { return out[i].NameEn < out[j].NameEn })
    return out
}

Searching the meaning as well as the name is what makes a name picker useful. A parent can type "noble" or "praised" and get matching names.

5. Download once, then cache on disk 

// Load reads the cache file if it is fresh, otherwise downloads and caches it.
func Load(url, cachePath string, maxAge time.Duration) (*Dataset, error) {
    if st, err := os.Stat(cachePath); err == nil && time.Since(st.ModTime()) < maxAge {
        if b, err := os.ReadFile(cachePath); err == nil {
            var d Dataset
            if json.Unmarshal(b, &d) == nil {
                return &d, nil
            }
        }
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    resp, err := client.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unexpected status %s", resp.Status)
    }
    var d Dataset
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&d); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if b, err := json.Marshal(d); err == nil {
        _ = os.WriteFile(cachePath, b, 0o644)
    }
    return &d, nil
}

Two details matter here. Always set a client Timeout, because Go's default client waits forever. And if the cache file is corrupt, the code just falls through and downloads a fresh copy.

6. The HTTP microservice 

type apiName struct {
    Arabic  string `json:"arabic"`
    English string `json:"english"`
    Gender  string `json:"gender"`
    Meaning string `json:"meaning"`
}

// Handler serves GET /names?gender=female&lang=ur&q=noble
func Handler(d *Dataset) http.HandlerFunc {
    return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        lang := r.URL.Query().Get("lang")
        if lang == "" {
            lang = "en"
        }
        res := []apiName{}
        for _, n := range Filter(d.Items, r.URL.Query().Get("gender"), r.URL.Query().Get("q"), lang) {
            res = append(res, apiName{n.NameAr, n.NameEn, n.Gender, n.Meaning(lang)})
        }
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8")
        w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=3600")
        _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]any{"count": len(res), "lang": lang, "names": res})
    }
}

Starting res as []apiName{} rather than nil means an empty result is encoded as [], not null. Front-end code will thank you.

7. Wire up the CLI 

func main() {
    gender := flag.String("gender", "", "male or female (empty = both)")
    lang := flag.String("lang", "en", "en, ur, fr, de, tr, ms, ru, zh-CN, ja")
    query := flag.String("q", "", "search the name or its meaning")
    serve := flag.String("serve", "", "listen address, e.g. :8080 (starts the HTTP API)")
    flag.Parse()

    d, err := Load(sourceURL, "islamic-names.cache.json", 24*time.Hour)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if *serve != "" {
        http.HandleFunc("/names", Handler(d))
        log.Printf("listening on %s", *serve)
        log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(*serve, nil))
    }
    for _, n := range Filter(d.Items, *gender, *query, *lang) {
        fmt.Printf("%-10s %-8s %-7s %s\n", n.NameEn, n.NameAr, n.Gender, n.Meaning(*lang))
    }
}

8. Run it 

$ go run . -gender female
Aisha      عَائِشَة female  Living, prosperous — wife of Prophet (SAW)
Fatima     فَاطِمَة female  One who abstains — daughter of Prophet (SAW)

$ go run . -lang ur -q yusuf
Yusuf      يُوسُف   male    اللہ بڑھاتا ہے — حضرت یوسف علیہ السلام

And as a service:

$ go run . -serve :8080
$ curl 'localhost:8080/names?gender=male&lang=de'
{"count":3,"lang":"de","names":[{"arabic":"عَلِي","english":"Ali","gender":"male","meaning":"Hoch, edel"},{"arabic":"مُحَمَّد","english":"Muhammad","gender":"male","meaning":"Gepriesener — Name des letzten Propheten"},{"arabic":"يُوسُف","english":"Yusuf","gender":"male","meaning":"Allah mehrt"}]}

(Arabic and Urdu are right-to-left. In a terminal the column alignment can look a little off. In a browser, wrap them in an element with dir="rtl".)

9. Tests without the network

httptest.NewServer gives the loader a fake upstream, so the tests check the cache logic and never call the real API:

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "path/filepath"
    "testing"
    "time"
)

var sample = []Name{
    {NameAr: "عَلِي", NameEn: "Ali", Gender: "male", Translations: map[string]string{"en": "High, elevated, noble", "ur": "بلند، عالی، شریف"}},
    {NameAr: "فَاطِمَة", NameEn: "Fatima", Gender: "female", Translations: map[string]string{"en": "One who abstains"}},
}

func TestFilterQueryMeaning(t *testing.T) {
    if got := Filter(sample, "", "noble", "en"); len(got) != 1 || got[0].NameEn != "Ali" {
        t.Fatalf("got %+v", got)
    }
}

func TestMeaningFallback(t *testing.T) {
    if m := sample[1].Meaning("ur"); m != "One who abstains" {
        t.Fatalf("fallback failed: %q", m)
    }
}

func TestLoadAndCache(t *testing.T) {
    calls := 0
    srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        calls++
        _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(Dataset{Title: "Islamic Names", Items: sample})
    }))
    defer srv.Close()
    cache := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "c.json")
    for i := 0; i < 2; i++ {
        if d, err := Load(srv.URL, cache, time.Hour); err != nil || len(d.Items) != 2 {
            t.Fatalf("load %d: %v", i, err)
        }
    }
    if calls != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 1 network call, got %d", calls)
    }
}

func TestHandler(t *testing.T) {
    rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
    Handler(&Dataset{Items: sample})(rec, httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/names?gender=male&lang=ur", nil))
    var body struct {
        Count int       `json:"count"`
        Names []apiName `json:"names"`
    }
    if err := json.Unmarshal(rec.Body.Bytes(), &body); err != nil || body.Count != 1 || body.Names[0].Meaning != "بلند، عالی، شریف" {
        t.Fatalf("bad body %s", rec.Body.String())
    }
}

$ go test ./...
ok      names   0.006s

10. Going further

  • Add background for well-known names. Many Muslim names are names of prophets (such as Yusuf) or companions (such as Ali). You can show a short biography next to them with the Prophets Stories (Ambiya) API and the Sahaba API.
  • Names of Allah are a different list. If you also want the 99 Names (Asma ul Husna), use the Asma ul Husna API instead of mixing them into a baby-name list.
  • Deploy. The binary is a single static file. CGO_ENABLED=0 go build and copy it to any small VPS or container.

Source and links

  • SunnahSource Islamic Names API: https://sunnahsource.org/apis/islamic-names/
  • All SunnahSource Islamic APIs (Quran, Hadith, Duas, Prayer Times and more): https://sunnahsource.org/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/sunnahsourceofficial-droid/sunnahsource-islamic-api

If you build something with it, share it in the comments.

title: Typed State Machines for React Email Verification
description:
Email verification looks like a small form feature: collect an address, send a code, wait for a message, and let the user continue. In a real product, it is an asynchronous workflow with several ways to get stuck.

The UI are not just waiting for a promise. It is waiting for a message that may arrive late, may be unreadable, or may belong to an older attempt. A typed state machine gives the React layer a small, explicit contract for those situations.

Why email verification needs explicit UI states

The usual implementation starts with three booleans: isSending, isWaiting, and hasError. That works until a user clicks resend during polling, changes the address, or opens a verification link in another tab. Then combinations appear that the product never intended to show, such as a success message beside an expired-code error.

Instead, model the meaningful states:

  • idle: no address has been submitted
  • sending: the request to create a verification attempt is in progress
  • waiting: the attempt exists and the client is waiting for a matching message
  • verified: the server accepted the code or link
  • expired: the attempt lease ended
  • failed: the user can retry after a recoverable error

This rules out accidental combinations. It also makes the copy, disabled buttons, and accessibility announcements easier to review together.

Model the flow as a discriminated union

TypeScript can make invalid rendering paths harder to write. Each state carries only the data that makes sense for it:

type VerificationState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending"; email: string }
  | { kind: "waiting"; email: string; attemptId: string; expiresAt: number }
  | { kind: "verified"; email: string }
  | { kind: "expired"; email: string }
  | { kind: "failed"; email: string; message: string; canRetry: boolean };

The attemptId is important. It prevents a late response from an older request changing the current screen. The expiry timestamp is useful too: the client can show a countdown, but the server must still enforce the actual lease.

I prefer a reducer for transitions because each event is visible in one place. A resend action should create a new attempt, clear the old polling task, and move back through sending; it should not quietly mutate a few unrelated flags.

Keep polling and inbox access behind a boundary

React should not know how a message is found. The component can call a small API such as waitForVerification(attemptId), while the service handles bounded polling, correlation IDs, and cleanup.

For staging and automated checks, an isolated disposable email generator can help inspect the message without mixing it with a personal inbox. It is test data, not proof that a production identity is trustworthy. Give each run a unique recipient and a short expiry.

The service boundary might look like this:

async function waitForVerification(
  attemptId: string,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): Promise<{ code: string }> {
  for (let tryNumber = 0; tryNumber < 12; tryNumber += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/verification/${attemptId}`, { signal });

    if (response.status === 200) return response.json();
    if (response.status === 410) throw new Error("verification expired");
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error("verification lookup failed");

    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1500));
  }

  throw new Error("verification timed out");
}

In production, the server should usually push a completion event or expose a carefully bounded endpoint. The loop is mainly useful as a simple adapter and for test environments. It need a cancellation path: when the address changes or the component unmounts, abort the old attempt.

If your workflow runs in CI, pair the adapter with an AWS deployment drift check so environment differences do not look like random email failures. For browser tests, inbox lease patterns for Cypress retries are a useful reminder that a retry needs a new, identifiable fixture.

Render useful React feedback

Keep the component focused on user decisions. In waiting, show the destination in a privacy-conscious way, offer “use a different address,” and provide a resend action only when the current attempt allows it. Do not expose the full verification token in the DOM or logs.

An aria-live="polite" region can announce “Verification email sent” and later “Code expired, request a new one.” Reserve space for these messages so the form does not jump around. A bit more clear copy usually beats a clever animation here.

People also search for phrases like temp gamil com when they are trying to find a temporary inbox. That typo can be useful in support analytics, but it should never become a label or a reason to weaken validation.

Testing the transitions

Test events and transitions, not just the final happy-path screenshot. At minimum, cover:

  1. A successful send moves from idle to waiting.
  2. A late response from an old attemptId is ignored.
  3. A 410 response renders the expired state and enables a new request.
  4. Aborting the request on unmount does not show an error toast.
  5. A matching code moves to verified, while an unrelated message is rejected.
  6. Keyboard users can reach resend and change-address actions in the right order.

The test don't need a real mailbox for every transition. Inject the verification service and return deterministic results. Reserve a smaller end-to-end suite for checking that the sender, inbox adapter, and application agree on the correlation contract.

Questions developers usually ask

Should the client poll forever?

No. Set a server-enforced expiry and a client timeout. “Try again” is more honest than a spinner that never ends.

Is a disposable temporary email safe for production accounts?

No. Use isolated test fixtures only, and never place recovery credentials or private customer data in them. A disposable inbox is a development tool with a narrow purpose.

Do I need a state machine library?

Not always. A discriminated union and reducer are enough for a compact flow. A library becomes more useful when verification is part of a larger process with parallel tasks, retries, and persisted transitions.

Final takeaway

Email verification becomes easier to ship when the UI treats it as a contract instead of a collection of flags. Define the states, correlate every attempt, bound the wait, and test the transitions that users actually see. The result is more predictable React code, cleaner TypeScript types, and fewer mysterious “the email never arrived” reports.

title: Nodus vs Spheron: which is better for running training?
description:
Nodus is the better way to run a training job you want finished: it lists the NVIDIA H100 at $2.60/hr against $2.65 to $2.98 for on-demand H100s on Spheron, and it restores your checkpoint on a new machine when one is lost. Spheron is the better pick when you want the cheapest reclaimable GPU and are happy to restart runs yourself, or when you want a bare-metal server or AMD hardware to manage by hand.

We build Nodus. Every Spheron fact below links to Spheron's own site or docs, the arithmetic is shown once, and one section covers where Spheron wins.

How do Nodus and Spheron compare at a glance?

They sell different things. Spheron says it "pools capacity from multiple providers and exposes it through a single API and dashboard" (Spheron overview). You pick an offer, get a VM or a bare-metal server, and run your training on it. Nodus takes a command or a training job, picks the machine, checkpoints your state directory and starts a replacement attempt if the machine goes away.

Spheron Nodus
What you launch A spot or dedicated VM, a bare-metal server, a container, or a reserved cluster A Job, TrainingJob, Workspace or Function that Nodus places for you
How prices work Live rates per GPU that follow partner supply Live quotes per machine, frozen when capacity is acquired
H100 listed rate $2.98 on-demand and $2.20 spot on the pricing page; $2.65 dedicated on the H100 page $2.60/hr
Billing Prepaid credits, billed per minute after a 20-minute minimum runtime Prepaid credits; each run shows boot, running and teardown cost
Spot capacity Reclaimed at any time with no warning; on the Spheron ES provider the spot price can change every 15 minutes Opt in per run with --interruptible; urgent checkpoint on a reclaim notice
After a reclaim or failure You redeploy and load your own checkpoint from a volume New attempt with your state directory restored
Coding agents MCP connector for Claude, ChatGPT and Codex CLI MCP server for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor
Multi-node Bare-metal clusters up to 80 x H100 (10 nodes); custom reserved clusters of 8 to 512+ GPUs Beta, up to 8 nodes
Hardware beyond NVIDIA AMD Instinct MI300X, Intel Gaudi2 NVIDIA only on the pricing page

Sources: Spheron pricing, Spheron H100 page, Spheron instance types, Spheron billing, Spheron AI connections, the Nodus pricing page, the Nodus usage and costs and multi-node training docs. Prices checked November 23, 2026.

Is Nodus cheaper than Spheron for an 8 x H100 training run?

On on-demand rates, yes, though the H100 gap is small. We priced the same job, 8 x H100 for 10 hours, which is 80 GPU-hours, from each company's public pages on November 23, 2026.

Option Rate per GPU-hour 80 GPU-hours
Nodus $2.60 $208.00
Spheron dedicated (H100 page) $2.65 $212.00
Spheron on-demand (pricing page) $2.98 $238.40
Spheron spot, no reclaim $2.20 $176.00

Prices checked November 23, 2026: Spheron pricing, Spheron H100 page and the Nodus pricing page. GPU rates only, no storage.


Nodus is 13% cheaper than Spheron's pricing-page on-demand rate; Spheron spot is cheapest if nothing is reclaimed.

Two Spheron numbers appear because Spheron's rates are live and its pages showed both on the same day. Its H100 page says the rates "move with partner supply". Nodus quotes are live too, so run nodus run --dry-run for your exact job instead of trusting any table, including this one.

The gap is wider on other cards. Spheron's pricing page lists the A100 80 GB at $1.43, the H200 at $4.80 and the L40S at $0.96 per GPU-hour on demand. The Nodus pricing page lists them at $1.09/hr, $3.593/hr and $0.793/hr. The B200 is the outlier: $11.06 on demand on Spheron against $5.50/hr on Nodus, though Spheron's B200 spot rate is $5.22.


On every card in this chart, the Nodus rate is lower than Spheron's on-demand rate.

When does Spheron spot stop being the cheaper option?

After about 1.8 hours of lost work on that run. Spheron spot instances "can be interrupted at any time" and are reclaimed "with no warning", so you lose everything since the last checkpoint your script wrote (Spheron instance types). A reclaim stops billing, so you pay for the hours the machine ran, and then pay again to redo the lost work.

Each lost hour on 8 x H100 spot costs 8 x $2.20 = $17.60 to redo. The spot run starts $32.00 below Nodus ($208.00 minus $176.00), and $32.00 / $17.60 = 1.82 hours. Here is how the total moves:

  • No lost work: $176.00
  • 1 hour lost: $176.00 + $17.60 = $193.60
  • 2 hours lost: $176.00 + $35.20 = $211.20
  • 3 hours lost: $176.00 + $52.80 = $228.80


Two lost hours of work make the spot run more expensive than the Nodus run.

That count is the floor, not the full bill. On Spheron ES the spot price itself can change as often as every 15 minutes and is capped at the dedicated price for the same machine, so $2.20 is the price at launch, not a promise. And every reclaim costs elapsed time while you notice, redeploy and reload data.

If you checkpoint every 30 minutes, two reclaims cost at most an hour of work and spot still wins. If your script saves once an hour, two badly timed reclaims can cost up to 2 hours and erase the saving.

Our rule: use Spheron spot for runs where your own restart script is already tested. Use Nodus when you want the restart handled and a cost estimate before you launch.

What happens to a training run when the machine is lost?

On Spheron, recovery is yours to build. Spheron's docs tell you to save checkpoints to a persistent volume and resume from them after a reclaim, with a torch.save example writing to /checkpoints (Spheron instance types). You then deploy a new instance, mount the volume and start your script again. Bare-metal and reserved instances can't be stopped or restarted from the dashboard at all (Spheron instance lifecycle).

On Nodus, your script writes its state to /nodus/state and loads it on start. When capacity gives notice that it is about to be reclaimed, Nodus asks your program for an urgent checkpoint and prepares a replacement machine at the same time. A machine that stops sending heartbeats gets a replacement prepared after 20 seconds and, on shared capacity, is declared lost after 60. The new attempt starts with your state directory restored, so a checkpointed run loses at most the work since its last committed checkpoint (attempts and recovery).

Neither platform resumes your training loop for you. Your program still has to read its last checkpoint when it starts. Our post on how to resume training after a spot preemption has the code.

What do you pay when a GPU sits idle?

On Spheron, a running instance bills until you stop or terminate it, after a 20-minute minimum runtime that applies even to a 5-minute job (Spheron pricing). Spheron gives you timers to limit the damage: stop an instance after 0.5 to 720 hours of running, or terminate it at a set time. A stop-when-idle timer exists too, but it needs GPU usage readings that only Agent GPU Sandbox instances report. A stopped instance still bills its disk at the provider's stopped rate (Spheron instance lifecycle).

On Nodus, a Job ends when your command exits. Nodus keeps the capacity warm for 60 seconds in case you launch again, and --no-warm releases it at once. --max-cost stops the run at a dollar cap you set (nodus run reference).

Spheron's timers are a sensible fix, but you have to set one on every instance. On Nodus, stopping when the work is done is the default.

Can you connect a Spheron account to Nodus?

No. Nodus can run work in some cloud accounts you already have, such as AWS, GCP, Azure and a list of API-key providers, but Spheron is not one of them (connect your cloud accounts). If you use both, you keep two accounts with separate credit balances.

Where is Spheron the better choice?

Pick Spheron in these cases:

  • You want the lowest price and handle restarts yourself. Spheron spot H100s are $2.20 per GPU-hour against $2.60/hr on Nodus, and B200 spot is $5.22 against $5.50/hr (Spheron pricing).
  • You need AMD or Intel hardware. Spheron offers AMD Instinct MI300X at $3.59 per GPU-hour on demand (Spheron pricing) and Intel Gaudi2 through one of its providers (Spheron instance types). The Nodus pricing page lists only NVIDIA GPUs.
  • You want bare metal. Spheron's Dedicated Bare Metal offers give you the whole server with no hypervisor, with NVLink or NVSwitch on SXM offers, and dedicated instances carry a 99.95% SLA (Spheron instance types).
  • You need a large InfiniBand cluster now. Spheron's H100 page lists bare-metal clusters of up to 80 x H100 across 10 nodes with 400 Gb/s InfiniBand, and Spheron sources custom reserved clusters of 8 to 512+ GPUs (Spheron H100 page, reserved GPUs). Multi-node training on Nodus is in Beta with a ceiling of 8 nodes, and public traffic between nodes is not encrypted in the Beta.
  • You want to pay in stablecoins, or keep credit indefinitely. Spheron takes USDC, and its credits never expire (Spheron billing).

How do you move a training script from Spheron to Nodus?

If your script already saves to a Spheron volume, change only the path. Keep /checkpoints as the fallback so the same script runs on both:

import os

# On Nodus this is /nodus/state; on Spheron, your mounted volume
STATE_DIR = os.environ.get("NODUS_STATE_DIR", "/checkpoints")

Then install the CLI, sign in, check the estimate and launch with a cap a little above it:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login
nodus run --dry-run --gpu H100:8 --expected-duration 10h -- torchrun --nproc_per_node 8 train.py
nodus run --gpu H100:8 --checkpoint /nodus/state --max-cost 230 -d -- torchrun --nproc_per_node 8 train.py

Add --interruptible to let Nodus use interruptible capacity for the same run, and check the dry-run estimate before you launch. If you are weighing other options too, our RunPod alternatives guide compares more platforms, and which GPU platforms checkpoint and resume training for you goes deeper on recovery.

FAQ

Is Spheron spot capacity cheaper than dedicated?

Spheron says spot is typically 30 to 60% cheaper than dedicated (Spheron instance types). On Spheron ES you can set a max price, and the instance stops automatically if the live spot price climbs above it, though that does not stop a reclaim.

Does a stopped Spheron instance keep its GPU?

Not always. Some Spheron providers release the hardware while an instance is stopped, so a start can be refused when that machine type is sold out (Spheron instance lifecycle). Nothing is lost when that happens; you try again when stock returns.

Does Nodus offer managed fine-tuning as well as raw jobs?

Yes, in Beta. Nodus TrainingJobs run managed runtimes for SFT with full, LoRA or QLoRA training, DPO, GRPO, distillation and continued pretraining, and a dry run prices the job before anything runs.

Is there a free tier on either platform?

Neither lists one. Spheron needs a minimum deposit of $15 by card (Spheron billing), and the public Nodus starter credit has ended, so new Nodus accounts add prepaid credit or use an approved promotional offer (Nodus credits).

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: How I built a SQL injection scanner for Java using ASTs (as a sophomore)
description:
I'm a CS sophomore at George Mason. This semester I wanted to understand how tools like CodeQL actually find bugs, so I built a small version myself. It's a GitHub Action that scans Java code for SQL injection and hardcoded secrets and marks the exact line on your pull request.

Here's what I learned building it.

Why regex isn't enough

My first idea was to just search for strings like "SELECT " +. That breaks fast. The SQL might be built in a variable three lines up, or split across a StringBuilder. Regex only sees text. It doesn't know what the code means.

What an AST is

An AST (abstract syntax tree) is the code turned into a tree of what it actually does: this is a method call, this is a string, this is a variable being added to a string. I used JavaParser to turn each Java file into a tree, then wrote "visitor" rules that walk the tree.

For SQL injection, the rule looks for a database call like executeQuery(...) where the query was built by gluing user input onto a string, instead of using a PreparedStatement with ? placeholders.

The hard part: false alarms

Finding secrets sounds easy: look for things like password = "...". But real code is full of fake ones, like test values, placeholders and example configs. My first version flagged way too much.

So I ran it on 31 open source projects (27,552 files) and went through the results by hand. I added rules to skip test folders, obvious placeholders and so on. False alarms on secrets went from 156 to 27, about 83% fewer, and every real secret in that survey was still caught.

That was the most useful part of the project. Making a scanner that finds stuff is easy. Making one people won't mute is hard.

Suggesting fixes with a local LLM

There's an optional step that sends a finding to a local model through Ollama to suggest a fix. I don't trust the output blindly. The fix gets parsed again to make sure it's valid Java before it's shown. There are 57 JUnit tests covering the rules.

Try it

It takes about 2 minutes. Create .github/workflows/security-scan.yml in your repo:

name: Security scan
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: noorhusaan302-png/ast-security-reviewer@v1.1.0

Then open the Actions tab. Any finding shows the file, the line and the problem.

I know CodeQL and Semgrep are way more complete. This was a learning project, but I'd love to make it useful for student and small projects. If you try it and hit a false positive, please open an issue.

title: Building Better Web Experiences with React: From Components to Full-Stack Integration
description:
Modern web applications require more than attractive designs. They need to be interactive, responsive, maintainable, and capable of communicating with backend services. React.js has become a popular choice for frontend development because it helps developers build dynamic user interfaces through a component-based approach.

As part of my software development internship at Valentius Kryptix, I worked on improving an existing portfolio web application by transitioning its frontend towards React. This experience helped me understand how frontend development works in practical projects and how individual technologies come together to create a complete web application.

Understanding React and Component-Based Development

React is a JavaScript library used to develop user interfaces. Its biggest advantage is component-based architecture. Instead of creating an entire website in one large file, developers can divide it into smaller, independent components.

For example, a portfolio application can contain separate components for navigation, project cards, login forms, dashboards, and project details. These components can be reused across multiple pages, reducing code duplication and making maintenance easier.

React also provides hooks such as useState and useEffect to manage application data and handle side effects. These features make it easier to build interfaces that respond to user interactions and changing information.

Technologies Behind a React Frontend

Building a functional frontend involves multiple technologies working together. React.js handles the user interface, while Vite provides a fast development environment. HTML and CSS define the structure and appearance, and JavaScript manages application logic.

React Router DOM helps implement navigation between pages without unnecessary full-page reloads. On the backend, Node.js and Express.js can provide APIs, while MongoDB stores application data.

Understanding how these technologies communicate is important for developing full-stack applications.

Connecting Frontend with Backend

A modern frontend should display real information rather than relying entirely on static content. API integration makes this possible.

For example, when a user opens a particular project page, React Router can extract its project ID using useParams. The frontend can then send a request to the backend and display the corresponding project information.

During development, handling loading indicators, errors, and successful responses is equally important. These details improve usability and make applications more reliable.

Challenges and Learning Outcomes

Working on an existing project introduced practical challenges, including organizing folders, correcting component import paths, implementing navigation, and connecting frontend components with backend APIs.

Debugging these issues helped me understand the importance of reading terminal errors, checking browser console messages, and testing API responses.

The experience strengthened my understanding of reusable components, state management, routing, asynchronous JavaScript, and frontend-backend communication.

Conclusion

React frontend development is not simply about creating visually appealing pages. It involves structuring applications, managing data, implementing navigation, integrating APIs, and providing a smooth user experience.

This internship project has helped me connect theoretical knowledge with practical development. It has also encouraged me to explore more advanced React concepts and continue improving my full-stack development skills.

Read the full article: https://valentiuskryptix.com/how-to-build-a-react-frontend-my-development-journey/

Author: Sonali Shukla

title: How to Use the Same Component on Multiple Websites (and Update It Once, Everywhere)
description:
Copies drift, npm packages make every site rebuild, and a hosted script can break the page. Component publishing keeps one versioned, isolated copy and delivers it to every site with one snippet.

There are four common ways to use one component on several websites: write a native Web Component, share an npm package (or a monorepo), embed an iframe, or load a hosted script.

If every site is built from the same codebase, by the same team, on the same framework, use a package or a monorepo. If the component can live in a fixed box, an iframe is enough. If the sites run on different stacks and the component has to be part of the page, you need a hosted script, which is safe only with three things in place: isolation, versions and a way back. A hosted script with all three is called component publishing, and that is what Taggor does.

What are the four ways, and where does each one fit?

1. A native Web Component, written by hand

How it works. You write a custom element with the browser's own APIs, put it in a .js file and load that file on each site.

Where it fits. A small element with no dependencies, on sites where you control the hosting.

Where it hurts. A Web Component is a format, not a delivery system. Where the file lives, how a new version reaches each site and how you go back are yours to solve. Copy the file into each project, and the original problem is back.

2. A shared npm package or a monorepo

How it works. The component lives in a package. Each site installs it, imports it and builds it into its own bundle.

Where it fits. One framework, one team, sites that have a build step. You get types, tests and code review. In this case it is the right answer.

Where it hurts. You publish the package, then every site bumps the version, rebuilds and deploys. Five sites are five deploys, and a site that skips one drifts. A WordPress theme has no npm install at all.

3. An iframe

How it works. You host the component as a small page of its own, and each site embeds that page with an <iframe> tag.

Where it fits. A self-contained widget that can live in a fixed box: a map, a video player, a booking calendar. Styles do not cross the frame in either direction, and one change to the hosted page reaches every site.

Where it hurts. The widget is a separate document. It does not grow with its content unless you write messaging code between the frame and the page, and it does not inherit the page's fonts and colors. An update overwrites the hosted page, with no versions and no way back unless you build them.

4. A hosted script (a remote embed)

How it works. The component is served from one address. Each site carries a script tag and the component's tag, and the component renders inside the page itself.

Where it fits. Sites on different stacks, or sites you cannot rebuild, when the component has to look and behave like part of the page. A single change reaches every site without a deploy on each.

Where it hurts. Reaching every site at once is also the risk, and the section after the diagram explains why. It is also the approach Taggor makes safe.

Why can a hosted script break the page?

Styles collide. The page's CSS reaches into your component, and your component's CSS leaks out into the page.

One error spreads. A script that throws can take other things on the page down with it, and a bad update does that on every site at once.

There is no way back. Say you overwrite widget.js. The old file is gone, and "undo" means fixing forward under pressure.

What is component publishing?

Component publishing is building a piece of a website as its own isolated, versioned unit and delivering it to any site with one snippet.

Here is how Taggor answers the three problems:

  • Isolation. Each component is mounted in a Shadow DOM inside the page, so styles stay on their own side, and an error boundary wraps it. What you write inside the component's tag is fallback content: the visitor sees it until the component loads, or permanently if it cannot load.
  • Versions. Every publish creates a version, and a version's code is immutable.
  • A way back. Sites do not point at a version. They follow a channel, Staging or Production, and a channel points at a version. Going back is moving the pointer.

The snippet is one async script tag per site. It loads a small loader that fetches only the components that site uses. The loader sets no cookies and uses no browser storage.

Taggor also covers the work around the script:

  • Checks before anything goes out. Every publish passes gates for types, size and security, and a file that looks like a secret stops the upload.
  • Your source is kept. Every publish stores the component's source, and npx taggor pull brings it back on any computer.
  • Forms have somewhere to go. A component can declare a collection, and Taggor stores what visitors submit, with anti-spam and export. The data is yours.
  • Your agent can write it. The docs have quickstarts for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor that publish a first component from one prompt.

What does it look like in practice?

The example is a signup form, signup-inline. The finished version in the picture comes from Taggor's own showcase: an email field and a button in one pill, storing each signup in a subscribers collection. The steps below use the starter that init generates, so you can follow them exactly on a new account and put your own form in later.

Sign in, create the project, preview the component and run the checks:

npx taggor login
npx taggor init --component signup-inline
cd <the folder init printed>
npm install
npx taggor dev
npx taggor check

init creates the project in ~/.taggor/projects/<workspace>/ and prints the path. The starter is one defineTaggorComponent call in components/signup-inline/src/index.tsx, with a single prop, headline. That file is where your form goes. dev serves it on a deliberately hostile test page with aggressive CSS, so collisions show up on your machine, not on a client's site. check runs the publication gates.

Create a test site and publish to it:

npx taggor sites create --name "Test site" --domain <test-hostname> --environment staging
npx taggor publish --site <site key>

sites create prints the site key and the snippet, and npx taggor sites snippet <site key> prints the snippet again whenever you need it. publish builds the component remotely, creates version 1.0.0, moves the Staging channel to it and attaches the component to the site. Paste the snippet once into the page, then write the component's tag where the form should appear:

<script async src="https://cdn.taggorcdn.com/s/<site-key>.js"></script>

<signup-inline headline="Join the list">
  <a href="mailto:hello@example.com">Write to us to join the list</a>
</signup-inline>

The link inside the component's tag is the fallback: with the CDN blocked, it is what stays on the page. The showcase form takes label in place of headline.

A client's live site is a Production site. Create it, attach the component, and paste that site's own snippet and the same component tag into its page. Then move Production to the version you just checked:

npx taggor sites create --name "Client A" --domain <client-a-hostname> --environment production
npx taggor attach signup-inline --site <site key>
npx taggor promote signup-inline --to production

Every further client is the first two commands again: per the docs, all Production sites show the version the Production channel points to. How many sites a workspace can have depends on its plan. On Free, sites create is refused above the plan's site limit; the pricing page has the numbers. The docs have platform guides for WordPress, Shopify, Webflow, Wix, Framer, Squarespace and more.

Update once, change everywhere

Now change the component and publish again:

npx taggor publish
npx taggor promote signup-inline --to production

publish creates a new version (1.0.1 in our run) and moves the Staging channel, so the test site shows it first while Production stays on 1.0.0. promote moves the Production channel, and every Production site follows. No page was edited and no site was rebuilt. The CLI says sites pick up the change within about 60 seconds; the docs allow up to about two minutes, because the loader is cached for a short time.

If the new version is wrong:

npx taggor rollback signup-inline --channel production
npx taggor versions signup-inline

rollback points the Production channel back to 1.0.0, on every Production site at once. versions lists each version and the channels that point to it.

When should you not use this?

  • One codebase, one framework, one team. A package or a monorepo does the job inside the tools you already have.
  • A fixed box is enough. For a widget that does not have to blend into the page, an iframe is simpler.
  • You need a different version on each Production site. In Taggor, two Production sites show the same version of a component. To show different versions, publish the component under another name.
  • You want to keep your existing framework components as they are. A Taggor component is written with the Taggor SDK and renders a Preact view, so existing ones have to be ported.

The short version

Copies drift, a package costs one deploy per site, and an iframe keeps the component in a box. A hosted script changes every site at once, so it needs isolation, versions and a way back.

Taggor gives you those three, plus the checks, the hosting and the form data, behind one snippet per site. If your sites are on different stacks, Taggor takes about ten minutes to try: the CLI quickstart goes from signing in to a component on a page of your own. Start at taggor.dev.

title: Compare intrinsic and rendered image widths when debugging layout
description:
Start with two numbers when a photo preview looks blurry. After the image loads, read its naturalWidth and its getBoundingClientRect().width. The first is the intrinsic width in CSS pixels. The second is the width of the rendered box. Use an image with no border or transform for this check.

If the intrinsic width is 400 CSS pixels and the box is 600 CSS pixels wide, look for the layout rule that widens the preview. For an image with responsive sources, check currentSrc as well. It shows which resource the browser selected.

Put both widths and the viewport size in the bug report. That gives the next person enough information to reproduce the same layout.

description:
Evaluator-Optimizer with Spring AI: One Model Writes, Another Critiques

Anyone who writes for a living knows the rhythm of revision. You draft something, reread it with fresh eyes, notice what is weak, and rewrite. The second draft is almost always better than the first, and the reason is not talent. It is the separation between producing a text and judging it. When the same mind does both at once, it tends to accept its own first answer.

The evaluator-optimizer pattern applies that rhythm to LLM systems. One model generates a solution. A second evaluation step judges it against explicit criteria and returns feedback. If the solution does not pass, the feedback goes back to the generator, and the loop continues until the evaluator accepts the result. Anthropic describes this workflow in its research on building effective agents, and the sample in the spring-ai-examples repository implements it with Spring AI.

This article walks through that sample: how the loop is built, what the prompts ask each model to do, and where the code needs guardrails before it is safe to run unattended. Some of those guardrails are missing from the sample, and I point them out, because the loop as written has no stopping limit.

Where the pattern fits

Anthropic's taxonomy separates workflows, where code decides the control flow, from agents, where the model decides its next action. Evaluator-optimizer is a workflow. The loop structure is fixed: generate, evaluate, and either return or retry. What changes from run to run is the content, and how many times the loop turns.

The pattern earns its cost when three conditions hold. First, you have criteria for what a good answer looks like, and you can state them in a prompt. Second, a critique can make the next attempt measurably better. Third, the first attempt is often close but not quite right. Translation with nuance, code that must meet a specification, and drafts that must follow a style guide all fit that profile. A simple factual question does not, because there is nothing for a critic to improve.

It is also a different shape from the other patterns in this series. Parallelization splits independent work and merges it. Routing picks one specialist. Orchestrator-workers plans subtasks at runtime. Evaluator-optimizer repeats the same work with feedback, which makes it the only one of the five that revisits its own output.

The sample task

The sample asks the model to implement a stack in Java with three operations: push, pop, and getMin, where all operations must run in O(1) time. The task also sets two style rules: inner fields must be private, and any use of a field must be prefixed with this..

The task is small, but it has the properties that make the pattern interesting. The O(1) requirement is easy to violate by accident: a naive getMin that scans the stack is correct but too slow. The style rules are easy to forget on a second draft. A critic that checks both is more useful than one that only checks that the code compiles.

The records

The pattern is described by three records in EvaluatorOptimizer:

public static record Generation(String thoughts, String response) {
}

public static record EvaluationResponse(Evaluation evaluation, String feedback) {

    public enum Evaluation {
        PASS, NEEDS_IMPROVEMENT, FAIL
    }
}

public static record RefinedResponse(String solution, List<Generation> chainOfThought) {
}

Generation is what the generator returns: a short statement of its approach and the proposed solution. EvaluationResponse is what the evaluator returns: a verdict from a fixed set of three values, and feedback in prose. RefinedResponse is what the caller receives: the final solution and the full history of generations, so you can see how the solution evolved.

The enum matters more than it looks. Because the verdict is a closed set, the code can branch on it. The loop in this sample only stops on PASS. NEEDS_IMPROVEMENT and FAIL both send the work back for another round, which is a reasonable choice for a demo but one you should revisit in production, since a FAIL often means the approach itself is wrong, not that it needs polishing.

The generator prompt

The generator prompt is unusual because it is almost entirely about format. Before it describes the task, it asks for a single line of valid JSON, with every newline and quote escaped:

Your response must be a SINGLE LINE of valid JSON with NO LINE BREAKS except those explicitly escaped with \n.
{"thoughts":"Brief description here","response":"public class Example {\n    // Code here\n}"}

This is a practical lesson. Code contains quotes, backslashes, and line breaks, and asking a model to put it inside a JSON string is a reliable source of malformed output. The prompt tries to prevent that with rules and an example. The rules help, but they are not a guarantee. The sample depends on Spring AI's structured output to parse the result, so a malformed response fails the whole run. The fix is not a better prompt alone. It is a retry on parse failure, which the sample does not have.

The generator prompt also tells the model to reflect on feedback from earlier rounds. That instruction is what turns a single call into a refinement step. Without it, each round would be a fresh attempt that ignores what went wrong before.

The evaluator prompt

The evaluator prompt is shorter, and it sets the criteria explicitly:

Evaluate this code implementation for correctness, time complexity, and best practices.
Ensure the code have proper javadoc documentation.
Respond with EXACTLY this JSON format on a single line:
{"evaluation":"PASS, NEEDS_IMPROVEMENT, or FAIL", "feedback":"Your feedback here"}
Use "PASS" only if all criteria are met with no improvements needed.

The criteria are concrete: correctness, time complexity, best practices, and Javadoc. A vague instruction such as "make sure it's good" gives the critic nothing to check, and its feedback becomes generic. The line "Use PASS only if all criteria are met" pushes the evaluator toward strictness, which matters because a lenient critic ends the loop too early.

This prompt is written for code. Change the criteria and you change the pattern's application. For a translation, the criteria would be fidelity, register, and idiom. For a summary, they would be coverage and length. The structure of the loop does not change; the evaluator's checklist does.

The loop

The core of the pattern is a short recursive method:

private RefinedResponse loop(String task, String context, List<String> memory,
        List<Generation> chainOfThought) {

    Generation generation = generate(task, context);
    memory.add(generation.response());
    chainOfThought.add(generation);

    EvaluationResponse evaluationResponse = evalute(generation.response(), task);

    if (evaluationResponse.evaluation().equals(EvaluationResponse.Evaluation.PASS)) {
        return new RefinedResponse(generation.response(), chainOfThought);
    }

    StringBuilder newContext = new StringBuilder();
    newContext.append("Previous attempts:");
    for (String m : memory) {
        newContext.append("\n- ").append(m);
    }
    newContext.append("\nFeedback: ").append(evaluationResponse.feedback());

    return loop(task, newContext.toString(), memory, chainOfThought);
}

Read it step by step. The generator produces a solution, which is recorded in memory and chainOfThought. The evaluator judges it. If the verdict is PASS, the method returns. Otherwise it builds a new context that lists every previous attempt and the latest feedback, and calls itself with that context.

The design choice to keep every previous attempt in the context is worth thinking about. It lets the generator see what it already tried, which helps it avoid repeating a mistake. It also means the prompt grows on every round. A third attempt carries two previous solutions and two rounds of feedback. For code, that growth is manageable. For a long document, it can become expensive quickly.

The missing stopping rule

This is the most important gap in the sample, and I would not run it without fixing it. The loop has no iteration limit. It only stops when the evaluator returns PASS. If the evaluator never passes the solution, because the criteria are too strict, or the generator cannot satisfy them, or the evaluator keeps finding something new to criticize, the recursion never ends. The most likely outcome is either an unbounded number of model calls or a StackOverflowError when the recursion gets deep enough.

A fix is simple. Pass a round counter, and stop after a fixed number of rounds:

private static final int MAX_ROUNDS = 4;

public RefinedResponse loop(String task) {
    List<String> memory = new ArrayList<>();
    List<Generation> chainOfThought = new ArrayList<>();
    String context = "";

    for (int round = 1; round <= MAX_ROUNDS; round++) {
        Generation generation = generate(task, context);
        memory.add(generation.response());
        chainOfThought.add(generation);

        EvaluationResponse evaluation = evalute(generation.response(), task);
        if (evaluation.evaluation() == EvaluationResponse.Evaluation.PASS) {
            return new RefinedResponse(generation.response(), chainOfThought);
        }
        context = buildContext(memory, evaluation.feedback());
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException("No passing solution after " + MAX_ROUNDS + " rounds");
}

A loop also makes the control flow easier to read and easier to test than recursion. Whether you return the best attempt so far or throw an error when the budget runs out is a product decision. The important part is that the decision exists.

Other gaps

Three more issues are worth knowing about before you build on the sample.

The generator and the evaluator use the same ChatClient, so they are the same model. A model judging its own output shares its blind spots, and it may approve a solution it would have rejected from a different viewpoint. For high-stakes work, use a different model or a different prompt persona for the evaluator, and test whether the critic catches what the generator misses.

The FAIL verdict is treated like NEEDS_IMPROVEMENT. The evaluator is asked to say FAIL, but the code never uses that signal. In practice, FAIL should mean the approach is unsalvageable: stop, or switch strategy, instead of asking for polish.

The sample has no protection against a parse failure. Both entity(Generation.class) and entity(EvaluationResponse.class) throw if the model returns malformed JSON. Add a retry for those calls, separate from the refinement loop, so one bad response does not end the run.

The sample prints every generation and every evaluation to standard output. That is useful while you learn the loop and noisy in production. Replace the prints with a logger that records the round number, the verdict, and the length of the feedback. Log the full code only in a debug mode.

Testing the loop

The loop is straightforward to test, because EvaluatorOptimizer takes a ChatClient in its constructor. Use a stub client that returns a sequence of canned generations and evaluations. A good test set covers four cases:

  • The first generation passes, so the loop returns after one round.
  • The first evaluation fails and the second passes, so the final solution is the second generation and the chain of thought has two entries.
  • The evaluator never passes, so the loop stops at the round limit and does not recurse forever.
  • The evaluator returns malformed JSON, so the retry logic is exercised.

Testing the prompts is harder, and it is where most of the quality comes from. Keep a small set of tasks with clear acceptance criteria. Run the loop on each task, read the feedback the evaluator gives, and check whether the feedback is specific enough to act on. If the feedback is vague, tighten the evaluator's criteria before changing anything else.

When to choose this pattern

I use three questions. Can I write down what a good result looks like, in terms a critic can check? If not, the evaluator will be guessing. Does a second pass measurably improve the result? If the first answer is usually good enough, the extra calls are waste. Can I afford several rounds of latency and tokens, and can I bound them? If the answer to the last question is no, use a single well-written prompt and a cheaper check.

The pattern is also a good place to add a human. The evaluator can flag a solution for review when it reaches the round limit, instead of failing silently. That combines automated refinement with a person's judgment on the cases the loop cannot settle.

Running the sample

To run the sample you need Java 17 or later and a configured model. The project includes properties for OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama. The sample configures gpt-4o for OpenAI, so set that key, or change the properties to the provider you use. Start the application with the Maven wrapper. The console shows each generation and each evaluation, and the final output prints the solution and the chain of thought.

Watch the first few rounds closely. You will see the evaluator's feedback become more specific as the generator fixes earlier problems, and you will also see the prompt size grow. Both observations are the pattern working as intended, and both are the reason the round limit matters.

Key takeaways

  • Evaluator-optimizer separates generating from judging, and loops feedback back into the generator until the evaluator accepts the result.
  • The pattern is worth its cost when criteria are explicit, a critique measurably improves the output, and the first attempt is often close.
  • The sample's loop has no stopping limit, so an evaluator that never passes can run forever. Add a round budget before you use it.
  • Use a closed set of verdicts, and decide what FAIL means in your system instead of treating it like a polish request.
  • Add retries for malformed structured output, and consider a different model for the evaluator when the stakes are high.

The full sample is in the spring-ai-examples repository under agentic-patterns/evaluator-optimizer. The pattern is described in Anthropic's research on building effective agents, alongside the other workflows covered in this series.
