title: Ambient Mode – From Color Scheme to a Living Interface
description:
Originally published with interactive examples at lukiluki.me.

You open the same website at midday and late in the evening. The text stays familiar, but the light changes, the sky grows calmer and summer greens become winter outlines. Can an interface feel alive without making you learn new controls on every visit?

Ambient Mode adds atmosphere to light and dark reading colors: light, gradients, time of day or seasons change the background while content and controls stay dependable. This can give a website character and express personal preferences. Separate design layers, respect for system preferences and deliberate user control are essential. An attractive effect alone proves neither improved usability nor lower energy consumption.

Merksatz (Design principle):
Reading colors provide orientation, atmosphere sets the mood, and users decide how much change they want.

What changes between color scheme and atmosphere?

Dark and light modes first define which surfaces and text colors are readable together. Atmosphere can go further by borrowing light from content, representing a time of day or adding seasonal accents. Here, “Ambient Mode” is a design term, rather than the name of a single web standard.

A concrete product example is YouTube's Ambient Mode: video colors gently spread into the surrounding background. The effect complements the dark color scheme. A broader pattern follows: content or context supplies the mood, while the interface retains its purpose.

Three layers are useful for a digital garden:

  1. Reading: Text, reading surfaces, links and focus indicators need tested light and dark variants.
  2. Atmosphere: Sky, glow and landscape change; they convey no essential information.
  3. Meaning: Categories keep their colors, whether it is autumn or nighttime.

Colors and spacing are stored as design tokens (Named design values, such as text color, background, spacing or category accent, shared by components.). A warm evening sky can sit behind a clearly recognizable pink design tile. The season determines the surroundings; the category explains the content.

Who decides: the system, the clock or the person?

The system preference is a good starting point because people may already have chosen reading colors in their operating system or browser. The CSS query prefers-color-scheme exposes that preference. It says nothing about actual room lighting or the local position of the sun.

Mode What controls the interface? Suitable for Limitation
System The light or dark browser/OS scheme; the season follows the calendar. A respectful default without an additional decision. The system does not provide a time-of-day atmosphere.
Auto Local time and calendar determine reading colors and atmosphere. A page whose mood follows the day. Fixed times are not measured sunrise and sunset times.
Manual A chosen time and season determine the appearance. A personal mood independent of the actual date. This is a deliberate departure from the system preference.

Here in the garden, the page starts with System. Only Auto or Manual takes over control. Auto uses simple day boundaries of 06:30 and 18:30; the four seasons follow Northern Hemisphere meteorological months. This is a transparent design rule, rather than a location or weather sensor. The automatic season may therefore be unsuitable for visitors in the Southern Hemisphere.

Try Manual in the header, or Menu → Ambience on a phone: move the time from midday to night and switch from summer to winter. Sky, light and vegetation respond; navigation and categories stay familiar. Returning to System hands reading colors back to the browser and operating system. This experiment demonstrates the design; it does not measure energy savings.

How do transitions work with native CSS?

A convincing transition does not need a new background image for every hour. A few color stops and calculated intermediate values are enough for a calm progression through the day. In this garden, sky colors are mixed between such stops; sun, moon and seasonal shapes complete the scene. The reading scheme still switches between light and dark variants, rather than making every intermediate color a new text palette. Both variants and their actual backgrounds belong in the contrast check.

Native CSS provides useful building blocks for new interfaces: light-dark() chooses between two color values according to the active color-scheme; @property gives a custom CSS variable a type and enables interpolated animation. MDN lists the color variant of light-dark() as Baseline since May 2024, and @property since July 2024. That is useful compatibility guidance, rather than a guarantee for old browsers or embedded WebViews.

The following CSS is a small standalone recipe for an existing .reading-surface text area and a decorative .ambient-layer background. Both elements must exist, and the application must set data-time="evening" on the root element after an explicit time selection. Without that attribute, the initial state remains. The colors are examples, rather than a fully tested product palette.

@property --ambient-light {
  syntax: "<color>";
  inherits: true;
  initial-value: rgb(249 196 131 / 18%);
}

:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;
}
.reading-surface {
  color: #172033;
  background: #faf8f4;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  .reading-surface {
    color: #e8edf5;
    background: #171c29;
  }
}
@supports (color: light-dark(white, black)) {
  .reading-surface {
    color: light-dark(#172033, #e8edf5);
    background: light-dark(#faf8f4, #171c29);
  }
}
.ambient-layer {
  pointer-events: none;
  background: radial-gradient(
    ellipse at 75% 15%,
    var(--ambient-light),
    transparent 65%
  );
  transition: --ambient-light 700ms ease;
}
:root[data-time="evening"] .ambient-layer {
  --ambient-light: rgb(147 123 221 / 18%);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .ambient-layer {
    transition: none;
  }
}

The reading surface stays opaque and follows the system; the glow has its own responsibility. Without light-dark(), the preceding colors and media query apply. Without @property, changing the custom variable may be abrupt, but the content remains readable. Gentle transforms and opacity changes are another option for continuous sun paths. Add a large blur or continuously running canvas scene only after checking performance.

What does OLED actually have to do with energy?

On OLED (Organic Light-Emitting Diode: Pixels emit their own light instead of being lit by a shared backlight.) displays, darker pixels need less energy. That explains a potential advantage of dark surfaces. This pixel-level saving does not directly carry over to a conventional backlit LCD (Liquid Crystal Display: A screen whose liquid crystal pixels are illuminated by a backlight.). Dark Mode also has design and personal motivations and cannot be reduced to a single historical purpose.

The 2021 Purdue study examined six Android apps on four OLED smartphones, each during 60 seconds of use. At 30–50 percent brightness, Dark Mode saved an average of 3–9 percent of total phone power; at 100 percent brightness, savings were 39–47 percent. These results describe the devices and workflows studied, rather than savings for every website or current hardware.

A glow is not evidence of energy savings
Bright backgrounds and additional animation can increase display and
computation costs. Ambient Mode can use less or more energy; without
measurement on the target device, the balance remains unknown.

Battery life between charges, battery lifespan and display aging are also different questions. Longer runtime between charges does not establish a longer device lifespan. Apple describes OLED burn-in as a possible result of high-contrast static images displayed for long periods at high brightness, and recommends automatic brightness and a short screen lock interval among other measures. An animated website offers no guaranteed protection; bright icons that remain in place in Dark Mode are still static image elements.

When does atmosphere help, and when does it distract?

A garden, portfolio or media site can gain a recognizable character from subtle changes in light. An administrative interface, long work form or focused reading view may be better served by a quiet background. This is a design hypothesis: whether atmosphere improves recognition, time spent or enjoyment must be tested with real users.

Readability matters between the attractive end states too. Version 2.2 of the WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: The W3C's guidelines for accessible web content.) requires at least 4.5:1 contrast for normal text and 3:1 for qualifying large text. Behind translucent surfaces, a moving glow can alter the actual visible background. Check intermediate states or use an opaque reading surface.

Motion is a separate decision. prefers-reduced-motion signals a preference for less nonessential animation. Sun and moon can remain still while selected colors and seasons continue to work. For a complete product, a separate control to disable decorative effects is also useful; a system preference alone does not cover every wish.

Four checks before using it

  • Respect the system: Without a saved, deliberate override, the page starts in the browser/OS scheme and follows changes to it.
  • Read intermediate states: Check midday, twilight, night and every season; text and focus indicators remain visible against their actual backgrounds.
  • Keep controls calm: Enable reduced motion and use sliders, mode selection and seasons by keyboard; decoration must not intercept clicks.
  • Measure the cost: On a less powerful target device, check CPU and GPU activity and smooth scrolling; energy claims also need appropriate hardware measurements.

Sources and next steps

Source research and verification in the original article: October 7, 2026. The Purdue figures explicitly come from 2021; the garden rules are an original implementation example.

  • YouTube: Ambient Mode – a concrete use in a media product.
  • MDN: prefers-color-scheme, light-dark() and @property – system preferences and native color features.
  • Purdue: Dark Mode measurements and original paper by Dash and Hu, MobiSys 2021 – method and limitations of OLED energy claims.
  • Apple: OLED displays – image persistence, burn-in and brightness.
  • W3C: Minimum contrast and MDN: Reduced motion – boundaries for comfortable design.

The Accessibility tile explores contrast and usability further. Explainable Text shows another kind of adaptation: readers choose the depth of information there, and the atmosphere here.

Read the original guide & explore the interactive playground on *lukiluki.me*.

title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update @ai-sdk/harness-fx to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.

title: CVE-2026-114938 Java4Shell: Pre-Auth RCE in OpenJDK Base64 Decoder — Analysis & Mitigation
description:
CVE-2026-114938 Java4Shell: Pre-Auth RCE in OpenJDK Base64 Decoder — Analysis & Mitigation

On November 17, 2026, the security firm Calif disclosed a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK that it named Java4Shell. Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, the flaw is a heap out-of-bounds write in the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder that HotSpot uses to speed up java.util.Base64. A single malformed Base64 string, supplied before any login, can corrupt the Java heap — and Calif demonstrated that the corruption can be turned into remote code execution in the default setups of some of the most widely deployed Java applications on the internet. This analysis explains what the flaw is, how it works in general terms, who is exposed, how to check your own systems, and what to patch first.

The short version: if you run OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later, or OpenJDK 21, 25 or 27, on an x86-64 server whose CPU supports AVX-512 VBMI, you are affected. Upgrade to the fixed builds released on November 17, 2026 — 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 or 27.0.1.1 — rebuild any container images that bundle Java, and restart every JVM. If you cannot patch immediately, a single JVM flag, -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, disables the vulnerable code path. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 are not affected.

What Is Java4Shell?

Java4Shell is a memory-corruption vulnerability in the OpenJDK Base64 decoder. Base64 is the encoding Java applications use constantly: HTTP Basic authentication credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, JSON Web Tokens, MIME attachments and API keys are all routinely Base64-decoded before a user is authenticated. That is what makes this flaw so dangerous — the vulnerable code runs on data an attacker controls, before any login check.

The bug lives in a hand-written, hardware-accelerated routine inside the HotSpot compiler. When the just-in-time compiler sees a hot Base64 decode loop on a capable CPU, it swaps the portable Java decoder for a vectorized native stub that uses AVX-512 VBMI instructions to decode many bytes at once. The flaw is in that stub, in the component OpenJDK lists as hotspot/compiler. Because the bug is in the JVM itself rather than in any application, no application code change can dodge it — every Java application running on a vulnerable JVM is exposed through the same path.

Calif found the flaw with AI assistance and reported it to Oracle ahead of the scheduled fix. The name Java4Shell follows the pattern of earlier landmark Java flaws: a single crafted input, no authentication, and a straight line to code execution. The vulnerable code was introduced as a performance optimization in OpenJDK pull request #4368, merged on June 25, 2021 — which means the flaw has been present in every affected release line for more than five years before anyone noticed it.

How CVE-2026-114938 Works

To understand the flaw, it helps to know how Base64 decoding works. Valid Base64 input comes in groups of four characters, each group decoding to three bytes, with = padding filling out the final group when the input length is not a multiple of three. The decoder computes how many output bytes a given input will produce, allocates a destination buffer of that size, and then writes the decoded bytes into it.

The bug is in how the accelerated decoder handles malformed padding. When the input ends with padding that should not be there — for example, a complete set of valid groups followed by a stray = — the decoder strips the padding with a subtraction that goes negative. That underflow produces a wrong output length, and the mask the decoder builds from it opens wider than the destination buffer. The vector write then lands past the end of the allocated buffer, corrupting adjacent memory on the Java heap.

At best, that corruption crashes the JVM, which is a denial of service. At worst, an attacker who controls the decoded data can overwrite heap structures — object headers, array lengths and pointers — in a way that eventually redirects execution to attacker-controlled code. That is how a decoding error becomes remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution in the default setups of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and post-authentication code execution in Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Each target needs its own exploit chain, the attack is sensitive to network latency, and a failed attempt can crash the JVM — but the demonstrations prove the path from a malformed Base64 string to code execution is real.

Calif has published a bounded trigger that proves a JVM is vulnerable, and crash-level proof-of-concept code is public. The full application exploit chains are being held back by the researchers for now, which is the window defenders have: inventory and patch before those chains circulate. There is also a client-side route — a Java client that decodes Base64 from a malicious server over a TLS connection can be attacked the same way — so the exposure is not limited to servers.

Impact and Exposure

The exposure is large because Java is everywhere, but it is narrower than the headline suggests, and defenders should understand the two conditions that must both be true. First, the JVM must be a vulnerable build: OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later, or any release of the 21, 25 or 27 lines before the November 17 fixes, from any vendor — Oracle, Temurin, Corretto, Zulu, Microsoft, Red Hat, Liberica, SapMachine or GraalVM. Second, the server must run on an x86-64 CPU that exposes the AVX-512 VBMI instructions — Intel Xeon from Ice Lake onward, or AMD EPYC from Zen 4 onward, which includes common cloud instance types. ARM servers are not affected, and neither are older x86-64 CPUs without those instructions.

Both conditions must hold, and the application must also decode attacker-controlled Base64 — which, as noted above, most web applications do before login. Red Hat notes that HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens and MIME encoded words are routinely decoded before authentication, which is why internet-facing identity and collaboration software tops the priority list: Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate first, then Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker, and then every product, appliance or container image that bundles its own Java runtime.

Two facts keep the situation from being worse. First, as of late November 2026, the flaw has not been added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and Cisco and AWS have said they know of no malicious use. Second, fixed packages reached the major Linux distributions within days: by November 20, RHEL 8, 9 and 10, Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine and Amazon Linux had shipped fixed Java packages. That is not a reason to relax. A public crash proof of concept already exists, the full exploit chains are only being held back rather than impossible, and history says the window between disclosure and weaponization is short.

Who Is Affected

OpenJDK lineAffected versionsFixed build
1717.0.6 through 17.0.21.017.0.21.1
2121 through 21.0.13.021.0.13.1
2525 through 25.0.5.025.0.5.1
2727 through 27.0.1.027.0.1.1
18–20, 22–24, 26Every release (end-of-life lines)No fix — upgrade to a supported line
8 and 11Not affectedNo change needed

Two scoring disagreements are worth understanding, because they explain why different advisories quote different numbers for the same flaw. OpenJDK and the CVE record publish a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1, with a high attack-complexity metric, because exploitation needs both a vulnerable CPU and an application that decodes attacker-supplied Base64. Calif, the discoverer, scores it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and Red Hat's preliminary score is 9.8. Atlassian also scores it 9.2. The gap is a judgement about how common the preconditions are, not a disagreement about the bug. For an internet-facing Java application, the preconditions are common enough that the higher scores are the honest ones to plan around — and this post carries both, so readers can see the full picture.

One trap deserves a warning. The Java version a server reports does not always tell you whether it is patched. Vendors ship fixed builds under the same feature version, and container images bundle their own JVMs, so checking java -version on the host is not enough. Check the exact build number, check the Java bundled inside every container image and appliance, and confirm against your vendor's advisory. A server that looks old but is actually fixed can be left alone, but a server that looks fine while its container still carries a vulnerable JVM is the one that gets compromised.

How to Detect It

Detection is harder than usual for this flaw, and defenders should know why before they start hunting. The attack traffic is an ordinary-looking request carrying a malformed Base64 value — a credential, a token, a SAML artifact — inside an encrypted TLS connection. Web access logs show almost nothing distinctive about an attempt, and the vulnerable code runs before authentication, so there is no failed-login trail to follow either.

Start with JVM stability, because a memory-corruption attempt usually leaves crashes behind before anything else. Look for JVM crashes, heap corruption errors and unexpected JVM restarts on Java services, and correlate them with inbound traffic. Repeated crashes on a Java service that decodes attacker-controlled Base64, especially alongside spikes in connections, should be investigated rather than dismissed as routine instability. A failed exploitation attempt can crash the JVM, so a cluster of crashes may be the first sign that someone is working through the exploit chain.

Next, inventory rather than hunt. The most reliable detection for this flaw is knowing where vulnerable JVMs run. List every Java runtime in the environment — hosts, containers, appliances and build pipelines — and record the exact build and the CPU it runs on. Anything on OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later, or on the 21, 25 or 27 lines before the November 17 builds, running on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, is exposed. Prioritize internet-facing identity and collaboration software first, then anything that decodes Base64 from untrusted input, then the long tail of bundled JVMs in appliances and images.

Then check processes and the network. A Java process that spawns a shell, or any unexpected child process running under the application user, is the loudest single signal of a successful compromise. Look for new or modified files under the application directory outside a change window, and for outbound connections from Java servers to unfamiliar hosts after a burst of requests. If the endpoint was reachable from the internet, check the host for compromise before patching over it — patching removes the hole, but it does not remove an attacker who already got in.

How to Fix It

Patching is straightforward, and the order matters. First, upgrade the Java runtime to a fixed build: 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 or 27.0.1.1, or your Linux distribution's fixed package. Oracle's fixed releases shipped on November 17, 2026, and the major distributions followed within days. Rebuild every container image that bundles Java — patching the host JVM does nothing for a container that carries its own — and restart every JVM. A running JVM keeps using the old, vulnerable code until it restarts, so the restart step matters as much as the upgrade.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, disable the vulnerable code path with a single JVM flag: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. That turns off the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder and falls back to the portable implementation, which is not affected. Vendors confirm the flag has no meaningful performance impact for most applications, and it works on every affected version, so it is the right emergency mitigation while patching is scheduled. End-of-life lines — 18 through 20, 22 through 24 and 26 — have no fix at all and must be upgraded to a supported line.

After patching, verify rather than assume. Confirm the running build number on every JVM, including the ones inside containers, and re-run the exposure check. Calif's bounded trigger can prove whether a JVM is still vulnerable, which is more reliable than trusting a version string. Treat any internet-facing Java service that was reachable before the patch as potentially probed: review its logs and process history for the crash and compromise signals described above.

Lessons for Defenders

The first lesson is about where trust lives in a Java stack. Applications assume the JVM is a safe foundation, and most of the time it is — but Java4Shell is a reminder that the runtime itself is attack surface. A flaw in a standard-library decoder reaches every application that uses it, without a single line of application code being wrong. Runtime patching belongs in the same priority tier as application patching, and container images that bundle their own JVM need the same discipline as the hosts they run on.

The second lesson is about performance optimizations. The vulnerable code was a hand-written, hardware-specific fast path, introduced to make Base64 decoding faster on modern CPUs. Hand-written vector code is exactly the kind of code where a small arithmetic mistake becomes a memory-safety catastrophe, and it is also the kind of code that is hardest to review — the bug survived five years in one of the most scrutinized codebases in the world. When a fast path handles untrusted input, it deserves the same scrutiny as any parser.

The third lesson is about preconditions. Java4Shell needs a specific CPU, a specific JVM range and attacker-controlled Base64 — and yet it still reaches the most important Java applications on the internet, because those preconditions are ordinary in production. "It needs a modern server CPU" is not a meaningful defense when modern server CPUs are the default. Score a vulnerability by how common its preconditions are in your environment, not by how many conditions it has.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Java4Shell being exploited in the wild?

As of late November 2026, no exploitation in the wild has been reported, and the flaw is not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Calif has demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution in the lab and is holding back the full exploit chains. The absence of reported exploitation is a window, not a verdict.

Am I affected if my server uses an ARM CPU?

No. The vulnerable code only runs on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI instructions. ARM servers, and older x86-64 CPUs without those instructions, do not take the vulnerable path. Check your CPU flags before assuming either way.

Does Java 8 or Java 11 need patching?

No. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 do not contain the vulnerable code. Oracle's Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack has a fixed build, 8u513-perf, for the performance-pack variant only.

What does the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics flag do?

It disables the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder and makes the JVM use the portable Java implementation instead. That removes the vulnerable code path entirely, with no meaningful performance impact for most applications. It is the recommended emergency mitigation while patching is scheduled.

Why do different advisories show different CVSS scores?

OpenJDK and the CVE record score it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1, with high attack complexity, because exploitation needs a vulnerable CPU and an application that decodes attacker-controlled Base64. Calif scores it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 and Red Hat's preliminary score is 9.8, reflecting the view that those preconditions are common in production. Both scores describe the same flaw.

title: How to Add Interactivity to a Webpage Using JavaScript: A Beginner-Friendly Tutorial
description:
Have you ever clicked a button on a website and watched something happen instantly?

Perhaps a heading changed, a menu opened, a message appeared, or a counter increased without the entire webpage reloading.

Have you ever wondered how developers make these interactions possible?

The answer often involves JavaScript, a programming language that allows websites to respond to user actions and update content dynamically.

If you're learning web development, understanding JavaScript can feel much easier when you build something small and see the result for yourself.

You don't need to start with a complicated web application. You don't need hundreds of lines of code. You can begin with something as simple as a heading and a button.

In this tutorial, we'll build a small interactive webpage step by step. You'll learn how HTML, CSS, and JavaScript work together, and you'll practise important concepts such as variables, functions, DOM selection, event listeners, and updating text content.

By the end, you'll have a practical example you can experiment with and expand.

Let's get started! 🚀

What Are We Going to Build?

We'll create a webpage containing a heading and a button.

Initially, the heading will display:

Welcome to My Website!

When someone clicks the button, the heading will change to:

You just made this page interactive!

It may seem like a small project, but it introduces several important concepts used in frontend development.

Here's how the three core technologies will contribute:

HTML: Creates the heading and button.

CSS: Styles the button.

JavaScript: Detects the click and changes the heading.

Let's build it one step at a time.

Step 1: Create the HTML Structure

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It defines the structure and meaning of webpage content.

For our project, we need two elements: a heading and a button.

Create a file named index.html and add the following code:

<!DOCTYPE html>




My Interactive Webpage

Welcome to My Website!

Click Me

Let's understand a few important parts.

The

element represents the main heading on the page.

The element creates a button that users can click.

But what are id="heading" and id="changeButton" doing?

An id gives an HTML element a unique identifier within the document. JavaScript can use these identifiers to locate the specific elements it needs to work with.

For example, heading identifies our heading, while changeButton identifies our button.

At this stage, we have the structure, but the button doesn't yet change the heading.

That's perfectly fine. We'll add that behaviour shortly.

Step 2: Style the Button With CSS

Now let's improve the appearance of the button.

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It controls how HTML elements are presented, including their colours, spacing, borders, typography, and layout.

Create another file named style.css.

Add the following code:

body {
font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
text-align: center;
padding: 60px 20px;
}

h1 {
color: #2E2E2E;
}

button {
background-color: #800020;
color: white;
padding: 12px 20px;
border: none;
border-radius: 6px;
cursor: pointer;
font-size: 16px;
}

button:hover {
opacity: 0.9;
}

Here's what these styles accomplish:

font-family sets the font used on the page.

text-align: center centres the text horizontally.

padding creates space inside the button and around the page content.

background-color gives the button a burgundy background.

color: white makes the button text white.

border-radius rounds the button's corners.

cursor: pointer indicates that the button is clickable when using a mouse.

button:hover changes the button's appearance slightly when a mouse pointer hovers over it.

But there's one more thing to do.

We need to connect our CSS file to the HTML document.

Inside the element of index.html, add this line:

Your page now has a structure and a visual design.

However, the button still needs JavaScript to perform our intended action.

Step 3: Select the HTML Elements With JavaScript

Here's where things get interesting.

JavaScript allows us to access HTML elements and change their content, attributes, and other properties.

For this project, we need to select the heading and the button.

Create a file named script.js.

Add the following code:

const heading = document.getElementById("heading");
const button = document.getElementById("changeButton");

Let's break this down.

Understanding variables

A variable provides a name through which we can access a value.

In this example, we use const to declare two variables:

heading

button

The first variable stores a reference to the HTML heading element.

The second variable stores a reference to the HTML button element.

Why use const?

It declares a binding that cannot be reassigned to a different value. In this example, we don't need to reassign either variable.

Understanding DOM selection

DOM stands for Document Object Model.

The browser represents the HTML document as a structured model that JavaScript can access and modify.

The method document.getElementById() searches the document for an element with the specified ID.

For example:

document.getElementById("heading");

This retrieves the element whose ID is heading.

Because our HTML heading has that ID, JavaScript can now access it through the heading variable.

The same process allows us to access the button.

Why is this important?

JavaScript needs a way to identify the elements it should work with. DOM selection provides that connection between your JavaScript code and the webpage.

Step 4: Create a Function to Change the Heading

Now that JavaScript can access the heading, let's define what should happen when we want to change its text.

Add this code to script.js:

function changeHeading() {
heading.textContent = "You just made this page interactive!";
}

Let's examine the important concepts.

What is a function?

A function is a reusable block of code that performs a particular task when called.

Here, we've created a function named changeHeading.

The instructions inside the function tell JavaScript to update the heading's text.

Notice that defining the function doesn't automatically execute it. We still need to tell JavaScript when to run it.

What does textContent do?

The textContent property lets JavaScript read or update the text contained in an element.

This statement:

heading.textContent = "You just made this page interactive!";

replaces the heading's existing text with the new message.

Initially, the heading says:

Welcome to My Website!

After the statement executes, it says:

You just made this page interactive!

The heading element itself remains on the page. Only its text changes.

This is a simple example of DOM manipulation.

Step 5: Listen for a Click Event

We've created a function that changes the heading. Now we need to connect it to the button.

Add this line to script.js:

button.addEventListener("click", changeHeading);

Let's understand what this means.

What is an event?

An event is an occurrence that JavaScript can respond to.

Examples include:

A user clicking a button.

A user typing into an input field.

A form being submitted.

A keyboard key being pressed.

In our project, the event is a button click.

What is an event listener?

An event listener allows JavaScript to wait for a particular event and execute a function when that event occurs.

The addEventListener() method accepts the event type and the function that should run in response.

In our example:

button.addEventListener("click", changeHeading);

button refers to our HTML button.

"click" specifies the event we want to listen for.

changeHeading is the function that should execute when the click occurs.

Notice that we write changeHeading, not changeHeading().

We are passing the function itself as a callback so the browser can call it when the click happens.

If we wrote changeHeading() directly as the second argument, we would execute the function immediately rather than register it as the click handler.

This small distinction is important when learning JavaScript events.

Step 6: Connect JavaScript to HTML

We've written the JavaScript, but the browser needs to load the file.

Open index.html and add this script element just before the closing tag:

Placing the script at the end of the body in this example ensures that the heading and button have been parsed before the script tries to select them.

Your HTML file should now look like this:

<!DOCTYPE html>




My Interactive Webpage


Welcome to My Website!

Click Me

You now have three files:

index.html — the webpage structure.

style.css — the visual styling.

script.js — the interactive behaviour.

Make sure all three files are saved in the same folder, as shown in this example.

Step 7: Test Your Webpage in the Browser

It's time to see your code in action!

Open index.html in your browser.

You should see a heading that reads:

Welcome to My Website!

Below it, you'll see your styled button.

Now click the button.

The heading should change to:

You just made this page interactive!

Congratulations! 🎉 You've created a webpage that responds to a user's action.

Let's review the sequence:

The browser loads your HTML.

CSS styles the heading and button.

JavaScript selects the heading and button.

The browser waits for a click on the button.

When the click occurs, the event listener calls changeHeading().

The function updates the heading through textContent.

The browser updates the displayed text without requiring a full-page reload.

That's a simple but important example of JavaScript in action.

Step 8: Troubleshoot Common Problems

If your webpage doesn't behave as expected, don't panic. Debugging is part of programming.

Here are a few things to check.

The button does nothing

Make sure the script is connected correctly:

Check that the file is named script.js and is located where the HTML expects it to be.

The heading doesn't change

Check that the ID in your HTML matches the ID used in JavaScript.

Your HTML should contain:

Welcome to My Website!

Your JavaScript should use:

document.getElementById("heading");

Remember that spelling and capitalization matter.

The button isn't styled

Confirm that this line appears in the HTML's :

Also check the filename and folder location.

You're still stuck

If you're using a desktop browser, open the developer tools and inspect the Console for JavaScript errors. A message about a missing element or file can help you identify the problem.

If your browser reports that an element is null, check whether the element exists and whether the script runs after the element has been parsed.

Debugging isn't a sign that you're bad at programming. It's part of learning how your code works.

Step 9: Challenge Yourself With Small Improvements

Once the basic interaction works, try changing the project.

These small challenges will help you practise what you've learned.

Challenge 1: Change the message

Replace the existing message with something of your own.

For example:

heading.textContent = "Keep learning and keep building!";

Challenge 2: Change the button text

Can you also change the text displayed on the button after it's clicked?

Hint: The button element has a textContent property too.

Challenge 3: Create a counter

Instead of changing a heading, create a number that increases each time someone clicks a button.

This will help you practise variables and updating the DOM.

Challenge 4: Create a show-and-hide feature

Make a button that reveals additional text when clicked and hides it when clicked again.

This introduces the idea of changing an element's visibility and tracking its current state.

Challenge 5: Add a second button

Create another button that changes the heading back to its original message.

This will help you practise working with multiple events and functions.

You don't have to complete every challenge immediately. Start with one, make it work, and then move to the next.

Why This Small Project Matters

You might be thinking, "It's only a button that changes some text. Is that really useful?"

Yes—because the purpose of this exercise is not to create a sophisticated application. It's to understand the basic mechanism behind many interactive features.

The same fundamental ideas can contribute to much larger projects.

A shopping cart responds to button clicks and updates information.

A search interface responds to input and displays results.

A form can listen for submission events and provide feedback.

A dashboard can update its interface when new data arrives.

Larger applications introduce additional concepts, but understanding events, functions, DOM selection, and content updates gives you a foundation for learning them.

The best way to understand JavaScript is to connect what you learn with something you can build and test.

Conclusion: Start Small, Then Build Bigger

Adding interactivity to a webpage doesn't have to be complicated.

In this tutorial, you created an HTML heading and button, styled the button with CSS, selected the elements with JavaScript, defined a function, listened for a click event, and updated the heading's text.

Along the way, you practised five important concepts:

Variables.

DOM selection.

Functions.

Event listeners.

Updating text with textContent.

More importantly, you saw how these concepts work together to create a result you can observe in your browser.

Remember the roles of the three technologies:

HTML = Structure

CSS = Presentation

JavaScript = Behaviour

You don't need to master JavaScript before building your first project. You can start with one small interaction, learn from it, and gradually take on more challenging ideas.

Save your code. Experiment with it. Break something and figure out how to fix it.

Every experiment gives you another opportunity to learn.

Your Turn!

💬 If you could build your next JavaScript project, which would you choose?

A click counter.

A simple calculator.

A show-and-hide menu.

An interactive form.

Share your choice in the comments—and keep building!

title: Using JackedIN with AI agents
description:
Using JackedIN with AI agents

This article describes JackedIN 1.2.1, plus a safety rule being built for the next release. Human approval before any change is not in 1.2.1 yet. The canonical version is on the product site: Using JackedIN with AI agents.

JackedIN is an SSH, Telnet and serial terminal for Windows, Linux and Raspberry Pi. The same program is a desktop window, a command line, a local API, and a stdio MCP server. Built-in profiles for Junos, Cisco IOS/NX-OS, Arista, Nokia, MikroTik and more.

Use it only on devices you own or are allowed to manage. Examples use 192.0.2.10 and router1. Keep passwords out of the command line; set JACKEDIN_PASSWORD or a credential reference instead.

Human approval before any change (coming in the next release)

This is the safety rule being built for AI sessions, and it is not in JackedIN 1.2.1 yet:

  • Show-type commands run freely.
  • A command that changes something runs only after a human approves it.
  • The agent can never approve itself.

Until that ships, treat exec as able to send any command you allow it to run, and limit the agent by how you prompt it and which tools you enable.

The problem agents hit

If you pipe a command into a raw SSH/serial session, end-of-file often ends the session while the device is still paging, or after it printed an error the agent never read. The agent moves on as if the change landed.

JackedIN is built so that does not happen.

Wait for the prompt, then read the complete output

jackedin exec reads the whole command list first, sends one command, and waits until the device prompt is back before it sends the next. It pages through --More--, ---(more)---, ---(more 100%)---, and similar markers, then returns the complete output. A stdin pipe on connect also waits for the prompt after each line; after stdin ends, it waits for the prompt that follows the last line, then exits.

There is no --terminator flag. The device prompt, and those pager markers, are how JackedIN knows a command has finished. --prompt REGEX replaces the prompt JackedIN detects. --vendor NAME forces a profile; omit it and the prompt or banner picks one.

Pacing, when a slow console needs it:

  • --line-delay MS — gap between lines (serial defaults to 100 ms if you omit it)
  • --char-delay MS — pause between characters
  • --wait-for-echo — wait until the device echoes a line before sending the next
  • !sleep 500 in a command list — wait 500 ms and send nothing
  • --timeout SEC — cap each wait; omit it and JackedIN waits as long as the device needs

The same pacing fields on the API and MCP are lineDelayMs, charDelayMs, and waitForEcho.

--dry-run prints the plan and connects to nothing. Prefer exec over piping into connect.

jackedin exec --host 192.0.2.10 --user admin --trust-host-key \
  --json --timeout 8 --cmd 'show version'

JSON output

--json and --output json are the same flag. JACKEDIN_JSON=1 matches them. On exec, each command is returned as structured data: command, ok, output, prompt, matched_error, timed_out, duration_ms. ok is false if any command, timeout, or verify check failed. fleet and inventory sync also accept JSON output.

On Windows, capture that output with jackedin.com, not jackedin.exe.

MCP server

jackedin mcp is a stdio MCP server for the local API. It dials 127.0.0.1 only. It is not a public URL.

  1. Install JackedIN 1.2.1 from the download section (72-hour full trial; a license is needed after that).
  2. Turn the local API on in Settings. It stays off until you do. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only (port 47321 unless you change it) and requires a Bearer token.
  3. Leave the window open, or run jackedin headless (the API must still be enabled).
  4. Point the client at the stdio command: 
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "jackedin": {
      "command": "jackedin",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "env": {
        "JACKEDIN_API_TOKEN": "paste-the-token-from-settings",
        "JACKEDIN_API_PORT": "47321"
      }
    }
  }
}

The packaged examples include this snippet for generic clients, Cursor, and Claude Desktop. The token is JACKEDIN_API_TOKEN if that variable is set, otherwise the token saved in Settings.

Tools: list_sessions, open_session, send_session, exec, send_break, read_session, close_session, wait_for_output, scan_ports, ping_host, trace_host, read_events. Prefer exec. exec and send_break do not require the automationApi setting; wait, scan, ping, trace, and events do. scan_ports tells the caller to only scan devices they are allowed to test.

The local API, off by default

The same work is available over HTTP on the local machine: POST /v1/exec, POST /v1/sessions/{id}/exec, and the other routes in the packaged docs/openapi.yaml. The listener is off until you enable it, bound to 127.0.0.1, and token-protected. Do not expose it on a network.

Safe use

  • Only connect to or scan devices you are allowed to test.
  • Do not put secrets in argv, MCP config files you will share, or logs. Use environment variables and the credential store.
  • Prefer --dry-run and show commands until you are sure of the plan.
  • A changed SSH host key is refused in the background; --trust-host-key accepts a new key, not a changed one.

Coming in the next release: human approval before any change

The same rule as the headline above. It is being built for the next release and is not in 1.2.1: in AI sessions, show-type commands run freely; a command that changes something waits for a human; the agent cannot approve its own change.

Try it

  • Download: getpathprobe.com/jackedin/#download
  • Buy (launch price $19, after the 72-hour trial): getpathprobe.com/jackedin/#pricing
  • Release and SHA256SUMS: JackedIN 1.2.1 on GitHub
  • User's guide: JackedIN-Users-Guide.md

We build JackedIN. This article describes the current 1.2.1 app, and marks human approval before any change as coming in the next release.

title: What is an embedding, really? Building an AI agent from scratch in Java, part 2
description:
Not one word in common. No synonyms file, no tags, no LLM writing an answer. Just Postgres, a column of numbers, and an ORDER BY.

Some context first. This is part 2 of a series where I learn AI engineering by building everything by hand. In part 1 I wrote an MCP server, an MCP client and an agent loop in plain Java, with no AI frameworks, so a local Qwen model running in Ollama could read and write my notes file.

That agent has a catch, though. Its read tool hands the model the whole notes file, pasted into the prompt. Fine for a short to-do list. Point it at a wiki with hundreds of pages, and the prompt gets huge: slow, expensive, the model starts missing things, and eventually it doesn't fit at all. What the agent really needs is to pull in only the few paragraphs that matter for the question. To find those, it has to search by meaning.

That piece is the embedding, and it's the foundation under semantic search, recommendations and most of the "add your own data to AI" stuff.

Here's the plan for this post. We take a handful of short notes, turn each one into numbers with an embedding model, store them in Postgres, then search them by meaning instead of by exact words. No chat model, no MCP, no agent: just an embedding model and a database. By the end, things to buy finds Grocery list on your own machine.

To see why that's worth doing, start with how search usually works.

Keyword search matches words, not meaning

Classic search (SQL LIKE, MySQL FULLTEXT, Postgres full-text search, even Elasticsearch out of the box) works on words. Split the text into words, clean them up a bit (lowercase, calling → call), and find documents that contain the same ones.

That's great when you know the exact word. It falls over when you don't:

You search for The note says Keyword search
things to buy Grocery list: rice, lentils, ginger ❌ no shared words
reset my password Account recovery steps ❌
car my vehicle insurance renewal ❌

Humans read meaning, not spelling. To search the way humans read, we need a way to turn meaning into something a computer can compare. That's what an embedding is.

What an embedding is: text in, numbers out

An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. You get one by sending text to an embedding model.

I run mine locally with Ollama:

ollama pull nomic-embed-text

curl http://localhost:11434/api/embed -d '{
  "model": "nomic-embed-text",
  "input": "things to buy"
}'

The response, trimmed:

{
  "model": "nomic-embed-text",
  "embeddings": [[0.0123, -0.0456, 0.0331, 0.0718, -0.0092, ...]]
}

That inner list has 768 numbers. Every piece of text you send, whether it's three words or three paragraphs, comes back as exactly 768 numbers. That fixed length is what makes texts comparable.

  • An embedding model is not a chat model. It's a neural network, but a small one (nomic-embed-text is about 270 MB, versus 4.7 GB for the Qwen model I chat with). It can't write a sentence. Text goes in, numbers come out, and that's its entire job.
  • Nobody chose what the numbers mean. There's no "number 42 = food". The model invented its own 768 features during training. You can't read them, but you can compare them, and comparing them is the whole point.

Direction is meaning, length is "how much"

768 numbers are impossible to picture, so let's cheat. Pretend the model only produced 3 numbers, and each one meant a topic: [food, tech, travel].

Text Embedding
"pasta recipe" [0.9, 0.1, 0.0]
a 5-page article on Italian cooking [2.7, 0.3, 0.0]
"setting up Docker" [0.0, 0.9, 0.1]
"best ramen in Sapporo" [0.6, 0.0, 0.7]

Now picture each embedding as an arrow from the origin, pointing somewhere in that 3D space. Two things describe an arrow: which way it points, and how long it is.

  • Direction = what the text is about. "Pasta recipe" and the cooking article point the same way: mostly food, a bit of tech (recipe sites, I guess), no travel. "Setting up Docker" points somewhere else entirely.
  • Length = how much, not what. The article's numbers are three times bigger because it's longer and says more about food. It's not about a different topic, just more of the same one.
  • Mixed topics point in between. "Best ramen in Sapporo" sits between food and travel, which is exactly what it is.

That is what stood out for me: similar meaning = similar direction. Real embeddings work the same way, just in 768 dimensions with features nobody can name.

How close is close? Cosine

If meaning is direction, we need a number that says how alike two directions are. For text, that number is cosine distance. It measures only the angle between two arrows and ignores their length:

  • Same direction → distance 0 → same meaning.
  • Different direction → bigger distance → different meaning.

Why ignore length? Search "pasta recipe" and the 5-page cooking article points the same way, so cosine calls it a near-perfect match. A ruler-style distance would call it far away just for being longer, which is backwards for search.

Other measures exist (Euclidean, inner product) for other kinds of data, like map coordinates or recommendation scores. You don't have to pick: your embedding model's docs tell you which one it was trained for, and for text models that's almost always cosine. Just make sure you use the same model for what you store and what you search with.

Semantic search in Postgres with pgvector

You don't need a special vector database to try this. Postgres with the pgvector extension stores embeddings as a normal column type, and a search is a normal SELECT. The whole flow:

A chunk is a piece of a bigger document, roughly a paragraph, so each vector stands for one idea. In this post each short note is its own chunk.

I run the official pgvector/pgvector:pg17 Docker image. Setup:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE notes (
    id        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    title     text NOT NULL,
    body      text NOT NULL,
    embedding vector(768)          -- 768 must match the model's output
);

For each note, a small script asks Ollama for the embedding and stores it. pgvector accepts the vector as plain text:

INSERT INTO notes (title, body, embedding)
VALUES ('Grocery list', 'rice, lentils, ginger, chili', '[0.0123, -0.0456, ...]');

At search time, the request is embedded the same way, then:

SELECT title,
       1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS similarity      -- $1 = the query's vector
FROM notes
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1                      -- <=> is cosine distance
LIMIT 3;

    title          | similarity
-------------------+-----------
 Grocery list      |   0.71
 Dinner plans      |   0.48
 Ollama setup      |   0.39

That's it. Semantic search is an ORDER BY on a distance. The <=> operator is cosine distance (0 = same direction), so 1 - distance gives a similarity score where higher is better.

One honest note: results always come back sorted, even when nothing is relevant. Search for "quantum physics" in a grocery wiki and you'll still get three rows, so keep an eye on the scores.

What embeddings are bad at

Embeddings are fuzzy by design. That's perfect for "things to buy", but bad when the exact word matters: error codes (ERR_4021 vs ERR_4022 look nearly identical), invoice IDs, or "notes NOT about Docker" (Docker notes still rank first). Keyword search handles those, which is why real search systems often run both, called "hybrid search".

Wrap-up

The whole idea in five lines:

  1. An embedding model turns text into a fixed-length list of numbers, a vector.
  2. Think of each vector as an arrow. Direction is meaning; length is mostly noise.
  3. Cosine distance measures the angle between arrows. For text, it's the default.
  4. Use the same model for what you store and what you search with.
  5. Semantic search is just ORDER BY embedding <=> query LIMIT k. No chat model involved.

What clicked for me is how unmagical it is. "Understands meaning" turns out to be arrows and angles, and a database that can sort by an angle.

Next up

So far, nothing in this post talks back. It's just search. In part 3 the agent from part 1 finally gets to use it: I'll add a new search tool to my Java MCP server that embeds the question, runs this exact pgvector query and hands back the closest chunks. Then the agent can stop reading the whole notes file and just ask for the few paragraphs it needs.

Co-written with Claude, who patiently answered "but what does that mean?" about forty times.

title: Bitmap: uma estrutura de dados com mais de 70 anos de história
description:
Bitmap é uma técnica de representação de dados que utiliza bits para armazenar informações de maneira compacta e permitir operações eficientes.

Embora o termo seja frequentemente associado a imagens e arquivos .bmp, seu uso na computação vai muito além dos formatos gráficos.

Representações baseadas em bits aparecem em sistemas operacionais, bancos de dados, mecanismos de busca, algoritmos de jogos e aplicações que precisam manipular grandes conjuntos de informações.

E o mais interessante: a ideia já era utilizada nos primeiros anos da computação digital, muito antes dos computadores pessoais.

Neste artigo, vamos entender sua história, seu funcionamento, suas aplicações e como utilizá-la em Java.

O que é um bitmap?

Um bitmap é uma representação de informações por meio de uma sequência de bits.

Cada bit pode assumir apenas dois estados:

  • 0: desligado, falso ou ausente.
  • 1: ligado, verdadeiro ou presente.

O significado desses estados depende do problema que queremos resolver.

Imagine que precisamos armazenar um conjunto contendo os números 1, 4 e 6.

Uma implementação convencional poderia utilizar um array:

int[] numbers = {1, 4, 6};

Em um bitmap, podemos representar o mesmo conjunto assim:

Posição:  0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
          ---------------
Bits:     0 1 0 0 1 0 1 0

Cada posição corresponde a um número.

Se o bit estiver ativado, o número pertence ao conjunto.

Assim, consultar o número 4 significa verificar diretamente o bit da posição 4.

Não é necessário percorrer os demais números.

Essa forma de representar pertencimento a conjuntos é conhecida como bitset, ou vetor de bits.

É importante distinguir os termos: bitmap é um conceito amplo de representação de informações por bits; bitset costuma designar especificamente uma estrutura utilizada para representar conjuntos.

Uma história que começa nos anos 1950

Não existe uma data universalmente reconhecida para a invenção do bitmap como estrutura de dados.

Entretanto, representações semelhantes aos bitsets atuais já eram utilizadas nos primeiros computadores digitais.

1952: o programa de damas de Christopher Strachey

Uma das aplicações históricas mais interessantes aparece no programa de damas desenvolvido pelo cientista da computação britânico Christopher Strachey.

Em 1952, seu programa já conseguia disputar partidas completas no computador Ferranti Mark 1, da Universidade de Manchester.

Um dos desafios era representar o estado do tabuleiro utilizando recursos computacionais extremamente limitados.

A solução empregava três palavras de 32 bits, utilizadas para identificar posições de peças pretas, peças brancas e damas.

Cada uma das 32 casas jogáveis do tabuleiro correspondia a uma posição de bit.

Ao ativar ou desativar determinados bits, o programa podia representar alterações no estado do jogo.

Essa técnica ficou conhecida como bitboard.

Em vez de armazenar cada casa como uma estrutura independente, era possível representar grande parte do estado do tabuleiro utilizando apenas algumas palavras de memória.

Essa abordagem também permitia aproveitar operações lógicas e deslocamentos de bits para trabalhar com posições e movimentos.

O projeto foi posteriormente reconstruído e documentado pela Computer Conservation Society.

1959: Arthur Samuel e o aprendizado de máquina

Outro exemplo histórico aparece no trabalho de Arthur Samuel, pesquisador da IBM.

Em 1959, ele publicou o artigo Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers.

O estudo apresentava um programa capaz de melhorar seu desempenho no jogo de damas a partir da experiência.

Para representar o tabuleiro, Samuel utilizava posições de bits dentro de palavras de memória do IBM 704.

Com essa representação, operações de deslocamento e operações lógicas podiam auxiliar nos cálculos relacionados ao jogo.

É interessante observar que técnicas de manipulação de bits já eram utilizadas em pesquisas pioneiras de inteligência artificial.

A lógica por trás da otimização continua relevante: representar dados adequadamente pode reduzir significativamente o trabalho necessário para processá-los.

Como um bitmap funciona na memória?

Para entender sua eficiência, precisamos olhar um pouco mais de perto para a representação binária.

Um byte contém oito bits.

Portanto, com apenas um byte, conseguimos representar oito condições independentes.

Por exemplo:

Bits:  1 0 1 0 0 1 1 0

Dependendo da aplicação, cada posição poderia representar uma permissão, um recurso ocupado ou a presença de determinado elemento.

Em Java, o tipo long possui 64 bits.

Isso significa que podemos representar 64 indicadores de pertencimento utilizando apenas um long.

long bitmap = 0L;

Inicialmente, todos os bits estão desligados.

Para ativar o bit da posição 5:

bitmap |= (1L << 5);

O operador << desloca os bits para a esquerda.

A expressão 1L << 5 cria uma máscara com o bit 5 ativado.

Já o operador |= realiza uma operação OR bit a bit, preservando os bits anteriormente ativados.

Para verificar se o bit está ligado:

boolean exists =
    (bitmap & (1L << 5)) != 0;

O operador & realiza um AND bit a bit.

Se o resultado for diferente de zero, significa que o bit consultado estava ativado.

Para desativar a posição:

bitmap &= ~(1L << 5);

E para alternar seu estado:

bitmap ^= (1L << 5);

Com essas operações conseguimos manipular conjuntos de informações diretamente sobre a representação binária.

Representando milhares de valores

Um único long consegue representar até 64 posições.

Mas e se precisarmos representar 10 mil valores possíveis?

Podemos utilizar um array de long:

long[] bitmap = new long[157];

Cada long possui 64 bits.

Portanto:

10.000 / 64 = 156,25

Arredondando para cima: 157 longs

Como cada long ocupa oito bytes:

157 × 8 = 1.256 bytes

Isso representa aproximadamente 1,23 KiB de dados, desconsiderando o cabeçalho do array e seu alinhamento na JVM.

Para ativar o bit correspondente ao valor 5411, primeiro precisamos encontrar a posição correta.

int value = 5411;

int wordIndex = value >>> 6;
int bitIndex = value & 63;

O resultado será:

wordIndex = 84
bitIndex  = 35

O deslocamento de seis bits equivale à divisão inteira por 64 para valores não negativos.

Já a operação & 63 equivale a obter o resto dessa divisão.

Agora podemos ativar o bit:

bitmap[wordIndex] |= 1L << bitIndex;

E consultá-lo:

boolean exists =
    (bitmap[wordIndex] & (1L << bitIndex)) != 0;

Assim, uma consulta encontra diretamente a palavra e o bit desejados, sem realizar uma busca sequencial.

Para um domínio numérico limitado e diretamente indexável, o custo da consulta é O(1).

Java já possui a classe BitSet

Não é necessário implementar manualmente todas essas operações.

A biblioteca padrão do Java disponibiliza a classe java.util.BitSet desde suas primeiras versões.

Ela oferece uma API para armazenar e manipular conjuntos representados por bits.

Veja um exemplo:

import java.util.BitSet;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BitSet numbers = new BitSet();

        numbers.set(1);
        numbers.set(4);
        numbers.set(6);

        System.out.println(numbers.get(4)); // true
        System.out.println(numbers.get(3)); // false

        System.out.println(numbers); // {1, 4, 6}
    }
}

O método set() ativa um bit.

O método get() verifica seu estado.

O método clear() permite desativá-lo.

A classe também disponibiliza outras operações:

Método Finalidade
set(index) Ativa um bit
get(index) Consulta um bit
clear(index) Desativa um bit
flip(index) Inverte um bit
cardinality() Conta os bits ativados
and(other) Interseção
or(other) União
xor(other) Diferença simétrica
nextSetBit(index) Encontra o próximo bit ativado

A documentação completa está disponível em java.util.BitSet — Java 21.

Um detalhe importante: BitSet é uma estrutura mutável e não é automaticamente segura para modificações concorrentes. Aplicações multithread precisam considerar sincronização, encapsulamento ou publicação de estruturas que não serão modificadas.

Operações entre conjuntos utilizando bits

Uma das características mais interessantes dos bitmaps é a possibilidade de combinar conjuntos por meio de operações bitwise.

Imagine dois conjuntos:

A = {1, 3, 5}
B = {3, 4, 5}

Suas representações binárias seriam:

Posição:  0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7

A:        0 1 0 1 0 1 0 0
B:        0 0 0 1 1 1 0 0

Se quisermos encontrar os elementos presentes nos dois conjuntos, basta utilizar AND:

A:        0 1 0 1 0 1 0 0
B:        0 0 0 1 1 1 0 0
          ---------------
AND:      0 0 0 1 0 1 0 0

O resultado representa o conjunto {3, 5}.

Em Java:

BitSet a = new BitSet();
a.set(1);
a.set(3);
a.set(5);

BitSet b = new BitSet();
b.set(3);
b.set(4);
b.set(5);

a.and(b);

System.out.println(a); // {3, 5}

Uma operação AND sobre palavras de 64 bits consegue combinar até 64 posições por palavra processada.

Isso é especialmente útil quando precisamos comparar ou combinar grandes conjuntos de informações.

Onde os bitmaps são utilizados?

A representação por bits aparece em diferentes áreas da computação.

1. Bancos de dados

Bancos de dados podem utilizar bitmap indexes para representar conjuntos de registros que atendem a determinadas condições.

Imagine uma tabela de usuários com informações sobre status e permissões.

Um bitmap pode representar os usuários ativos:

Ativos:     1 0 1 1 0 1

Outro pode representar usuários com determinada permissão:

Permissão:  1 1 0 1 0 1

Aplicando AND:

Resultado:  1 0 0 1 0 1

O resultado identifica os registros que atendem às duas condições.

Essa ideia é utilizada em mecanismos de indexação de bancos como o Oracle, especialmente em cenários analíticos e colunas com poucos valores distintos.

Os índices bitmap possuem características próprias e não substituem automaticamente índices B-tree.

Referência: Oracle Database — Bitmap Indexes.

2. Sistemas operacionais

Bitmaps podem representar recursos livres ou ocupados.

Por exemplo, um sistema pode utilizar bits para acompanhar a disponibilidade de blocos de armazenamento ou unidades de alocação.

Um bit indica que o recurso está livre; outro estado indica que está ocupado.

Isso permite representar grandes quantidades de estados utilizando relativamente pouca memória.

3. Controle de permissões e flags

Bits também podem representar permissões independentes.

Considere três permissões:

int READ    = 1 << 0;
int WRITE   = 1 << 1;
int EXECUTE = 1 << 2;

Podemos combiná-las:

int permissions = READ | WRITE;

E consultar uma permissão:

boolean canWrite =
    (permissions & WRITE) != 0;

Esse exemplo utiliza uma máscara de bits dentro de um único inteiro, em vez de um bitset extensível, mas o princípio de representação binária é o mesmo.

4. Mecanismos de busca e processamento analítico

Conjuntos de identificadores podem ser representados por bitmaps para acelerar operações de interseção, união e filtragem.

Uma família de estruturas especialmente interessante é a dos Roaring Bitmaps.

Ela combina diferentes representações internas, incluindo arrays e estruturas baseadas em bits, para lidar eficientemente com conjuntos de inteiros de diferentes densidades.

O objetivo é equilibrar consumo de memória e desempenho.

Mais informações: Roaring Bitmaps.

Bitmap, array ou HashSet?

Apesar das vantagens, bitmap não é necessariamente a melhor escolha para qualquer conjunto de valores.

Considere um problema de pertencimento:

Estrutura Busca Característica
Array não ordenado O(n) Simples, compacto para conjuntos pequenos
Array ordenado com busca binária O(log n) Pouca memória e busca por divisão
HashSet O(1) esperado Flexível para diferentes tipos de chaves
Bitmap diretamente indexado O(1) Eficiente para domínios numéricos limitados

Um bitmap diretamente indexado reserva posições de acordo com o domínio dos valores.

Se precisamos representar números de 0 a 9999, isso é relativamente barato.

Mas se os identificadores estiverem distribuídos por um domínio numérico extremamente grande, reservar um bit para cada valor possível pode ser inviável.

Por exemplo, um conjunto contendo apenas os números 1, 100 e 1.000.000.000 ocuparia pouquíssima memória em um array.

Já um bitmap diretamente indexado precisaria representar mais de um bilhão de posições, consumindo aproximadamente 125 MB apenas para três elementos.

Nesse caso, um array ou uma estrutura hash provavelmente seria mais apropriado.

É por isso que existem também estruturas de bitmap comprimido.

A escolha ideal depende da quantidade de elementos, da extensão do domínio numérico, da densidade do conjunto, das operações necessárias e do perfil de acesso.

Bitmap e performance

Uma característica importante dessa estrutura é que o espaço total reservado não corresponde à quantidade de memória acessada em cada consulta.

Um bitmap pode reservar milhares de bits, mas uma consulta individual normalmente precisa acessar apenas a palavra que contém o bit desejado.

Isso pode tornar verificações de pertencimento bastante rápidas.

Por outro lado, um bitmap grande pode ocupar mais espaço nos caches da CPU quando muitas estruturas diferentes são utilizadas.

Arrays pequenos, por sua vez, podem apresentar excelente localidade de memória e ser competitivos mesmo utilizando busca linear.

Portanto, não basta observar a complexidade O(1) do bitmap ou O(n) do array para determinar qual implementação terá menor latência real.

É necessário considerar custos constantes, layout de memória, distribuição dos dados, comportamento da CPU e resultados de benchmarks representativos.

Conclusão

Bitmap é uma técnica de representação de dados simples em sua ideia fundamental, mas com aplicações importantes em diversas áreas da computação.

Sua história remonta aos primeiros computadores digitais, passando por programas de jogos na década de 1950, sistemas de bancos de dados e aplicações modernas de processamento de informações.

Ao representar estados e conjuntos por meio de bits, podemos aproveitar diretamente operações lógicas oferecidas pelos processadores.

Entretanto, seu principal valor não está apenas na velocidade.

Está em permitir que determinados problemas sejam representados de uma forma mais adequada às características dos dados.

Antes de escolher um array, uma tabela hash ou uma estrutura mais sofisticada, vale compreender o domínio dos valores e as operações necessárias.

A maneira como representamos os dados pode ser tão importante quanto o algoritmo utilizado para processá-los.

Referências

  • Computer Conservation Society — Christopher Strachey's Draughts Program
  • Arthur Samuel — Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers (1959)
  • Oracle — java.util.BitSet
  • Oracle Database — Bitmap Indexes
  • Roaring Bitmaps

Today, AWS announces the general availability of the metal size for Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) G7 instances, accelerated by NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. G7 instances deliver up to 4.6x AI inference performance and up to 2.1x graphics performance compared to G6.
