title: How to Compare Cloud Storage Providers for Direct Browser Uploads — Go
description:
Short answer: compare the tenant boundary before comparing upload latency. For a logistics receipt workflow, the browser should receive a short-lived upload URL for one server-selected object key, while the storage policy must prevent that URL from crossing tenants. S3, Cloudflare R2, and Wasabi can all be evaluated through that same contract because the important test is the trust boundary: who chooses the bucket, key, headers, and expiry, and what happens when a client retries?

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. Those alerts changed how I look at direct uploads. A successful HTTP response is not proof that the receipt is attached to the right shipment. A retry can create a second object, and a copied upload URL can expose another tenant's prefix. The provider comparison belongs after those cases are defined.

What can a browser upload safely?

The browser needs permission to send bytes, not permission to invent identity. The application authenticates the operator, resolves the tenant and shipment on the server, and creates an object key from trusted values. The response can contain an upload URL, an expiry, and the exact headers the browser must send. It should not accept a client-supplied bucket or an arbitrary key as an authority decision.

For example, the key can be derived from an internal tenant ID and receipt ID:

package upload

import "fmt"

func receiptKey(tenantID, receiptID string) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("receipts/%s/%s/original", tenantID, receiptID)
}

That function is deliberately boring. Its input should already be validated identifiers, not a path copied from the browser. Keep the original file under a stable key, record the expected content length and media type in the database, and make the receipt ID idempotent. If the request is retried, the service returns the same pending upload record instead of creating a second logical receipt.

CORS is part of the browser contract, not an access-control substitute. The storage endpoint must allow the application origin and the required request method and headers, while the authorization decision remains in the signed request and storage policy. MDN's CORS guidance is useful here because a browser may block a response even when the server received the request; that is an operational failure mode worth testing separately.

Where did the tenant boundary fail?

The incident shape is easy to reproduce. Tenant A requests a receipt URL, then a worker or test tool changes the key to receipts/tenant-b/... before sending the request. A second case uses a valid URL after its intended expiry. A third sends a different content type than the one signed. These are not throughput tests. They answer whether the URL represents one narrow capability or a general storage credential.

I start with a matrix and keep the expected result explicit:

Test Expected result Why it matters
Valid key and signed headers Upload succeeds Confirms the normal browser path
Key changed to another tenant Rejected Tests tenant isolation
Signed URL after expiry Rejected Limits copied links
Same receipt request repeated Same logical receipt Prevents duplicate delivery records
Interrupted large upload resumed One finalized object Tests retry behavior

The last row deserves care. A multipart upload is a sequence, not one request. S3's multipart documentation describes separate initiation, part uploads, and completion, which means the application needs a cleanup policy for abandoned uploads. The browser can retry a part, but the service still needs to know which receipt owns that upload and when an incomplete upload should be removed.

Here is the server-side shape I use for the authorization decision. The signer is intentionally an interface, so the same test suite can exercise different S3-compatible backends without turning the article into a provider setup guide.

package upload

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Signer interface {
    PresignPut(ctx context.Context, bucket, key, contentType string, expires time.Duration) (string, error)
}

type ReceiptRequest struct {
    TenantID    string
    ReceiptID   string
    ContentType string
}

func CreateUpload(ctx context.Context, s Signer, r ReceiptRequest) (string, string, error) {
    if r.TenantID == "" || r.ReceiptID == "" || r.ContentType == "" {
        return "", "", errors.New("missing receipt identity or content type")
    }

    key := receiptKey(r.TenantID, r.ReceiptID)
    url, err := s.PresignPut(ctx, "receipts", key, r.ContentType, 10*time.Minute)
    if err != nil {
        return "", "", fmt.Errorf("presign receipt upload: %w", err)
    }
    return key, url, nil
}

The ten-minute value is an example policy, not a universal setting. Choose it from the expected upload duration, clock skew, and the consequences of a leaked URL. Persist the key and an upload state such as pending, complete, or expired; do not infer completion solely from the browser's callback. A worker can verify the object metadata, then atomically mark the receipt complete.

How should I compare cloud storage providers for direct browser uploads?

The protocol surface is similar enough to make a common test harness practical, but “S3-compatible” does not mean identical operations or identical operational behavior. S3 is the reference point for the multipart and lifecycle concepts in the supplied documentation. R2 exposes an S3-compatible API and documents presigned URLs, while Wasabi documents presigned URL workflows. For this use case, the difference to measure is the surrounding behavior: endpoint configuration, policy language, CORS controls, multipart limits, lifecycle cleanup, and the observability available to explain a rejected upload.

I would record the result as evidence rather than as a ranking:

Provider surface Check in the harness Decision signal
S3 API behavior Presigned PUT, multipart completion, lifecycle rule Does the workflow match the retention and cleanup model?
R2 S3-compatible endpoint Signature, endpoint, CORS, multipart behavior Are endpoint-specific settings explicit in deployment configuration?
Wasabi S3-compatible endpoint Signature, bucket policy, CORS, multipart behavior Can the same tenant-denial tests run without hidden exceptions?

No row answers tenant isolation by itself. A bucket policy can be carefully written and still be undermined by an application that signs the wrong key. Conversely, an application can derive the right key and still fail browser uploads because CORS does not allow the signed headers. Keep those layers separate in logs and tests.

Avoid making price the deciding argument. Storage and request economics change, and the receipt workflow has costs that a headline comparison misses: abandoned multipart parts, reprocessing, audit retention, cross-region movement, and the engineer-hours needed to diagnose a provider-specific rejection. A neutral comparison should carry those variables as measured inputs, not as a permanent cheapest-provider claim.

What should happen when the browser or worker retries?

A receipt has two identities: the business identity and the object identity. The business identity might be (tenant_id, receipt_id). The object identity is the server-derived key. Make the database uniqueness constraint match the first one, and make the key deterministic from it. That is the simplest guard against duplicate delivery records.

For completion, accept an event or callback only after checking the tenant, receipt ID, object key, size, and expected media type. Then use a compare-and-set transition so two workers cannot both perform the final side effect. The original file remains available for audit, while downstream processing can use a separate derived object or record.

A small state machine is easier to page on than a pile of booleans:

package upload

type State string

const (
    Pending  State = "pending"
    Complete State = "complete"
    Expired  State = "expired"
)

func CanComplete(current State, key, expectedKey string) bool {
    return current == Pending && key == expectedKey
}

The real implementation must perform the transition transactionally and verify object metadata through the storage API. This helper only makes the invariant visible: an expired or already-complete receipt cannot be completed by a late retry.

For large files, use multipart upload only when the reliability benefit outweighs the cleanup and state-management cost. The browser needs a resumable plan; the service needs an abort path and a scheduled check for stale uploads. S3's lifecycle documentation covers lifecycle management as a storage-side control, but the application still needs a receipt state and an audit trail. Storage cleanup cannot tell you whether a shipment's original was successfully processed.

The runbook I would ship

First, log a request ID, tenant ID, receipt ID, object key, provider label, and upload state. Do not log the signed URL. Second, alert on pending receipts older than the normal upload window, failed completions by tenant, and growth in incomplete multipart uploads. Third, keep a replay-safe reconciliation job that compares pending records with object metadata and makes no assumption that one notification arrived exactly once.

Before deployment, run the matrix against each configured endpoint from a real browser origin. Repeat it after changing CORS, signing libraries, bucket policies, or endpoint settings. Include clock skew in the test environment. A green unit test around key construction is valuable, but it cannot prove that a browser preflight, signature check, and storage policy agree.

The advice has a boundary. If receipts are tiny, uploads are infrequent, and the server already handles the file safely, a direct browser path may add more lifecycle work than it removes. The trade-off is operational: this design does not fit a team that cannot maintain upload state, validate object metadata, or operate cleanup for abandoned multipart work; choose a server-mediated upload when that control plane would be simpler. If an auditor requires immutable retention, add the relevant retention and deletion controls to the decision record; a presigned URL is an upload mechanism, not an audit policy.

The provider choice should be the final implementation detail. The durable decision is that a tenant can upload only the object the server assigned, retries preserve one receipt identity, and operators can explain every pending or rejected upload. That contract gives S3, R2, and Wasabi a fair test, and it keeps a storage outage from becoming an accounting mystery.

Sources

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://docs.wasabi.com/docs/how-do-i-create-a-pre-signed-url

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Branded caller ID label was truncated in the Outbound Number selector when the agent application language was set to French Canadian.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls experienced significant delays in connecting after being assigned to an agent.

  • Fixed an issue where whisper announcements played more than once and the call panel was slow to load in the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce case creation was delayed until the end of a call for inbound callers without a matching contact record.

  • Fixed an issue where callbacks to Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish landline numbers were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix, causing the calls to fail.

  • Fixed an issue where merged call recordings incorrectly reported only the duration of the first segment in the Calls API.

  • Salesforce account linking now completes only in the browser that started it. An authorization link opened in another browser or an incognito window is refused and can't be reused afterwards, and an administrator's Link New User action must be finished by the same signed-in administrator. Android and iOS agent apps link as before. This behavior is off by default and can be enabled per instance.

  • Fixed an issue that affected call connection stability during active calls for instances using Agent Assist.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent callback calls incorrectly required manual acceptance even when queues were configured for Auto-Answer.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx and Twilio virtual agent calls remained stuck in a connected state for an extended period if the carrier didn't send a terminal status callback.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS replies to auto-dismissed chats were incorrectly recorded as an agent timeout instead of an end-user timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where the Unanswered Transferred Call Expiration setting wasn't enforced for calls parked in an overcapacity deflection state.

  • Fixed an issue that affected connection stability and prevented calls from being accurately recorded as end-user hangups when callers hung up while waiting in a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing the queue service level field.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were disconnected when an agent finished their wrap-up following a queue transfer to a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls escalated from a virtual agent to a human agent reported inaccurate call-level queue and wait durations in reporting and data exports.

  • Fixed an issue where unrecorded voicemails incorrectly created Salesforce cases even when the Create CRM records for abandoned calls setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where activating a new language in the CCaaS portal caused the Languages & Messages page to crash or display an infinite loading spinner.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata files were duplicated across different day folders in external storage when re-uploads occurred after midnight.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became permanently stuck in a queued status without reaching a terminal state.

  • Fixed an issue where active agents were incorrectly signed out due to inactivity because the system didn't recognize activity outside the embedded call panel.

  • Fixed an issue where a permanent loading spinner appeared in the agent desktop top bar for instances with the email channel disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound keypad (DTMF) entries didn't reach the virtual agent during periods of stream instability or reconnection.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing required parameters.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls involving a virtual agent didn't record an end time and duration when deflected to an overcapacity queue.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings weren't fetched or saved when CRM ticket creation failed.

  • Fixed an issue where after-hours phone deflections didn't appear in the Deflections dashboard if the outbound dial timed out or failed.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled phone number obfuscation caused degraded performance for live calls.

  • Fixed an issue where CRM ticket assignees weren't consistently updated following an agent's pickup of a chat.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became stuck in a queued state after a caller selected a callback during a cold transfer to a specific agent.

  • Fixed an issue where Smart Disposition suggestions weren't pre-selected on the wrap-up screen, causing the disposition field to remain empty after a call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were incorrectly routed to agents even when the minimum available agent floor wasn't met.

  • Fixed an issue where cold transfers to a direct agent extension didn't trigger overcapacity deflection, leaving callers on hold until they disconnected.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent replies were cut off or silenced when using bidirectional streaming with barge-in disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where JSON chat transcripts in external storage contained unredacted message text even when the setting to store unredacted transcripts was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where the Keep Waiting label in the overcapacity deflection screen displayed an inconsistent font style compared to other menu options.

*useCallback *

-> When depedency values changes it creates a new function reference

eg:

const display = useCallback(() => {
console.log(count);
}, [count]);

count same → same function reference
count changed → new function reference

react compare the previous value {count} and the current value {count}

title: Project setup — Fastify with TypeScript (part 3/18)
description:
Project setup

Third chapter of the "Fastify with TypeScript" series. Before writing a single line of business logic, you need a properly configured project: a package.json, two tsconfig files (one for type-checking, one for the production build), and a folder structure that scales. At the end of the chapter we'll run four commands to check that everything works.

Requirements: Node.js ≥ 22.19 (24 LTS recommended) and TypeScript 6.x. Type stripping runs flag-free from Node 22.19 / 23.6 / 24; on older 22.x you'd need --experimental-strip-types.

Initialization 

mkdir my-fastify-app && cd my-fastify-app
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install fastify
npm install -D typescript@6 @types/node
mkdir src test

package.json

npm init created a package.json for you. Open it and change three fields, main, scripts and engines, leaving everything else as it is (in particular the dependencies and devDependencies that npm just wrote):

{
  "name": "my-fastify-app",
  "type": "module",
  "main": "dist/server.js",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "node --watch --env-file-if-exists=.env src/server.ts",
    "build": "tsc -p tsconfig.build.json",
    "start": "node --env-file-if-exists=.env dist/server.js",
    "test": "node --test 'test/**/*.test.ts'",
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit"
  },
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=22.19.0"
  }
}

node --watch restarts the server on every file change and --env-file-if-exists loads a local .env when there is one, so the project never needs dotenv. start uses the same flag so you can run the built output locally; in production there is no .env file and the variables come from the real environment. Note that typescript is only a devDependency: in development Node runs the .ts files directly.

.env and .gitignore

Create the .env file now, even though it only holds one value for the moment:

echo "PORT=3000" > .env
printf 'node_modules\ndist\n.env\n' > .gitignore

Two reasons. The .env file will soon contain secrets, so it must never be committed: that's what the .gitignore line is for. And in watch mode Node also watches the .env file for changes, so on some versions npm run dev stops with an ENOENT error if the file isn't there.

tsconfig.json (type-checking)

This file is only used by tsc --noEmit and by your editor: the code is executed by Node with type stripping, no compilation involved.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2024",
    "lib": ["ES2024"],
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "types": ["node"],
    "rootDir": ".",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts", "test/**/*.ts"]
}

A few notes specific to TypeScript 6:

  • strict is now true by default, but we keep it explicit so the intent is obvious to anyone reading the file.
  • types is no longer auto-discovered (it defaults to []), so ["node"] is required or process, Buffer and friends won't exist.
  • rootDir is no longer inferred from your sources; set it explicitly.
  • erasableSyntaxOnly makes the compiler reject the TypeScript syntax that Node's type stripping can't handle (see the note below). This is the single most useful flag in this file.
  • verbatimModuleSyntax forces import type for type-only imports, which type stripping requires.
  • allowImportingTsExtensions + rewriteRelativeImportExtensions let you write import './app.ts' (what Node needs at runtime) and have tsc rewrite it to ./app.js in the build output.

tsconfig.build.json (production build) 

{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "noEmit": false,
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "declaration": true,
    "sourceMap": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"]
}

A note on type stripping: Node removes type annotations without transforming code, so your source must avoid the TypeScript features that generate JavaScript: enum, namespace, constructor parameter properties (constructor(private x: string)) and import x = require(). With erasableSyntaxOnly: true, tsc reports an error on each of these, so you find out before Node does. Decorators are the exception: tsc accepts them, but Node can't run them, so the series doesn't use them. Finally, always use import type for types, and import local files with their .ts extension.

Check that it works

There is no application yet, so let's write a throwaway entry point just to try the four scripts. We'll replace it in the next chapter.

// src/server.ts — temporary: we replace it in the next chapter
const port: number = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

console.log(`Setup works. The server will listen on port ${port}.`);

npm run typecheck   # prints nothing: no type errors
npm run dev         # Setup works. The server will listen on port 3000.

npm run dev stays alive waiting for changes: edit the message, save, and it runs again. Stop it with Ctrl+C, then try the production path:

npm run build       # creates dist/server.js (plus .d.ts and source map)
npm start           # same message, this time from the compiled JavaScript

One last experiment, to see erasableSyntaxOnly earn its place. Add this line at the end of src/server.ts:

enum Color { Red }

npm run typecheck now fails with This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled, and Node itself refuses to run the file (TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode). Remove the line before going on.

Recommended project structure

This is where the project is heading over the next chapters:

src/
  app.ts               # builds the Fastify instance (no listen() here)
  server.ts            # entry point: imports app.ts and starts the server
  config.ts            # environment variables validated against a schema
  plugins/             # shared plugins (database, auth, security...)
  users/               # one folder per module, with everything that module needs
    users.route.ts       # the route plugin: routes + handlers
    users.schema.ts      # TypeBox schemas
    users.service.ts     # business logic and domain errors (chapter 13)
    users.repository.ts  # data access (chapter 13)
  auth/
    auth.route.ts
    auth.schema.ts
    auth.service.ts      # login rules (chapter 13)
test/
  helper.ts
  users.test.ts
  users.service.test.ts

The code is grouped by module, not by technical layer: there is no top-level routes/, services/ or repositories/ folder, and no modules/ wrapper either. Each module is a folder directly under src/: everything about users lives in src/users/, so working on a feature means working in one folder, and removing a feature means deleting one. plugins/ is the only folder that isn't a module: it holds the infrastructure shared by all of them.

Separating app.ts from server.ts is a very common convention in the Fastify ecosystem: app.ts exports a factory function that builds and configures the Fastify instance (routes, plugins, hooks) without ever binding to a network port; server.ts is the only file responsible for starting the listener. The main benefit is that in your tests you can import buildApp() from app.ts and use inject() without opening a TCP port (we'll cover this in the testing chapter).

⬅️ Previous chapter: Fastify core concepts · ➡️ Next chapter: Your first server (app.ts, server.ts, config.ts)

This article is part of the "Fastify with TypeScript" series — chapter 3 of 18.

title: Lazy-Loading Images on Guide Pages Only — Never on Tool Pages
description:
I made a lazy-loading decision on ramrom.io that sounds backwards at first: the guide pages lazy-load their images, and the tool pages do not lazy-load anything at all. It is not an oversight. It is the one place where I deliberately do not apply a performance best practice, because on the tool pages it would make things worse.

The two kinds of page

The site has two kinds of page, and they behave very differently. A tool page is one job: paste a link, tap download, get the file. It has almost no images — a logo, maybe a small illustration in the 3-step guide, and that is it. A guide page is a long read, a couple of thousand words explaining how a downloader works or what to watch out for, with screenshots and diagrams scattered down the page.

That split is what drives the decision. Lazy loading exists to stop the browser downloading images the visitor may never scroll to. On a guide page that is a real win: most readers never reach the bottom, so why fetch every screenshot up front? On a tool page there is nothing below the fold worth deferring. Every image on the page is already visible, so lazy-loading it would only delay something the visitor needs right now.

What the guide pages do

On guide pages every content image gets loading="lazy" and decoding="async", and — this is the part people skip — explicit width and height attributes. The lazy attribute stops the download until the image nears the viewport. The width and height stop the page jumping when the image finally arrives, because the browser reserves the space before it knows the file.

That last point matters more than the lazy loading itself. I chased layout shift to zero on the tool pages and I am not about to reintroduce it on the guides. A page that reflows while you read is worse than a page that loads a fraction slower. So the rule on guides is: lazy, but with the box already reserved.

I also keep the first image on a guide page eager. It is usually the header illustration, it sits above the fold, and deferring it would delay the largest contentful paint for no benefit. The lazy attribute goes on everything from the second image down.

What the tool pages do instead

Tool pages carry no loading="lazy" at all. The logo and the 3-step visual guide are above the fold and part of the first paint, so the browser should fetch them immediately. Making them lazy would mean the logo pops in a beat after the rest of the page, which looks broken, and it would push the largest contentful paint later on the exact pages where speed matters most — the pages a visitor lands on, uses, and leaves in under a minute.

The deeper reason is that tool pages barely have images in the first place. The whole homepage stays under 100KB. There is no hero photograph, no carousel, no stock imagery. When a page has two small images, the optimisation is not lazy loading; it is not having a dozen images to defer. The performance budget is enforced by what I choose not to put on the page, not by clever attributes.

The check that keeps me honest

The rule is simple enough to test by hand. Open a guide page, watch the network tab, and confirm only the first image loads before scrolling. Open a tool page and confirm everything is there on first paint with no pop-in. If a new guide image ever ships without width and height, the layout shift shows up immediately in the field data, and that is the signal to fix it.

Lazy loading is a good default. It is just not a universal one. The question is never "should I lazy-load images" — it is "which images does the visitor actually need right now". On my site the answer splits cleanly down the middle: guides, yes, from the second image down; tool pages, no, because everything on them is already the job.

title: NariQ: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file
description:
We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding.

To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.

Benchmarks (BF16 / 3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit):

- DeepSWE: 39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6

- Terminal-Bench 2.1: 62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4

- AIME 25+26: 97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0

- MSGM: 94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6

- RealWorldQA: 82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9

Decode speed is comparable to other quants on an RTX PRO 6000. Context-length results below

(3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit / Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS):

- 4K: 88.9 / 99.2 / 111.7 / 94.7

- 16K: 84.5 / 93.8 / 105.1 / 89.8

- 64K: 70.7 / 77.5 / 85.0 / 74.8

Running these currently require our llama.cpp fork: (https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp)

Feedback and questions welcome. We'd love to hear how these perform on your workloads.

title: Replaceable Object Storage Service for Signed SaaS File Export Download URLs
description:
Object storage with presigned download URLs is the simplest fit for private e-commerce media and export files when customers need temporary access, not permanent public URLs. Keep the bucket private. Let the application decide who owns each object, then mint a short-lived link only after authorization.

TL;DR: put a narrow ExportStore contract between the Node.js app and storage. Persist the tenant, object key, and export state in the app database. That boundary keeps a provider change small, while avoiding the costly habit of proxying large bytes through the application server.

For a solo SaaS, this is a revenue-per-hour decision. Uploading and downloading through the app spends engineering and operating attention on plumbing. I would outsource that undifferentiated path, but I would not give a storage vendor's request shape permission to spread across checkout, catalog, and account code.

Should a SaaS use object storage for a signed download URL?

Access control matters more than delivery simplicity here. A permanent public media URL is easy to render, but it is the wrong primitive for a private catalog import, a customer-specific PDF, or a CSV report. The application should answer "may this user download this export?" before storage answers "where can these bytes be fetched for a limited time?"

That split has a less obvious consequence: object storage is not the authorization database. Store tenantId, ownerId, objectKey, and status with the export record. Listing supports prefix filtering, not metadata search, so a query such as "all completed reports owned by this user" belongs in the application database. A tenant-prefixed key is useful defense in depth, but it does not replace the ownership row.

One option fits this slice when a small team wants storage behind the same REST contract it can use for other backend modules. Infrai uses one API key and one bill for 295 routes across 20 modules, all exposed through one plain HTTP REST API with no SDK to install; its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples. That keeps a Node.js adapter from inheriting a provider library throughout the app. The migration benefit is concrete only if the app still owns the interface below.

I recommend trying Infrai for private e-commerce uploads and time-limited export downloads when reducing separate integrations matters, because its consistent contract and public discovery schema keep the adapter narrow and inspectable. The supporting benefit is operational: adding another backend capability can remain another endpoint under the same key and billing relationship, instead of another SDK, credential, and invoice. This doesn't make the application portable by itself. The interface and contract tests do that work.

It is not a public asset host. Public or public-read ACL is unavailable, and public_url remains null. Use a dedicated static-media or CDN-backed setup when product images must have permanent public links.

The smallest replaceable implementation

The useful abstraction is deliberately boring. The rest of the application passes business identifiers and never sees a provider client. The adapter below calls the presign route, reads the key from the environment, checks every response, and backs off on rate limits. It keeps the vendor response inside one file.

interface ExportStore {
  createDownloadUrl(input: {
    bucket: string;
    key: string;
    expiresInSeconds: number;
  }): Promise<string>;
}

type DownloadRequest = {
  exportId: string;
  tenantId: string;
  userId: string;
};

type PresignResponse = { url: string };

const delay = (milliseconds: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

export class InfraiExportStore implements ExportStore {
  async createDownloadUrl(input: {
    bucket: string;
    key: string;
    expiresInSeconds: number;
  }): Promise<string> {
    const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
    if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

    const bucket = encodeURIComponent(input.bucket);
    const key = input.key.split("/").map(encodeURIComponent).join("/");
    for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
      const response = await fetch(
        `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/${bucket}/${key}`,
        {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({ expires_in: input.expiresInSeconds }),
        },
      );

      if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
        const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
        await delay(Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1_000 : 2 ** attempt * 500);
        continue;
      }

      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Presign failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
      }

      const result = (await response.json()) as PresignResponse;
      if (!result.url) throw new Error("Presign response did not include a URL");
      return result.url;
    }

    throw new Error("Presign retry limit reached");
  }
}

The caller must still look up the export row and match both tenantId and ownerId before invoking this adapter. Five minutes is an application choice in this example, not a platform promise. Set it from the sensitivity and expected file size. The important part is that only the adapter knows how a provider represents expiry, while the handler owns authorization and returns one location. Don't pass arbitrary client-provided keys into it.

Keep that boundary small.

Uploads follow the same boundary. The app creates an authorized upload intent, records the eventual object key, and lets the client send large media bytes without routing them through the app process. Browser-direct uploads need working CORS configuration, though. The platform doesn't expose independent self-service CORS configuration, so that requirement can move the decision to a direct provider.

Where each option earns its place

There is no universal winner. AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Alibaba Cloud OSS, and Tencent Cloud COS are direct choices when a team wants to own the provider relationship and its specialist controls. The aggregated option can route storage across S3, R2, OSS, and COS behind one surface; it does not cover Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2. B2 therefore belongs on the direct-provider shortlist.

Option Best fit in this workflow Boundary to examine
AWS S3 A direct specialist integration is acceptable More provider-specific application and operational coupling
Cloudflare R2 R2 is already the chosen storage relationship Use the direct surface when self-managed provider controls matter
Alibaba Cloud OSS The deployment is already centered on OSS Direct integration trades portability for provider control
Tencent Cloud COS COS is the established object store The app owns the COS-specific adapter and migration work
Backblaze B2 B2 is a deliberate direct-provider choice It is outside Infrai's current storage vendor coverage
Aggregated REST API One contract across several backend capabilities is valuable No permanent public URLs, versioning, object lock, or cross-region replication

This limitation is a fair place to be strict. If immutable retention, recovery from accidental overwrite, automatic cross-region replication, or bulk cross-cloud migration is a requirement, a direct specialist is the better choice. Infrai isn't suitable there: it has no object versioning or object lock, no automatic cross-region replication, and no bulk migration tool. Strict concurrent writes also need queue or database coordination because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable.

Those are architecture limits, not footnotes.

What I would change at scale

First, I would make object keys collision-resistant and tenant-scoped, then put creation and completion states in the database. Retries for a write need an idempotency key so an interrupted request cannot apply twice. Infrai specifies Idempotency-Key as a platform convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window, but the application should still reconcile its own export state.

Second, I would add a retention policy. Lifecycle cleanup can delete old exports, with a minimum retention of 1 day. That works for nightly cleanup of reports, but it cannot enforce hour-level deletion. Multipart fragments also lack an automatic cleanup rule, so upload abandonment needs explicit operational handling. This trade-off is easy to miss during a quick prototype: URL expiry stops later access through that link, while lifecycle retention governs when the stored object is deleted. They are separate clocks, and the database should make the distinction visible to support and operations.

Finally, I would test migration instead of declaring it. Keep contract tests that upload a small fixture, request a temporary URL, download it, and verify the bytes. Run the same suite against each adapter before moving production objects. Ship weekly, but keep the exit door unlocked.

The decision rule is short: use private object storage plus temporary links for delayed customer downloads; use a specialist or direct provider when public hosting, browser CORS control, immutable retention, provider-specific controls, or unsupported vendors dominate the design. If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage discovery schema before implementing the adapter.

Further reading

  • Infrai storage presign discovery
  • MDN: Content-Disposition
  • Backblaze B2 pricing and service overview

title: I Built Two AI Tools for Developers – Here's What I'm Learning Along the Way
description:
Building AI-powered tools sounds exciting, but turning an idea into something developers can actually use is a completely different experience.

I've been working on two projects as part of my development journey: Elite Article Engine and MakeYourUI.

Both solve different problems, but they share one goal: making AI more useful in real-world development workflows.

I wanted to share what I've been building, some of the challenges I've faced, and get honest feedback from the developer community.

1. Elite Article Engine – More Than Just an AI Writer

Most AI writing tools focus on generating text. But generating 2,000 words doesn't necessarily mean producing a useful technical article.

That's one of the problems I wanted to address with Elite Article Engine.

I'm building it around a research-driven content generation workflow.

Some of its features include:

  • Real-time research to provide relevant information before generation.
  • AI-powered article structure and topic-specific headings.
  • Technical explanations with practical examples.
  • Code playgrounds and working code examples.
  • Charts and visual elements where they make sense.
  • Automatically selected diagrams, including flowcharts, mind maps, timelines, and lifecycle diagrams.

One particularly challenging part is selecting the right diagram for each topic.

For example, a comparison between Java and Python needs a different visual structure from an article explaining a software development lifecycle.

I'm continuously improving the selection logic and content quality because I don't want the tool to generate visuals just for decoration.

Project: https://makemychance.com/elite-engine2/

2. MakeYourUI – Generate Frontend Code From Natural Language

My second project, MakeYourUI, focuses on frontend development.

The concept is simple: select your technology stack, describe the interface you want, and generate frontend code.

Some of its capabilities include:

  • Generate UI components from text prompts.
  • Support for different CSS and JavaScript frameworks.
  • Generate interfaces using Tailwind, Bootstrap, React, Vue, Next.js, Svelte, Angular, and more.
  • Upload an image or Figma screenshot as a reference.
  • Preview generated interfaces directly in the browser.
  • Inspect and copy the generated code.
  • Refine an existing design using additional prompts.
  • Test layouts at different viewport sizes.

I particularly wanted to make the generated output accessible to developers rather than limiting everything to a static visual result.

There is still room for improvement in code consistency, complex layouts, and maintainability, but that's part of the development process.

Project: https://makemychance.com/makeyourui/

3. What Building These Projects Has Taught Me

Working on both products has given me a different perspective on AI development.

A few things I've learned:

  • Better prompts alone don't guarantee better results.
  • Research and context are important for reliable AI-generated content.
  • Generated code should be editable, understandable, and reusable.
  • Visual quality and code quality are two different things.
  • Adding more features doesn't automatically make a product better.
  • Real user feedback is essential for improving an AI product.

One thing I've realized is that AI tools should help developers work more efficiently, not create another layer of complexity.

4. I'd Like Feedback From the Developer Community

These projects are still evolving, and I'd genuinely appreciate feedback from developers who work with frontend technologies, AI tools, and content generation.

I'm particularly interested in a few questions:

  1. What do you think is the biggest limitation of current AI article generators?
  2. When using an AI UI generator, would you prefer generating complete pages or individual reusable components?
  3. How important is screenshot-to-code functionality in your frontend workflow?
  4. What would make an AI-generated codebase easier to maintain?
  5. Which features would you actually use in tools like these?

You can explore both projects here:

  • Elite Article Engine: https://makemychance.com/elite-engine2/
  • MakeYourUI: https://makemychance.com/makeyourui/

I'm building these products and would rather receive honest technical criticism than generic praise.

If you've tried similar tools, I'd love to hear what worked, what didn't, and what you think is still missing.

title: Website Design Associations
description:
Website Design Associations: A Critical Examination of Conventional Approaches

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, it is imperative to acknowledge the shortcomings of standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms in website design. These conventional approaches often fail to deliver optimal results due to their inherent lack of customization and adaptability to specific business needs. The one-size-fits-all methodology neglects the unique value proposition, brand identity, and target audience of each organization, ultimately leading to a subpar user experience and diminished conversion rates.

A deeper analysis reveals that generic templates and forms are designed to cater to a broad spectrum of users, resulting in a diluted and unremarkable design that fails to resonate with the intended audience. Furthermore, the absence of a tailored approach to website design associations leads to a disconnect between the user's expectations and the actual experience, culminating in increased bounce rates and decreased engagement.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key takeaways that can be derived from this analysis:

  1. Customization is crucial: A bespoke approach to website design, one that takes into account the specific needs and objectives of the organization, is essential for creating a compelling and effective user experience.
  2. User-centric design is paramount: The design process should be informed by a deep understanding of the target audience, including their preferences, behaviors, and pain points, to ensure that the website meets their needs and expectations.
  3. Data-driven decision making is essential: The use of data analytics and user feedback should be integral to the design process, allowing for iterative improvements and optimizations that enhance the overall user experience and conversion rates.

In conclusion, the limitations of standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms in website design are clear. To create a truly effective and engaging online presence, organizations must adopt a more nuanced and tailored approach to website design associations.

title: Amazon CloudFront Announces HTTP/2 Support for Connections to Origins
description:
Amazon CloudFront now supports HTTP/2 connections to custom origins and VPC origins. HTTP/2 lets CloudFront send many requests over fewer connections to your origin. This means fewer connections and TLS handshakes for your origin to handle, which improves performance for API and agentic workloads, such as AI agents calling MCP servers or mobile and web apps calling backend APIs.

Until now, CloudFront connected to origins only over HTTP/1.1, which handles one request at a time per connection. When traffic spiked, for example when an AI agent made many tool calls at once, CloudFront had to open more origin connections. Each new connection added latency and load. With HTTP/2, those requests share connections, so your origin does less work and responds faster. HTTP/2 is also supported for WebSocket connections that support extended CONNECT. If your origin doesn't support HTTP/2, CloudFront automatically falls back to HTTP/1.1, so you don't need to change anything on your origin.

HTTP/2 to origins is available from all CloudFront edge locations. There is no additional cost for using HTTP/2 to origins. To learn more, visit Origin HTTP version in the CloudFront Developer Guide.

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.

title: How to Schedule Storage for Saving User Documents: Throughput Signals
description:
Short answer: for saving user documents, compare storage adapters with interrupted multi-gigabyte uploads and duplicate retention jobs; select the integration whose recovery and audit boundaries fit the training pipeline.

The decision rule is straightforward: schedule retention from a durable manifest, and choose the storage adapter that keeps large training artifacts moving after an interrupted transfer. Small-document upload latency is not a useful proxy for this workload.

For a B2B SaaS training pipeline, I would test a 10 MB document, a 500 MB archive, and a multi-gigabyte artifact before committing to an integration. Record completed bytes, retry count, p50 and p95 upload time, and the time until the object is readable. Then make retention a versioned state transition rather than a nightly script that guesses what is safe to delete.

That approach answers the practical question behind comparing storage services for user documents. The service name matters less than the transfer boundary, authorization model, event behavior, and evidence available when a scheduled job runs twice. I used to treat the upload callback as the finish line; missed jobs and duplicate deliveries are why I now treat it as an input to reconciliation.

The scheduler is the boundary.

At first, I assumed a successful upload response was enough to start training. The failure appears later: a worker receives two completion events, one manifest write is delayed, and a retention pass sees a different state from the processor. That chain is why the verification record needs the object identity, byte count, policy revision, and downstream enqueue result together. When a 4 GB transfer fails near completion, those fields tell the on-call engineer whether to resume, inspect, or safely replay the job; without them, the team is left comparing timestamps and guessing which copy is authoritative.

How should storage handle saving user documents at scale?

An uploaded training artifact is both data and a future job. The bytes may be a compressed dataset, an evaluation bundle, or an exported notebook. The scheduler later decides whether that object is active, eligible for deletion, or already gone. Those decisions need a stable identity.

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat an upload-complete notification as an at-least-once signal. It is not proof that the manifest was committed, the checksum was verified, or downstream processing succeeded. A worker must be safe to run twice. Boring retries are a design requirement.

Use a key that includes the tenant identifier, training-run identifier, artifact identifier, and schema version. Do not put an expiration date in the key. Retention rules change; object names tend to survive those policy changes. Keep the policy revision, checksum algorithm, byte count, and lifecycle state in a database manifest.

The object store owns bytes. The manifest explains why they should still exist.

How should the large-file path be measured?

Measure the failure path.

Start with a failure late in the transfer. Interrupt a 4 GB artifact after several gigabytes, retry with the same artifact identity, and compare resumed work with a second full upload. A happy-path benchmark hides the most expensive mistake: a retry that starts over while the first attempt still occupies bandwidth or storage.

The test harness should hold constant the region class, object sizes, concurrency, retry budget, checksum rule, and client/server path. Run direct client uploads separately from server-mediated uploads. Proxying a multi-gigabyte object through an application instance changes memory pressure, connection failure behavior, and throughput, so combining those measurements produces a misleading result.

I would record these fields for every attempt:

  • artifact identity and policy revision
  • attempt number and bytes acknowledged
  • checksum algorithm and final object generation
  • authorization result and time to readable state
  • event delivery delay and retention-deletion confirmation time

The comparison target is not a single upload speed. It is the amount of coordination required to make the result trustworthy. Supabase Storage documents an S3-compatible protocol and database-backed policy integration. Firebase Cloud Storage for Firebase uses Google Cloud Storage buckets with Firebase Security Rules. Amazon S3 exposes multipart upload primitives. Those are different integration boundaries, not a ranking.

Test each behind the same application interface. A useful result says which adapter resumes an interrupted transfer, how incomplete work is cleaned up, and which system owns the final authorization decision. It does not declare a universal winner.

Build the retention state machine before the worker

Keep the first state machine small: active, eligible, deleting, and deleted. The upload path creates an active manifest only after identity and size verification. A policy evaluation moves it to eligible with the policy revision that made the decision. A scheduled worker claims it, attempts deletion, and records the response. A retry can safely inspect the object and repeat the operation.

The application boundary should expose generic operations, not provider-specific calls. Here is a compact Go shape for a storage adapter and an upload verification step:

package retention

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
)

type ObjectStore interface {
    Put(ctx context.Context, key string, body io.Reader, size int64) error
    Head(ctx context.Context, key string) (size int64, generation string, err error)
    Delete(ctx context.Context, key string) error
}

type Manifest struct {
    Key            string
    Size           int64
    Generation     string
    PolicyRevision string
    State          string
}

func VerifyUpload(ctx context.Context, store ObjectStore, key string, expectedSize int64) (Manifest, error) {
    gotSize, generation, err := store.Head(ctx, key)
    if err != nil {
        return Manifest{}, fmt.Errorf("inspect %s: %w", key, err)
    }
    if gotSize != expectedSize || generation == "" {
        return Manifest{}, errors.New("object identity check failed")
    }
    return Manifest{Key: key, Size: gotSize, Generation: generation, State: "active"}, nil
}

The adapter must define what generation means. It can be an object version, an opaque provider generation, or another documented identity. Do not compare unlike identifiers and call the result a checksum. For content integrity, use the storage system's documented checksum semantics and record the algorithm explicitly.

The worker needs an atomic claim in the manifest store. Two deliveries for the same eligible row should produce one logical deletion, even if both processes reach the provider. A lease or compare-and-swap claim can prevent concurrent work; idempotent delete behavior and an audit record handle a retry after a process crash. The exact mechanism is less important than making the state transition observable.

What does a fair storage comparison include?

Concern Test condition Evidence to retain
Large-file throughput 10 MB, 500 MB, and 4 GB artifacts at fixed concurrency p50 and p95 duration, completed bytes, retry count
Resume behavior Drop the connection after several gigabytes resumed bytes, duplicate objects, final generation
Authorization Repeat the same request for permitted and forbidden tenants decision latency and audit event
Retention Run two workers against the same eligible manifest one claim, repeatable delete, durable tombstone
Event handling Delay or duplicate completion notifications manifest state and downstream enqueue count

Supabase Storage, Firebase Cloud Storage for Firebase, and Amazon S3 can all be evaluated against this matrix, but their primitives do not remove the application work. A Firebase rules decision still needs to align with the tenant recorded in the manifest. S3 multipart work still needs a policy for abandoned uploads. An S3-compatible endpoint still needs a test for the exact features and checksum behavior used by the adapter.

That is the trade-off I would put in the review record: which boundary is simpler for the existing identity system, which one gives the training pipeline reliable large-file recovery, and which one leaves the clearest deletion evidence. Avoid turning a provider's client ergonomics into a proxy for operational correctness.

Verify rollout, then make rollback boring

Before enabling deletion, replay a fixture containing active artifacts, already-deleted artifacts, missing objects, expired policy revisions, and two workers claiming one row. The expected outcome is one durable state transition per artifact. Add a deliberate connection drop during a large upload. A test that never interrupts the stream is not exercising the incident path.

Use dry-run mode first. It should record the candidate key, policy revision, and reason without deleting bytes. Once deletion is enabled, keep the manifest tombstone and audit record for the period required by the data policy. Configure alerts for stuck deleting rows, abandoned multipart work where supported, repeated authorization failures, and a gap between an upload event and an active manifest.

Rollback should stop new deletion claims and leave existing object state untouched. Restoring a deleted artifact from backup is a recovery procedure, not a rollback button. If the policy logic is wrong, deploy a new policy revision and reconcile manifests explicitly; silently changing the meaning of an old revision makes the next postmortem much harder.

For cached responses, set directives deliberately. Cache-Control: no-store is appropriate when content must not be stored by caches. A bounded freshness policy can fit immutable, access-controlled artifacts served through a signed URL. Caching rules do not replace authorization or retention policy.

The final decision should fit in one review note: measured large-file behavior, failure recovery, tenant authorization, lifecycle evidence, and the operational work left to the team. If those facts are recorded, changing the storage adapter later is a controlled migration instead of a rewrite of the scheduler.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control
  • https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage
  • https://firebase.google.com/docs/storage
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
