title: Twenty's Open CRM Architecture: How Agent-First Design Turns Customer Data into Executable Workflows
description:
Twenty bills itself as "designed for AI," but what does that mean when you trace the plumbing? Most CRMs treat automation as an afterthought: webhook endpoints bolted onto a UI-first data model, with agents forced to scrape HTML or reverse-engineer undocumented APIs. Twenty flips the contract. Its GraphQL schema exposes contacts, deals, tasks, and pipeline stages as introspectable primitives. Agents read and mutate CRM state the same way humans do, through a typed API surface that treats customer lifecycle events as first-class resources.

This matters for financial and sales automation. Lead scoring, pipeline progression, outreach sequencing, and revenue forecasting all depend on reading relationship state and writing back decisions. Twenty's architecture reveals how a modern CRM becomes agent infrastructure: PostgreSQL for queryable state, NestJS for mutation boundaries, and a workflow engine that surfaces field changes and stage transitions as event streams.

GraphQL as the Agent Contract

Twenty's primary interface is a GraphQL API. No REST fallback, no legacy SOAP layer. The schema defines every entity (Person, Company, Opportunity, Task) and every relationship (Person.company, Opportunity.pointOfContact) as typed fields. Agents introspect the schema at runtime, discover available mutations, and construct queries without hardcoded field names.

Key primitives for agents:

  • Queries: findManyPeople, findOneOpportunity, searchCompanies return paginated, filterable result sets. Agents can pass GraphQL variables for dynamic filtering (e.g., where: { stage: { eq: "QUALIFIED" } }).
  • Mutations: createOnePerson, updateOneOpportunity, deleteOneTask accept input objects that match the schema. State transitions (moving a deal from "Qualified" to "Proposal") are just field updates on the Opportunity.stage enum.
  • Subscriptions: Real-time updates when records change. An agent watching for new leads subscribes to personCreated and receives push notifications without polling.

The schema is code-generated from TypeScript decorators in the NestJS backend. When you define a new custom field in Twenty's UI, the GraphQL schema regenerates automatically. Agents see the new field in the next introspection query.

PostgreSQL Data Model and State Management

Twenty stores all CRM data in PostgreSQL. Each workspace gets its own schema (logical isolation within a single database). The core tables mirror the GraphQL types:

  • person: contacts with email, phone, LinkedIn URL
  • company: organizations with domain, employee count, industry
  • opportunity: deals with amount, stage, close date
  • activity: tasks, notes, emails linked to people or companies
  • workflow_run: execution history for automated sequences

State transitions are row updates. When an agent moves a deal to "Closed Won," it issues an updateOneOpportunity mutation that writes a new stage value and closedAt timestamp. PostgreSQL triggers can fire on these updates to log audit events or cascade changes (e.g., updating a company's total deal value when an opportunity closes).

Multi-tenancy boundaries: Each workspace is a separate schema. Agents operating across workspaces must authenticate per-workspace and cannot query across schema boundaries without explicit federation. This prevents accidental data leakage but complicates cross-workspace orchestration (e.g., a holding company agent managing deals across subsidiary workspaces).

Workflow Engine and Event-Driven Triggers

Twenty includes a workflow engine that turns CRM events into agent triggers. Workflows are defined as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) where nodes represent actions (send email, update field, call webhook) and edges represent conditional logic.

Event sources that trigger workflows:

  • Field changes: When Opportunity.stage moves from "Proposal" to "Negotiation," fire a workflow that notifies the sales manager and schedules a follow-up task.
  • Record creation: When a new Person is created with leadSource: "Website", enrich the contact with Clearbit data and assign to the inbound sales queue.
  • Time-based: Daily cron job that finds all opportunities with closeDate in the past and stage != "Closed Lost" and sends a reminder.

Webhook delivery for external orchestrators: Twenty can POST workflow events to external URLs. An agent orchestrator (LangGraph, Temporal, n8n) listens for these webhooks and decides whether to intervene. For example:

  1. Deal moves to "Negotiation."
  2. Twenty fires a webhook to https://orchestrator.example.com/deal-negotiation.
  3. Orchestrator queries the deal details via GraphQL, runs a pricing model, and posts a recommended discount back to Twenty as a note on the opportunity.

The workflow engine tracks execution state in workflow_run and workflow_step tables. If a webhook fails, Twenty retries with exponential backoff. Agents can query these tables to audit past runs and debug stuck workflows.

Agent Tool Boundaries and Mutation Surface

From an agent's perspective, Twenty exposes these tool categories:

Tool Category Example Operations State Changes
Contact Management createPerson, updatePerson, searchPeople Inserts/updates in person table
Deal Progression createOpportunity, updateOpportunity.stage Updates opportunity.stage, logs audit event
Task Orchestration createActivity, updateActivity.status Inserts/updates in activity, triggers reminders
Enrichment enrichCompany (custom function) Calls external API, writes to company.metadata JSONB field
Reporting aggregateOpportunities (custom resolver) Read-only query across opportunity with SUM/AVG

Custom functions as agent tools: Twenty lets you define custom GraphQL resolvers in TypeScript. An agent can call enrichCompany(domain: "example.com") which internally hits Clearbit, Apollo, or another data provider and writes enriched fields back to the company record. These custom resolvers are versioned alongside the schema, so agents always see the latest tool signature.

Permission boundaries: Twenty uses role-based access control (RBAC) at the GraphQL resolver level. An agent authenticated with a service account token inherits the permissions of that account's role. If the role lacks update:opportunity permission, the agent's mutation fails with a 403. This prevents rogue agents from escalating privileges or mutating sensitive records.

Audit Logging and Agent Attribution

Every mutation in Twenty writes to an audit log table (audit_event). The log captures:

  • Actor: user ID or service account ID (agent token)
  • Action: CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE
  • Entity: table name and record ID
  • Changes: JSON diff of old vs. new field values
  • Timestamp: when the mutation occurred

Distinguishing agent actions from human actions: Service accounts are flagged with isServiceAccount: true. Queries against audit_event can filter by actor type to separate agent-initiated mutations from human edits. This is critical for compliance (e.g., proving that a discount was applied by an AI agent following a pricing policy, not a rogue salesperson).

Replay and rollback: Because the audit log stores JSON diffs, you can reconstruct the state of any record at any point in time. If an agent makes a bad decision (e.g., marks all deals as "Closed Lost"), you can query the audit log, identify the offending mutations, and issue compensating transactions to revert the changes.

Deployment Shape and Observability

Twenty ships as a Docker Compose stack for self-hosting or runs on their managed cloud. The core services:

  • twenty-server: NestJS backend, GraphQL API, workflow engine
  • twenty-frontend: React SPA, admin UI
  • postgres: PostgreSQL 15 with pgvector for semantic search
  • redis: Job queue for async workflows and webhook retries
  • worker: Background job processor (emails, enrichment, scheduled workflows)

Observability hooks for agents:

  • Metrics: Prometheus endpoint at /metrics exposes GraphQL query latency, mutation error rates, and workflow execution counts.
  • Traces: OpenTelemetry instrumentation tags each GraphQL operation with operation_name, user_id, and workspace_id. Agents can correlate their tool calls with backend traces in Jaeger or Honeycomb.
  • Logs: Structured JSON logs include correlation_id for tracing a single agent request across multiple services (e.g., GraphQL mutation triggers workflow, workflow calls webhook, webhook updates record).

Failure modes agents must handle:

  • Rate limits: Twenty enforces per-workspace rate limits (e.g., 1000 requests/minute). Agents must implement exponential backoff and respect Retry-After headers.
  • Schema drift: If a custom field is deleted, agents querying that field receive a GraphQL error. Agents should catch schema errors and re-introspect before retrying.
  • Webhook delivery failures: If an agent's webhook endpoint is down, Twenty retries for 24 hours then marks the workflow as failed. Agents must monitor workflow_run.status and manually replay failed runs.

Code Example: Agent Tool for Deal Progression

Here's how an agent would wrap Twenty's GraphQL API as a tool for moving deals through the pipeline:

import { GraphQLClient } from 'graphql-request';

class TwentyCRMTool {
  private client: GraphQLClient;

  constructor(apiUrl: string, apiKey: string) {
    this.client = new GraphQLClient(apiUrl, {
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` }
    });
  }

  async moveDealToStage(opportunityId: string, newStage: string): Promise<void> {
    const mutation = `
      mutation UpdateOpportunity($id: ID!, $stage: String!) {
        updateOneOpportunity(
          where: { id: $id }
          data: { stage: $stage }
        ) {
          id
          stage
          updatedAt
        }
      }
    `;

    const variables = { id: opportunityId, stage: newStage };
    const result = await this.client.request(mutation, variables);

    console.log(`Deal ${result.updateOneOpportunity.id} moved to ${result.updateOneOpportunity.stage}`);
  }

  async getDealsInStage(stage: string): Promise<any[]> {
    const query = `
      query FindOpportunities($stage: String!) {
        findManyOpportunities(
          where: { stage: { eq: $stage } }
          orderBy: { closeDate: ASC }
        ) {
          id
          name
          amount
          closeDate
          pointOfContact { name email }
        }
      }
    `;

    const variables = { stage };
    const result = await this.client.request(query, variables);
    return result.findManyOpportunities;
  }
}

// Agent usage
const crm = new TwentyCRMTool('https://api.twenty.com/graphql', process.env.TWENTY_API_KEY);

// Get all deals in "Negotiation" stage
const deals = await crm.getDealsInStage('NEGOTIATION');

// Move the first deal to "Closed Won"
if (deals.length > 0) {
  await crm.moveDealToStage(deals[0].id, 'CLOSED_WON');
}

The agent treats moveDealToStage and getDealsInStage as tools. The GraphQL client handles retries, error parsing, and token refresh. The agent's orchestrator (LangGraph, CrewAI, etc.) calls these tools based on its decision logic.

Security Boundaries and Token Scoping

Twenty uses JWT tokens for authentication. Each token is scoped to a workspace and a role. Agents receive service account tokens with limited permissions:

  • Read-only tokens: Can query all entities but cannot mutate. Useful for reporting agents that aggregate pipeline metrics.
  • Write tokens: Can create and update records but cannot delete. Useful for enrichment agents that add data without removing it.
  • Admin tokens: Full CRUD access. Reserved for orchestrators that manage workspace configuration.

Token rotation: Service account tokens expire after 90 days. Agents must implement token refresh logic or store tokens in a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) that rotates them automatically.

IP allowlisting: Self-hosted Twenty instances can restrict API access to specific IP ranges. Agents running in a VPC must route through a NAT gateway with a static IP.

Technical Verdict

Use Twenty when:

  • You need a CRM that agents can introspect and mutate without custom integration code.
  • Your sales or financial workflows require reading pipeline state and writing back decisions (lead scoring, discount approval, forecast updates).
  • You want audit logs that distinguish agent actions from human actions for compliance.
  • You're comfortable running a TypeScript/PostgreSQL stack and need to extend the CRM with custom resolvers.

Avoid Twenty when:

  • You need a CRM with pre-built integrations to legacy systems (Salesforce has 3000+ connectors, Twenty has dozens).
  • Your agents must operate across multiple CRMs and you need a unified abstraction layer (consider a middleware like Merge or Vessel instead).
  • You require real-time collaboration features (live cursors, conflict resolution) for human-agent co-editing.
  • Your compliance regime prohibits self-hosting or requires FedRAMP/HIPAA certification (Twenty's managed cloud is not yet certified).

Twenty's architecture is a blueprint for agent-first SaaS: expose your data model as a typed API, surface state changes as events, and let agents treat your product as infrastructure. The GraphQL contract and PostgreSQL backing store make it straightforward to build agents that read, write, and orchestrate customer lifecycle workflows without wrestling with REST pagination or webhook flakiness.

Source Links

  • Twenty GitHub Repository
  • Twenty Documentation

title: A better empty state for template search: keep the query
description:
A customer success lead types “People sign up, but they never invite the rest of their team.” There’s no template with that title. What should the search page do with the sentence?

I ran into this while building the template library for Rewuu Feedback Forms, our AI customer feedback software. The obvious thing to improve was retrieval: a search in everyday language ought to find a relevant template even when the words are different. But retrieval only solves half the problem. Sometimes there really isn’t a good match.

A missed search can be the first field of a form

A typical empty state asks the visitor to try a broader term. “Onboarding” might produce more results, but the most useful part of the original input was the bit about inviting colleagues. I didn’t want someone to throw that away just to move forward.

In Rewuu, when a search doesn’t turn up a suitable template, the visitor can carry what they wrote into a form of their own. The purpose opens for editing. That last part matters: something typed in a search box is a rough expression of intent. It deserves a second look before it becomes a brief for a conversation with a customer.

Take that opening example. “People sign up, but they never invite the rest of their team” is the business’s observation. It quietly assumes everyone intended to invite someone. I’d edit the purpose to:

Learn what the customer wanted to do after signup and what happened when they tried.

Now “I only needed an account for myself” is a useful answer. So is “I sent an invitation and it landed in spam.” Those answers send the team in different directions.

Let the visitor test the handoff

A purpose is easier to judge once you’ve tried answering the form. The template page lets you do that from the customer’s side. You can choose a preset rule set or add a rule of your own. For this example, mine would be: “Don’t ask for the colleague’s email address.” Knowing where an invitation got stuck is useful; collecting the address isn’t necessary to understand that experience.

If you decide to use the form, signup carries the purpose and rules forward. That gave me three concrete checks for the flow:

  1. Search in the customer’s vocabulary. Describe the problem without using a template title. Can you tell why a result might fit?
  2. Try a purpose the catalogue doesn’t cover. Can you see and edit the words you already typed, or do you meet another blank box?
  3. Change something before signup. Add one rule, try the form, then take it through signup. Does the form you keep still contain your edit?

The third check changed how I thought about onboarding. If someone has already chosen the purpose, set a boundary and tried a customer’s answer, they’ve started using the product. Asking them to build it all again after creating an account would make the preview feel like a different product.

You can explore the template library, try the customer onboarding template, or open the custom form page. If you build search for a catalogue, here’s the question I’d start with: what useful work has the visitor already done by the time your search returns nothing?

Disclosure: This article was written with AI assistance using the founder’s account of building Rewuu’s template library.

title: MongoDB to BigQuery Without Datastream or Kafka: A Change Stream CDC Tutorial
description:
BigQuery wants columns, and MongoDB hands you documents that get rewritten in place. A MongoDB to BigQuery pipeline has to close both gaps: turn fields into columns, and carry every update and delete across instead of shipping yesterday's export.

The common ways to move the data:

  • mongoexport to JSON, then bq load. A script, a scheduler and a staging bucket. Freshness is hours to daily, and every run is a full reload, so updates and deletes never arrive as changes.
  • Datastream for MongoDB. Google's managed service reads change streams into native BigQuery datasets, near real time by Google's description. There is nothing to run, and BigQuery is the only reader of the result.
  • Debezium, Kafka and a BigQuery sink. Changes arrive in seconds, and you operate Kafka, Kafka Connect, Debezium and a sink connector per collection.
  • Managed extract, load, transform (ELT) tools such as Fivetran, Estuary or Airbyte Cloud. Nothing to host, and freshness in minutes depending on the plan. You pay per row, per GB or per connector for a second copy in BigQuery.

This tutorial takes a fifth route. OLake Go, an open source (Apache 2.0) replication tool, reads the MongoDB change stream with change data capture (CDC) and commits each collection as an Apache Iceberg table into BigLake, Google Cloud's Iceberg representational state transfer (REST) catalog. The files stay in a Cloud Storage bucket you own, and BigQuery reads them in place.

I ran it against MongoDB 7 as a single-node replica set in Docker and a bucket in us-central1, with OLake Go v1.1.0. The first sync copied 48 documents in 34 seconds, and a second sync replayed 12 change events in 33 seconds. Every figure in this post is from that run.

What you need for this MongoDB to BigQuery pipeline

MongoDB 4.0 or later running as a replica set (self-hosted or Atlas), Docker, and a Google Cloud project where you can enable an API and create a service account. The account that runs the BigQuery queries needs the BigQuery Job User role plus read access to the catalog. Set aside about 30 minutes.

Step 1: A replica set, a user and two collections

Change streams exist only in replica set mode, and one node is enough. On a self-hosted server, start mongod with --replSet rs0 and run this in mongosh on the primary:

rs.initiate({ _id: "rs0", members: [{ _id: 0, host: "<host>:27017" }] })

use admin
db.createUser({
  user: "olake", pwd: "<password>",
  roles: [{ role: "read", db: "shop" }, { role: "clusterMonitor", db: "admin" }]
})

// oplog size in bytes; raise it with replSetResizeOplog if it is small
use local
db.oplog.rs.stats().maxSize

The read role lets OLake Go copy the collections. clusterMonitor (or readAnyDatabase) grants the oplog access that the change stream needs.

Confirm there is one PRIMARY and that the user exists:

rs.status().members.map(m => m.stateStr)
db.getSiblingDB("admin").getUsers().users.map(u => u.user)

Next, the data. Use your own collections, or seed the same 8 customers and 40 orders I used, with money stored as NumberDecimal:

use shop
const seededAt = new Date();
const people = [
  [1, 'Aarav Mehta',  'Mumbai',    'gold'],
  [2, 'Priya Sharma', 'Bengaluru', 'silver'],
  [3, 'Liam Carter',  'Austin',    'bronze'],
  [4, 'Sofia Rossi',  'Milan',     'gold'],
  [5, 'Kenji Tanaka', 'Tokyo',     'silver'],
  [6, 'Emma Schulz',  'Berlin',    'bronze'],
  [7, 'Noah Kim',     'Seoul',     'gold'],
  [8, 'Zara Ali',     'Dubai',     'silver']
];
db.customers.insertMany(people.map(([id, name, city, tier]) => ({
  _id: id, name, email: name.split(' ')[0].toLowerCase() + '@example.com', city, tier,
  created_at: seededAt, updated_at: seededAt
})));

const products = ['Laptop', 'Headphones', 'Monitor', 'Keyboard', 'Mouse', 'Webcam'];
const statuses = ['placed', 'shipped', 'delivered'];
db.orders.insertMany(Array.from({ length: 40 }, (_, i) => {
  const n = i + 1;
  return {
    _id: n, customer_id: 1 + (n % 8), product: products[n % 6],
    amount: NumberDecimal((20 + ((n * 7919) % 120000) / 100).toFixed(2)),
    status: statuses[n % 3], created_at: seededAt, updated_at: seededAt
  };
}));

On Atlas, skip rs.initiate, because clusters are already replica sets. Create the user under Database Access with the same two roles, and allow OLake Go's IP under Network Access.

⚠️ The oplog is the replay window. Atlas and most self-hosted installs keep 24 hours or less of it by default, and a job paused past that window cannot resume and needs a fresh snapshot.

Step 2: Bucket, service account and key on Google Cloud

All of this happens in the Google Cloud console.

  1. Enable the BigLake API under APIs and services, Enable APIs and services.
  2. Create a bucket in Cloud Storage, in the region where BigQuery will run the queries. Its name becomes the catalog name in BigQuery SQL, so choose one you do not mind typing.
  3. Create a service account under IAM and Admin, Service Accounts. IAM is short for Identity and Access Management. Grant the account BigLake Editor on the project and Storage Object User on the bucket.
  4. Download a JSON key from the service account's Keys tab: Add key, Create new key, JSON. The console hands it over once.

You do not create the catalog yourself. BigLake makes a single-bucket catalog named after the bucket the first time OLake Go calls the endpoint with gs://<bucket> as the catalog path.

Step 3: Start OLake UI and connect MongoDB 

curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-ui/master/docker-compose-v1.yml | docker compose -f - up -d

Open http://localhost:8000 and sign in with admin / password.

Go to Sources, Create Source and pick MongoDB. Leave Enable CDC on, then fill in the connection details. Mine were host host.docker.internal:27017 (MongoDB ran in another container), Database Name shop, Auth DB admin, user olake and Replica Set rs0, with Read Preference left on primary.

Click Set up source. OLake Go tests the connection, confirms that it can open a change stream, and reports the oplog window. A window under 7 days is shown as a warning, not a blocker.

Step 4: Point the destination at BigLake

Go to Destinations, Create Destination, choose Apache Iceberg as the connector and BigLake as the catalog type.

Field Value
REST Catalog URI https://biglake.googleapis.com/iceberg/v1/restcatalog
BigLake Catalog Path gs://<bucket>, with no folder after it
Authentication Type GCP
GCP Service Account JSON the full contents of the key file
Catalog Name olake_iceberg
GCP Project ID your project ID
Enable Arrow Writes off

Create runs a test: OLake Go calls the endpoint, creates the catalog on first contact, then writes and drops a test table in the bucket. A missing role fails this test with a 403 from biglake.googleapis.com or storage.googleapis.com, and the host tells you which grant to add.

⚠️ Keep the catalog in its default end-user credential mode. OLake Go 1.1.0 does not send the X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation header, so a catalog switched to vended credentials rejects its commits.

Step 5: Create the job and run the first sync

Open Jobs, click Create Job, name it mongodb_to_bigquery, set a schedule and select the source and destination.

Under Advanced Settings, set Target Query Engines to Google BigQuery, Apache Spark and DuckDB. OLake Go then offers only the delete formats all three can read, which are equality and positional deletes. Deletion vectors drop off the list because BigQuery reads them only in preview.

Click Next, tick customers and orders, and keep Full Refresh + CDC with Upsert. The Upsert Type in my run was Positional Deletes. Then click Create Job, and choose Sync Now from the job's menu.

The first sync copied 8 customers and 40 orders (48 documents, 6.40 KB) in 34 seconds, container start included. It opened the change stream and saved a resume token before reading the collections in parallel chunks, so writes made during the copy are not lost.

OLake Go names the BigLake namespace after the job and the source database, which gave mongodb_to_bigquery_shop. The Iceberg DB field at the top of the Streams page changes that before the first sync.

Step 6: Query the collections in BigQuery

There is no dataset to create and no external table to declare. In BigQuery the bucket is the catalog, the namespace is the dataset, and you address a table by a four-part name in backticks:

SELECT _id, name, city, tier
FROM `<project-id>.<bucket>.mongodb_to_bigquery_shop.customers`
ORDER BY _id;

SELECT status, count(*) AS n, round(sum(cast(amount AS NUMERIC)), 2) AS total
FROM `<project-id>.<bucket>.mongodb_to_bigquery_shop.orders`
GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

Two details matter. Run the query in the bucket's region, which you set in the editor under More, Query settings. And cast amount, because a Decimal128 field arrives in BigQuery as STRING.

From a terminal, the same statements run with bq:

bq query --project_id=<project-id> --location=<region> --use_legacy_sql=false "<sql>"

Step 7: Change documents and sync again

Now the part a nightly export cannot do. Back in mongosh, on database shop, make 12 changes: 7 inserts and 5 updates.

const now = new Date();
db.customers.insertMany([
  { _id: 9,  name: 'Maya Patel',  email: 'maya@example.com',  city: 'Pune',      tier: 'silver', created_at: now, updated_at: now },
  { _id: 10, name: 'Lucas Silva', email: 'lucas@example.com', city: 'São Paulo', tier: 'bronze', created_at: now, updated_at: now }
]);
db.orders.insertMany([
  { _id: 41, customer_id: 9,  product: 'Laptop',   amount: NumberDecimal('1299.00'), status: 'placed', created_at: now, updated_at: now },
  { _id: 42, customer_id: 9,  product: 'Mouse',    amount: NumberDecimal('25.50'),   status: 'placed', created_at: now, updated_at: now },
  { _id: 43, customer_id: 10, product: 'Monitor',  amount: NumberDecimal('349.99'),  status: 'placed', created_at: now, updated_at: now },
  { _id: 44, customer_id: 3,  product: 'Keyboard', amount: NumberDecimal('89.00'),   status: 'placed', created_at: now, updated_at: now },
  { _id: 45, customer_id: 7,  product: 'Webcam',   amount: NumberDecimal('79.90'),   status: 'placed', created_at: now, updated_at: now }
]);
db.customers.updateOne({ name: 'Liam Carter' }, { $set: { tier: 'gold', updated_at: now } });
db.customers.updateOne({ name: 'Zara Ali' },    { $set: { city: 'Abu Dhabi', updated_at: now } });
db.orders.updateMany({ _id: { $in: [1, 4, 7] } }, { $set: { status: 'delivered', updated_at: now } });

Click Sync Now again. The second sync read 12 change events (1.60 KB) from the stream and finished in 33 seconds.

For customers, OLake Go wrote one new data file holding 4 rows: the 2 inserts and the new versions of the 2 updated documents. One small positional delete file retires the 2 old versions. The commit report in the sync log says the same thing: addedDataFiles=1, addedRecords=4, addedPositionalDeleteFiles=1, addedPositionalDeletes=2.

orders has the same shape, with 8 rows and 3 deletes. Rerun the first SELECT in BigQuery, with no refresh and no ALTER TABLE:

Liam Carter is gold, Zara Ali has moved to Abu Dhabi, and customers 9 and 10 are present. BigQuery applies the positional deletes while reading, so each key still returns one row. Add _op_type to the query to see how each row arrived: r for the snapshot, c for an insert and u for an update.

Read the same tables from DuckDB

No export is involved here. DuckDB attaches the BigLake catalog with a Google access token and reads the files OLake Go wrote.

Because the catalog is in end-user mode, DuckDB brings its own storage credentials. That is a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) key for the service account, created under Cloud Storage, Settings, Interoperability.


INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;
INSTALL httpfs;  LOAD httpfs;

-- gcloud auth print-access-token, or a token minted for the service account
CREATE SECRET biglake_catalog (
  TYPE iceberg,
  TOKEN '<access token>',
  EXTRA_HTTP_HEADERS MAP {'x-goog-user-project': '<project-id>'}
);
-- the HMAC key pair for the bucket
CREATE SECRET biglake_files (TYPE gcs, KEY_ID '<hmac access id>', SECRET '<hmac secret>');

ATTACH 'gs://<bucket>' AS biglake (
  TYPE iceberg,
  ENDPOINT 'https://biglake.googleapis.com/iceberg/v1/restcatalog',
  SECRET biglake_catalog
);

SHOW ALL TABLES;
SELECT _id, name, city, tier FROM biglake.mongodb_to_bigquery_shop.customers ORDER BY _id;

DuckDB 1.5.5 returned the same 10 customers as BigQuery, and Spark 4.0.1 with Iceberg 1.10.0 did as well. The orders roll-up matched MongoDB to the cent in all three engines: 16 delivered orders for 8659.68, 18 placed for 10522.26 and 11 shipped for 6397.25. In DuckDB and Spark the cast is sum(cast(amount AS decimal(12,2))).

The access token lasts an hour. When a query fails with 401, run CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET with a fresh one.

Tips from the run

  • Documents are flattened one level. Top-level fields become columns. Nested objects and arrays arrive as JSON text in a STRING column, which PARSE_JSON or JSON_VALUE can unpack.
  • Store doubles if you want to skip the cast. Decimal128 always arrives as text, and an ObjectId key arrives as its 24-character hex string.
  • A new field becomes a new column on the next sync, with nulls for older rows. A field whose type changes in an incompatible way fails the sync instead of corrupting the table.
  • Watch metadata.json. BigLake keeps every snapshot in it and rejects a file above 1 MB, which a busy table reaches after a few thousand syncs. Expire snapshots and compact on a schedule with Spark's expire_snapshots and rewrite_data_files.

How the MongoDB to BigQuery options compare

Method Freshness Updates and deletes Where the data lands What you run
mongoexport plus bq load hours to daily no, full reloads only native BigQuery tables a script, a scheduler, a staging bucket
Datastream for MongoDB near real time, by Google's description yes native BigQuery datasets nothing; a stream in the console
Debezium, Kafka, BigQuery sink seconds yes, in upsert mode Kafka topics, then BigQuery tables Kafka, Kafka Connect, Debezium, sinks
Managed ELT minutes, by plan varies by tool a second copy in BigQuery nothing; per row, GB or connector pricing
OLake Go to BigLake (this post) CDC on a schedule down to one minute yes, as row-level deletes open tables BigQuery, Spark and DuckDB read one Docker Compose stack, your bucket

Datastream is the simpler choice when BigQuery is the only reader and you prefer a managed Google service. The route in this post has two more limits worth stating plainly:

  • A catalog table is read from Parquet in the bucket on every query, so it will not match native BigQuery speed. Load the hot slice into a native table on a schedule if a dashboard needs that.
  • Deletion vectors are out while BigQuery is a reader. BigQuery reads them only in preview, with a cap of 100,000 deletion vector entries per query.

FAQ

How fresh can the BigQuery tables be?

As fresh as the job's schedule, which goes down to one minute. Each run drains the change stream and ends with one commit to BigLake, and BigQuery sees that snapshot on its next query. It is CDC on a schedule, not a continuous stream.

Can I run this from the command line instead of the UI?

Yes. The olakego/source-mongodb:latest image has check, discover and sync commands driven by JSON config files. Positional deletes keep a small index between runs, so mount a persistent directory through OLAKE_INDEX_DB_DIR and pass --state on every run after the first.

What does it cost to keep running?

Storage is billed at Cloud Storage rates for the Parquet and delete files, and the BigLake catalog has no per-table charge. BigQuery bills queries by bytes scanned on demand, or by slot time on an edition. OLake Go runs on whatever machine hosts Docker.

Where to go from here

  • Point the source at your real replica set or Atlas cluster. On Atlas, paste the cluster host with Use SRV on.
  • The full guide, with the CLI configs, the Spark connection and the complete data type table, is on olake.io.

If something here does not match what you see, post the exact message in the comments.

title: What a Farmers Market Website in Dubai Needs to Get Right on Market Day
description:
A farmers market in Dubai lives or dies on one morning a week. The website has one job: get the right people to the right place with the right expectations, before the stalls sell out. Most market sites we review fail at that job in the same three places.

1. Put this week's market first, not the market's history

Visitors open the site on Friday evening or Saturday morning. They want three facts: is it on this week, where exactly, and what time does it open. If those facts sit below a long story about the market's founding, the visitor leaves and asks on social media instead. The current date, the location, and the opening hours belong at the top of the page, updated every week without fail. A seasonal schedule page that lists every market date for the season earns the bookmark; a single static date does not.

2. Make every stall findable before arrival

A farmers market is not one shop, it is forty small businesses sharing a field. Shoppers come for a specific vendor — the cheese stall, the honey seller, the plant nursery. A stall directory with a short line per vendor, what they sell, and whether they take card payments turns browsing into a plan. When a vendor is absent for a week, say so on their listing. Nothing frustrates a regular more than arriving for a stall that never came.

3. Treat the vendor enquiry like a real application

Markets grow by adding good vendors, and good vendors apply through the website. A vendor enquiry page needs the honest questions up front: what do you sell, what space do you need, what power or refrigeration do you need, and which dates can you commit to. Collect it in one form, answer it within a couple of days, and keep a waiting list when the market is full. A market that answers vendors quickly gets first pick of the best stalls.

4. Design for a phone in one hand and a shopping bag in the other

Nobody browses a farmers market site at a desk. The visitor is standing in a car park, checking the location pin and the opening time. The map link, the parking note, and the WhatsApp enquiry route must work with one thumb and load fast on a weak connection. Big tap targets, short lines, and no image-heavy hero that delays the facts.

5. Let the season do the talking

Farmers markets change with the season, and the website should show it. A short weekly update — what is fresh this week, which stalls are new, what sold out last week — gives regulars a reason to return to the site instead of only to the market. Three lines and one honest photo beat a gallery of stock images every time.

6. Measure the Saturday, not the month

After launch, the number that matters is Saturday-morning behaviour: how many visitors checked the date and location, and how many tapped through to WhatsApp with a question. If enquiries spike on Friday evening, the schedule page is working. If they ask where the market is, the location section is not.

A farmers market website is a practical tool, not a brochure. It should answer the three questions every visitor asks, help vendors join, and stay current every single week. We build websites for Dubai businesses and booking apps for markets and events — if you run a market, start with the Saturday-morning test above and fix whatever fails it first. More about our work is on RapidBizz.

title: Alternativa offline a Descript y CapCut: quitar silencios, comprimir vídeos <10 MB y subtítulos con FFmpeg 9.1 y Whisper
description:
Si editas podcasts, tutoriales, gameplay o Shorts, seguramente ya conoces el peaje habitual de la nube: $20–$30 al mes en suscripciones como Descript, CapCut Pro o OpusClip, subidas lentas de archivos de varios gigas y marcas de agua si no pagas.

La buena noticia en 2026 es que FFmpeg 9.1 (ya con soporte nativo para whisper.cpp offline) permite hacer todo el trabajo pesado 100% en local a la velocidad nativa de tu PC, sin subir ni un byte a internet.

Aquí tienes las 4 recetas exactas listas para copiar y pegar, además de una Calculadora Exact-MB de Bitrate y Comandos FFmpeg 9.x gratuita (sin registro) para calcular los parámetros exactos de cualquier vídeo.

1. Comprimir un vídeo al tamaño exacto para Discord (<10 MB) o WhatsApp (15 MB) sin perder calidad

El error clásico al comprimir con CRF fijo es quedarse corto (calidad borrosa) o pasarse por 1 MB y que Discord rechace el archivo. La fórmula exacta de 2 pasadas (2-pass) usa todo el presupuesto de bits disponible:

bitrate_video_kbps = floor((objetivo_MB * 8192 * 0.94) / duracion_segundos) - bitrate_audio_kbps

# Ejemplo: vídeo de 60 segundos ajustado a 9.5 MB (audio 96k -> vídeo 1124k)
ffmpeg -y -i entrada.mp4 -c:v libx264 -b:v 1124k -pass 1 -an -f mp4 NUL && \
ffmpeg -y -i entrada.mp4 -c:v libx264 -b:v 1124k -pass 2 -c:a aac -b:a 96k salida_discord.mp4

En nuestras pruebas reales, un clip de 11,55 MB bajó a 0,62 MB exactos manteniendo el vídeo nítido. Puedes calcular el comando automático para cualquier duración en la Calculadora Exact-MB gratis.

2. Masterizar audio de podcast o vídeo a -16 LUFS sin recodificar el vídeo (-c:v copy)

La mayoría de editores re-renderizan todo el vídeo H.264 solo para subir el volumen de la voz. Con loudnorm y -c:v copy limpias graves (<75 Hz), eliminas ruido de fondo y clavas -16 LUFS (estándar de YouTube, Spotify y Apple Podcasts) en segundos y sin pérdida de imagen:

ffmpeg -y -i grabacion.mp4 -c:v copy -af "highpass=f=75,afftdn=nf=-25,loudnorm=I=-16:TP=-1.5:LRA=11" -c:a aac -b:a 192k master_16lufs.mp4

3. Reencuadrar vídeo 16:9 a formato vertical 9:16 (YouTube Shorts, Reels y TikTok)

title: Best tools for testing your own app's SMS and OTP flows (2026): cloud numbers, test numbers and SMS inboxes
description:
I work with DuoPlus, on the growth marketing side, so it's on this list and it sits near the top. Keep that in mind. Everything I say about the other five tools comes from their own websites and docs, which I opened again on 24 November 2026. I've left prices out. Pricing pages change too often to copy.

One more thing before the list. Everything here is about testing your own app: your signup screen, your password reset, your login code, your "we've sent you a text" step. None of it is about getting through someone else's phone verification. That's a different conversation and not one I'm having.

Why SMS flows are annoying to test

The bug reports always sound the same. "Code never arrived." "Code arrived but autofill didn't." "Worked in the US build, not the Brazil one." The usual fix is a teammate's personal phone, until that teammate is on leave or the test needs a country nobody lives in.

So the tools below split into roughly three kinds:

  • Fake numbers that never send a real SMS. Fast, free-ish, good for CI. They don't tell you whether a real message actually lands.
  • Real numbers that receive real SMS and expose them to your tests. Slower, but closer to what your users actually see.
  • A real Android device to read it on. Half the bugs are on the phone side: keyboard, autofill, the app killed in the background while the user checks Messages.

1. DuoPlus â€” for walking through the whole flow on a real Android device, in the country you care about

What it is: a cloud phone platform. You get real ARM Android cloud phones (Android 10, 11, 12 and 15) that you open in a browser, in the Windows or Mac client, or through the Android and iOS apps that control the cloud phone. The DuoPlus homepage lists a separate Cloud Number product, described as "online physical and virtual numbers for receiving SMS", next to the cloud phones.

Why it's on a list about SMS testing: the cloud phone itself doesn't have a real SIM, so when I'm walking through my own app's signup, I pair it with a DuoPlus cloud number that receives the code. The phone gives me the device side (install the APK, run the flow, see what the keyboard and autofill actually do) and the number gives me the message side.

Where it fits best:

  • Regional checks. The site lists location and SIM-card data settings for 150+ countries and regions. If your OTP copy, sender name or timing changes by market, you can sit in that market's environment instead of guessing from a VPN.
  • Handing a broken state to a teammate. Team collaboration is built in, so if the code arrives but the verify button hangs, I share the same cloud phone instead of writing a ten-step repro.
  • Version spread. One device on Android 10, one on 15, same build, same flow. That's usually where the "autofill works on my phone" bugs show up.
  • Batch setup. Bulk install, uninstall and launch, plus an API and ADB access if you want to spin devices up from a script. Root is available for the few test cases that need it.
  • Short sessions. Billing is per minute, which suits SMS checks; most of mine are fifteen or twenty minutes, not a full day.

Honest drawbacks:

  • It's Android only, and it won't place voice calls. If your app offers "call me with the code instead", you need something else for that path. iOS testing needs a different tool.
  • It's not an assertion library. If what you really want is for the SMS body to land inside a Playwright or Cypress test so your suite can check the code automatically, the next tool on this list is built for exactly that. DuoPlus is better at the "a human walks through it on a real device" side.

Link: duoplus.net. If you want to look around first, the DuoPlus market page is a decent starting point.

2. Mailosaur â€” for putting SMS codes straight into automated tests

Best known for email testing, Mailosaur also has an SMS product, and it's the most direct CI fit here. Their SMS page says you can test "using dedicated numbers across supported regions, without relying on phones or live SIMs", and that you can run "SMS OTP testing, verification code flows, and SMS notification tests" through their API with Cypress, Playwright, Selenium and others.

The docs show the pattern: assign a Mailosaur phone number to your test, trigger your app to send the SMS, then pull the message back in your test code and assert on it. They also mention project permissions for teams.

Where it fits: you want "receives code, enters code, gets in" to run on every build, not as a manual pre-release check.

What to watch: it tests the message, not the device. It won't tell you whether your Android autofill picks up the code. It also covers "supported regions", so check their list against your markets before you commit.

3. Firebase Authentication test phone numbers â€” free, fast, and fake on purpose

If you already use Firebase phone sign-in, start here. The Firebase docs let you set up fictional phone numbers and codes in the console. According to the docs, this lets you test without using your SMS quota, without sending an actual SMS, and without getting throttled when you run the same number over and over. It also works in an Android emulator without Google Play Services.

The limits are written down plainly: you can add up to 10 test numbers, they must be fictional (the docs suggest 555-prefixed US numbers), they go through the same format validation as real numbers, and Google recommends making the codes hard to guess and rotating them.

Where it fits: integration tests, app-review accounts, and days when you just need login to work.

What it can't tell you: whether a real SMS reaches a real phone in a real country. By design, nothing is sent.

4. Twilio test credentials and magic numbers â€” for testing the sending side of your code

If your backend sends codes through Twilio, their test credentials let you call parts of the REST API without being charged and without touching real phone numbers. The docs list what's supported: buying phone numbers, sending SMS, making calls, and Lookup. There are also "magic input" values that always produce a specific result, for example the number +15005550000 always returns a "number unavailable" error when you try to buy it, which is handy for testing your own error handling.

Two caveats from the same page. First, SMS sent with test credentials don't trigger status callbacks, so your delivery-status webhook path isn't covered. Second, and this one matters for new teams: Twilio now says you can't create test credentials in the new Twilio console. Credentials created in the legacy console keep working; otherwise they point you to a trial account.

Where it fits: backend tests for the "send code" call and its error paths. Not for checking what the user sees.

5. Telnyx Numbers â€” for buying real numbers by API in a lot of countries

Telnyx is a number provider rather than a testing tool, but some teams prefer to own a pool of real test numbers. Their numbers page lists local, national, toll-free and short code numbers across 130+ countries, a Numbers API to search, reserve and buy them, and "multi-function" numbers that handle voice, SMS, MMS and fax on the same number. They say they hold carrier licences in 30+ countries.

Where it fits: you want permanent test numbers in specific markets, managed in code, and you're fine wiring inbound messages to your own webhook.

What to watch: you build the "read the code" part yourself, and availability and paperwork differ by country.

6. Plivo phone numbers â€” a simpler number provider with a console

Plivo's numbers page says you can "instantly buy local, mobile, and toll-free numbers in more than 50 countries" through their API and console, with voice and SMS-enabled local and mobile numbers.

Where it fits: like Telnyx, for teams happy to handle inbound SMS on their own server, with a console for anyone who'd rather not script purchases. It lists fewer countries than Telnyx.

How I'd actually set it up

If I were starting fresh on a small app team:

  1. Firebase test numbers (or your provider's equivalent) for everyday dev and CI.
  2. Mailosaur, or a Telnyx/Plivo number wired to your own webhook, for one or two real end-to-end SMS tests that run on every release build.
  3. DuoPlus cloud phones plus cloud numbers for the human pass: one device per target market, Android 10 and 15 side by side, before a regional launch or a signup-screen change.
  4. Twilio test credentials only if you're already on Twilio and have legacy test credentials; otherwise, a trial account.

The fake numbers keep you fast. The real numbers keep you honest. And a real device in the right country is where you find out the code arrived fine but the screen didn't.

If you want to try the device side, DuoPlus is where I'd start, but I'm biased, so test it against your own flow before you take my word for it.

title: How to migrate Google Custom Search API in Python
description:
Google's Custom Search JSON API is shutting down on January 1, 2027. If your Python app still calls service.cse().list(...).execute(), you'll need to replace that integration before the deadline. Google has already closed the API to new customers. Its official notice points existing users toward a different product for searches limited to 50 domains, or a sales-led option for broader web search.

If you need search results as data rather than a search widget or a generated answer, Spidra Search is one option. It returns titles, links, descriptions, and source-specific fields as JSON. This walkthrough replaces the usual googleapiclient call with a Python client, handles Spidra's asynchronous responses and pagination, and provides a small compatibility helper for existing code that expects Google's title, link, and snippet fields.

The example uses requests so the HTTP changes are visible. Spidra also has a Python SDK that handles job polling if you're writing a new integration rather than migrating an old one.

Start with the Google code you're replacing

A common Custom Search implementation looks like this:

from googleapiclient.discovery import build


def google_search(search_term, api_key, cse_id):
    service = build("customsearch", "v1", developerKey=api_key)
    response = service.cse().list(
        q=search_term, cx=cse_id, num=10
    ).execute()
    return response.get("items", [])

The function returns a list of results containing fields such as title, link, and snippet. Returning response.get("items", []) matters because Google omits items when a search has no matches.

Migrating involves more than changing the endpoint. A Custom Search request uses an engine ID (cx) and numbered offsets (start). Spidra takes the query and any domain restrictions in its JSON request, returns url and description instead of link and snippet, and uses opaque tokens to continue a result set.

Existing Google code Spidra equivalent
q, cx query, optionally includeDomains
num=10 limit=10 (up to 20 per source)
items[].link, items[].snippet web[].url, web[].description
start, queries.nextPage pageTokens, nextPageTokens
siteSearch, siteSearchFilter includeDomains, excludeDomains
searchType="image" sources=["images"]
dateRestrict="d7" startDate/endDate, or coarser timeRange

The rest of the Google response is not automatically preserved. We'll handle the fields most applications use and identify the important gaps later.

Make your first Spidra search in Python

Use Python 3.9 or newer. Install requests and create an API key in the Spidra dashboard. New accounts include 300 free credits without requiring a payment card.

pip install requests
export SPIDRA_API_KEY="spd_YOUR_API_KEY"

Spidra accepts POST /search with an Authorization: Bearer header. Passing "wait": true often gives you the finished result in the same response, but searches that take longer return a job ID. Your code still needs to poll for completion.

Save this complete client as spidra_cse_migration.py. It includes the normal search request, pagination, and the compatibility helper we'll use below.

"""Google Custom Search JSON API migration helpers for Spidra Search.

Install: pip install requests
Set: export SPIDRA_API_KEY='spd_YOUR_API_KEY'
Run: python spidra_cse_migration.py

The legacy helper preserves only the common title/link/snippet fields,
not Google's complete response schema or its search rankings.
"""

import os
import time

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.spidra.io/api"
IN_PROGRESS = {"queued", "pending", "active", "running"}


class SpidraAPIError(RuntimeError):
    def __init__(self, status, details):
        super().__init__(f"Spidra API error ({status}): {details}")
        self.status = status
        self.details = details


class SearchClient:
    def __init__(self, api_key=None, session=None):
        self.api_key = api_key or os.environ["SPIDRA_API_KEY"]
        self.session = session or requests.Session()
        self._legacy_cache = {}

    def _request(self, method, path, payload=None):
        response = self.session.request(
            method,
            f"{BASE_URL}{path}",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {self.api_key}"},
            json=payload,
            timeout=30,
        )
        try:
            body = response.json()
        except ValueError as exc:
            raise SpidraAPIError(response.status_code, "Non-JSON response") from exc
        if response.status_code >= 400:
            raise SpidraAPIError(response.status_code, body)
        return body

    def search(self, query, *, sources=None, limit=10, timeout=180, **options):
        """Return the completed REST API envelope, including result/data."""
        payload = {
            "query": query,
            "sources": sources or ["web"],
            "limit": limit,
            "wait": True,
            **options,
        }
        envelope = self._request("POST", "/search", payload)
        deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
        while envelope.get("status") in IN_PROGRESS:
            job_id = envelope.get("jobId")
            if not job_id:
                raise SpidraAPIError("missing jobId", envelope)
            if time.monotonic() >= deadline:
                raise TimeoutError(f"Search {job_id} did not finish within {timeout}s")
            time.sleep(min(2, max(0, deadline - time.monotonic())))
            envelope = self._request("GET", f"/search/{job_id}")
        if envelope.get("status") != "completed":
            raise SpidraAPIError(envelope.get("status", "unknown"), envelope.get("error"))
        if not isinstance(envelope.get("result"), dict):
            raise SpidraAPIError("missing result", envelope)
        if envelope["result"].get("success") is False:
            raise SpidraAPIError("unsuccessful search", envelope.get("error"))
        return envelope

    @staticmethod
    def items(envelope, source="web"):
        return envelope["result"]["data"].get(source, []) or []

    @staticmethod
    def next_token(envelope, source="web"):
        return (envelope["result"]["data"].get("nextPageTokens") or {}).get(source)

    def collect(self, query, *, target=30, limit=10, max_pages=10, source="web", **options):
        """Collect distinct search results, bounded by page count and target."""
        items, seen = [], set()
        token = None
        for _ in range(max_pages):
            page_options = dict(options)
            if token:
                page_options["pageTokens"] = {source: token}
            envelope = self.search(query, sources=[source], limit=limit, **page_options)
            page = self.items(envelope, source)
            if not page:
                break
            for item in page:
                if item.get("url") and item["url"] not in seen:
                    seen.add(item["url"])
                    items.append(item)
                    if len(items) >= target:
                        return items
            token = self.next_token(envelope, source)
            if not token:
                break
        return items

    def cse_items(self, query, *, num=10, start=1, site=None):
        """Return a list of Google-style title/link/snippet items.

        This supports the common `return res.get('items', [])` pattern.
        It is not a complete cse().list().execute() replacement.
        """
        if not 1 <= num <= 10 or start < 1 or start + num - 1 > 100:
            raise ValueError("Expected 1 <= num <= 10 and a window within 1..100")
        options = {"includeDomains": [site]} if site else {}
        # Tuple components are hashable, unlike raw includeDomains lists.
        cache_key = (query, site)
        pages = self._legacy_cache.setdefault(cache_key, [])
        need = start - 1 + num
        have = sum(len(self.items(p)) for p in pages)

        while have < need and len(pages) < 10:
            call_options = dict(options)
            if pages:
                token = self.next_token(pages[-1])
                if not token:
                    break
                call_options["pageTokens"] = {"web": token}
            envelope = self.search(query, limit=10, **call_options)
            if not self.items(envelope):
                break
            pages.append(envelope)
            have += len(self.items(envelope))

        raw = [item for page in pages for item in self.items(page)]
        return [
            {
                "title": item.get("title", ""),
                "link": item.get("url", ""),
                "snippet": item.get("description") or "",
            }
            for item in raw[start - 1:need]
        ]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    client = SearchClient()
    response = client.search("google custom search json api migration", limit=10)
    for hit in client.items(response)[:2]:
        print(hit["title"])
        print(hit["url"])

Run it with:

python spidra_cse_migration.py

The following two URLs were returned for the same query in the supplied November 24 live run (the output is shortened to the first two results):

Migrate from Custom Search Site Restricted JSON API
https://docs.cloud.google.com/generative-ai-app-builder/docs/migrate-from-cse
Custom Search JSON API | Google for Developers
https://developers.google.com/custom-search/v1/overview

Inside search(), a successful result is under envelope["result"]["data"]["web"]. The items() helper gives you that list directly. You don't have to build your own result parser, and an empty result set gives you an empty list rather than a missing-key exception.

The client also checks terminal job states and raises a useful error if the request fails. That matters in a production integration: a search that returns a job ID is not a completed search yet.

Replace offset pagination with cursor pagination

Google's start=11 fetches the second page of ten results. Spidra instead returns a token for the next page inside nextPageTokens. You send it back in pageTokens along with the same query and filters.

The collect() method in the file handles that loop, stops after a configured number of pages, and removes repeated URLs. Here's how to ask for up to 30 unique search results:

from spidra_cse_migration import SearchClient

client = SearchClient()
hits = client.collect(
    "google custom search json api migration",
    target=30,
    limit=10,
    max_pages=5,
)

In the supplied live verification, that query produced 30 distinct results across three pages, with the positions continuing from 1 through 30. A deeper run also found one repeated URL across 100 results. This is why collect() keeps a seen set rather than assuming every new page contains entirely new URLs.

Don't build the loop around totalResults, even if your previous CSE implementation did. Spidra doesn't provide that estimate. It provides a next-page token while further results are available. The explicit max_pages bound also protects you from unintentionally collecting far more than your application needs.

Preserve the fields your existing code expects

You might not be ready to update every function that uses Google's link and snippet keys. The included cse_items() method lets those callers keep reading the same three fields while you migrate their search provider:

from spidra_cse_migration import SearchClient

client = SearchClient()
items = client.cse_items(
    "python tutorial", num=10, start=11,
    site="docs.python.org",
)

for item in items:
    url = item["link"]
    description = item["snippet"]

cse_items() converts url to link and description to snippet. It also walks earlier cursor pages when callers request an offset such as start=11, and caches those pages in memory so subsequent calls don't fetch them again in the same client instance.

This is a compatibility helper for the common items list, not a drop-in replacement for the entire service.cse().list(...).execute() interface. It doesn't reproduce Google's engine configuration, totalResults, pagemap, spelling suggestions, or arbitrary CSE parameters. The cache is intentionally per-process; start a new client when you need fresh results.

There's another cost to offset compatibility: fetching start=11 on a new client needs the first page's cursor before it can fetch page two. If you control the application, moving it to collect() or native cursor pagination is better than maintaining offset behavior indefinitely.

Carry your search restrictions over

Domain-restricted search is straightforward when you know the sites your product should search. Rather than configuring a cx engine, send the domains with each request:

client = SearchClient()
response = client.search(
    "python tutorial", limit=10,
    includeDomains=["docs.python.org"],
)

Spidra enforces includeDomains and excludeDomains on web results. You can specify up to 20 domains in one filter. If your old CSE setup depended on a larger collection of domains or custom engine refinements, audit that configuration before switching. A domain list isn't a replacement for every engine setting.

Date restrictions also need attention. Google's dateRestrict="d7" meant a specific recent period. Spidra's timeRange="week" favors recent results but is not a strict date filter. Use explicit dates if your application needs a bounded period:

response = client.search(
    "artificial intelligence", limit=10,
    startDate="2026-11-01",
    endDate="2026-11-20",
)

Don't send timeRange and startDate/endDate in the same request. Spidra returns a validation error when you combine them. For language preferences, pass language="de"; treat it as a preference, not a guarantee that every result will have a German title. SafeSearch is available as safeSearch="strict" or "off", without Google's intermediate setting. These options are described in the Search API reference.

For image results, change the source rather than adding Google's searchType parameter:

response = client.search(
    "mechanical keyboard", sources=["images"], limit=10
)
images = client.items(response, "images")

Image items can include imageUrl, thumbnailUrl, and the URL of the page hosting the image. If you're migrating image handling, update the consuming code as well as the query.

Go beyond an ordinary list of links

If you're replacing CSE inside a research tool or an AI agent, you may need more than web search results. Spidra can search multiple sources in one request, with separate result lists for web, news, images, videos, research papers, and GitHub issues or repositories.

For example, a product research tool can get web pages and news in one job:

response = client.search(
    "artificial intelligence announcement",
    sources=["web", "news"], limit=10,
)
web_results = client.items(response, "web")
news_results = client.items(response, "news")

When an application needs the source page itself, scrapeOptions can fetch Markdown content for the top web results as part of the same search job:

response = client.search(
    "posthog before_send config",
    sources=["web"], limit=3,
    scrapeOptions={"formats": ["markdown"], "maxResults": 2},
)

The selected results can include a markdown field. Pages that can't be read may lack it, so handle that as an optional field. Content fetching also takes longer and is charged separately from the search. See Search API versus scraping API for when it's worth retrieving page content instead of stopping at the URLs.

Check these differences before switching production traffic

Google's service is retiring, but a migration still needs to preserve the behavior your application depends on. These are the differences I'd test against actual production queries:

  • Rankings won't match exactly. Spidra returns search results as data, not a copy of your old Google Programmable Search Engine configuration. Check result relevance on a representative set of queries.
  • No totalResults or Google pagemap. Page on tokens. For page content, request Markdown with scrapeOptions; structured page data is only available for some results, not a guaranteed replacement for pagemap.
  • Domain filters aren't engine definitions. They restrict results to the domains you send, but they don't reproduce Google's promotions or refinements.
  • Some options work only on certain sources. For example, sort="date" is for news; date filtering and SafeSearch support also vary by source. Inspect warnings if you combine sources and filters.
  • Search results can overlap across pages. Keep a URL deduplication step, especially for longer pagination chains.

One billing detail is easy to miss during testing. Spidra charges one credit per ten results per source, rounded up, and a source returning no results is free. Re-submitting the same search within five seconds can reuse its existing job ID. If you're reconciling search usage from response envelopes, deduplicate by job ID rather than counting the same job twice. The credit rules explain the underlying charges.

For a production cutover, run a sample of your existing queries through both providers while CSE is still available. Compare the fields your code reads, check the behavior of filters and empty result sets, and validate your cost assumptions. Switch the traffic only when the new responses meet the needs of your application.

You now have a Python client for Spidra Search, a bounded cursor paginator, and a compatibility helper for the most common Google result fields. If your application needs only search-result URLs and snippets, the migration can stay small. If it needs page content or additional search sources, the same API can support those workflows without a separate discovery step.

Create a free account at Spidra, set SPIDRA_API_KEY, and run the example against a query your application actually uses.

Frequently asked questions

When does the Google Custom Search JSON API shut down?

Google says existing customers must transition by January 1, 2027. The API is already closed to new customers. Google's published guidance points to Vertex AI Search for searches covering up to 50 domains, or a separate full-web search discussion for broader requirements.

Is Spidra Search a drop-in replacement for googleapiclient?

No. Spidra has a different HTTP request and response model, and it does not reproduce Google's cx engine or every response field. The cse_items() helper above adapts common result fields during migration, but broader integrations must be updated deliberately.

Can I retrieve more than Google's 100-result limit?

Spidra's cursor pagination can continue beyond 100 results when further results are available. The supplied live verification retrieved more than 100. Always set a maximum page count and deduplicate URLs in long-running collection jobs.

Can I migrate an image search or domain-restricted search?

Yes. Set sources=["images"] for image results or use includeDomains and excludeDomains for supported search sources. Image metadata and domain filtering aren't identical to Google's response and engine settings, so test the fields and restrictions your application uses.

title: CC50 gratuito: Ciência da Computação de Harvard em português
description:
Um percurso para começar do zero

O CC50 é a versão legendada em português brasileiro do CS50, curso de Ciência da Computação produzido e licenciado por Harvard. Gratuito e online, reúne 25 horas de aulas gravadas, com duração indicada de 12 semanas e aulas para acompanhar no próprio ritmo. A proposta é construir uma base em computação e programação, inclusive para quem nunca teve contato com o tema.

O primeiro módulo é dedicado a Scratch; em seguida, o percurso passa por C. Exercícios práticos, projetos e estudos de caso ajudam a colocar os conceitos em uso enquanto o aluno desenvolve o raciocínio lógico e aprende a resolver problemas de programação.

Algoritmos, memória e estruturas de dados

Depois de C, a trilha avança por arrays, algoritmos, memória e estruturas de dados. Esses módulos organizam parte importante dos fundamentos da Ciência da Computação: pensar em etapas, escolher como representar informações e compreender como os programas trabalham com elas. O foco também inclui formas eficientes de resolver problemas.

Segurança e engenharia de software estão entre os temas do curso. A combinação desses fundamentos amplia o contexto para entender como programas são construídos e quais aspectos precisam ser considerados além de escrever código. Ética aparece em um módulo próprio ao final da sequência.

Python, SQL e desenvolvimento web

Python entra na trilha depois dos módulos de fundamentos, acompanhado por um módulo dedicado a inteligência artificial. Mais adiante, o conteúdo inclui SQL e desenvolvimento web com HTML, CSS e JavaScript. Flask também tem um módulo próprio, aproximando a sequência de ferramentas ligadas à construção de aplicações web.

O contato com várias linguagens permite observar diferentes partes da programação ao longo do percurso. O programa indicado inclui C, Python, SQL, JavaScript, HTML e CSS, além de Scratch e Flask. Assim, a trilha não fica restrita a uma única linguagem ou área: conecta fundamentos, dados, web e inteligência artificial.

Exercícios e projeto final

A prática acompanha o aprendizado por meio de exercícios desafiadores, projetos e estudos de caso. No encerramento, cada aluno desenvolve um projeto final e o apresenta aos colegas. Esse trabalho também pode ser colocado no portfólio, como registro concreto do que foi construído durante o curso.

Há ainda acesso a uma comunidade de jovens com diferentes níveis de experiência e interesse em comum. As aulas são gravadas, então o formato permite estudar no próprio ritmo. O certificado de conclusão é emitido pela Fundação Estudar.

Para quem é a trilha

O CC50 é voltado a quem quer dar os primeiros passos em programação, incluindo estudantes do ensino médio ou da faculdade e pessoas em transição de carreira. Também faz sentido para quem tem curiosidade sobre desenvolvimento e quer praticar o pensamento lógico antes de seguir para estudos mais específicos.

Com aulas de Harvard legendadas em português brasileiro, uma sequência que vai de Scratch e C a Python, SQL e desenvolvimento web, e um projeto final para apresentar, o CC50 oferece um caminho estruturado para explorar fundamentos de computação sem custo. A carga horária, os exercícios e os temas do programa ajudam a avaliar se essa trilha combina com o tempo disponível e os objetivos de aprendizagem.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/cursos/cc50-ciencia-da-computacao-de-harvard-em-portugues/

title: How we keep a Laravel log ingest endpoint fast (Valkey buffer, batched ClickHouse writes)
description:
We're building a hosted log tool on Laravel 13, and the part that took the most thought was ingestion. Clients send logs in bursts, sometimes thousands of lines a second, and the endpoint can't sit waiting on a database while that happens.

The request does almost nothing

It checks the token, pushes the batch into Valkey (Redis-compatible) and returns a 202. There are no MySQL queries in that path and no queue job per line.

Drainers do the writing

Separate long-running drainer processes, one per buffer shard, claim a batch of 500 to 1000 lines, insert it into ClickHouse, and only acknowledge it after the insert succeeded. Popping first and writing second looks simpler, but it loses lines if the process dies in between.

Replays without duplicates

That raises the opposite problem: if a drainer dies after inserting but before acknowledging, the batch gets inserted again on restart. ClickHouse's insert_deduplication_token handles that. Every batch carries a token, and a repeat with the same token is ignored, so a replay doesn't create duplicates.

Reads start with source and time

Every query filters by source and time range first, because that's what the table's primary key is built on. Without that, ClickHouse has to scan far more than it needs to.

Live tail is the cheap part

After storing a batch, the drainer broadcasts it on a private Laravel Reverb channel and the browser appends the lines. Nothing extra is stored for it.

Happy to go deeper on any of this in the comments. If you want to poke at it, Tailcove is on DevHunt this week and has a free plan: https://devhunt.org/tool/tailcove

title: Make your React/Vite SPA readable by AI crawlers without rewriting it
description:
Short answer: a React or Vite app sends an empty <div id="root"></div> and builds the page in the browser. AI crawlers don't run that JavaScript, so to ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity your site has no text. Pre-render it: build the HTML of each route at deploy time with a 15-line script, and React takes over in the browser as usual. You don't need to rewrite anything in Next.js.

When I audited 286 developer portfolios for an earlier study, 98 of them (34%) showed fewer than 20 words to a bot that doesn't run JavaScript. Most were React, Vue or Vite single-page apps. They look great to a person and blank to a crawler.

Check your site in 10 seconds

Ask for your page the way a crawler does and search for your main heading:

curl -s -A "GPTBot/1.1" https://yourdomain.com/ | grep -i "your main heading"

If nothing prints, AI crawlers can't see that text. You can also open view-source:https://yourdomain.com in the browser. If the body is a lone <div id="root"></div>, that's what the bots get.

The fix: 4 small changes

Vite can build your app twice: once for the browser and once for Node. The Node build can turn a route into an HTML string, and a short script saves one file per route. I tested this with Vite 8, React 19 and React Router 8.

1. Add a placeholder in index.html:

<div id="root"><!--app--></div>

2. Create src/entry-server.jsx, which renders a route to a string:

import { renderToString } from "react-dom/server";
import { StaticRouter } from "react-router";
import App from "./App.jsx";

export function render(url) {
  return renderToString(<StaticRouter location={url}><App /></StaticRouter>);
}

3. In src/main.jsx, change createRoot to hydrateRoot, so React reuses the HTML that's already there instead of building it from scratch:

import { hydrateRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { BrowserRouter } from "react-router";
import App from "./App.jsx";

hydrateRoot(
  document.getElementById("root"),
  <BrowserRouter><App /></BrowserRouter>
);

4. Add prerender.js at the project root and list your public routes:

import fs from "node:fs";
import { render } from "./dist-ssr/entry-server.js";

const routes = ["/", "/projects", "/about"];
const template = fs.readFileSync("dist/index.html", "utf8");

for (const url of routes) {
  const html = template.replace("<!--app-->", render(url));
  const file = `dist${url === "/" ? "" : url}/index.html`;
  fs.mkdirSync(file.replace("/index.html", ""), { recursive: true });
  fs.writeFileSync(file, html);
}

Then point the build script in package.json at the three steps:

"build": "vite build && vite build --ssr src/entry-server.jsx --outDir dist-ssr && node prerender.js"

Run the build and dist/projects/index.html now has your real heading, text and links. Run the curl again after you deploy and you should see it.

Things that break (and how to fix them)

  • window or localStorage at the top of a component. The Node build doesn't have them. Move that code into a useEffect, which only runs in the browser.
  • Different output in Node and in the browser. If something like Date.now() or Math.random() changes what's rendered, React warns about a hydration mismatch. Render the same thing in both places, and update it in a useEffect.
  • Routes with parameters. /blog/:slug isn't a list the script can guess. Build the list from your data (the same JSON or Markdown files your app reads) and add those URLs to routes.
  • The <title>. Every page still has the title from index.html. If you want one per route, replace it in the same loop, with a .replace() on the <title> tag.
  • Testing locally. vite preview returns the home page for /projects and the right file for /projects/. Static hosts like Vercel and Netlify serve dist/projects/index.html for /projects before applying the SPA rewrite, so it works when deployed.

When this isn't the right fix

If your content changes per visitor or every few minutes (a dashboard, prices in real time), pre-rendering at deploy time won't keep up. That's a job for server-side rendering, and at that point a framework like Next.js or React Router's framework mode is worth it. For a portfolio, a landing page or a small business site, pre-rendering is enough.

Don't want to touch your build?

If your site is a React or Vite SPA and you'd rather not deal with it, I can do it for you. I pre-render your public pages, check that AI crawlers can read them, and leave your app working exactly as it does now.
