title: Model a Trust Boundary for OAuth Email Fixtures
description:
OAuth flows are often tested as if the inbox were a harmless test detail. It is not. An inbox that receives a verification code, magic link, or recovery message is a capability. Anyone who can read it may be able to move the flow forward.

That makes a test inbox part of your OAuth trust boundary. You can use a create temp mail workflow or a disposable email address generator for isolated fixtures, but the fixture still needs ownership, expiry, and audit rules. The goal is to make assumptions visible.

Why an inbox is an OAuth trust boundary

An OAuth test usually has several actors: the browser, the client application, the authorization server, and an email system. The email system is easy to forget because it sits outside the redirect flow, yet it can deliver a link that proves address control or resets a credential.

Treat that message as a short-lived capability, similar to a code or session token. A test inbox needs a clear owner and narrow purpose. It should never be a shared mailbox containing real customer messages, production reset links, or credentials copied from another environment.

This distinction matters: a disposable address is test data, not an identity guarantee. A passing test proves only that configured actors completed the flow.

A small threat model for email fixtures

Start with how a fixture can cross its intended boundary:

  • Cross-test reading: two parallel jobs use one inbox, so a code from one run is accepted by another. A shared fixture make this failure quiet.
  • Redirect confusion: the application accepts a redirect URI from a loose environment variable, allowing a token or link to land somewhere unexpected.
  • Log leakage: the full verification URL is printed by a failed test, a CI artifact, or a browser trace.
  • Long retention: old messages remain after the test. Cleanup is not a nice-to-have; it are part of the security control.
  • Account reuse: a fixture address is reused across branches, teams, or environments, making it hard to know which run created a message.

Some teams search for “tempail mail” when they are trying to find temporary test mail. The spelling is not the security issue; the important question is whether the mailbox can be isolated and deleted on a predictable clock.

Pair the fixture with a deletion clock for privacy-safe email tests. Deletion should be explicit, not a hope that a provider eventually removes old data.

Design the fixture boundary

Give every test run a fixture identity: run ID, environment, creation time, expiry time, and owner. Your application should still verify that the address belongs to the current run before accepting a message.

Make these rules explicit:

  1. One run, one fixture. Do not let parallel jobs poll the same address. If a provider cannot isolate it, add locking or use a different strategy.
  2. Short lease, enforced server-side. Store an expiry timestamp. Do not rely only on a CI timeout, because cancelled jobs do not always execute their final step.
  3. No production access. Keep test inbox credentials and OAuth client credentials in the test environment. Never make a test address a recovery route for a real account.
  4. Minimum message exposure. Extract the code or link, redact it from logs, and delete the message after the assertion.
  5. A dry-run path. Before sending, validate the recipient, environment, redirect URI, and lease. A dry-run contract for automation makes these checks repeatable.

This can feel over careful for staging, but staging often contains realistic configuration and copied data. A small boundary is cheaper than investigating a leaked token later.

Implement safer verification flows

Keep the email adapter behind a narrow interface. The test should ask for a message belonging to its run, not search a global inbox for the newest message:

async function waitForVerificationLink({ inbox, runId, expiresAt }) {
  const message = await inbox.waitForMessage({
    recipient: `oauth-${runId}@test.invalid`,
    after: new Date().toISOString(),
    until: expiresAt,
  });

  if (!message || message.runId !== runId) {
    throw new Error("verification message is outside the fixture boundary");
  }

  return extractVerificationLink(message.text);
}

The adapter should reject messages without the expected run correlation. If a test fail here, that is valuable evidence: the contract is incomplete or the system sent mail to the wrong place. Do not “fix” it by accepting the newest message from any recipient.

Validate the link before opening it: host, scheme, state, registered redirect URI, and the current browser session. Never print the complete link; log a hash or redacted route if debugging is needed.

Finally, make cleanup idempotent. A failed test, retry, and manual rerun should all call cleanup without turning a missing message into a second failure. The clean up step removes the mailbox or revokes its lease, then records only audit metadata.

A practical review checklist

Before merging an OAuth flow that depends on email, ask:

  • Is the test inbox isolated by run, environment, and owner?
  • Can one job read or consume another job’s verification message?
  • Are redirect URIs and state values checked before a link is opened?
  • Could a CI log, trace, screenshot, or artifact contain a token?
  • Does the fixture expire if the job is cancelled halfway through?
  • Is cleanup safe to run more than once?
  • Can an operator explain which messages existed without reading their contents?

Good audit data says what happened, when, and under which run ID. It does not preserve the secret that made the test pass.

Questions teams usually ask

Should temporary email be used for production authentication tests?

Use it for controlled test accounts and isolated environments, not as a substitute for identity verification. Production tests need synthetic data and monitoring that prevents a test account becoming a recovery path.

Is deleting the inbox enough?

No. Check application logs, CI artifacts, browser traces, provider logs, and caches too. A mailbox can be gone while its verification URL remains in a retained artifact.

What is the safest default when a message is ambiguous?

Fail closed. Require the exact run correlation, recipient, time window, and expected sender or message shape. A little extra polling is better than accepting an unrelated message.

Final takeaway

Email fixtures are part of the authentication system’s attack surface, even when they exist only for tests. Give each fixture a short lease, bind it to a run, validate every link before use, and remove both messages and derived secrets from retained artifacts.

The surprized result is usually positive: once the boundary is explicit, flaky OAuth tests become easier to debug as well as safer to operate. Security controls and reliable test design are pulling in the same direction here.

title: The rule that pays for a Chinese workplace injury lives in four documents
description:
I spent a morning trying to answer one question: what does an employer in China owe after a workplace injury? The short answer is a State Council regulation with four benefit bands. The longer answer is that three of the numbers people quote are not in that regulation at all, and one of them changes every January.

This is a note on how the chain fits together, and on the checks that caught my own misreadings.

The regulation is the easy part

The work injury regulation (State Council Order 375, rewritten by Order 586 in 2010) is a tidy document. Ten disability grades, a fixed number of months of the worker's wage for each, plus a monthly allowance for the top six. The wage it multiplies is not the salary in the contract: article 64 uses the average monthly contribution wage over the 12 months before the injury, then clamps it to 300% and 60% of the local average wage.

That clamp is the first place a hand calculation goes wrong. If a worker earns 30,000 a month in a city whose average wage is 8,000, the benefit is priced at 24,000. If a worker earns 3,500, it is priced at 4,800 — higher than what they actually earned. Both directions are in the same sentence, and the mechanism is contribution-based, so an employer that reported a low base produces a low payout.

A small function makes the rule testable:

GRANT = {1: 27, 2: 25, 3: 23, 4: 21, 5: 18, 6: 16, 7: 13, 8: 11, 9: 9, 10: 7}
ALLOWANCE = {1: 0.90, 2: 0.85, 3: 0.80, 4: 0.75, 5: 0.70, 6: 0.60}

def priced_wage(last12_avg, city_avg):
    lo, hi = 0.6 * city_avg, 3.0 * city_avg
    return min(max(last12_avg, lo), hi)

def one_off(grade, wage):
    return GRANT[grade] * wage

assert priced_wage(30_000, 8_000) == 24_000   # ceiling
assert priced_wage(3_500, 8_000) == 4_800     # floor
assert one_off(10, 10_000) == 70_000
assert one_off(1, 10_000) == 270_000

Number one that is not in the regulation: the death grant

Article 39 says a work-related death pays three items. Two of them are computed on figures that have nothing to do with the worker's wage: the burial grant is six months of the local average wage, and the one-off death grant is 20 times the previous year's national urban per-capita disposable income.

The 20 is in the regulation. The income figure is not. It arrives with the statistics bureau's January release. For deaths in 2026 the number is 56,502 CNY, so the grant is 1,130,040. For 2025 the figure was 54,188 and the grant was 1,083,760.

Two consequences worth writing down: the death grant is identical in every city, while the burial grant is not, because one uses a national income average and the other a local wage average. And if a death happens in the first weeks of January, before the release, a 2013 ministry opinion allows payment on the previous year's figure with a top-up later. A benefit table that hardcodes one year's number is wrong by the next January.

Checking is cheap here: recompute the prior year, subtract, and see whether the difference matches the published growth rate.

Number two: when the 48-hour clock starts

The regulation treats a sudden illness at work that kills within 48 hours as a work injury, and never says when the 48 hours begin. A 2004 ministry letter does: from the first diagnosis at a medical institution.

The interesting part is that this letter predates the 2010 rewrite, and part of it is visibly stale. One item still quotes the old commute clause, which covered motor vehicle accidents; the rewrite replaced it with any accident where the worker is not mainly responsible, across road, rail, ferry and train. So the letter is half-live: its 48-hour reading is still cited by the ministry, while its other items describe text that no longer exists.

That is the failure mode I keep running into with Chinese administrative law. An interpretive letter stays in force until something repeals it, even when the thing it interprets has been rewritten underneath it. The only reliable check is to read the letter and the current regulation side by side, and to note which items still map onto a live article.

Number three: the two subsidies only provinces can price

When the employment ends after a graded injury, two more payments appear: a medical subsidy from the fund and an employment subsidy from the employer. The regulation sets no amounts and hands them to each province.

Guangdong's statute gives grade 5 ten months of medical subsidy and fifty months of employment subsidy, down to grade 10 at one month and four months. At a 10,000 monthly wage, a grade 10 injury adds 50,000 to the 70,000 grant; a grade 5 adds 600,000 to the 180,000.

So "the compensation for a grade 10 injury" has no national answer. It has a national core plus a provincial tail, and the tail is larger than the core for low grades.

GD_MED = {5: 10, 6: 8, 7: 6, 8: 4, 9: 2, 10: 1}
GD_EMP = {5: 50, 6: 40, 7: 25, 8: 15, 9: 8, 10: 4}

def gd_termination(grade, wage):
    return GD_MED[grade] * wage, GD_EMP[grade] * wage

assert sum(gd_termination(10, 10_000)) == 50_000
assert sum(gd_termination(5, 10_000)) == 600_000

What I'd check first next time

Three questions, in this order, for any benefit that looks like a simple multiple:

  1. Is the multiplier applied to the worker's wage, a local average, or a national statistic? Article 39 uses all three in one paragraph.
  2. Is the base the wage paid or the wage contributed on? In China those diverge, and the benefit follows the contribution.
  3. Which document actually sets the amount? A regulation that says "the province decides" is a pointer, not an answer.

None of this is exotic. It is the ordinary work of reading a spec that is split across four files, where one file changes annually and one is older than the file it interprets.

I wrote the full version, with every article number and source date, at notebookfield.com.

Drafted with an AI assistant from my own reading of the primary documents; every clause number and link here was checked against the source.

title: Why UUIDv4 Causes PostgreSQL/InnoDB B-Tree Bloat — and How RFC 9562 UUIDv7 Fixes It
description:
Using random UUIDv4 values as database primary keys looks clean at 100k rows and turns painful past 20M rows. The bottleneck is not UUID size (16 bytes)—it is write locality inside B-Tree indexes.

1. What Random UUIDv4 Does to B-Tree Pages

Sequential keys append to the rightmost leaf page of a B-Tree, so hot index writes stay inside RAM (shared_buffers in PostgreSQL, innodb_buffer_pool in MySQL).

Completely random UUIDv4 keys scatter inserts across the entire index:

  • Half-full page splits inflate index size by 30–50% and drive random disk I/O.
  • In MySQL InnoDB, because the primary key is clustered and copied into every secondary index, random UUIDv4 keys degrade cache hit ratios across all indexes on the table.

2. How RFC 9562 UUIDv7 Keeps 16 Bytes and Restores Locality

UUIDv7 fits inside the exact same standard UUID column type, placing a 48-bit big-endian Unix millisecond timestamp in the first 6 bytes:

  • Bits 0..47: Unix epoch timestamp in milliseconds
  • Bits 48..51: Version 7 (0111)
  • Bits 52..63: 12 bits of sub-millisecond monotonicity / randomness
  • Bits 64..65: RFC 9562 variant 10
  • Bits 66..127: 62 random bits

Because keys increase monotonically with time, inserts land at the rightmost leaf pages—and you can decode exact creation timestamps straight out of any UUIDv7 without touching the database.

3. Zero-Dependency CLI & Browser Inspector

I built a small MIT CLI (uuidv7-inspect, zero dependencies, node --test passing) to generate RFC 9562 UUIDv7s and inspect embedded timestamps, paired with client-side browser tools (0 bytes uploaded):

  • Open-Source CLI (uuidv7-inspect, MIT): https://github.com/JangYS0/uuidv7-inspect
  • Browser UUIDv7 / UUIDv4 Generator & Inspector: https://global-utils.com/en/uuid-generator
  • Unix Timestamp Converter: https://global-utils.com/en/timestamp-converter
  • UUIDv7 & Snowflake ID Suite: https://global-utils.com/en/assets/uuidv7-snowflake-high-throughput-id-suite

title: SwiftPY 0.3.5 Beta: I Need Python Developers Who Will Try to Break It
description:
Most framework announcements say "try it". This one says something slightly different:

Please try to break it.

SwiftPY is an ASGI native, Eloquent style Python web framework I have been building for one reason. After more than ten years of backends with Laravel, and a recent stretch of AI projects on FastAPI, I wanted the async first speed of the Python ecosystem together with the structure, conventions and tooling I had learned to love. That framework did not exist, so I started building it.

SwiftPY is now at version 0.3.5, it is on PyPI, and it is still in beta. Before I call anything 1.0.0, I want people other than me to push on it.

GitHub: https://github.com/Obrainwave/swiftpy

Why beta testers matter more than any feature

I use SwiftPY on real projects, including its own documentation site (Next.js on the frontend, SwiftPY on the backend). Real use is the best bug finder I have, but it has a hard limit: it only exercises the paths I happen to take.

Every developer builds differently. You will name your models differently, nest your routes differently, deploy behind a different proxy and hit combinations I never imagined. That is exactly the information a 1.0.0 release needs.

The changelog shows what this loop looks like in practice. In 0.3.5 alone, the entries under "Fixed" include:

  • a comma separated trusted_proxies string that passed validation but later broke every request.ip() call
  • a scheduler loop that listed every schedule on each wake up instead of reading the earliest due time
  • overlap locks that could expire while a long running job was still executing

Each one is a small, specific, fixable problem. Finding them early, in public, is the whole point.

What is already in the box

SwiftPY is not a toy router. Over the last few weeks the beta has grown into a full framework:

  • An async Active Record ORM with typed models, eager loading, dirty tracking, HasMany, HasOne, BelongsTo and BelongsToMany, plus relationship existence queries such as has() and where_has()
  • A fluent query builder and migrations with Blueprint, pagination, group_by, having, and PostgreSQL advisory locks
  • Validation through FormRequest and validate(), failing closed before your handler runs
  • Authentication with JWT pairs, refresh token rotation, API keys, Auth.attempt(), remember me sessions, auth lifecycle events and built in login throttling
  • A native task scheduler with a strict five field cron engine, time zone support and a durable Redis store, driven by schedule:work
  • Queues, events, cache, storage, mail and WebSockets
  • A native AI subsystem for OpenAI and Anthropic: streaming, embeddings, vector stores, RAG, tool calling agents, and versioned prompt templates
  • A CLI that writes the boring code

A taste of the developer experience:

# Controller routing with per request dependency injection
router.get("/users", UserController.index)

# Credential login with throttling, events and optional remember me
await Auth.attempt({"email": email, "password": password, "active": 1}, remember=True)

# Update a model, respecting __fillable__ / __guarded__
await user.update({"name": "Alice"})

swiftpy new my_service
swiftpy make:model Post -m
swiftpy make:request CreateOrderRequest
swiftpy make:agent SupportAssistant
swiftpy make:prompt summarise.v2
swiftpy migrate
swiftpy db:seed
swiftpy schedule:work

Secure by default, and I want that tested hardest

Security is where outside eyes help most. These defaults already ship, and I would love you to attack them:

  • Mass assignment is denied unless a model declares __fillable__ or __guarded__
  • A WHERE less update() or delete() raises an error unless you opt in with .allow_all()
  • Client IP detection ignores forwarded headers unless you configure trusted proxies, and it resolves them right to left with strict bounds
  • Login throttling buckets IPv6 clients by /64, so rotating addresses inside one prefix cannot dodge a lockout
  • Scheduled tasks carry an HMAC signature, and tampered records are marked failed and never executed
  • Queue envelopes are signed before any class is imported
  • Production mode refuses weak secrets and never leaks tracebacks

If you find a hole, I want to hear about it. For anything security sensitive, please message me privately before posting it publicly.

How to get started

You need Python 3.12+, PostgreSQL and Redis. The scaffold ships with a Docker setup for the last two.

pip install swiftpy-framework
swiftpy new my_service
cd my_service
swiftpy migrate
swiftpy start --reload

The step by step guides live in the repository's documentations folder, and the full documentation site at https://swiftpy.net arrives with 1.0.0.

Five ways to help, from 15 minutes to a weekend

  1. Build something small. A blog API, a todo service, an auth flow, a job that sends email. Whatever you would normally build, build it with SwiftPY.
  2. Stress the risky corners. Try your real database schemas with the migrations, relationships you actually use with the ORM, the scheduler across multiple workers, or login throttling behind your own proxy.
  3. Try your own platform. Windows, macOS, Linux, Docker Desktop, a cheap VPS. Environment bugs are invisible to a single developer.
  4. Report what you find. Open an issue on GitHub with what you expected, what happened and how to reproduce it. "This confused me" is a valid bug report, because confusing documentation is a bug.
  5. Contribute. Tests, examples, documentation fixes and code are all welcome. You do not need prior open source experience.

What to expect

This is a beta, so expect rough edges and the occasional breaking change before 1.0.0. Every release lists what was added, changed, fixed and secured in the public changelog, so nothing changes quietly.

I am also not going to rush 1.0.0 just to have a stable looking number. It ships when I am confident the framework is stable, secure and reliable enough for production. Your testing is how I get there.

Join in

  • Star and explore the repo: https://github.com/Obrainwave/swiftpy
  • Open an issue for anything you find
  • Or send me a DM with "SWIFTPY TESTER" and I will help you get started

Building a framework is one thing. Building one other developers can trust is another. Help me earn that trust before 1.0.0.

SwiftPY: Building towards 1.0.0.

title: Halo: Campaign Evolved Lands on PS5, Xbox, and PC July 28
description:
Halo: Campaign Evolved Lands on PS5, Xbox, and PC July 28

The wait is almost over for fans of the iconic Halo franchise. 343 Industries, the developers behind the beloved series, have announced that Halo: Campaign Evolved will be released on July 28, 2023, for PlayStation 5, Xbox, and PC. This new iteration promises to bring a fresh perspective to the classic Halo experience, with a focus on reimagining the campaign for a new generation of gamers.

What's New in Halo: Campaign Evolved?

The latest installment in the Halo series is designed to appeal to both new and veteran players. The campaign has been reworked to provide a more immersive and engaging experience, with a greater emphasis on storytelling and character development. The game's narrative will explore the aftermath of the events in Halo 5: Guardians, delving deeper into the struggles of the Master Chief and his allies as they face an uncertain future.

New Missions and Gameplay Mechanics

Halo: Campaign Evolved will introduce new missions, each with its unique challenges and objectives. These missions will be designed to showcase the game's improved graphics, sound design, and gameplay mechanics. Players can expect to encounter a range of new enemies, including some familiar faces from the series' past.

Enhanced Graphics and Sound Design

The game's visuals have been significantly upgraded, with 343 Industries utilizing the latest technology to create a more realistic and immersive environment. The sound design has also been overhauled, with a greater emphasis on creating a more immersive audio experience. The game's soundtrack, composed by Martin O'Donnell, is expected to be just as epic as its predecessors.

Multiplayer and Co-op

Halo: Campaign Evolved will also feature a robust multiplayer mode, allowing players to engage in competitive and cooperative gameplay. The game will include a range of modes, including PvP, PvE, and co-op, ensuring that there's something for every type of player.

Key Takeaways

  • Halo: Campaign Evolved is a reimagined campaign for the classic Halo series, designed to appeal to both new and veteran players.
  • The game features new missions, improved graphics, and enhanced sound design.
  • Multiplayer and co-op modes are included, offering a range of gameplay options for players.
  • The game is set to release on July 28, 2023, for PlayStation 5, Xbox, and PC.

Why This Matters

The Halo franchise has a dedicated fan base, and the announcement of Halo: Campaign Evolved is likely to generate significant excitement. The game's reworked campaign and improved graphics will provide a fresh perspective on the classic Halo experience, making it an attractive option for both new and veteran players. The inclusion of multiplayer and co-op modes will also ensure that the game has broad appeal, making it a must-play for fans of the series.

Conclusion

Halo: Campaign Evolved is shaping up to be an exciting addition to the Halo franchise, offering a reimagined campaign, improved graphics, and enhanced sound design. The game's release on July 28, 2023, is eagerly anticipated by fans of the series, and its inclusion of multiplayer and co-op modes will ensure that it has broad appeal. Whether you're a new or veteran player, Halo: Campaign Evolved is definitely worth keeping an eye on.

title: Built in the open: four repositories, one rule — declare what's absent
description:
I'm a solo builder. Everything below is public on GitHub, free for non-commercial use with attribution under my Dual License Agreement v4.9. I'm not selling anything. This is a record of what exists, written for the people who judge work by running it.

The work's home on the web is https://www.livingphiphysics.com.

Living-Phi-Physics — the flagship proofs

https://github.com/pluscoder30-cpu/Living-Phi-Physics

Nine papers (P1–P9), committed August 19, 2026: phi-form laws with a classical limit (κ_φ → 0), including work on Navier–Stokes, Yang–Mills, and the Riemann hypothesis. The claim and the papers are dated by GitHub's own timestamps. Read them, check the dates, argue with the math — that's what they're there for.

Portable-XRF — the instrument package

https://github.com/pluscoder30-cpu/Portable-XRF

Software for a portable XRF spectrometer: 222 files, ~19,500 lines of Python, ESP32 firmware, ten papers. On a clean machine the test suite runs 236 passed / 9 skipped / 2 failed of 247 — both failures are the same self-declared absence (a vendor cross-check package that isn't public, named as absent in the code). Every reading carries a receipt with a verdict code — [VERIFIED] [REAL] [DECLARED] [PREDICTED] [SIMULATED] [ABSENT] — and Law 1347 keeps the core spectroscopy in exact classical form, enforced by a dedicated honesty test.

Omega_Field_GPU_Ultimate — the field processor

https://github.com/pluscoder30-cpu/Omega_Field_GPU_Ultimate

A self-defining field matrix processor with a holographic codec (real numpy encode/decode via pseudo-inverse). It ships with its own claim-checker: run VERIFY_CLAIMS.py and every check passes — the summary matches the README to the digit. Don't take the README's word; run the file that argues with it.

The-future-of-vehicles — the fleet

https://github.com/pluscoder30-cpu/The-future-of-vehicles

51 complete build packages — 1,138 files: priced parts lists from real suppliers, wiring and mechanical docs, assembly steps written so a 12-year-old can follow them, safety, and the physics for each. Total fleet cost ~$35,000 per the README. This one is a gift artifact: take a package and build the thing.

The rule that ties them together

Every package declares what it is and what it isn't. Verdicts are printed, absences are spoken, and the receipts are kept by third parties — GitHub's timestamps, hash chains — not by me. Judge it the way builders judge anything: clone it, run it, and see what holds.

— Christopher David Ayotte (pluscoder30-cpu)

title: Design for the slowest moment: why you should judge a logistics product in a yard
description:
Software is usually shown at its fastest. A demonstration happens on a good laptop, on office wifi, with tidy sample data and a presenter who knows exactly where to click. Freight happens somewhere else.

That gap is the subject of chapter 9 of my book, One Shared Record, and it ends on a line I keep coming back to: the honest way to judge a logistics product is to try it in a yard.

Six in the morning, one bar of signal

A driver has just finished unloading at a warehouse on the edge of an industrial estate. It is early, it is cold, the signal is poor and the next slot is ninety minutes away. They need to submit proof of delivery and leave.

Everything about that moment is a constraint. The screen has to work on a phone, with gloves on if necessary. It has to ask for as little as possible. When the connection drops halfway, it has to keep what was entered and send it when the signal returns, without the driver ever needing to know that anything went wrong.

If that step takes four minutes and fails one time in ten, drivers stop using it. Paper comes back, and the shared record gets a hole exactly where the most disputed evidence should be.

Month end, two hundred invoices

At the other extreme sits a finance officer on the last working day of the month, with a long queue of invoices to approve. Their constraint is not signal. It is attention.

They need to see, for each invoice, whether the evidence behind it is already accepted, and to approve many at once where nothing is unusual. What they should never have to do is open each shipment to check whether the delivery note was signed. A shared record helps this person more than almost anyone, because the checking already happened upstream, but only if the screen shows it plainly.

What slow moments decide

These moments decide architecture, not only screens:

  1. Confirmations must be quick and predictable. A person at a dock will not wait and wonder. The answer has to feel immediate every time, not on average.
  2. The system must be honest about what is pending. "Sent, waiting for confirmation" and "confirmed" are different, and the user should be able to tell.
  3. No technical decisions for non-technical people. No fees to choose, no network to select, no error message in the vocabulary of the ledger.
  4. Failure has to be ordinary. Connections drop and services restart. Good design assumes that and recovers without drama.

I have learned to distrust any feature that only works under demonstration conditions. Before you believe a demo, ask to see it on a cheap phone, at six in the morning, with one bar of signal.

The book

One Shared Record: What a blockchain can and cannot prove in European freight is a short book in twelve chapters about giving every company on a shipment one shared, tamper-evident record.

  • Kindle: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HSN18N4N
  • Paperback: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HSN5YJ6D
  • Author page: https://www.amazon.com/author/pratyushshivam

Pratyush Shivam is the CTO of Konfidio GmbH (Berlin) and leads the technology behind TrustedTrucks. More at https://www.pratyushshivam.com

title: Hardcharger Tops DB Olympics at 1 TB: Most Queries per Second, Lowest Cost, All 409 Answers Correct
description:
Philip Moore · 2026-11-23

Source: https://gizmodata.com/blog/dbolympics-hardcharger-1tb

DB Olympics is a new, open benchmark of 409 SQL queries asked by AI agents playing the staff of an online retailer. At 1 TB, Hardcharger 2.14.0 answered 4.74 queries per second, 1.85 times CedarDB and almost twice DuckDB, ran all 409 for $0.068, and is the only released database to answer all 409 correctly on every machine at every scale. Where we aren't first, the query that made us fork DuckDB, and the DuckDB Labs work it all stands on.

DB Olympics is a new, open SQL benchmark from Altan Birler and Tobias Schmidt of the database group at the Technical University of Munich. Instead of a fixed set of textbook queries, it simulates an online retailer, Tidewick Commerce, and lets AI agents play its people: the CEO, the CFO, data analysts, the security chief and more. Their questions became 409 SQL queries, which every system runs on AWS machines at four sizes, from 1 GB to 1 TB, with each answer checked against a reference result.

We submitted Hardcharger 2.14.0 on November 22, and DB Olympics ran it the next day. At 1 TB, Hardcharger has the highest throughput and the lowest cost of every system on the board, and it is the only released database that answered all 409 queries correctly on every machine at every scale.

Leaderboards move, and this one is only weeks old. We expect the other systems to catch up, some of them soon. But on November 23, at 1 TB, Hardcharger is on top, and we'll take it.

DB Olympics' Figure 1 at 1 TB: queries per second against the cost of all 409 queries, each system on its most efficient machine. Up and to the left is better. Hardcharger is listed as a variant of DuckDB, so to see it on the live chart, click the DuckDB row in the table below the chart to expand it. Screenshot of dbolympics.com, November 23, 2026.

The results at 1 TB

DB Olympics scores a system by the time it takes to run all 409 queries once after its last data load. Queries per second is 409 divided by that time, and cost is that time at the machine's AWS on-demand price. A query that runs past the timeout (30 seconds at 1 TB) counts as the full 30 seconds. This is every system on the largest machine, a c8a.24xlarge with 96 vCPUs and 192 GB of memory, each with its own storage format:

System Queries per second Cost of all 409 Slowdown Correct
Hardcharger 4.74 $0.124 1.40× 409
CedarDB 2.56 $0.229 1.35× 408
DuckDB 2.40 $0.244 1.58× 407
Hyper 1.70 $0.346 1.66× 404
ClickHouse 1.09 $0.538 4.20× 349
DataFusion (Parquet) 0.97 $0.605 4.84× 317
Firebolt 0.61 $0.959 4.39× 381

DB Olympics' Table 1 on the c8a.24xlarge. The site lists Hardcharger as a variant of DuckDB, the engine it builds on, and ranks only the base systems, so Hardcharger's row (highlighted) has no rank number of its own. Screenshot of dbolympics.com, November 23, 2026.

Hardcharger answers 1.85 times as many queries per second as CedarDB and almost twice as many as DuckDB, for about half the cost. The lowest cost on the board comes from a smaller machine: on a c8a.12xlarge (48 vCPUs, 96 GB), Hardcharger ran all 409 queries for $0.068, against $0.126 for DuckDB and $0.129 for CedarDB there. Its 4.31 queries per second on that machine are more than any other system managed on any machine.

Slowdown is DB Olympics' other measure: the geometric mean of how far each query is from the fastest system's time on it. It rewards the typical query rather than the total, and on the largest machine CedarDB is ahead on it, 1.35 to our 1.40. On the c8a.12xlarge and c8a.16xlarge, Hardcharger's slowdown is the lowest. CedarDB is faster than Hardcharger on more than half of the individual queries at 1 TB; Hardcharger wins on the total because it has no slow outliers. Its slowest query took 6.3 seconds. CedarDB's slowest answer took 16.6 seconds, and one more query timed out; DuckDB had two timeouts.

A note on what was measured. DuckDB runs embedded inside the benchmark program. Hardcharger runs as a server: the benchmark sent every query to hardcharger-server through the Hardcharger ADBC driver, over Chargewire on the same machine, and fetched every result. So Hardcharger's times include a client-server round trip that the embedded DuckDB entry doesn't pay.

All 409, everywhere

DB Olympics ran Hardcharger in 16 configurations: four scale factors (1 GB, 10 GB, 100 GB and 1 TB), each on three or four machine sizes. Hardcharger answered all 409 queries correctly in all 16, with no wrong result, no error and no timeout. The only other system to do that is Querybrew on ClickHouse, an experimental system from the DB Olympics authors in which their research database, Umbra, rewrites every query for ClickHouse; it isn't a released product, and at 1 TB it ran at about a quarter of Hardcharger's throughput. Among released systems at 1 TB, CedarDB answered 408 and DuckDB 407.

The query that started a fork

Query 318 was asked by the simulated Chief Information Security Officer:

"Since shopper accounts have 0% MFA, what actually stands in for a second factor today: are most shoppers authenticating through an OAuth provider (Google/Apple/etc., which carries its own security), or are they overwhelmingly raw password-only accounts with no backup at all?"

At its heart is a join of shoppers to their login attempts on the tenant and either the user ID or the email address:

join login_attempts la
  on la.tenant_id = s.tenant_id
 and (la.user_id = s.id or la.email = s.email)

The tenant is a weak key: it matches every shopper of a merchant to every login attempt of that merchant, and the or can't be used to look rows up, so an engine ends up checking a huge number of candidate pairs. At 1 TB on the c8a.24xlarge:

System Query 318 at 1 TB
Hardcharger 0.25 s
Querybrew on ClickHouse (experimental) 0.55 s
ClickHouse 6.15 s
Firebolt 7.29 s
CedarDB, DuckDB, Hyper, DataFusion (Parquet) and Hardcharger (Parquet) timed out at 30 s

Query 318 at 1 TB as DB Olympics shows it. Screenshot of dbolympics.com, November 23, 2026.

We'll be upfront: this is the query that made us fork. DB Olympics' first run of Hardcharger, version 2.0.0 on stock DuckDB 2.0.0 in late October, timed out on it at 10 GB and above, and the fix needed a change inside DuckDB's optimizer. So we started Hardcharger Engine, our performance fork of DuckDB, to ship and test such changes on Hardcharger's release schedule. Its first optimizer rule handles joins of this shape in general, not query 318 by name: for an eligible inner join under a DISTINCT, it builds two selective joins, one on tenant and user ID and one on tenant and email, and lets the existing DISTINCT remove the overlap. It applies only when it can prove the answer is unchanged, and it ships with its own regression tests. In our own test at 10 GB on a laptop, swapping stock DuckDB 2.0.1 for our engine took query 318 from 3.67 seconds to 19 milliseconds.

How Hardcharger Engine runs query 318's join. Left: stock DuckDB joins on tenant_id alone and checks the OR condition on every candidate pair. Right: Hardcharger Engine runs two selective joins and lets the query's own DISTINCT remove the overlap. An illustration, not to scale.

Two caveats, because they matter. Our Parquet configuration still timed out on query 318, so the rule doesn't help there yet. And at 100 GB, query 318 is what puts Hardcharger ahead: without it, CedarDB would be slightly faster on the c8a.12xlarge, 26.7 queries per second to our 25.1. At 1 TB the lead holds without it. Take query 318 out of every system's total on the c8a.24xlarge and Hardcharger still answers 4.74 queries per second, against 3.15 for CedarDB and 2.91 for DuckDB. At 10 GB and 1 GB, CedarDB leads outright.

One more: query 360

The simulated Head of Pricing and Promotions asked whether free deliveries going to customers whose subscription had already been canceled were "a slow-burning historical gap, steady, or accelerating". Here we don't win: at 1 TB on the c8a.24xlarge, CedarDB answered in 97.5 milliseconds and Hardcharger in 144. But stock DuckDB timed out at 30 seconds, and the next systems took from 0.9 to 2.5 seconds. The query joins orders to calendar days and exchange rates on a timestamp cast to a date, the shape another of our engine changes is aimed at: a better estimate of how many rows such a join produces. We haven't isolated that change as the reason (the DuckDB entry ran 2.0.0, a patch release behind our engine's base), so we'll just report the times.

Query 360 at 1 TB as DB Olympics shows it. Screenshot of dbolympics.com, November 23, 2026.

Standing on the shoulders of ducks

None of this exists without DuckDB. Hardcharger Engine 2.0.1 is DuckDB 2.0.1 with 14 performance commits on top, plus the hooks the Hardcharger server needs. The SQL, the execution engine, the storage and the database file format are DuckDB's, built by the incredible team at DuckDB Labs and DuckDB's many contributors, and released under the MIT license. Thank you. The 409 queries ran on your work.

One of those contributors, in a small way, is our founder, Philip Moore (prmoore77). Three of his pull requests are in DuckDB itself: the struct_insert function, HUGEINT support for bit_count and new information_schema views. Not many, but it means we've helped build the engine we know and love, not just build on it.

We'll take a little of the credit too. Our share of the result is:

  • The engine changes. Besides the join rule, the fork estimates timestamp-to-date joins better, applies integer range filters in one pass, reuses checks in filtered column scans, starts scan read-ahead sooner, and speeds up substring search and regular expression extraction. Each change is documented with its limits, its tests and what we measured.
  • The server around it. Hardcharger turns the engine into a multi-user server with sign-in, access control and an Arrow-native protocol, Chargewire, and it scored these numbers as a server, answering over the wire.

Thank you as well to Altan Birler and Tobias Schmidt for DB Olympics: an open benchmark where anyone can add a system, every result is checked, and the queries come from questions people would actually ask. Finding query 318 made our engine better.

And on ClickBench

We submitted Hardcharger 2.14.0 to ClickBench as well, and it was merged on November 22. On ClickBench's default combined score, as of November 23, Hardcharger places 6th of 93 entries on the c7a.metal-48xl and 6th of 91 on the c8g.metal-48xl, the highest-placed DuckDB-based system on both, behind Rayforce, CedarDB, ClickHouse and chDB. On the smaller c6a.4xlarge it is 9th of 102, a hair behind our own GizmoSQL entry from May. Cold runs, the first run of each query after a restart, are our weak spot there, and the next thing we want to improve.

The details

  • Hardcharger: version 2.14.0 on Hardcharger Engine 2.0.1 (DuckDB 2.0.1), queried through the Hardcharger ADBC driver 2.7.2. The DuckDB entry ran DuckDB 2.0.0.
  • Run: by DB Olympics' own runner on November 23, 2026, on AWS c8a machines (AMD EPYC), each system limited to the machine's cores and 80% of its memory, with data loaded from Parquet in five periods and the queries timed after the last load.
  • Numbers: computed from DB Olympics' published data with its own formulas (the site rounds them); prices are AWS on-demand, $2.5865 an hour for the c8a.12xlarge and $5.173 for the c8a.24xlarge.
  • See it for yourself: the results, query 318, the methodology and Hardcharger's entry in the DB Olympics repository. Hardcharger isn't one of the site's core systems: it is listed under DuckDB, so click the DuckDB row in the results table to expand it, and Hardcharger then appears in the table and on the chart.

Try Hardcharger

Start free with $25 of launch credit, applied automatically. No credit card needed. Run it on GizmoData Cloud, or install the open-source server on your own machine in a minute.

Install Hardcharger

CedarDB, ClickHouse, Hyper, DataFusion, Firebolt and other names are trademarks of their respective owners. DB Olympics ran every system; the numbers above are computed from its published data.

title: Building a reading speed test that can't be gamed by skimming
description:
Our book review site needed a feature readers would actually use, and that other sites would want to link to. We settled on a reading speed test, then found that most existing tests share a flaw: skim the passage, press stop, and you're suddenly reading at 1,000 words per minute.

Here's how we built one that pushes back, in a single React client component inside a Next.js app.

The flow

The component is a small state machine with four stages: intro → reading → quiz → result.

const [stage, setStage] = useState<"intro" | "reading" | "quiz" | "result">("intro");

We wrote three original passages (about 300 words each), each with three multiple-choice questions. Original text matters: nobody has read it before, and there's no copyright question.

Timing with performance.now()

Date.now() can jump if the system clock changes, so we time with performance.now(). The visible timer updates four times a second, but the score uses the exact start and end values:

function finishReading() {
  const s = (performance.now() - startedAt) / 1000;
  if (s < 5) return; // nobody reads 300 words in under 5 seconds
  setSeconds(s);
  setStage("quiz");
}

const wpm = Math.round(words / (seconds / 60));

The "I'm done" button stays disabled for the first 5 seconds, so a reflex click can't produce a score.

Guarding against skimming

Two checks keep the result honest.

Comprehension questions. After reading, the passage disappears and three questions appear. The result shows the score, and if you got fewer than two right, we suggest retaking at a slower pace.

A credibility cap. Anything above 900 wpm is labelled "Too fast to measure" and isn't saved:

const MAX_CREDIBLE_WPM = 900;

if (score <= MAX_CREDIBLE_WPM) {
  try {
    localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, String(score));
  } catch {
    // storage may be blocked
  }
}

Why 900? A 2016 review of speed-reading research (Rayner and colleagues, Psychological Science in the Public Interest) found that comprehension drops sharply when people push far past normal reading speeds, so 900 is a generous ceiling. The baseline we compare against is Brysbaert's 2019 meta-analysis of 190 studies, which puts adult silent reading at about 238 wpm for non-fiction and 260 wpm for fiction.

Note the try/catch around localStorage: in some private browsing modes it throws, and the tool should still work there.

The book-time calculator

A speed on its own is a curiosity. "This book will take you 9 hours" is useful. The Open Library search API is free, needs no key and allows cross-origin requests from the browser, so we query it directly with a timeout:

const ctrl = new AbortController();
const t = setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(), 12000);
const res = await fetch(
  `https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}` +
    `&fields=key,title,author_name,number_of_pages_median&limit=6`,
  { signal: ctrl.signal }
);
clearTimeout(t);

Asking only for the fields we need keeps the response small. number_of_pages_median gives a sensible page count across editions. If the search fails, the user can still type a page count.

The maths is simple:

const totalWords = pages * wordsPerPage; // 275 by default
const minutes = totalWords / speed;
const days = Math.ceil(minutes / minutesPerDay);

What we'd do next

  • More passages, so repeat visitors get a fresh one
  • Separate averages for reading on a phone and on a desktop

You can try it here: Reading Speed Test

If you've built anything similar, I'd like to hear how you handled the skim problem.

title: Replying to Codex desktop 26.11 sessions from your phone: what Kiteline 3.49.52 can and can't do
description:
Codex desktop 26.11 stopped exposing session control to other apps. Any tool that followed Codex sessions through that interface dropped to read-only: you could watch a session, not answer it. Kiteline is an open-source remote for coding agents (desktop on Mac, Windows and Linux; iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, plus a WeChat Mini Program for Android). Its Mac app 3.49.52 adds a way to send messages again.

What works. From the phone you can reply to sessions in the new Codex desktop app, and to Codex sessions running in a terminal with --no-daemon. If Codex is idle the message goes out immediately; if it is working, the message is queued and sent when the current turn ends. If you interrupt Codex, the message waits until you continue or send again, so it is not lost. The session has to have been opened in Codex at least once.

What still doesn't. Approving permissions, answering Codex's questions and interrupting still have to be done in Codex itself. The phone shows the state but can't click for you, because the new version no longer offers an entry point for those.

Two other changes in the same stretch. The data-flow screen (3.49.50) now cuts between close-up, overview and oblique views; a card that is working lights up, and the link for an operation in progress keeps flowing until its result returns. In the session list (3.49.53), messages sent between sessions no longer bump "last activity", so ordering and previews reflect only conversations you are part of.

Kiteline doesn't change how you launch agents, doesn't sign in to AI services and never reads API keys; it reads the transcripts agents already write locally. Source: github.com/hon6/kiteline (AGPL-3.0), site tars.betac.cn.

title: Two batches of 73 rows. Why did I get 133 candles?
description:
The 17:00 candle turned up twice. So did the one at 17:05. I was joining two six-hour slices of the same HYPEUSDT market-data file, and both slices included their endpoints.

The first slice starts at noon and ends at 18:00 Hong Kong time. The second starts at 17:00 and ends at 23:00. There are twelve five-minute steps from 17:00 to 18:00, but thirteen timestamps if you count both ends. That accounts for all 13 extra rows when you append the batches.

Here’s the whole check. Download the five-minute futures archive for November 14 and run the following Python code with pandas in the same directory as the ZIP.

import pandas as pd

archive = "HYPEUSDT-5m-2026-11-14.zip"
fields = ["open", "high", "low", "close", "volume"]
bars = pd.read_csv(archive, usecols=["open_time", *fields])
bars.index = pd.to_datetime(bars.pop("open_time"), unit="ms", utc=True)
bars.index = bars.index.tz_convert("Asia/Hong_Kong")
day = "2026-11-14 "
original = bars.loc[day + "12:00":day + "23:00"]
a = original.loc[:day + "18:00"]
b = original.loc[day + "17:00":]

shared = a.index.intersection(b.index)
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(a.loc[shared], b.loc[shared], check_exact=True)
joined = pd.concat([a, b])
recovered = joined.loc[~joined.index.duplicated(keep="first")]
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(recovered, original, check_exact=True)
print(len(a), len(b), len(joined), len(shared), len(recovered))

Output: 73 73 146 13 133. The last assertion compares the prices, volume and row order with the original window.

In this experiment both batches came from one file, so the overlapping values should match. With two independently collected batches, I’d keep the first assertion before dropping anything. If the closing prices at 17:00 disagree, keeping the first row would quietly discard that difference. For a feed with several instruments or intervals, the key needs the symbol and interval as well as the opening timestamp.

AI disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance. The example was run against the linked archive.

title: MDX – Markdown Meets React Components
description:
Originally published with interactive examples at lukiluki.me.

You are writing technical documentation in Markdown. Plain text works until the reader needs a calculator, a live example or a reusable warning box. Copying HTML fragments across articles makes them harder to maintain. How can a document stay readable while using the same components as the application?

MDX combines Markdown with JSX, so documents can import and render React components. In the Next.js App Router, local MDX can participate in server rendering while interactive components live behind explicit client boundaries. This makes shared styling and focused interaction possible. The result still depends on the imported components: using MDX alone does not guarantee static output, type-safe metadata or zero client JavaScript.

Merksatz (Key takeaway):
Use Markdown for the learning path and components for tasks that need them. Keep interactive state in separate client components and check what reaches the browser.

How MDX works in the App Router

The MDX compiler turns a document into JavaScript that renders React elements. Headings and paragraphs become elements; imported components appear where they are used in the document. The MDX format guide explains the combination of Markdown, JSX, expressions and module imports.

With @next/mdx, Next.js processes local .mdx files through its build pipeline. An RSC (React Server Component: A component evaluated on the server whose rendered output can be composed with interactive Client Components.) can render the document and include client components where needed. Client components still need their JavaScript and hydration; importing one does not make the entire surrounding article a client component.

Document element Role What to verify
Markdown headings, paragraphs and lists Structure and readable explanations The rendered heading hierarchy and semantics
Shared component mapping Consistent design-system presentation Mapping does not introduce unnecessary client dependencies
Imported client component State, event handlers or browser APIs The interaction works and has accessible controls
Metadata and frontmatter Search, page titles and exports The project explicitly parses and validates the fields

Map standard elements to the design system

The App Router uses mdx-components.tsx to define component mappings. This allows a Markdown code fence or heading to reuse a styled application component. Next.js documents this setup, including the required mapping file and local MDX imports.

For example, a shared code component can provide syntax highlighting, a frame and a copy button for every article. Keeping that behavior in one place is easier to maintain than repeating styled HTML snippets. It also means the document inherits the behavior and client requirements of that shared component.

Frontmatter (Metadata stored at the start of a document, often as YAML between delimiter lines; parsing and validation must be configured by the application.) is not automatically a validated schema. In this garden, a build script parses metadata and checks it with Zod before generating the index. That is project infrastructure on top of MDX.

Keep interaction in a separate component

Before using this pattern, configure @next/mdx and the component mapping for your Next.js project. The example assumes an App Router application with an @/ source alias. The component file is ordinary TSX; the article imports it rather than defining hooks inside the MDX document.

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";

export default function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <button
      type="button"
      onClick={() => setCount((value) => value + 1)}
      className="min-h-11 rounded-lg border px-4 py-2"
    >
      Clicks: {count}
    </button>
  );
}

Save that component as src/components/Counter.tsx. The corresponding article can then contain:

import Counter from "@/components/Counter";

## Try the example

Activate the button by mouse or keyboard and watch the count change.

<Counter />

The expected result is a heading, an explanatory paragraph and a button whose count changes. Build the page, then test the interaction in the browser. A successful MDX compilation alone does not verify keyboard behavior, layout stability or the correctness of a larger interactive tool.

Use components where they improve the document

Markdown is a good default for explanations, lists and comparison tables. A reusable callout helps when it gives a warning a clear role. An interactive tool is useful when inputs change real data or behavior. A collection of preset comparisons can usually remain a table.

Keep large dependencies behind deliberate boundaries and load them when the reader needs them. Avoid placing client hooks directly in an article or importing an entire component catalog for one small example. Review the resulting bundle rather than assuming an island is free.

One design system, multiple reading depths
Shared components can keep documentation consistent with the application. UI Components discusses component libraries, while Explainable Text shows how optional explanations can stay in the reading flow.

MDX checklist

  • [ ] Put state, event handlers and browser APIs in separate client files.
  • [ ] Keep the page's H1 in its wrapper and use a coherent H2/H3 structure in the article.
  • [ ] Parse metadata explicitly and validate it against the page configuration.
  • [ ] Build the application, then test any imported interaction in a real browser.
  • [ ] Inspect the text export so important explanations survive without JSX.

Sources and next steps

  • MDX: What is MDX? – syntax, imports and embedded components.
  • Next.js: MDX guide – local integration and component mapping; check the guide for your installed version.

For shared UI choices, continue with UI Components. For optional depth within a paragraph, see Explainable Text.

Read the original guide & explore the interactive playground on *lukiluki.me*.

title: Model Consolidation as a History of Membership, Not a List of Current Contents
description:
Picture a bag that left the hub this afternoon. This morning it held twelve customer packages. One was pulled for review before departure. Tonight a destination team wants to know what actually traveled, and a customer wants to know which handling fees apply to the package that stayed behind.

If the platform stores only the group's current contents, both answers may already be gone. The bag now looks as though the removed package was never there. Billing cannot tell a service performed on the package from a charge that belonged to the group. Customer status has nothing reliable to show.

This is the records problem behind consolidation at a multi-market hub. I have worked on a Caribbean cross-border forwarding platform for a Miami hub serving 9+ markets, where receiving, grouping, destination-specific charges, and handoffs have to remain explainable after the freight has moved. The design note below is a recommended model. It is not a dump of a client's production database.

GS1 identifies a logistics unit with an SSCC, and GS1 materials on shipping management describe relationships between units, shipments, and consolidated consignments. An SSCC should not be treated as interchangeable with a parcel carrier's tracking number. You do not need to adopt every identifier standard on day one. You do need identities that grouping cannot destroy.

Four identities, plus an event log

I would distinguish:

  1. The individual package the customer cares about.
  2. Any physical grouping (a bag, carton, pallet, or master unit).
  3. The onward dispatch or shipment that is supposed to leave the hub.
  4. External references: inbound tracking, an SSCC if you use one, a carrier tracking number for the onward movement.

The current membership of a group can be a view. It should not be the only table you have.

create table package (
  id                   bigserial primary key,
  customer_account_id  bigint not null,
  origin_reference     text,            -- inbound tracking or purchase ref
  destination_market   text not null,   -- a specific market, not a catch-all
  current_status       text not null    -- received, held, assigned,
                                        -- departed, arrived, exception
);

create table logistics_unit (
  id                      bigserial primary key,
  unit_type               text not null,  -- package, bag, carton, pallet, master
  sscc                    text,           -- optional; not a parcel tracking number
  carrier_tracking_number text,
  purpose                 text not null,  -- receiving, consolidation, onward_shipment
  created_at              timestamptz not null default now()
);

-- A package may also be represented as a logistics_unit of type 'package'.
create table package_unit (
  package_id  bigint primary key references package(id),
  unit_id     bigint not null unique references logistics_unit(id)
);

create table unit_membership_event (
  id              bigserial primary key,
  child_unit_id   bigint not null references logistics_unit(id),
  parent_unit_id  bigint not null references logistics_unit(id),
  event_type      text not null,   -- assigned, removed, held, handed_over, received
  occurred_at     timestamptz not null,
  actor_id        bigint,
  reason          text,
  location_id     bigint,          -- hub or destination office
  evidence        text
);

create table dispatch (
  id                   bigserial primary key,
  destination_market   text not null,
  master_unit_id       bigint references logistics_unit(id),
  planned_departure_at timestamptz,
  departed_at          timestamptz,
  arrived_at           timestamptz
);

-- A point-in-time list of what was expected or what actually moved.
create table dispatch_membership_snapshot (
  id               bigserial primary key,
  dispatch_id      bigint not null references dispatch(id),
  package_id       bigint not null references package(id),
  included         boolean not null,
  snapshot_at      timestamptz not null,
  snapshot_reason  text not null,  -- planned, departed, arrived
  unique (dispatch_id, package_id, snapshot_reason, snapshot_at)
);

Current contents can then be derived, instead of being edited in place:

-- Latest membership event per child/parent pair.
create view unit_current_membership as
select distinct on (child_unit_id, parent_unit_id)
  child_unit_id,
  parent_unit_id,
  event_type,
  occurred_at
from unit_membership_event
order by child_unit_id, parent_unit_id, occurred_at desc, id desc;

A package is in a group now only if its latest event for that parent is assigned or handed_over, not removed or held. That rule should be explicit in code. Do not infer it from a missing row.

Departed means "verified membership at the handoff," not "everyone who was ever assigned"

The bug I want to prevent is this: a package is assigned, then removed; the dispatch later departs; a report of "packages on dispatch X" is written as where dispatch_id = X against a current-contents table that no longer mentions the removal. The destination team cannot see the hole. Billing may still attach a group-level fee to a package that never left, or fail to bill a hold that did occur.

function removePackageFromDispatch(package, dispatch, actor, reason):
  parent = dispatch.master_unit
  child  = unit for package

  append unit_membership_event(
    child, parent,
    event_type = "removed",
    occurred_at = now(),
    actor, reason,
    location = current hub
  )

  set package.current_status = "held" or "exception",
      according to the reason

  mark any group-level checks as needing review
    (weight, piece count, documents, seal)

  do not edit earlier membership events
  do not assume destination charges or handling fees
    should move to the group or disappear

function closeDispatchForDeparture(dispatch, actor):
  members = packages whose latest event on dispatch.master_unit
            is an included type (assigned or handed_over)

  write dispatch_membership_snapshot(
    dispatch,
    every package ever assigned, with included = true/false,
    snapshot_reason = "departed",
    snapshot_at = now()
  )

  set dispatch.departed_at = now()
  set current_status = "departed" only for members actually included

  packages removed or held stay on their own status
  their history remains queryable against the same dispatch

Two billing rules fall out of the same model:

  • A service performed on the package (repacking, storage, a hold, a destination charge for that market) should reference the package, the account, and the time it was recorded.
  • A service charged to the group (a master-bag handling fee, a shared transport cost) should reference the dispatch and the snapshot that was in effect, not a later rewrite of membership.

If you only store the second kind of charge, and membership is a mutable list, you will not be able to explain either one.

Test a difficult dispatch, not only a clean bag

Walk the model through four cases before you trust a "add to consolidation" button:

  1. A normal consolidation that departs as planned.
  2. A package removed before departure, with a reason and an owner.
  3. A held item that never joins a dispatch.
  4. A destination discrepancy: the arrived snapshot does not match the departed snapshot.

For each case, ask:

  • Which record explains what was expected?
  • Which record confirms what was handed over?
  • Can staff trace the package without opening the group?
  • Can billing distinguish package-level services from group-level services?

Those questions are the requirements. The schema above is only useful if it can answer them after the freight has left the building.

This is the kind of exception that custom cross-border forwarding software has to hold if a corridor app only tracks the group that exists right now. Buy the existing product if it already preserves membership history, departed snapshots, and package-level charges. Extend or build when that history still lives in a spreadsheet.

This article is a rewritten engineering treatment of a subject I first discussed for operators, originally published on Consolidation Should Not Erase Individual Package History.

Hasnain Qureshi is co-founder of BlinkShift, which builds custom software for forwarding, consolidation, and destination-charge workflows.

title: what a shopify app stack really costs
description:
I built a Shopify app-cost calculator. The results changed how I price shop.

Quick context: I work on an ecommerce platform, and to understand our competition I did what any engineer would do — I turned pricing pages into math. The result is a calculator (launchstore.io/savings) that adds up what a real Shopify store pays monthly. This post walks through the model, because the totals surprised even me.

The pricing model nobody sees

Shopify's Basic plan is $39/mo. That's the number everyone quotes. But the platform ships deliberately lean, and the app store fills the gaps. Here's the stack a typical growing store ends up with, from the pricing pages as of writing:

Function Typical app Listed price
Email marketing Klaviyo $45–500/mo (subscriber tiers)
Live chat / support Tidio $29–749/mo (conversation tiers)
Product reviews Loox $10–300/mo
Page builder Shogun $39–499/mo
WhatsApp marketing various $30–100/mo
Loyalty program Smile.io $19–99/mo
SEO tools Plug in SEO $29–79/mo

Add those up and the plan fee — the only number in the ads — is a minority of the bill. A modest stack lands around $210–2,300/mo on top of Shopify itself. The realistic band for a store doing real volume is $300–900/mo total, which matches what we see when merchants import their actual invoices into the calculator. [VERIFY: re-run the calculator with current app pricing before publishing; screenshots of the calculator make this post much stronger.]

Why stores end up here (it's not stupidity)

Every line starts as a free trial solving a real problem. Reviews: you need social proof. Klaviyo: abandoned carts are 10–15% of recoverable revenue. Nobody signs up for a $500/mo stack — they accrete one $29 at a time, and every app individually seems cheaper than engineering around it.

The interesting engineering question: why is the stack the default? Because the platform's business model is the app store. Extract the same features into the platform and the economics invert — which is exactly the bet we made at LaunchStore ($9/mo, everything included; there's my affiliation, grain of salt).

The calculator, as a build

For the #showdev crowd: it's a static page, no backend — pricing data is a small JSON model with tier functions (Klaviyo's subscriber math is the fiddly one), and the calculator solves the inverse problem: given your order volume and subscriber count, which tier does each app put you in? The fun part was encoding tier boundaries as data rather than code, so updating Klaviyo's pricing next quarter is a one-line change.

The full breakdown of Shopify's real costs (including transaction fees and theme costs) is in our long-form post — but the calculator is the honest version, because you can put in your own numbers and check my math.

Takeaways, even if you never use our platform

  1. When you evaluate any platform, price the stack, not the plan. The plan is a lower bound.
  2. Audit your app subscriptions quarterly. The data is consistent: stores routinely pay for two apps solving the same problem after a trial they forgot to cancel.
  3. If you're building SaaS: the app-store model prints money precisely because each individual charge feels small. Your users' invoice totals are your churn risk.

title: Treat unavailable localStorage differently from an empty shortlist
description:
I build Riddle List, a daily-puzzle discovery directory with a browser-local shortlist. That makes a small UI distinction important: “there is nothing saved” and “the browser could not read storage” should not mean the same thing.

This is a standalone educational example, not a copy of the site's production storage format. Do not paste it over an existing application's keys or migrate real users without a separate compatibility plan. This article and example were prepared with AI assistance and reviewed and tested during the project work.

Four read states, not one empty array

A helper that catches every exception and returns [] is convenient until another effect writes that empty array back. A failed read can then look like an intentional empty shortlist. The same problem occurs if an old payload uses an unsupported schema version.

The reader below returns an explicit status:

  • missing: the key does not exist.
  • ok: the version and every ID are valid, including an intentionally empty array.
  • invalid: the key exists, but the data cannot be understood.
  • unavailable: accessing storage threw an exception.

Reading never writes, repairs or deletes the original value. The caller can show a recovery option for invalid data and keep the current in-memory list when persistence is unavailable.

// Standalone educational example, not Riddle List application source.
export function loadShortlist(storage, key) {
  let raw;
  try { raw = storage.getItem(key); }
  catch { return { status: 'unavailable', ids: [] }; }
  if (raw === null) return { status: 'missing', ids: [] };
  try {
    const value = JSON.parse(raw);
    if (value.version !== 1 || !Array.isArray(value.ids) ||
        !value.ids.every(id => typeof id === 'string' && id.length > 0)) {
      return { status: 'invalid', ids: [] };
    }
    return { status: 'ok', ids: [...new Set(value.ids)] };
  } catch { return { status: 'invalid', ids: [] }; }
}

export function saveShortlist(storage, key, ids) {
  if (!Array.isArray(ids) || !ids.every(id => typeof id === 'string' && id.length > 0)) {
    return { status: 'invalid' };
  }
  try {
    storage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify({ version: 1, ids: [...new Set(ids)] }));
    return { status: 'saved' };
  } catch { return { status: 'unavailable' }; }
}

Keep persistence out of the hydration effect

Load once into a result object. Do not immediately save result.ids on every result status. A missing key can initialize an empty list; an ok result can hydrate a list; an invalid or unavailable result needs a separate UI decision.

Likewise, the save function returns saved only after setItem succeeds. An app can continue working with an in-memory shortlist after an unavailable result, but should tell the user it could not persist the change. Silently displaying “saved” would promise durability the code has not established.

Deduplication preserves the first occurrence's order. It does not rename IDs or map them to a new catalog. Stable identity and route migrations deserve their own compatibility tests.

What I checked

The standalone module passed six Node test cases using fake storage objects: missing versus stored-empty, a blocked read, malformed/wrong-version/wrong-type payloads, ordered deduplication without overwriting bad data, a failed write, and valid-write round trips with invalid-input protection. These are unit checks of the example, not a claim that every browser storage policy was exercised.

To exercise the real UI, also check a reload in the same browser, an environment where persistence is unavailable, and the message shown when saving fails. Keep a disposable key for demonstrations. Never use another site's live storage as a test fixture.

The product boundary matters too

A directory bookmark and a game's progress are different records. Saving a game in Riddle List means adding it to that browser's shortlist. It does not save the publisher's puzzle attempt or create cloud synchronization. Keeping that boundary visible in the interface is as useful as catching the exception in code.

The MDN Web Storage API documentation explains availability checks and storage operations. Use the browser's actual behavior as the evidence for the message you display.
