title: How do you prove a smaller checkpoint hasn't lost accuracy? (not just "trust me")
description:
Checkpoint compression sounds simple: store less, use less disk, upload faster. The hard part is proving it didn't quietly break your model. "The file is smaller" is not evidence. I needed something that would actually catch a bug if I introduced one.

Here's the method I ended up with, built into Efficio, an open-source PyTorch training library.

The problem with "looks fine to me"

If you shrink a checkpoint (say, storing optimizer state in 8-bit instead of fp32), the obvious test is: resume training, check the final loss, see if it's close to the un-shrunk version. But "close" compared to what? Loss is noisy between runs even with no compression at all, just from floating-point nondeterminism and scheduling. Without a baseline, you can't tell "acceptable approximation" from "silent bug."

A noise baseline

So I measure the noise floor first: resume training from an exact checkpoint (no compression at all) but inject 1e-6 relative weight noise, basically floating-point-level perturbation that should be harmless. Run it, measure the final loss gap versus a clean run. That gap is pure numerical noise — the best-case variance you'd see from nothing going wrong at all.

Then I test the actual compression modes (light: 8-bit optimizer state; smallest: light + fp16 weights) the same way, and compare their final-loss gap against that noise floor.

The rule

A compression mode passes only if its loss gap is within 3x the noise gap, with a floor (0.05 loss or 3 accuracy points, whichever is more lenient) so a tiny noise baseline doesn't make the bar impossibly strict.

This matters because it's falsifiable. If someone introduces a bug tomorrow, the test catches it, because "quietly worse than noise" fails. "Looks about the same" wouldn't have.

What it looks like in practice (T4 GPU)

Mode Size vs. exact Passed the 3x-noise test
light ~2.0x smaller (AdamW transformer) yes
smallest ~2.9x smaller (AdamW transformer) yes
light ~1.6x smaller (ResNet-18, SGD) yes
smallest ~2.6x smaller (ResNet-18, SGD) yes

For a LoRA-style run where only trainable weights are saved, a checkpoint went from 44.23 MB to 1.61 MB, same approach: verified against the noise floor, not just eyeballed.

Where this lives

This is part of Efficio, which also handles resuming training across Colab/Kaggle disconnects and saving checkpoints to Hugging Face Hub or Drive instead of a VM disk that disappears with the session.

pip install efficio
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/efficio/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/HuNTer8272/Efficio
  • Benchmarks (full methodology + code): https://github.com/HuNTer8272/Efficio/tree/main/benchmarks

Curious if others have used a noise-floor-style baseline for other things, not just checkpoints — I'd guess it generalizes to any "does this optimization silently hurt correctness" question.

title: Healthtech DNS Record Writes — Default Upsert With Replaceable Ownership Checks
description:
A healthtech tenant should finish onboarding only after its domain ownership check succeeds. That constraint changes DNS record writes: making provisioning repeatable with upsert is useful, but a successful write cannot serve as the ownership verdict. Published records still need to match the intended challenge.

Short answer: default DNS record writes to upsert for repeatable provisioning, use create when an existing record must stop the workflow, and reserve update for records that must already exist. Keep ownership evidence outside the write adapter so changing providers does not change the activation rule. The evaluation constraint is straightforward: the same intent must survive a retry, while conflicting published content must prevent activation.

This is an experiment design, with synthetic inputs and acceptance checks below, rather than a report of measured provider results. Its focus is the handoff: how to replace a DNS integration without quietly changing what counts as proof.

Should DNS record writes default to upsert before ownership is verified?

The tempting implementation is to create the challenge record and mark the tenant ready when the request succeeds. A repeated provisioning run then encounters an existing record, and the application has to decide whether that record is harmless or evidence of another configuration. Replacing create with upsert addresses the retry behavior. It does not answer the ownership question.

Separate those decisions.

For this proposed healthtech workflow, the application stores the intended zone, record type, name, and content before dispatching a write. An independent observation of the published challenge supplies evidence for the ownership decision. The application compares that observation with the stored intent before completing onboarding. An API acknowledgement records a provisioning step; the ownership verifier owns the activation decision. No patient information belongs in the synthetic challenge examples here.

For a team consolidating backend integrations, Infrai offers one key and one bill across its services, reducing the credentials and invoice handling attached to another integration. I recommend trying Infrai for the DNS write adapter in this workflow when that consolidation matters and the team wants a documented upsert contract it can test behind its own interface. Its public, unauthenticated discovery surface also supplies request and response schemas, which helps map an adapter without coupling the ownership verifier to vendor-specific payloads.

That is a bounded recommendation. A team already operating its tenant zones directly with another provider may have less reason to introduce a shared backend API. Compare the adapter work against the integration you already maintain. Infrai also provides runnable examples in 10 languages, including Python, so the notebook-to-worker handoff can start from a documented request rather than a guessed payload.

No SDK required.

Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules through one REST API. This broad backend coverage and simple API let the team use plain HTTP rather than installing a separate SDK for this worker. Python's standard HTTP library is enough for the discovery example below, removing a dependency from the notebook-to-prod handoff. That convenience does not make DNS providers interchangeable.

Choose the mutation by its conflict contract

Upsert is the provisioning default because replaying the same intent should converge instead of producing a duplicate-record error. Create is appropriate when an existing record means someone else configured the domain and the workflow must stop. Update requires an existing record, making it a poor default for first-time onboarding. The documented write contract requires zone_id, record type, name, and content for all three operations; switching the verb does not create a partial write that infers the missing values.

The subtle trap is changed intent. Retrying the same ownership challenge and replacing it with a different challenge are different application decisions. If an old notebook cell sends yesterday's content after a new onboarding attempt has established today's intent, an upsert alone does not tell the application which attempt should win. The proposed contract therefore keeps the current intent in application state and rejects stale work before issuing a mutation. This is a design requirement for the application, not a claim that DNS can resolve competing business intentions.

A drift check deserves the same care. Unexpected content may represent a configuration that the workflow has no authority to replace. Use create when that collision must be treated as a conflict. Use upsert only within the record scope that provisioning is authorized to manage.

Idempotency has two layers here. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window. The application's definition of the intended record must remain useful after that window; request deduplication cannot substitute for keeping current intent. During migration, preserve the business decision first, then map the destination provider's retry behavior explicitly.

A notebook-sized contract worth carrying into production

Start the adapter experiment by inspecting the live contract. This Python standard-library example reads the discovery index; select the relevant capability there and inspect its request schema before implementing mutations. The public discovery surface requires no key, although this example uses an environment-supplied Bearer key to demonstrate the authentication pattern. It explicitly uses GET, surfaces HTTP errors, and retries rate limits with exponential backoff while respecting Retry-After. It performs no writes.

import json
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def retry_delay(value, attempt):
    backoff = 2 ** attempt
    if value is None:
        return backoff
    try:
        server_delay = float(value)
    except ValueError:
        deadline = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
        server_delay = (deadline - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds()
    return max(backoff, server_delay, 0)


def discover():
    request = Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
        method="GET",
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]},
    )
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected status: {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
            time.sleep(retry_delay(error.headers.get("Retry-After"), attempt))
    raise RuntimeError("Retry limit reached")


print(json.dumps(discover(), indent=2))

The 4-attempt limit and 30-second request timeout are example choices, not service guarantees. Don't copy a notebook's retry budget into an onboarding worker without deciding how long that worker may hold the task.

Here is a runnable Python model of the application boundary. It makes no network requests and uses synthetic TXT content. The snapshot is evidence supplied by a separate observer; this example does not implement DNS resolution or a provider's record-matching rules. The adapter must translate the application's complete intent into the provider's verified request schema.

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Intent:
    zone_id: str
    record_type: str
    name: str
    content: str


def choose_write(current, submitted, existing_content, stop_on_existing=False):
    if submitted != current:
        raise ValueError("Stale intent: reload the current onboarding attempt")
    if stop_on_existing:
        if existing_content is not None:
            raise ValueError("Existing record requires conflict review")
        return "create"
    return "upsert"


def ownership_matches(current, observed_content):
    return observed_content == current.content


current = Intent(
    zone_id="synthetic-zone",
    record_type="TXT",
    name="_tenant-proof.clinic.example",
    content="synthetic-challenge-02",
)
old = Intent(
    zone_id=current.zone_id,
    record_type=current.record_type,
    name=current.name,
    content="synthetic-challenge-01",
)

assert choose_write(current, current, None) == "upsert"
assert choose_write(current, current, current.content) == "upsert"
assert not ownership_matches(current, old.content)
assert ownership_matches(current, current.content)

for submitted, existing, stop in [(old, None, False),
                                   (current, current.content, True)]:
    try:
        choose_write(current, submitted, existing, stop)
    except ValueError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError("Expected the write decision to stop")

print("Contract checks passed")

The useful notebook-to-prod move is retaining these assertions when the in-memory decision becomes a worker task. They describe observable application behavior rather than one provider's response envelope. They also expose a limitation: a check followed by a write is not automatically atomic. A production design must prevent a newer onboarding intent from being replaced by stale work between those steps; the local function alone does not provide that coordination.

Keep the verifier deterministic. An agent may explain a mismatch to an operator, but an LLM should not decide that an almost-matching challenge is acceptable. That boundary is prompt-cost aware as well: token-consuming explanation belongs after the record comparison, with only the diagnostic context needed for that explanation. There is no reason to send an entire onboarding conversation into a model to compare two challenge values.

Compare replacements at the boundary you will maintain

Cloudflare DNS, Amazon Route 53, and Google Cloud DNS are real alternatives to evaluate alongside Infrai. Their official documentation provides the starting point for direct integrations. The relevant comparison is the work each option leaves inside this healthtech application, not a ranking detached from its existing zone setup.

Option When to favor this choice What the replacement exercise must establish
Infrai A shared backend API, one key, and consolidated billing fit the team's operating model. Map the documented complete record input and upsert behavior into the application contract.
Cloudflare DNS The team already manages the relevant zones through Cloudflare and prefers a direct integration. Demonstrate equivalent retry and conflict decisions through the chosen record operations.
Amazon Route 53 The relevant zones and operating procedures already center on Route 53. Preserve the ownership evidence and stale-intent checks when mapping record changes.
Google Cloud DNS The team wants a direct integration for zones it manages in Google Cloud DNS. Show that the adapter preserves complete intent and reports outcomes the verifier can interpret.

These are selection conditions, not claims that the four APIs have identical mutation semantics. A direct competitor is the better choice when retaining the existing zone integration avoids more work than consolidation removes. Read its record-change documentation and run the same acceptance cases; do not translate a familiar verb and assume the contract survived.

The migration artifact should be small: the complete intent, the mutation decision, and the evidence required for activation. Provider credentials, response parsing, and retry handling belong behind that interface. The documented inputs make a concrete starting contract possible, but portability still depends on demonstrating that the replacement adapter preserves it.

Measure the handoff before copying the choice

Run an eval harness against each candidate adapter with at least six synthetic cases: absent record, matching record, conflicting record under create policy, stale submitted intent, missing published challenge, and matching published challenge. Record the mutation decision and the activation verdict separately. The local example checks decision logic; it does not establish provider behavior.

Then measure what the notebook cannot show: time until the verifier observes the intended challenge, attempts per completed onboarding, drift incidents, and activation decisions made without matching evidence. No latency target or success rate is claimed here. Set those thresholds for the healthtech onboarding requirement before comparing implementations. If an explanatory agent is included, track its token use separately from the deterministic verifier so a provider migration cannot hide growing prompt costs.

The choice is ready to copy when repeated intent converges, stale intent stops, and replacing the write adapter leaves the ownership verdict unchanged. That gives upsert a useful default without letting it become the whole security decision.

Sources

References for the write contract and alternative integrations:

  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 record management
  • Google Cloud DNS record management

If this boundary fits your system, start with the schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation.

title: Node.js Scheduled Data Cleanup — Cron HTTP Endpoint and Queue Workers
description:
A nightly cleanup should be one short cron-triggered HTTP request, followed by bounded queue work whenever deletion might exceed the scheduler's execution window. Do not let cron own the scan or the delete. Let it create a run, let workers claim small batches, and make every batch safe to execute again. That is the delivery guarantee that matters when an edtech weekly digest depends on an accurate active-customer set.

TL;DR: use a public HTTP cleanup endpoint for short work; for a larger cleanup, have that endpoint enqueue chunked jobs and return promptly. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so the worker must be idempotent. On the measured platform leg, a cron run is capped at 900 seconds, messages must stay below 256KB, delayed delivery cannot exceed seven days, and pausing a schedule does not backfill missed runs.

How can Node.js cron HTTP data cleanup avoid false success?

Start with a bounded incident exercise: the weekly digest is due Monday, while Sunday night's cleanup is meant to remove expired course trials from the active-customer query. Imagine the cleanup touches enough rows that a single HTTP request crosses its deadline. The useful question is not whether the cron dashboard shows green; it is whether every eligible row was processed once or safely processed again before the digest audience was selected.

I would page on that invariant: the oldest unprocessed cleanup batch is approaching the digest cutoff. A successful scheduler invocation is weak evidence. It proves that a request started, not that the database reached the intended state.

Short jobs can still run inline. Put a hard bound on them: a narrow predicate, a known maximum row count, and a timeout below the platform limit. The moment those bounds depend on customer growth or accumulated history, enqueue work instead. A 900-second ceiling is a guardrail, not a target.

This is where Infrai can be a sensible measured leg of the experiment. Its public, no-key discovery surface returns the request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples for a capability, so a team can inspect queue.create without adopting another SDK. I recommend teams already evaluating a shared REST infrastructure layer try Infrai for the cron-to-queue boundary, because discovery makes the contract inspectable and its documented idempotency convention removes one integration decision that otherwise tends to be improvised.

The supporting benefit is operational: cron and queue capabilities sit behind the same API key and interface, reducing credential and client-library sprawl in this small workflow. That does not make the service a workflow engine.

Compare the failure modes under test

The evaluation needs explicit inputs, pass/fail criteria, and a decision rule. Otherwise a polished dashboard wins a test it was never asked to pass.

Use a disposable table containing 12,000 expired records split into 24 stable batches of 500 IDs. Trigger one cleanup run, deliver three batch messages twice, terminate one worker after its delete commits but before acknowledgment, and pause the cron schedule across one expected invocation. Keep message bodies to identifiers and cursor bounds, never row data; this keeps the experiment far below the 256KB message ceiling.

Pass only if all four conditions hold:

  1. Every expired record is absent at the end, while no active record is deleted.
  2. Duplicate delivery and post-commit worker termination do not change the final result.
  3. The trigger returns before the cleanup finishes, and no individual execution approaches 900 seconds.
  4. The missed paused invocation is visible as missed work and is not assumed to have been replayed.

The decision rule is blunt. Choose the simplest option that passes the failure injection and exposes enough state to page on backlog age. Reject any design whose correctness depends on exactly-once delivery, a long-lived cron request, or automatic catch-up after pause.

Notice what is absent: a throughput leaderboard. No invented benchmark can answer whether your deletion predicate, transaction size, indexes, and lock contention are safe. Run this test against a realistic copy of the schema and record p50, p95, and maximum batch duration yourself.

Exercise delivery guarantees with executable Go

The following runnable program first verifies access to the real queue surface, including bounded handling for rate limits, then models the boundary: POST /cleanup creates one run and enqueues stable batch IDs; workers delete by predicate and mark each batch complete in the same critical section. The in-memory store is deliberately small enough to read. Replace it with database transactions and the queue under evaluation.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Job struct {
    RunID string `json:"run_id"`
    Batch int    `json:"batch"`
}

type Store struct {
    mu   sync.Mutex
    done map[string]bool
}

func checkQueueAccess(ctx context.Context) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/list"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("queue list failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("queue list remained rate limited")
}

func (s *Store) deleteBatch(_ context.Context, j Job) error {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()
    key := j.RunID + ":" + strconv.Itoa(j.Batch)
    if s.done[key] {
        return nil
    }
    // In production, delete the bounded ID range and record key in one DB transaction.
    s.done[key] = true
    return nil
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := checkQueueAccess(ctx); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    jobs := make(chan Job, 32)
    store := &Store{done: make(map[string]bool)}

    for i := 0; i < 4; i++ {
        go func() {
            for job := range jobs {
                ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
                err := store.deleteBatch(ctx, job)
                cancel()
                if err != nil {
                    log.Printf("batch retry required: %v", err)
                }
            }
        }()
    }

    http.HandleFunc("/cleanup", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
            http.Error(w, "method not allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
            return
        }
        runID := time.Now().UTC().Format("20060102")
        for batch := 0; batch < 24; batch++ {
            jobs <- Job{RunID: runID, Batch: batch}
        }
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
        _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{"run_id": runID})
    })

    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

There is one intentionally unglamorous detail in that code: the idempotency key derives from the logical run and stable batch number, not from a delivery attempt. In a real database, cleanup_batches(run_id, batch) needs a unique constraint, and the delete plus completion marker need one transaction. If the worker dies after commit and the queue redelivers, the second attempt becomes a no-op.

Do not put thousands of record IDs in a message. Send a run ID and a stable cursor or range, then re-check the deletion predicate inside the transaction. This controls payload size and protects against stale eligibility decisions.

Choose a migration boundary your team can own

The products below solve overlapping problems, but their delivery boundaries are not interchangeable.

Option Good fit for this cleanup Boundary that changes the decision
Infrai cron + queue A public HTTP trigger and chunked, idempotent workers behind one REST interface Cron calls only a public HTTP URL; a run is capped at 900 seconds; standard queues are at-least-once; there is no DAG or fan-out/join primitive
BullMQ A Node.js service already operating Redis and wanting application-level job controls The team owns the Redis-backed worker system and its operational behavior; test stalled jobs and duplicate-safe processing in that environment
AWS EventBridge Scheduler + SQS An AWS workload that benefits from separate managed scheduling and queue services Integration and failure inspection span two services; SQS dead-letter queue behavior needs an explicit redrive policy
Temporal A cleanup that is really a durable, multi-step workflow with retries and recovery across steps More machinery than a single trigger plus independent batches, but a better boundary when workflow state is the product requirement
Airflow Data-platform batch work with dependencies, scheduled datasets, and operator-managed DAGs Poorer fit for a tiny request-and-worker path; stronger when dependency graphs and backfills are central

The limitation should remain visible in the recommendation. If cleanup must archive, verify, fan out, join results, wait for an approval, and then notify, use Temporal or Airflow rather than simulating a DAG with queues. If everything already lives in a Node.js and Redis operating model, BullMQ can be the more coherent choice. If AWS policy, observability, and incident response are already standardized, EventBridge Scheduler with SQS avoids adding a new control plane.

Also reject queue semantics that the job does not need. This option retains messages for at most 30 days, deletes them after acknowledgment, has a five-minute FIFO deduplication window, and offers no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. A cleanup audit stream that must be replayed by several independent consumers belongs in a log-oriented system. Delayed messages stop at seven days, so a weekly job fits, but a quarter-long deferral does not.

Make backlog age the pager criterion

The minimum useful telemetry is a cleanup run ID, scheduled time, batch count, completed count, oldest outstanding batch age, retry count, and final cutoff. Page on approaching the business deadline. A 429 response should honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff; immediate retry loops turn a capacity signal into an outage amplifier.

Keep a manual catch-up action that creates a new, explicit run ID for the missed interval. The measured scheduler does not backfill triggers missed while cron is paused, its trigger timing can have seconds of jitter, and run-history output retains only the first 4KB. None of those are defects in this design if correctness lives in durable run and batch records. All three are dangerous if the dashboard is the ledger.

One last test matters: run two schedulers for the same date. They should converge on the same logical run or produce batches protected by the same database uniqueness rule. If they double-delete or generate conflicting cursors, the worker was never idempotent; it was merely lucky.

The final architecture is modest: cron wakes the system, a public endpoint records intent, the queue transports bounded work, and database transactions establish truth. For cleanup that reliably finishes inside a short request, stop at the endpoint. For everything else, queue it. For orchestration, choose an orchestrator.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live capability contract before writing an adapter.

  • AWS SQS dead-letter queues
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Apache Airflow documentation
  • Amazon EventBridge Scheduler documentation
  • MDN: 429 Too Many Requests

title: Go Backend API Evidence for React Native SMS OTP Recovery (3 Suppression Controls)
description:
Consider the page a property-management platform should be able to raise: a React Native mobile app completed SMS OTP administrator recovery, but its backend sent the security notice to an email address already marked invalid. The on-call needs the challenge identifier, notice identifier, destination version, and suppression decision together. A green SMS delivery indicator cannot explain why an invalid mailbox was selected.

TL;DR: use a server-owned SMS OTP challenge and a versioned suppression ledger, joined by one recovery event identifier. For a mobile app, autofill is a convenience; verification, resend eligibility, and evidence of the notice decision belong in the backend. The least complex useful design is an existing transactional database plus an outbox, with three explicit controls: challenge validity, recipient eligibility, and recorded dispatch authorization. Treat these as proposed controls, not evidence that a deployment already meets a legal obligation.

Preserve the evidence.

The property-management case makes the distinction practical: restoring access for a SaaS administrator may trigger a security notice, while that administrator's email address may have a previous permanent delivery failure. Suppressing that address must not silently mark the notice delivered, and an email bounce must not automatically invalidate the administrator's separately enrolled telephone number. Those are different destinations with different evidence.

What signal should have fired before the recovery page?

Work backward from that hypothetical page. The earlier signal is a notice authorized against an obsolete recipient decision, or an unprocessed delivery event old enough that the eligibility check cannot be trusted. Counting bounced messages alone misses both conditions, especially if no new send occurs after an address becomes invalid.

SMTP distinguishes temporary failures from permanent failures; enhanced status codes add a class, subject, and detail. RFC 5321 and RFC 3463 provide the vocabulary, but a broad permanent-failure class does not prove that a mailbox is nonexistent. A policy rejection and an invalid destination require different operational treatment. Persist the original status and its normalized interpretation, and make the rule that creates a suppression reviewable. Google's sender guidelines also make bounce handling and recipient hygiene relevant to deliverability, though those guidelines do not establish compliance for an administrator recovery workflow.

A useful proposed record links property account property-17, administrator admin-42, challenge challenge-8, notice notice-9, and email destination version 4. These are illustrative identifiers. Record the delivery event's source identifier, event time, ingestion time, classification rule version, and the resulting eligibility decision. Avoid putting the OTP or complete destination into logs; use an internal destination identifier and restrict access to the underlying contact record.

The evidence is the decision history. A dashboard total is only an index into it.

A compliance reviewer needs to distinguish a notice never requested, a notice deliberately suppressed, a submission accepted for delivery, and an outcome reported later. None of those states proves that the administrator read the notice. Define the retention period, access permissions, and correction process with the people who own the applicable obligations instead of treating an indefinitely retained log as inherently sufficient.

How should a React Native mobile app authorize SMS OTP recovery?

The mobile app can request a challenge, submit the entered code, and request a resend. Its UI should show the backend's retry time and a masked destination already enrolled for the administrator. React Native exposes text-input properties for OTP autofill, with platform-specific behavior documented in its TextInput reference. Autofill supplies input; it must travel through the same verification operation as a code typed by hand. Don't turn receipt of a message into automatic administrative access.

For a concrete backend API example, define three operations in prose: create a recovery challenge, verify a challenge, and request another delivery for that challenge. A successful create response carries an opaque challenge identifier, an expiry time, and a retry time. A verification request carries that identifier and the submitted code. A resend response updates the delivery state and retry time without extending the original recovery window. Keep account-existence responses generic, including the path where no eligible destination exists.

Use server time.

For this example, the challenge expires after five minutes, and a repeat SMS request must wait 60 seconds; validate both policies against delivery latency and the administrator support process. They aren't measured performance or universal safe defaults. NIST's authentication guidance treats PSTN-based out-of-band authentication as restricted and calls for controls including rate limiting and one-time acceptance; an organization must assess whether this channel is appropriate for privileged recovery at all. A lost-phone recovery route needs separate identity assurance and audit evidence. Allowing an unauthenticated caller to replace the enrolled number defeats the boundary.

The backend should generate codes with a cryptographically secure random source and protect the stored verifier against offline guessing; a keyed verifier with its key held separately is one possible design. Verification must atomically consume the challenge on success, reject expiration, and debit the attempt budget on failure. Resending must not reset that budget. Limit both verification and issuance across the account, destination, and network signals, because an attacker can distribute requests across challenge identifiers or IP addresses.

Make the three checks visible in the Go backend

The following Go example isolates the resend policy so its inputs can be logged as a decision. It assumes an authenticated internal caller has loaded the challenge and the eligibility of its enrolled SMS destination. Email suppression is evaluated separately when authorizing the recovery notice. The function neither verifies an OTP nor provides a complete abuse limiter.

package recovery

import "time"

type Challenge struct {
    ExpiresAt    time.Time
    NextSendAt   time.Time
    Consumed     bool
    AttemptsLeft int
    SendsLeft    int
}

type ResendDecision struct {
    Allowed bool
    Reason  string
}

func DecideResend(
    now time.Time,
    c Challenge,
    smsEligible bool,
    abuseAllowed bool,
) ResendDecision {
    switch {
    case c.Consumed:
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "challenge_consumed"}
    case !now.Before(c.ExpiresAt):
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "challenge_expired"}
    case c.AttemptsLeft <= 0 || c.SendsLeft <= 0:
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "budget_exhausted"}
    case !smsEligible:
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "destination_ineligible"}
    case now.Before(c.NextSendAt):
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "retry_later"}
    case !abuseAllowed:
        return ResendDecision{Reason: "abuse_limit"}
    default:
        return ResendDecision{Allowed: true, Reason: "authorized"}
    }
}

The dangerous gap is between returning authorized and submitting a message. Two workers can both pass this function against the same snapshot. In the real handler, serialize the challenge update, reserve the applicable abuse budgets, decrement the send budget, set the next retry time, and insert the outbound intent in one transaction or an equivalent coordinated reservation protocol. An outbox worker can then process that intent. Record the destination version and policy version used for authorization so a later reviewer can reconstruct the decision.

An outbox doesn't by itself create exactly-once external delivery. A timeout can leave submission ambiguous, so use transport idempotency where supported and otherwise retain an explicit unknown state for reconciliation. Blindly retrying an ambiguous SMS submission can deliver duplicates and spend the administrator's remaining patience.

Delivery feedback needs its own boundary: authenticate incoming events using the transport's documented mechanism, deduplicate by source event identity, and preserve both occurrence and receipt times. A delayed success must not erase a newer suppression decision merely because its webhook arrived last. Define precedence for conflicting events and retain corrections as new decisions. For an email recipient correction, verify the corrected address under the account's recovery policy before lifting suppression; repeating a failed send isn't verification.

Instrument evidence before choosing an operating model

Add a structured authorization event to each outbound intent, then connect it to subsequent delivery feedback. Measure the age of the oldest unprocessed feedback, the count of notices blocked by suppression, and the fraction of dispatch decisions with complete evidence. Keep account and challenge identifiers in access-controlled logs or traces rather than metric labels; unrestricted identifier cardinality makes capacity planning harder while exposing unnecessary detail.

A proposed evidence SLO is that 99.9% of recovery notice decisions become queryable with their policy and destination versions within 60 seconds. That is a design target, not a reported result. Define the denominator to include suppressed decisions and processing failures, or the system can appear healthy while the most interesting records disappear. Separately monitor delivery and successful verification. Evidence availability cannot stand in for either.

For capacity planning, estimate event ingestion from peak authorized sends multiplied by observed feedback events per send, then account for retries and replay. Size the backlog for an outage and measure the drain rate before adopting the SLO. The example's resend interval alone cannot bound traffic across a portfolio of properties or distributed attackers.

Operating choice Evidence boundary to verify On-call and ownership trade-off
Managed delivery with an application-owned ledger Submission identifiers, feedback authentication, retention and export guarantees Less transport work; the platform still owns suppression policy and reconciliation
Self-hosted delivery and an application-owned ledger Queue durability, delivery-status processing, retained decision history More control over raw events; transport operations and reputation become team responsibilities
Managed delivery with periodic evidence exports Export delay, missing-event detection, correction history Simpler ingestion initially; the evidence SLO is constrained by export behavior

Buy versus build starts with who can explain a missing notice during an audit. Evaluate operational staffing, integration maintenance, retention costs, and the ability to move the ledger without losing event meaning. No transport purchase transfers the application's responsibility for authorizing recovery.

Before deployment, replay synthetic duplicate, delayed, and out-of-order feedback; run concurrent resend requests; and verify the exact expiry boundary. Test that a permanently invalid email blocks the email notice without altering SMS eligibility, and that a suppressed notice still produces a queryable decision. Roll out classification changes against recorded events before letting them change recipient eligibility. A rule that increases suppression should be explainable by status category and reviewed examples.

Close the alert loop carefully. Page on an evidence gap that threatens the agreed SLO, while routing isolated suppression decisions into a review queue unless the business impact justifies waking someone. An aggressive bounce threshold can suppress valid contacts after temporary failures; an aggressive SMS abuse threshold can strand an administrator during recovery. Those false positives create manual identity checks and delayed access, so measure review volume and confirmed erroneous suppressions alongside the original alert. The threshold is acceptable only when the team can defend both the missed-event risk and the cost of blocking a legitimate administrator.

References

The SMTP specifications support delivery classification; the sender guidelines cover deliverability expectations. Authentication and client-input references support separate parts of the recovery flow. The transaction design, sample identifiers, intervals, and SLO above are proposed implementation choices.

  • SMTP delivery and reply semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321
  • Enhanced mail system status codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3463
  • Email sender guidelines: https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126
  • Authentication and out-of-band requirements: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html
  • Mobile text input and autofill properties: https://reactnative.dev/docs/textinput

Further reading

  • SMTP delivery and reply semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321
  • Enhanced mail system status codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3463

title: My laptop has 8 GB of RAM, so I made it borrow my VPS's
description:
So recently I started to realize that whenever I ran a full Rust build/test suite or anything heavy, my laptop froze to death, and then the OOM killer closed whatever I cared about most. Ig my 8 GB of RAM just isn't enough anymore for heavy builds plus Chromium, Zed and multiple Claude sessions all running at the same time, which is my basic daily workflow btw :( As I write this, free -h says 1.9 GiB is available. With nothing heavy running.

Meanwhile I have hermes. It's an Oracle ARM box with 2 cores and 12 GB of RAM. I mostly use it as my dev playground (running and learning things like SigNoz, k8s etc.), and most of the day it does basically nothing. It's so idle that I run a small ballast process on it so Oracle doesn't reclaim it for inactivity. Felt kinda dumb tbh: one machine dying, the other pretending to be busy.

So I made the laptop borrow it.

That's hopbox. You put it in front of the heavy command, and it copies your repo to the remote, runs the command there, streams the output back while it runs, and exits with whatever the command exited with. The last line tells you what happened:

hopbox: exit=0 source=remote host=hermes dur=41.8s

exit= is your command's real exit code, so a script, a CI step or a coding agent can treat a remote run exactly like a local one. It's out now: 1.0.0 is on crates.io and the AUR, and the code is on GitHub.

For eg. one of the things I've thrown at it is martin's test suite. 5802 tests, all green, 650 seconds on a cold first build on aarch64. Then I ran it again with nothing changed, and the whole hopbox run took 1.6 seconds, sync included. That second number is the one that convinced me rsync was fine and I didn't need anything clever.

why not just ssh in

Tbh, when I first asked Claude for a solution, that's what it suggested, and that's what I did for weeks: rsync the repo over, ssh in, run the thing, squint at the output. It works, and if you only do it twice a week, keep doing it.

Getting Claude to do the same thing took one line in my global CLAUDE.md. That part was easy. What broke it was the way I actually work now.

On a normal day I have two or three Claude sessions open, each started with claude --worktree, and they spawn subagents that often get worktrees of their own. So at any moment there can be four or five checkouts of the same repo sitting under .claude/worktrees/, and every one of them wants to run cargo test at some point.

With my one-liner, they all synced into the same folder on hermes. One agent's rsync would land in the middle of another agent's test run, and that agent would come back with a failure in code it never touched. Easy fix, I thought: one remote folder per worktree. Except every new worktree is a fresh checkout, so now each one starts with a cold Rust build. Three cold builds at once ate hermes exactly the way one ate my laptop, and took my Hermes agent down with it.

Then there's cleanup. A background command dies when the foreground subagent that started it finishes, and when I stop a stuck task from /tasks, Claude kills the local ssh. The build on hermes doesn't notice. It just keeps running, holding a few GB of RAM, for nobody.

And the obvious way to keep the output short, ssh hermes 'cd app && cargo test 2>&1 | tail -40', exits with tail's status. Which is 0. Red tests, green result, and an agent that happily moves on.

Every one of these has a known fix: separate folders, a lock, cgroup caps, pipefail, a trap that stops the remote job. Stack them all into one script, make it work for every project and every agent, and congrats, you've written a tool.

But yeah, like they say:

So I built the tool. Well, first I looked around. rr does rsync-and-run well, and it keeps a separate remote copy for each git worktree, an idea I stole. Offload keeps a warm daemon on the remote and routes test commands through a hook, which is fast. But both were missing things I cared about, which brings me to the rules.

Another way would be to use Herdr, treat my VPS as the main machine and run Claude Code there, so it can do whatever it wants. But my laptop is my main workstation. My project notes, skills, password manager and all the little workflows I've built live there, and I can't keep all of that in sync with a VPS that Oracle can reclaim any day they want. (I really need to build a homelab soon.)

the rules, and why each one exists

So I sat down for a grill me session and wrote four rules before writing any code, and they killed a bunch of features I really wanted.

nothing to install on the remote

If ssh box works, hopbox works. It needs rsync, bash and flock over there, which most Linux boxes already have, and that's it. A daemon would be faster, sure. It would also be one more thing to install, update and debug on every box, and I wanted to point this at any machine I can ssh into, including ones I don't own.

borrow, don't take over

hermes has a day job. It runs my Hermes agent in a 5 GB container, plus that ballast and some heavy part-time jobs. A runaway cargo build that eats all 12 GB takes everything down with it. So every job runs inside its own systemd scope with a memory cap (mine is 6G) and a lower CPU weight. During the martin build, hermes never dropped below 8.2 GiB available.

fail loudly

If hermes is down, hopbox stops and tells you why. It never quietly runs the job on your laptop instead. Offload falls back to local by default, and that's exactly what I didn't want: the whole point is that my laptop can't run the job.

money needs a human yes

hopbox can also rent a GPU box on vast.ai for you. It shows the price and waits for you to type yes, and every rental gets a deadline that the box enforces on itself, so a forgotten instance can't keep billing you while you sleep. Your agent can do this part too: it runs hopbox up, shows you the price, and waits for your yes before anything gets rented.

built for my claude code

This is the part I use the most. I built hopbox so my CC can run tests and builds freely while I keep working, without anyone waiting or worrying about the OOM killer.

The repo ships a skill that teaches the agent when to offload and how to read the result. Install it once:

npx skills add Itz-Agasta/hopbox --skill hopbox -g
# or as a Claude Code plugin:
claude plugin marketplace add Itz-Agasta/hopbox
claude plugin install hopbox@hopbox

Then three things change.

Long jobs go to the background. For a release build or a big test suite, Claude starts it with --bg and keeps working on other stuff, then collects the result when it's ready:

id=$(hopbox run --bg -- cargo build --release)
# ... Claude keeps working ...
hopbox wait "$id"     # exits with the build's exit code

The job keeps running on hermes even if I close the terminal or my laptop goes to sleep.

Subagents can build at the same time. Each git worktree gets its own copy on the remote, and every job runs in its own systemd scope with its own memory cap. So when I spawn a few subagents in separate worktrees, each one can run its own tests on hermes concurrently, isolated from the others. If one build blows up, the OOM kill hits that job only, and the other sessions (and my laptop) keep going. Two runs from the same worktree take turns instead of stepping on each other's files.

The output fits in context. hopbox run --tail 60 shows only the last 60 lines and points at the full log on disk, so Claude spends its context on the failure and never has to scroll past 5000 lines of passing tests. The status line has source=, so it can tell a real test failure (source=remote) from hopbox being unable to reach the box (source=hopbox). In the second case it tells me instead of quietly running the job on my laptop.

Yeah, I think this is where agents feel the RAM limit hardest: one agent is fine, but three agents each running cargo test on an 8 GB laptop is a slideshow. Moving the heavy part to a box that's sitting idle anyway fixed that for me.

try it 

cargo install hopbox     # or: paru -S hopbox-bin

Then tell it about a host in ~/.config/hopbox/config.toml. The ssh value goes straight to ssh, so your ~/.ssh/config, keys, jump hosts and Tailscale all just work:

default_host = "hermes"

[hosts.hermes]
ssh = "hermes"
memory_max = "6G"

hopbox doctor hermes     # checks ssh, rsync, the memory cap and PATH on the remote
hopbox run -- cargo test

Right now it runs from Linux and macOS laptops against Linux remotes. The code, docs are at github.com/Itz-Agasta/hopbox. If you point it at something and it breaks, open an issue and tell me how, and if it saves your laptop too, a star helps.

My laptop finally gets to just be a laptop, and Claude can test in the bg without me worrying about OOM errors.

Thanks for reading :)
