title: Build a hosting company homepage in Laravel, with plans and a billing snapshot
description:
Part 1 of Small Business Sites.

A hosting company homepage has one job: show the plans clearly enough that a visitor can pick one without opening a support ticket. Most small hosts I see either hard code their prices into the page, so every price change means editing HTML in four places, or they install a billing system built for a company ten times their size before they have ten customers.

This build sits between those two. The plans live in a database table, so the homepage reads them the way any Laravel page reads data. The price toggle switches between monthly and yearly without a page reload. A billing snapshot panel shows a signed in customer their invoices, due dates, and payment status, read only. Payments themselves stay outside this build, and I say where they would connect at the end.

Put the plans in a table first

Three plans are enough for a small host. The table needs the facts a buyer compares: name, disk space, bandwidth, email accounts, and the two prices. Store the monthly and yearly price as separate columns. Working the yearly price out from the monthly one inside the view sounds tidy and breaks the first time you run a yearly offer that is not a round multiple.

Schema::create('plans', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->string('name');
    $table->unsignedInteger('disk_gb');
    $table->string('bandwidth');
    $table->unsignedInteger('email_accounts');
    $table->decimal('monthly_price', 8, 2);
    $table->decimal('yearly_price', 8, 2);
    $table->boolean('featured')->default(false);
    $table->unsignedInteger('sort_order')->default(0);
    $table->timestamps();
});

Seed it with your real plans and your real prices. The names and numbers in my screenshots are sample data from my own template work, and yours should be the plans you can actually deliver. A plan card is a promise. If the disk figure on the homepage is larger than the disk you give the account, the page is lying in a way a customer will find in the first week.

The controller for the homepage stays small:

public function home()
{
    $plans = Plan::orderBy('sort_order')->get();

    return view('home', compact('plans'));
}

That is the whole point of the table. Adding a fourth plan next year is a row in the database, not an afternoon of HTML edits.

Draw the plan cards and the toggle

Each plan becomes one card. The card shows the name, the price, and the comparison rows in the same order on every card, so a visitor can read down one column and across the next. Keep the rows identical across cards. A row that appears on one card and not the next reads as a hidden limit, even when it was only a layout slip.

@foreach($plans as $plan)
    <article class="plan-card {{ $plan->featured ? 'featured' : '' }}">
        <h3>{{ $plan->name }}</h3>
        <p class="price">
            <span data-monthly="{{ $plan->monthly_price }}"
                  data-yearly="{{ $plan->yearly_price }}">
                ${{ $plan->monthly_price }}
            </span>
            <span class="per">/mo</span>
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li>{{ $plan->disk_gb }} GB disk space</li>
            <li>{{ $plan->bandwidth }} bandwidth</li>
            <li>{{ $plan->email_accounts }} email accounts</li>
        </ul>
    </article>
@endforeach

The toggle is two buttons and a few lines of JavaScript. Both prices are already on the page inside the data attributes, so switching needs no request to the server and works even on a slow connection.

document.querySelectorAll('[data-cycle]').forEach(function (button) {
    button.addEventListener('click', function () {
        const cycle = button.dataset.cycle;
        document.querySelectorAll('[data-monthly]').forEach(function (el) {
            el.textContent = '$' + (cycle === 'yearly' ? el.dataset.yearly : el.dataset.monthly);
        });
        document.querySelectorAll('.per').forEach(function (el) {
            el.textContent = cycle === 'yearly' ? '/yr' : '/mo';
        });
    });
});

Check the cards at phone width before you call this section done. At 390px the cards stack in one column, the price stays on one line, and no card is wider than the screen. A pricing table that needs sideways scrolling on a phone loses the visitors most likely to be comparing plans away from their desk.

The billing snapshot panel

Once a visitor becomes a customer, the question changes from what does it cost to what do I owe and when. A snapshot panel answers that on one screen: the current plan, the invoices, each due date, and each status. It reads data. It does not take money, and it should not pretend to.

Invoices need their own small table: the customer, the plan, the amount, an issue date, a due date, and a status field that holds plain words like unpaid, paid, and overdue.

public function billing()
{
    $invoices = auth()->user()->invoices()
        ->orderByDesc('due_date')
        ->take(10)
        ->get();

    return view('billing', compact('invoices'));
}

In the view, show the status as text a person uses, with the due date next to it, and let overdue rows stand out by colour alone. Do not hide an unpaid invoice behind a tab. The panel earns its place the day a customer checks it instead of opening a ticket to ask when their renewal is due. When you later connect a payment gateway, it connects here: the gateway marks the invoice paid, and this panel keeps doing the same read it always did.

The domain box and the support section, kept small

A domain search box belongs on the homepage, as a front end form. Give it an input, a button, and an answer area. Until a real domain API connects to it, the honest version checks nothing and says so in the small print under the box, or stays off the page. A box that invents availability results is worse than no box.

The support section needs three things: the hours a person actually answers, a link to open a ticket or a contact page, and a status note the owner can edit by hand when something is wrong. One edited line that says the mail server restart finished at a real time builds more trust than a green all systems normal badge that never changes.

Trust sections that do not fake numbers

A new hosting company has no honest big numbers. It has no thousands of customers, no years of uptime record, and no wall of testimonials. Templates often ship with those numbers filled in, and leaving them in is the fastest way to make a real company look fake to anyone who reads closely.

What a new host can show is smaller and stronger. The exact plan limits, printed on the cards where the buyer compares them. The support hours it really keeps. How to reach a person, with a named page and a working form. The terms, privacy, and refund pages written as plain templates the owner has read. And the status note above, edited by hand. Each of those can be checked by a visitor, and a claim that can be checked is the kind that holds up.

Add the other numbers later, one at a time, when they are true. A first testimonial with a real customer name on it is worth more than a row of invented ones, and it cannot be taken apart in a comment thread.

What stays static and what goes dynamic

Keep the static parts static. The explanation of what shared hosting and VPS mean, the support hours text, the legal pages, and the company story do not change by the week, and plain Blade views with no queries keep them fast and hard to break.

Make dynamic only what changes or what belongs to a person: the plans and prices, because an offer or a new plan should not need a code edit; the status note, because it changes during an incident; and the billing panel, because it shows one customer's own invoices. That split is most of the maintenance story for a small host. The homepage stays quick, and the parts an owner edits from an admin screen are the parts that were going to change anyway.

Where this leaves you

With the plans in a table, the toggle on the cards, and the snapshot panel reading real invoices, a small hosting homepage in Laravel is a weekend of work and a short list of pages. If you would rather start from the finished version, HostNest is this homepage finished as a 10 page template. If you need the whole site and not only the homepage, it is $24 on Gumroad: https://mehedirafi.gumroad.com/l/hostnest

I am Mehedi Mansur Rafi, a freelance Laravel developer (B.Sc. in Computer Science & Engineering). I build hospital, clinic, and small business websites. My full store is at https://mehedirafi.gumroad.com/ and my site is https://mehedimansurrafi.online

title: Alternatives to EKS, GKE, and AKS in 2026: What Staying Costs and What Changes When You Move
description:
The best alternative to EKS, GKE, or AKS depends on why you are leaving: cost, the operations work a cluster still needs, lock-in to one cloud, or control. Control Plane takes cluster operations off your team on one cloud or several. Serverless container services and the providers’ own managed modes remove most node work inside one cloud, smaller providers lower the control plane fee for teams that keep running Kubernetes themselves, and self-managed distributions give the most control for the most work.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Staying costs more in team time than in fees, and each alternative fits a different reason for leaving.

  • Cost of staying. The cluster fee is small. The real cost is the upgrade cycle, node management, and add-on maintenance your team still owns.
  • Managed modes. EKS Auto Mode, GKE Autopilot, and AKS Automatic hand off node patching and scaling but keep you on one cloud. GKE Autopilot and AKS Automatic also run cluster-version upgrades; on EKS Auto Mode your team still starts them.
  • Alternatives by reason. Control Plane to take Day 2 operations and the cluster lifecycle off your team on one cloud or several, managed modes and serverless containers to reduce node work inside one cloud, smaller providers for a lower control plane fee, enterprise Kubernetes for governance, self-managed distributions for control, and Nomad or Swarm for non-Kubernetes simplicity.
  • What a move changes. Deployments and ConfigMaps move with few changes. Pod identity, ingress, persistent volumes, and image registry access are tied to one cloud and need a plan.
  • Control Plane. Handles Day 2 operations, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security, on Kubernetes clusters it orchestrates across AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions. It converts Kubernetes manifests with its cpln convert command and offers a 99.999% availability SLA for workloads running at least two replicas across at least two locations.

What does staying on EKS, GKE, or AKS cost and leave to your team?

EKS, GKE, and AKS each set a cluster fee and a version-support window, but the larger cost is the work your team still owns after the control plane is running.

Provider Cluster fee Version support What your team still does Managed mode that takes over nodes
Amazon EKS $0.10/cluster/hour standard; $0.60/cluster/hour extended support 14 months standard, then 12 months extended; a cluster not upgraded before extended support ends is auto-upgraded Start each upgrade one minor version at a time, update nodes, update VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy; deploy patched AMIs for managed node groups; configure Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter; own IAM, pod security, runtime security, network security EKS Auto Mode
Google GKE $0.10/cluster/hour; free-tier credit covers one Autopilot or zonal Standard cluster; $0.60/cluster/hour for Extended channel clusters in extended support 14 months standard; Extended channel adds ~10 months of security patches; GKE auto-upgrades all clusters over time Node pool sizing, autoscaling settings, security configuration, and add-ons on Standard clusters; Pod resource requests, VPC, and cluster configuration on Autopilot GKE Autopilot
Azure AKS Free tier (no SLA), Standard tier with uptime SLA, Premium tier for Long Term Support About 12 months of community support; Long Term Support (~24 months per version) requires Premium tier Node pools, upgrades (manual by default), networking, identity, and security on AKS Standard clusters AKS Automatic

Upstream Kubernetes supports each minor version for roughly 14 months and maintains the three most recent minor releases. On standard EKS your team starts each upgrade, one minor version at a time, and updates nodes and add-ons to match. On EKS, extended support is on by default, so a cluster that misses the standard window moves to six times the standard rate. GKE charges the same $0.60 only for clusters enrolled in its Extended channel and auto-upgrades the rest. AWS’s own pricing example shows a cluster that is never upgraded averages $0.33 per hour over 26 months. Node patching, autoscaler tuning, and security configuration add staff hours every month, a cost that weighs most on teams managing clusters without a platform team.

Why do teams look for alternatives to managed Kubernetes?

Four patterns explain most moves away from EKS, GKE, or AKS.

Cost. The cluster fee is predictable, but compute, storage, cross-zone data transfer, NAT gateways, and observability ingestion are billed separately and often exceed the cluster fee. Idle node capacity held for bursts and failover adds to it.

Operations work. With a managed control plane, your team still owns version upgrade planning and testing, node patching, autoscaler configuration, CNI and CSI add-on updates, ingress controllers, and security policies. Each provider handles upgrades, node pools, and add-ons differently, so a multi-cloud team needs a runbook for each.

Lock-in to one cloud. Pod identity, ingress, and persistent storage all tie a workload to a single provider. EKS Pod Identity maps an IAM role to a Kubernetes service account, GKE Workload Identity Federation grants Google IAM roles to Kubernetes entities, and AKS workload identity federates with Microsoft Entra ID. Teams looking to manage Kubernetes across multiple clouds without vendor lock-in hit these walls quickly.

Control. Some workloads must run on premises, at the edge, or on bare metal, outside any hyperscaler region. Regulated industries may need to own the full stack for audit and compliance reasons.

Should you switch to EKS Auto Mode, GKE Autopilot, or AKS Automatic first?

The hyperscalers’ own managed modes take over node operations, while the cluster stays on one cloud and your team keeps the VPC and cluster configuration.

EKS Auto Mode uses Karpenter-based scaling, takes responsibility for node OS configuration, patching, and health, enforces a 21-day maximum node lifetime, and builds in pod networking, network policy, local DNS, GPU plug-ins, and EBS CSI storage. Customers keep responsibility for application containers, the VPC, and cluster configuration. Auto Mode adds a management fee per EC2 instance on top of the EC2 price, varying by instance type.

GKE Autopilot goes further. Google manages nodes, scaling, security settings, and upgrades of the control plane and worker nodes. General-purpose Autopilot pods are billed per second for the CPU, memory, and ephemeral storage they request, which removes idle-node waste but requires careful resource-request tuning.

AKS Automatic handles node management, scaling, security, and preconfigured settings, and automatically patches nodes and cluster components. It includes a financially backed 99.95% Kubernetes API server availability SLA.

All three managed modes take node patching and scaling off your team. GKE Autopilot and AKS Automatic also upgrade the cluster version through a release channel, and your team keeps workloads compatible with each new Kubernetes version. On EKS Auto Mode, your team still starts each control plane upgrade. None of them remove the VPC and cluster configuration work or the tie to a single cloud’s identity, ingress, and storage systems. A managed mode reduces node work on the cloud you already use, while the cluster itself, its configuration, and compatibility testing stay with your team.

What are the best alternatives to managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS)?

The right alternative maps to the reason you are leaving, whether you need the Kubernetes API, and how much work you want to own.

Option Examples Reason it fits Keeps the Kubernetes API What your team still runs Where it runs
Control Plane Control Plane Day 2 operations, total cost including staff time, and lock-in, on one cloud or several Yes on clusters joined through CPLN BYOK, Control Plane’s bring-your-own-Kubernetes option, or run by Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes; on built-in locations, manifests convert with cpln convert and a Kubernetes operator lets kubectl and Argo CD manage Control Plane resources Container images and workload settings AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions plus Kubernetes clusters you run or Control Plane runs for you, including on your own servers on premises
Managed modes of the same provider EKS Auto Mode, GKE Autopilot, AKS Automatic Operations work, staying on one cloud Yes Apps, VPC, cluster configuration One cloud
Serverless containers Amazon ECS with Fargate, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps Operations work No Services, scaling settings, networking One cloud
Smaller managed Kubernetes providers DigitalOcean Kubernetes, Linode Kubernetes Engine, Civo, OVHcloud Lower control plane fee Yes Nodes, upgrades, add-ons That provider
Enterprise Kubernetes Red Hat OpenShift (including ROSA and ARO), SUSE Rancher for managing many clusters Governance across many clusters Yes The platform and its clusters, shared with Red Hat and the cloud on ROSA and ARO Several clouds and data centers
Self-managed lightweight Kubernetes K3s, Talos Linux Control, edge, bare metal Yes Everything including control plane and upgrades Anywhere
Non-Kubernetes orchestrator HashiCorp Nomad, Docker Swarm mode Simplicity, mixed workloads No The cluster, servers, and upgrades Anywhere

Control Plane takes Day 2 operations off your team and orchestrates hardened, security-isolated Kubernetes clusters across regions of the major clouds. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s named set of locations, lets you add a location to roll every workload out there and remove one to withdraw them. Locations can be AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions that Control Plane operates, plus Kubernetes clusters you run yourself or that Control Plane runs for you. cpln convert turns Kubernetes Deployments, StatefulSets, CronJobs, Secrets, ConfigMaps, PersistentVolumeClaims, and Ingresses into Control Plane workloads, secrets, volume sets, and domains. Control Plane also leads the wider list of best alternatives to Kubernetes, which compares Kubernetes and non-Kubernetes paths.

Managed modes reduce node work for a team staying on one cloud, while VPC and cluster configuration stay with that team.

Serverless containers remove the Kubernetes API from your team’s work. Amazon ECS has no additional charge for orchestration and Fargate bills per second with a one-minute minimum for Linux tasks. AWS App Runner is closed to new customers; AWS recommends Amazon ECS Express Mode instead. Google Cloud Run runs code as a service, job, worker pool, or instance, and a service with no incoming requests scales to zero. Azure Container Apps is powered by Kubernetes, Dapr, KEDA, and Envoy but does not provide direct access to the Kubernetes APIs. ECS, Cloud Run, and Container Apps each run on one cloud.

Smaller managed Kubernetes providers keep the Kubernetes API at a lower price. DigitalOcean Kubernetes includes the control plane at no cost and charges $40 per month for a high-availability control plane. Linode Kubernetes Engine includes the control plane at no additional cost, with its HA control plane starting at $60 per month per cluster depending on region. Civo says clusters launch in 90 seconds with an always-free control plane. OVHcloud Managed Kubernetes has a free plan and a Standard plan at $0.099 per cluster per hour. Your team still owns nodes, upgrades, and add-ons.

Enterprise Kubernetes targets governance across many clusters. Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS (ROSA) is jointly operated by Red Hat and AWS, and Azure Red Hat OpenShift (ARO) is jointly engineered by Red Hat and Microsoft. SUSE Rancher provisions clusters on hosted providers including EKS, GKE, and AKS, or imports existing clusters, and manages them; it does not replace them. Rancher and OpenShift also appear in the comparison of the best Kubernetes management platforms.

Self-managed lightweight Kubernetes gives the most control for the most work. K3s is a fully compliant Kubernetes distribution with SQLite as the default datastore, packaged as a single binary of less than 100 MB. Talos Linux is an immutable, API-driven OS for Kubernetes with no SSH, shell, or package manager. Both run anywhere, but your team owns everything including the control plane and upgrades.

Non-Kubernetes orchestrators suit teams that do not need the Kubernetes API. HashiCorp Nomad is a single binary for clients and servers with no external services for coordination or storage, and runs Docker, Java, Qemu VMs, and standalone binaries. Nomad 1.7.0 and later are under the Business Source License 1.1. Docker Swarm mode is built into Docker Engine; the older Classic Swarm is no longer actively developed. Both require your team to run the cluster, servers, and upgrades.

What changes when you move off EKS, GKE, or AKS?

Most Kubernetes objects are portable, but the integrations that connect a workload to cloud services are not.

What you have today Why it is tied to that cloud What a move takes
Deployments, StatefulSets, and CronJobs Standard Kubernetes API objects Copy manifests; adjust resource requests, node selectors, and tolerations that reference cloud-specific labels such as instance types or node groups
Container images in Amazon ECR, Artifact Registry, or Azure Container Registry Nodes pull images using that cloud’s IAM identity Grant the new environment pull access with registry credentials, or replicate images to a registry it can reach
ConfigMaps and Secrets Standard API objects, but values synced from a cloud secrets manager through External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI Driver depend on that cloud Point the sync at a secrets store the new environment can reach, or move values to the new platform’s secrets manager, without exporting plaintext Secrets
Ingress and load balancers AWS Load Balancer Controller creates ALBs; GKE creates Google load balancers from Gateway resources; Application Gateway for Containers is Azure’s managed L7 ingress Replace provider-specific annotations and controllers with the new platform’s ingress or Gateway API model; reissue TLS certificates held in the provider’s certificate service
Pod identity (EKS Pod Identity or IRSA, GKE Workload Identity Federation, AKS workload identity) Each maps a Kubernetes service account to that cloud’s IAM system Re-create identity bindings in the target cloud or use a cross-cloud identity layer
Persistent volumes An EBS volume and its instance must be in the same AZ; a zonal Persistent Disk is accessible only within one zone. Block volumes belong to one cloud. Copy data with file-level backups or database replication, since EBS and Persistent Disk snapshots restore only in their own cloud, or move it to a managed or replicated database first
Logging, metrics, and tracing CloudWatch Container Insights, Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus, and Azure Monitor use each cloud’s agents and backends Move to OpenTelemetry or Prometheus-compatible collectors, or the target platform’s built-in observability, and rebuild dashboards and alerts
Network policies and private connectivity NetworkPolicy enforcement depends on the CNI, and AWS PrivateLink, Google Private Service Connect, and Azure Private Link are cloud-specific Re-create policies for the target CNI or platform; re-establish private paths and IP allowlists to databases and third-party services
Helm charts Portable if templates do not hard-code cloud-specific resources Audit templates for provider-specific storage classes, annotations, and service types
Operators and CRDs Portable unless they manage cloud resources, as AWS Controllers for Kubernetes, Google Config Connector, and Azure Service Operator do Test each operator on the target platform; replace operators that manage one cloud’s resources with the target cloud’s equivalent
GitOps with Argo CD Argo CD itself is portable; the manifests it deploys may not be Update repo manifests to target the new cluster; adjust secrets and image registries
Version upgrades Each provider sets its own support windows and upgrade mechanics Adopt the target platform’s upgrade cadence and tooling; plan for different extended-support terms

The safest approach is to move in steps. Set up workload identity in the target environment first and start replicating data early, because data takes longest to copy and its final cutover needs a write freeze or a replica promotion. Run old and new environments side by side behind weighted DNS records, with TTLs lowered well before cutover, so you can shift traffic gradually and roll back. Cut over one service, or one group of tightly coupled services, at a time, since calls between clouds add latency and egress charges, and budget for running both environments during the overlap. Decommission the old cluster only after the last service is stable and traffic to it has drained.

How do you choose an alternative to managed Kubernetes?

Five questions narrow the choice.

  1. Why are you leaving? Cost, operations work, lock-in, and control each point to a different category of alternative.
  2. Do you need the Kubernetes API, operators, or CRDs? If your CI/CD, observability, and deployment tooling depends on the Kubernetes API, eliminate serverless containers and non-Kubernetes orchestrators.
  3. How many clouds or regions do you need? Managed modes and serverless containers stay on one cloud, a platform that removes cluster operations works in one region as well as many, and a multi-cloud team needs a platform that spans providers.
  4. Who will run upgrades? If you do not have a platform team, choose an option that handles the upgrade cycle for you.
  5. Where does your data live? Persistent volumes and managed databases are the hardest things to move. Start your decision from the data layer.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security.

Control Plane is based on Kubernetes, works without in-depth Kubernetes knowledge, and augments and extends clusters you already run. Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s identity for workloads, creates an IAM role, GCP service account, or Azure managed identity in your own account, so no long-lived AWS, GCP, or Azure keys sit in your code.

CPLN BYOK, Control Plane’s bring-your-own-Kubernetes option, registers a cluster you already run as a location in a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC). It supports the three most recent Kubernetes minor releases and brings its own Istio-based service mesh. This lets a team keep an existing EKS, GKE, or AKS cluster in the same GVC as Control Plane’s cloud regions during a migration, so you can move services one at a time without a hard cutover. During the move, cpln convert maps Secrets to secrets, ConfigMaps to dictionary secrets, PersistentVolumeClaims to volume sets, and Ingresses to domains, and Universal Cloud Identity takes the place of pod identity bindings. Data on the old volumes is copied separately.

Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), Control Plane’s service that provisions and operates clusters for you, handles cluster creation, upgrades, and scaling across cloud platforms and private environments and is CNCF certified.

Workload types cover most production patterns: serverless (request-driven, scales to zero), standard (long-running services), stateful (stable per-replica identity and persistent storage), cron, and vm (a KubeVirt-backed virtual machine). Each workload gets a canonical endpoint, Control Plane’s per-workload HTTPS URL that uses DNS to route clients to the nearest healthy location.

cpln helm deploys Control Plane resources from Helm charts as versioned releases with rollback. The Control Plane Kubernetes Operator manages Control Plane resources from a Kubernetes cluster through CRDs, enabling GitOps with Argo CD. Control Plane’s Template Catalog installs over 80 open-source projects, including PostgreSQL, Redis, and Kafka, into a GVC as versioned releases you can upgrade or roll back.

Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to a workload running at least two replicas across at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. Teams that want the benefits of Kubernetes without a platform team run production workloads in one region or across several clouds without owning the cluster lifecycle.

FAQ

Common questions from teams evaluating a move off managed Kubernetes.

What are the best alternatives to managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS)?

Control Plane is the strongest fit for teams leaving because of operations work, on one cloud or several, because it handles Day 2 operations including autoscaling, observability, and security, takes the cluster lifecycle off your team, and removes the tie to one provider. Managed modes like EKS Auto Mode, GKE Autopilot, and AKS Automatic reduce node work for teams staying on one cloud. Serverless containers like Amazon ECS with Fargate, Google Cloud Run, and Azure Container Apps remove the Kubernetes API from your team’s work but lock you to one provider. Smaller managed Kubernetes providers like DigitalOcean, Linode, Civo, and OVHcloud lower the control plane fee. Self-managed distributions like K3s and Talos Linux give full control. Nomad and Docker Swarm mode suit teams that do not need the Kubernetes API.

What are the best managed Kubernetes providers?

Control Plane operates the Kubernetes clusters behind its AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure locations, provisions and operates CNCF-certified clusters for you on your infrastructure through Managed Kubernetes, and joins clusters you already run through CPLN BYOK. Amazon EKS, Google GKE, and Azure AKS remain the largest providers with the broadest service ecosystems. DigitalOcean Kubernetes, Linode Kubernetes Engine, Civo, and OVHcloud offer lower-cost control planes for teams that want Kubernetes without hyperscaler pricing. The comparison of the top managed Kubernetes services covers the major providers in more detail.

Is EKS Auto Mode or GKE Autopilot an alternative to managed Kubernetes?

No. They are managed modes of EKS and GKE, so they reduce work inside managed Kubernetes and keep you on it. They take over node patching and scaling, and GKE Autopilot also runs cluster upgrades, but you still run a Kubernetes cluster on a single cloud with that cloud’s identity, ingress, and storage systems. They reduce operations work without addressing lock-in or multi-cloud requirements. On Control Plane’s built-in locations, Control Plane operates the clusters, so your team does not start or schedule Kubernetes version upgrades, in one region or across clouds.

How much does it cost to run EKS, GKE, or AKS?

EKS and GKE both charge $0.10 per cluster per hour in standard support. EKS charges $0.60 per cluster per hour in extended support, and GKE charges the same for clusters on its Extended channel once their version leaves standard support. GKE offers a free-tier credit covering one Autopilot or zonal Standard cluster. AKS offers a Free tier with no financially backed SLA, which Microsoft recommends for clusters under 10 nodes, a Standard tier with an uptime SLA, and a Premium tier required for Long Term Support. The cluster fee is a small part of the bill. Compute, storage, networking, observability, and engineering time for upgrades and security make up most of the total.

What is the cheapest alternative to EKS?

Control Plane is the strongest option when total cost includes staff time: it takes cluster upgrades and node management off your team, and Control Plane says customers see 30 to 50 percent lower compute costs compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. For the lowest control plane fee while keeping your own Kubernetes operations, DigitalOcean Kubernetes, Linode Kubernetes Engine, Civo, and OVHcloud all include the control plane at no cost or at a lower rate than EKS. DigitalOcean charges $40 per month for a high-availability control plane, Linode’s HA control plane starts at $60 per month depending on region, Civo offers an always-free control plane, and OVHcloud has a free plan. Compute costs and staff time for ongoing operations decide total cost, so the cheapest control plane is not always the cheapest overall.

Can I keep my Helm charts and operators if I leave EKS?

Yes, in most cases. Helm charts that produce standard Kubernetes objects move to another Kubernetes provider with changes only where templates reference cloud-specific storage classes, annotations, or service types. On Control Plane, cpln convert converts Kubernetes manifests into Control Plane resources, and cpln helm installs charts whose templates define Control Plane resources as versioned releases with rollback. Operators and CRDs that extend the Kubernetes API run on a Kubernetes cluster, which can be a cluster you join through CPLN BYOK or a Managed Kubernetes cluster that Control Plane operates on your infrastructure.

How do I migrate from EKS to another platform?

Start by inventorying AWS-specific dependencies: EKS Pod Identity or IRSA bindings, AWS Load Balancer Controller annotations, EBS-backed persistent volumes, images in Amazon ECR, and references to AWS services such as Secrets Manager or RDS. Set up identity in the new environment and start replicating data early, since data takes longest to move. Run the old EKS cluster and the new environment side by side behind weighted DNS with low TTLs, shift traffic service by service, and decommission the old cluster only after every service is validated. On Control Plane, CPLN BYOK can register the EKS cluster as a location in the same GVC as Control Plane’s regions while cpln convert turns each service’s manifests into workloads, and Universal Cloud Identity replaces Pod Identity or IRSA bindings with an IAM role in your AWS account.

What is the best alternative to EKS for running across multiple clouds?

Control Plane is the best fit. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s named set of locations, can span AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure regions, and a workload runs in every location of its GVC. CPLN BYOK lets you register an existing EKS cluster as a location in the same GVC, so you can migrate incrementally. Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s identity for workloads, creates the IAM role, GCP service account, or Azure managed identity in each cloud account, so a workload reaches services on all three with no long-lived keys in its code.

How does Control Plane compare to EKS, GKE, and AKS?

EKS, GKE, and AKS each manage a Kubernetes control plane on a single cloud and leave node operations, upgrade planning, identity, ingress, and security configuration to your team. Their managed modes take over node operations within that cloud, and GKE Autopilot and AKS Automatic also run version upgrades; identity, ingress, and VPC configuration stay with your team. Control Plane handles Day 2 operations, including autoscaling, observability, and security, on Kubernetes clusters it orchestrates in one region or across multiple clouds. Its 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas across at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers.

title: HTTP não é REST
description:
GET /usuarios/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.exemplo.com
Accept: application/json

POST /api HTTP/1.1
Host: api.exemplo.com
Content-Type: application/json

{ "acao": "buscarUsuario", "id": 42 }

As duas requisições buscam o mesmo usuário. As duas usam HTTP.

Qual delas é REST?

Se você respondeu "a primeira", faz sentido: ela usa o método GET e uma URL que representa o usuário. Mas usar GET, URLs bonitas e JSON não é o que define REST. E a segunda continua sendo HTTP válido, mesmo parecendo "errada".

A confusão vem de usarmos os dois termos juntos o tempo todo, como se fossem sinônimos. Não são: HTTP é um protocolo. REST é um estilo de arquitetura.

Este é o sétimo artigo da série "Coisas que usamos todo dia, mas raramente paramos para entender." No artigo sobre o que acontece quando digitamos uma URL, a navegação passava pelo HTTP a caminho da renderização. Agora vamos parar nessa etapa.

1. HTTP: uma conversa feita de mensagens

HTTP é um protocolo de requisição e resposta. O cliente envia uma mensagem, o servidor devolve outra.

Uma requisição tem:

  • Método: o que queremos fazer (GET, POST, PUT...).
  • Alvo: o caminho do recurso (/usuarios/42).
  • Headers: metadados, como formato aceito, autenticação e cache.
  • Body (opcional): o conteúdo enviado.

Uma resposta tem:

  • Status: como a requisição terminou (200, 404...).
  • Headers: tipo de conteúdo, regras de cache, cookies.
  • Body (opcional): o conteúdo devolvido.

Vamos ver isso acontecendo. Salve como servidor.cjs:

const http = require("node:http");
const crypto = require("node:crypto");

const usuario = { id: 42, nome: "Ana" };

const servidor = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  console.log(`${req.method} ${req.url}`);

  if (req.method === "GET" && req.url === "/usuarios/42") {
    const querHtml = (req.headers.accept || "").includes("text/html");

    const corpo = querHtml
      ? `<h1>${usuario.nome}</h1><p>ID: ${usuario.id}</p>`
      : JSON.stringify(usuario);

    const etag = `"${crypto.createHash("sha1").update(corpo).digest("hex")}"`;

    if (req.headers["if-none-match"] === etag) {
      res.writeHead(304, { ETag: etag, "Cache-Control": "no-cache", Vary: "Accept" });
      return res.end();
    }

    res.writeHead(200, {
      "Content-Type": querHtml ? "text/html; charset=utf-8" : "application/json",
      ETag: etag,
      "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
      Vary: "Accept",
    });
    return res.end(corpo);
  }

  res.writeHead(404, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ erro: "Recurso não encontrado" }));
});

servidor.listen(3000, () => console.log("Ouvindo em http://localhost:3000"));

Execute:

node servidor.cjs

Em outro terminal:

curl -v http://localhost:3000/usuarios/42

Uma saída resumida (as linhas com > são a requisição, as com < são a resposta):

> GET /usuarios/42 HTTP/1.1
> Host: localhost:3000
> User-Agent: curl/8.x
> Accept: */*
>
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Content-Type: application/json
< ETag: "..."
< Cache-Control: no-cache
< Vary: Accept
< Date: ...
< Content-Length: 22
<
{"id":42,"nome":"Ana"}

Os headers exatos variam com a versão do curl e do Node.js. O formato é o que importa: método, alvo, headers e body de um lado; status, headers e body do outro.

Repare que o servidor não usa nenhum framework. Ainda não falamos de REST, e o HTTP já está funcionando.

2. Métodos têm significado

Os métodos não são só nomes. A especificação do HTTP (RFC 9110) define propriedades para eles:

  • Seguro: não pede mudança de estado no servidor.
  • Idempotente: repetir a mesma requisição tem o mesmo efeito que fazer uma vez.
  • Cacheável: a resposta pode ser guardada para reuso.
Método Seguro Idempotente Cacheável
GET Sim Sim Sim
HEAD Sim Sim Sim
OPTIONS Sim Sim Não
PUT Não Sim Não
DELETE Não Sim Não
POST Não Não Só em casos específicos
PATCH Não Não Só em casos específicos

Duas consequências práticas:

  • GET não deveria alterar nada. Navegadores podem fazer prefetch e crawlers seguem links contando com isso. Um GET /pedidos/42/cancelar pode cancelar um pedido sem ninguém clicar.
  • PUT e PATCH não são intercambiáveis. O PUT substitui o recurso inteiro, então repetir a mesma requisição leva ao mesmo resultado. O PATCH aplica uma mudança parcial, e a idempotência depende de como a mudança é descrita: "defina o nome como Ana" pode ser repetido; "some 1 ao estoque", não.

Essas regras são do HTTP, não do REST. Qualquer cliente, proxy ou biblioteca de retry pode contar com elas.

3. Status codes também

O status é a forma padronizada de dizer como a requisição terminou:

Faixa Significado Exemplos
1xx Informativo 101 Switching Protocols
2xx Sucesso 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xx Redirecionamento ou cache 301, 304 Not Modified
4xx Erro do cliente 400, 401, 403, 404, 409
5xx Erro do servidor 500, 502, 503

Uma API que responde 200 OK com { "sucesso": false } no body funciona para quem lê o JSON, mas engana tudo que olha só o status: monitoramento, cache, retry e o próprio DevTools.

4. Cache é parte do protocolo

Voltando ao nosso servidor, ele devolveu um header ETag: uma identificação daquela versão do conteúdo. O cliente pode mandar esse valor de volta e perguntar se algo mudou.

Copie o valor do ETag da resposta anterior e execute:

curl -i -H 'If-None-Match: "COLE_O_ETAG_AQUI"' http://localhost:3000/usuarios/42

Saída:

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "..."
Cache-Control: no-cache
Vary: Accept
...

Sem body. O servidor só confirmou que a versão que o cliente já tem continua válida.

O Cache-Control: no-cache que usamos não significa "não guarde". Significa "guarde, mas confirme com o servidor antes de reutilizar". É exatamente o fluxo que acabamos de ver: o ETag é o validador, e o 304 é a confirmação.

Tudo isso, de novo, é HTTP. Navegadores fazem essas requisições condicionais sozinhos.

5. Stateless: o protocolo não lembra de você

Cada requisição HTTP é independente. O servidor não guarda, no protocolo, o contexto da requisição anterior.

É por isso que o token ou o cookie de sessão precisam ir em toda requisição: o servidor não lembra que você fez login há cinco minutos. Ele confere o que chegou naquela mensagem.

Aplicações constroem estado por cima disso, com cookies, sessões no servidor ou tokens. O protocolo, em si, continua sem memória.

6. Então o que é REST?

REST (Representational State Transfer) foi descrito por Roy Fielding em 2000, no capítulo 5 da sua tese de doutorado. Fielding descreve um estilo de arquitetura para sistemas distribuídos de hipermídia, ou seja, um conjunto de restrições que, aplicadas juntas, produzem certas propriedades, como escalabilidade e evolução independente de cliente e servidor.

Ele também participou da escrita das especificações do HTTP e das URIs. A própria tese conta que o REST foi usado para guiar o desenho da arquitetura da Web moderna. Por isso os dois parecem tão próximos: o HTTP foi desenhado com o REST em mente, mas um não é o outro.

As restrições do REST são:

Restrição Ideia
Cliente-servidor Interface separada do armazenamento; os dois evoluem de forma independente
Stateless Cada requisição carrega tudo que é necessário para ser entendida
Cache Respostas indicam se podem ser reutilizadas
Interface uniforme Uma forma padronizada de interação entre os componentes
Sistema em camadas O cliente não precisa saber se fala com o servidor final ou com um intermediário
Code-on-demand (opcional) O servidor pode enviar código para o cliente executar

Repare que várias delas o HTTP já facilita: stateless, cache e intermediários fazem parte do protocolo. Não é coincidência.

7. Recurso e representação

Dois conceitos centrais do REST aparecem no nosso servidor.

O recurso é a coisa que identificamos: o usuário 42, identificado por /usuarios/42.

A representação é a forma como esse recurso é transferido num momento: um JSON, um HTML, um XML.

Teste:

curl -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:3000/usuarios/42
curl -H "Accept: text/html" http://localhost:3000/usuarios/42

Saída:

{"id":42,"nome":"Ana"}
<h1>Ana</h1><p>ID: 42</p>

O mesmo recurso, duas representações. O cliente indicou o que aceitava com o header Accept, e o servidor avisou com Vary: Accept que a resposta depende dele, para que um cache não entregue o HTML a quem pediu JSON.

O nome REST vem daí: transferimos representações do estado de um recurso.

8. Interface uniforme e hipermídia

A interface uniforme é a restrição que mais diferencia o REST de outros estilos. Fielding a define com quatro partes:

  1. Identificação de recursos.
  2. Manipulação de recursos por meio de representações.
  3. Mensagens autodescritivas.
  4. Hipermídia como motor do estado da aplicação (HATEOAS).

As três primeiras aparecem em muitas APIs. A quarta quase nunca.

Hipermídia significa que a resposta diz ao cliente o que ele pode fazer em seguida, em vez de o cliente depender de uma documentação externa para montar a próxima URL:

{
  "id": 42,
  "nome": "Ana",
  "_links": {
    "self": { "href": "/usuarios/42" },
    "pedidos": { "href": "/usuarios/42/pedidos" },
    "desativar": { "href": "/usuarios/42/desativacao", "method": "POST" }
  }
}

É assim que a Web funciona com HTML: você não decora URLs, segue links e envia formulários que a própria página oferece.

Em 2008, Fielding escreveu um texto direto sobre isso: se a API não é guiada por hipertexto, ela não pode ser chamada de REST. Por esse critério, a maior parte das APIs que chamamos de REST não é.

9. HTTP sem REST, e REST sem HTTP

Agora a frase do título fica mais clara.

HTTP sem REST é muito comum:

  • A segunda requisição do começo, com POST /api e a ação no body, é um estilo RPC sobre HTTP.
  • GraphQL normalmente usa um único endpoint HTTP para todas as operações.
  • SOAP também trafega sobre HTTP.

Nenhum desses está "usando HTTP errado". Eles só seguem outro estilo de arquitetura.

REST sem HTTP também é possível, ao menos na teoria: REST descreve restrições, não um protocolo específico. O HTTP é só a implementação mais conhecida delas.

10. Um meio-termo: o Modelo de Maturidade de Richardson

Para conversar sobre o que fica no meio do caminho, Leonard Richardson propôs um modelo em níveis, popularizado por Martin Fowler:

Nível O que aparece Exemplo
0 HTTP só como transporte POST /api com a ação no body
1 Recursos /usuarios/42, mas tudo com POST
2 Métodos e status do HTTP GET /usuarios/42, DELETE /usuarios/42, 404
3 Controles de hipermídia Respostas com links para as próximas ações

A maioria das APIs que usamos no dia a dia está no nível 2. Isso não é um problema por si só, mas ajuda a ser preciso: uma API de nível 2 é uma boa API HTTP, e pelo critério de Fielding ainda não é REST.

Vale o aviso que o próprio Fowler faz: o modelo é uma forma de entender os elementos do REST, não uma definição oficial de níveis de REST.

11. Como isso aparece no trabalho?

Retry e idempotência. Bibliotecas de retry costumam repetir automaticamente só métodos idempotentes. Se uma criação de pagamento usa POST, repetir a requisição depois de um timeout pode criar uma cobrança duplicada. Já trabalhei com integrações de pagamento e webhooks, e é por isso que tantas APIs de pagamento usam chaves de idempotência: o HTTP não garante idempotência no POST, então a aplicação precisa garantir.

Status code mentindo. Um 200 com erro no body faz o monitoramento achar que está tudo bem e impede o cliente de reagir pelo status. Escolher o status certo é usar o protocolo a seu favor.

GET com efeito colateral. Links de "confirmar" ou "cancelar" com GET podem ser disparados por prefetch, crawler ou pré-visualização de link em aplicativos de mensagem.

Cache de graça. ETag, Cache-Control e 304 já estão no protocolo. Antes de criar uma camada de cache própria para dados que mudam pouco, vale ver o que o HTTP e uma CDN já resolvem.

Precisão na conversa. Quando alguém pede "uma API REST", quase sempre quer uma API HTTP de nível 2: recursos, métodos e status bem usados. Saber a diferença ajuda a perguntar o que realmente se espera, em vez de discutir rótulos.

Conclusão

As duas requisições do começo usam HTTP. A primeira se aproxima do estilo REST, com recurso identificado e método com significado. A segunda segue um estilo RPC. Nenhuma das duas, sozinha, vira REST só por usar GET, JSON ou URLs bonitas.

O HTTP define a conversa: métodos, status, headers, cache e mensagens sem memória entre si. O REST define um conjunto de restrições sobre como sistemas distribuídos devem se organizar, e o HTTP foi desenhado para facilitar várias delas.

Entender a diferença não é sobre ganhar discussão de nomenclatura. É sobre aproveitar o que o protocolo já oferece e saber quando estamos, de fato, seguindo o estilo.

HTTP é o protocolo que transporta a conversa. REST é um conjunto de escolhas sobre como organizá-la.

Na API em que você trabalha hoje, em que nível do modelo de Richardson ela estaria?

Referências

  • Roy Fielding — Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, capítulo 5: REST
  • Roy Fielding — REST APIs must be hypertext-driven
  • RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics
  • MDN — HTTP request methods
  • MDN — HTTP conditional requests
  • Martin Fowler — Richardson Maturity Model

title: Shadow AI Discovery and Data Loss Prevention Playbook
description:
Shadow AI discovery is the part of AI governance that IT teams inherit without being asked. Nobody sends a memo announcing that the sales team pasted a customer contract into a chat tool, that an engineer connected a coding assistant to the production repository, or that finance trials four summarisation tools on last quarter's board pack. The usage simply exists, and the first question leadership asks is one nobody can answer from existing dashboards: how much of this is happening, and what data has left the building?

The comfortable answer, that the company has a policy and a list of approved tools, describes intent rather than reality. Discovery is a separate discipline with its own data sources, its own blind spots, and its own false positives. This playbook is the version I would run at a 100 to 1,000 person company with a small IT team and no enterprise SIEM: what signals to collect, what risks those signals reveal, and which controls are worth buying before the rest.

This sits inside the wider program described in the small business AI governance framework and the shadow AI risk overview. The written rules live in an AI acceptable use policy, and the vendor side of the problem, where a purchased tool overstates its controls, is covered in the AI washing vendor audit. The framework this article leans on is the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, which treats inventory and measurement as prerequisites rather than afterthoughts.

How Do IT Teams Identify Shadow AI Usage across Enterprise Networks?

No single feed finds shadow AI. Six signals, combined, produce a defensible inventory, and each one has a specific blind spot you need to know before you trust the count.

Signal What it detects Blind spot
SSO application inventory and OAuth grants Tools that authenticate through your identity provider, and the scopes employees granted them Consumer tools reached with a personal login never appear
DNS and secure web gateway logs Domains resolved and requests made from managed devices Personal devices, mobile hotspots, and DoH resolvers inside apps
Browser extension inventory Assistant extensions with page-read permissions Extensions sideloaded outside management policy, and desktop apps
Expense and SaaS spend data Seats bought on corporate cards, including team-level purchases Free tiers and reimbursed personal subscriptions
Endpoint telemetry Local model runtimes, CLI assistants, and installers Web-only usage that leaves no process trace
Egress volume anomalies Unusual upload volume to newly seen destinations Small, repeated exfiltration that stays under thresholds

Three practical observations from running this.

Start with identity, because it is free and authoritative. Pull the SSO application report and the OAuth grant list for every user. Any assistant that asked for Drive, SharePoint, email, or repository scopes is an integration, not a chat session, and those grants are the highest-risk items in the inventory because they persist after the trial ends.

DNS logs are the best coverage-per-dollar signal for managed devices. A secure web gateway or filtered DNS provider gives you request volume by domain, which converts "someone might be using AI" into "these fourteen domains had traffic from these users this month". It will not see a personal phone on a cellular connection, and you should say so in the report rather than implying full coverage.

Expense data is the signal finance already owns. Card statements and reimbursement queues surface tools nobody would confess to buying. It lags by a month and misses free tiers, but it catches the purchases that create contractual obligations.

The output of discovery is not a list of names. It is a short register of four fields per tool: who uses it, what they do with it, what data classes can reach it, and whether it is sanctioned, tolerated, or prohibited. That register is what the rest of the program operates on.

What Are the Main Data Loss Prevention Risks of Employee AI Tools?

The risk is not that a model learns your secrets. It is that data leaves your boundary on a path you can no longer inspect, and the paths are predictable.

1. Prompt exfiltration. Employees paste customer records, contracts, source code, and HR documents into a chat box to get help. The data leaves with no inspection, no retention guarantee, and no record on your side. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications names this risk class directly as LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure, and it also applies to your own assistants when retrieval or logging puts data where it should not be.

2. Connector over-permission. An assistant that connects through OAuth to a drive, mailbox, or repository inherits broad read access, often with a scope the user did not read. The tool does not need to be malicious to be dangerous: a summariser that indexes everything the employee can see now holds a copy, and offboarding the employee does not revoke the tool's access to what it already indexed.

3. Retention and training posture. Consumer tiers frequently reserve the right to use inputs for improvement, while business tiers contractually do not. That distinction is a purchase decision, not a technical control, and it belongs in the register next to the tool name.

4. Generated content risk. Outputs can carry third-party IP, factual errors, or fabricated citations. An employee who pastes a generated paragraph into a customer proposal has introduced a risk that no firewall sees, which is why the copyright liability question belongs in the same policy as the data handling rules.

5. Insecure output handling. Generated text that lands in a ticket, a page builder, or a code path can carry instructions or markup that the downstream system executes. This is the same class of problem as prompt injection in web applications, arriving through a channel your security team never approved.

The pattern across all five is the same: the risk scales with the sensitivity of the data an employee can already reach, multiplied by the breadth of access the tool asks for. Rank tools by that product and the inventory becomes a prioritisation list.

How Do Mid-Market Companies Enforce AI Governance without Enterprise SIEM Budgets?

You do not need a SIEM to run this program. You need controls at three layers, in this order, and a decision about what you will not attempt to control.

Layer one: identity and policy, which cost nothing extra.

  • Publish an acceptable use policy that names sanctioned tools, prohibited data classes, and the approval path. Vague guidance produces workarounds.
  • Enforce SSO for sanctioned tools so revocation is one action and usage is attributable.
  • Review OAuth grants quarterly and remove scopes nobody uses. Start with mailbox and drive-wide read access, which is where most oversharing lives.
  • Turn on the identity provider's conditional access for unmanaged devices, at least as a reporting mode, so you can see what is connecting from where.

Layer two: network and browser controls, which cost a modest subscription.

  • Filter DNS and web traffic for unmanaged AI domains, and log rather than block in the first month. Blocking before you have data drives usage onto mobile hotspots.
  • Manage browser extensions by allowlist. Page-reading assistant extensions are the most under-reported data path in most companies.
  • Put an egress DLP policy on the one or two systems that hold the crown jewels, such as the CRM or the finance share, rather than trying to inspect all traffic.

Layer three: DLP and monitoring, where budget actually buys coverage.

  • Prefer DLP that can act at the browser or identity layer over network-only inspection, because most AI traffic is HTTPS to a small number of domains and network DLP sees only metadata.
  • Alert on volume and pattern, not on keywords. A single prompt containing "confidential" will generate noise; a user uploading 40 MB to a newly seen domain will not.
  • Keep a weekly review with a named owner and a 15-minute agenda: new domains, new OAuth grants, DLP hits above threshold, and open exceptions.

What to skip at this size: full CASB deployment, a custom model-monitoring platform, and formal data classification of every repository. Each is defensible later; starting there means the program stalls before it produces its first register.

A 30-Day Discovery and Control Sprint

Week one: assemble the register from data you already have. Export SSO applications and OAuth grants, pull 30 days of DNS or proxy logs for AI-related domains, list managed browser extensions, and pull the last two months of card and expense lines that look like AI subscriptions. Produce the four-field register and an honest coverage statement for each signal.

Week two: classify and prioritise. Tag each tool with the data classes it can reach this month and the access breadth it requested. Anything with mail or drive scope plus a consumer tier is a priority-one conversation, not a policy email.

Week three: publish and enforce the boundaries that matter. Ship the policy update with the sanctioned list, enable SSO for those tools, revoke grants nobody uses, and turn on logging for the domains you are not ready to block. Communicate the approval path so the answer to "can I use this" is a form, not a no.

Week four: baseline the metrics and pick the next control. Report sanctioned-tool share, unapproved-domain request volume, DLP events above threshold, and time to revoke. Then choose exactly one new control for next month, based on what the data says is the largest uncovered path.

Metrics That Show the Program Is Working

  • Sanctioned share of AI sessions. The portion of observed AI traffic going to approved tools. This is the number that moves when the program is healthy, because it measures migration rather than prohibition.
  • Unapproved domain requests per 100 managed devices. Trend, not absolute. A falling number means discovery and policy are working together.
  • OAuth grants with high-risk scopes. Count and age. A grant older than two quarters with mailbox access is a finding.
  • DLP events above threshold, and their disposition. Volume without disposition is noise; the useful metric is how many were investigated and closed.
  • Time from discovery to revocation. Target same business day for priority-one tools. If revocation takes a week, the program is documentation rather than control.

Five Failure Modes

Failure What it looks like Fix
Policy without telemetry A signed AI policy and no ability to say which tools are in use Run the six-signal discovery before the next policy revision
Block-everything rollout Usage moves to personal devices and mobile hotspots, invisible to you Log first, then block the highest-risk domains with a documented exception path
DLP that only logs Dashboards full of events nobody reviews Weekly review with a named owner and a disposition for every threshold hit
Broad OAuth grants left in place A summariser holds an indexed copy of a departed employee's access Quarterly grant review, least-scope re-consent, revoke with offboarding
No deprovisioning path Ex-employees keep AI tool access because the tool sits outside the identity provider SSO for every sanctioned tool, and an offboarding checklist that includes them

Conclusion

Shadow AI is not a discipline problem. It is an inventory and telemetry problem, and at mid-market scale the data already exists in four systems the company is paying for: identity, DNS or proxy, the browser, and the expense report. Combining them produces a register precise enough to argue about, which is a much better position than a policy that assumes compliance.

The sequence that works is unglamorous: inventory what you already have, classify by data reach, sanction a short list, make approval easy, and report a handful of metrics that leadership can read. The alternative, buying a control platform before you know what you are controlling, is how mid-market AI programs spend their first year's budget and still cannot answer the question the board actually asked.

title: Mechanics of AI Interface Feedback Loops: Capturing User Corrections Without Breaking UX
description:
You’ve just finished typing a prompt or tweaking an AI-generated suggestion, maybe correcting a label, adjusting a value, or rejecting a mistaken completion, and you expect the UI to instantly update, ready for your next move. But sometimes, the interface feels sluggish, or worse, your correction disappears, the AI’s response overwrites your input, and you think, “Why can’t this just behave like a normal app?”

That frustration hit me recently while working on a project with live AI-assisted forms. The core challenge? Capturing user corrections and feedback in real time without breaking the flow or introducing weird latency. Turns out, the mechanics of this feedback loop are subtle and surprisingly tricky.

Let’s break down what’s really going on under the hood when AI interfaces try to capture your input, handle your corrections, and update the UI smoothly.

The Feedback Loop: More Than Just Input and Output

At first glance, it seems straightforward: the user types or clicks, the AI responds, the UI updates. But that ignores a crucial reality, AI-generated content is often streaming in, partial, and probabilistic. Meanwhile, the user might be interacting with the UI, correcting or tweaking things mid-stream.

For example, imagine an AI autocomplete suggesting a phrase as you type. You spot a typo and try to fix it while the suggestion is still arriving. If the UI just blindly replaces the input with the latest AI output, your correction is lost. That’s a broken experience.

The key is managing two intertwined states:

  1. The user’s local input and corrections
  2. The AI’s generated response as it streams or updates

These have to coexist and merge carefully.

Event and State Management: Coordinating User Edits and AI Updates

How do interfaces keep your input intact while updating AI suggestions?

1. Local State vs Remote AI State

Typically, the UI maintains a local state reflecting your input and edits. Meanwhile, AI responses come asynchronously, often as partial streams. The interface needs to reconcile these two sources.

A common pattern is to treat user edits as authoritative until the AI finishes or the user signals completion. This means:

  • While you’re typing or correcting, your local input state overrides incoming AI updates.
  • The AI’s output is merged in only when it doesn’t conflict or after you pause.

This demands a nuanced event system that:

  • Detects user edits (input, selection, cursor position)
  • Temporarily suspends AI state updates that would overwrite user changes
  • Resumes syncing once the user stops typing

2. Debouncing and Throttling AI Updates

Since AI suggestions can stream rapidly, bombarding the UI with updates risks causing jitter or lost focus.

Throttling or debouncing AI updates helps:

  • Batch rapid AI output into manageable chunks
  • Avoid interrupting user input with constant overwrites

For instance, holding off AI state merges for 100-200ms after user input lets the user finish their edit before the AI response updates the UI.

3. Cursor and Selection Preservation

One subtle but critical piece is preserving cursor position during updates.

If the UI replaces text without maintaining cursor or selection, the user can lose their spot or type in the wrong place. This is especially tricky when AI updates insert or remove characters.

Many implementations track:

  • The cursor index before AI update
  • The diff between old and new text
  • Adjust cursor position accordingly

Failing to do this causes the cursor to jump unexpectedly, confusing users.

Design Tradeoffs: Balancing Latency, Responsiveness, and Clarity

Even with careful state management, tradeoffs remain.

Optimistic UI vs Consistency

Should the UI show AI suggestions immediately, or wait until the AI response is stable?

  • Showing suggestions early feels responsive but risks flicker or overwriting user edits.
  • Waiting for stable output reduces flicker but introduces latency.

A middle ground is incremental updates with clear UI cues (like loading spinners or subtle placeholders).

User Control: Letting Users Override AI

Good AI UX lets users override or dismiss suggestions without frustration.

Implementing undo, manual override, or explicit accept/reject actions helps prevent the AI from fighting the user.

Feedback Capture Without Interruptions

If the AI UI aggressively resets input on every model update, users get annoyed.

Instead, triggering AI updates only when the user pauses or via explicit action reduces interference.

Real-World Example: Live Code Completion Editors

I’ve seen these mechanics in action in live AI code editors:

  • The editor buffers your keystrokes locally.
  • AI completions stream in asynchronously.
  • The UI merges completions only if they don’t conflict with your edits.
  • Cursor position is preserved using diff algorithms.
  • Updates are throttled to avoid UI jank.

This orchestration creates smooth interactions where the AI assists but never steals control.

Wrapping Up

Building AI interfaces that capture user corrections without breaking UX requires juggling asynchronous AI streams, local user edits, and precise event coordination.

It’s a dance of state management and event handling, preserving your intent while letting the AI help.

Next time your AI UI feels smooth and responsive, you can thank the careful mechanics working quietly behind the scenes.

Helpful learning resources

  • W3C WAI accessibility guidance
  • W3Schools accessibility tutorials
  • MDN Web Docs Originally published at Under The Hood. Get the next deep dive in your inbox: subscribe to Under The Hood.

title: How to Use a Proxy in Go: net/http, HTTP_PROXY, and Why GOPROXY Is Something Else
description:
By Leo Lin, Product Manager at FlashIP (https://www.flaship.com/), Singapore. Disclosure: I work on FlashIP.

Go has two settings with "proxy" in the name. They do different jobs, and people mix them up all the time. HTTPS_PROXY is a network proxy that your traffic passes through. GOPROXY is a module mirror that go get downloads code from. If you're behind a corporate gateway and go mod download times out, changing GOPROXY won't help. If your company runs a private module mirror, setting HTTPS_PROXY won't point Go at it.

Below is how each one works, based on the official Go docs and a few tests I ran on Go 1.27 against a dead proxy at 127.0.0.1:9. Hostnames and credentials are placeholders.

1. net/http reads HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY

http.DefaultTransport, which http.Get and http.DefaultClient use, picks up its proxy from the environment through http.ProxyFromEnvironment. It reads HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY, or their lowercase versions, and chooses the proxy by the request's scheme:

export HTTPS_PROXY=http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080
export HTTP_PROXY=http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080
export NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,.internal.example.com,10.0.0.0/8
go run .

Some details that trip people up:

  • The scheme decides. An https:// URL uses HTTPS_PROXY only. In my test, setting only HTTP_PROXY sent https://example.com direct (200 OK). With HTTPS_PROXY set, the same request failed with proxyconnect tcp: ... connection refused.
  • The value can be a full URL or just host[:port]. With host[:port], Go assumes http.
  • localhost is never proxied. ProxyFromEnvironment returns no proxy when the request host is localhost.
  • The environment is read once. In my test, calling os.Setenv("HTTPS_PROXY", ...) after the first request had no effect, and the second request still went direct. Set the variables before the process starts, or set the proxy in code (section 3).

2. NO_PROXY syntax in Go

According to the golang.org/x/net/http/httpproxy docs, NO_PROXY is a comma-separated list. Each entry can be:

  • an IP prefix (1.2.3.4) or a CIDR block (10.0.0.0/8)
  • a domain name, which matches the name and all its subdomains (example.com matches example.com and api.example.com)
  • a domain with a leading dot, which matches subdomains only (.example.com doesn't match example.com)
  • an IP or domain with a port (1.2.3.4:80)
  • *, which turns proxying off completely

Parsing is best effort and errors are ignored. A typo won't throw an error. Go just ignores that entry and proxies the request.

3. Set the proxy in code (including SOCKS5)

To use a proxy that doesn't depend on the environment, set Transport.Proxy:

proxyURL, _ := url.Parse("http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080")
client := &http.Client{
    Transport: &http.Transport{Proxy: http.ProxyURL(proxyURL)},
}
resp, err := client.Get("https://example.com")

Transport.Proxy supports the http, https, socks5 and socks5h schemes. If the scheme is empty, Go uses http. Go treats socks5 the same as socks5h. Username and password in the URL are sent in a Proxy-Authorization header. If Proxy is nil, Go doesn't use a proxy. So a Transport you build yourself without setting Proxy ignores HTTPS_PROXY entirely. To keep the environment behavior on a custom transport, set Proxy: http.ProxyFromEnvironment.

My test confirmed SOCKS5 works from both places: http.ProxyURL with a socks5:// URL and HTTPS_PROXY=socks5://127.0.0.1:9 both tried the dead proxy and failed.

4. GOPROXY is a module mirror, not a network proxy

GOPROXY tells the go command where to download modules. Its default value is:

https://proxy.golang.org,direct
  • direct means fetch from the version control repository, off means don't fetch at all, and the separator controls fallback. After a comma, Go tries the next entry only on a 404 or 410 response. After a pipe (|), it tries the next entry on any error, timeouts included.
  • GOPRIVATE=*.corp.example.com lists module path patterns that should never be requested from a proxy. It's the default for both GONOPROXY and GONOSUMDB.
  • A private mirror can take credentials in the URL: GOPROXY=https://user:pass@proxy.corp.example.com.

To save these settings, use go env -w GOPROXY=.... It writes to a config file in your user config directory, and GOENV changes where that file lives. go env -w only accepts Go's own variables, though. go env -w HTTPS_PROXY=... failed with unknown go command variable HTTPS_PROXY, so the network proxy still belongs in your shell or service environment.

The go command does honor HTTPS_PROXY when it talks to a module mirror. With a dead proxy in HTTPS_PROXY, go mod download failed with a proxyconnect error against proxy.golang.org. For direct fetches Go runs git, and Git has its own http.proxy setting. Its docs describe that setting as overriding http_proxy/https_proxy/all_proxy.

Quick triage

  • curl uses the proxy but your Go binary doesn't → check that HTTPS_PROXY is set for the process, and that a custom Transport sets Proxy.
  • An internal host still goes through the proxy → check NO_PROXY for typos. Remember the leading-dot rule.
  • go get is blocked by the network → set HTTPS_PROXY, not GOPROXY.
  • Private modules return 404/410 or fail checksum lookups → set GOPRIVATE.

If you're testing against an external proxy, FlashIP (https://www.flaship.com/) offers HTTP(S) and SOCKS5 endpoints with username:password or IP whitelist authentication. The URL formats above work for either type.

Sources

  • net/http package docs: https://pkg.go.dev/net/http
  • httpproxy package (NO_PROXY rules): https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/net/http/httpproxy
  • Go Modules Reference (GOPROXY, GOPRIVATE): https://go.dev/ref/mod
  • cmd/go (go env -w, GOENV): https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go
  • git-config (http.proxy): https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config

title: Secure Database Access for AI Agents with db-mcp-gateway
description:
AI agents are useful when they can inspect data, but giving them direct database credentials creates a large security problem. A connection string in an agent prompt or a local environment variable is hard to rotate and easy to leak. db-mcp-gateway addresses this by acting as a self hosted MCP gateway between AI agents and databases. The agent sends a query request through MCP. The gateway checks identity and permissions before the database responds.

The repository is available at https://github.com/developerz-ai/db-mcp-gateway.

Credential isolation

The core rule is simple. Database credentials live only in the gateway. An AI agent receives query results, not connection strings. This removes the need to place a database URL on a developer laptop or inside an agent configuration file.

The gateway also avoids credential leakage in logs, errors, and responses. That matters because agents can produce verbose output, and debugging tools may capture more than expected. When the database password never enters the agent context, there is less to leak.

A typical request path looks like this. The AI agent calls an MCP tool. The gateway checks the caller identity and the grant. The gateway opens the database connection using its own credentials. The database returns rows. The gateway returns only the requested data to the agent.

Identity and SSO

db-mcp-gateway uses browser based SSO for authentication. Supported identity providers include Okta, Google Workspace, Entra, Authentik, and Keycloak. The agent does not need an embedded browser. The login flow happens through the user's normal browser session.

Every query can be traced from SSO user to group to grant to audit row. This gives security teams a clear attribution path. If an investigation asks who ran a query, the answer is not a shared service account. It is the identity that authenticated through SSO.

Group based permissions keep access manageable. A platform team can map an SSO group to a grant, and the grant can be reviewed like code.

Grants as code

Permissions are defined in YAML. There is no in band admin UI by design. This makes the permission model reviewable through pull requests and compatible with GitOps workflows.

A grant can specify the group, databases, actions, schemas, row limits, and whether a reason is required.

grants:
  - group: backend-devs
    databases: [production_postgres]
    actions: [query_read]
    constraints:
      schemas: [public, analytics]
      row_limit: 1000
      require_reason: true

This example allows the backend-devs group to run read queries against production_postgres. It limits the grant to the public and analytics schemas. It caps rows at 1000 and requires a reason for the query.

The gateway is read only by default. Writes are opt in per grant. Per database least privilege roles can be used, and statement timeouts and row caps are enforced at both the database and the gateway. Grants can also allow or deny schemas and define time windows.

Audit trail

Database access for AI agents needs an audit trail that is useful during an incident review. db-mcp-gateway records query history and stores gateway state and audit logs in PostgreSQL. The MCP tool surface includes get_query_history, which lets operators inspect prior queries.

The audit trail should answer who accessed a database and what query was run. It should also show which grant was used. This supports compliance efforts by providing access control and query logging. It does not make the project a certified compliance product, but it gives teams evidence they can review.

Deployment model

The gateway is distributed as a single Docker container. Configuration is one YAML file. PostgreSQL is used for gateway state and audit logs. The project targets PostgreSQL and MongoDB. MySQL and MSSQL are rejected at boot, which keeps the supported database surface explicit.

A basic run looks like this.

docker pull ghcr.io/developerz-ai/db-mcp-gateway:1.1.1
docker run -p 8080:8080 -v $(pwd)/config.yaml:/app/config.yaml ghcr.io/developerz-ai/db-mcp-gateway:1.1.1

This deployment style is small enough for a platform team to operate without a large control plane. The important operational control is the configuration file, because it defines grants and identity behavior.

MCP tool surface

The gateway exposes a small set of MCP tools. list_databases shows available databases. describe_schema returns table structure and relationships. sample_table previews data before a full query. run_query executes SELECT queries. explain helps with query analysis. get_query_history exposes the audit trail.

This tool surface is useful for AI agents because it gives them a safe way to explore data before running expensive queries. It also gives platform teams a narrow interface to monitor and restrict.

Who benefits

Platform and SRE teams get a way to enable AI agent database access without spreading credentials. Backend developers can query production data with their own SSO identity instead of a shared password. Security and compliance teams get centralized access control and query logging. They also get user attribution.

The main tradeoff is that the gateway becomes a required component for agent database access. That is usually acceptable when credential isolation and auditability are the goal.

Start with the repository

The project README includes the security model, grant examples, and deployment steps. Start by defining one read only grant for a non production database. Review the audit output. Then expand to production only after the identity and grant model is clear.

The repository is at https://github.com/developerz-ai/db-mcp-gateway. #MCP #DatabaseSecurity
