description:
Today's Storylines

Three Numbers That Belong on the Same Slide

The daily AI news for November 24 is about three capabilities arriving together: agents that can now approve code, sanctions that reshape chip supply, and a privacy shift that changes what models remember. Each moves the industry one step from demo to infrastructure.

The Five-Minute Version

  • Anthropic launched Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix and approve code changes in GitHub and GitLab.
  • US imposed sanctions on a Singaporean firm at the center of the Nvidia chip scandal, blacklisting Megaspeed.
  • Google Gemini now decouples chat history from AI training data, adding new user controls.
  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned after board reinstatement amid national security scrutiny.
  • Open source AI desktop app TheGitAI released for macOS, Windows and Linux.
  • Matching Sonnet 5.5 on medical chart review at 3% of the cost shows shrinking inference economics.

Anthropic Launches Claude Ship: Agents That Review, Fix and Approve Code

What Claude Ship Does

Anthropic announced Claude Ship on November 23, a new product that lets AI agents participate directly in code review workflows. The agents can read pull requests, suggest fixes, and now approve or request changes — the same actions a human reviewer takes.

The system integrates with GitHub and GitLab. When a pull request opens, Claude Ship agents analyze the diff, run tests in a sandbox, and post review comments. They can also apply fixes directly to the branch.

The Approve Button Changes the Workflow

Until now, AI code assistants stopped at suggestions. The human had to read, verify and click merge. Claude Ship adds the approve action, meaning an agent can now be the final gate before code lands.

Anthropic says the agent follows the same review standards the team configures: passing tests, style guides, security scans. The human sets the policy; the agent enforces it.

Why This Matters for Developer Velocity

Code review is often the bottleneck in shipping. Large teams wait hours or days for human reviewers. An agent that can approve routine changes — dependency updates, test additions, documentation fixes — removes that queue.

For risky changes, the agent requests human review. The workflow becomes: agent handles the 80% that are safe, humans focus on the 20% that need judgment.

Sources

  • TechCrunch: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix and approve code changes

US Sanctions Singapore Firm at Center of Nvidia Chip Scandal

Megaspeed Blacklisted

The US Commerce Department added Singapore-based Megaspeed to the Entity List on November 23. The company is accused of diverting Nvidia AI chips to China in violation of export controls.

Reuters reports the blacklist cuts Megaspeed off from US technology and banking. The move follows a Washington Post report that the Commerce Department approved 580,000 Nvidia chips for China in exchange for a revenue share.

The Singapore Connection

Megaspeed operated as a transshipment hub. Chips shipped legally to Singapore were re-exported to Chinese buyers. The firm's directors include individuals with ties to Chinese military procurement networks.

Nvidia stopped disclosing Singapore sales in its latest earnings. The subpoena from California prosecutors and the Megaspeed blacklist suggest the channel was larger than previously acknowledged.

What This Means for Supply Chains

Companies buying Nvidia GPUs now face stricter due diligence on Singapore intermediaries. The Entity List designation means any US person or company dealing with Megaspeed needs a license — effectively a ban.

For AI labs planning compute purchases, the message is clear: the provenance of every GPU will be audited. Gray-market chains are being closed.

Sources

  • Reuters: US blacklists Megaspeed chip firm linked to Nvidia scandal
  • NY Times: Trump administration blacklists Megaspeed over Nvidia chip trade

Google Gemini Decouples Chat History from AI Training

New User Controls

Google announced updated controls for Gemini on November 23. Users can now choose whether their conversations are used to improve the model. The setting is off by default for new users.

Previously, chat history fed directly into training pipelines. The change separates the product experience (conversation continuity) from the model improvement loop.

Why the Default Changed

Regulatory pressure from the EU AI Act and US state privacy laws forced the shift. Google also faces a class action alleging unauthorized use of chat data.

The new architecture stores conversations in a user-controlled vault. Training pipelines pull from anonymized, aggregated datasets that users explicitly opt into.

Impact on Model Quality

Google says the quality impact is minimal because the opted-in corpus is still large. But the change sets a precedent: user data is no longer free training fuel by default.

Other labs will face the same pressure. The era of implicit consent for AI training data is ending.

Sources

  • Google Blog: Updated controls for Gemini app

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Reinstated Amid National Security Scrutiny

Board Overruled Management

Bloomberg reported on November 23 that Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO without consulting the management team. Huang had stepped aside temporarily amid a federal investigation into chip diversions to China.

The board's unilateral move is rare. It signals that Huang's control over the company's China strategy is seen as a national security matter, not just a governance issue.

Foreign Policy Calls It a Scandal

Foreign Policy published an essay calling Huang's return "the biggest national security scandal in US history." The argument: the CEO who oversaw the Singapore diversion channel is now back in charge of the company that supplies the chips.

Republicans in Congress are breaking with the administration over the reinstatement. The NY Times reports GOP members demand a full briefing on what the board knew.

Market Reaction

Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday, November 20, the day after the Anthropic IPO erased Nasdaq gains. The stock has not recovered. Short sellers who bet against Nvidia's China exposure were vindicated.

Sources

  • Bloomberg: Nvidia board reinstated CEO without consulting management
  • Foreign Policy: Huang's return is a national security scandal
  • NY Times: Republicans break with Trump over Jensen Huang

TheGitAI Desktop App Released for All Platforms

Open Source AI Coding Assistant

TheGitAI released its desktop application on November 23 for macOS, Windows and Linux. The app brings local AI coding assistance with Git integration, running models locally or via API.

The project is open source. Users can connect their own Ollama instance, LM Studio, or cloud API keys. The app handles context gathering from the repository, diff generation, and commit message drafting.

Why Local Matters

Enterprise policies often block cloud AI tools. A desktop app that runs entirely locally — model, context, diffs — satisfies compliance while delivering AI assistance.

The release adds to the growing local-first AI tooling ecosystem: Cursor, Windsurf, and now TheGitAI all offer varying degrees of local execution.

Sources

  • TheGitAI Desktop App

Matching Sonnet 5.5 on Medical Chart Review at 3% of the Cost

Propensity Labs Case Study

Propensity Labs published a case study on November 23 showing their Cortex Charts system matching Claude Sonnet 5.5 on medical chart review tasks at roughly 3% of the inference cost.

The system uses a smaller specialized model fine-tuned on de-identified clinical notes. It achieves comparable accuracy on ICD-10 coding, discharge summary quality, and comorbidity extraction.

The Economics Shift

Frontier model API pricing has been the ceiling for AI applications. A 97% cost reduction for a specific domain task changes the ROI calculation for healthcare AI deployments.

Hospitals and insurers running millions of chart reviews per year can now justify automated coding that was previously too expensive.

Sources

  • Propensity Labs: Cortex Charts case study

FAQ

What is Claude Ship and how does it differ from Copilot?

Claude Ship is an AI agent that participates directly in code review on GitHub and GitLab. Unlike Copilot which suggests code while you write, Claude Ship reviews pull requests after they are opened, runs tests, suggests fixes, and can approve or request changes — acting as an automated reviewer.

Did the US really blacklist a Singapore company over Nvidia chips?

Yes. The Commerce Department added Megaspeed to the Entity List on November 23 for diverting Nvidia AI chips to China. This follows reports that 580,000 Nvidia chips were approved for China sales with a revenue share arrangement.

Can I opt out of Gemini training on my chats?

Yes. Google added new controls on November 23 that let users choose whether conversations are used for model training. The setting is off by default for new users.

Why did Nvidia's board reinstate Jensen Huang without consulting management?

The board's unilateral move suggests Huang's role in China chip strategy is viewed as a national security matter. Foreign Policy called it "the biggest national security scandal in US history."

The Bottom Line

What to Watch Next

Watch whether Claude Ship's approve action becomes a standard CI gate. If agents can reliably approve routine changes, the code review bottleneck shrinks — but the liability question when an agent approves a bug remains open.

Watch the Megaspeed case for precedent. If Singapore transshipment hubs are systematically shut down, the gray market for AI chips contracts, and legitimate buyers face longer procurement cycles.

The Pattern Today

Three of today's stories are about control shifting to automated systems: agents approving code, export controls enforced via Entity List, and users controlling their training data. The industry is building the governance layer that was missing in the pure capability phase.

title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
description: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

title: Token Pass credit now applies automatically across AI Gateway
description:
Token Pass credit now applies automatically to included model usage through AI Gateway, whether a request authenticates with an API key, OIDC token, or fx login. No dedicated Token Pass API key is required, though you can still create one from the dashboard or the CLI for keys scoped only to featured models and providers.

When Token Pass credit runs out for the billing period, requests from a standard key or OIDC token fall back to your team's AI Gateway credits. Token Pass keys still stop until the next billing period.

Requests served through the Token Pass provider remain Zero Data Retention (ZDR). Fallback requests follow your team's setting. With team-wide ZDR enabled, they route only to ZDR providers.

Available now for Token Pass subscribers on Pro teams. If you created a Token Pass key during setup, switch to a standard API key or OIDC token to get fallback. Learn more in the Token Pass documentation.

title: I Stopped Hand-Tweaking shadcn/ui CSS Variables — Build the Whole Theme in Minutes Instead
description:
shadcn/ui gives you beautiful components and exactly one rite of passage: an afternoon inside globals.css, hand-tuning CSS variables, wondering why your primary color looks perfect in light mode and like a crime scene in dark mode.

--primary, --primary-foreground, --ring, --chart-3... every variable has a partner, contrast is a real constraint, and "just make it blue" turns into forty small decisions. There's a faster way to get a theme that's actually coherent.

🛠️ Free Tool: shadcn Theme Generator — WebToolsHub — pick colors visually, preview light and dark mode live, and export ready-to-paste CSS variables. Free, in-browser.

Why Hand-Tuned Themes Drift

A shadcn theme isn't one color. It's a system:

  • Backgrounds and foregrounds that must pair correctly
  • Primary, secondary, accent, and destructive — each with a foreground that stays readable on top of it
  • Border, input, and ring colors that harmonize instead of matching by accident
  • Chart colors that look like they belong to the same product
  • A radius that changes the entire personality of the UI

Change one value in isolation and the system quietly breaks somewhere else — usually the place a user finds first, like a disabled button nobody can read.

The Workflow That Respects Your Afternoon

  1. Start from intent, not hex codes. "Warm and trustworthy" or "sharp and technical" — pick the feeling, then the base color that carries it.
  2. Preview in both modes simultaneously. Dark mode is not inverted light mode. If you're only checking one, you're shipping the other on faith.
  3. Check the pairings, not the colors. Text on primary, text on destructive, muted text on background — contrast lives in pairs.
  4. Export and paste. The output should be the full variable block for globals.css, ready for Tailwind v4's @theme or the classic :root / .dark setup.

That's the whole loop the shadcn theme generator is built around: visual picking, live component preview in both modes, and a clean export you paste once.

Your Components Were Never the Problem

shadcn's components are consistent by design — which means when a UI looks "off," it's almost always the theme layer underneath. Fix the system once, and every button, card, and dialog you add inherits the fix.

Spend the afternoon building features. Let the theme take ten minutes.

title: Building Bilingual (Arabic + English) Shopify Themes: Practical RTL Lessons
description:
If you build storefronts for clients in the Gulf, sooner or later someone asks for an Arabic version of their Shopify store. Shopify Markets and the translation tools handle the words, but the theme has to handle direction. Right-to-left (RTL) support is where many otherwise solid themes fall apart: arrows point the wrong way, carousels slide backwards, prices wrap strangely and icons sit on the wrong side of their labels.

Here are the lessons that have saved us the most time when building bilingual themes.

1. Set the direction once, at the root

Do not sprinkle dir="rtl" across individual sections. Set it on the <html> element based on the active locale, so the whole document flips consistently:

{%- liquid
  assign rtl_locales = 'ar,he,fa,ur' | split: ','
  assign page_dir = 'ltr'
  if rtl_locales contains request.locale.iso_code
    assign page_dir = 'rtl'
  endif
-%}
<html lang="{{ request.locale.iso_code }}" dir="{{ page_dir }}">

With direction set at the root, the browser handles text alignment, table columns and form fields for you. Your job becomes fixing the places where the CSS fights the browser.

2. Replace physical CSS properties with logical ones

The single biggest improvement is moving from left/right to logical properties. Instead of:

.card__badge { left: 12px; }
.price { margin-right: 8px; text-align: left; }

write:

.card__badge { inset-inline-start: 12px; }
.price { margin-inline-end: 8px; text-align: start; }

margin-inline-start, padding-inline-end, inset-inline-start, border-inline-start and text-align: start all follow the document direction automatically. One stylesheet now works for both languages, and you avoid maintaining a separate rtl.css file that drifts out of sync.

Browser support for logical properties is excellent in every evergreen browser, so there is little reason to avoid them on new builds.

3. Flip directional icons, not all icons

Arrows, chevrons and "back" icons should mirror in RTL. Search, cart, user and close icons should not. A small utility class keeps this explicit:

[dir="rtl"] .icon--directional { transform: scaleX(-1); }

Apply icon--directional only to icons that imply movement or reading order. Logos, product images and anything containing Latin text should never be flipped.

4. Watch out for sliders and JavaScript positioning

Carousel libraries often calculate positions with scrollLeft or translate values that assume left-to-right flow. Before shipping:

  • check whether your slider library has an RTL option and pass it based on document.dir,
  • test swipe gestures on a real phone, because swipe direction should feel natural for Arabic readers, and
  • check scrollLeft behaviour, since browsers report negative values in RTL containers.

A quick guard in your theme JavaScript helps:

const isRTL = document.documentElement.dir === 'rtl';
slider.init({ rtl: isRTL });

5. Handle mixed-direction content carefully

Product titles in Arabic stores often contain English brand names, model numbers or sizes. The Unicode bidirectional algorithm usually copes, but numbers and punctuation at the edges of a string can jump to the wrong side. Wrap user-generated or mixed values with <bdi>:

<span class="product-sku"><bdi>{{ variant.sku }}</bdi></span>

Prices deserve extra testing. Check how the currency code or symbol renders next to Arabic text, and make sure phone numbers in the footer stay readable in both directions.

6. Choose fonts that support Arabic properly

Many popular Latin web fonts have no Arabic glyphs, so the browser falls back to a system font and the store suddenly looks inconsistent. Pick a pairing with a proper Arabic companion, set it with a locale-based class, and increase the line height slightly. Arabic script generally needs more vertical space to stay readable.

[lang="ar"] body { font-family: 'Noto Kufi Arabic', system-ui, sans-serif; line-height: 1.8; }

7. Test the whole purchase path, not just the homepage

The homepage is usually fine after the steps above. Problems hide in the cart drawer, quantity selectors, filters, account pages and the order confirmation email. Walk through a complete order in Arabic on mobile before calling the job done.

Closing thoughts

RTL support is much easier when it is planned from the first line of CSS rather than patched at the end. Set the direction at the root, use logical properties, be deliberate about icons and sliders, and test real purchase flows. If you would rather hand the work to a team that does this regularly, a specialist Shopify Development Dubai studio can build bilingual themes from the ground up, and the same principles apply to any custom Web Design Dubai project that has to serve both Arabic and English audiences.

The Edge UI now fetches API products on demand when you open the Add Product dialog, improving initial page load performance.
576859695 Edge UI Fixed an issue in the Analytics Error Code Analysis dashboard where 504 Gateway Timeout responses caused by target timeouts were excluded from the Proxy errors charts. Target timeout 504 responses are now counted under Proxy errors.
188163219 Edge UI Fixed a UI formatting issue in the Analytics Custom Reports list view so that dimensions display without overlapping.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.16.14

On November 11, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.16.14.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.16.14.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies now support function calling

The SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies now handle LLM function calling (tool use) flows. Two new optional XML elements extract function calling content for Model Armor sanitization:

  • <FunctionResponseSource> in SanitizeUserPrompt: extracts function/tool response data from user turns. Used as a fallback when <UserPromptSource> returns empty on function calling turns.
  • <FunctionCallSource> in SanitizeModelResponse: extracts function call arguments from model responses. Used as a fallback when <LLMResponseSource> returns empty.

Default templates target the Gemini format and require no additional configuration. For OpenAI and Anthropic formats, configure custom JSONPath templates. For more information, see FunctionResponseSource and FunctionCallSource.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
575563262 Updated the Google Cloud client library stack to match Apigee hybrid 1.17 (protobuf 4.x, gRPC 1.82, GAX 2.83, Guava 33.5). With this update: (1) a malformed inbound gRPC request frame is now reported to the client as grpc-status INTERNAL (13) and recorded in analytics as x-apigee.grpc.status=13, instead of an Apigee ServiceUnavailable fault (UNAVAILABLE, 14) with no x-apigee.grpc.status; (2) an ExternalCallout policy whose Google service account does not exist now fails with gRPC UNAUTHENTICATED (16) instead of UNAVAILABLE (14); and (3) Gson parse-error messages, such as in proxy validation errors, now end with a link to Gson's troubleshooting guide.
572875915 Fixed an issue where the apigee-env Helm chart and Apigee operator ignored the synchronizer pollInterval configuration (synchronizer.pollInterval, envs[].pollInterval, and envs[].components.synchronizer.pollInterval); configured values now take effect, and values below 60 seconds are raised to 60.
572025634 Fixed an issue where responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow returned a corrupted body; compressed text/event-stream responses now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact.
560272924 Apigee hybrid now supports continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Fixed an issue where Model Armor policies did not honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: when set, Model Armor callouts now bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic, while streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
549779897 Apigee analytics now reports the Model Armor template, verdict, and matched filters for each request on both the prompt and model-response directions.
524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
519116013 Disabled weak Diffie-Hellman (DH) TLS cipher suites on port 7070 (Prometheus jmx_exporter) in the apigee-hybrid-cassandra container.
500345401 The apigee-telemetry Helm chart now supports independent tolerations and nodeSelector configuration for the OpenTelemetry Collector (metrics.collector), Prometheus Adapter (metrics.adapter), and Stackdriver Exporters (metrics.proxyStackdriverExporter and metrics.appStackdriverExporter).

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

End-user safety identifier labels for abuse monitoring

End-user safety_identifier request labels are available in General Availability (GA) for Gemini (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) and Veo (predictLongRunning) API calls. API resellers and multi-tenant apps can pass an anonymized per-user ID in labels to attribute policy violations to individual end users. Targeted attribution helps prevent enforcement actions across an entire Google Cloud project.

For formatting requirements and code samples, see Pass an end-user safety identifier in API calls.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.21.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Sandboxed build commands and patch refresh: When sandboxing is enabled, cm build and cm fix build validation now run build.command inside the sandbox, and cm fix refreshes stored patch diffs after build validation finishes.
  • Read-only host toolchains and isolated caches: Sandboxed cm build, cm fix, and cm verify runs now mount host toolchain and package-manager directories read-only and redirect supported compiler and package caches to session-scoped temporary directories.
  • Command environment isolation: Disabled repository Git hooks, isolated host Git configuration, and ignored repository Python bytecode caches (__pycache__) during command and build runs.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a 30-minute timeout for silent active turns so stalled sessions cancel and recover cleanly.
    • Preserved proof-of-concept execution output when reproducer errors occur, retaining stdout and stderr to help diagnose build failures, timeouts, and setup issues.
    • Fixed an issue where patch generation failed on mid-run sandbox failures by automatically retrying with a fresh sandbox environment.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

Gemini 4 Carbon in CodeMender (Preview)

CodeMender now supports Gemini 4 Carbon. To use it, pass --model gemini-4-carbon to cm find, cm verify, or cm fix. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Specifying the model.

Feature

Govern agents on any CNCF-conformant Kubernetes cluster with Agent Gateway for cross-cloud (Limited Preview)

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available in Limited Preview. It extends Agent Platform governance to agents that run on Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF)-conformant Kubernetes clusters outside of Google Cloud, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Red Hat OpenShift, and bare-metal clusters. Your agents keep running where they are, but you govern them from one place: give each agent a verifiable identity, register agents and MCP servers in Agent Registry, and route their LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic through local Agent Gateway proxies by using your existing service mesh or network stack. Those proxies enforce access and Model Armor safety policies, and send access logs and agent traces to Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace.

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available at no charge during Limited Preview. Other products that you configure with it, such as Model Armor, Cloud Logging, and Cloud Trace, are billed at their standard rates. To request access, complete the access request form.

For more information, see Set up Agent Gateway for cross-cloud.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.34.1100-gke.125 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud 1.34.1100-gke.125 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.12-gke.500.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Feature

The following changes were added in 1.34.1100-gke.125:

  • Updated system components and container base images to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs and reject compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs.
  • Upgraded Container-Optimized OS (COS) to milestone 121 (cos-121-18867-652-7), which removes the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs.
  • Updated the Ubuntu 22.04 node and admin workstation base image to ubuntu-gke-op-2204-1-33-v20261024 to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) root CAs (USN-8944-1).

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1100-gke.125:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a user cluster left an orphaned k8s-health-check-reader-binding-<cluster-namespace> ClusterRoleBinding on the admin cluster. Health check permissions now use a namespaced RoleBinding, and legacy ClusterRoleBinding objects are automatically cleaned up.
  • Fixed an issue where adding IP addresses to an existing MetalLB address pool of an advanced user cluster left the cluster stuck in the UPDATING state. The update is now rejected during validation; to add IP addresses, add a new address pool instead.
  • Fixed an issue where preflight checks erroneously required the control plane VIP (loadBalancer.vips.controlPlaneVIP) to be in the control plane node subnet when the control plane load balancer mode is set to manual.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.34.1100-gke.125 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.34.1100-gke.125 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.12-gke.500.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Feature

The following changes were added in 1.34.1100-gke.125:

  • Updated system components and container base images to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs and reject compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1100-gke.125:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a user cluster left an orphaned k8s-health-check-reader-binding-<cluster-namespace> ClusterRoleBinding on the admin cluster. Health check permissions now use a namespaced RoleBinding, and legacy ClusterRoleBinding objects are automatically cleaned up.
  • Fixed a race condition where bmctl check cluster --snapshot could fail with a panic: send on closed channel error when taking Node Agent snapshots.
  • Fixed an issue where removing a node from a cluster left behind its local PersistentVolume resources instead of garbage collecting them. This fix applies to Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal local PersistentVolume resources created after upgrading to 1.34.1100-gke.125; existing orphaned PersistentVolume resources must be deleted manually.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where resetting or removing a control plane node could remove the wrong etcd or etcd-events member if another control plane node's IP address shared the same prefix (for example, 10.201.0.2 and 10.201.0.26), causing the affected node to become NotReady and stalling cluster upgrades.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Issue

On nodes that have Linux syscall auditing enabled, such as Container-Optimized OS nodes where you enabled Linux auditd logging, mounting Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver volumes can hang indefinitely. Pods that use these volumes don't start and remain in a status such as Init:0/1 or ContainerCreating. Pods that are being deleted remain in the Terminating state, and node drains, including drains during node pool upgrades, might not complete. Pod events show errors similar to the following:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = Aborted desc = An operation with the given volume key TARGET_PATH already exists

The following GKE versions are affected:

  • 1.31.14-gke.2963000 and later
  • 1.32.13-gke.2714000 and later
  • 1.33.13-gke.1973000 and later
  • 1.34.12-gke.1209000 and later
  • 1.35.8-gke.2014000 and later
  • 1.36.5-gke.1817000 and later
  • 1.37.1-gke.1777000 and later

In these versions, the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver uses a Debian 13 base image whose mount utility uses the newer Linux mount API. When syscall auditing is active, the mount operation can hang in the kernel before the FUSE file system is initialized. Restarting the gcsfusecsi-node Pod doesn't resolve the issue. Nodes that don't have syscall audit rules loaded aren't affected.

Workaround: Disable Linux auditd logging in clusters that use the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver, and then re-create the affected nodes to clear the audit rules that are loaded on them. If you must keep auditd logging enabled, contact Cloud Customer Care.

A fix is in progress.

Feature

Capacity buffers, including active and standby capacity buffers, are generally available for GKE Standard and Autopilot clusters running version 1.37.1-gke.3020000 or later. Capacity buffers let you pre-provision and optionally suspend standby compute capacity using the CapacityBuffer custom resource (autoscaling.x-k8s.io/v1beta1) to accelerate workload scaling and mitigate capacity constraints. To get started, see About capacity buffers.

  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.24

The latest version in the Regular channel is Looker 26.20.

title: 5 Ways to Shape Node.js Tenant Document Uploads — MinIO or Spaces
description:
The least complex production choice for an edtech app with predictable traffic is managed object storage: DigitalOcean Spaces removes the storage-server work. Choose MinIO when your team can own disks, upgrades, failure recovery, and compliance controls. A third shape, one REST layer over storage plus document processing, can reduce integration glue when one key and one bill matter more than separate specialists.

System shape Best fit Invariant Main cost
Managed bucket Predictable traffic and a small platform team Tenant keys stay private; downloads are signed Less infrastructure control
Self-hosted S3-compatible cluster An infrastructure team with a reason to own storage Replication, capacity, restores, and upgrades are yours More operational surface
One REST surface A small team crossing upload and PDF-processing boundaries One credential policy covers both calls One vendor becomes a trust boundary

My recommendation is conditional: use Spaces for a normal production path with stable traffic; use MinIO when self-hosting is a requirement rather than a preference. Infrai is worth testing for the third shape because storage and PDF processing share one plain REST base URL and one key. Its limitations matter, so this is a workflow fit, not a universal storage verdict.

1. Keep the tenant boundary outside the bucket name

For a document belonging to tenant school_42, use a key such as tenants/school_42/submissions/2026/10/assignment-183.pdf. Authorize the tenant before creating or returning a signed download URL. Keep the bucket private. A successful upload must not imply a public URL.

That invariant applies to MinIO, Spaces, Amazon S3, and an API layer in front of object storage. A browser should never receive a provider credential.

This matters for student records even when the file is only a worksheet.

Spaces buys delivery simplicity. Its pricing model includes storage and transfer, while DigitalOcean operates the storage service. MinIO provides S3-compatible APIs and infrastructure flexibility, but the team running it owns setup, maintenance, capacity planning, and recovery. “S3-compatible” describes the request surface. It does not remove the hard parts underneath.

2. Should your app use MinIO self-hosted or DigitalOcean Spaces?

Disk replacement, monitoring, network paths, upgrade sequencing, and a restore drill are part of self-hosting. MinIO is a strong fit when those responsibilities already belong to an infrastructure practice. It is a poor fit when the app team wants to ship uploads and has no spare operator.

Spaces is easier to manage for production environments with predictable traffic. Amazon S3 is the broader managed baseline if you already depend on AWS identity, lifecycle tooling, or regional architecture. Cloudflare R2 is another managed alternative worth checking when its delivery model and current feature set fit the application. These are different advantages, not four names for the same product.

3. Put upload and document processing behind one seam

An S3 plus Cloudinary or Imgix stack means two signups, two credential sets, two usage views, and glue that moves an object reference from the uploader to the processor. That separation can be correct; specialists are valuable. It is still work.

Infrai exposes storage routes and PDF processing routes under the same base URL, with the same Bearer key. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities, schemas, billing, and runnable examples. The practical benefit is smaller integration glue for a CLI or SDK: storage and processing do not need separate credential plumbing.

This example keeps the object private, uploads a PDF, obtains a signed read URL, downloads through that URL without forwarding the Infrai key, and passes those bytes to the PDF parser with the same API key.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function infrai(path: string, init: RequestInit): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(new URL(path, baseUrl), {
      ...init,
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`, ...(init.headers ?? {}) },
    });
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
      return response;
    }
    const waitMs = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1") * 1000;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Math.min(waitMs, 8000)));
  }
  throw new Error("Rate limit retry budget exhausted");
}

const bucket = "tenant-documents";
const key = "tenants/school_42/submissions/2026/10/assignment-183.pdf";
const pdf = new Uint8Array(await Bun.file("assignment-183.pdf").arrayBuffer());

await infrai(`/storage/object/put/${bucket}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`, {
  method: "PUT",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/pdf", "Idempotency-Key": `upload-${key}` },
  body: pdf,
});

await infrai(`/storage/object/set_acl/${bucket}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ acl: "private" }),
});

const signedResponse = await infrai(`/storage/object/presign/${bucket}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ expires_in: 900 }),
});
const { url } = (await signedResponse.json()) as { url: string };
const privateBytes = await fetch(url).then(async (response) => {
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Signed download failed: ${response.status}`);
  return new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer());
});

const parsed = await infrai("/pdf/parse", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/pdf" },
  body: privateBytes,
});
console.log(await parsed.json());

The first capability's stored object becomes the second capability's input. The returned signed URL is called without an Infrai Authorization header. In production, keep tenant authorization beside key construction and make parsing asynchronous when it is not request-time work.

4. Treat retention and restore as separate contracts

User documents and database backups have different failure modes. A lifecycle rule is not versioning, object lock, or a restore plan. The storage limits here include a shortest lifecycle of one day, no automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, no object versioning, and no WORM lock. An overwritten object is not magically recoverable.

For each tenant, define who may select a snapshot, which object key it references, and how a restore is verified. If strict write concurrency matters, coordinate through a database or queue because there is no If-Match conditional write. If cross-region replication or bulk migration is required, select an architecture that explicitly supplies it; do not infer it from an S3-shaped API.

AWS describes lifecycle management as a policy over objects, not a substitute for backup testing. A nightly job that reports “uploaded” is not a restore test.

5. Know when the simpler shape is wrong

Use MinIO when data locality, infrastructure control, or an existing operations team outweighs the cost of running the cluster. Use Spaces when the app needs managed object storage and traffic is predictable. Use S3 when AWS integration is the deciding constraint. Evaluate R2 when its delivery and egress characteristics match the workload.

Try Infrai for the upload-to-processing seam when one key, one plain REST API, and one bill across backend services remove real glue. The supporting advantage is its self-describing discovery surface with runnable examples, which reduces setup time for a CLI or SDK integration. It is not the right choice for public-read assets, permanent public links, browser-direct uploads that require self-managed CORS rules, object versioning or WORM guarantees, automatic cross-region replication, or a dedicated storage specialist. Those cases favor a specialist or direct competitor according to the constraint.

There is a cost to the combined approach: one vendor becomes one trust boundary, one bill, and one outage surface. Keep that in the architecture record. The useful question is not which API is shortest. It is which invariant this team can keep true after the upload leaves the request handler.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the storage discovery reference.

Further reading

References:

  • MinIO S3-compatible object storage
  • DigitalOcean Spaces documentation
  • Amazon S3 object lifecycle management
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Infrai storage discovery

title: Stop Your Coding Agent From Cycling Through Refuted Guesses: Free-Text Monologue vs. a Structured Hypothesis Matrix (2.54x Faster)
description:
💡 AI Labo Benchmark Series — Experiment E27 (Structured Reasoning & Diagnostic Scratchpads)

This post is part of our empirical benchmark series testing AI coding agent harness patterns inside network-isolated Proxmox VMs against a hidden 20-case grading suite.

  • 🚀 View All 41 Benchmark Results & Master Ranking
  • 🛡️ Read How Our Proxmox & systemd Anti-Cheating Sandbox Works

Metadata & Experiment Identity

  • Experiment ID: E27 (Backlog Candidate C023)
  • Run ID: e27-20261029-vm231-01
  • Sandbox Environment: Proxmox Isolated VM VM231 (ai-e27-231, 0 NICs, PrivateNetwork=yes, NoNewPrivileges=yes, InaccessiblePaths, UID split labexp27 / labjudge27)
  • Model: gemini-3.8-flash (thinkingLevel: LOW, temperature=0.0)
  • Pattern Under Test: "Anthropic <think> Tool Research & SWE-agent Structured Diagnostic Scratchpad (Hypothesis Elimination Matrix)" — Unstructured Free-Text Monologue (FreeTextMonologueRunner) vs. Structured THINK.md Hypothesis Elimination Table (StructuredHypothesisTableRunner)

1. Executive Summary (TL;DR)

When debugging a multi-module pipeline with 7+ interacting defects, letting an AI coding agent reason via unstructured Free-Text Monologue ("Let me think... maybe the settlement total is off because of integer division? Or wait, did we check that earlier?") leads to Hypothesis Cycling: as tool logs grow across turns, the model loses track of which candidate root causes were already falsified and which boundary contracts remain unverified.

Inspired by Anthropic's <think> scratchpad research and SWE-agent diagnostic matrices, we tested replacing free-text debugging monologues with a mandatory Structured Hypothesis Elimination Table (THINK.md) inside isolated VM VM231 on the 3-module enterprise payment settlement pipeline (validator.py ➔ settlement.py ➔ statement.py):

  • Mode A (FreeTextMonologueRunner): Reasons through unstructured free-text monologue logs (92,463 tool output chars across Turns 1–2) before submitting on Turn 3.
  • Mode B (StructuredHypothesisTableRunner): Requires a fixed-schema Hypothesis Elimination Matrix (STRUCTURED_HYPOTHESIS_TABLE_MD) mapping Hyp ID ➔ Target Module ➔ Suspected Defect ➔ Diagnostic Probe ➔ Status (CONFIRMED/REFUTED) ➔ Canonical Fix before any code edit.

Key Result

Mode A missed validator_01 (19 / 20, 95.0%) after 3 turns (48,712 input tokens) because it over-constrained set(item.keys()) != required_keys instead of stripping extra keys into a clean 5-key dictionary. Mode B achieved a 20 / 20 (100%) pass in 1 turn, cutting LLM calls by -66.7% (3 ➔ 1), cumulative input tokens by -95.0% (48,712 ➔ 2,450 tokens—a 19.88x reduction), API cost by -83.6% ($0.0478 ➔ $0.0079), and running 2.54x faster (33.66s ➔ 13.28s, -60.6%).

2. The Verified THINK.md Hypothesis Elimination Matrix (input-03.json)

Instead of rambling in prose, Mode B locked this 7-row structured diagnostic matrix (+795 tokens) before touching a single line of code:

Hyp ID Target Module Suspected Defect / Boundary Diagnostic Probe & Elimination Result Status Required Canonical Fix
H-01 validator.py ALLOWED_CURRENCIES missing "JPY" & empty list [] allowed validate_txns([]) did not raise; "jpy" rejected CONFIRMED Set ALLOWED_CURRENCIES = ("USD", "EUR", "JPY") and reject len(raw_txns) == 0
H-02 validator.py isinstance(True, int) passes in Python & cents <= 0 rejects $0 auth tx_count=True accepted; unit_cents=0 raised ValueError CONFIRMED Check isinstance(x, bool) before isinstance(x, int); enforce cnt > 0, cents >= 0, 0 <= bps <= 1000
H-03 validator.py In-place mutation item["merchant_id"] = ... & extra keys retained Caller dict mutated; "extra": 1 leaked into output CONFIRMED Construct a fresh 5-key dict (merchant_id, currency, tx_count, unit_cents, chargeback_bps)
H-04 settlement.py sorted(order) destroys first-seen merchant-currency order M-Z before M-A reordered to M-A, M-Z CONFIRMED Iterate for k in order: (never sorted(order))
H-05 settlement.py Chargeback reserve >= 300 vs strictly > 300 bps 300 bps charged 10% reserve instead of 0 CONFIRMED Charge (gross * 10) // 100 strictly when g["chargeback_bps"] > 300
H-06 settlement.py Tier discount > 15000 vs inclusive >= 15000 & rebate cap subtotal == 15000 missed discount; rebate > after_discount went negative CONFIRMED Use subtotal >= 15000 (GROWTH 10%/0%; ENTERPRISE 20%/10%) and min(fee_rebate, after_discount)
H-07 statement.py : separator and unsigned "0" on zero discount/rebate Output had M-1:USD and TIER_DISCOUNT: 0 CONFIRMED Format {merchant_id}#{currency} and always prefix -: TIER_DISCOUNT: -{batch['tier_discount']}

3. Why Free-Text Monologue Missed validator_01 (19/20)

In Mode A (freetext-monologue-bundle.json), without H-03 explicitly distinguishing "rejecting missing required keys" from "stripping unapproved extra keys into a fresh 5-key dict", Mode A wrote:

# ❌ Mode A (FreeTextMonologueRunner — Turn 3 Final validator.py, 19/20)
        required_keys = {"merchant_id", "currency", "tx_count", "unit_cents", "chargeback_bps"}
        if set(item.keys()) != required_keys:  # <-- BUG: Raises ValueError when caller passes {"extra": 1} instead of stripping it!
            raise ValueError("invalid keys")

Mode B, guided by row H-03 ("extra": 1 leaked into output ➔ Construct a fresh 5-key dict), extracted the 5 required fields and dropped extra keys cleanly without raising a false-positive ValueError.

4. Drop-In Implementation Recipe: HypothesisTableGate 

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class HypothesisRow:
    hyp_id: str
    target_module: str
    suspected_defect: str
    probe_result: str
    status: str  # "CONFIRMED" or "REFUTED"
    canonical_fix: str

class HypothesisTableGate:
    """Blocks code edits until all target modules have confirmed/refuted rows in THINK.md."""
    def __init__(self, required_modules: set[str]):
        self.required_modules = required_modules
        self.confirmed_rows: list[HypothesisRow] = []

    def register_table(self, rows: list[HypothesisRow]) -> str:
        covered = {r.target_module for r in rows if r.status in {"CONFIRMED", "REFUTED"}}
        missing = self.required_modules - covered
        if missing:
            raise ValueError(f"THINK.md table incomplete; missing modules: {sorted(missing)}")
        self.confirmed_rows = [r for r in rows if r.status == "CONFIRMED"]
        return f"THINK.md locked with {len(self.confirmed_rows)} confirmed root causes."

5. Practical Takeaway: Force Tabular State for Multi-Bug Debugging

  1. Replace unstructured CoT monologues with a fixed-column Markdown table (THINK.md) on multi-bug tasks: A 6-column table acts as an external working-memory register where every confirmed bug maps 1-to-1 to a required code change.
  2. Keep REFUTED rows visible: Recording why a hypothesis was ruled out (status: REFUTED) prevents the agent from re-trying the same failed guess three turns later.

title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
description:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.

title: Choose AI Gateway providers by headquarters country
description:
Provider headquarters sends your AI Gateway requests only to providers headquartered in countries you choose, so you can meet compliance and procurement rules about where your AI vendors are located.

You can configure provider headquarters to be an allowlist of the countries to use, or a denylist of the countries to block. AI Gateway skips providers in blocked countries and routes requests to the rest of the list, so a model stays accessible as long as it is available in one of its allowed provider locations.

Use provider headquarters with regional hosting and regional inference to control where a request is received, where the model runs, and who runs it.

Set provider headquarters for your team

Pro and Enterprise customers can apply their provider headquarters list to every AI Gateway request across their team. Configure the list in AI Gateway settings.

Provider headquarters settings are applied automatically as AI Gateway adds models and providers. Providers without a headquarters country on record never receive your requests.

Set provider headquarters per request

On any plan, set headquarters in the gateway provider options to restrict a single request. Pass country codes for an allowlist, or prefix every code with ! for a denylist, as in ['!US']. If your team has a list, a request can only narrow it.

In the examples below, requests are only sent to providers based in the US and Germany:

Both settings filter providers, so a model stays available as long as one of its providers is based in an allowed country. If no provider is available in an allowed country, AI Gateway tries your fallback models. If no fallback models are available in allowed countries, or if no fallback models are configured, the request will fail without trying to route to providers in other locations.

Read the provider headquarters documentation for the countries supported, pricing and setup details.
